questions.stem:
A company produces resistors with resistance being normally distributed ($\mu=50\,\Omega$, $\sigma=2\,\Omega$).

Resistors below $48\,\Omega$ or exceeds $52\,\Omega$ are defective.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the percentage of defective resistors.

dif.r: empirical rule: outside 1 sd is 32%

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: In a batch of 1000 resistors, how many are expected to be non-defective?

dif.r: scale percentage to 1000

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Defective resistors lie more than one standard deviation from the mean ($48=50-2$, $52=50+2$). By the empirical rule, $68\%$ lie within one standard deviation:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{defective}) &= P(X<48)+P(X>52)\\ &= 1-68\%\\ &= 32\% \end{aligned}$$

From (a), $100\%-32\%=68\%$ are non-defective:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000(1-32\%) &= 1000\times 0.68\\ &= 680 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 680 resistors are expected to be non-defective.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\tan x\right)=e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)$$

dif.r: product rule then sec^2 = 1 + tan^2

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence evaluate

$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)\,dx$$

dif.r: substitute limits into primitive from (a)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
Then, using $\sec^2 x=\tan^2 x+1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\tan x\right) &= e^x\tan x+e^x\sec^2 x\\ &= e^x\left(\sec^2 x+\tan x\right)\\ &= e^x\left(\tan^2 x+1+\tan x\right)\\ &= e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Sets up the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From (a), $e^x\tan x$ is a primitive of $e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} e^x\left(\tan^2 x+\tan x+1\right)dx &= \Big[e^x\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &= e^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-e^0\tan 0\\ &= \sqrt{3}\,e^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac{3k}{4}$, $P(B)=k$ and $P(\overline{A}\cap B)=k^2$ where $0<k<1$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the expression of $P(A\cap B)$ in terms of $k$.

dif.r: symbolic Venn decomposition of B

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that the two events are independent, find the value of $k$.

dif.r: independence gives quadratic in k, reject k=0

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram with complement-of-A intersect B shaded

solutions.latex:
The events are independent, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$. Using (a):
$$\begin{aligned} k-k^2 &= \dfrac{3k}{4}\cdot k\\ 4k-4k^2 &= 3k^2\\ 7k^2-4k &= 0\\ k(7k-4) &= 0\\ k &= 0 \text{ or } k=\dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$k=0$ is not allowed since $0<k<1$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{4}{7}$$
criteria: Uses $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The amount of time for Opstra Telecom. to respond to a customer query follows the probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{(5x-1)^2}, & x\ge 1\\[6pt] 0, & 0<x<1\end{cases}\qquad\text{where } x \text{ is time in hours.}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=20$.

dif.r: improper integral equals 1, show k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the median response time.

dif.r: F(m)=0.5 with rational CDF

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the probability that the company spends more than 2 hours but less than 3 hours to respond to the customer query?

dif.r: one direct definite integral

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total area under a probability density function is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^{\infty}\dfrac{k}{(5x-1)^2}\,dx &= 1\\ k\int_1^{\infty}(5x-1)^{-2}\,dx &= 1\\ k\left[\dfrac{(5x-1)^{-1}}{-1\times 5}\right]_1^{\infty} &= 1\\ -\dfrac{k}{5}\left[0-\dfrac{1}{4}\right] &= 1\\ \dfrac{k}{20} &= 1\\ k &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the correct integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let the median be $m$. Half the probability lies below the median:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^m\dfrac{20}{(5x-1)^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ -4\left[\dfrac{1}{5x-1}\right]_1^m &= 0.5\\ -\dfrac{4}{5m-1}+1 &= 0.5\\ \dfrac{4}{5m-1} &= 0.5\\ m &= \dfrac{9}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The median response time is $\dfrac{9}{5}$ hours ($1.8$ hours).
criteria: Writes the correct integral equation, or equivalent merit
Shows correct working, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle is given by $\dot{x}(t)=8t^3e^{t^4}$, where $\dot{x}(t)$ is velocity in metres per second and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the times(s) the particle is at rest.

dif.r: v=0 with e^{t^4}>0, one step

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the displacement function is $x(t)=2e^{t^4}-2$.

dif.r: reverse chain rule integral with e^{t^4}, find C

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what time does the particle reach a displacement of 100 metres? (Give your answer to 2 d.p.)

dif.r: solve exponential equation with logs, fourth root

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$8t^3e^{t^4}=0$$
$e^{t^4}>0$ for all $t$, so $t^3=0$.
$$\therefore\ t=0$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity. The derivative of $t^4$ is $4t^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 8t^3e^{t^4}\,dt\\ &= 2\int 4t^3e^{t^4}\,dt\\ &= 2e^{t^4}+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle is at the origin: when $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^0+C &= 0\\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=2e^{t^4}-2$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the handwritten line $2e^0+C=-2$ should read $2e^0+C=0$, which gives the stated $C=-2$.

solutions.latex:
Let $x(t)=100$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{t^4}-2 &= 100\\ e^{t^4} &= 51\\ t^4 &= \ln 51\\ t &\approx 1.41 \text{ s} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The mass of oranges at Fruit King farm are normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

It is known that 25.78% of these oranges have mass more than 190 g and 34.46% of them have mass more than 180 g.

Using the table of z scores below, answer the following questions.

\extable{1358_q28_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

dif.r: two table z-values give simultaneous equations for mu, sigma

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Two oranges from Fruit King farm are chosen at random.

Given that the mass of both oranges is greater than 180 grams, what is the probability that both of them have a mass less than 194 g. Give your answer as a percentage to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: conditional on two independent oranges, squared ratio of areas

solutions.latex:
$25.78\%$ of oranges are heavier than 190 g, so $100\%-25.78\%=74.22\%$ are lighter. From the table, this corresponds to $z=0.65$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.65 &= \dfrac{190-\mu}{\sigma}\\ 0.65\sigma &= 190-\mu \quad (1) \end{aligned}$$
Similarly, $100\%-34.46\%=65.54\%$ corresponds to $z=0.4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.4 &= \dfrac{180-\mu}{\sigma}\\ 0.4\sigma &= 180-\mu \quad (2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtract (2) from (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 0.25\sigma &= 10\\ \sigma &= 40 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $\sigma=40$ into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 0.4(40) &= 180-\mu\\ \mu &= 164 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The mean is 164 g and the standard deviation is 40 g.
criteria: Sets up two correct equations, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $100\%-25.75\%$ should be $100\%-25.78\%$ (the given percentage); the result $74.22\%$ is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
$z$-score for 194 g, using $\mu=164$ and $\sigma=40$ from (a):
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{194-164}{40}\\ &= 0.75 \end{aligned}$$
From the table, $77.34\%$ of the oranges have mass less than 194 g.

Let the mass of an orange be $X$. For one orange, by conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<194\mid X>180) &= \dfrac{P(180<X<194)}{P(X>180)}\\ &= \dfrac{77.34\%-65.54\%}{34.46\%}\\ &= 34.24\% \end{aligned}$$
The two oranges are independent:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both}) &= (34.24\%)^2\\ &= 11.73\% \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the conditional probability $34.24\%$, or equivalent merit

Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find, in terms of $a$, the total sum of the areas of all the squares.

dif.r: limiting sum of areas, a_1^2/(1-r)

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: right-angled triangle ABC with right angle at B and a sequence of decreasing squares a1, a2, ... along BC touching hypotenuse AC
solution sketch: annotated triangle: a - a1 on AB, areas A1, A2, A3, BC = 2a

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1358_q29_s1}
$$\dfrac{AB}{BC}=\dfrac{a}{2a}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The small triangle above the first square (vertical side $a-a_1$, horizontal side $a_1$) is similar to $\triangle ABC$ (corresponding angles, both right-angled):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a-a_1}{a_1} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\\ 2a-2a_1 &= a_1\\ 2a &= 3a_1\\ a_1 &= \dfrac{2a}{3} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Each square sits on the one before in the same way as in (a), so
$$a_2=\dfrac{2}{3}a_1,\quad a_3=\dfrac{2}{3}a_2,\ \ldots$$
Using (a), the areas are
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= (a_1)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}a^2\\ A_2 &= (a_2)^2 = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}a_1\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}\cdot\dfrac{4}{9}a^2 = \left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^2a^2\\ A_3 &= (a_3)^2 = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}a_2\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}\cdot\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^2a^2 = \left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)^3a^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The areas of the squares form a geometric sequence with $r=\dfrac{4}{9}$.
criteria: Shows successive areas, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The areas form a geometric series with first term $A_1=\dfrac{4}{9}a^2$ and $r=\dfrac{4}{9}$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum is $S_\infty=\dfrac{A_1}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{\frac{4}{9}a^2}{1-\frac{4}{9}}\\ &= \dfrac{4}{5}a^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the limiting sum formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=(x+1)e^x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f''(x)=(x+3)e^x$.

dif.r: product rule twice to show f''

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any stationary points of $f(x)$, determine their nature, and find any points of inflection.

dif.r: stationary point and inflection of (x+1)e^x, standard tests

Product rule.reason: Differentiating the product e^x(x+2) for f''.

Derivatives of exponential functions.evidence: Possible points of inflection occur when f''(x)=0: e^x(x+3)=0
Derivatives of exponential functions.reason: f'' of e^x(x+2) must be found.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Sketch the curve $f(x)$, labelling any stationary points, points of inflection and intercepts with the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis.

\exfigure{1358_q30_1}

dif.r: sketch from found features plus asymptote y=0 to the left

figures.cap: blank grid with x and y axes and origin O for sketching
solution sketch: sketch of y=(x+1)e^x with (0,1), (-1,0), minimum (-2,-e^-2), inflection (-3,-2e^-3), x-axis asymptote on the left

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+1 & v&=e^x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= e^x+(x+1)e^x\\ &= e^x(x+2) \end{aligned}$$
Again with the product rule, $u=x+2$, $v=e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= e^x+(x+2)e^x\\ &= e^x(x+3) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$. From (a), $f'(x)=e^x(x+2)$:
$$e^x(x+2)=0$$
$e^x>0$ for all $x$, so $x+2=0$, $x=-2$.
$$f(-2)=(-2+1)e^{-2}=-e^{-2}$$
Nature: $f''(-2)=e^{-2}>0$, so the curve is concave up.

$\therefore$ $\left(-2,-e^{-2}\right)$ is a local minimum turning point.

Possible points of inflection occur when $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} e^x(x+3) &= 0\\ x &= -3 \end{aligned}$$
$$f(-3)=-2e^{-3}$$
Check the concavity either side of $x=-3$:

\extable{Ts1102_1}

Concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $\left(-3,-2e^{-3}\right)$.
criteria: Finds the stationary point and its nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point, or equivalent merit

As $x\to\infty$, $y\to\infty$.

As $x\to-\infty$, $y\to 0^-$, so the $x$-axis is an asymptote.

parts.label: b

figures.cap: region under L1 from x=0 to 1 split by the parabola L2 into S1 (left, against y-axis) and S2 (right)

solutions.latex:
The curves intersect where the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} -x^2+1 &= ax^2\\ (a+1)x^2 &= 1\\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{a+1}\\ x &= \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}} \end{aligned}$$
$x\ge 0$ is given, so $x=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= a\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}\right)^2\\ &= \dfrac{a}{a+1} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $y=a\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{a+1}}\right)^2=\dfrac{a}{a+1}$ (the factor $a$ was missing).

solutions.latex:
Method 1

$S_1+S_2$ is the area under $L_1$ from $x=0$ to $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_1+S_2 &= \int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx\\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\ &= \left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-(0-0)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
But $S_1=S_2$, so $2S_1=\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $S_1=S_2=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

$S_1$ lies between $L_1$ (above) and $L_2$ (below), from $x=0$ to the intersection in (a):
$$\begin{aligned} S_1 &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}(-x^2+1-ax^2)\,dx\\ &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}\left(1-(1+a)x^2\right)dx\\ &= \left[x-\dfrac{1+a}{3}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}\\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}-\dfrac{1+a}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\right)-0\\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}\left(1-\dfrac{1+a}{3(1+a)}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $S_1=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}\left(1-\dfrac{1+a}{3(1+a)}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{3}\\ 2(1+a) &= (1+a)\sqrt{1+a}\\ 4(1+a)^2 &= (1+a)^2(1+a)\\ (1+a)^2(1+a)-4(1+a)^2 &= 0\\ (1+a)^2(1+a-4) &= 0\\ a &= -1 \text{ or } a=3 \end{aligned}$$
$a>0$, so $a=3$.

Method 2

$S_2=\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx-S_1$ and $S_1=S_2$, so
$$S_1=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx$$
then continue as in Method 1.

Method 3

From Method 1:
$$S_1=\dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}$$
$S_2$ is the area under $L_2$ up to the intersection, plus the area under $L_1$ from the intersection to $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_2 &= \int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}ax^2\,dx+\int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}^1(1-x^2)\,dx\\ &= \left[\dfrac{a}{3}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}+\left[x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}}^1\\ &= \dfrac{a}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}+\left(1-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}-\dfrac{1}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2+2a}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} \end{aligned}$$
Equating $S_1$ and $S_2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} &= \dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2(1+a)}{3(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}}\\ \dfrac{2(1+a)}{(1+a)\sqrt{1+a}} &= 1\\ 2(1+a) &= (1+a)\sqrt{1+a}\\ 4(1+a)^2 &= (1+a)^3\\ (1+a)^2(a-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$a=-1$ is outside the domain.
$$\therefore\ a=3$$
criteria: Forms an equation in $a$, such as $\dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{1+a}}=\dfrac{1}{3}$, or equivalent merit

Writes an integral for $S_1$ with limits $0$ and $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+a}}$, or finds $S_1+S_2=\dfrac{2}{3}$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: trapezium ABCD with AB at the bottom, DC at the top, P on DC near C, segment AP drawn; NOT TO SCALE
solution sketch: trapezium annotated with feet E, H, F, height h, AE = BF = 1, DC = 2, AB = 4, angle 60 degrees

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1358_q32_s1}

The trapezium is symmetric ($AD=BC$, equal base angles), so $\triangle ADE\equiv\triangle BCF$ and
$$AE=BF=\dfrac{4-2}{2}=1 \text{ km}$$
In right-angled $\triangle ADE$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{1}\\ h &= \sqrt{3} \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
In right-angled $\triangle APH$, using the sine ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= \dfrac{h}{AP}\\ AP &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sin\theta} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the triangle with $\tan 60^\circ=\dfrac{h}{1}$ is $\triangle ADE$, not $\triangle APE$.

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle APH$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{h}{AH}\\ AH &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta} \end{aligned}$$
$DPHE$ is a rectangle, so $DP=EH$:
$$\begin{aligned} DP &= AH-AE\\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta}-1 \end{aligned}$$

From (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} AP &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sin\theta}\\ PC &= CD-DP\\ &= 2-\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta}-1\right)\\ &= 3-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta} \end{aligned}$$
Total cost (\$ per km times km):
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 100\,000\,AP+80\,000\,PC\\ &= 100\,000\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sin\theta}+80\,000\left(3-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\tan\theta}\right)\\ &= 100\,000\sqrt{3}(\sin\theta)^{-1}+240\,000-80\,000\sqrt{3}(\tan\theta)^{-1} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating, using
$$\dfrac{\sec^2\theta}{\tan^2\theta}=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}\times\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}$$
$$\begin{aligned} C' &= \dfrac{-100\,000\sqrt{3}\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{80\,000\sqrt{3}\sec^2\theta}{\tan^2\theta}\\ &= \dfrac{-100\,000\sqrt{3}\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{80\,000\sqrt{3}}{\sin^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $C'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -100\,000\sqrt{3}\cos\theta+80\,000\sqrt{3} &= 0\\ \cos\theta &= \dfrac{80\,000\sqrt{3}}{100\,000\sqrt{3}}\\ &= \dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$
so $\theta\approx 36.9^\circ$.

Check the sign of $C'$ either side:

\extable{Ts1108_1}

$\therefore$ The cost is a minimum when $\cos\theta=\dfrac{4}{5}$.

parts.latex: Solve the equation: $|2x - 3| = 9x$

dif.r: absolute value equation, reject extraneous solution

solutions.latex:
$|2x-3|=9x$ means $2x-3=9x$ or $-(2x-3)=9x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x - 3 &= 9x & \qquad -2x + 3 &= 9x \\ -3 &= 7x & 3 &= 11x \\ x &= -\dfrac{3}{7} & x &= \dfrac{3}{11} \end{aligned}$$
Test the solutions in the original equation.

$x=-\dfrac{3}{7}$:
$$\left|2 \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{7}\right) - 3\right| = \dfrac{27}{7},\qquad 9 \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{7}\right)=-\dfrac{27}{7}$$
These are not equal, so $x = -\dfrac{3}{7}$ is not a solution.

$x=\dfrac{3}{11}$:
$$\left|2 \times \dfrac{3}{11} - 3\right| = \dfrac{27}{11},\qquad 9 \times \dfrac{3}{11}=\dfrac{27}{11}$$
These are equal.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{3}{11}$$

Rearrange the line to gradient–intercept form:

questions.stem: A continuous probability distribution is given by $f(x) = \dfrac{3x^2}{279}$, defined in the domain $[4, 7]$.

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is the area under $f$ from 4 to $x$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_4^x \dfrac{3t^2}{279}\,dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^3}{279}\right]_4^x \\ &= \dfrac{x^3}{279} - \dfrac{4^3}{279} \\ &= \dfrac{x^3 - 64}{279} \end{aligned}$$
for $4\le x\le 7$.

solutions.latex:
The median $x$ satisfies $F(x)=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x^3 - 64}{279} &= 0.5 \\ x^3 - 64 &= 139.5 \\ x^3 &= 203.5 \\ x &= \sqrt[3]{203.5} \\ &= 5.881951\ldots \\ &\approx 5.9 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The median is approximately 5.9.
criteria: Correctly equates to 0.5, allow for 1 error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1+x & v&=e^{-2x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2e^{-2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= e^{-2x} - 2(1 + x)e^{-2x} \\ &= e^{-2x}\left(1 - 2(1 + x)\right) \\ &= e^{-2x}(-1 - 2x) \\ &= -e^{-2x}(1 + 2x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y' = 0$:
$$-e^{-2x}(1 + 2x)=0$$
$e^{-2x}>0$ for all $x$, so $1+2x=0$ and $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-2 \times \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}\\ &= \dfrac{e}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{e}{2}\right)$ is a stationary point.

Only $1+2x$ decides the sign of $y'$. Testing either side:

\extable{Ts1140_1}

$\therefore$ Maximum turning point at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{e}{2}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $y'=-e^{-2x}(1+2x)$ with the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$:
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-e^{-2x} & v&=1+2x\\ u'&=2e^{-2x} & v'&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'' &= 2e^{-2x}(1 + 2x)-2e^{-2x} \\ &= 2e^{-2x}(-1 + 1 + 2x) \\ &= 4xe^{-2x} \end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflection occur when $y'' = 0$:
$$4xe^{-2x}=0$$
$e^{-2x}>0$ for all $x$, so $x = 0$.

At $x = 0$, $y = 1$, so $(0, 1)$ is a possible point of inflection.

Only $4x$ decides the sign of $y''$. Testing either side:

Concavity changes, so $(0, 1)$ is a point of inflection.

questions.stem: A particle moves with velocity given by $v = 12\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2}$, where $v$ and $t$ are measured in cm/s and seconds respectively. The particle was initially at rest at $x = \dfrac{-24}{\pi}$.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 12\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2}\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{-12\cos\frac{\pi t}{2}}{\frac{\pi}{2}} + C \\ &= -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{2} + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $x = -\dfrac{24}{\pi}$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{24}{\pi} &= -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 0\right) + C \\ C &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = -\dfrac{24}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{2}$$

parts.latex:
A vertical tower of height $h$ metres stands on horizontal ground. From a point $P$ on the ground due east of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $45^\circ$. From a point $Q$ on the ground due south of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $30^\circ$. If the distance $PQ$ is 40 metres, find the exact height of the tower.

\exfigure{1359_q29_1}
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: 3D set-up: two elevation triangles combined via Pythagoras, exact values.

figures.cap: 3D diagram: tower RT of height h, P and Q on the ground, angles of elevation 45 at P and 30 at Q, PQ = 40 m, north arrow

solutions.latex:
Let $R$ be the base of the tower. In right-angled triangles $PRT$ and $QRT$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 45^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \qquad \tan 30^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ 1 &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ PR &= h & QR &= \sqrt{3}h \end{aligned}$$
$P$ is due east and $Q$ due south of $R$, so $\angle PRQ = 90^\circ$. Using Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle PRQ$:
$$\begin{aligned} 40^2 &= h^2 + \left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2 \\ 1600 &= 4h^2 \\ h^2 &= 400 \\ h &= \pm 20 \end{aligned}$$
$h > 0$, so $h = 20$ m.

parts.latex:
A population of insects varies according to the formula $P = 3000n^{\frac{t}{10}}$, where $n$ is a positive constant and $t$ is the time in days.

The initial population was 3000. After 20 days the population had grown to 12 000.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of increase is 6000 insects per day.

dif.r: twin of 2021 Q23: find base, differentiate a^{kt}, solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Initially $P=3000$; after 20 days $P=12\,000$. Find $n$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12000 &= 3000n^{\frac{20}{10}} \\ n^2 &= 4 \\ n &= \pm 2 \end{aligned}$$
$n > 0$, so $n = 2$ and $P=3000\times 2^{\frac{t}{10}}$.

Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=k\ln a\cdot a^{kt}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 3000 \times \ln 2 \times \dfrac{1}{10} \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 6000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6000 &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{20}{\ln 2} \\ \dfrac{t}{10} &= \log_2\left(\dfrac{20}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \log_2 20 - \log_2(\ln 2) \\ t &= 10\left(\dfrac{\ln 20}{\ln 2} - \dfrac{\ln(\ln 2)}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &\approx 48.5 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Three of: finds $n$, finds $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, substitutes 6000 into $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, calculates $t$ (or 1 error), or equivalent merit
Two of the above (or 2 errors), or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

The probability that Young's soccer team wins this weekend is $\dfrac{4}{9}$. The probability that Young's rugby league team wins this weekend is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

What is the probability that neither team wins this weekend?

dif.r: product of two complements

solutions.latex:
Let $S$ be "soccer team wins" and $R$ be "rugby team wins". The results are independent, so multiply the complements:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(\overline{S}\cap\overline{R}\right)&=\left(1-\dfrac{4}{9}\right)\times\left(1-\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\\&=\dfrac{5}{9}\times\dfrac{1}{4}\\&=\dfrac{5}{36}\end{aligned}$$

Using $P(B\cap A)=P(A|B)\times P(B)$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(B|A)&=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)}\\&=\dfrac{P(A|B)\times P(B)}{P(A)}\\&=\dfrac{0.6\times0.3}{0.45}\\&=0.4\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_2(1-x)+\log_2(3-x)=3$.

dif.r: log law to quadratic, reject root 5 by domain

The logarithms need $1-x>0$ and $3-x>0$, so $x<1$.

Using the log law $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2[(1-x)(3-x)]&=3\\(1-x)(3-x)&=2^3\\x^2-4x+3&=8\\x^2-4x-5&=0\\(x-5)(x+1)&=0\\x&=5 \text{ or } x=-1\end{aligned}$$
$x=5$ does not satisfy $x<1$.
$$\therefore\ x=-1$$

parts.latex: Teachers with more than 14 years of teaching experience are known as highly accomplished teachers. Use the Empirical rule to find, to the nearest whole number, the percentage of highly accomplished teachers who have more than 26 years teaching experience.

dif.r: decode wording as conditional, ratio of empirical-rule areas

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ with $\mu=20$, $\sigma=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}z_{14}&=\dfrac{14-20}{6}=-1\\z_{32}&=\dfrac{32-20}{6}=2\end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule:
$$\begin{aligned}P(z\le-1)&=16\%\\P(z\ge2)&=2.5\%\end{aligned}$$
Teachers with at most 14 years' experience:
$$0.16\times4800=768$$
Teachers with at least 32 years' experience:
$$0.025\times4800=120$$
$$768-120=648$$
$\therefore$ There are 648 more teachers with at most 14 years' experience than with at least 32 years' experience.

26 years has $z=\dfrac{26-20}{6}=1$, and 14 years has $z=-1$.

The highly accomplished teachers are those with $z>-1$. The required percentage is a conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned}P(z>1\mid z>-1)&=\dfrac{P(z>1)}{P(z>-1)}\\&=\dfrac{16}{84}\\&\approx19\%\end{aligned}$$

A product is zero when one of its factors is zero:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta-1&=0\\\sqrt{3}\sin\theta-\cos\theta&=0\\\sqrt{3}\sin\theta+\cos\theta&=0\end{aligned}$$
First factor:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=1\\\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\sin\theta&=-\cos\theta\\\tan\theta&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\\theta&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\&=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v(t)=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. The particle starts at $O$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $x(t)=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.

dif.r: integrate (t+1)^{1/2}, find C, rearrange

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find when and where the particle is at rest in relation to the fixed point $O$.

dif.r: solve v=0 then substitute into x(t)

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 24 seconds.

dif.r: distance with rest point given; add legs

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} v(t)&=3\sqrt{t+1}-9\\ &=3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\\ x(t)&=\int\left(3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\right)dt\\ &=\dfrac{3(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C\\ &=2\sqrt{(t+1)^3}-9t+C\\ &=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t+C \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at $O$, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=2(1)\sqrt{1}-9(0)+C\\ \therefore\ C&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2 \text{ as required}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates $v(t)$ but does not evaluate the constant of integration or makes an error, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct solution with appropriate and logical steps shown

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9&=0\\ \sqrt{t+1}&=3\\ t+1&=9\\ \therefore\ t&=8 \end{aligned}$$
Using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} x(8)&=2(8+1)\sqrt{8+1}-9(8)-2\\ &=-20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The particle is at rest after 8 seconds, 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of motion.
criteria: Finds when the particle is at rest, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct solution, accept 20 m away from the origin
meta.marker_note: Accept 20 m away from the origin.

solutions.latex:
Using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} x(24)&=2(25)\sqrt{25}-9(24)-2\\ &=32 \end{aligned}$$
The particle travels from $x=0$ to $x=-20$ (at rest at $t=8$), then to $x=32$ in the first 24 seconds.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=20+20+32\\ &=72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Using $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=(1+\tan x)^2\\ &=1+2\tan x+\tan^2x\\ &=2\tan x+1+\tan^2x\\ &=2\tan x+\sec^2x\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct solution with all steps shown

solutions.latex:
$y=(1+\tan x)^2\ge 0$ for all $x$, so the area is the integral.

By part (a), $y=2\tan x+\sec^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left(2\tan x+\sec^2x\right)dx\\ &=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left(\dfrac{2\sin x}{\cos x}+\sec^2x\right)dx\\ &=\Big[-2\ln|\cos x|+\tan x\Big]_{-\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\ &=\left(-2\ln\left|\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right|+\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\left(-2\ln\left|\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right|+\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\\ &=-2\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-\left(-2\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\\ &=-2\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+2\ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates but makes an error in evaluating, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3 x\right)=3\cos x-3\cos^3 x$.

dif.r: chain rule then sin^2 = 1 - cos^2

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos^3 x\,dx$.

dif.r: rearrange (a) to express cos^3, evaluate exactly

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule and $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)\\ &=3\sin^2x\cos x\\ &=3\cos x\left(1-\cos^2x\right)\\ &=3\cos x-3\cos^3x\\ &=\text{RHS as required} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly but does not make the required identity, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct solution with all appropriate steps shown

solutions.latex:
Rearranging part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)&=3\cos x-3\cos^3x\\ \therefore\ \cos^3x&=\cos x-\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)\right] \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos^3x\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left(\cos x-\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)\right]\right)dx\\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos x\,dx-\dfrac{1}{3}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^3x\right)\right]dx\\ &=\Big[\sin x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}-\dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\sin^3x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\ &=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin(0)-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\sin^3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin^3(0)\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}-0-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{8}-0\right)\\ &=\dfrac{11}{24} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly rearranges the answer to part (a) to integrate, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation $x^{\ln(2)}=8$.

dif.r: take logs of variable base with log exponent

B.note: unknown in the base: take ln, power law, then ln x = 3

Exponential equations.reason: Unknown is in the base (x^{ln2}=8), not the index; solved by Logarithm laws (agreed).

solutions.latex:
Taking natural logs of both sides and using the log law $\ln a^n=n\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^{\ln 2}&=8\\ x^{\ln 2}&=2^3\\ \ln\left(x^{\ln 2}\right)&=\ln\left(2^3\right)\\ \ln 2\,\ln x&=3\ln 2\\ \ln x&=3\\ x&=e^3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies one log law, or equivalent merit

\exfigure{1361_q32_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$ coordinates, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, of the points of intersection of the two curves are the solutions of the equation $\tan x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: equate curves, divide by cos x

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence show that the region enclosed by the two curves has an area of 4 square units.

dif.r: find both intersections, set up and evaluate trig area

figures.cap: graphs of y = root3 sin x and y = cos x for 0 to 2pi, region between their intersections shaded

solutions.latex:
At the points of intersection the two equations are equal. Dividing both sides by $\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{3}\sin x&=\cos x\\ \sqrt{3}\tan x&=1\\ \tan x&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the point of intersection requires that the equations must equal each other, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$\tan x>0$ in the first and third quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan x&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ x&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Between these points $y=\sqrt{3}\sin x$ is above $y=\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{7\pi}{6}}\left(\sqrt{3}\sin x-\cos x\right)dx\\ &=\Big[-\sqrt{3}\cos x-\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{7\pi}{6}}\\ &=\left(-\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)-\sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\right)-\left(-\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\\ &=\left(\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)-\left(-\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\\ &=\left(\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\left(-\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{8}{2}\\ &=4\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct primitive function, or equivalent merit
Solves $\tan x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ to find the intersection points and forms an appropriate integral for the area, or equivalent merit
Solves $\tan x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ to find the intersection points or forms an appropriate integral for the area, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
\exfigure{1361_q33_1}

A metal container of volume $0.66\pi\ \text{m}^3$ is to be made in the shape of a hollow cylinder of radius r metres and height h metres, closed at the bottom and capped at the top with a hemispherical shell of the same radius. The area of the metal required is $A\ \text{m}^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that a sphere with radius $r$ has volume $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ and surface area $4\pi r^2$ and a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ has volume $\pi r^2 h$ and surface area $2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$, show that $A=\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}+\dfrac{5\pi r^2}{3}$.

dif.r: eliminate h via volume constraint, build surface area

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the dimensions of such a container that uses the least amount of metal.

dif.r: given A: derivative, cube root, find h, test minimum

figures.cap: container: cylinder capped with a hemisphere

solutions.latex:
The volume is a hemisphere plus a cylinder:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3+\pi r^2h&=0.66\pi\\ \dfrac{2}{3}r^3+r^2h&=0.66\\ 2r^3+3r^2h&=\dfrac{99}{50}\\ 3r^2h&=\dfrac{99}{50}-2r^3\\ h&=\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The metal is a hemispherical shell, the base circle and the curved side of the cylinder:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\pi r^2+\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\ &=2\pi r^2+\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\ &=3\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)\\ &=3\pi r^2+\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}-\dfrac{4\pi r^2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}+\dfrac{5\pi r^2}{3}\ \text{as required} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an equation for the surface area in terms of $r$ (eliminating $h$), or equivalent merit
Writes an equation for the volume incorporating the given volume, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{33\pi}{25r}+\dfrac{5\pi r^2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{33\pi}{25}r^{-1}+\dfrac{5\pi}{3}r^2\\ A'&=-\dfrac{33\pi}{25}r^{-2}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3}r\\ A''&=\dfrac{66\pi}{25}r^{-3}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{10\pi r}{3}-\dfrac{33\pi}{25r^2}&=0\\ \dfrac{10\pi r^3}{3}-\dfrac{33\pi}{25}&=0\\ \dfrac{10\pi r^3}{3}&=\dfrac{33\pi}{25}\\ r^3&=\dfrac{99}{250}\\ \therefore\ r&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$
Second derivative test:
$$\begin{aligned} A''&=\dfrac{66\pi}{25}\left(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}\right)^{-3}+\dfrac{10\pi}{3}\\ &=10\pi \end{aligned}$$
$A''>0$, so $A$ is a minimum at $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}$.

Using $h$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} h&=\dfrac{33}{50r^2}-\dfrac{2r}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100r^3}{150r^2}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^3}{150\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{99-100\left(\frac{99}{250}\right)}{150\left(\frac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\\ &=\dfrac{99-\frac{990}{25}}{150}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{297}{750}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^1\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\ \therefore\ h&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The dimensions are $r=h=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}}$ m.

Alternative end of solution, from the volume equation in part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} 2r^3+3r^2h&=1.98\\ h&=\dfrac{1.98-2r^3}{3r^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1.98-2\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^3}{3\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{99}{250}}\right)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1.98-\frac{99}{125}}{3}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{99}{250}\times\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{99}{250}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\\ \therefore\ h&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{99}{250}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides correct dimensions or justifies that the determined $r$ value gives a minimum, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $r$ that makes $A'=0$, or equivalent merit
Differentiates $A$ with respect to $r$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct dimensions with relevant working including justification that the given r value gives a minimum SA

parts.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are two independent events with $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{5}{8}$ and $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{6}$.

What is the value of $P(B)$?

dif.r: addition rule with independence, solved in reverse

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
By the addition rule, $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.

$A$ and $B$ are independent, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)\left[1-P(A)\right]\\ \dfrac{5}{8}&=\dfrac{1}{6}+P(B)\left[1-\dfrac{1}{6}\right]\\ \dfrac{5}{8}-\dfrac{1}{6}&=P(B)\times\dfrac{5}{6}\\ \dfrac{15-4}{24}&=P(B)\times\dfrac{5}{6}\\ P(B)&=\dfrac{11}{24}\times\dfrac{6}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{11}{20} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\log_a xy=\log_a x+\log_a y$ and $\log_a a=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\log_2 2+\log_2\sqrt{2}+\log_2\sqrt{2}\\ &=1+\log_2\left(\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}\right)\\ &=1+\log_2 2\\ &=1+1\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$
Or:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\log_2\left(2\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}\right)\\ &=\log_2(2\times 2)\\ &=\log_2 2^2\\ &=2\log_2 2\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A ball is dropped from a height of 2 metres onto a hard floor and bounces. After each bounce, the maximum height reached by the ball is 75\% of the previous maximum height. Thus, after it first hits the floor, it reaches a height of 1.5 metres before falling again, and after the second bounce, it reaches a height of 1.125 metres before falling again. Correct answers to 4 significant figures.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from page image (solutions copy with handwritten markers' annotations)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the maximum height reached after the fifth bounce.

dif.r: GP term; index off-by-one risk

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the total distance travelled by the ball from the time \underline{after} reaching the maximum height with the 5\textsuperscript{th} bounce.

dif.r: limiting sum from 5th bounce, doubled path

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Let $h_n$ be the height after the $n$th bounce. Each bounce multiplies the height by $0.75$:
$$\begin{aligned} h_1&=2\times 0.75=1.5\\ h_2&=2\times 0.75^2=1.125\\ h_3&=2\times 0.75^3\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ h_5&=2\times 0.75^5\\ &=0.474609375\\ &=0.4746 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
Downward motion:
$$2+2\times 0.75+2\times 0.75^2+\dots+2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6+\dots$$
From $2\times 0.75^5$ on, this is a geometric series with $a=2\times 0.75^5$ and $r=0.75$; $|r|<1$, so the limiting sum exists.

Upward motion:
$$2\times 0.75+2\times 0.75^2+\dots+2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6+\dots$$
From $2\times 0.75^6$ on, this is a geometric series with $a=2\times 0.75^6$ and $r=0.75$; $|r|<1$, so the limiting sum exists.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance after 5th bounce}&=\dfrac{2\times 0.75^5}{1-0.75}+\dfrac{2\times 0.75^6}{1-0.75}\\ &=\dfrac{2\times 0.75^5+2\times 0.75^6}{0.25}\\ &=3.3222\ldots\\ &\approx 3.322 \text{ (4 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the upward limiting sum, or equivalent merit
Finds the downward limiting sum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\sec^2 A\equiv\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} A}{\operatorname{cosec} A-\sin A}$.

dif.r: routine identity: reciprocal, compound fraction, Pythagorean identity

solutions.latex:
Using $\operatorname{cosec}A=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}A}{\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A}\\ &=\operatorname{cosec}A\div\left(\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}\div\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin A}-\sin A\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}\div\dfrac{1-\sin^2A}{\sin A} \end{aligned}$$
Since $\cos^2A+\sin^2A=1$, $\cos^2A=1-\sin^2A$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}\times\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos^2A}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2A}\\ &=\sec^2A\\ &=\text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$
Or, using $\sec^2A=1+\tan^2A$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\sec^2A\\ &=1+\tan^2A\\ &=1+\dfrac{\sin^2A}{\cos^2A}\\ &=1+\dfrac{\sin^2A}{1-\sin^2A}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^2A+\sin^2A}{1-\sin^2A}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin^2A}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\sin A}}{\frac{1}{\sin A}-\frac{\sin^2A}{\sin A}}\\ &=\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}A}{\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A}\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct manipulation using $\cos^2A=1-\sin^2A$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: near twin of 2023 Q24(a) set-up plus A=xy

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the \underline{exact value of} $x$ such that the area of the frame and photograph combined is a \underline{minimum}. \underline{Show that} your answer gives a minimum area.

dif.r: quotient rule, quadratic with surd root, justify minimum

figures.cap: photograph (20 cm^2) inside a frame of length x cm with 1 cm top/bottom and 2 cm side borders

solutions.latex:
Let the width of the frame be $y$ cm. The photograph is $(x-4)$ cm by $(y-2)$ cm:
$$\begin{aligned} (x-4)(y-2)&=20\\ y-2&=\dfrac{20}{x-4}\\ y&=\dfrac{20}{x-4}+2\\ &=\dfrac{20+2(x-4)}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{20+2x-8}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{12+2x}{x-4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=x\times y\\ &=x\times\dfrac{12+2x}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{12x+2x^2}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{2x^2+12x}{x-4} \end{aligned}$$
Or let the width of the photo be $y$, so $(x-4)\times y=20$ and $y=\dfrac{20}{x-4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=x(y+2)\\ &=x\left(\dfrac{20}{x-4}+2\right)\\ &=x\times\dfrac{20+2(x-4)}{x-4}\\ &=x\times\dfrac{20+2x-8}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{x(12+2x)}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{12x+2x^2}{x-4}\\ &=\dfrac{2x^2+12x}{x-4} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an expression for the width in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: expression for the width in terms of $x$
meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x^2+12x & v&=x-4\\ u'&=4x+12 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx}&=\dfrac{(x-4)(4x+12)-(2x^2+12x)\times 1}{(x-4)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{4x^2+12x-16x-48-2x^2-12x}{(x-4)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{2x^2-16x-48}{(x-4)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{2(x^2-8x-24)}{(x-4)^2} \end{aligned}$$
The minimum or maximum area occurs when $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$x^2-8x-24=0$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{64-4\times 1\times(-24)}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{64+96}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{160}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{8\pm 4\sqrt{10}}{2}\\ &=4\pm 2\sqrt{10} \end{aligned}$$
$x>0$, so $x=4+2\sqrt{10}\approx 10.32$.

Testing the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side:

\extable{Ts1241_1}

$\therefore$ The area is a minimum when $x=4+2\sqrt{10}$ cm.
criteria: Obtains $x=4+2\sqrt{10}$ (discarding the negative solution), or equivalent merit

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Using the trapezoidal rule with 3 function values, find an approximation to the area between the curve $y=2xe^x$ and the $x$ axis from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

Express your answer correct to three significant figures.

dif.r: two-strip trapezoidal, direct evaluation

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Comparing your answers for parts (b) and (c), comment on the concavity of $y=2xe^x$.

dif.r: overestimate implies concave up, justify

A.note: compare exact and trapezoidal estimate to deduce concave up

B.note: over-estimate implies concave up; Concavity skill counts_when (sign of f'') not met

Concavity and points of inflection.evidence: trapezoidal area greater than integral, so y=2xe^x must be concave up

figures.cap: solution sketch: small sketch of a concave-up curve with a chord from x=0 to x=1 lying above it

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x+4 & v&=e^x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left((2x+4)e^x\right)&=e^x\times 2+(2x+4)\times e^x\\ &=e^x\left[2+2x+4\right]\\ &=e^x(2x+6) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\int e^x(2x+6)\,dx=(2x+4)e^x+c$$

From part (a):
$$\int\left(2xe^x+6e^x\right)dx=(2x+4)e^x+c$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 2xe^x\,dx&=\Big[(2x+4)e^x\Big]_0^1-\int_0^1 6e^x\,dx\\ &=(2+4)e^1-4e^0-6\Big[e^x\Big]_0^1\\ &=6e-4-6\left[e-1\right]\\ &=6e-4-6e+6\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses part (a) correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
3 function values means $n=2$ strips (not $n=3$), with $a=0$ and $b=1$:
$$h=\dfrac{b-a}{n}=\dfrac{1-0}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
so the $x$ values are $0$, $\dfrac{1}{2}$, $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y_1&=2\times 0\times e^0=0\\ y_2&=2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times e^{\frac{1}{2}}=e^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ y_3&=2\times 1\times e^1=2e \end{aligned}$$
Using the trapezoidal rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{b-a}{2n}\left[f(a)+f(b)+2f(x_1)\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{1-0}{2\times 2}\left[0+2e+2\times e^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\left[2e+2e^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]\\ &\approx 2.1835\\ &\approx 2.18 \text{ (3 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct function values and $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

The area using the trapezoidal rule is greater than the area using integration ($2.18>2$), so $y=2xe^x$ must be concave up between $x=0$ and $x=1$.

solutions.latex:
For $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(3\sin 2x-3\sin 2a)\,dx=0$, the area below the line $y=3\sin 2a$ (from $0$ to $a$) must equal the area above it (from $a$ to $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$):
$$\int_0^a(3\sin 2a-3\sin 2x)\,dx=\int_a^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(3\sin 2x-3\sin 2a)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[3x\sin 2a-\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2x\right)\right]_0^a&=\left[-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2x-3x\sin 2a\right]_a^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\ 3a\sin 2a+\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2a-\left(0+\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 0\right)&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\sin 2a-\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2a-3a\sin 2a\right)\\ 3a\sin 2a+\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2a-\dfrac{3}{2}&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\times 0-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\sin 2a+\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2a+3a\sin 2a\\ -\dfrac{3}{2}&=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\sin 2a\\ -6&=-3\pi\sin 2a\\ \sin 2a&=\dfrac{6}{3\pi}=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\\ 2a&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)=0.6901070914\\ a&=0.3450535457\\ &=0.345 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
Alternative (direct): $3\sin 2a$ is a constant, so
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}3\sin 2x\,dx=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}3\sin 2a\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[-\dfrac{3}{2}\cos 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}&=\Big[3x\sin 2a\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\ \dfrac{3}{2}&=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\sin 2a\\ a&=0.345 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes a correct area statement, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Consider the graph of a hyperbola $y=f(x)$, as shown below.

\exfigure{1362_q28_1}
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from page image (solutions copy with handwritten markers' annotations)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Justify that the equation of $y=f(x)$ is $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x-1}$. Show full working.

dif.r: justify hyperbola equation from asymptotes and a point

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the exact value of $m$ for which the equation $f(x)=mx$ is a tangent to $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x-1}$.

dif.r: tangent condition via discriminant on rational equation

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

figures.cap: hyperbola y=f(x) with asymptotes x=1 and y=1, passing through the origin

solutions.latex:
The graph has asymptotes $x=1$ and $y=1$, so it is a translation of $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-1&=\dfrac{k}{x-1}\\ y&=1+\dfrac{k}{x-1} \end{aligned}$$
The curve passes through $(0,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=1+\dfrac{k}{-1}\\ k&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y&=1+\dfrac{1}{x-1}\\ &=\dfrac{x-1+1}{x-1}\\ &=\dfrac{x}{x-1} \end{aligned}$$
Checking the asymptotes:
$$\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x-1}\right)=1+0=1$$
so the horizontal asymptote is $y=1$.

The domain is $x\ne 1$, so the vertical asymptote is $x=1$.
criteria: Uses the asymptotes or a transformation of $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).
meta.marker_note: Stating $x\ne 1$, $y\ne 1$ without justification is not sufficient.

solutions.latex:
The line $y=mx$ is a tangent when $\dfrac{x}{x-1}=mx$ has exactly one solution, that is, $\Delta=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=mx(x-1)\\ x&=mx^2-mx\\ 0&=mx^2-mx-x\\ 0&=mx^2-(m+1)x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta&=b^2-4ac\\ &=\left(-(m+1)\right)^2-4\times m\times 0\\ &=(m+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$\Delta=0$ when $m=-1$.

Calculus approach: the curve passes through $(0,0)$, so the tangent through the origin touches at $x=0$. Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=x-1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{1(x-1)-x\cdot 1}{(x-1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-1}{(x-1)^2}\\ m&=f'(0)=\dfrac{-1}{(-1)^2}=-1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the quadratic and discriminant (or derivative), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The line $y=c-\dfrac{x}{2}$ is a normal to the curve $y=x^3+ax^2+bx-4$ at the point $(2,\,7)$.

What are the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$?

dif.r: normal gives tangent gradient; point and gradient give simultaneous a,b

solutions.latex:
$y=x^3+ax^2+bx-4$ passes through $(2,7)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7&=8+4a+2b-4\\ 3&=4a+2b &&(1) \end{aligned}$$
$y'=3x^2+2ax+b$. The normal $y=-\dfrac{x}{2}+c$ has gradient $m_N=-\dfrac{1}{2}$, so the tangent gradient at $(2,7)$ is $m_T=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=3\times 2^2+2a\times 2+b\\ 2&=12+4a+b\\ -10&=4a+b &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
$(1)-(2)$:
$$b=13$$
Substituting into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=4a+2\times 13\\ 4a&=3-26=-23\\ a&=-\dfrac{23}{4}=-5\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$(2,7)$ is on $y=-\dfrac{x}{2}+c$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7&=-\dfrac{2}{2}+c\\ 7&=-1+c\\ c&=8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=-5\dfrac{3}{4},\quad b=13,\quad c=8$$
criteria: Finds the tangent gradient $m_T=2$ and forms the second equation, or equivalent merit
Forms the equation from the point $(2,7)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Sketch the curve $y=\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{x^2}{4}-3x+1$ by finding all stationary points and testing their nature.

Also, find the points of inflection and the $y$ intercept.

dif.r: routine cubic: stationary points, inflection, sketch

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of the cubic with maximum (-3, 7 3/4), inflexion (-1/2, 2 13/24), minimum (2, -2 2/3), y-intercept 1

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{x^2}{4}-3x+1\\ y'&=\dfrac{3x^2}{6}+\dfrac{2x}{4}-3 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x}{2}-3\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(x^2+x-6)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(x+3)(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x=-3&: &y&=\dfrac{-27}{6}+\dfrac{9}{4}+9+1=\dfrac{31}{4}=7\dfrac{3}{4}\\ x=2&: &y&=\dfrac{8}{6}+\dfrac{4}{4}-6+1=-\dfrac{8}{3}=-2\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature with $y''=x+\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-3: &y''&=-3+\dfrac{1}{2}=-2\dfrac{1}{2}<0 &&\text{maximum turning point at } \left(-3,\,7\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\\ x&=2: &y''&=2+\dfrac{1}{2}=2\dfrac{1}{2}>0 &&\text{minimum turning point at } \left(2,\,-2\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflexion occur when $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x+\dfrac{1}{2}&=0\\ x&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\dfrac{-1}{8\times 6}+\dfrac{1}{4\times 4}-3\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{48}+\dfrac{1}{16}+\dfrac{3}{2}+1\\ &=\dfrac{61}{24}=2\dfrac{13}{24}\approx 2.5416 \end{aligned}$$
Testing the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts1250_1}

There is a change in concavity, $\therefore$ there is a point of inflexion at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2},\,2\dfrac{13}{24}\right)$.

The $y$-intercept occurs when $x=0$: $y=0+0-0+1=1$.

\exfigure{1362_q30_s1}

Finds the stationary points and their nature, and the point of inflexion with a change of concavity, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points and determines their nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis such that at a time $t$ seconds its displacement from the origin is $x$ metres. The acceleration of the particle is given by $a=\dfrac{8}{e^{2t}}+\dfrac{3}{e^t}$.

Initially its velocity is $-6$ m/s and its displacement is 5 m.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from page image (solutions copy with handwritten markers' annotations)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the equation for the displacement ($x$) of the particle in terms of $t$.

dif.r: integrate exponential acceleration twice with two constants

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what time and where does the particle come to rest?

dif.r: hidden quadratic in e^{-t}, reject negative, then find x

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

req: Particles at rest and changing direction
Particles at rest and changing direction
B.note: quadratic in e^-t

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: v and x were found in part (a); this part solves v=0 and evaluates x, covered by agreed skills.

e and natural logarithms.reason: ln step is part of the agreed Exponential equations; x evaluated to decimals, e^{ln} property not needed.

solutions.latex:
$$a=8e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}$$
Integrating to find the velocity:
$$v=\dfrac{8e^{-2t}}{-2}+\dfrac{3e^{-t}}{-1}+c$$
When $t=0$, $v=-6$:
$$\begin{aligned} -6&=-4e^0-3e^0+c\\ -6&=-7+c\\ c&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$v=-4e^{-2t}-3e^{-t}+1$$
Integrating again:
$$x=\dfrac{-4e^{-2t}}{-2}-\dfrac{3e^{-t}}{-1}+t+k$$
When $t=0$, $x=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5&=2e^0+3e^0+0+k\\ 5&=5+k\\ k&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}+t\\ &=\dfrac{2}{e^{2t}}+\dfrac{3}{e^t}+t \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct velocity, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-4e^{-2t}-3e^{-t}+1\\ 0&=4e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}-1\\ &=4(e^{-t})^2+3e^{-t}-1 \end{aligned}$$
Let $m=e^{-t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4m^2+3m-1\\ &=(4m-1)(m+1)\\ m&=\dfrac{1}{4} \text{ or } m=-1 \end{aligned}$$
$e^{-t}=-1$ has no solution, since $e^{-t}>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{-t}&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \ln e^{-t}&=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}\\ -t&=\ln 4^{-1}=-\ln 4\\ t&=\ln 4=1.386294361 \end{aligned}$$
When $t=\ln 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2e^{-2\ln 4}+3e^{-\ln 4}+\ln 4\\ &=2e^{\ln 4^{-2}}+3e^{\ln 4^{-1}}+\ln 4\\ &=2\times 4^{-2}+3\times 4^{-1}+\ln 4\\ &=\dfrac{2}{16}+\dfrac{3}{4}+\ln 4\\ &=\dfrac{7}{8}+\ln 4\\ &=2.261294361 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The particle is at rest when $t=\ln 4\approx 1.386$ seconds, at $x\approx 2.26$ m.
criteria: Forms the quadratic in $e^{-t}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Four students want to organise a netball game. All four students have the same probability, $P(T)$, of being available next Tuesday. All four students have the same probability, $P(W)$, of being available next Wednesday. Josie is one of the four students.

It is known that $P(T)=\dfrac{2}{5}$, $P(W\mid T)=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $P(T\mid W)=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
questions.review_note: scan path: transcribed from page image (solutions copy with handwritten markers' annotations)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Is Josie's availability next Tuesday independent from her availability next Wednesday? Justify your answer.

dif.r: twin of 2023 Q31(a): compare P(T|W) with P(T)

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the probability that Josie is available next Wednesday is $\dfrac{3}{10}$.

dif.r: twin of 2023 Q31(b): chain two conditionals

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the probability that at least one of the four students is NOT available next Wednesday?

solutions.latex:
If $T$ and $W$ are independent, then $P(T\mid W)=P(T)$ and $P(W\mid T)=P(W)$.

But $P(T\mid W)=\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $P(T)=\dfrac{2}{5}$.

$\therefore P(T\mid W)\ne P(T)$

$\therefore T$ and $W$ are \underline{not} independent.

Using $P(W\mid T)=\dfrac{P(W\cap T)}{P(T)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{4}&=\dfrac{P(W\cap T)}{\frac{2}{5}}\\ P(W\cap T)&=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{2}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{20}=\dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}$$
Using $P(T\mid W)=\dfrac{P(T\cap W)}{P(W)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{10}}{P(W)}\\ P(W)&=\dfrac{1}{10}\div\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{10}\times\dfrac{3}{1}\\ &=\dfrac{3}{10} \end{aligned}$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
"At least one not available" is the complement of "all four available", and the students are independent:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-P(\text{all available on }W)&=1-\left(\dfrac{3}{10}\right)^4\\ &=1-\dfrac{81}{10\,000}\\ &=\dfrac{9919}{10\,000} \end{aligned}$$

parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: 3D set-up combining depression angles, bearings and cosine rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
At 9 a.m., two destroyers start travelling from $A$ and $B$ in the direction of $C$ and continue past $C$ in the same straight lines. The destroyer at $A$ travels along $AC$ with a uniform speed of $20$ km/h, while the destroyer at $B$ travels along $BC$ with a uniform speed of $50$ km/h.

Show that the distance between the two destroyers after travelling for $t$ hours is $10\sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2}$.
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

dif.r: Model moving distances, cosine rule with careful algebraic expansion

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
The destroyers are known to be “on alert” when they are less than $40$ km apart.

During what times will the two destroyers be “on alert”?
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

dif.r: Set up and solve quadratic inequality, convert to clock times

figures.cap: 3D diagram: helicopter at H above C, angles of depression 60 and 30 degrees to A and B, AB = 100 sqrt13 km, AC = x km
solution sketch: sketch of the upward parabola in t, negative between its roots

solutions.latex:
Using the bearings from $C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ACB&=250^{\circ}-130^{\circ}\\ &=120^{\circ} \end{aligned}$$
Let $AC=x$. In right-angled triangle $AHC$, the angle of depression gives $\angle HAC=60^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^{\circ}&=\dfrac{h}{x}\\ x&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 60^{\circ}}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\\ h&=\sqrt{3}x \end{aligned}$$
In right-angled triangle $BHC$, $\angle HBC=30^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 30^{\circ}&=\dfrac{h}{BC}\\ BC&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 30^{\circ}}=\dfrac{h}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}=\sqrt{3}h\\ &=\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}x=3x \end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $ABC$, $AB^2=AC^2+BC^2-2\times AC\times BC\times\cos 120^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(100\sqrt{13}\right)^2&=\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2-2\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}h\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ 10\,000\times 13&=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+3h^2+h^2\\ 130\,000&=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+4h^2=\dfrac{13h^2}{3}\\ 13h^2&=3\times 130\,000\\ h^2&=3\times 10\,000\\ h&=\pm\sqrt{30\,000} \end{aligned}$$
$h>0$, so $h=\sqrt{30\,000}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ AC=x&=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{30\,000}}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{10\,000}=100\text{ km}\\ BC&=\sqrt{3}h=\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{30\,000}=\sqrt{90\,000}=300\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
Or, using $BC=3x$:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2&=x^2+(3x)^2-2\times x\times 3x\times\cos 120^{\circ}\\ \left(100\sqrt{13}\right)^2&=x^2+9x^2-6x^2\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ 10\,000\times 13&=10x^2+3x^2\\ 130\,000&=13x^2\\ x^2&=10\,000 \end{aligned}$$
$x>0$, so $x=100$, and $BC=3x=300$ km.
criteria: Uses the cosine rule correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds $AC$ and $BC$ in terms of $h$ (or $BC=3x$), or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: BC = 300 km (all distances are in km), not 300 m.

solutions.latex:
After $t$ hours the distances $AC$ and $BC$ are $100-20t$ and $300-50t$ respectively. The angle at $C$ is still $120^{\circ}$, so by the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2&=(100-20t)^2+(300-50t)^2-2(100-20t)(300-50t)\cos 120^{\circ}\\ &=10\,000-4000t+400t^2+90\,000-30\,000t+2500t^2-2\left(30\,000-5000t-6000t+1000t^2\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=130\,000-45\,000t+3900t^2\\ &=100\left(1300-450t+39t^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
$AB>0$, so
$$\begin{aligned} AB&=\sqrt{100\left(1300-450t+39t^2\right)}\\ &=10\sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes the correct distances after $t$ hours into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct distances after $t$ hours in the cosine rule
meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).
meta.marker_note: $100+20t$ and $300+50t$ were also accepted.

solutions.latex:
The destroyers are on alert when $AB<40$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2}&<40\\ \sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2}&<4 &&(\text{divide by } 10)\\ 1300-450t+39t^2&<16 &&(\text{square})\\ 39t^2-450t+1284&<0 &&(\text{subtract } 16) \end{aligned}$$
Solving $39t^2-450t+1284=0$ with the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{450\pm\sqrt{450^2-4\times 39\times 1284}}{2\times 39}\\ &=\dfrac{450\pm\sqrt{2196}}{78}\\ &=\dfrac{75\pm\sqrt{61}}{13} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1362_q33_s1}

The parabola is concave up, so it is negative between its roots:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{450-\sqrt{450^2-4\times 39\times 1284}}{78}&<t<\dfrac{450+\sqrt{450^2-4\times 39\times 1284}}{78}\\ 5.168442333&<t<6.370019206 \end{aligned}$$
$$5\text{ h }10\text{ min }6.39\text{ s}<t<6\text{ h }22\text{ min }12.07\text{ s}$$
where $t$ is the time after 9 am.

$\therefore$ The destroyers are on alert between 2:10 pm and 3:22 pm.
criteria: Solves the quadratic inequality for $t$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the range of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{x-2}}+1$?

dif.r: range of reciprocal root plus shift, open endpoint

solutions.latex:
Let $u=\sqrt{x-2}$, where $u>0$.

As $u\to\infty$, $\dfrac{3}{u}+1\to 1$.

As $u\to 0$, $\dfrac{3}{u}+1\to\infty$.

The function approaches 1 but never reaches it, so the range is $(1,\infty)$.

parts.latex: Given that $a=\log 5$ and $b=\log 2$, what is the expression of $\log 100$ in terms of $a$ and $b$?

dif.r: 100 as (5x2)^2, product and power laws

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\log x^n=n\log x$ and $\log xy=\log x+\log y$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log 100&=\log 10^2\\ &=2\log 10\\ &=2(\log 2+\log 5)\\ &=2(a+b) \end{aligned}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: log 10 = log 2 + log 5 = a + b, not log(a + b); so log 100 = 2(a + b).

parts.latex: If $\tan x=3$ and $\sin x<0$, what is the exact value of $\cos x$?

dif.r: quadrant from signs, Pythagoras, exact cos

figures.cap: solution sketch: axes with reference triangle in the third quadrant: adjacent 1, opposite 3, angle x at the origin

solutions.latex:
$\tan x=3>0$ and $\sin x<0$, so $x$ is in the third quadrant.

\exfigure{1364_q3_s1}

By Pythagoras' theorem, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{3^2+1^2}=\sqrt{10}$.

$\cos x$ is negative in the third quadrant, hence
$$\cos x=\dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{10}}$$

parts.latex:
Three runners compete in a race.

The probabilities that the three runners finish the race in under 10 seconds are $\dfrac{1}{4}$, $\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $\dfrac{2}{5}$ respectively.

What is the probability that at least one of the three runners will finish the race in under 10 seconds?

dif.r: three complements multiplied then complement

solutions.latex:
The probabilities that each runner does not finish in under 10 seconds are
$$\begin{aligned} P(A)&=1-\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{3}{4}\\ P(B)&=1-\dfrac{1}{6}=\dfrac{5}{6}\\ P(C)&=1-\dfrac{2}{5}=\dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$$
The runners are independent:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{none})&=P(A)\times P(B)\times P(C)\\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{5}{6}\times\dfrac{3}{5}=\dfrac{3}{8} \end{aligned}$$
"At least one" is the complement of "none":
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one})&=1-\dfrac{3}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{5}{8} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
It is known that for a particular function, $y=f(x)$, that

$$\begin{gathered}f(2)=-5\\ f'(2)=0\\ f''(2)=3\end{gathered}$$

Which statement below is true regarding the graph of $y=f(x)$?

dif.r: MCQ: f'=0 and f''>0 means minimum

options.label: B
options.latex: There is a local minimum at $(2,-5)$

options.label: D
options.latex: There is a point of inflexion at $(2,4)$

solutions.latex:
$f'(2)=0$, so there is a stationary point at $(2,-5)$.

$f''(2)=3>0$, so the curve is concave up there.

Hence at $x=2$ there is a local minimum.

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the test uses f''(2) = 3 > 0 at the point, not f''(x) > 0 in general.

parts.latex:
The curve $y=2x^3-ax^2+6x$ has a point of inflection at $x=4$.

What is the value of $a$?

dif.r: MCQ: set f''(4)=0, solve for a

solutions.latex:
At a point of inflection $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2x^3-ax^2+6x\\ y'&=6x^2-2ax+6\\ y''&=12x-2a \end{aligned}$$
At $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=12(4)-2a\\ 2a&=48\\ a&=24 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{4}\sqrt{16-x^2}\,dx$?

dif.r: recognise semicircle area, no integration

solutions.latex:
$y=\sqrt{16-x^2}$ is the top semicircle with radius 4, so the integral is its area:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-4}^{4}\sqrt{16-x^2}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\pi\times4^2\\ &=8\pi \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Which of the following is the exact area bounded by $y=\sin x$, $y=\cos x$, $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and the $y$-axis?

\exfigure{1364_q9_1}

dif.r: MCQ: area between curves, split at intersection pi/4

figures.cap: y = cos x and y = sin x on [0, pi/2], crossing at pi/4; regions between the curves shaded up to x = pi/2

solutions.latex:
The curves meet at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. $\cos x\ge\sin x$ on $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$ and $\sin x\ge\cos x$ on $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(\sin x-\cos x)\,dx\\ &=\Big[\sin x+\cos x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}+\Big[-\cos x-\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=2\sqrt{2}-2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A YouTuber predicts that every person who views their latest video will share it with 5 other people after a day.

The YouTuber shares the video to 8 people in the first day.

After how many whole days should the YouTuber reach 1 million unique views?

dif.r: GP sum = 10^6 then logs

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
This is a geometric progression with $a=8$ and $r=5$.

1 million unique views requires the sum of the geometric progression. Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000000&=\dfrac{8(5^n-1)}{4}\\ 1000000&=2(5^n-1)\\ 5^n-1&=500000\\ 5^n&=500001\\ n\ln 5&=\ln 500001\\ n&=\dfrac{\ln 500001}{\ln 5}\\ &=8.1533\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Therefore it takes 9 full days to reach 1 million unique views.
criteria: Correctly solves the required equation using logarithm laws, or equivalent merit
Identifies that a sum of a geometric progression is required and obtains the equation $1000000=\dfrac{8(5^n-1)}{4}$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly determines the number of days after solving the geometric progression equation using logarithm laws
meta.marker_note: Many students used $T_n$ rather than $S_n$; 2 marks were awarded if $T_n$ was used. Coincidentally, using $T_n$ produces the same answer.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: 5^n = 500 001 (from 5^n - 1 = 500 000), not 5 000 001; the value n = 8.1533... already uses 500 001.

questions.stem:
The population of stray cats can be modelled by the equation $P=P_0e^{kt}$, where $P_0$ and $k$ are constants.

Initially, a town had 30 stray cats. In 12 days, the population of cats increased to 120.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $P_0=30$.

dif.r: substitute t=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the exact value of $k$.

dif.r: exponential formula used in reverse with logs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine the population of cats in 30 days.

dif.r: substitute t=30

solutions.latex:
Initially ($t=0$), $P=30$:
$$\begin{aligned} 30&=P_0e^{k\times0}\\ 30&=P_0\times1\\ P_0&=30 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Substitutes $t=0$ and $P=30$ into the equation and solves to obtain $P_0=30$
meta.marker_note: Very well done.

solutions.latex:
When $t=12$, $P=120$:
$$\begin{aligned} 120&=30e^{12k}\\ 4&=e^{12k}\\ \ln 4&=\ln e^{12k}\\ 12k&=\ln 4\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln 4}{12} \end{aligned}$$
Optionally,
$$k=\dfrac{\ln 4}{12}=\dfrac{2\ln 2}{12}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{6}$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes values for $t$ and $P$ into the equation, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly obtains the exact value of $k$ by substituting values then solving for $k$
meta.marker_note: Very well done; bizarrely, many students when dividing 120 by 30 wrote 40 rather than 4.

solutions.latex:
Substituting $t=30$ and $k=\dfrac{\ln 4}{12}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=30e^{\frac{\ln 4}{12}\times30}\\ &=960 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Obtains 960 by substituting in correct values for $t$ and $k$
meta.marker_note: Very well done.

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{2x^2}{x^2-4}$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that there is a horizontal asymptote at $y=2$.

dif.r: limit at infinity of rational function

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the vertical asymptotes of the function.

dif.r: denominator zero, one step

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the function, showing all asymptotes and intercepts.

dif.r: sketch rational function with asymptotes and branches

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y = 2x^2/(x^2-4) with asymptotes x = -2, x = 2, y = 2; local maximum at origin

solutions.latex:
The horizontal asymptote is at $y=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)$. Dividing the numerator and denominator by $x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)\\ &=\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{2x^2}{x^2-4}\\ &=\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{\frac{2x^2}{x^2}}{\frac{x^2}{x^2}-\frac{4}{x^2}}\\ &=\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{2}{1-\frac{4}{x^2}}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{1-0}\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly uses limits to show that the horizontal asymptote is at $y=2$
meta.marker_note: All students were given a mark for this question due to its difficulty and the vagueness of the syllabus.

solutions.latex:
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator of $f(x)$ is zero:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-4&=0\\ x^2&=4\\ x&=\pm2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Very well done by the cohort. A few forgot about the plus-minus sign.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1364_q14_s1}
criteria: One portion of the graph is correct, with all asymptotes and intercept labelled, OR the correct graph is produced with all asymptotes and intercepts labelled but the curve does not correctly approach the asymptote, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Graph is the correct shape and in the correct position, with all asymptotes drawn
meta.marker_note: Students need to take care sketching their graphs: many graphs showed poor attention to detail, such as the curve "bouncing" up once it reaches the asymptote, or the symmetry (the function is even).

parts.latex:
The quadratic equation $x^2+(m+6)x+8m=0$ has two distinct roots.

By considering the discriminant or otherwise, determine all the possible values of $m$.

dif.r: discriminant in m, quadratic inequality

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

figures.cap: solution sketch: concave-up parabola in m crossing the m-axis at 2 and 18

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \Delta&=b^2-4ac\\ &=(m+6)^2-4(1)(8m)\\ &=m^2+12m+36-32m\\ &=m^2-20m+36 \end{aligned}$$
For two distinct roots, $\Delta>0$:
$$\begin{aligned} m^2-20m+36&>0\\ (m-2)(m-18)&>0 \end{aligned}$$
The graph of $m^2-20m+36$ is above the axis outside its roots 2 and 18:

\exfigure{1364_q15_s1}
$$\therefore\ m<2 \text{ or } m>18$$
criteria: Substitutes correct values into the discriminant formula, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Determines all possible values of $m$ by correctly solving $(m-2)(m-18)>0$
meta.marker_note: Many students failed to consider the inequality. Two marks maximum for stating $m=2$ and $m=18$ without identifying that $\Delta>0$.

parts.latex:
In a workplace of 25 employees, each employee speaks either French or German, or both.

It is known that 36% of the employees speak German, and 20% speak both French and German.

Calculate the probability one person chosen could speak German if they could speak French.

Give your answer to the nearest percent.

dif.r: deduce P(F) from both-or-either condition, then conditional

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram F and G: F only 0.64 (16), both 0.20 (5), G only 0.16 (4)

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1364_q16_s1}

Everyone speaks French or German, so
$$P(F)=1-P(\text{German only})=1-(0.36-0.20)=0.84$$
Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(G\mid F)&=\dfrac{P(G\cap F)}{P(F)}\\ &=\dfrac{0.20}{0.84}\\ &=0.238\ldots\\ &=24\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the correct formula with a correct probability, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b

Which team is more successful at scoring goals?

Justify your answer using summary statistics.
parts.note: quartiles and box plots of a data set: not in the 2024 Advanced syllabus · Standard: MST-11-08

dif.r: Compare box-plots and justify conclusion with summary statistics; simple interpretation.

solution sketch: Team A box-plot: min 19, Q1 23, median 26, Q3 27, max 28, drawn above Team B

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1364_q17_s1}
criteria: Correct shape plus 3 correct values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: Team B is more successful at scoring goals, as each value in its five-number summary is higher than Team A's equivalent value.

meta.top_criterion_original: justification which includes correct terminology and reference to at least one of the quartiles or median without additional information not supporting the correct solution
meta.marker_note: Students needed to select only reasoning that supported Team B being more successful, and state that; not additional information, even if correct (e.g. Team B being slightly positively skewed or symmetrical). The question said to use summary statistics. Correct terminology was required (median, not med), and correct percentages needed to be quoted. The justification required correct context: scores given were match scores, so a percentage of scores must be in this context (e.g. Team B scored more than 27 goals in $50\%$ of matches). A higher interquartile range or larger range does not justify higher scores (consider a team with $Q_1=10$ and $Q_3=20$, or lowest and highest scores 8 and 23). Reasoning had to be supported by the data: a higher median for Team B is shown by the data, a higher mean is not. Students who gave more than one reason needed both to be correct to get the mark. Mark awarded for a justification with correct terminology referring to at least one of the quartiles or the median, without additional information that does not support the answer.

The table below lists the average life span (in years) and average sleeping time (in hours/day) of 9 animal species.

\extable{1364_q18_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Using sleeping time as the independent variable, calculate the least squares regression line.

Give your answers correct to two decimal places.
parts.note: Least-squares regression line by calculator: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

dif.r: Routine calculator regression; must assign independent variable correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
A wallaby species sleeps for 4.5 hours on average, each day.

Use your equation from part (a) to predict its expected life span, to the nearest year.
parts.note: Prediction from a least-squares regression line: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

dif.r: Single substitution into the regression line, then rounding.

solutions.latex:
Using the calculator's linear regression with sleeping time as the independent variable:
$$\text{Life span}=42.89-2.85\times\text{sleeping time}$$
criteria: Correct $A$ or $B$ or both, or the correct equation found with sleeping time as the dependent variable, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substituting a sleeping time of 4.5 hours into the equation from part (a):

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

dif.r: E(X^2) minus mean squared, square root

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0+1\times0.3+2\times0.5+3\times0.1+4\times0.1\\ &=0.3+1+0.3+0.4\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$

Using the reference sheet formula $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X)&=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2\\ &=\left(0+1^2\times0.3+2^2\times0.5+3^2\times0.1+4^2\times0.1\right)-2^2\\ &=(0.3+2+0.9+1.6)-4\\ &=0.8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \sigma&=\sqrt{0.8}\\ &=0.8944\ldots\\ &=0.9\ \text{(to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct answer not supported by using the formula on the reference sheet, or correctly calculates the variance, or finds the standard deviation from the variance, or equivalent merit
