questions.stem:
Natalie and her friends have made a post-HSC adventure bucket list. One of their bucket list items is to visit the Figure Eight rock pools and a visit to Figure Eight rock pools requires extreme caution. At all times it is very important to check the depth of water before entering the pools.

The depth of water at Figure Eight rock pools can be modelled by the equation

$$d=2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\,,\ \text{for } 0\le t\le12$$

where $d$ is in metres and $t$ is time after 7 am.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the depth of the water at high tide?

dif.r: centre plus amplitude

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Figure Eight rock pools is only safe to visit when the depth of the water is below 1.75 m.

Between what times is it safe to visit the pools?

dif.r: solve sine inequality, interpret interval as clock times

solutions.latex:
High tide is when $d$ is greatest, that is when $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}d&=2+\dfrac{1}{2}(1)\\&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The depth of water at high tide is $2.5$ m.

The pools are safe when $d<1.75$:
$$\begin{aligned}2+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<1.75\\\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<-0.25\\\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&<-0.5\end{aligned}$$
Solve $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t=-0.5$. The related angle is $\sin^{-1}(0.5)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and sine is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6} &&\text{so } t=7\\\dfrac{\pi}{6}t&=2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&\text{so } t=11\end{aligned}$$
By checking the graph or testing values, $d<1.75$ for $7<t<11$.

As $t$ is the number of hours after 7 am, $t=7$ is 2 pm and $t=11$ is 6 pm.

$\therefore$ It is safe to visit the pools between 2 pm and 6 pm.
criteria: Solves for the values of $t$ using trigonometric equation techniques, or equivalent merit
Makes $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}t$ the subject, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A wire of length 28 m is to be cut into two pieces. One of the pieces is to be made into a square and the other into a circle.

Let $r$ metres be the radius of the circle and $x$ metres be the length of each side of the square.

The combined perimeter is given as $2\pi r+4x=28$ and the combined area, $A$, is given by:

$$A=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\ \ (\textbf{DO NOT PROVE THIS})$$

What should be the lengths of each piece so that the combined area of the circle and the square is minimum? Leave your answer in simplest exact form.

dif.r: A given; solve A'=0, convert x to piece lengths exactly

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the given area to find the stationary point:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\\A'&=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot2(14-2x)(-2)+2x\\&=-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x\\A''&=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2\end{aligned}$$
Set $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x&=0\\-\dfrac{56}{\pi}+\dfrac{8x}{\pi}+2x&=0\\-56+8x+2\pi x&=0\\2x(4+\pi)&=56\\x&=\dfrac{28}{4+\pi}\end{aligned}$$
$A''=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2>0$ for all $x$ (concave up), so $x=\dfrac{28}{4+\pi}$ gives a minimum.

The square has perimeter $4x$ and the circle has the rest of the wire, so the lengths of the two pieces are
$$4x=\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}\text{ m}$$
and
$$\begin{aligned}28-4x&=28-\dfrac{112}{4+\pi}\\&=\dfrac{28\pi}{4+\pi}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantially correct solution, or equivalent merit
Some correct working towards the correct solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t$, the change in the population from $t=0$ to $t=4$ is
$$\begin{aligned}P(4)-P(0)&=\int_0^4\left(9e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}-2t\right)dt\\&=9\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt-\int_0^42t\,dt\end{aligned}$$
With $P(0)=34$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(4)&=9\int_0^4e^{\frac{t^2}{5}}\,dt-\Big[t^2\Big]_0^4+P(0)\\&=9(22.26)-16+34\\&=218.34\ldots\\&\approx218\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantially correct solution, or equivalent merit

meta.overwritten_from_source: source dropped the factor 9 before the integral of e^{t^2/5}; restored (P=218 unchanged)

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $P=218$ when $t=4$. Substitute into $P=Ate^{-0.05t}-100$:
$$\begin{aligned}218&=A(4)e^{-0.05\times4}-100\\318&=4Ae^{-0.2}\\A&=\dfrac{318}{4e^{-0.2}}\\&=97.10151927\ldots\\&\approx97\end{aligned}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: source bracket enclosed -100: 218=A(4)(e^{-0.2}-100); now 218=4Ae^{-0.2}-100 (A=97 unchanged)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=t & v&=e^{-0.05t}\\u'&=1 & v'&=-0.05e^{-0.05t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P&=97te^{-0.05t}-100\\P'&=97\left(1\times e^{-0.05t}-0.05te^{-0.05t}\right)\\&=97e^{-0.05t}(1-0.05t)\end{aligned}$$
For a maximum, $P'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}97e^{-0.05t}(1-0.05t)&=0\\e^{-0.05t}\left(1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-0.05t}\ne0$, $1-\dfrac{t}{20}=0$, so $t=20$.

Since $97e^{-0.05t}>0$, the factor $1-0.05t$ decides the sign of $P'$. Test either side of $t=20$:

\extable{Ts2365_1}

$\therefore\ t=20$ is a maximum.

When $t=20$:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=97(20)e^{-1}-100\\&=613.6861159\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum population}=613$$

parts.latex: Consider the function $f(x)=|x+2|+1$. Which of the following is a true statement?

dif.r: recognise corner of absolute value graph

options.label: A
options.latex: The function is continuous and differentiable for every value of $x$.

options.label: B
options.latex: The function is not continuous but differentiable for every value of $x$.

options.label: C
options.latex: The function is not continuous and not differentiable for every value of $x$.

options.label: D
options.latex: The function is continuous but not differentiable for every value of $x$.

solutions.latex:
$f(x)=|x+2|+1$ is the graph of $y=|x|$ translated 2 units left and 1 unit up.

It has no breaks, so it is continuous for every $x$.

It has a sharp corner at $x=-2$, so it is not differentiable at $x=-2$.

Hence $f$ is continuous everywhere but not differentiable everywhere.

parts.latex: Consider the function $f(x)=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)$. Which of the following describes $f(x)$?

dif.r: Proving oddness needs a non-obvious rationalisation of f(-x); also monotonicity reasoning.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f(-x)&=\ln\left(\sqrt{x^2+1}-x\right)\\&=\ln\dfrac{(x^2+1)-x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1}+x}\\&=\ln\dfrac{1}{x+\sqrt{x^2+1}}\\&=-\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)\\&=-f(x)\end{aligned}$$
So $f$ is odd.

$x+\sqrt{x^2+1}$ is increasing, so $f$ is increasing and therefore one-to-one.

Hence $f$ is an odd one-to-one function.

parts.latex: For what values of $k$ does the quadratic equation $x^2+kx-2k=0$ have real roots?

dif.r: discriminant >= 0 gives quadratic inequality in k

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
The equation has real roots when $\Delta\ge0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta&=k^2-4(1)(-2k)\\&=k^2+8k\\&=k(k+8)\ge0\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}k&\le-8 &&\text{(both factors negative or zero)}\\k&\ge0 &&\text{(both factors positive or zero)}\end{aligned}$$
So $k\in(-\infty,-8]\cup[0,\infty)$, with the end points included because $\Delta=0$ gives a repeated real root.

parts.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are events such that:

$$P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{2}{5}\quad\text{and}\quad P(A\cap B')=\dfrac{3}{7}$$

Which of the following is the value of $P(B'|A)$ ?

dif.r: P(A) from two intersections, then conditional

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
$$P(A)=P(A\cap B)+P(A\cap B')=\dfrac{2}{5}+\dfrac{3}{7}=\dfrac{29}{35}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P(B'\mid A)&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B')}{P(A)}\\&=\dfrac{3}{7}\div\dfrac{29}{35}\\&=\dfrac{15}{29}\end{aligned}$$

dif.r: MCQ: E(X) range from parameter constraints; table unseen

A.note: E(X) range with parameter b in [0,0.2]; Global maxima tag is a judgement

B.note: E(X)=5b^2+8b-0.8 bounded on 0<=b<=0.2 (from probabilities >=0); monotonicity by calculus or parabola

Global maxima and minima.evidence: This is increasing for 0≤b≤0.2 ... E(X)=−0.8 at b=0
Global maxima and minima.reason: Calculus endpoint check is one method; quadratic vertex outside the interval or option checking also works.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned}a+b+b+2b+0.2&=1\\a&=0.8-4b\end{aligned}$$
Since $b\ge0$ and $a\ge0$, we have $0\le b\le0.2$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-2a+0\times b+b\times b+2b\times2b+4\times0.2\\&=-2(0.8-4b)+5b^2+0.8\\&=5b^2+8b-0.8\end{aligned}$$
This is increasing for $0\le b\le0.2$ (its derivative $10b+8$ is positive):
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-0.8 &&\text{at } b=0\\E(X)&=1 &&\text{at } b=0.2\end{aligned}$$
Hence $-0.8\le E(X)\le1$.

parts.latex:
The graph of a function $f$ is obtained when the graph of function $g$ with the rule $g(x)=x^2-3x-10$ is translated by 7 units in the vertical direction followed by a reflection across the $y$-axis.

Which of the following is the rule for the function $f$?

dif.r: vertical shift then y-axis reflection of quadratic

Reflections of graphs.evidence: Reflecting in the y-axis replaces x with -x

solutions.latex:
Translating up 7 units:
$$x^2-3x-10+7=x^2-3x-3$$
Reflecting in the $y$-axis replaces $x$ with $-x$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=(-x)^2-3(-x)-3\\&=x^2+3x-3\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: If $\displaystyle\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx=8$, to which of the following is $\displaystyle\int_4^8 2f(x-2)\,dx$ equal?

dif.r: MCQ: translation and dilation of integral

solutions.latex:
Let $u=x-2$. When $x=4$, $u=2$; when $x=8$, $u=6$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_4^82f(x-2)\,dx&=2\int_2^6f(u)\,du\\&=2\times8\\&=16\end{aligned}$$

Katie has deliberately designed a biased six-sided die with the following probability distribution for $X$, the number showing on the uppermost face when the die is rolled.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What values of $\theta$ allow for $P(X)$ to be a probability distribution function?

dif.r: use 0<=P<=1 on each probability to bound theta

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(1\le X\le 4)$ in terms of $\theta$.

dif.r: add four expressions in theta

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the probability of rolling an even number in terms of $\theta$.

dif.r: add three expressions in theta

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1 for every $\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sum P(X=x)&=\dfrac{3(1-\theta)}{6}+\dfrac{3(1+\theta)}{6}\\&=1\end{aligned}$$
So this gives no restriction on $\theta$.

Each probability must also satisfy $0\le P(X=x)\le1$:
$$\begin{aligned}0\le\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}\le1 &&\text{gives}&& -5\le\theta\le1\\0\le\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}\le1 &&\text{gives}&& -1\le\theta\le5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -1\le\theta\le1$$
criteria: Solves both inequalities $0\le P(X=x)\le1$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: $-1\le\theta\le 1$. Must show $\sum P(X=x)=1$. Many students wrote $-1<\theta<1$ (incorrect).
meta.marker_note: Must show $\sum P(X=x)=1$. Many students wrote $-1<\theta<1$ (incorrect).

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}P(1\le X\le4)&=\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}\\&=\dfrac{4-2\theta}{6}\\&=\dfrac{2-\theta}{3}\end{aligned}$$

The even outcomes are $2$, $4$ and $6$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(X\text{ even})&=\dfrac{1-\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}+\dfrac{1+\theta}{6}\\&=\dfrac{3+\theta}{6}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Janet and Alan are playing a tennis match. The probability of Janet winning the first set is 0.3. After that, Janet’s probability of winning a set is 0.6 if she won the previous set, or 0.4 if she lost the previous set. The match will continue until either Janet or Alan wins two sets.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Draw a probability tree diagram to describe the match.

dif.r: model dependent set probabilities as a tree

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the expected value of the number of sets that the match will last.

dif.r: build distribution of match length from tree, E(X)

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the probability that Alan wins, given the match lasted 3 sets.

dif.r: conditional probability on three-set branches

figures.cap: solution sketch: probability tree for three sets with outcome probabilities JJ 0.18, JAJ 0.048, JAA 0.072, AJJ 0.168, AJA 0.112, AA 0.42

criteria: Tree diagram correct to the 2nd set, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: tree diagram correct to the 3rd set

solutions.latex:
Let $X$ be the number of sets.
$$\begin{aligned}P(X=2)&=0.18+0.42=0.6\\P(X=3)&=0.4\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=2\times0.6+3\times0.4\\&=2.4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Probability distribution for $X$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Alan wins in 3 sets by $JAA$ or $AJA$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{A wins}\mid3\text{ sets})&=\dfrac{0.072+0.112}{0.048+0.072+0.168+0.112}\\&=\dfrac{0.184}{0.4}\\&=0.46\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Two sectors $A_1$ and $A_2$ are constructed along the interval $AC$. $AO=4$ and $OC=3$ as shown in the diagram below.

parts.latex: If the area of $A_1$ is twice the area of $A_2$, find the value of $\theta$.

dif.r: set up sector-area equation with pi-theta, solve

figures.cap: semicircular sector A1 of radius 4 m (A to B) and sector A2 of radius 3 m (D to C) with angle theta at O

solutions.latex:
Sector area $=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, and $A_1=2A_2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{2}(4)^2(\pi-\theta)&=2\times\dfrac{1}{2}(3)^2\theta\\8(\pi-\theta)&=9\theta\\17\theta&=8\pi\\\theta&=\dfrac{8\pi}{17}\end{aligned}$$
This is $84^\circ42'$, or $84.71^\circ$.
criteria: Correct equation using the sector area formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove: $\dfrac{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}{\tan x+\sin x}=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x$

dif.r: compound fractions in cot/cosec, factorise and cancel 1+cos x

solutions.latex:
Method 1: multiply the numerator and denominator by $\sin x\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}+\frac{1}{\sin x}}{\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}+\frac{\sin x}{1}}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x(\cos x+1)}{\sin^2x+\sin^2x\cos x}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x(1+\cos x)}{\sin^2x(1+\cos x)}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: write the numerator using $\cot x=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan x}+\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right)\times\dfrac{1}{\tan x+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x+\tan x}{\tan x\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\tan x+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct simplification of the compound fraction, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $2\cos^2 x-3\cos x=2$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: quadratic in cos x, reject cos=2, two exact solutions

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to a quadratic in $\cos x$ and factorise:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2x-3\cos x-2&=0\\(2\cos x+1)(\cos x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos x=2$.

$\cos x=2$ has no solution, since $-1\le\cos x\le1$.

For $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ the related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is negative in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Factorises to $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ (rejecting $\cos x=2$), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $3\sin x+\sqrt{3}\cos x=0$ over the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: divide by cos to get tan equation, two quadrants

solutions.latex:
Divide both sides by $\cos x$:
$$\begin{aligned}3\sin x&=-\sqrt{3}\cos x\\3\tan x&=-\sqrt{3}\\\tan x&=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and tangent is negative in the 2nd and 4th quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
criteria: One correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Write expressions for $AD$ and $BD$ in terms of $h$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the exact value of $h$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: Combine Pythagoras and cosine rule with algebraic sides; solve quadratic exactly.

figures.cap: circle centre O on a vertical wall; A below O at height h, B on the circle with angle AOB = 90 degrees; D on the ground with elevations 30 and 60 degrees and angle ADB = 30 degrees (not to scale)

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle with the angle of elevation $30^\circ$ at $D$ and height $h$ at $A$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin30^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{AD}\\AD&=\dfrac{h}{\sin30^\circ}=2h\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is $10$ m above $A$ and $OB$ is horizontal, so $B$ is $h+10$ m above the ground:
$$BD=\dfrac{h+10}{\sin60^\circ}=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$$
criteria: One correct expression, $AD=2h$ or $BD=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle OAB$, $OA=OB=10$ and $\angle AOB=90^\circ$, so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$AB=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt{2}$$
In $\triangle ABD$, use the cosine rule with $\angle ADB=30^\circ$:
$$\left(10\sqrt{2}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+(2h)^2-2\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)(2h)\cos30^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned}200&=\dfrac{4h^2+80h+400}{3}+4h^2-4h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2+80h+400+12h^2-12h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2-40h+400\\0&=4h^2-40h-200\\&=4\left(h^2-10h-50\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$h=\dfrac{10\pm\sqrt{300}}{2}=5\pm5\sqrt{3}$$
Since $h>0$:
$$\therefore\ h=5+5\sqrt{3}\approx13.66$$
criteria: Correct quadratic equation in $h$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the curve $y=x^3-6x^2+7$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: differentiate cubic, solve, second derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any points of inflexion.

dif.r: y''=0 linear, check concavity change

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the graph, clearly showing all the points found in (a) and (b) and $y$-intercepts. You do NOT need to find $x$-intercepts.

dif.r: sketch from points already found

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = x^3 - 6x^2 + 7 with maximum (0,7), inflexion point and minimum (4,-25)

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3x^2-12x&=0\\3x(x-4)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}y(0)&=7\\y(4)&=64-96+7=-25\end{aligned}$$
Use the second derivative, $y''=6x-12$:
$$\begin{aligned}y''(0)&=-12<0 &&\text{maximum at } (0,7)\\y''(4)&=12>0 &&\text{minimum at } (4,-25)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Appropriate method for determining the nature and finding the $y$-coordinates, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For a point of inflexion, $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}6x-12&=0\\x&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$y(2)=8-24+7=-9$$
Test the concavity either side of $x=2$:

\extable{Ts2391_1}

The concavity changes at $x=2$, so there is a point of inflexion at $(2,-9)$.
\exfigure{355_q17_s1}
criteria: All points from (a) and (b) marked with the general cubic shape, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Differentiate $xe^{5x}$ with respect to $x$.

dif.r: direct product rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{10} 5xe^{5x}\,dx$

dif.r: add/subtract e^5x to use (a), exact evaluation

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=e^{5x}\\u'&=1 & v'&=5e^{5x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{5x}\right)&=e^{5x}+x\cdot5e^{5x}\\&=e^{5x}(5x+1)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: One correct term of the product rule, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct derivative (1 per correct term of the product rule)

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $5xe^{5x}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{5x}\right)-e^{5x}$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{10}5xe^{5x}\,dx&=\int_0^{10}\left(5xe^{5x}+e^{5x}-e^{5x}\right)dx\\&=\left[xe^{5x}-\dfrac{e^{5x}}{5}\right]_0^{10}\\&=10e^{50}-\dfrac{e^{50}}{5}-\left(0-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)\\&=\dfrac{49e^{50}+1}{5}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the result from (a), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $f(x)=x^2-4x+5$ from first principles.

dif.r: first principles on quadratic, full working

solutions.latex:
From first principles:
$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{(x+h)^2-4(x+h)+5-\left(x^2-4x+5\right)}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{(x+h-x)(x+h+x)-4h}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{h(2x+h)-4h}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to0}(2x+h-4)\\&=2x-4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expands and simplifies, or equivalent merit
Correct substitution into the first principles definition, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle travelling on the $x$ axis is given by $v(t)=\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $t\ge 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the particle is stationary when $t=1$.

dif.r: substitute t=1

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Explain why the particle is moving to the left for all times $t>1$.

dif.r: a<0 so v decreasing from v(1)=0; explain

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds, correct to one decimal place.

dif.r: split at t=1, integrate 1/(t+1), log evaluation

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}v(1)&=\dfrac{1}{1+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
So the particle is stationary at $t=1$.

meta.top_criterion_original: must show substitution AND concluding statement
meta.marker_note: Must show the substitution and a concluding statement.

solutions.latex:
$$a(t)=v'(t)=-\dfrac{1}{(t+1)^2}$$
$a(t)<0$ for all $t\ge0$, so $v$ is decreasing.

Since $v(1)=0$ and $v$ is decreasing, $v<0$ for all $t>1$, so the particle always moves to the left for $t>1$.
criteria: Mathematical reasoning, e.g. finding $a(t)$ or use of inequalities, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$v(0)=\dfrac{1}{2}>0$, $v(1)=0$ and $v$ is decreasing, so the direction changes at $t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving right}\\v&<0 &&\text{for } t>1 &&\text{moving left}\end{aligned}$$
So the distance is
$$d=\int_0^1\left(\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt+\left|\int_1^3\left(\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\left[\ln|t+1|-\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_0^1+\left|\left[\ln|t+1|-\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_1^3\right|\\&=\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}-(0-0)+\left|\ln4-\dfrac{3}{2}-\ln2+\dfrac{1}{2}\right|\\&=\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}+\ln2-\ln4+1\\&=\ln\dfrac{2\times2}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The distance travelled is $0.5$ m.

meta.top_criterion_original: correct substitution and answer. No marks awarded if the integrated expression has no logs.
meta.marker_note: No marks are awarded if the integrated expression has no logs.

questions.stem:
The curves $y=e^{-x}$ and $y=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{4}$ intersect at the point $P$ as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{355_q21_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the point of intersection, $P$, is $\left(\ln 4,\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$.

dif.r: verify intersection with log/exponent laws

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the area bounded by the two curves and the $y$-axis, as shaded in the diagram.

dif.r: exponential area to ln4, exact evaluation

figures.cap: graphs of y = e^{-x} and y = e^{-x/2} - 1/4 meeting at P, region between them and the y-axis shaded

solutions.latex:
At the intersection, $e^{-x}=e^{-\frac{x}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{4}$.

Multiply both sides by $4e^{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=4e^{\frac{x}{2}}-e^{x}\\e^{x}-4e^{\frac{x}{2}}+4&=0\\\left(e^{\frac{x}{2}}-2\right)^2&=0\\e^{\frac{x}{2}}&=2\\\dfrac{x}{2}&=\ln2\\x&=\ln4\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into $y=e^{-x}$:
$$y=e^{-\ln4}=\dfrac{1}{4}$$
So $P$ is $\left(\ln4,\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$.

meta.top_criterion_original: clear working (substitution method allowed). Common mistake: $\ln\dfrac{1}{4}=\ln e^{-x}-\ln e^{-\frac{x}{2}}$.
meta.marker_note: Clear working is required (substitution method allowed). Common mistake: $\ln\dfrac{1}{4}=\ln e^{-x}-\ln e^{-\frac{x}{2}}$.

solutions.latex:

$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{\ln4-1}{4}\text{ units}^2\ (\approx0.097)$$

questions.stem:
A discrete random variable has a probability distribution as shown in the table below where $n$ is a finite, positive integer and $r$ is any real number other than 1.

\extable{355_q23_t1}

parts.latex: Show that $E(X)=n(2r-1)$.

dif.r: twin of 2021 HSC Q34: GP sum condition then general E(X)

solutions.latex:
Each term of $E(X)$ is $x\times P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=r\cdot r^n+r^2\cdot r^{n-1}+r^3\cdot r^{n-2}+\cdots\\&\quad+r^k\cdot r^{n-k+1}+\cdots+r^n\cdot r\\&=r^{n+1}+r^{n+1}+\cdots+r^{n+1}\\&=nr^{n+1} &&(1)\end{aligned}$$
The probabilities sum to 1, and they form a geometric series with first term $r$, common ratio $r$ and $n$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned}r^n+r^{n-1}+r^{n-2}+\cdots+r&=1\\\dfrac{r(r^n-1)}{r-1}&=1\\r^{n+1}-r&=r-1\\r^{n+1}&=2r-1\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$E(X)=n(2r-1)\quad\text{as required}$$
criteria: $\sum P(X=x)=1$ with working, e.g. recognising the GP, or equivalent merit
Correct expression for $E(X)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider $f(x)=\ln\left[\cos(3x)\right]$ where $-\dfrac{\pi}{6}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $f'(x)$ in simplest form.

dif.r: chain rule ln(cos3x) to -3tan3x

parts.label: b
parts.latex:

$y=6x+1-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.latex:
Find the area bound by the curve $y=\tan 3x$, the tangent and the $x$ axis.

Give your answer correct to four decimal places.

dif.r: tan3x primitive via (a), curve area minus triangle

A.note: model solution uses part (a) result and a triangle; not stated as hence

B.note: Area under tan3x minus a triangle; primitive taken from (a) (or tan as f'/f)

Integration using a given derivative.evidence: Using d/dx ln cos3x=−3tan3x from part (a)

Integrals giving logarithms.reason: ∫tan3x as f'/f is an alternative to reversing part (a).

figures.cap: solution sketch: y = tan 3x and tangent y = 6x + 1 - pi/2 with the bounded region shaded, x-intercepts pi/12 - 1/6 and pi/12

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with $u=\cos3x$:
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{-3\sin3x}{\cos3x}=-3\tan3x$$

When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$:
$$y=\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{12}=\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}=1$$
so the point is $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12},1\right)$.
$$y'=3\sec^23x$$
The gradient at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ is
$$m_T=3\sec^2\dfrac{\pi}{4}=3\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^2=6$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-1&=6\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)\\y-1&=6x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\y&=6x+1-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$$

The $x$-intercept is where $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}6x+1-\dfrac{\pi}{2}&=0\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}-\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: correct answer ($\dfrac{\frac{\pi}{2}-1}{6}$ accepted, simplified version preferred)
meta.marker_note: The equivalent form $\dfrac{\frac{\pi}{2}-1}{6}$ is accepted; the simplified version is preferred.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{355_q24_s1}

The area is the area under the curve from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$, minus the triangle between the tangent, the $x$-axis and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ (base $\dfrac{1}{6}$, height $1$):
$$A=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{12}}\tan3x\,dx-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}-\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}-\dfrac{1}{6}\right)\right)(1)$$
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\cos3x=-3\tan3x$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned}A&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{12}}-3\tan3x\,dx-\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)(1)\\&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\Big[\ln\cos3x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{12}}-\dfrac{1}{12}\\&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\dfrac{1}{12}\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\sqrt{2}-\dfrac{1}{12}\\&=0.032191\ldots\\&\approx0.0322\text{ (4 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows $\ln\cos3x$ from part (a), or equivalent merit
Correct expression (integral minus triangle), or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The depth of the water in a harbour changes due to the tides and can be modelled with the equation $d=12+4\cos\left(\dfrac{t}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, where $d$ is the depth of the harbour in metres and $t$ is the number of hours since midnight on Tuesday morning.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Draw a neat sketch of the depth of the water $d$ for $t\in[0,6\pi]$.

dif.r: sketch: factor phase shift, period 6pi, amplitude about centre

parts.label: b
parts.latex: A boat needs 10 metres of water to be operated in the harbour, although if it motors out of the harbour, the water is always deep enough to operate. The boat uses 6 litres of petrol every hour that it is being used. If the boat is launched at 7:30 AM and leaves the harbour, and it takes 12 minutes to motor each way in and out of the harbour, what is the minimum amount of petrol that the boat must hold to make it back to its starting point? Answer to the nearest litre.

dif.r: multi-stage context: solve cos, pick window, travel times, fuel

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of d = 12 + 4cos(t/3 - pi/6) for t from 0 to 6pi: max (pi/2, 16), min (7pi/2, 8), endpoints at 12 + 2sqrt3

solutions.latex:
$$d=12+4\cos\left(\dfrac{t}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=12+4\cos\dfrac{1}{3}\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$$
The amplitude is 4 about the centre line $d=12$, so $8\le d\le16$.
$$\text{Period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{1}{3}}=6\pi$$
\exfigure{355_q25_s1}
criteria: Two of: correct minimum and maximum (both coordinates clearly labelled), correct shape, both end points, or equivalent merit
One of: correct minimum and maximum (both coordinates clearly labelled), correct shape, both end points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The boat can operate when the depth is at least 10 m. Find when $d=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}12+4\cos\left(\dfrac{t}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)&=10\\\cos\left(\dfrac{t}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{t}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{3},\ \ldots$$
Multiply by 3 and add $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}&=2\pi,\ 4\pi,\ 8\pi,\ 10\pi,\ \ldots\\t&=\dfrac{5\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{9\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{21\pi}{2},\ \ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$t=7.85\ldots,\ 14.137\ldots$$
which are 7:51 am and 2:08 pm.

The boat can re-enter the harbour at 2:08 pm, and returns to the dock at 2:20 pm.

It needs fuel from 7:30 am to 2:20 pm, which is 6 h 50 min:
$$6\dfrac{5}{6}\times6=41\text{ L (minimum)}$$
criteria: Explanation: re-enters the harbour at 2:08 pm and docks at 2:20 pm, or equivalent merit

A long rectangular sheet of metal 28cm wide is to be made into a gutter by turning up sides of equal height $x$cm, perpendicular to the base as shown below:

\exfigure{355_q27_1}

parts.label: a

$$A=28x-2x^2$$

dif.r: base 28-2x times height

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Explain why this formula is only valid for $x\in(0,14)$.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the maximum value of $A$.

dif.r: vertex of simple quadratic via derivative

figures.cap: gutter formed from a 28 cm wide sheet with sides of height x cm turned up; cross-section A shaded

solutions.latex:
Turning up two sides of height $x$ leaves a base of
$$28-x-x=28-2x$$
and the cross-section is a rectangle of height $x$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=x(28-2x)\\&=28x-2x^2\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: At least two steps must be shown.

solutions.latex:
The height $x$ must be positive, and the base $28-2x$ must be positive:
$$\begin{aligned}x&>0 &&\text{if } x=0 \text{ there is no height}\\28-2x&>0 &&\text{if } x=14 \text{ there is no base, so } x<14\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x\in(0,14)$$

meta.top_criterion_original: clear explanation for both $x=0$ and $x=14$ (e.g. $A>0$ using the parabola, and $x>0$); $-1$ if only one end of the domain discussed
meta.marker_note: Both ends of the domain must be explained, e.g. $A>0$ using the parabola and $x>0$; $-1$ if only one end is discussed.

solutions.latex:
For the maximum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}28-4x&=0\\x&=7\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=-4<0$$
so there is a maximum at $x=7$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\max}&=7(28-14)\\&=98\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Tests the nature at $x=7$ (second derivative or relating to a parabola), or equivalent merit

parts.label: c
parts.latex: People can swim in the lake once the amount of the toxic substance is less than 50. In how many years can this happen, to the nearest year?

dif.r: exponential inequality solved with logs

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=6$ and $A=2400$:
$$\begin{aligned}2400&=3000m^{-0.2(6)}\\\dfrac{4}{5}&=m^{-\frac{6}{5}}\\m&=\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{-\frac{5}{6}}\\&=1.2\text{ (1 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Some students gave $0.8$.

solutions.latex:
With $m=1.2$, $A(t)=3000(1.2)^{-0.2t}$. Fish can be reintroduced when $A'(t)>-20$:
$$\begin{aligned}3000\ln(1.2)\times(-0.2)(1.2)^{-0.2t}&>-20\\-600\ln(1.2)(1.2)^{-0.2t}&>-20\\(1.2)^{-0.2t}&<\dfrac{1}{30\ln1.2}\end{aligned}$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}-0.2t\ln1.2&<-\ln(30\ln1.2)\\t&>\dfrac{\ln(30\ln1.2)}{0.2\ln1.2}\\&=46.5993724\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Fish can be reintroduced after $46.6$ years (1 d.p.).
criteria: Correct change of base or similar operation, or equivalent merit
Writes $A'(t)>-20$ with the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned}3000(1.2)^{-0.2t}&<50\\-0.2t\ln1.2&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{60}\right)\\t&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{60}\right)}{-0.2\ln1.2}\\&=112.283611\ldots\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln 2)\sqrt{x^3}} & \text{for } k\le x\le 8\\[2ex] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \text{ in } \mathbb{R}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$. Leave your answer as an exact value.

dif.r: simplify pdf, log base 2 integral, solve for lower limit

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the median value of $X$ as an exact value.

dif.r: median from log integral with surd limit, exact

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

req: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf
A.note: median from integral of pdf = 0.5; CDF tag is a judgement

req: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

Cumulative distribution functions.reason: No cdf is found or used; the pdf is integrated directly to 0.5 (Median skill, agreed).

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^3}}=\dfrac{1}{x}$, the density is $\dfrac{3}{2(\ln2)x}$, and
$$\int\dfrac{3}{2(\ln2)x}\,dx=\dfrac{3}{2}\log_2x=\log_2\sqrt{x^3}$$
The total probability is 1:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_k^8\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln2)\sqrt{x^3}}\,dx&=1\\\left[\log_2\sqrt{x^3}\right]_k^8&=1\\\log_2\sqrt{8^3}-\log_2\sqrt{k^3}&=\log_22\\\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{8}{k}\right)^3}&=2\\\dfrac{8}{k}&=\sqrt[3]{4}\\k&=\dfrac{8}{\sqrt[3]{4}}=4\sqrt[3]{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integral of $f(x)$ from $k$ to $8$ equal to $1$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Variants accepted: $\sqrt[3]{2^7}$, $\dfrac{8}{2^{2/3}}$, $e^{\frac{\ln128}{3}}$, $\approx5.03968$.

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_k^mf(x)\,dx=0.5$, with $k=4\sqrt[3]{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{4\sqrt[3]{2}}^{m}\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2(\ln2)\sqrt{x^3}}\,dx&=0.5\\\log_2\sqrt{m^3}-\log_2\sqrt{\left(4\sqrt[3]{2}\right)^3}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\\log_2m^3-\log_2\left(2\times4^3\right)&=\log_22\\\dfrac{m^3}{2\times4^3}&=2\\m&=4\sqrt[3]{4}\end{aligned}$$
The median value is $4\sqrt[3]{4}\approx6.3496$.
criteria: Integral from $k$ to $m$ equal to $0.5$, or equivalent merit

The graph touches the $x$-axis at $x=-2$ (double root) and crosses at $x=1$ and $x=3$, so the factors are $(x+2)^2$, $(x-1)$ and $(x-3)$, up to sign.

Both ends of the graph go down, so the leading coefficient is negative and the last factor must be $(3-x)$.
$$y=(x+2)^2(x-1)(3-x)$$
The other options fail: one has a positive leading coefficient, one has a root at $x=-3$ and one touches the axis at $x=1$ instead of $x=-2$.

dif.r: MCQ: quotient rule from table; twin of 2022 Q5

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=f(x) & v&=g(x) \\ u'&=f'(x) & v'&=g'(x) \end{aligned}$$
From the table, at $x=2$: $f(2)=4$, $f'(2)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $g(2)=-2$, $g'(2)=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} h'(2)&=\dfrac{f'(2)g(2)-f(2)g'(2)}{[g(2)]^2} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}(-2)-4(2)}{(-2)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{-1-8}{4} \\ &=-\dfrac{9}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent is $-\dfrac{9}{4}$.

parts.latex:
A function $f(x)$ is such that

$$\int_{-k}^{k}f(x)\,dx=2\int_{0}^{k}f(x)\,dx$$

Which of the following could $f(x)$ be?

dif.r: MCQ: recognise even function

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The condition is
$$\int_{-k}^{k}f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^k f(x)\,dx$$
This holds when $f$ is an even function, $f(-x)=f(x)$, because the areas on either side of the $y$-axis are equal.

$\cos 2x$ is even, whereas $\sin 2x$, $\tan 2x$ and $\operatorname{cosec}2x$ are odd.

So $f(x)=\cos 2x$ is the function that could satisfy the condition.

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3(2x+1)^2\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2\times3}\Big[(2x+1)^3\Big]_1^3 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\left[(2\times3+1)^3-(2+1)^3\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}(343-27) \\ &=\dfrac{158}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Given that $E(X)=2.5$, find $a$ and $b$.

\extable{361_q14_t1}

dif.r: sum to 1 and E(X)=2.5 simultaneous equations

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} a+b+0.5&=1 \\ a+b&=0.5 &&(1) \end{aligned}$$
Using $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)=2.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.3+2a+3b+4\times0.2&=2.5 \\ 2a+3b&=1.4 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
From (1), $b=0.5-a$. Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 2a+3(0.5-a)&=1.4 \\ 2a+1.5-3a&=1.4 \\ -a&=-0.1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore a=0.1,\ b=0.4$$
criteria: Correct setting for two equations, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The first term of an arithmetic series is 7, the common difference is 2 and the sum of the first $n$ terms is 247. Find the value of $n$.

dif.r: quadratic in n from S_n=247

solutions.latex:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$ with $a=7$ and $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\times247&=n\left(14+2(n-1)\right) \\ 494&=14n+2n^2-2n \\ 2n^2+12n-494&=0 \\ n^2+6n-247&=0 \\ (n+19)(n-13)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $n=-19$ or $n=13$. The number of terms is positive, so
$$\therefore n=13$$

questions.stem: A population of bacteria is modelled by the function $P(t)=P_0\times e^{kt}$, where $P(t)$ is the population at time $t$ (in hours), $P_0$ is the initial population, and $k$ is the constant growth rate.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that the initial population $P_0$ is 100 bacteria and the population triples every 4 hours, show that value of $k=\dfrac{\ln 3}{4}$.

dif.r: tripling gives e^(4k)=3, take logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the population of bacteria after 12 hours.

dif.r: substitute t=12

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the time it takes for the population to reach 100,000 bacteria. Leave your answer to the nearest minute.

dif.r: solve exponential with logs, convert to minutes

solutions.latex:
The population triples every $4$ hours, so $P(4)=3\times100=300$:
$$\begin{aligned} 300&=100e^{4k} \\ 3&=e^{4k} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k=\dfrac{\ln 3}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(12)&=100e^{12\times\frac{\ln 3}{4}} \\ &=100\times e^{\ln 3^3} \\ &=2700 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

Setting $P(t)=100\,000$ and using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 100\,000&=100e^{\frac{t\ln 3}{4}} \\ 1000&=e^{\ln 3^{\frac{t}{4}}} \\ 1000&=3^{\frac{t}{4}} \\ \dfrac{t}{4}&=\log_3 1000 \\ t&=\dfrac{4\ln 1000}{\ln 3} \\ &\approx25.15 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
Converting the decimal part to minutes:
$$\begin{aligned} t&\approx25+0.15\times60 \\ &=25 \text{ hours } 9 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given the function $f(x)=2x^3-\dfrac{5}{2}x^2-4x+2$. Determine the interval(s) where $f(x)$ is decreasing.

dif.r: differentiate cubic, factorise, quadratic inequality

A.note: quadratic solve is assumed algebra; solution also classifies stationary points but f'<0 suffices

B.note: Solution classifies with f'' but only the sign of f' is needed; f'(x)<0 is a quadratic inequality.

Quadratic inequalities.reason: Answer is the solution of a quadratic inequality.

solutions.latex:
Decreasing where $f'(x)<0$. Find the stationary points:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-5x-4 \\ f'(x)=0:\ x&=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{25+4\times6\times4}}{12} \\ &=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{121}}{12} \\ &=\dfrac{5\pm11}{12} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{4}{3} \text{ or } x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$$
Test the nature using $f''(x)=12x-5$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=-6-5=-11<0 &&\text{maximum} \\ f''\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)&=16-5=11>0 &&\text{minimum} \end{aligned}$$
So $f(x)$ is decreasing between the maximum and the minimum:
$$-\dfrac{1}{2}<x<\dfrac{4}{3}$$
criteria: Correctly determines the nature of the stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points with working, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Given the following two functions $f(x)=x^2-3$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{2-x}$.

Find the domain and range of $f(g(x))$.

dif.r: composite simplifies; range must use restricted domain

solutions.latex:
Substitute $g(x)=\sqrt{2-x}$ into $f(x)=x^2-3$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(g(x))&=\left(\sqrt{2-x}\right)^2-3 \\ &=2-x-3 \\ &=-x-1 \end{aligned}$$
The square root needs $2-x\ge0$, so the domain is $x\le2$.

For the range, work from the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} x&\le2 \\ -x&\ge-2 &&(\text{multiply by } -1) \\ -x-1&\ge-3 &&(\text{subtract } 1) \end{aligned}$$
So the range is $[-3,\infty)$.
criteria: Correct composite function, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Prove

$$\dfrac{\sec^2(2\theta)}{\sec^2(2\theta)-1}=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta).$$

dif.r: routine identity proof via Pythagorean identities

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, solve $\dfrac{\sec^2(2\theta)}{\sec^2(2\theta)-1}=2$ where $0\le\theta\le\pi$.

dif.r: hence cosec^2=2, plus/minus roots, doubled domain, four solutions

solutions.latex:
Using $\sec^2(2\theta)=\tan^2(2\theta)+1$, so that $\sec^2(2\theta)-1=\tan^2(2\theta)$, and $1+\cot^2(2\theta)=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\tan^2(2\theta)+1}{\tan^2(2\theta)} \\ &=1+\dfrac{1}{\tan^2(2\theta)} \\ &=1+\cot^2(2\theta) \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta) \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, writing $\sec$ in terms of $\cos$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}}{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}-1} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\cos^2(2\theta)}}{\frac{1-\cos^2(2\theta)}{\cos^2(2\theta)}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\cos^2(2\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2(2\theta)} \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta) \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses trigonometric identities to simplify the LHS to $1+\dfrac{1}{\tan^2 2\theta}$ or $\dfrac{1}{1-\cos^2 2\theta}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a) the equation becomes $\operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta)=2$. The domain is
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le\theta\le\pi \\ 0&\le2\theta\le2\pi &&(\text{multiply by } 2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{cosec}^2(2\theta)&=2 \\ \operatorname{cosec}(2\theta)&=\pm\sqrt{2} \\ \sin(2\theta)&=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so in $0\le2\theta\le2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \\ \theta&=\dfrac{\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{8},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{8} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Changes the domain to $0\le2\theta\le2\pi$, or equivalent merit
Uses part (a) to simplify the equation to $\sin(2\theta)=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: bearings diagram: P to Q 150 km on bearing 060 degrees, Q to R 200 km on bearing 160 degrees; 'Diagram not to scale'
solution sketch: bearings diagram annotated with 120 degrees and angle PQR = 80 degrees, PR joined

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{361_q23_s1}

The north lines at $P$ and $Q$ are parallel, so the bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $060^\circ+180^\circ=240^\circ$, and
$$\angle PQR=240^\circ-160^\circ=80^\circ$$
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle PQR$:
$$\begin{aligned} PR&=\sqrt{150^2+200^2-2(150)(200)\cos80^\circ} \\ &=228.21 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows that $\angle PQR=80^\circ$ or applies the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle PQR$ with $QR=200$:
$$\cos\angle QRP=\dfrac{200^2+PR^2-150^2}{2(200)(PR)}$$
so $\angle QRP=40.33800\ldots^\circ$.

The bearing of $Q$ from $R$ is $160^\circ+180^\circ=340^\circ$, and $P$ lies $\angle QRP$ anticlockwise from $Q$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing}&=360^\circ-20^\circ-\angle QRP \\ &=299.661\ldots^\circ \\ &=300^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows that $\angle QRP=40^\circ$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Solve the following equation:

$$x-2x^2+x^3-2x^4+x^5-2x^6+\cdots=-\dfrac{2}{5}$$

Where $-1\le x\le 1$

dif.r: group pairs into GP, S_inf eqn, quadratic, check domain

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Group the terms in pairs; each pair is a term of a geometric series:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=x-2x^2 \\ T_2&=x^3-2x^4 \\ T_3&=x^5-2x^6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} r&=\dfrac{x^3-2x^4}{x-2x^2} \\ &=\dfrac{x^3(1-2x)}{x(1-2x)} \\ &=x^2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $-1\le x\le1$, $r<1$, so the series has a limiting sum:
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{x-2x^2}{1-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x-2x^2}{1-x^2}&=-\dfrac{2}{5} \\ 5x-10x^2&=-2+2x^2 \\ 12x^2-5x-2&=0 \\ (3x-2)(4x+1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ or } x=-\dfrac{1}{4}$$
criteria: Correct limiting sum of the GP, or equivalent merit
Correct ratio with working, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and $y=2$ when $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, find $y$ in terms of $x$.

dif.r: trig primitive then constant from condition

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\int\cos\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)dx \\ &=\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, $y=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+C \\ 2&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+C \\ C&=1 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The quantity Q in mL of a certain chemical in the body varies during the day and is given by the formula $Q(t)=4+3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$

where $t$ measures hours from midnight.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the period in hours of the function Q.

dif.r: period 2pi/(pi/4)

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what time or times of the day is the quantity a minimum?

dif.r: locate minimum, repeat by period within the day

A.note: min where cos=-1, then period; solution uses Q'=0 as alternative

B.note: Minimum where cos=-1, repeated every period; solution's Q'(t)=0 is optional.

Trigonometric equations.reason: Minimum times can be read from the graph (as the solution does) or by solving cos(pi t/4) = -1; method free.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the minimum quantity of the chemical the body will contain?

dif.r: centre minus amplitude

parts.label: d
parts.latex: A hospital patient requires a pill to temporarily boost the amount of the chemical whenever the quantity in his body falls to 1.5 units. At what time will a nurse have to wake the patient to give him his first pill of the day? Give your answer to nearest minute.

dif.r: non-exact inverse cos, choose first time, convert to minutes

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of Q(t) from 7 at t=0 down to minimum 1 at t=4 and back to 7 at t=8

solutions.latex:
The period of $\cos(nt)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$; here $n=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} T&=\dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &=8 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{361_q30_s1}

The minimum occurs where $Q'(t)=0$, at $t=4$ hours. The period is $8$ hours, so the minimum recurs every $8$ hours:
$$t=4,\ 12,\ 20$$
that is, at 4 am, 12 pm and 8 pm.
criteria: Draws the graph, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} Q(4)&=4+3\cos\pi \\ &=4-3 \\ &=1 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$

Set $Q(t)=1.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1.5&=4+3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{2.5}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Cosine is negative, so take the second-quadrant angle (the first time the quantity falls to $1.5$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=\pi-\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right) \\ &=2.5559\ldots \\ t&=2.5559\ldots\times\dfrac{4}{\pi} \\ &=3.254\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So the nurse wakes the patient at $3$ h $15$ min, that is 3:15 am.

questions.stem: Given that $y=x^2\ln(x)$

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x\ln(x)+x$$

dif.r: direct product rule show

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence, show that

$$\int x\ln(x)\,dx=\dfrac{x^2\ln(x)}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{4}+C$$

dif.r: integrate (a), rearrange, halve for int x ln x

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln(x) \\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x\ln(x)+x^2\times\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &=2x\ln(x)+x \end{aligned}$$

Integrating the result of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \int\left(2x\ln(x)+x\right)dx&=x^2\ln(x) \\ 2\int x\ln(x)\,dx+\int x\,dx&=x^2\ln(x) \\ 2\int x\ln(x)\,dx&=x^2\ln(x)-\int x\,dx \\ \int x\ln(x)\,dx&=\dfrac{x^2\ln(x)}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\int x\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{x^2\ln(x)}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{x^2}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{x^2\ln(x)}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{4}+C \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: The first two terms of an infinite geometric sequence are $T_1=20$ and $T_2=16\sin^2\theta$, where $0<\theta<2\pi$, $\theta\ne\pi$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the range of the ratio $(r)$ in this geometric sequence.

dif.r: range of r from sin^2 bounds

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By developing an expression for the sum of the infinite sequence, find the values of $\theta$ which give the greatest sum.

dif.r: maximise S_inf over theta; like 2024 Q30 reasoning

can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} r&=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} \\ &=\dfrac{16\sin^2\theta}{20} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{5}\sin^2\theta \end{aligned}$$
For $0<\theta<2\pi$ with $\theta\ne\pi$, $\sin\theta\ne0$, so $0<\sin^2\theta\le1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&<\sin^2\theta\le1 \\ 0&<\dfrac{4}{5}\sin^2\theta\le\dfrac{4}{5} &&\left(\text{multiply by } \dfrac{4}{5}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore 0<r\le\dfrac{4}{5}$$

meta.overwritten_from_source: source gave 0<r<=4/5 OR r in [0,4/5]; r=0 not attained (sin theta != 0), now 0<r<=4/5 only

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{20}{1-\frac{4}{5}\sin^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{20\times5}{5-4\sin^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{100}{5-4\sin^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=100 & v&=5-4\sin^2\theta \\ u'&=0 & v'&=-8\sin\theta\cos\theta \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dS}{d\theta}=\dfrac{-100\left(-8\sin\theta\cos\theta\right)}{\left(5-4\sin^2\theta\right)^2}$$
$\dfrac{dS}{d\theta}=0$ when $\sin\theta\cos\theta=0$. In the domain $\sin\theta\ne0$, so $\cos\theta=0$:
$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \text{ or } \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
Test the values of $S$ just either side of each:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\theta&\dfrac{\pi}{2}-0.01&\dfrac{\pi}{2}&\dfrac{\pi}{2}+0.01\\\hline S&99.96&100&99.96\end{array}$$
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\theta&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}-0.01&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+0.01\\\hline S&99.96&100&99.96\end{array}$$
$\therefore$ the sum is greatest at $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ or $\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

parts.latex:
A flood insurance company determines that N, the number of claims received in a month, is a random variable with

$$P(N=n)=\dfrac{2}{3^{n+1}},\ \text{for } n=0,1,2,\ldots.$$

The numbers of claims received in different months are independent.

In any consecutive two-month period, calculate the probability that more than one claim will be received, given that zero claims were received at least one of the two months.

dif.r: conditional on at least one zero month with discrete distribution

figures.cap: solution sketch: tree diagram for two months: zero claims probability 2/3, not zero claims 1/3

solutions.latex:
From $P(N=n)=\dfrac{2}{3^{n+1}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(N=0)&=\dfrac{2}{3} \\ P(N=1)&=\dfrac{2}{9} \\ P(N\ge2)&=\dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Solution 1:

\exfigure{361_q34_s1}
$$P(\text{at least one month with zero claims})=1-\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
More than one claim in total, given a zero month, means one month has zero claims and the other has $2$ or more:
$$\begin{aligned} P(N>1\mid\text{at least one zero month})&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{9}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{9}}{\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{4}{27}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Solution 2:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-\dfrac{P(0)P(0)+P(0)P(1)+P(1)P(0)}{P(0,0)+P(0,n)+P(n,0)} \\ &=1-\dfrac{\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2}{9}+\frac{2}{9}\times\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=1-\dfrac{\frac{4}{9}+\frac{8}{27}}{\frac{8}{9}} \\ &=1-\dfrac{5}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly recognises the sum of three combination events in the numerator, or equivalent merit

meta.checked_source_ok: verified: (4/27)/(8/9)=1/6 and 1-(20/27)/(8/9)=1/6; both clean restatements match the source answer

questions.stem: Melinda visits a bank and makes a single deposit of \$$Q$. The annual interest rate is 3.5%.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Melinda wishes to withdraw \$8000 at the end of each year for a period of $n$ years. Show that an expression for the minimum value of $Q$ is

$$\dfrac{8000}{1.035}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^2}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^3}+\cdots+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^n}$$

dif.r: A_n=0 then divide by 1.035^n to reach present-value sum

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the minimum value $Q$ that would permit Melinda to withdraw annual amounts of \$8000 indefinitely. Give your answer to the nearest dollar.

dif.r: recognise GP, indefinitely means limiting sum

solutions.latex:
Let $A_n$ be the balance after the $n$th withdrawal. Each year the balance is multiplied by $1.035$, then $\$8000$ is withdrawn:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=Q\times1.035-8000 \\ A_2&=A_1\times1.035-8000 \\ &=\left(Q\times1.035-8000\right)1.035-8000 \\ &=Q\times1.035^2-8000\times1.035-8000 \\ A_3&=A_2\times1.035-8000 \\ &=Q\times1.035^3-8000\times1.035^2-8000\times1.035-8000 \\ &=Q\times1.035^3-8000\left(1.035^2+1.035+1\right) \end{aligned}$$
Continuing the pattern,
$$A_n=Q\times1.035^n-8000\left(1+1.035+\cdots+1.035^{n-1}\right)$$
The minimum value of $Q$ leaves nothing after $n$ withdrawals, $A_n=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} Q\times1.035^n&=8000\left(1+1.035+1.035^2+1.035^3+\cdots+1.035^{n-1}\right) \\ Q&=\dfrac{8000}{1.035^n}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^{n-1}}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^{n-2}}+\cdots+\dfrac{8000}{1.035} \\ &=\dfrac{8000}{1.035}+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^2}+\cdots+\dfrac{8000}{1.035^n} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct expression for $A_n$, or equivalent merit
Writes the correct expression for $A_1$, $A_2$ or $A_3$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The expression in part (a) is a geometric series with
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{8000}{1.035} \\ r&=\dfrac{1}{1.035} \end{aligned}$$
Withdrawing indefinitely means $n\to\infty$, so the minimum value is the limiting sum (as $|r|<1$):
$$\begin{aligned} Q&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{8000}{1.035}}{1-\frac{1}{1.035}} \\ &=\$228\,571.43 \\ &\approx\$228\,571 \text{ (nearest dollar)} \end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution: the yearly interest must cover the withdrawal, so
$$\begin{aligned} Q\times3.5\%&=8000 \\ Q&=\dfrac{8000}{3.5\%} \\ &=\$228\,571.43 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the correct limiting sum expression to find the minimum value, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the question asks for the nearest dollar, so the answer is $\$228\,571$; the guideline stopped at $\$228\,571.43$.

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows a large bio-diversity precinct the council is planning to build inside a large park. $OAB$ is a sector with centre $O$, and radius $x$ kilometres. Arc $AB$ subtends an angle of $\theta$ radians at $O$. The equilateral triangle $BCO$ adjoins the sector.

\exfigure{361_q36_1}

parts.latex:
The perimeter of the precinct as shown in the diagram is given to be $\left(12-2\sqrt{3}\right)$ kilometres.

Calculate the maximum area of the precinct $(OABC)$. Leave your answer in exact form.

dif.r: unscaffolded: build perimeter and area, eliminate theta, optimise exactly

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

figures.cap: sector OAB with radius x and angle theta at O, joined along OB to equilateral triangle BCO with sides x

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is $OA+\text{arc }AB+BC+CO$, where $OA=BC=CO=x$ (radius, and equilateral triangle $BCO$), so
$$\text{Arc } AB=12-2\sqrt{3}-3x$$
Arc length is $x\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} x\theta&=12-2\sqrt{3}-3x \\ \theta&=\dfrac{12}{x}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{x}-3 \end{aligned}$$
Triangle $BCO$ is equilateral, so $\angle BOC=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area } \triangle OBC&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x^2\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x^2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Area of sector}=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\theta=\dfrac{x^2}{2}\theta$$
Area of the precinct is the area of the triangle plus the area of the sector:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4}+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\left(\dfrac{12}{x}-\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{x}-3\right) \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}x^2}{4}+6x-\sqrt{3}x-\dfrac{3x^2}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x^2}{4}+(6-\sqrt{3})x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x}{2}+(6-\sqrt{3})$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{(\sqrt{3}-6)x}{2}+(6-\sqrt{3})&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{-2(6-\sqrt{3})}{\sqrt{3}-6} \\ &=\dfrac{2(\sqrt{3}-6)}{\sqrt{3}-6} \\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}-6}{2}<0$, $x=2$ gives a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{4(\sqrt{3}-6)}{4}+2(6-\sqrt{3}) \\ &=6-\sqrt{3} \text{ km}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct expression for the total area of the precinct, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct expression for the area of the triangle or the area of the sector in terms of $x$ or $\theta$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The gradient of a curve, $y=f(x)$ is given by $f'(x)=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{x}}$. The curve passes through the point $(4,5)$. Find the equation of the curve.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{x}} \\ &=\dfrac{x}{2}+4x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: At what length should $x$ be cut to minimise the total area of the circle and square? Give your answer to the nearest centimetre.

dif.r: A given; solve A'=0 linear, round, justify minimum

figures.cap: 100 cm wire with point P; first piece of length x

solutions.latex:
The piece of length $x$ is the circumference of the circle:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi r&=x \\ r&=\dfrac{x}{2\pi} \end{aligned}$$
The other piece has length $100-x$ and is the perimeter of the square, so each side is $\dfrac{100-x}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{circle}}&=\pi\left(\dfrac{x}{2\pi}\right)^2 \\ A_{\text{square}}&=\left(\dfrac{100-x}{4}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total area}&=\dfrac{\pi x^2}{4\pi^2}+\left(\dfrac{100-x}{4}\right)^2 \\ &=\dfrac{x^2}{4\pi}+\dfrac{(100-x)^2}{16} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the area of the circle or the area of the square, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{x^2}{4\pi}+\dfrac{(100-x)^2}{16} \\ A'&=\dfrac{2x}{4\pi}-\dfrac{2(100-x)}{16} \\ &=\dfrac{x}{2\pi}-\dfrac{100-x}{8} \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{2\pi}-\dfrac{100-x}{8}&=0 \\ \dfrac{4x-\pi(100-x)}{8\pi}&=0 \\ 4x-100\pi+\pi x&=0 \\ x(4+\pi)&=100\pi \\ x&=\dfrac{100\pi}{4+\pi} \\ &=43.99\ldots \\ &\approx44 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Check that $44$ cm gives a minimum:
$$\begin{aligned} A''&=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}+\dfrac{1}{8} \\ &=0.28\ldots \\ &>0 \text{ for all } x \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $44$ cm is a minimum, so the wire should be cut at $44$ cm to minimise the total area of the square and the circle.

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct answer, with the minimum verified

parts.latex: What is the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+1}{4-x^2}$?

dif.r: ratio of leading coefficients gives y=-1

solutions.latex:
Divide the numerator and denominator by $x^2$:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{1+\frac{1}{x^2}}{\frac{4}{x^2}-1}$$
As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{1}{x^2}\to0$ and $\dfrac{4}{x^2}\to0$, so
$$f(x)\to\dfrac{1}{-1}=-1$$
The horizontal asymptote is $y=-1$.

parts.latex: If the red area is three times larger than the blue area, find the value of $n$.

dif.r: general x^n areas in terms of n, solve ratio

figures.cap: y=x^n with red region R between curve and y-axis from y=a^n to y=b^n, blue region B under curve from x=a to x=b; Not to scale

solutions.latex:
Let $B$ be the area of the blue region, $W$ the area of the small rectangle and $A$ the area of the big rectangle.
$$\begin{aligned} B&=\int_a^b x^n\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left[x^{n+1}\right]_a^b \\ &=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} W&=a\times a^n \\ &=a^{n+1} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=b\times b^n \\ &=b^{n+1} \end{aligned}$$
The big rectangle is made up of the blue region, the red region ($3B$) and the small rectangle:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=B+3B+W \\ &=4B+W \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} b^{n+1}&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right)+a^{n+1} \\ b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right) \\ 1&=\dfrac{4}{n+1} \\ 4&=n+1 \\ n&=3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the correct relationship between the areas, or equivalent merit
Finds the blue area and both rectangle areas, or equivalent merit
Finds the blue area or both rectangle areas, or equivalent merit

Factorise and cancel $x-7$ (since $x\ne7$ in a limit):

parts.latex: For what values of $a$ does the equation $ax^2+5x+a=0$ have no solution?

dif.r: discriminant < 0 gives a^2 > 25/4, two regions

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
The equation has no real solution when $\Delta<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 25-4a^2&<0 \\ 4a^2&>25 &&(\text{add } 4a^2) \\ a^2&>\dfrac{25}{4} &&(\text{divide by } 4) \end{aligned}$$
So $a<-\dfrac{5}{2}$ or $a>\dfrac{5}{2}$.

parts.latex:
Olivia and Sarah are participating in a fitness program. The probability that Olivia will complete the program is $0.8$, and the probability that Sarah will complete the program is $0.7$.

What is the probability that only one of them will complete the program?

dif.r: only one: two products added

req: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events
A.note: independence implicit not stated; could be Multistage events instead

Multistage events and tree diagrams.reason: Multiplying along two paths and adding them.

Complementary events.reason: Needs P(not complete)=1−P(complete) for each person.

Independent events.reason: Events not stated independent; multiply-and-add along paths is Multistage events.

Addition rule and mutually exclusive eve.reason: not_when: adding end-branch probabilities is part of Multistage events.

solutions.latex:
Either Olivia completes and Sarah does not, or Sarah completes and Olivia does not:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{only one})&=0.8\times0.3+0.2\times0.7 \\ &=0.24+0.14 \\ &=0.38 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is the derivative of $e^{3^x x^6}$.

dif.r: chain with product of 3^x and x^6, factorise to match

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3^x & v&=x^6 \\ u'&=3^x\log_e3 & v'&=6x^5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3^xx^6\right)=3^x\log_e3\cdot x^6+6x^5\cdot3^x=3^xx^5\left(6+x\log_e3\right)$$
By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{g(x)}=g'(x)e^{g(x)}$:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{3^xx^6}=3^xx^5\left(6+x\log_e3\right)e^{3^xx^6}$$

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Using the sketch from part (i) or otherwise, solve

$$|x-1|=2x+4$$

dif.r: absolute value equation, reject invalid case

can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y = |x - 1| on [-4, 4] with the line y = 2x + 4 drawn, meeting it at (-1, 2)

solutions.latex: \exfigure{373_q11_s1}

Graphically, the line $y=2x+4$ meets $y=|x-1|$ at $x=-1$ (the line must be sketched on the graph from part (a)).

Alternatively, solve algebraically in two cases.

Case 1, $x-1\ge0$, so $|x-1|=x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x-1&=2x+4 \\ -x&=5 \\ x&=-5 \end{aligned}$$
This does not satisfy $x\ge1$, so reject.

Case 2, $x-1<0$, so $|x-1|=-(x-1)=1-x$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-x&=2x+4 \\ -3x&=3 \\ x&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $-1<1$, so this satisfies $x-1<0$.
$$\therefore x=-1$$

$$\int 2\Big(\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right)\Big)\,dx$$

dif.r: match integrand to (a) after expanding

solutions.latex:
Write $x\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{x}{\sin x}$ and use the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\operatorname{cosec}x\right)&=\dfrac{\sin x-x\cos x}{\sin^2x} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}-\dfrac{x\cos x}{\sin^2x} \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}x-x\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative by the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By part (a), $\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right)$ is the derivative of $x\operatorname{cosec}x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int 2\Big(\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right)\Big)\,dx&=2\int\operatorname{cosec}x\left(1-x\cot x\right)\,dx \\ &=2x\operatorname{cosec}x+C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\left(x+\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^2$ at the point where $x=2$.

Write the equation of the normal using general form.

dif.r: chain rule with x+2/x, normal in general form

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\left(x+2x^{-1}\right)^2 \\ &=x^2+4+4x^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=2$:
$$y=\left(2+\dfrac{2}{2}\right)^2=9$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x-8x^{-3} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent at $x=2$ is
$$m=2(2)-8(2)^{-3}=3$$
so the gradient of the normal is $-\dfrac{1}{3}$ (perpendicular lines have $m_1m_2=-1$).

The equation of the normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-9&=-\dfrac{1}{3}(x-2) \\ 3y-27&=-x+2 \\ x+3y-29&=0 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient of the tangent at $x=2$, or equivalent merit

$$P\left(\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}\right)$$

dif.r: complement of union

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

req: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events
A.note: requires P(A and B) from conditional probability and union rule

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula, $P(A|B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{0.2} \\ P(A\cap B)&=0.1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &=0.3+0.2-0.1 \\ &=0.4 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
There are 4 red and 3 black discs in a bag. Ms Kim and Ms Lee are playing a game in which they take turns drawing a disc from the bag and then replacing it.

To win the game, Ms Kim must draw a red disc and for Ms Lee to win, she must draw a black disc. They continue taking turns until there is a winner. Ms Kim draws a disc first.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the probability that Ms Kim wins on her first draw.

dif.r: single direct probability 4/7

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the probability that Ms Kim wins in three or less of her turns.

dif.r: model turn sequences, sum three growing paths

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the probability that Ms Kim wins the game.

dif.r: recognise infinite GP of rounds, limiting sum

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

req: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences
A.note: infinite game: GP with r=12/49

B.note: Probability of winning is an infinite GP of path probabilities.

Applications of arithmetic and geometric.evidence: This is a GP with a=4/7 and r=3/7 x 4/7

figures.cap: solution sketch: tree diagram of Kim and Lee draws over five turns, red 4/7 and black 3/7
solution sketch: tree diagram continuing turns 5 to 7 (Kim, Lee, Kim)

solutions.latex: Ms Kim wins on her first draw if she draws a red disc, so $P=\dfrac{4}{7}$.

criteria: Correct expression for the three winning sequences, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{373_q17_s2}

Ms Kim wins by drawing red ($\dfrac{4}{7}$); each earlier round has her draw black ($\dfrac{3}{7}$) and Ms Lee draw red ($\dfrac{4}{7}$):
$$\begin{aligned} P(1 \text{ turn})&=\dfrac{4}{7} \\ P(2 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2 \\ P(3 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^3 \\ P(4 \text{ turns or less})&=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^3+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^3\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^4 \end{aligned}$$
So for $n$ turns,
$$P(n \text{ turns or less})=\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{7}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^2+\cdots+\left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{7}\right)^n$$
This is a GP with $a=\dfrac{4}{7}$ and $r=\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}$. The probability that Ms Kim wins the game is its limiting sum:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{4}{7}}{1-\frac{3}{7}\times\frac{4}{7}} \\ &=\dfrac{28}{37} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct limiting sum expression, or equivalent merit
Identifies a GP with $r=\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{7}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Prove the following identity:

$$\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=2\sec\theta.$$

dif.r: common denominator, Pythagorean identity, factor and cancel

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over the common denominator $\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)$, and use $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\cos^2\theta+(1+\sin\theta)^2}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta+1+2\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2+2\sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2(1+\sin\theta)}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{\cos\theta} \\ &=2\sec\theta \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines fractions and uses $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, show that the ratio of the area of $\triangle ABC$ to the area of $\triangle ADC$ is $\sqrt{3}:2$.

dif.r: area ratio, sin105=sin75, use ratio from (a)

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

figures.cap: triangle ABD with C on BD; BC = x, CD = y; angle ABC 45 degrees, angle ACD 75 degrees, angle ADC 60 degrees

solutions.latex:
From the diagram, $\angle ACB=180^\circ-75^\circ=105^\circ$, so $\angle BAC=180^\circ-45^\circ-105^\circ=30^\circ$, and $\angle CAD=180^\circ-75^\circ-60^\circ=45^\circ$.

Sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{AC}{\sin45^\circ}&=\dfrac{x}{\sin30^\circ} \\ \dfrac{AC}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}&=\dfrac{x}{\frac{1}{2}} \\ \sqrt{2}AC&=2x \\ AC&=\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{2}} &&(1) \end{aligned}$$
Sine rule in $\triangle ADC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{AC}{\sin60^\circ}&=\dfrac{y}{\sin45^\circ} \\ \dfrac{AC}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}&=\dfrac{y}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \\ \dfrac{2AC}{\sqrt{3}}&=\sqrt{2}y \\ AC&=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}y}{2} &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
Equate (1) and (2):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{2}}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}y}{2} \\ \dfrac{x}{y}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $AC$ in terms of $x$ and in terms of $y$, or equivalent merit
One correct sine rule expression for $AC$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: Since $\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta$, the smallest positive value is $\alpha=180^\circ$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}_{\triangle ABC}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times x\times AC\times\sin105^\circ \\ \text{Area}_{\triangle ADC}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times AC\times y\times\sin75^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Taking the ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{Area}_{\triangle ABC}}{\text{Area}_{\triangle ADC}}&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}x\,AC\sin105^\circ}{\frac{1}{2}y\,AC\sin75^\circ} \\ &=\dfrac{x\sin105^\circ}{y\sin75^\circ} \\ &=\dfrac{x\sin(180^\circ-75^\circ)}{y\sin75^\circ} \\ &=\dfrac{x\sin75^\circ}{y\sin75^\circ} \\ &=\dfrac{x}{y} \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore \text{Area}_{\triangle ABC}:\text{Area}_{\triangle ADC}=\sqrt{3}:2$$
criteria: Correct ratio of the two area formulas, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle is moving such that its displacement in metres after $t$ seconds is given by the equation

$$x=-1.5+3\sin 2t$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: State the maximum displacement of the particle.

dif.r: amplitude: max of sine plus shift

can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the first four times when the particle is at the origin.

dif.r: sin2t=1/2, doubled domain, list first four solutions

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of x = -1.5 + 3 sin 2t for 0 <= t <= 2 pi, range -4.5 to 1.5, crossing zero four times

solutions.latex:
The maximum value of $\sin(2t)$ is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x_{\max}&=-1.5+3\times1 \\ &=1.5 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{373_q21_s1}

The particle is at the origin when $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1.5+3\sin(2t)&=0 \\ 3\sin(2t)&=1.5 \\ \sin(2t)&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$; sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, and the pattern repeats every $2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 3\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the first four times the particle is at the origin are
$$t=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{12} \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Four correct values of $2t$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle travels in a straight line. Its velocity $\dot{x}$ at time $t$ is given by

$$\dot{x}=\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)\ \text{metres per second}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the expression for the particle's displacement $x$ in terms of $t$, if the particle was initially at $x=2$.

dif.r: integrate quadratic velocity, find C

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find an expression for the particle's acceleration in terms of $t$.

dif.r: differentiate velocity once

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what times is the particle at rest?

parts.label: d
