dif.r: Second derivative test fails; must test gradient sign, horizontal inflexion

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the points of inflexion.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 given, check concavity change at x=3

solutions.latex:
Stationary points are where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$-e^{-x}(1-x)^2=0$$
Since $e^{-x}>0$, $x=1$, and $y=\left(1^2+1\right)e^{-1}=\dfrac{2}{e}$.

At $x=1$ the second derivative is $0$, so the second derivative test does not decide the nature.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=e^{-1}\left(1^2-4(1)+3\right)=0$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side of $x=1$.

\extable{Ts3072_1}

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-e^{-x}(x-1)^2\le0$: the gradient is negative on both sides of $x=1$.

$\therefore$ a horizontal point of inflexion at $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$
criteria: Finds $x=1$ and tests the gradient either side, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $x=1$; 1 for the table of values; 1 for the horizontal point of inflexion at $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{e}\right)$
meta.format_note: Checked the given $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ by differentiating $-e^{-x}(x-1)^2$.

Possible points of inflexion are where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{-x}\left(x^2-4x+3\right) &= 0 \\ e^{-x}(x-3)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$x=3$ or $x=1$ ($x=1$ is the point found in part (i)).

Test whether the concavity changes at $x=3$.

\extable{Ts3073_1}
$$y=\left(3^2+1\right)e^{-3}=\dfrac{10}{e^3}$$
$\therefore$ a point of inflexion at $\left(3,\dfrac{10}{e^3}\right)$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x+x}\,dx$, expressing the answer in the form $\ln a$ for some constant $a$.

dif.r: Recognise f'/f form; log laws simplify exact limits to ln 2

solutions.latex:
The numerator $e^x+1$ is the derivative of the denominator $e^x+x$, so $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$ applies with $f(x)=e^x+x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\dfrac{e^x+1}{e^x+x}\,dx &= \Big[\ln|e^x+x|\Big]_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4} \\ &= \ln|e^{\ln 4}+\ln 4|-\ln|e^{\ln 2}+\ln 2| \\ &= \ln|4+\ln 4|-\ln|2+\ln 2| \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{4+\ln 4}{2+\ln 2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Using $\ln 4=2\ln 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{4+2\ln 2}{2+\ln 2}\right) &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2(2+\ln 2)}{2+\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive and substitution of limits, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By the symmetry of the graphs about $(\pi,0)$, the two shaded regions have equal area.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\left(2\sin x-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right)dx \end{aligned}$$
Since $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\,dx=0$ (a whole number of periods):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}2\sin x\,dx \\ &= 4\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore a=4$

solutions.latex:
Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{6}$:
$$2\sin x\ \text{becomes}\ \dfrac{2}{6}\sin x=\dfrac{1}{3}\sin x$$
Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ replaces $x$ by $3x$:
$$\dfrac{1}{3}\sin x\ \text{becomes}\ \dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x$$
criteria: Gives one correct dilation, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the vertical dilation factor $\dfrac{1}{6}$; 1 for the horizontal dilation factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$

solutions.latex:
Both graphs have the same shape each side of $x=\pi$, so the area is twice the area for $0\le x\le\pi$. For even $n$, $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\dfrac{1}{n}\sin nx\,dx=0$ (a whole number of periods).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}m\sin x\,dx \\ &= 2m\Big[-\cos x\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2m\left(-\cos\pi+\cos 0\right) \\ &= 2m(1+1) \\ &= 4m \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Checked numerically ($m=3$, $n=4$: area $12$).

solutions.latex:
For odd $n$, $\cos(n\pi)=-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\left(m\sin x-\dfrac{1}{n}\sin nx\right)dx \\ &= 2\left[-m\cos x+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos nx\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left\{\left(-m\cos\pi+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos n\pi\right)-\left(-m\cos 0+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\cos 0\right)\right\} \\ &= 2\left\{\left(m-\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)-\left(-m+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)\right\} \\ &= 2\left\{2m-\dfrac{2}{n^2}\right\} \\ &= 4m-\dfrac{4}{n^2} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore a=4$ and $b=-4$
criteria: Correct primitive and substitution, or equivalent merit

The heights of students in a class are represented in the boxplot below.

dif.r: Read quartiles, compute IQR, apply outlier fence: two routine steps.

figures.cap: boxplot of height (cm)

solutions.latex:
From the boxplot, $Q_1=155$ and $Q_3=170$.
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= 170-155 \\ &= 15 \end{aligned}$$
A value is an outlier if it is below $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$.
$$Q_1-1.5\times IQR=155-1.5\times15=132.5$$
So $132.5$ cm is the lowest height that is not an outlier.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\left(x^2+1\right)\cdot 1-x\cdot 2x}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2+1-2x^2}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1-x^2}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$

The point is $\left(2,\dfrac{2}{5}\right)$.

parts.latex:
Let $f'(x)=x^2+kx$.

The line $y=2x+1$ is a tangent to the graph of $y=f(x)$ at the point where $x=-1$.

Find $f(x)$.

dif.r: Use tangent gradient and point conditions, integrate, then find the constant.

solutions.latex:
The tangent has gradient $2$ at $x=-1$, so $f'(-1)=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} (-1)^2+k\times(-1) &= 2 \\ 1-k &= 2 \\ k &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=x^2-x$. Integrate to find $f(x)$.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$$
The tangent touches the curve where $x=-1$, so $f(-1)=2(-1)+1=-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} -1 &= \dfrac{(-1)^3}{3}-\dfrac{(-1)^2}{2}+C \\ -1 &= -\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}+C \\ C &= -\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{1}{6}$$

questions.stem: Helga is training for a marathon. Her training includes a run every Sunday, starting with a run of 3 km on the first Sunday. Each Sunday she increases the length of her run from the previous Sunday by 2 km.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that on the 5$^{\text{th}}$ Sunday of training, she runs 11 km.

dif.r: Substitute into the arithmetic nth-term formula.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find a simplified expression for length of her training run on the $n$th Sunday.

dif.r: Write the general arithmetic term and simplify.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: On the $n$th Sunday, Helga runs 43 km. Find the value of $n$.

dif.r: Solve a one-step linear equation using the previous expression.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the total distance she runs on Sundays, in 15 weeks of training.

dif.r: Substitute directly into the arithmetic series sum formula.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The lengths form an arithmetic sequence with first term $a=3$ and common difference $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ T_5 &= 3+(5-1)\times 2 \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 9,\ 11$ (adding $2$ each time).

So on the $5^{\text{th}}$ Sunday she runs $11$ km.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $a=3$ and $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= 3+(n-1)\times 2 \\ &= 2n+1 \end{aligned}$$

Put $T_n=43$ using $T_n=2n+1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2n+1 &= 43 \\ 2n &= 42 \\ n &= 21 \end{aligned}$$

The sum of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$, with $a=3$, $d=2$, $n=15$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left(2\times 3+(15-1)\times 2\right) \\ &= 255 \end{aligned}$$
So she runs $255$ km in total.
criteria: Substitutes into the sum formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let $A$ and $B$ be two events such that $P(A)=0.4$, $P(B)=0.55$ and $P(B\mid A)=0.6$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent events.

dif.r: Direct comparison of P(B|A) with P(B) using independence definition

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(A\cup B)$.

dif.r: Two steps: intersection from conditional, then addition rule

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Two events are independent if $P(B\mid A)=P(B)$.
$$P(B\mid A)=0.6 \ne 0.55=P(B)$$
$\therefore$ $A$ and $B$ are not independent.

Use $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. First find $P(A\cap B)$ from the conditional probability.
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B) &= P(B\mid A)\times P(A) \\ &= 0.6\times 0.4 \\ &= 0.24 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B) &= 0.4+0.55-0.24 \\ &= 0.71 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: For what values of $x$, in the interval $0\le x\le 2\pi$, does the line $y=-1$ intersect the graph of $y=2\cos 3x$?

dif.r: Trig equation with tripled angle, six solutions over extended domain

solutions.latex:
Set the function equal to $-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos 3x &= -1 \\ \cos 3x &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$3x=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
Since $0\le x\le 2\pi$, we need $0\le 3x\le 6\pi$, so add $2\pi$ and $4\pi$ to these angles.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}+2\pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+2\pi,\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}+4\pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+4\pi \\ &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{14\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{16\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The next angle, $\dfrac{20\pi}{3}$, is greater than $6\pi$, so it is too big. Divide by $3$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{10\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{14\pi}{9},\ \dfrac{16\pi}{9}$$
criteria: Finds the first angles for $3x$, $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $2\cos 3x=-1$; 1 for the first angles for $3x$; 1 for all six values of $x$ (and no others)

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=3x-\sin x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ is an odd function.

dif.r: Routine substitution of -x to verify odd function

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that $f(x)\ge 0$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, find the area bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis, from $x=-\pi$ to $x=\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: Use odd symmetry for area below axis, then exact integration

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
A function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= 3(-x)-\sin(-x) \\ &= -3x+\sin x \\ &= -(3x-\sin x) \\ &= -f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $f(x)$ is an odd function.

$f(x)$ is odd, so the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin and the area from $-\pi$ to $0$ equals the area from $0$ to $\pi$.
$$A=2\int_0^{\pi}(3x-\sin x)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+\cos x\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left[\left(\dfrac{3\pi^2}{2}+\cos\pi\right)-(0+\cos 0)\right] \\ &= 2\left[\dfrac{3\pi^2}{2}-2\right] \\ &= 3\pi^2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=(3\pi^2-4)\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Writes the integral using symmetry, $2\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}(3x-\sin x)\,dx$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A ship ($S$) leaves Port ($P$) travelling on a bearing of $072^\circ$.

After travelling 25 kilometres, the ship is due South of a lighthouse ($L$).

The ship continues on this bearing for a further 4 kilometres, then measures the bearing of the lighthouse to be $316^\circ$.

\exfigure{162_q13_2}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\angle PSL=64^\circ$.

dif.r: Bearings with co-interior angles and back bearing, two steps

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Calculate the distance $LS$ from the ship to the lighthouse at this time.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

dif.r: Must construct triangle LMS, deduce angles from bearings, sine rule

figures.cap: diagram of ships course P to S with bearings 72 and 316 degrees, lighthouse L due north of the 25 km point
solution sketch: the ship diagram marked up with the angles 44 and 72 inside the triangle and 44 at S

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{162_q13_s1}

The bearing of $L$ from $S$ is $316^\circ$, so $L$ is $360^\circ-316^\circ=44^\circ$ west of north from $S$.

The north lines at $P$ and $S$ are parallel, so co-interior angles give the angle between north at $S$ and $SP$.
$$180^\circ-72^\circ=108^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle PSL &= 108^\circ-44^\circ \\ &= 64^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave only '360-316=44' and '180-72-44=64'; the reasons (co-interior angles between parallel north lines) were added by us. Solution figure 162_q13_s1 kept.

solutions.latex:
Let $M$ be the point due south of $L$, where the ship had travelled $25$ km, so $MS=4$ km. In $\triangle LMS$:
$$\angle LMS=72^\circ,\qquad \angle MLS=44^\circ$$
$\angle LMS=72^\circ$ because $LM$ is a north line and $S$ is on bearing $072^\circ$ from $M$. $\angle MLS=44^\circ$ because $LS$ is $44^\circ$ from the south line $LM$ (the back bearing of $316^\circ$ is $136^\circ$). Use the sine rule.
$$\dfrac{LS}{\sin 72^\circ}=\dfrac{4}{\sin 44^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} LS &= \dfrac{4\sin 72^\circ}{\sin 44^\circ} \\ &= 5.5 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the sine rule equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Split the area under the graph into regions, counting area below the $x$-axis as negative.

From $x=0$ to $x=3$ the region is a trapezium with parallel sides $3$ and $2$ and height $2$. From $x=3$ to $x=4$ the region is a $1\times 1$ rectangle below the axis. From $x=4$ to $x=6$ the region is a triangle with base $2$ and height $2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6 f(x)\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{2}(3+2)-1\times 1+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 2 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Regions checked against the graph: trapezium (0 to 3) area 5, rectangle below axis -1, triangle (4 to 6) area 2.

solutions.latex:
Split the integral. From part (a) and the graph, $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx=5-1=4$ (trapezium minus the rectangle below the axis).
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4\left(f(x)-2\right)dx &= \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx-\int_0^4 2\,dx \\ &= 4-\left[2x\right]_0^4 \\ &= 4-(2\times 4-0) \\ &= -4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Splits the integral, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric rewritten top-down. Value 4 checked against the graph: 5 - 1.

solutions.latex:
By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(a)$, with $f(6)=0$ and $f(5)=1$ read from the graph.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_5^6 f'(x)\,dx&=\Big[f(x)\Big]_5^6\\&=f(6)-f(5)\\&=0-1\\&=-1\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Values f(6)=0 and f(5)=1 are read from the figure in the question; not checked against the figure here.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx$.

dif.r: Expand then reverse chain rule for cos x sin^2 x

solutions.latex:
Expand the integrand, then integrate each term.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx&=\int\cos x\,dx-\int\cos x\sin^2 x\,dx\\&=\sin x-\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3}+C\end{aligned}$$
The second integral has the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=\sin x$, $n=2$.
$$\therefore\ \int\cos x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)dx=\sin x-\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3}+C$$
criteria: Expands the integrand, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for expanding the integrand; 1 for $\sin x$; 1 for $-\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3}+C$
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Middle rows worded by us.

parts.latex:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by the formula

$S_n=3n^2-17n$, where $n>0$. Find an expression for the $n$th term of the series.

dif.r: Use T_n = S_n - S_(n-1) with careful algebra

solutions.latex:
For any series, the $n$th term is the difference of consecutive sums, $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=S_n-S_{n-1}\\&=3n^2-17n-\left[3(n-1)^2-17(n-1)\right]\\&=3n^2-17n-3\left(n^2-2n+1\right)+17n-17\\&=3n^2-17n-3n^2+6n-3+17n-17\\&=6n-20\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_n=6n-20$$

meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: T_1=S_1=-14=6-20.

questions.stem:
The population of parrots, $P$, is modelled by the function $P=P_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is time in years since May 2004.

In May 2004, there were 2500 parrots and by May 2014 the population had decreased to 1750.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $P_0=2500$.

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into exponential model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$. (Answer correct to four decimal places).

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for k using logarithms

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If the population continues to decrease in this manner, what will be the expected population in May 2024? Answer to the nearest whole number.

dif.r: Substitute t=20 into established model

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$ the population is $P=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}2500&=P_0e^{-k\cdot 0}\\&=P_0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P_0=2500$$

In May 2014, $t=10$ and $P=1750$, with $P_0=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}1750&=2500e^{-10k}\\\dfrac{7}{10}&=e^{-10k}\\\ln\dfrac{7}{10}&=-10k\\k&=-\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{7}{10}\\&=0.0357\ \text{(to 4 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $1750=2500e^{-10k}$; 1 for $k=0.0357$ (only the first mark is circled in the scan)
meta.format_note: Source scan circled only the first mark; rubric rewritten top-down. Checked: -ln(0.7)/10 = 0.035667.

solutions.latex:
May 2024 is $t=20$. Since $e^{-10k}=\dfrac{7}{10}$, we have $e^{-20k}=\left(\dfrac{7}{10}\right)^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2500e^{-20k}\\&=2500\times 0.49\\&=1225\ \text{parrots}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the substitution with $t=20$; 1 for 1225 (follow through from the previous answer)
meta.marker_note: Follow through from the answer to part (b) is accepted.
meta.format_note: Source skipped the value of k; working completed using e^{-10k}=7/10. Checked: 2500e^{-0.714} = 1224.9, rounds to 1225.

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows a shaded sector in a circle with radius $r$ and centre $O$.

The sector subtends an angle of $\theta$ at the centre of the circle.

The area of the sector is $49\ \text{cm}^2$.

\exfigure{162_q14_2}

Show that $\theta=\dfrac{98}{r^2}$ and hence show that the minimum perimeter of the sector will occur when the arc length of the sector is equal to the diameter of the circle.

dif.r: Optimisation set-up for sector perimeter, verify minimum, interpret arc

figures.cap: circle with centre O and a shaded sector of radius r and angle theta

solutions.latex:
The sector area is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta=49$.
$$\begin{aligned}r^2\theta&=98\\\theta&=\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is two radii plus the arc $r\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2r+r\theta\\&=2r+r\cdot\dfrac{98}{r^2}\\&=2r+98r^{-1}\\\dfrac{dP}{dr}&=2-98r^{-2}\\&=2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}\end{aligned}$$
A stationary point occurs when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{98}{r^2}&=0\\2r^2&=98\\r^2&=49\end{aligned}$$
Since $r>0$, $r=7$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=196r^{-3}=\dfrac{196}{r^3}$$
When $r=7$, $\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{196}{343}=\dfrac{4}{7}>0$, so $P$ is a minimum.

Then the arc length is
$$r\theta=7\times\dfrac{98}{7^2}=14=2\times 7.$$
$\therefore$ the perimeter is a minimum when the arc length equals the diameter of the circle.

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $\theta=\dfrac{98}{r^2}$; 1 for $P=2r+98r^{-1}$; 1 for $r=7$ (as $r>0$) from $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$; 1 for arc length $=14=2\times 7$
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: 196/343 = 4/7 = 0.571.

questions.stem:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.

dif.r: One step: turning point of quadratic velocity

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.

dif.r: Solve v=0, integrate with initial condition, substitute

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

dif.r: Distance needs splitting at direction change, absolute value of integral

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of v against t: downward parabola from v=4 at t=0, crossing the t-axis at t=2, with the area from 0 to 3 shaded

solutions.latex:
The velocity $v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$ is a concave-down parabola, so its maximum is at the turning point, where $v'(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}v'(t)&=-4t+2\\0&=-4t+2\\t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ s}$$
criteria: Recognises the maximum occurs at the turning point, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for recognising the maximum occurs at the turning point; 1 for $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2t^2+2t+4&=0\\-2\left(t^2-t-2\right)&=0\\-2(t-2)(t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=2$ or $t=-1$; since $t\ge 0$, $t=2$.

Integrate the velocity to find the position.
$$x(t)=\int v\,dt=-\dfrac{2t^3}{3}+t^2+4t+C$$
Initially $x(0)=4$, so $C=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}x(2)&=-\dfrac{2\times 2^3}{3}+2^2+4\times 2+4\\&=\dfrac{32}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is }\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m to the right of the origin}$$
criteria: Integrates to find $x(t)$, or equivalent merit
Factorises and solves $v=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for factorising and solving $v=0$; 1 for integrating to get $x(t)$; 1 for $x(2)=\dfrac{32}{3}$ m
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: -16/3+4+8+4 = 32/3.

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$, at $t=2$ (part (b)), so the distance is the total area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, counting the part below the axis as positive.

\exfigure{162_q15_s1}

$$\int_0^2 v\,dt+\left|\int_2^3 v\,dt\right|$$
Using the antiderivative $F(t)=-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3+t^2+4t$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance}&=F(2)-F(0)+\big|F(3)-F(2)\big|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}-0+\left|3-\dfrac{20}{3}\right|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}+\dfrac{11}{3}\\&=\dfrac{31}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance travelled is }\dfrac{31}{3}\text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the two integrals, the second in absolute value, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the two integrals (second in absolute value); 1 for the evaluation
meta.format_note: Checked: F(2)=20/3, F(3)=3, v(3)=-8 so the particle is moving left on (2,3).

parts.latex:
The function $y=f(x)$ is defined as

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}1 & \text{for } -3\le x\le 0\\ -x^2+1 & \text{for } x>0\end{cases}$$

Determine whether $y=f(x)$ is both continuous $\textbf{and}$ differentiable at $x=0$.

Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.

dif.r: Justify continuity and differentiability by matching values and gradients

solutions.latex:
Check continuity at $x=0$: both pieces must give the same value.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{left: } f(0)&=1\\\text{right: } -0^2+1&=1\end{aligned}$$
So $f$ is continuous at $x=0$.

Check the gradients from each side. Each piece is differentiable for all real $x$ on its own.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{left: } f'(x)&=0\\\text{right: } y&=-x^2+1\\y'&=-2x,\ \text{so } y'(0)=0\end{aligned}$$
The gradients agree ($0=0$), so $f$ is differentiable at $x=0$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)\text{ is both continuous and differentiable at } x=0$$
criteria: Shows continuity at $x=0$ (both pieces give $1$), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for showing continuity at $x=0$ (both pieces give 1); 1 for showing differentiability (both gradients are 0)
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down.

questions.stem:
On a given day, the height of the water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right),$$

where $h$ is the height of the water, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 12 am.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the height of the water at 12 am?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $h(t)=5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)$, in the domain $[0,16]$.

dif.r: Sketch sine with amplitude, midline, period over two cycles

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
A family decides to go on a picnic by the river from 12 pm to 2 pm.

It is only safe to swim in the river if the height of the water is less than 4 metres.

When is the earliest time the family can swim in the river after 12 pm?

Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Solve trig equation, select correct solution after t=12 in context

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of h(t) over [0,16]: sine curve with midline 5, maximum 7 and minimum 3, period 8

solutions.latex:
At 12 am, $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}h(0)&=5+2\sin 0\\&=5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

criteria: Shows the vertical transformation (midline $5$, amplitude $2$) or the horizontal transformation (period $8$), or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the vertical transformation (midline 5, amplitude 2); 1 for the horizontal transformation (period 8)
meta.format_note: Sketch is the existing figure 162_q15_s2; not checked against the working here. Rubric rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
The water is safe when $h<4$. Find when $h=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}5+2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)&=4\\\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{4}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{19\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{23\pi}{6},\ \ldots$$
Multiplying by $\dfrac{4}{\pi}$:
$$t=\dfrac{14}{3},\ \dfrac{22}{3},\ \dfrac{38}{3},\ \dfrac{46}{3},\ \ldots$$
At 12 pm ($t=12$), $h=5>4$, and the first solution with $t\ge 12$ is $t=\dfrac{38}{3}=12\dfrac{2}{3}$ hours. After this the height is below $4$ m.
$$\therefore\ \text{the earliest time is } 12{:}40\text{ pm}$$
criteria: Finds the angles, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{2}$; 1 for the angles; 1 for 12:40 pm
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: sin(19*pi/6)=-1/2 and h is below 4 on (38/3, 46/3).

parts.latex: Which of the quadratic equations has 2 distinct real and rational roots?

dif.r: Discriminant check across options, needing perfect-square condition for rational roots.

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
Real rational roots need $\Delta=b^2-4ac$ to be a positive perfect square.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{A: } \Delta&=(-3)^2-4(-1)(5)=29\ \text{(not a square)}\\\text{B: } \Delta&=(-1)^2-4(4)(-5)=81=9^2\\\text{C: } \Delta&=0-4(-1)(-4)=-16\ \text{(no real roots)}\\\text{D: } \Delta&=0\ \text{(one repeated root)}\end{aligned}$$
Only B has $\Delta$ positive and a perfect square, so B has 2 distinct real rational roots.

parts.latex: The point $P(-2,3)$ lies on $y=f(x)$. What are the coordinates of the image point, $P'$ on the graph of $y=3f(x-4)+1$

dif.r: Applies combined dilation and translations to a single point.

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=3f(x-4)+1$ is a translation right 4, a vertical dilation of factor 3, then a translation up 1, so $(x,y)$ maps to $(x+4,\,3y+1)$.
$$\begin{aligned}x'&=-2+4=2\\y'&=3\times 3+1=10\end{aligned}$$
So $P'=(2,10)$, which is option A.

parts.latex: Pearl invests \$12000 into a saving account that offers an interest rate of $4.15\%$ p.a. compounded yearly. Gary invests \$12000 into an account with a different interest rate that compounds monthly. What interest rate as a $\%\ p \cdot a.$ does Gary's bank offer if after 4 years both Pearl and Gary have the same amount in their accounts?

dif.r: Equates compound growth, solves for monthly rate using fractional power.

solutions.latex:
Pearl's balance after 4 years is
$$12000(1.0415)^4=14119.47$$
Gary's account has monthly compounding for $48$ months at $\dfrac{r}{12}$ per month. For equal balances:
$$\begin{aligned}12000\left(1+\dfrac{r}{12}\right)^{48}&=14119.47\\\left(1+\dfrac{r}{12}\right)^{48}&=(1.0415)^4\\1+\dfrac{r}{12}&=(1.0415)^{\frac{1}{12}}\\r&=12\left[(1.0415)^{\frac{1}{12}}-1\right]\approx 0.0407\end{aligned}$$
So Gary's rate is $4.07\%$ p.a., which is option B.

meta.format_note: Source stopped at the equation; working completed and checked numerically (r = 0.040731).

dif.r: Reads inflection point, finds a from a point, compares constants.

skills: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

figures.cap: graph of a cubic through (4,1) with stationary point of inflexion at (5,-1)

solutions.latex:
For $f(x)=a(x-b)^3+c$, the point of inflection is at $(b,c)$. The graph has its inflection at $(5,-1)$, so $b=5$ and $c=-1$.

The graph is decreasing, so $a<0$. Using the point $(4,1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}1&=a(4-5)^3-1\\1&=-a-1\\a&=-2\end{aligned}$$
So $a=-2<c=-1<b=5$, which is option B.

meta.format_note: Graph values (inflection at (5,-1), point (4,1)) are from the source working; figure not checked here.

parts.latex: Find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^5|x-3|\,dx$.

dif.r: Integral of absolute value evaluated as triangle areas.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=|x-3| with value 3 at x=0, vertex at x=3 and point (5,2)

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=|x-3|$ is a V with vertex at $(3,0)$. The integral is the area under it from $x=0$ to $x=5$: two triangles.

\exfigure{292_q8_s1}

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^5|x-3|\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 3+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 2\\&=4.5+2\\&=6.5\end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
The cumulative distribution function for the continuous random variable $X$ is graphed below. What is the mode of the probability density function?

\exfigure{292_q9_1}

dif.r: Must link mode to steepest gradient of the CDF graph.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf
Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: graph of a cumulative distribution function with dashed lines at A, B, C, D

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)$ and the probability density function is $f(x)=F'(x)$.

The mode is where $f(x)$ is greatest, which is where the gradient of the graph of $F$ is steepest, at point $B$.

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x), logarithmic curve through (1,0)
graph of y=g(x), between 0 and 1 with dashed line y=1

solutions.latex:
The range of $g$ is $[0,1)$. The inputs to $f$ that can be used lie in the interval $(0,1)$.

On $(0,1)$ the graph of $f$ takes the values $(-\infty,0)$.

So the range of $f(g(x))$ is $(-\infty,0)$, which is option A.

parts.latex: Solve $\dfrac{3x}{x+2}=4$.

dif.r: Simple rational equation, cross-multiply and solve linear.

solutions.latex:
Since $x\ne -2$, multiply both sides by $x+2$.
$$\begin{aligned}3x&=4(x+2)\\3x&=4x+8\\x&=-8\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Evaluate the following expressions.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\log_2 4x+\log_2 8x-2\log_2 x$

dif.r: Several log laws combined to simplify to a constant.
Index laws with prime-base rewriting of 25 and 15.

solutions.latex:
Use the log laws to combine the terms.
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 4x+\log_2 8x-2\log_2 x&=\log_2\left(32x^2\right)-\log_2 x^2\\&=\log_2\left(\dfrac{32x^2}{x^2}\right)\\&=\log_2 32\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines the logarithms, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric in the source was tick marks only; rows written by us.

solutions.latex:
Write every base as a power of $5$ or $3$, using $25=5^2$ and $15=5\cdot 3$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{25^x\times 3^{2x+5}}{15^{2x+1}}&=\dfrac{5^{2x}\times 3^{2x+5}}{5^{2x+1}\times 3^{2x+1}}\\&=5^{2x-(2x+1)}\times 3^{2x+5-(2x+1)}\\&=5^{-1}\times 3^4\\&=\dfrac{81}{5}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rewrites the expression in terms of powers of $5$ and $3$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{(2-x^2)^3}\,dx$.

dif.r: Standard reverse chain rule with constant adjustment, negative power.

solutions.latex:
Adjust the integrand to the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=2-x^2$, $f'(x)=-2x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{x}{(2-x^2)^3}\,dx&=\int x(2-x^2)^{-3}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\int-2x(2-x^2)^{-3}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{(2-x^2)^{-2}}{-2}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}(2-x^2)^{-2}+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Chloe sits a marine biology test and receives a mark of 60. The mean mark on the test was 50 with a standard deviation of 10. What percentage of her cohort did she score higher than?

dif.r: z-score then empirical rule to get percentage below.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.latex: Chloe also sits a test on mythological creatures. The mean mark is 57 with a standard deviation of 13. Chloe received a mark of 71. Which test did she do better in compared with her cohort? Justify your answer.

dif.r: Compare two z-scores, routine standardised comparison.

figures.cap: solution sketch: normal curve shaded to the left of 60 with 50 and 60 marked

solutions.latex:
The $z$-score measures how many standard deviations the mark is above the mean.
$$z=\dfrac{60-50}{10}=1$$
By the empirical (68-95-99.7) rule, $68\%$ of scores lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so $34\%$ lie between the mean and $z=1$.

\exfigure{292_q16_s1}

$$P(z<1)=50\%+34\%=84\%$$
So Chloe scored higher than $84\%$ of her cohort.

Compare the $z$-scores of the two tests.
$$\begin{aligned}z_{\text{marine biology}}&=1\\z_{\text{mythological creatures}}&=\dfrac{71-57}{13}=\dfrac{14}{13}\approx 1.08\end{aligned}$$
Since $1.08>1$, she did better in mythological creatures because her $z$-score is higher.

parts.label: c

parts.note: Annuity future value interest-factor TABLE look-up: 2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only

dif.r: Combines compound growth of balance with new quarterly annuity.

solutions.latex:
Instalments are made every 6 months for 8 years: $16$ instalments, at $\dfrac{4}{2}=2\%$ per period. The table factor for $2\%$ and $16$ periods is $18.63929$.
$$\begin{aligned}10000&=18.63929\times m\\m&=\dfrac{10000}{18.63929}\\&=\$536.50\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric in the source was tick marks only; rows written by us. Checked: 10000/18.63929 = 536.50 and the factor equals the sum of 1.02^k, k=0..15.

After 2 years there have been $4$ instalments at $2\%$ per period, with table factor $4.12161$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=536.50\times 4.12161\\&=\$2211.24\end{aligned}$$

For the remaining 6 years there are $6\times 4=24$ quarters at $\dfrac{4}{4}=1\%$ per quarter. The balance after 2 years grows by compound interest, and the new instalments are an annuity with table factor $26.97346$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2211.24\times(1.01)^{24}+536.50\times 26.97346\\&=\$17278.95\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Excess}&=17278.95-10000\\&=\$7278.95\end{aligned}$$
So she has $\$7278.95$ more than her goal.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=-x^2+4x-1$ at the point $(1,2)$.

dif.r: Derivative, perpendicular gradient, point-gradient line: standard normal.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The normal intersects $y=-x^2+4x-1$ again at point $P$. Find the coordinates of point $P$.

dif.r: Equate line and parabola, solve factorable quadratic, find second point

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent is $y'$ at $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=-2x+4\\y'(1)&=-2+4=2\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}y-2&=-\dfrac{1}{2}(x-1)\\y-2&=-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\y&=-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient of the tangent, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric in the source was tick marks only; rows written by us.

solutions.latex:
Equate the normal and the curve.
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{5}{2}&=-x^2+4x-1\\-x+5&=-2x^2+8x-2\\2x^2-9x+7&=0\\(x-1)(2x-7)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=1$ (the given point) or $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$.

When $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$, $y=-\dfrac{7}{4}+\dfrac{5}{2}=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$\therefore\ P=\left(\dfrac{7}{2},\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$$
criteria: Forms and factorises the quadratic $2x^2-9x+7=0$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{1-\tan^2 x}{1+\tan^2 x}=1-2\sin^2 x$.

dif.r: Standard identity proof using 1+tan^2=sec^2 and Pythagorean identity

solutions.latex:
Use the identity $1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x$ in the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1-\tan^2 x}{\sec^2 x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sec^2 x}-\dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\sec^2 x}\\&=\cos^2 x-\dfrac{\frac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}}{\frac{1}{\cos^2 x}}\\&=\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x\\&=\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)-\sin^2 x\\&=1-2\sin^2 x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Simplifies to $\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A geometric sequence is formed by

$$f(x)+f'(x)+f''(x)+f'''(x)+\cdots$$

where $f(x)=e^{\frac{1}{2}x}$. Find the limiting sum in terms of $x$.

dif.r: Differentiate repeatedly to find ratio, then apply limiting sum formula

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the first terms.
$$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=e^{\frac{1}{2}x}\\f'(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{1}{2}x}\\f''(x)&=\dfrac{1}{4}e^{\frac{1}{2}x}\end{aligned}$$
Each term is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ of the one before, so the series is geometric with $a=e^{\frac{1}{2}x}$ and $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$. Since $|r|<1$ the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\&=\dfrac{e^{\frac{1}{2}x}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}\\&=2e^{\frac{1}{2}x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the common ratio $r=\dfrac{1}{2}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A ball is thrown upwards from the edge of a cliff and hits the ground below. Its vertical height ($h$) in metres above the ground is given by the formula $h=-t^2+2t+3$ where $t$ is the time in seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: At what time does the ball hit the ground?

dif.r: Solve factorable quadratic, reject negative time

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what time is the ball stationary?

dif.r: Differentiate quadratic and set velocity to zero

skills: Velocity as a rate of change

parts.label: c
parts.latex: In the box below, graph the velocity function of the ball from the time it is launched until it hits the ground.

dif.r: Graph linear velocity function on restricted domain

skills: Velocity as a rate of change

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the total vertical distance travelled by the ball.

dif.r: Must distinguish distance from displacement, combine up and down motion

figures.cap: solution sketch: velocity graph: straight line from (0,2) through (1,0) to (3,-4)

solutions.latex:
The ball hits the ground when $h=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-t^2+2t+3&=0\\t^2-2t-3&=0\\(t-3)(t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=3$ or $t=-1$; since $t>0$, $t=3$ seconds.

The ball is stationary when its velocity $h'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}h'&=-2t+2\\0&=-2t+2\\t&=1\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$

The velocity is $v=h'=-2t+2$, a straight line from $t=0$ to $t=3$ with $v(0)=2$, $v(3)=-4$ and $v=0$ at $t=1$.

\exfigure{292_q24_s1}
criteria: Plots the end points $(0,2)$ and $(3,-4)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric: end points (1), half for shape, half for x-intercept; rewritten top-down. Line equation and values added; drawing is the existing figure 292_q24_s1 (not checked here).

solutions.latex:
The distance is the total area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, taken as positive: the triangle above the axis ($0\le t\le 1$) and the triangle below it ($1\le t\le 3$).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 1\times 2+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 4\\&=1+4\\&=5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex:

figures.cap: rectangle of width x and height y topped by a semicircle

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is the base $x$, two sides $y$, and a semicircular arc of radius $\dfrac{x}{2}$, length $\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x$.
$$\begin{aligned}250&=2y+x+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi x\\2y&=250-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{2}\\y&=125-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{4}\end{aligned}$$
The area is a rectangle plus a semicircle of radius $\dfrac{x}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=xy+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2\\&=x\left(125-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{4}\right)+\dfrac{\pi x^2}{8}\\&=125x-\dfrac{4x^2+2\pi x^2}{8}+\dfrac{\pi x^2}{8}\\&=125x-x^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the area as rectangle plus semicircle and substitutes for $y$, or equivalent merit
Finds $y=125-\dfrac{2x+\pi x}{4}$ from the perimeter, or equivalent merit

For a maximum, solve $A'=0$ and test the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned}A'&=125-2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)x\\0&=125-\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}x\\x&=\dfrac{500}{\pi+4}\approx 70.012\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$A''=-\dfrac{\pi+4}{4}<0$$
So $A$ is a maximum at this value of $x$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\max}&=125(70.012\ldots)-(70.012\ldots)^2\left(\dfrac{\pi+4}{8}\right)\\&\approx 4375.8\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: If Eugene saves \$500 000 dollars at the end of 25 years, find the size of his deposits.

dif.r: Substitute into given formula and solve for deposit

solutions.latex:
Interest is $\dfrac{4}{2}=2\%$ per 6 months, so each year the balance is multiplied by $(1.02)^2$. A deposit $P$ is made at the start of each year.
$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=P(1.02)^2\\A_2&=\left(P(1.02)^2+P\right)(1.02)^2\\&=P(1.02)^4+P(1.02)^2\\A_3&=\left(P(1.02)^4+P(1.02)^2+P\right)(1.02)^2\\&=P(1.02)^6+P(1.02)^4+P(1.02)^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $A_2$ (or $A_3$) in terms of the previous balance, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had no marks breakdown; rubric written by us. Reason for the factor (1.02)^2 added.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), the pattern of the terms continues, with $n$ deposits.
$$\begin{aligned}A_n&=P(1.02)^{2n}+P(1.02)^{2n-2}+\cdots+P(1.02)^2\\&=P(1.02)^2\left[1+1.02^2+1.02^4+\cdots+1.02^{2n-2}\right]\end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.02^2$ and $n$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{r^n-1}{r-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_n&=P(1.02)^2\times\dfrac{\left(1.02^2\right)^n-1}{1.02^2-1}\\&=P\cdot\dfrac{1.0404}{0.0404}\left(1.02^{2n}-1\right)\\&=\dfrac{2601}{101}P\left(1.02^{2n}-1\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.02^2$ and $n$ terms, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x-1 & v&=\sin x\\u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[(x-1)\sin x\big]&=\sin x+(x-1)\cos x\\&=\sin x+x\cos x-\cos x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrate both sides of the result of part (a).
$$\int\left(\sin x+x\cos x-\cos x\right)dx=(x-1)\sin x+C$$
$$-\cos x+\int x\cos x\,dx-\sin x=(x-1)\sin x+C$$
Make $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$ the subject.
$$\begin{aligned}\int x\cos x\,dx&=(x-1)\sin x+\cos x+\sin x+C\\&=x\sin x-\sin x+\cos x+\sin x+C\\&=x\sin x+\cos x+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates both sides of the result of part (a), or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The depth ($d$) in metres of the water in a wave pool varies as waves are sent out. The depth is measured from the floor and can be modelled by the equation $d=\dfrac{4}{5}\sin at+\dfrac{3}{2}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds and $a$ is a constant. Each wave has a period of 2.5 seconds measured from the peak of the wave to the peak of the next wave.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sine graph of depth over 0 to 5 s, max 2.3, min 0.7, midline 3/2

solutions.latex:
The period is $2.5$ seconds, and the period of $\sin at$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{a}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{a}&=2.5\\a&=\dfrac{2\pi}{2.5}=\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\end{aligned}$$

The maximum of $\sin at$ is $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}d_{\max}&=\dfrac{4}{5}+\dfrac{3}{2}\\&=2.3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{292_q31_s1}
criteria: Two of: correct shape, correct period, correct labelling of the $y$-axis, or equivalent merit
One of: correct shape, correct period, correct labelling of the $y$-axis, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric was 1 mark each for shape, period and y-axis; rewritten top-down. Drawing is the existing figure 292_q31_s1 (not checked here).

solutions.latex:
She can touch the bottom when $d<1.7$. First find when $d=1.7$.
$$\begin{aligned}0.8\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{5}t+1.5&=1.7\\\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{5}t&=\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{292_q31_s2}

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{4\pi}{5}t&=0.2526\ldots,\ \pi-0.2526\ldots\\t&=0.1005,\ 1.149\end{aligned}$$
So $d>1.7$ for $0.1005<t<1.149$ in each $2.5$-second period, and the same proportion holds over the first $5$ seconds (two periods).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{proportion above }1.7\text{ m}&=\dfrac{1.149-0.1005}{2.5}\\&=42.0\%\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{she can touch the bottom for }100-42.0=58.0\%\text{ of the time}$$

parts.latex:
The lengths of fish in metres in the harbour are distributed according to the equation,

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-2x(x^2-1)^3+0.5 & \text{for } 0<x\le 1\\[4pt] -\dfrac{x-2}{2} & \text{for } 1<x<2\\[4pt] 0 & \text{for } x>2\end{cases}$$

People are only permitted to catch a fish whose length is between 0.45 m and $L$ m long. If 60\% of fish in the harbour are within this legal limit, find the value of $L$ correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Piecewise pdf, substitution integral, decide which piece, solve quadratic

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The probability of a length between $0.45$ and $L$ is the area under $f$, so we need $\displaystyle\int_{0.45}^{L}f(x)\,dx=0.6$.

Total probability on $0<x\le1$: use the substitution $u=x^2-1$, $du=2x\,dx$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \big(-2x(x^2-1)^3+0.5\big)dx &= \left[-\dfrac{(x^2-1)^4}{4}+0.5x\right]_0^1 \\ &= \left(0+0.5\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \\ &= 0.75 \end{aligned}$$
Probability from $0.45$ to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{0.45}^1 f(x)\,dx &= 0.75-\int_0^{0.45} f(x)\,dx\\ &= 0.75-\left[-\dfrac{(x^2-1)^4}{4}+0.5x\right]_0^{0.45} \\ &= 0.75-0.37387\ldots \\ &= 0.37613\ldots \end{aligned}$$
This is less than $0.6$, so $L>1$ and we need a further $0.6-0.37613=0.22387$ from the second piece.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^L -\dfrac{x-2}{2}\,dx &= \left[x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right]_1^L \\ &= L-\dfrac{L^2}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} L-\dfrac{L^2}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4}&=0.22387 \\ L^2-4L+3.8955&=0 \\ L&=2\pm\sqrt{4-3.8955} \\ &=2\pm 0.3233 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1<L<2$, take the smaller root.
$$\therefore\ L\approx 1.68 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Forms and solves the quadratic in $L$, or equivalent merit
Finds $\displaystyle\int_{0.45}^{1}f(x)\,dx$ and sets up $\displaystyle\int_1^L f(x)\,dx$ equal to the remaining probability, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: scipy quad/brentq: int_0^1=0.75, int_0^0.45=0.373874, root L=1.676729 -> 1.68; int_1^2=0.25 so total 1 (valid pdf).
meta.format_note: Inequality in the first piece of f(x): 0.45 is in the first piece.

parts.latex: The function $y=\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}$ is dilated by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ horizontally and reflected about the $x$-axis. What is the new equation for this function?

dif.r: Apply a dilation then a reflection to a rational function, in order.

solutions.latex:
A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ replaces $x$ by $2x$.
$$y=\dfrac{2x-1}{2x+1}$$
A reflection in the $x$-axis replaces $y$ by $-y$.
$$\begin{aligned}-y&=\dfrac{2x-1}{2x+1}\\y&=\dfrac{1-2x}{2x+1}\end{aligned}$$
So the new equation is $y=\dfrac{1-2x}{1+2x}$, which is option C.

questions.stem: The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is given by $S_n=25n-2n^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the first term.

parts.latex: Show that the general term is given by $T_n=27-4n$.

dif.r: Substitute a and d into the arithmetic general term.

solutions.latex:
The first term is $T_1=S_1$.
$$\begin{aligned}S_1&=25(1)-2(1)^2\\&=23\end{aligned}$$
So the first term is $23$.

Find the first three terms from the sums, using $T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_1&=23\\S_2&=25(2)-2(2)^2=42,&T_2&=S_2-S_1=19\\S_3&=25(3)-2(3)^2=57,&T_3&=S_3-S_2=15\end{aligned}$$
The terms are $23,\ 19,\ 15,\ \ldots$
$$d=19-23=-4$$

Use $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $a=23$ and $d=-4$.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=23+(n-1)\times(-4)\\&=23-4n+4\\&=27-4n\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The circle $x^2+4x+y^2-6y+12=0$ is transformed by a vertical translation 3 units down and a horizontal translation 5 units right. What are the coordinates of the new centre of the transformed circle?

dif.r: Complete the square for the centre, then translate it.

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned}x^2+4x+y^2-6y+12&=0\\(x+2)^2-4+(y-3)^2-9+12&=0\\(x+2)^2+(y-3)^2&=1\end{aligned}$$
The original centre is $(-2,3)$.

Moving $5$ units right and $3$ units down gives the equation
$$(x-3)^2+y^2=1$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the new centre is }(3,0)$$
criteria: Completes the square to obtain $(x+2)^2+(y-3)^2=1$, or states the original centre $(-2,3)$

parts.latex: A factory gets permission to dispose, at the start of every day, 600kg of waste into a stream of water. The running stream removes 40% of any waste present, by the end of the day. Show that the amount of waste present in the stream at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ day is $900(1-0.6^n)$.

dif.r: Build a recurrence from context and recognise the geometric series.

solutions.latex:
The stream removes $40\%$, leaving $60\%$ at the end of each day. Let $W_n$ be the amount at the end of day $n$.
$$\begin{aligned}W_1&=0.6\times 600=360\\W_2&=0.6\left(W_1+600\right)=360+360\times 0.6\\W_3&=0.6\left(W_2+600\right)=360+360\times 0.6+360\times 0.6^2\end{aligned}$$
So
$$W_n=360+360\times 0.6+360\times 0.6^2+\cdots+360\times 0.6^{n-1}$$
This is a geometric series with $a=360$, $r=0.6$ and $n$ terms.
$$\begin{aligned}W_n&=\dfrac{360\left(1-0.6^n\right)}{1-0.6}\\&=\dfrac{360}{0.4}\left(1-0.6^n\right)\\&=900\left(1-0.6^n\right)\end{aligned}$$

Andrew places one grain of rice on the first square, two grains of rice on the second square, four grains on the third, eight on the fourth, and so on, until every square is covered.

The numbers of grains are $1,\ 2,\ 2^2,\ 2^3,\ \ldots$ with $a=1$. The ratio of consecutive terms is constant:

solutions.latex:
The board has $8\times 8=64$ squares, so the last square is the $64^{\text{th}}$ term.
$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=ar^{n-1}\\T_{64}&=1\times 2^{63}\\&=2^{63}\end{aligned}$$

The total is the sum of the first $64$ terms.

$$\begin{aligned}T_3&=ar^2=6 & T_5&=ar^4=\dfrac{3}{2}\\a&=\dfrac{6}{r^2} & a&=\dfrac{3}{2r^4}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{6}{r^2}&=\dfrac{3}{2r^4}\\12r^4&=3r^2\\3r^2\left(4r^2-1\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $r=0$ or $r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}$. But $r=0$ gives $ar^2=0\ne 6$, so $r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Then $a=\dfrac{6}{r^2}=\dfrac{6}{\frac{1}{4}}=24$.
$$\therefore\ r=\pm\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ and }a=24$$

parts.latex: If $4,\ x,\ y$ form a geometric sequence and $x,\ y,\ 12$ form an arithmetic sequence, find the values of $x$ and $y$.

dif.r: Combine geometric and arithmetic conditions into a quadratic system.

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
For the geometric sequence $4,\ x,\ y$ the ratios are equal.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x}{4}&=\dfrac{y}{x}\\x^2&=4y\\y&=\dfrac{x^2}{4}\qquad(1)\end{aligned}$$
For the arithmetic sequence $x,\ y,\ 12$ the differences are equal.
$$\begin{aligned}y-x&=12-y\\2y-x&=12\qquad(2)\end{aligned}$$
Substitute (1) into (2).
$$\begin{aligned}2\left(\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right)-x&=12\\\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x&=12\\x^2-2x-24&=0\\(x-6)(x+4)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=6$ or $x=-4$.

When $x=6$, $y=9$. When $x=-4$, $y=4$.
$$\therefore\ (x,y)=(6,9)\text{ or }(-4,4)$$
criteria: Forms a quadratic and solves for $x$
Forms a pair of equations to solve simultaneously

questions.stem:
$A$ and $B$ are two arithmetic series, where all the terms are positive.

In series $A$, the first term is $a$ and common difference is $d$. In series $B$, the first term is $M$ and the common difference is $D$.

Let $P=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $A$ and let $Q=$ the sum of the first $n$ terms of $B$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}$.

dif.r: General show-that, but just cancelling the sum formulas.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Express $\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}$ in terms of $a,\ d,\ M$ and $D$.

dif.r: Write down the general term formula with n=10.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Given that $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{5n+4}{9n+6}$, evaluate $\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}$.

dif.r: Insight needed: matching (n-1)/2=9 gives n=19; non-routine link between parts.

solutions.latex:
The sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]\\Q&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2M+(n-1)D\right]\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{P}{Q}&=\dfrac{\frac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]}{\frac{n}{2}\left[2M+(n-1)D\right]}\\&=\dfrac{2a+(n-1)d}{2M+(n-1)D}\\&=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly shows the sum of both AP's and simplifies to obtain the ratio needed
meta.format_note: Source also listed the nth-term formulas here; moved to part (b), where they are used.

solutions.latex:
The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of each series is $a+(n-1)d$ and $M+(n-1)D$. For $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of A}}{10^{\text{th}}\text{ term of B}}&=\dfrac{a+(10-1)d}{M+(10-1)D}\\&=\dfrac{a+9d}{M+9D}\end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{a+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)d}{M+\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)D}$. This matches the ratio of the $10^{\text{th}}$ terms in part (b) when $\dfrac{n-1}{2}=9$, so $n=19$.

Substitute $n=19$ into the given ratio.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{a+9d}{M+9D}&=\dfrac{5(19)+4}{9(19)+6}\\&=\dfrac{99}{177}\\&=\dfrac{33}{59}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source wrote 'substituting n=19 in (1)', a reference to a line not on the page; replaced by 'the given ratio'. Checked: 99/177 = 33/59.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=x^4+x^3+kx^2-3x-5$, where $k$ is a constant.

Find the values of $k$ for which $f(x)$ is always concave up.

dif.r: Combine second derivative with discriminant condition for positive definite quadratic

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
A function is concave up when $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=4x^3+3x^2+2kx-3\\f''(x)&=12x^2+6x+2k\end{aligned}$$
$f''(x)>0$ for all $x$ requires the quadratic $2\left(6x^2+3x+k\right)$ to have positive leading coefficient ($6>0$) and $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{aligned}3^2-4\times 6\times k&<0\\9-24k&<0\\k&>\dfrac{3}{8}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=e^x\sin x$ at the point $(\pi,0)$.

dif.r: Product rule gradient, negative reciprocal, point-gradient line

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent comes from the product rule applied to $y=e^x\sin x$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x$$
At $x=\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_T&=e^{\pi}\sin\pi+e^{\pi}\cos\pi\\&=-e^{\pi}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_N=-\dfrac{1}{m_T}=\dfrac{1}{e^{\pi}}$$
The normal through $(\pi,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-0&=\dfrac{1}{e^{\pi}}(x-\pi)\\e^{\pi}y&=x-\pi\\e^{\pi}y-x+\pi&=0\end{aligned}$$

Equate the line and the parabola.

solutions.latex:
Write $y$ as a power and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=(3x^2+6)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(3x^2+6)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 6x\\&=\dfrac{3x}{\sqrt{3x^2+6}}\end{aligned}$$

dif.r: Must recognise degrees need conversion to radians before differentiating.

solutions.latex:
Convert degrees to radians: $x^{\circ}=\dfrac{\pi}{180}x$ radians.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}x\right)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}x\right)\end{aligned}$$
or equivalently $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos x^{\circ}$.

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\log_e\sqrt{e^{x}(2x+1)}$

dif.r: Log laws simplify first, then routine differentiation.

solutions.latex:
Simplify first with the log laws $\ln\sqrt{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln A$ and $\ln(AB)=\ln A+\ln B$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left[e^x(2x+1)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln e^x+\ln(2x+1)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[x+\ln(2x+1)\right]\end{aligned}$$
Now differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{2x+1}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2x+1}\\&=\dfrac{(2x+1)+2}{2(2x+1)}\\&=\dfrac{2x+3}{4x+2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses at least one log law to simplify the question

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows the graph of the function $f(x)=\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.

The points $P(0,0)$ and $Q\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ both lie on the curve.

The point $R(t,\sin t)$ is also a point on the curve between $P$ and $Q$, such that $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{571_q21_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that $A$, the area of $\triangle PQR$, is given by

$$A=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\text{ when }t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$$

dif.r: Non-routine set-up: triangle area via trapezia, heavy algebra.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Find the maximum value of $A$, the area of $\triangle PQR$.

Justify your answer, leaving your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Optimise trig expression, inverse cosine, justify maximum numerically.

figures.cap: graph of y=sin x with points P, R, Q and triangle PQR shaded
solution sketch: annotated diagram of triangle PQR with rectangle and trapezoid areas

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{571_q21_s1}

The area of $\triangle PQR$ is the area under $PR$ plus the area under $RQ$, minus the area under $PQ$ (each a trapezium on the $x$-axis).
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}\,t\sin t+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-t\right)\left(\sin t+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
Expand and simplify.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}t\sin t+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin t+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi}{3}-t\sin t-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}t\right)-\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{6}\\&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\sin t-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}t\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds an area that will lead to significant progress to a solution

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and find the stationary point.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin t-3\sqrt{3}\,t\right)\\\dfrac{dA}{dt}&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\cos t-3\sqrt{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Stationary point where $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=0$:
$$\cos t=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{4\pi}$$
so $t=1.145\ldots$, which lies in $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dt^2}=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(-4\pi\sin t\right)$$
When $t=1.145$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dt^2}=-0.9534<0$, so the curve is concave down and this is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(4\pi\sin 1.145-3\sqrt{3}\times 1.145\right)\\&\approx 0.46\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum } A\approx 0.46$$
criteria: Satisfies one criteria point. Criteria points: finds $t$; test for concavity; finds maximum $A$

parts.latex:
The function $y=f(x)$ is transformed to $y=f\left(3\left(x+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)$.

dif.r: Identify horizontal dilation and translation from factored form

options.label: A
options.latex: Horizontal dilation factor of 3, followed by translation left 1 unit.

options.label: B
options.latex: Horizontal dilation factor of 3, followed by translation left $\dfrac{1}{3}$ unit.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.latex: Horizontal dilation factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$, followed by translation left $\dfrac{1}{3}$ unit.

solutions.latex:
Write $f\left(3\left(x+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)=f(3x+1)$. In the form $f\big(k(x+h)\big)$, the factor $k=3$ gives a horizontal dilation by factor $\dfrac{1}{k}=\dfrac{1}{3}$, and $x+h$ with $h=\dfrac{1}{3}$ gives a translation left $\dfrac{1}{3}$ unit.

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_1^a (4-2x)\,dx=-3$ where $a>0$. What is the value of $a$?

dif.r: Evaluate definite integral with unknown limit, solve quadratic

solutions.latex:
Integrate, then substitute the limits.

Since $a>0$, $a\ne 0$, so $a=4$ (option B).

parts.latex:
A particle is moving on the $x$ axis. Its velocity, $v$ metres per second, at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=3-6\cos t$.

Which expression is the displacement function in terms of $t$ ?

dif.r: Integrate velocity and use initial condition for constant

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=\int(3-6\cos t)\,dt\\&=3t-6\sin t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially $x(0)=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=0-0+C\\C&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x(t)=3t-6\sin t+4$, which is option A.

This is option A.

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=e^{2x}(x+2)$ at the point $(1,3e^2)$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^{2x}&v&=x+2\\u'&=2e^{2x}&v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e^{2x}\cdot 1+2e^{2x}(x+2)\\&=e^{2x}\left(1+2(x+2)\right)\\&=e^{2x}(2x+5)\end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=7e^2$, the gradient of the tangent.

The tangent through $(1,3e^2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-3e^2&=7e^2(x-1)\\y-3e^2&=7e^2x-7e^2\\0&=7e^2x-y-4e^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 7e^2x-y-4e^2=0$$

parts.latex: The graph of the function $f(x)=x^2$ is translated $m$ units to the left, dilated vertically by a scale factor of $k$ and then translated 7 units up. The equation of the transformed function is $g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{3}+2x+10$. Find $m$ and $k$.

dif.r: Same as anchor: equate coefficients or complete square

solutions.latex:
The transformed function is $g(x)=k(x+m)^2+7$ (translate $m$ units left, dilate by $k$, translate 7 up).
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=k\left(x^2+2mx+m^2\right)+7\\&=kx^2+2mkx+m^2k+7\end{aligned}$$
Equate coefficients with $g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{3}+2x+10$.

Coefficient of $x^2$: $k=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned}2mk&=2\\2\times m\times\dfrac{1}{3}&=2\\m&=3\end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution: complete the square.
$$\begin{aligned}g(x)&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(x^2+6x+30\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left(x^2+6x+3^2+30-3^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[(x+3)^2+21\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}(x+3)^2+7\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=3,\ k=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

solutions.latex:
Differentiate, and solve $f'(x)=0$ for the stationary points.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=12x^2-4x^3\\f''(x)&=24x-12x^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}12x^2-4x^3&=0\\4x^2(3-x)&=0\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=3\end{aligned}$$
When $x=0$: $y=3$ and $f''(0)=0$, so the second derivative test is inconclusive. Test the concavity either side of $x=0$:

\extable{Ts3278_1}

The concavity changes, so $(0,3)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

When $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3+4(3)^3-3^4=30\\f''(3)&=24(3)-12(3)^2=-36<0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore(3,30)$ is a local maximum turning point.
criteria: Finds the stationary points $(0,3)$ and $(3,30)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Ms Iacona notices that the number of emails she receives per week from students is cyclical. Every 12 weeks she receives the highest number of emails.

The number of emails Ms Iacona receives each week, $f(t)$, is modelled by the function

$$f(t)=a\cos(bt)+c$$

where $t$ is the number of weeks after 1 January 2023 and $0\le t\le 52$.

The lowest number of emails Ms Iacona receives is 15 per week and the highest number of emails per week is 45.

The number of emails is at a maximum on 1st January 2023 i.e., when $t=0$.

Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

dif.r: Find amplitude, period and centre from max/min data

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is half the difference between the highest and lowest values.
$$a=\dfrac{45-15}{2}=15$$
The period is $12$ weeks.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{b}&=12\\b&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$$
So $f(t)=15\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)+c$. The maximum is at $t=0$, so $f(0)=45$.
$$\begin{aligned}45&=15+c\\c&=30\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=15,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ c=30$$
criteria: Finds two of $a$, $b$, $c$ correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: The acceleration of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $a=4t+4$ . Initially the particle has a velocity of $-30$ m/s. When is the particle at rest?

dif.r: Integrate acceleration with initial condition, solve quadratic

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the integral of acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int(4t+4)\,dt\\&=2t^2+4t+c\end{aligned}$$
Initially $v=-30$, so when $t=0$, $c=-30$.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=2t^2+4t-30\\&=2(t^2+2t-15)\\&=2(t+5)(t-3)\end{aligned}$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$, so $t=-5$ or $t=3$. Since $t\ge 0$, $t=3$, option C.

parts.latex:
Consider the information about events $A$ and $B$.

\begin{itemize}
\item $P(B)=0.6$
\item $P(A|B)=0.4$
\item $P(A|\overline{B})=0.8$
\end{itemize}

What is the value of $P(B|A)$?

dif.r: Reverse conditional probability needing total probability step

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram with P(A and not B)=8/25 and P(A and B)=6/25

solutions.latex:
Use $P(B|A)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}$ and find each intersection from the conditional probabilities.
$$P(A|B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{0.6}=0.4\quad\text{so}\quad P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{6}{25}$$
$$P\left(A|\overline{B}\right)=\dfrac{P\left(A\cap\overline{B}\right)}{1-0.6}=\dfrac{P\left(A\cap\overline{B}\right)}{0.4}=0.8\quad\text{so}\quad P\left(A\cap\overline{B}\right)=\dfrac{8}{25}$$

\exfigure{638_q8_s1}

$$P(A)=P(A\cap B)+P\left(A\cap\overline{B}\right)=\dfrac{6}{25}+\dfrac{8}{25}=\dfrac{14}{25}$$
$$\therefore\ P(B|A)=\dfrac{\frac{6}{25}}{\frac{14}{25}}=\dfrac{3}{7}$$
This is option C.

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is
$$r=\dfrac{-16a}{64}=-\dfrac{a}{4}\qquad\left(\text{check: }\dfrac{4a^2}{-16a}=-\dfrac{a}{4}\right)$$
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$, that is $-1<r<1$. One operation per line:
$$\begin{aligned}-1&<-\dfrac{a}{4}<1\\-4&<-a<4&&(\text{multiply by }4)\\4&>a>-4&&(\text{multiply by }-1,\text{ reversing the inequalities})\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: A circle is divided into $n$ sectors in such a way that the angles of the sectors are in arithmetic progression. The smallest two angles are $3^\circ$ and $5^\circ$. Find the value of $n$.

solutions.latex:
The sector angles form an arithmetic series with $a=3^\circ$ and $d=2^\circ$, and they add to a full circle, so $S_n=360$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2\times 3+(n-1)\times 2\right]&=360\\n\left(2n+4\right)&=720\\2n^2+4n-720&=0\\n^2+2n-360&=0\\(n+20)(n-18)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=18$.

The derivative of $1+2x$ is $2$, so insert a factor of $2$ and compensate with $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+2x}}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2(1+2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{(1+2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}}+C\\&=\sqrt{1+2x}+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates correctly apart from the chain rule factor, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
In the diagram, $CD$ is an arc of a circle with radius 8 cm and centre $O$.

T is the midpoint of $OC$. It is given that $\angle COD=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ .

\exfigure{638_q19_1}

Calculate the perimeter of $CTD$ in exact form.

dif.r: Combine arc length and cosine rule, exact form

figures.cap: sector COD with T on OC, TD joined

solutions.latex:
The perimeter of $CTD$ is the arc $CD$ plus $CT$ plus $TD$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Arc }CD&=r\theta\\&=8\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{16\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$T$ is the midpoint of $OC$, so $CT=OT=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 8=4$.

In $\triangle OTD$, $OT=4$, $OD=8$ and $\angle TOD=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned}TD&=\sqrt{4^2+8^2-2\times 4\times 8\times\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}}\\&=\sqrt{80-64\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}\\&=\sqrt{112}\\&=4\sqrt{7}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P=\dfrac{16\pi}{3}+4+4\sqrt{7}\text{ cm}$$
criteria: Finds the arc length $CD$ or $CT$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The population of ants is growing exponentially according to the equation $P=50e^{kt}$ , where $t$ is the time in days after the insect is first counted. After four days, it is observed that the population has doubled from the initial amount.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the initial number of ants and show that $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$

dif.r: Initial value then routine log solve for k from doubling

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what rate (to the nearest whole number) is the population increasing at day 15?

dif.r: Differentiate exponential model and substitute t=15

parts.label: c
parts.latex: How many days will it take for the number of ants to first reach 1500?

dif.r: Solve exponential equation with logs, round to days

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$, $P_0=50e^0=50$, so the initial number of ants is $50$.

After four days the population has doubled, so $P=100$ when $t=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}100&=50e^{4k}\\e^{4k}&=2\\4k&=\ln 2\\k&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the initial number of ants, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $P=50e^{kt}$ with $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=50k\,e^{kt}$$
At $t=15$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=50\times\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\times e^{\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\times 15}\\&\approx 117\text{ ants per day}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us. Checked: 116.57.

solutions.latex:
Put $P=1500$ with $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$ and take natural logs.
$$\begin{aligned}1500&=50e^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t}\\30&=e^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t}\\\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t&=\ln 30\\t&=\dfrac{\ln 30}{\frac{1}{4}\ln 2}\\&\approx 19.6\\&\approx 20\text{ days}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms and simplifies $30=e^{kt}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The probability density function for the continuous random variable $X$ is given by:

$$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}kx(4-x), & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{array}\right\}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{9}$

dif.r: Standard: integrate pdf over domain, set equal to 1

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the mode of $X$.

dif.r: Mode is vertex of simple quadratic inside domain

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of f(x) with maximum at x=2, f=4/9

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^4 kx(4-x)\,dx&=1\\k\int_1^4\left(4x-x^2\right)dx&=1\\k\left[2x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4&=1\\k\left(\left(32-\dfrac{64}{3}\right)-\left(2-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)&=1\\9k&=1\\k&=\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $\displaystyle\int_1^4 kx(4-x)\,dx=1$ and integrates, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us.

solutions.latex:
The mode is the value of $x$ where $f(x)$ is greatest. With $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{9}x(4-x)$:

\exfigure{638_q24_s1}

The maximum is at $x=2$, which lies in $1\le x\le 4$, so the mode is $2$.

Alternatively, use calculus.
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\dfrac{4}{9}-\dfrac{2x}{9}\\f'(x)&=0\ \text{when}\ x=2\\f''(x)&=-\dfrac{2}{9}<0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=2$ is a maximum, and the mode is $2$.
criteria: Identifies that the mode is where $f(x)$ is a maximum, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x-x)=\ln x$

dif.r: One routine product rule verification

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^e \ln x^2\,dx$ .

dif.r: Log law rewrite then use given primitive to evaluate

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x&v&=\ln x\\u'&=1&v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x-x)&=1\times\ln x+x\times\dfrac{1}{x}-1\\&=\ln x+1-1\\&=\ln x\end{aligned}$$
which is the right-hand side.

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only; one-row rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $x\ln x-x$ is a primitive of $\ln x$. Also $\ln x^2=2\ln x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_1^e\ln x^2\,dx&=2\int_1^e\ln x\,dx\\&=2\Big[x\ln x-x\Big]_1^e\\&=2\Big[(e\ln e-e)-(1\cdot\ln 1-1)\Big]\\&=2\Big[(e-e)-(0-1)\Big]\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses $\ln x^2=2\ln x$ or the result of part (a), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A small school has counted the number of Year 12 students in Mathematics and Physics. They found that:

\begin{itemize}
\item 12 students study Mathematics only
\item 5 students study Physics only
\item 3 students study neither
\item $x$ students study both.
\end{itemize}

parts.latex: The curve $y=px^3+qx$ passes through the point $(1, 4)$. The tangent at this point is parallel to the line $y=2x-6$. Find the values of $p$ and $q$.

dif.r: Point and parallel-tangent conditions give simultaneous equations

solutions.latex:
The curve passes through $(1,4)$:
$$p+q=4\qquad(1)$$
Differentiate: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3px^2+q$. The gradient of the tangent at $(1,4)$ is $3p+q$. The tangent is parallel to $y=2x-6$, so its gradient is $2$:
$$3p+q=2\qquad(2)$$
From (1), $q=4-p$. Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{aligned}3p+4-p&=2\\2p&=-2\\p&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}q&=4-(-1)\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p=-1,\ q=5$$
criteria: Forms both equations $p+q=4$ and $3p+q=2$, or equivalent merit
Finds $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ or the gradient of the parallel line, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned}A_1&=P(1.003)-M\\A_2&=A_1(1.003)-M\\&=\left[P(1.003)-M\right](1.003)-M\\&=P(1.003)^2-M(1.003)-M\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$. Use the geometric series sum with $a=1$, $r=1.003$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=50\,000(1.003)^n-350\times\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}\\&=50\,000(1.003)^n-\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n+\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\\&=-\dfrac{200\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n+\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{200\,000}{3}\times 1.003^n&=\dfrac{350\,000}{3}\\1.003^n&=\dfrac{7}{4}\\n\log 1.003&=\log\dfrac{7}{4}\\n&=\dfrac{\log\frac{7}{4}}{\log 1.003}\\&=186.818\ldots\\&\approx 187\text{ months}\end{aligned}$$
It takes $187$ months, that is $15$ years and $7$ months, to pay off the loan.

solution sketch: right triangle with hypotenuse 6, legs x and y, angle tan^-1(2)

solutions.latex:
$OS=6$ (the radius of the circle $x^2+y^2=36$) and $OR=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle SOR&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times OS\times OR\times\sin\alpha\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6\times 4\times\sin\alpha\\&=12\sin\alpha\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only; one-row rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$T$ is on the $y$-axis, so $\angle ROT=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\angle TOS=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha$. With $OT=2$ and $OS=6$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area of }\triangle TOS&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6\times 2\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\right)\\&=6\cos\alpha\end{aligned}$$
The quadrilateral $ORST$ is $\triangle SOR$ and $\triangle TOS$ together.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=12\sin\alpha+6\cos\alpha\\&=6\cos\alpha\left(2\cdot\dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}+1\right)\\&=6\cos\alpha(2\tan\alpha+1)\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Use $A=12\sin\alpha+6\cos\alpha$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=12\cos\alpha-6\sin\alpha$$
Stationary point where $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}12\cos\alpha&=6\sin\alpha\\\tan\alpha&=2\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}=-12\sin\alpha-6\cos\alpha$$
When $\tan\alpha=2$, $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ (right-angled triangle with sides $1$, $2$, $\sqrt{5}$).
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}&=-\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{5}}-\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5}}\\&=-6\sqrt{5}\\&\approx-13.42<0\end{aligned}$$
so the area is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \tan\alpha=2\text{ gives the maximum area}$$

In a mathematics examination, 25% of students scored less than 40 marks, 75% of students scored less than 86 marks and the highest mark was 96.

Given that the distribution is symmetrical with no outliers, what is the lowest mark and the median of this data set?

dif.r: Uses symmetry twice: median from quartiles, then minimum from maximum

solutions.latex:
The distribution is symmetrical, so the lower quartile (40) and upper quartile (86) are the same distance from the median.
$$\text{Median}=\dfrac{40+86}{2}=63$$
The highest mark, 96, is $96-63=33$ above the median, so by symmetry the lowest mark is $63-33=30$.
$$\text{Lowest mark}=63-33=30$$
Lowest mark 30 and median 63.

parts.latex:
In an arithmetic series, the sum of the first three terms is 21 and the sum of the first four terms is 36.

What is the sum of the first five terms of this series?

dif.r: Two sum equations solved for a and d, then S5

solutions.latex:
In an arithmetic series the sum of three consecutive terms is three times the middle term.
$$3T_2=21\ \text{ so }\ T_2=7$$
The fourth term is the difference of the two sums.
$$T_4=S_4-S_3=36-21=15$$
Since $T_4-T_2=2d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2d &= 15-7 \\ &= 8 \\ d &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
The middle term of the first five terms is $T_3=7+4=11$, and the sum of five terms is five times the middle term.
$$S_5=5\times 11=55$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-1}$.

What is the domain and range for both $f\left(g(x)\right)$ and $g\left(f(x)\right)$?

dif.r: Domain and range of two composites, with restrictions checked carefully

solutions.latex:
For $f(g(x))=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{x-1}}$ we need $\dfrac{1}{x-1}\ge0$ and $x\ne1$, so the domain is $x>1$. Then $\dfrac{1}{x-1}$ takes every positive value, so the range is $y>0$.

For $g(f(x))=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}-1}$ we need $x\ge0$ and $\sqrt{x}\ne1$, so the domain is $x\ge0,\ x\ne1$.

The domain on which both composite functions are defined is $x>1$. For $x>1$, $\sqrt{x}-1$ takes every positive value, so $g(f(x))$ also has range $y>0$.
$$\text{Domain } (1,\infty),\quad \text{Range } (0,\infty)$$

parts.latex:
The limiting sum of a geometric series is $\dfrac{10}{9}$ and the sum of its first three terms is $\dfrac{26}{25}$.

What is the common ratio of this series?

dif.r: Combine limiting sum and S3 formulas; ratio gives 1 minus r cubed

solutions.latex:
The limiting sum is $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{a}{1-r} &= \dfrac{10}{9} \\ a &= \dfrac{10}{9}(1-r) \end{aligned}$$
The sum of the first three terms is $a(1+r+r^2)=\dfrac{26}{25}$. Substituting for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{10}{9}(1-r)(1+r+r^2) &= \dfrac{26}{25} \\ (1-r)(1+r+r^2) &= \dfrac{117}{125} \\ 1-r^3 &= \dfrac{117}{125} \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{8}{125} \\ r &= \dfrac{2}{5}=0.4 \end{aligned}$$

In a bag of $n$ coloured discs, exactly 7 are red.

Two discs are selected at random, without replacement.

The probability that both discs are red is $\dfrac{21}{55}$.

Which quadratic equation could be used to find the value of $n$?

dif.r: Without-replacement product probability rearranged into a quadratic

solutions.latex:
The probability that both discs are red is
$$\dfrac{7}{n}\cdot\dfrac{6}{n-1}=\dfrac{21}{55}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{42}{n(n-1)} &= \dfrac{21}{55} \\ \dfrac{2}{n(n-1)} &= \dfrac{1}{55} \\ n(n-1) &= 110 \\ n^2-n-110 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
This factorises as $(n+10)(n-11)=0$, so $n=11$.
