Two identical balls are dropped on the Moon and on Earth, each from a height of two metres, and they both eventually stop bouncing.

Calculate the difference in the total vertical distance travelled by these balls.

dif.r: Model bounce distances as limiting sums, handle initial drop

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: bouncing ball dropped from 2 metres

solutions.latex:
Each ball falls 2 m, then each bounce goes up and down, so the distance is a limiting sum of a G.P. with the initial 2 m subtracted.

Moon: $a=2$, $r=0.95$.
$$\begin{aligned} D_{\text{Moon}} &= \dfrac{2\times2}{1-0.95}-2 \\ &= 78 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Earth: $a=2$, $r=0.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} D_{\text{Earth}} &= \dfrac{2\times2}{1-0.5}-2 \\ &= 6 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Difference} &= 78-6 \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, a student who neglects the initial drop and finds $80-8=72$ m is awarded full marks (with correct working).
criteria: Correct Moon and Earth distances, or equivalent merit
One correct distance, or equivalent merit

dif.r: General tangent through origin, rearrange to h = tan h

figures.cap: y=sin x with tangent through origin touching at P(h, sin h)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $y=\sin x$:
$$y'=\cos x$$
At $x=h$ the gradient is $\cos h$.

The tangent at $P(h,\sin h)$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\sin h &= \cos h\,(x-h) \\ y &= (\cos h)x-h\cos h+\sin h \end{aligned}$$
The tangent passes through the origin $(0,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -h\cos h+\sin h \\ h\cos h &= \sin h \\ h &= \dfrac{\sin h}{\cos h} \\ &= \tan h \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=\tan h$$
criteria: Substitutes the origin into the tangent, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Trapezoidal rule with exact trig function values

solutions.latex:
With 3 function values on $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, there are 2 strips, so $h=\dfrac{\pi/2-0}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, and the $x$ values are $0$, $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

For $f(x)=x\sin^2x$:
$$f(0)=0,\qquad f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^2=\dfrac{\pi}{8},\qquad f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$
By the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left\{f(0)+2f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi/4}{2}\left\{0+2\times\dfrac{\pi}{8}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{8}\times\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{3\pi^2}{32} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct $y$-values and trapezoidal rule substitution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Derivation of $h$ added.

$$A=\int_0^1\left((e-1)x-(e^x-1)\right)dx$$

Using the definition of a cumulative distribution function

$$F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\ \text{ for } a\le x\le b$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.

Show that after seven months, the total amount Sergio owes is:

$$A_7=12500\times1.0075-R(6\times1.0075+1)$$

dif.r: Non-standard interest-free period before compounding recurrence begins

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the monthly repayment \$$R$ required to pay back the loan, correct to the nearest dollar.

dif.r: Generalise unusual recurrence, sum GP of 54 terms, solve for R

solutions.latex:
In the first six months no interest is charged, so each repayment reduces the balance by $R$:
$$A_1=12\,500-R,\quad A_2=12\,500-2R,\quad A_3=12\,500-3R$$
so $A_6=12\,500-6R$.

The monthly rate is $r=\dfrac{0.09}{12}=0.0075$.

In month 7, interest is added and then $R$ is paid:
$$\begin{aligned} A_7 &= A_6\times1.0075-R \\ &= (12\,500-6R)\times1.0075-R \\ &= 12\,500\times1.0075-6R\times1.0075-R \\ &= 12\,500\times1.0075-R(6\times1.0075+1) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.format_note: Source rubric was one-mark-per-step; rewritten top-down by us.

solutions.latex:
Continue the pattern, interest then repayment each month:
$$A_8=A_7\times1.0075-R=12\,500\times1.0075^2-R(6\times1.0075^2+1.0075+1)$$
$$A_9=12\,500\times1.0075^3-R(6\times1.0075^3+1.0075^2+1.0075+1)$$
Hence
$$A_n=12\,500\times1.0075^{n-6}-R\left(6\times1.0075^{n-6}+1+1.0075+\cdots+1.0075^{n-7}\right)$$
The loan lasts $n=5\times12=60$ months:
$$A_{60}=12\,500\times1.0075^{54}-R\left(6\times1.0075^{54}+\left(1+1.0075+\cdots+1.0075^{53}\right)\right)$$
The bracketed sum is a G.P. with $a=1$, $r=1.0075$ and $54$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{1.0075^{54}-1}{1.0075-1}$.

The loan is repaid, so $A_{60}=0$:
$$12\,500\times1.0075^{54}=R\left(6\times1.0075^{54}+\dfrac{1.0075^{54}-1}{0.0075}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} R &= \dfrac{12\,500\times1.0075^{54}}{6\times1.0075^{54}+\frac{1.0075^{54}-1}{0.0075}} \\ &\approx \$248.66 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ R\approx\$249$$
criteria: Correct equation for $R$, or equivalent merit
Develops the series, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{2x}$ is shown below.

\exfigure{1614_q18_1}

Upper and lower rectangles of width $0.5$ units are drawn from the $x$-axis to the curve between $x=1$ and $x=2$ as shown in the diagram.

By considering the areas of the rectangles, show that $\dfrac{7}{24}<\ln\sqrt{2}<\dfrac{5}{12}$.

dif.r: Compare rectangle sums with exact log integral to bound

figures.cap: y=1/(2x) with upper and lower rectangles between x=1 and x=2

solutions.latex:
The curve $y=\dfrac{1}{2x}$ is decreasing, so the lower rectangles have area less than the integral and the upper rectangles have area greater than it.

The heights are $y=\dfrac{1}{2}$ at $x=1$, $y=\dfrac{1}{3}$ at $x=1.5$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{4}$ at $x=2$.

Lower rectangles:
$$\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{7}{24}$$
Upper rectangles:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{5}{12}$$
The exact area is
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\dfrac{dx}{2x} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln x\right]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}(\ln2-\ln1) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln2 \\ &= \ln\sqrt2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{7}{24}<\ln\sqrt2<\dfrac{5}{12}$$
criteria: Both rectangle sums correct and integral evaluated to $\ln\sqrt2$, or equivalent merit
Both rectangle sums correct, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta}$?

dif.r: Common denominator then two Pythagorean identities.

solutions.latex:
Use a common denominator, then $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta} &= \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta + 1 - \sin\theta}{1 - \sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= 2\sec^2\theta \\ &= 2\left(1 + \tan^2\theta\right) \\ &= 2 + 2\tan^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: Which if the following is equivalent to $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\dfrac{\sqrt{x}\,(2x+1)}{3-4x^2}\right)$?

dif.r: Log laws to expand, then three chain-rule log derivatives; sign care.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws, expand the logarithm first.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\dfrac{\sqrt{x}\,(2x+1)}{3-4x^2}\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\ln x + \ln(2x+1) - \ln\left(3-4x^2\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2x} + \dfrac{2}{2x+1} + \dfrac{8x}{3-4x^2}\end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex: Which transformations listed are required to obtain the graph of $y = x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3$ from the graph of $y = 4x^2 + x$?

dif.r: Must recognise target as f(x/2)+3; horizontal dilation easily misread.

options.label: A
options.latex: Horizontal dilation by a factor of 2; vertical translation of 3 units upwards

options.label: B
options.latex: Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$; vertical translation of 3 units to downwards

options.label: C
options.latex: Vertical dilation by a factor of 2; horizontal translation of 3 units in to the right

options.label: D
options.latex: Vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$; horizontal translation of 3 units to the left

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x) = 4x^2 + x$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) + 3 &= 4\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right)^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3 \\ &= x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x + 3 \end{aligned}$$
The graph of $y = f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) + 3$ is obtained from $y = f(x)$ by a horizontal dilation of factor 2 and a vertical translation of 3 units upwards.

This is option A.

parts.latex:
The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is given by

$$P\left(X = 2^{-n}\right) = 0.1 \times 0.9^{n-1}, \text{ where } n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$$

What is the expected value of $X$?

dif.r: Infinite distribution; recognise expected value as geometric limiting sum.

solutions.latex:
$X$ takes the values $2^{-1}, 2^{-2}, 2^{-3}, \ldots$ with probabilities $0.1,\ 0.1 \times 0.9,\ 0.1 \times 0.9^2, \ldots$

The expected value is a geometric series with first term $2^{-1}\times 0.1$ and common ratio $2^{-1}\times 0.9$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(X) &= \left(2^{-1} \times 0.1\right) + \left(2^{-2} \times 0.1 \times 0.9\right) + \left(2^{-3} \times 0.1 \times 0.9^2\right) + \ldots \\ &= \dfrac{2^{-1} \times 0.1}{1 - 2^{-1} \times 0.9} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{11}\end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

questions.stem: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2-1}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $f'(x)$.

dif.r: Routine quotient rule with simplification.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the equation of the normal to the graph of $y = f(x)$ at the point where $x = 2$, in general form.

dif.r: Normal gradient, point-gradient form with fractions, general form.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=x^2-1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{x^2 - 1 - 2x^2}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-x^2 - 1}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f'(x) = \dfrac{-x^2 - 1}{\left(x^2-1\right)^2}$$
criteria: Uses the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Find the point and the gradient at $x=2$.
$$f(2) = \dfrac{2}{2^2 - 1} = \dfrac{2}{3}$$
$$f'(2) = \dfrac{-(2)^2 - 1}{\left(2^2 - 1\right)^2} = -\dfrac{5}{9}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_{\text{normal}} = \dfrac{9}{5}$$
The equation of the normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y - \dfrac{2}{3} &= \dfrac{9}{5}(x - 2) \\ 15y - 10 &= 27x - 54 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore 27x - 15y - 44 = 0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let there be two events, $A$ and $B$, such that $P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.55$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.8$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $P\left(\bar{A} \cap \bar{B}\right)$.

dif.r: One step complement of union.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the value of $P\left(A \mid \bar{B}\right)$.

dif.r: Fill Venn regions then apply conditional probability formula.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram

solutions.latex:
Neither $A$ nor $B$ occurs exactly when $A \cup B$ does not occur.
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(\bar{A} \cap \bar{B}\right) &= 1 - P(A \cup B) \\ &= 1 - 0.8 \\ &= 0.2 \end{aligned}$$

Draw a Venn diagram using the probabilities found.

\exfigure{833_q13_s1}

Using conditional probability,
$$\begin{aligned} P\left(A \mid \bar{B}\right) &= \dfrac{P\left(A \cap \bar{B}\right)}{P\left(\bar{B}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.25}{0.25 + 0.2} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{9} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The sum of the first $n$ terms in an arithmetic series is given by the formula

$$S_n = 3n^2 - 17n$$

where $n > 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the common difference is 6.

dif.r: Must use S1 and S2 to recover terms; unfamiliar to many.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the tenth term in the series.

dif.r: Direct substitution into arithmetic term formula.

solutions.latex:
The series is arithmetic, so $a = S_1$ and $T_2 = S_2 - S_1$.
$$S_1 = 3(1)^2 - 17(1) = -14$$
so $a=-14$.
$$S_2 = 3(2)^2 - 17(2) = -22$$
$$T_2 = -22 - (-14) = -8$$
The common difference is
$$\begin{aligned} d &= T_2 - T_1 \\ &= -8 - (-14) \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the first term of the arithmetic series, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$ with $a=-14$ and $d=6$,
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= -14 + (10 - 1) \times 6 \\ &= 40 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the correct formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Since the introduction of the internet, the number of emails sent has been modelled using the exponential equation

$$M = M_0 e^{kt}$$

where $M$ is the number of emails sent worldwide, in millions, and $t$ is the number of years after the year 1980.

Records show that $45\,000$ emails were sent in 1980 and 306 billion emails were sent in the year 2020.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $M_0$ and $k$, correct to three decimal places.

dif.r: Unit conversion to millions, then solve exponential for k with logs.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many emails, to the nearest million, are expected to be sent in the year 2025?

dif.r: Substitute t=45 into found model.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the rate at which the number of emails sent increased in the year 2000, correct to the nearest million per year.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential model, substitute t=20, interpret units.

criteria: Finds the value of $M_0$ or $k$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added final decimal line $k\approx0.393$ (computed: ln 6,800,000 ≈ 15.73, /40 ≈ 0.393), since question asks three decimal places; source stopped at exact form

solutions.latex:
In 2025, $t = 45$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 0.045e^{45 \times \frac{1}{40}\ln 6\,800\,000} \\ &\approx 2\,186\,679.032 \text{ million} \\ &\approx 2\,186\,679 \text{ million (to the nearest million)} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiating $M = M_0e^{kt}$ gives
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = kM_0e^{kt}$$
In 2000, $t = 20$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt} &= \dfrac{1}{40}\ln(6\,800\,000) \times 0.045e^{20 \times \frac{1}{40}\ln(6\,800\,000)} \\ &\approx 46.153 \text{ million per year} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore \text{rate} \approx 46 \text{ million/year (to the nearest million/year)}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative of $M$ with respect to time, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: At a local fast food restaurant, the probability, $W$, of the ice cream machine working on any given day is $40\%$. Ronald visits the restaurant on three consecutive days attempting to order an ice cream.

parts.label: a

dif.r: Complete tree, complement of all three working.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many days must Ronald visit in order to be $95\%$ confident that he will eventually visit the restaurant when the ice cream machine is working?

dif.r: Set up 1-0.6^n inequality, solve with logs, round up.

figures.cap: partially completed tree diagram
solution sketch: completed tree diagram

criteria: Finds the probability of the ice cream machine working on all three days, or equivalent merit
Completes the tree diagram, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Existing figure kept

solutions.latex:
The machine works on at least one of $n$ days unless it fails on every day.
$$P(W \text{ eventually}) = 1 - (0.6)^n$$
Set this equal to $0.95$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.95 &= 1 - (0.6)^n \\ (0.6)^n &= 0.05 \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln 0.05}{\ln 0.6} \\ &= 5.864\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ must be a whole number, Ronald must visit for $6$ days.
criteria: Establishes an equation in terms of the number of days required, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let $f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points on the graph of $y = f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of a cubic, factorise and second-derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, sketch the graph of $y = f(2x)$.

dif.r: Horizontal dilation of known cubic sketch, halving x-coordinates of key points

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the possible values of $a$ such that the graph of $y = f(2x) + a$ has only one $x$-intercept.

dif.r: Must reason vertical shift against turning values; dilation leaves y-values unchanged

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=f(2x)

solutions.latex:
Differentiating,
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2 + 2x - 1 \\ f''(x) &= 6x + 2 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2 + 2x - 1 &= 0 \\ (3x - 1)(x + 1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x = \dfrac{1}{3} \text{ or } x = -1$$
Test the nature using the sign of $f''(x)$.

parts.latex:
Solve $2\sin^2 x - 5\sin x\cos x + 3\cos^2 x = 0$, for $x \in [0, 2\pi]$.

Leave your answer in exact form

dif.r: Factorise homogeneous quadratic in sin, cos; two tan cases over domain

solutions.latex:
Factorise the left side.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin^2 x - 5\sin x\cos x + 3\cos^2 x &= 0 \\ (2\sin x - 3\cos x)(\sin x - \cos x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Case 1: $2\sin x = 3\cos x$, so $\tan x = \dfrac{3}{2}$.
$$x = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \text{ or } x = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$$
Case 2: $\sin x = \cos x$, so $\tan x = 1$.
$$x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } x = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Makes some progress towards solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Let $f'(x) = x^2 + kx$.

The line $y = 2x + 1$ is a tangent to the graph of $y = f(x)$ at the point where $x = -1$.

Find $f(x)$.

dif.r: Combine tangent gradient and point conditions with integration constant

solutions.latex:
Integrating $f'(x)$,
$$f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 + c$$
The tangent $y = 2x + 1$ touches the curve at $x = -1$, so $f'(-1) = 2$ and $f(-1) = 2(-1) + 1 = -1$.

From $f'(-1) = 2$:
$$(-1)^2 + k(-1) = 2$$
$$\therefore k = -1$$
From $f(-1) = -1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}(-1)^3 + \dfrac{1}{2}k(-1)^2 + c &= -1 \\ \dfrac{1}{2}k + c &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \\ \dfrac{1}{2}\times(-1) + c &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \\ c &= -\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 - \dfrac{1}{6}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Finds a valid primitive function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The account balance, $\$A_n$, at the end of $n$ months is given by the recurrence relation

$$A_n = \left(A_{n-1} + 500\right) \times q$$

What is the value of $q$?

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the time, to the nearest whole month, that it takes for Sienna to reach her savings goal.

dif.r: Build annuity pattern with start-of-month deposits, GP sum, solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Interest for the first month is the monthly rate times the balance of $\$500$.
$$X = \dfrac{4.2\%}{12}\times 500 = \$1.75$$
The balance is the previous balance, plus the deposit, plus the interest.
$$Y = 1005.26 + 500 + 5.27 = \$1510.53$$
criteria: Finds the value of $X$ or $Y$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The monthly growth factor is
$$q = 1 + \dfrac{4.2\%}{12} = 1.0035$$

Build up the balance month by month.
$$A_1 = 500\times 1.0035$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= \left(500(1.0035) + 500\right)\times 1.0035 \\ &= 500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_3 &= \left(500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) + 500\right)\times 1.0035 \\ &= 500(1.0035)^3 + 500(1.0035)^2 + 500(1.0035) \\ &= 500(1.0035)\left(1 + 1.0035 + 1.0035^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
Continuing the pattern, the bracket is a geometric series with $a = 1$, $r = 1.0035$ and $n$ terms.
$$A_n = 500(1.0035)\left(1 + 1.0035 + 1.0035^2 + \cdots + 1.0035^{n-1}\right)$$
Set $A_n = 50\,000$ and use the sum of a GP.
$$\begin{aligned} 50\,000 &= 500(1.0035)\times\dfrac{1.0035^n - 1}{0.0035} \\ \dfrac{2707}{2007} &= 1.0035^n \\ n &= \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{2707}{2007}\right)}{\log 1.0035} \\ &\approx 85.64 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore it will take 86 months for Sienna to reach her savings goal.
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Expresses $A_n$ in terms of a geometric progression, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
At a local bay, the tide height is measured by a buoy. Based on the data, the average tide height of the bay is modelled using the function

$$H(t) = 0.7\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-1)\right) + 0.8$$

where $H$ is the average tide height, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in hours, since 12.00 am midnight.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time when the maximum tide height occurs.

dif.r: Set sine term to 1 and solve for t, convert to clock time

parts.label: c

solutions.latex:
The maximum occurs when the sine term equals 1.
$$\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-1)\right) = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-1) &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t - 1 &= 3 \\ t &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the maximum tide height occurs at 4.00 am.
criteria: Recognises that the maximum average tide height occurs when the sine term equals 1, or equivalent merit

Two groups, Group $X$ and Group $Y$, compare the number of pushups their members can perform. Data from Group $X$ is normally distributed with a mean of 12 pushups. Data from Group $Y$ is normally distributed with a mean of 22 pushups. Both groups have the same standard deviation.

parts.label: a

solutions.latex:
The distributions have the same shape, so $P(X>a)=P(Y<a)$ when $a$ is midway between the means.
$$a = \dfrac{12 + 22}{2} = 17$$

$$\begin{aligned} P(17 \le Y \le 29) &= P(Y \le 29) - P(Y \le 17) \\ &= P(X \le 19) - P(X \le 7) &&(\text{the distribution of } Y \text{ is } X \text{ shifted up by } 10) \\ &= P(X \le 19) - P(X \ge 17) &&(\text{symmetry about } 12) \\ &= P(X \le 19) - \left(1 - P(X \le 17)\right) \\ &= 0.8275 - (1 - 0.7500) \\ &= 0.5775 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t) = -2t^2 + 2t + 4$$

where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.

dif.r: Maximum of quadratic velocity via derivative or vertex

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.

dif.r: Solve v=0, integrate velocity with initial position

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

dif.r: Split integral at direction change and add magnitudes

solutions.latex:
Method 1: maximum velocity occurs when $a(t) = 0$.

Differentiating $v(t) = -2t^2 + 2t + 4$,
$$a(t) = -4t + 2$$
$$\begin{aligned} -4t + 2 &= 0 \\ t &= 0.5 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: since velocity is a quadratic function, the maximum is at the vertex.
$$t = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{2}{2(-2)} = 0.5 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Attempts to solve $a(t) = 0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v(t) = 0$.
$$v(t) = 0 \text{ gives } t = -1 \text{ or } t = 2$$
Since $t \ge 0$, it first comes to rest at $t = 2$.

Since $x(0) = 4$, the position at $t = 2$ is
$$\begin{aligned} x(2) &= 4 + \displaystyle\int_0^2 v(t)\,dt \\ &= 4 + \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3 + t^2 + 4t\right]_0^2 \\ &= 10\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The particle is $10\dfrac{2}{3}$ metres to the right of the origin.
criteria: Finds the distance travelled in the first two seconds, or equivalent merit
Finds the time the particle comes to rest, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t = 2$, so the distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the displacements on $[0,2]$ and $[2,3]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance travelled} &= \int_0^2 v(t)\,dt + \left|\int_2^3 v(t)\,dt\right| \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \int_2^3 v(t)\,dt \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3 + t^2 + 4t\right]_2^3 \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \left[\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}(3)^3 + (3)^2 + 4(3)\right) - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}(2)^3 + (2)^2 + 4(2)\right)\right] \\ &= 10\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the distance travelled by the particle in the third second, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Non-routine composite solid set-up, exposed area insight, then optimise

figures.cap: cylinder of radius r on a cube

solutions.latex:
The volume is the cylinder plus the cube of side $2r$.
$$\pi r^2 h + (2r)^3 = 1.5$$
$$h = \dfrac{1.5 - 8r^3}{\pi r^2}$$
The coated surface is the 6 faces of the cube plus the curved surface of the cylinder. Let $S$ be this area.
$$S = 6\times(2r)^2 + 2\pi rh$$
Substituting $h$,
$$\begin{aligned} S(r) &= 24r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{1.5 - 8r^3}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 24r^2 + \dfrac{3 - 16r^3}{r} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating,
$$S'(r) = 48r - \dfrac{3}{r^2} - 32r$$
For a stationary point, $S'(r) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 16r &= \dfrac{3}{r^2} \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{3}{16} \end{aligned}$$
$$r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} \text{ since } r > 0$$
Test the nature using the sign of $S'(r)$.
$$\begin{aligned} S'(r) &< 0 &&\text{for } r \text{ just below } \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{decreasing}\\ S'(r) &= 0 &&\text{at } r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{stationary}\\ S'(r) &> 0 &&\text{for } r \text{ just above } \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}} &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
So this is a minimum.
$$S_{\min} = 24\left(\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{16}}\right)^2 + \dfrac{3 - 16\times\frac{3}{16}}{\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{16}}} \approx 7.86 \text{ m}^2$$
The minimum surface area is $7.86 \text{ m}^2$ (to 2 d.p.).
criteria: Finds the value of $r$ that minimises the surface area, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative of their equation for surface area, or equivalent merit
Finds an equation for the surface area in terms of one variable, or equivalent merit
Formulates equations to describe the information provided, or equivalent merit

why: Checker got a different answer — The stationary point r^3=3/16 gives h=(1.5-8r^3)/(πr^2)=0, so the 'minimum' is a bare cube with no pillar. The feasible domain is 0<r≤(3/16)^(1/3), and the stored test 'S'(r)>0 just above' uses infeasible r (h<0). 7.86 is only the endpoint value, so the question and solution are degenerate; the owner should review.

questions.stem:
The graphs of $y = \dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2}$ and $y = e^x - 2$ are shown in the diagram below. The two curves intersect at point $A$.

\exfigure{833_q27_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\ln 4$.

dif.r: Equate curves, quadratic in e^x, reject negative root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the exact area enclosed by the curves and the $y$-axis. Express your answer in the form $\ln a + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

dif.r: Area between curves needing f'/f integral and log simplification

figures.cap: graphs of y=3e^x/(e^x+2) and y=e^x-2 meeting at A

solutions.latex:
At the intersection the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2} &= e^x - 2 \\ 3e^x &= (e^x - 2)(e^x + 2) \\ 3e^x &= e^{2x} - 4 \\ e^{2x} - 3e^x - 4 &= 0 \\ (e^x + 1)(e^x - 4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^x > 0$, $e^x \ne -1$, so $e^x = 4$.
$$\therefore x = \ln 4$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve $y = \dfrac{3e^x}{e^x+2}$ is above $y = e^x - 2$ on $[0, \ln 4]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area} &= \int_0^{\ln 4} \left(\dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2} - \left(e^x - 2\right)\right)dx \\ &= \int_0^{\ln 4} \left(\dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2} - e^x + 2\right)dx \\ &= \left[3\ln\left(e^x + 2\right) - e^x + 2x\right]_0^{\ln 4} \\ &= \left(3\ln 6 - 4 + 2\ln 4\right) - \left(3\ln 3 - 1 + 0\right) \\ &= \ln 128 - 3 \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Describes the area using a definite integral, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has a median value of $m$ and a probability density function given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx & \text{if } 0 \leq x < 1 \\ kx^2 & \text{if } 1 \leq x \leq 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k = \dfrac{6}{55}$.

dif.r: Total probability equals 1 across two pieces

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function of $X$.

dif.r: Piecewise CDF, carrying accumulated probability into second piece

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the value of $m$, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Choose correct piece, solve F(m)=0.5 cube root

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1.
$$\displaystyle\int_0^1 kx\,dx + \int_1^3 kx^2\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k}{2}x^2\right]_0^1 + \left[\dfrac{k}{3}x^3\right]_1^3 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2} + \left(9k - \dfrac{k}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{55}{6}k &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k = \dfrac{6}{55}$$
criteria: Writes a valid equation involving the sum of all probabilities, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0 \le x < 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \dfrac{6}{55}\displaystyle\int_0^x t\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{6}{55}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}t^2\right]_0^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55}x^2 \end{aligned}$$
For $1 \le x \le 3$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}\displaystyle\int_1^x t^2\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}\left[\dfrac{1}{3}t^3\right]_1^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 - \dfrac{2}{55} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$F(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{55}x^2 & \text{if } 0 \le x < 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}x^3 & \text{if } 1 \le x \le 3 \end{cases}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Describes the cumulative distribution function using an integral, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Changed dummy variable in integrals from x to t (same mathematics).

solutions.latex:
Since $F(1) = \dfrac{3}{55} < 0.5$, the median satisfies $1 \le m < 3$, so use the second piece with $F(m) = 0.5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{55} + \dfrac{2}{55}m^3 &= 0.5 \\ 2 + 4m^3 &= 55 \\ m &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{53}{4}} \\ &\approx 2.37 \end{aligned}$$
The median is $m \approx 2.37$ (to 2 d.p.).
criteria: Recognises that $1 \le m < 3$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Two surveyors, $A$ and $B$, stand on level ground to observe a large tree. The tree is directly north of surveyor $A$ who sights the top of the tree at an angle of elevation of $52^\circ$.

Surveyor $B$ is 27 metres away from Surveyor $A$ on a bearing of $043^\circ$ and sights the top of the tree at an angle of elevation of $46^\circ$.

Find the height, $h$, of the tree correct to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tree seen from two points on level ground, elevation and bearings) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

dif.r: 3D elevations combined with cosine rule giving quadratic in h

figures.cap: solution sketch: diagram of surveyors and tree

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{833_q29_s1}

Let $C$ be the point at the base of the tree. Using the tangent ratio in the two right-angled triangles,
$$AC = \dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}, \qquad BC = \dfrac{h}{\tan 46^\circ}$$
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 27$ and $\angle CAB = 43^\circ$ (the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $043^\circ$ and $C$ is due north of $A$). Apply the cosine rule.
$$\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 46^\circ}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}\right)^2 + 27^2 - 2\times\dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}\times 27\times\cos 43^\circ$$
Rearranging,
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\tan^2 52^\circ} - \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 46^\circ}\right)h^2 - \dfrac{54\cos 43^\circ}{\tan 52^\circ}h + 27^2 \\ 0 &\approx -0.32215h^2 - 30.85539h + 729 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula, with $h > 0$,
$$h = \dfrac{30.855\ldots - \sqrt{30.855\ldots^2 - 4\times(-0.322\ldots)\times 729}}{2\times(-0.322\ldots)} \approx 19.6$$
$$\therefore h \approx 20 \text{ metres (to the nearest metre)}$$
criteria: Makes progress in solving for $h$, or equivalent merit
Forms a relationship, in terms of $h$, between the edges in the base triangle, or equivalent merit
Expresses the edge $AC$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Quadratic formula root choice: the negative-denominator form gives the positive root.

parts.latex:
The circle $(x-1)^2 + y^2 = 9$ is translated 3 units up and 2 units left.

What is the equation of the circle after these translations?

dif.r: Direct translation of circle equation, one routine step

solutions.latex:
Translating 2 units left replaces $x$ by $x+2$; translating 3 units up replaces $y$ by $y-3$.

$$(x-1+2)^2+(y-3)^2=9$$
so
$$(x+1)^2+(y-3)^2=9$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: The graph of $f(x)$ is obtained from $g(x) = \sqrt{x-6}$ by a dilation with a scale factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ from the $y$-axis. Which of the following is $f(x)$?

dif.r: Horizontal dilation: must know scale 1/3 replaces x by 3x

solutions.latex:
A dilation by scale factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$ from the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $3x$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= g(3x) \\ &= \sqrt{3x-6} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

solutions.latex:
The graph is flipped (reflected in the horizontal axis), so $k<0$, and $|k|=3$, hence $k=-3$.

The period is $4\pi$, and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{a}$, so
$$a=\dfrac{2\pi}{4\pi}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The centre line is the mean of the maximum and minimum values:
$$c=\dfrac{4+(-2)}{2}=1$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex: What is the range of the function $y = 2\sqrt{9 - x^2} + 1$ ?

dif.r: Bound semicircle expression then scale and shift to get range

solutions.latex:
The square root needs $9-x^2\ge 0$, so $x\in[-3,3]$.

Then $0\le\sqrt{9-x^2}\le 3$.

So the range is $[1,7]$, option A.

parts.latex: Explain why the graph of $y = \tan x$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ .

dif.r: Short explanation: cos zero makes tan undefined

solutions.latex:
Since $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, and at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ we have $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}=0$ while $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1$.

So $\tan x$ would be $\dfrac{1}{0}$, which is undefined.

Hence $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is a vertical asymptote.

parts.latex:
Consider the following data set.

$4\quad 7\quad 7\quad 9\quad 12\quad 15$

Which row of the table shows how the median and mean are affected when a score of 9 is added to the data set?

dif.r: Direct median and mean recalculation after adding one score

options.label: B
options.latex: Median: stays the same; mean: stays the same

options.label: C
options.latex: Median: changes; mean: stays the same

options.label: D
options.latex: Median: stays the same; mean: changes

solutions.latex:
Original data set (6 scores): the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th scores.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{median} &= \dfrac{7+9}{2} = 8 \\ \text{mean} &= \dfrac{4+7+7+9+12+15}{6} = \dfrac{54}{6} = 9 \end{aligned}$$
Add a score of 9: the data set is $4,\ 7,\ 7,\ 9,\ 9,\ 12,\ 15$ (7 scores), so the median is the 4th score.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{median} &= 9 \\ \text{mean} &= \dfrac{54+9}{7} = \dfrac{63}{7} = 9 \end{aligned}$$
The median changes from $8$ to $9$, and the mean stays at $9$ (adding a score equal to the mean does not change the mean).

Therefore the row is: median changes, mean stays the same.

Differentiating, we have the first and second derivatives.
$$f'(x) = 2x^3 - 18x^2 + 40x,\qquad f''(x) = 6x^2 - 36x + 40$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.

So $x = 0, 4, 5$.

The sign of $f''(x)$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=40>0 &&\text{minimum at } (0,0)\\ f''(4)&=-8<0 &&\text{maximum at } (4,64)\\ f''(5)&=10>0 &&\text{minimum at } (5,62.5) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A population, $P$, which is initially 40 500, varies according to the formula $P = 40500\,b^{\frac{-t}{5}}$ where $b$ is a positive constant and $t$ is time in years, $t \ge 0$

The population is 1500 after 15 years.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of decrease is 25 people per year.

dif.r: Find b, differentiate exponential base b, solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Substitute $P = 1500$, $t = 15$ to find $b$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1500 &= 40500\,b^{-\frac{15}{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{27} &= b^{-3} \\ 27 &= b^3 \\ b &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
We want $t$ when $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -25$.

Using $y = a^x$, $y' = \ln a \cdot a^x$ on $P = 40500 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 40500 \times \dfrac{-1}{5}\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} \\ &= -8100\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $-25$.
$$\begin{aligned} -8100\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} &= -25 \\ 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{324\ln 3} \\ -\dfrac{t}{5} &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{324\ln 3}\right)}{\ln 3} \\ t &= \dfrac{-5\ln\left(\frac{1}{324\ln 3}\right)}{\ln 3} \\ &= 26.737\ldots \\ &\approx 26.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t \approx 26.7 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds $b$, sets $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-25$ and finds a correct derivative, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: cylinder with radius r and height h

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cylinder is $V = \pi r^2 h$, and $V = 380$, so we make $h$ the subject.
$$380 = \pi r^2 h,\qquad h = \dfrac{380}{\pi r^2}$$
Substitute into $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{380}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{760\pi r}{\pi r^2} \\ &= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{760}{r} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Criteria rewritten top-down from source rows.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $A$ twice.
$$\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 4\pi r - \dfrac{760}{r^2},\qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} = 4\pi + \dfrac{1520}{r^3}$$
Since $r > 0$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} > 0$, therefore $A$ has a minimum value.

The minimum occurs when $\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4\pi r - \dfrac{760}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 4\pi r^3 &= 760 \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{760}{4\pi} \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{760}{4\pi}} \\ &\approx 3.925 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r \approx 3.925 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct first derivative and shows minimum using the second derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \ln x + \dfrac{x}{x} \\ &= \ln x + 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$$

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln x + 1 &= 0 \\ \ln x &= -1 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{e} \end{aligned}$$
This is the only solution, so there is one stationary point.
$$f(e^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{e}\ln e^{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{e}$$
The sign of $f''(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ decides the nature. The domain is $x > 0$, so $f''(x) > 0$.
$$\therefore\ \left(e^{-1}, -e^{-1}\right) \text{ is a minimum.}$$

questions.std: Standard, Year 11: Data analysis (MST-11-08)

parts.latex:
Harry's previous four test scores on Statistics were 93%, 94%, 96% and 98%.

In the next test, which is out of a maximum of 100 marks, he wants to achieve $x\%$ so that the average of all the scores is 97%.

What is the value of $x$?
parts.note: Mean of a data set (summary statistics) has no 2024 Advanced dot point.

dif.r: Mean equation in reverse, then must notice 104% is impossible.

solutions.latex:
The average of all five scores is 97%, so
$$\dfrac{93+94+96+98+x}{5}=97$$
The four scores sum to $381$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 381+x &= 485 \\ x &= 104 \end{aligned}$$
The test is out of 100, so $x=104$ is impossible.

Hence there is no solution for $x$.

dif.r: Read amplitude and period off a sine graph.

figures.cap: graph of a sine curve with amplitude 3 and period 4π

solutions.latex:
The graph is a sine curve through the origin, so $y=A\sin(kx)$.

The amplitude is $A=3$.

The period is $4\pi$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2\pi}{k} &= 4\pi \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=3\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$$

questions.review_note: Options A and B printed as 'sin 3' and '-3 sin 3' (no x); likely typo

parts.latex:
A function $f(x)$ has gradient function $f'(x) = \sin 3x$.

Which of the following represents the concavity of $f(x)$?

dif.r: One step: differentiate sin 3x to get f''.

solutions.latex:
Concavity is given by the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \sin 3x \\ f''(x) &= 3\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f''(x)=3\cos 3x$$

parts.latex: Find $x'(t)$ given $x(t) = \ln\left(2e^{-3t}\right)$

dif.r: Log derivative, or log laws first, then simplify to a constant.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $\ln f(t)$ gives $\dfrac{f'(t)}{f(t)}$, with $f(t)=2e^{-3t}$.
$$\begin{aligned} x'(t) &= \dfrac{2e^{-3t}\times(-3)}{2e^{-3t}} \\ &= -3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Once upon a time, world leaders Gary, Figen, John and Julian had a meeting and implemented policies to control the rising global temperature. The rise of temperature has been slowing down since then.

Let $T$ be the temperature $y$ years after the policies were implemented.

Which of the following graphs represent $T$ as a function of $y$?

dif.r: Turn 'rising more slowly' into increasing and concave down.

figures.cap: option A: T increasing at a decreasing rate
option B: T decreasing at a decreasing rate
option C: T increasing at an increasing rate
option D: T decreasing at an increasing rate

solutions.latex:
Temperature is still rising, but more slowly, so $T$ is increasing at a decreasing rate: the graph is increasing and concave down.

This is the graph in option A.

parts.latex: Which of the following is the anti-derivative of $x\left(1+\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\right)^4$?

dif.r: Reverse chain rule, inner derivative exactly x.

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle \int f'(x)\big(f(x)\big)^n\,dx=\dfrac{\big(f(x)\big)^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$ with $f(x)=1+\dfrac{1}{2}x^2$ and $f'(x)=x$:
$$\int x\left(1+\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\right)^4dx=\dfrac{1}{5}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\right)^5+C$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be an odd function and $g(x)$ be an even function.

Given that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are continuous and $k$ is a positive constant,

which of the following is NOT always true?

dif.r: Abstract odd/even composition and integral reasoning across four options.

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Option A: $g(f(-x))=g(-f(x))=g(f(x))$, which is even, so A is true.

Option B: $f(-2x)+2(-x)=-\big[f(2x)+2x\big]$, which is odd, so the integral is $0$ and B is true.

Option C: $g(-2x)f(-2x)=-g(2x)f(2x)$, which is odd, so the integral is $0$ and C is true.

Option D: $f(g(-x))=f(g(x))$ is even, and the integral of an even function can be zero, so D is not always true.

questions.stem:
The cumulative frequency graph, published by DAHTAH, shows the distribution of the number of app downloads made by 100 people in an hour.

\exfigure{1037_q11_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the interquartile range for the number of downloads.
parts.note: Interquartile range from a cumulative frequency graph (IQR is Standard statistics).

dif.r: Read two quartiles off a cumulative frequency graph, then subtract.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the mode for the number of downloads?

dif.r: Unusual: mode is where the cumulative graph rises most steeply.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
One minute, after representing the data on the graph, it was reported that 15 people made 10 downloads during that hour. This piece of data was delayed due to a technical glitch. If this new set of data is an outlier then DAHTAH will not update the graph. Otherwise, the graph has to be updated to include this piece of information.

Does DAHTAH need to update the graph to include this latest piece of information? Show your mathematical reasoning.
parts.note: Outlier test using IQR fences (Standard statistics).

dif.r: Outlier fence calculation and contextual decision; boundary case needs care.

figures.cap: cumulative frequency histogram and ogive of number of downloads

solutions.latex:
From the cumulative frequency graph:
$$Q_1=16,\quad Q_3=20$$
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3-Q_1 \\ &= 20-16 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds either $Q_1$ or $Q_3$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The mode is where the cumulative frequency graph rises most steeply (the greatest increase).
$$\text{Mode}=20$$

A value is an outlier if it is below $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1-1.5\times IQR &= 16-1.5\times 4 \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
The value 10 is not below the lower fence, so it is not an outlier.

Therefore the graph needs updating.
criteria: Calculates the lower fence, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $0 \le x \le 4\pi$

dif.r: Standard trig equation; adjust domain for x/3 and find two solutions.

solutions.latex:
Since $0\le x\le 4\pi$, we have
$$0\le \dfrac{x}{3}\le \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
Solving $\tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ (tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants):
$$\dfrac{x}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{2}$$
criteria: Provides some correct working, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a

dif.r: Read period and amplitude directly from the equation.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: $y = 2\cos(2x+\pi) - 1$ represents the temperature in a freezer in degrees Celsius at time $x$ hours, where $x=0$ corresponds to the time 9.20am. At what time is the temperature dropping most rapidly during the time interval $0 \le x \le \pi$ hours? Give your answer to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Read 'dropping fastest' as most negative gradient, choose root, convert time.

skills: Maxima and minima from the range

figures.cap: solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
For $y=a\cos(bx+c)+d$, the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$ and the amplitude is $|a|$.
$$\text{Period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$$
$$\text{Amplitude}=2$$
criteria: Correct period or amplitude, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-intercepts by letting $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos(2x+\pi)-1 &= 0 \\ \cos(2x+\pi) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

\exfigure{1037_q13_s1}
criteria: Correct shape and domain, or the $x$-intercepts, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw (key 1037_q13_s1). It should show maximum y=1 at x=pi/2 and y=-3 at x=0 and x=pi, with x-intercepts pi/3 and 2pi/3.

solutions.latex:
The line $y=4-x$ is above the curve on the interval, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_0^\pi \Big(4-x-\big(2\cos(2x+\pi)-1\big)\Big)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^\pi (5-x+2\cos 2x)\,dx \\ &= \left[5x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\sin 2x\right]_0^\pi \\ &= 5\pi-\dfrac{\pi^2}{2} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral and primitive, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The temperature drops most rapidly where the gradient is most negative, on the axis $y=-1$, since $\cos(2x+\pi)=-\cos 2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} -2\cos 2x-1 &= -1 \\ \cos 2x &= 0 \\ x &= \dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The curve is decreasing at $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, so choose $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\approx 2$ hours 21 minutes.

Adding this to 9:20 am gives
$$\therefore\ \text{the time is } 11{:}41 \text{ am}$$
criteria: Finds the correct $x$ value, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The function $y = \ln x$ is defined in the domain $e \le x \le e^2$.

Find the area between its graph and the $y$ axis.

dif.r: Area against y-axis: invert to x=e^y and change limits.

skills: Area with respect to the y-axis

solutions.latex:
Make $x$ the subject: $y=\ln x$ gives $x=e^y$.

When $x=e$, $y=1$; when $x=e^2$, $y=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_1^2 x\,dy \\ &= \int_1^2 e^y\,dy \\ &= \Big[e^y\Big]_1^2 \\ &= e^2-e \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Chi translated the function $f(x) = \sqrt{4-x^2}$ vertically by 2 units and then dilated it vertically by a factor of 3.

Find the expression for this new function, $g(x)$, and neatly sketch its graph.

dif.r: Order of translation then dilation; sketch a stretched semicircle.

figures.cap: solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Translating $f$ up by 2 units gives
$$h(x)=\sqrt{4-x^2}+2$$
Dilating vertically by a factor of 3 gives
$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &= 3h(x) \\ &= 3\sqrt{4-x^2}+6 \end{aligned}$$
The graph is a semi-ellipse arc with endpoints $(-2,6)$ and $(2,6)$ and maximum $(0,12)$.

\exfigure{1037_q15_s1}
$$\therefore\ g(x)=3\sqrt{4-x^2}+6$$
criteria: Correct function, or correct graph, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Find the first derivative of the following functions:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $y = \ln\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{x^2+1}\right)$

dif.r: Log laws to expand, then routine differentiation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $f(x) = \tan^3 2x$

dif.r: Chain rule applied twice to tan cubed.
Exponential with base 8; recognise 8^e is a constant.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: $y = e^{\cos 2x}\cos 2x$

dif.r: Product rule with chain-rule exponential factor.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$ and $\ln a^n=n\ln a$:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln x-\ln(x^2+1)$$
Differentiating,
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{2x}-\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$$
criteria: Applies the log laws correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, with $u=\tan 2x$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan 2x)=2\sec^2 2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3\tan^2 2x\cdot\sec^2 2x\cdot 2 \\ &= 6\tan^2 2x\sec^2 2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f'(x)=6\tan^2 2x\sec^2 2x$$
criteria: Sets up the chain rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(a^{kx}\right)=k\ln a\cdot a^{kx}$, and since $8^e$ is a constant:
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=e\ln 8\cdot 8^{ex}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{\cos 2x} & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=-2\sin 2x\, e^{\cos 2x} & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -2\sin 2x\, e^{\cos 2x}\cos 2x+e^{\cos 2x}(-2\sin 2x) \\ &= -2e^{\cos 2x}\sin 2x\,(1+\cos 2x) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=-2e^{\cos 2x}\sin 2x\,(1+\cos 2x)$$
criteria: Applies the product rule correctly in part, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source line had the product-rule terms in a different order and with $u'$ written as $-2\sin 2x\,e^{\cos 2x}$ split; the result is unchanged.

questions.stem: Find:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int e^{4-2x}\,dx$

dif.r: Direct integral of a linear-exponent exponential.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \left(1 - \tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right)^2 dx$

dif.r: Expand, use tan²=sec²−1, integrate tan via log; multi-idea.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_0^2 x\sin x^2\,dx$ Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Reverse chain rule definite integral, radian evaluation.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{e^x}{e^{-x}-e^x}\,dx$

dif.r: Must multiply by e^x to reach f'/f form.

solutions.latex:
Expanding the square and using $\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(1-\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2dx &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(1-2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}+\tan^2\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx \\ &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\sec^2\dfrac{x}{2}-2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx \\ &= \left[2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}+4\ln\left|\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\right|\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= 2+4\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \\ &= 2+\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(1-\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2dx=2+\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit
Expands and uses the identity, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\right)=2x$, write the integrand as $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2x\sin x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 x\sin x^2\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^2 2x\sin x^2\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos x^2\right]_0^2 \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos 4-1) \\ &\approx 0.83 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^2 x\sin x^2\,dx\approx 0.83$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{e^x}{e^{-x}-e^x}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{e^{2x}}{1-e^{2x}}\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{-2e^{2x}}{1-e^{2x}}\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|1-e^{2x}\right|+C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int\dfrac{e^x}{e^{-x}-e^x}\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|1-e^{2x}\right|+C$$

A local minimum occurs where $f'(x)=0$, that is $x=4$, and $f(4)=3$:

$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{4}-2x+7$$

The graph $y = f(x)$ consists of a straight interval and a quarter circle.

The $y$-intercept is 4 and the $x$ axis is tangential to the quarter circle at $x = a$

Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)\,dx$

Split the integral into areas: the triangle above the axis, the triangle below, and the region between the quarter circle and the $x$-axis (also below).
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^8 f(x)\,dx &= A-B-C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 4-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 2-\left(2\times 2-\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\times 2^2\right) \\ &= 8-2-4+\pi \\ &= 2+\pi \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos 2x)$

dif.r: Routine product rule.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int x\sin 2x\,dx$

dif.r: Rearrange derivative result and integrate; hence integration by parts.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos 2x)=\cos 2x-2x\sin 2x$$
criteria: Correct derivative of one factor or one term, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a),
$$2x\sin 2x=\cos 2x-\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos 2x)$$
Integrating both sides,
$$\int 2x\sin 2x\,dx=\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}-x\cos 2x+C_1$$
Dividing by 2,
$$\therefore\ \int x\sin 2x\,dx=\dfrac{\sin 2x}{4}-\dfrac{x\cos 2x}{2}+C$$
criteria: Rearranges the result of part (a), or equivalent merit

questions.stem: For the function $y = 4xe^{-x}$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary point and determine its nature.

dif.r: Standard stationary point and nature for xe^{-x}.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any point of inflection.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and test concavity change.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the function showing all important features.

dif.r: Sketch with asymptotic behaviour; mirrors anchor curve sketch.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find an estimation to the area under the graph in the domain $[0, 2]$ using the Trapezoidal rule with three function values.

dif.r: Trapezoidal rule, two strips, direct substitution.

parts.label: e
parts.latex: Explain whether the Trapezoidal rule over estimated or under estimated the exact area in part (d).

dif.r: Justify underestimate via concavity on interval.

figures.cap: solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 4e^{-x}-4xe^{-x} \\ &= 4e^{-x}(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. Since $e^{-x}>0$, $x=1$, and $y=4e^{-1}$.

To find the nature, use the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4e^{-x}(2-x)$$
At $x=1$,
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-4e^{-1}<0$$
$$\therefore\ (1,4e^{-1})\text{ is a maximum turning point}$$
criteria: Finds the stationary point and tests its nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$:
$$-4e^{-x}(2-x)=0$$
Since $e^{-x}>0$, $x=2$. Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} x=1.9:\ & \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=2.1:\ & \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, and $y=8e^{-2}$ when $x=2$.
$$\therefore\ (2,8e^{-2})\text{ is a point of inflection}$$

The curve passes through the origin, has a maximum at $(1,4e^{-1})$ and an inflection at $(2,8e^{-2})$, and approaches the $x$-axis as $x\to\infty$.

\exfigure{1037_q21_s1}
criteria: Correct shape, or correct coordinates of the points, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw (key 1037_q21_s1): origin, maximum $(1,4e^{-1})$, inflection $(2,8e^{-2})$, asymptote $y=0$.

solutions.latex:
Three function values on $[0,2]$ give two strips, so
$$h=\dfrac{2-0}{2}=1$$
The values are at $x=0,1,2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y(0)&=0\\ y(1)&=4e^{-1}\\ y(2)&=8e^{-2}\end{aligned}$$
By the trapezoidal rule,
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left(0+4e^{-1}\right)+\dfrac{1}{2}\left(4e^{-1}+8e^{-2}\right) \\ &= 4\left(e^{-1}+e^{-2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}\approx 4\left(e^{-1}+e^{-2}\right)\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
On $[0,2]$ the curve has a maximum at $x=1$ and the inflection is at $x=2$, so the curve is concave down throughout $0<x<2$.

The trapezium chords lie below a concave down curve.
$$\therefore\ \text{the trapezoidal rule underestimated the area}$$

meta.format_note: Added reason that the curve is concave down on $[0,2]$ (from $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0$ for $x<2$) and chords lie below it.

questions.stem: The water level, measured in meters, at a dam has been changing at a rate of $R = t^3 - 11t^2 + 35t - 29$ for $0 \le t \le 6$ years.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: When is the water level decreasing most rapidly?

dif.r: Minimise the rate itself; endpoint check overturns the stationary-point answer.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the change in water level of the dam for the 6 years?

dif.r: Integrate a rate over the interval to get net change.

solutions.latex:
The water level decreases most rapidly where $R$ is least, so find the stationary points of $R$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= 3t^2-22t+35 \\ &= (3t-7)(t-5) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dR}{dt}=0$ gives $t=\dfrac{7}{3}$ or $t=5$.

Nature, using the second derivative $\dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=6t-22$:
$$\begin{aligned} t=\dfrac{7}{3}:\ & \dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=-8<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ t=5:\ & \dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=8>0 &&\text{minimum, } R=-4\end{aligned}$$
Check the endpoints of the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:\ & R=-29\\ t=6:\ & R=1\end{aligned}$$
The least value of $R$ is $-29$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the water level decreases most rapidly at } t=0$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points and their nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The change in level is the integral of the rate:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6\left(t^3-11t^2+35t-29\right)dt &= \left[\dfrac{t^4}{4}-\dfrac{11t^3}{3}+\dfrac{35t^2}{2}-29t\right]_0^6 \\ &= -12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the water level decreased by } 12 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Using two applications of the Trapezoidal rule, find an estimate for the area of the irregular shape shown below. (Each square on the grid is one square unit.)

\exfigure{1544_q1_1}

dif.r: Direct trapezoidal rule using two strips read from a grid

figures.cap: irregular shape on grid, x from 0 to 4

solutions.latex:
Each trapezium has width $h=2$ units. The parallel sides $d_f$ and $d_l$ are the first and last vertical sides of each trapezium.

Using the trapezoidal rule, $A\approx\dfrac{h}{2}(d_f+d_l)$ for each trapezium:
$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{2}{2}(2+4)+\dfrac{2}{2}(4+3) \\ &=1(6)+1(7) \\ &=13 \text{ square units} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex:
The curve $y=\ln x$ is translated to the left by $\pi$ units and then dilated horizontally by a scale factor of 3.

What is the equation which describes this new curve?

dif.r: Order of translation then horizontal dilation is a common trap

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

solutions.latex:
To translate left by $a$ units, replace $x$ by $x+a$. So $x$ becomes $x+\pi$.

To dilate horizontally by a factor of $k$, replace $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{k}$. Then $x$ is replaced by $\dfrac{x}{3}$ in $\ln(x+\pi)$, so $x+\pi$ becomes $\dfrac{x}{3}+\pi$.

Hence $y=\ln x$ becomes
$$y=\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+\pi\right)$$
This is option A. (Option D, $\ln\left(\dfrac{x+\pi}{3}\right)$, is the result of dilating first and then translating.)

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the key was D; translating left by $\pi$ then dilating horizontally by 3 gives $\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+\pi\right)$, option A.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the key was D; translating left by $\pi$ then dilating horizontally by 3 gives $\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+\pi\right)$, option A.

parts.latex: Find the range of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{3}{2}\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$.

dif.r: Range from centre line and amplitude, routine

solutions.latex:
The curve oscillates about $y=\dfrac{1}{2}$ with amplitude $\dfrac{3}{2}$.

The minimum and maximum values are
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{3}{2}&=-1 \\ \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{3}{2}&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Range}=[-1,2]$$
This is option B.

questions.review_note: Option C is printed as a fraction with denominator 'ln(1/5) . (1/5) x' with the x set as a superscript-like character; transcribed as ln(1/5) . 1/5^x (best reading)

parts.latex: $$\int\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{x}dx$$

dif.r: Standard a^x integral, needs ln(1/5) simplification

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{5}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{x}dx&=\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^x}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}+C \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{5^x}}{\ln 1-\ln 5}+C \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{5^x}}{-\ln 5}+C \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{5^x}\times\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}+C \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5\cdot 5^x}+C \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Assume the weights of newborn babies are normally distributed with a mean of $\mu$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma$. A particular baby has a weight below the lower quartile of the distribution but not in the bottom 10% of the distribution. Which of the following best represents the region in which this baby's weight lies?

dif.r: Same as HSC melon item: locate percentiles in sigma regions

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

figures.cap: option A: normal curve, shaded below mu-2 sigma to about mu-1.5 sigma
option B: normal curve, shaded from far left up to about mu-0.7 sigma
option C: normal curve, shaded between about mu-1.7 sigma and mu-0.7 sigma
option D: normal curve, narrow shaded band between mu-2 sigma and mu-1.2 sigma

solutions.latex:
The baby is below the lower quartile (bottom $25\%$) but not in the bottom $10\%$, so its weight is between the 10th and 25th percentiles.

The lower quartile lies between $0$ and $-1$ standard deviations from the mean.

The 10th percentile lies between $-1$ and $-2$ standard deviations from the mean.

Only diagram C shades this region, so the answer is option C.

parts.latex: Differentiate $x\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$

dif.r: Product rule with chain rule on sin(1/x)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\dfrac{1}{x^2}\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\right]&=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)-\dfrac{x}{x^2}\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) \\ &=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)-\dfrac{1}{x}\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: Solve $\tan\left(x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $[-\pi\le x\le\pi]$

dif.r: Shifted tan equation, adjusting domain to select solutions

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta=x+\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$. Then $-\pi\le x\le\pi$ gives $-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\theta\le\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$, and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ has solutions $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}+n\pi$.

Listing solutions of $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$:
$$\theta=-\dfrac{11\pi}{6},-\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\dfrac{13\pi}{6}$$
Subtract $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ from each:
$$x=-\dfrac{16\pi}{6},-\dfrac{10\pi}{6},-\dfrac{4\pi}{6},\dfrac{2\pi}{6},\dfrac{8\pi}{6}$$
$$x=-\dfrac{8\pi}{3},-\dfrac{5\pi}{3},-\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
Only $-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lie in $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.

This is option C.

meta.format_note: Source wrote the domain as $[-\pi\le x<\pi]$ in its last line; the question has $\le$, so used that (same answers). Added a line on the range of theta, which is arithmetic from the question's domain.

parts.latex:
The probability density function of a random variable is given by:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{50}e^{-\frac{x}{50}} & x\ge 0\\[6pt] 0 & \text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$

What is the median to 1 decimal place?

dif.r: Integrate exponential pdf, set to 0.5, solve with logs

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies
$$\int_0^m\dfrac{1}{50}e^{-\frac{x}{50}}\,dx=0.5$$
Evaluating the integral:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=\left[-e^{-\frac{x}{50}}\right]_0^m \\ &=-e^{-\frac{m}{50}}+1 \end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} e^{-\frac{m}{50}}&=0.5 \\ -\dfrac{m}{50}&=\ln 0.5 \\ m&\approx 34.7 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

meta.format_note: Source used x as both the limit and the variable; the upper limit is renamed m.

questions.stem:
There are three candidates for team leader on a camp, Andie, Bec and Cat.

There are two candidates for team mascot at the camp, Miao and Woof.

Based on a survey of camp attendees, the probability tree shows the likelihood of the candidates being chosen for each position.

\exfigure{1544_q11_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that Andie will be leader with Miao as mascot?

dif.r: Multiply two branch probabilities on a tree

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability that Andie will be the leader or Miao will be the mascot, but not both?

dif.r: Identify three exactly-one outcomes and sum products

can_use: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

figures.cap: probability tree: leader A, B, C then mascot M, W

solutions.latex:
The leader and mascot choices are independent, so multiply the branch probabilities from the tree:
$$\begin{aligned} P(AM)&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

Exactly one of the two events happens in three outcomes: Andie with Woof, Bec with Miao, or Cat with Miao.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly one})&=P(AW)+P(BM)+P(CM) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{9}+\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{18} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates at least one of the relevant product probabilities correctly from the tree, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Chloe plans to build a rectangular enclosure for her new chickens against an existing wall, using 16 metres of wire fencing as shown below. She calls the dimensions of the enclosure $x$ and $y$.

\exfigure{1544_q12_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: She reasons that $2x+y=16$. Write $y$ in terms of $x$ and hence, show that the area of the enclosure can be written as $A=16x-2x^2$.

dif.r: Rearrange given constraint and substitute into area

parts.label: b

dif.r: Read two x-values from graph, compute y each

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine the dimensions (both $x$ and $y$) that will achieve the maximum possible area for the enclosure.

dif.r: Read vertex from graph and find y

figures.cap: rectangular enclosure against existing wall
graph of A=16x-2x^2

solutions.latex:
The fencing covers two sides of length $x$ and one of length $y$, so $2x+y=16$.

Making $y$ the subject:
$$y=16-2x$$
The area is length times width:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=xy \\ &=x(16-2x) \\ &=16x-2x^2 \end{aligned}$$

Draw the line $A=24$ on the graph. It meets the curve where $x=2$ and $x=6$.

These can be checked by solving $16x-2x^2-24=0$.

For each $x$, $y=16-2x$:
$$\begin{aligned} x=2&:\ y=12 \\ x=6&:\ y=4 \end{aligned}$$
The dimensions are $2$ m by $12$ m, or $6$ m by $4$ m.
criteria: Correct values of $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The maximum area on the graph is $32 \text{ m}^2$, at $x=4$.

Then
$$\begin{aligned} y&=16-2\times 4 \\ &=8 \end{aligned}$$
The dimensions are $4$ m by $8$ m.

questions.stem: Differentiate the following with respect to $x$:

dif.r: Power rule on negative index with constant e

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\dfrac{\log_e x}{x^2}$

dif.r: Quotient rule with ln x and simplification

parts.label: c
parts.latex: $\sqrt{\sin x}$

dif.r: Chain rule with fractional power of sin x

solutions.latex:
Rewrite as a power of $x$ and use the power rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{3e}{2}x^{-2}\right]&=-2\times\dfrac{3e}{2}x^{-3} \\ &=-\dfrac{3e}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{\ln x}{x^2}\right]&=\dfrac{\frac{x^2}{x}-2x\ln x}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{x-2x\ln x}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{x(1-2\ln x)}{x^4} \\ &=\dfrac{1-2\ln x}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write $\sqrt{\sin x}=(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and use the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\cos x\,(\sin x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos x}{2\sqrt{\sin x}} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vanna Beach.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Weston.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{1544_q14_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
It then plans to fly directly back to Underwood.

Calculate, to the nearest km, the distance that it will fly.

dif.r: Derive 85 degree angle from bearings, then cosine rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Determine the bearing (from Weston) on which it should fly to return to Underwood.

Give your answer to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Sine rule plus parallel-line angle reasoning to get bearing

figures.cap: journey U to V to W with bearings
solution sketch: journey diagram with north lines and angles, including start of working

solutions.latex:
Let $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be points due north of $U$, $V$ and $W$ respectively.

\exfigure{1544_q14_s1}

The angle at $V$ is
$$\angle UVW=55^\circ+30^\circ=85^\circ$$
Applying the cosine rule in triangle $UVW$:
$$\begin{aligned} UW^2&=70^2+82^2-2\times70\times82\times\cos 85^\circ \\ &\approx 10\,623.452 \end{aligned}$$
$$UW\approx 103.07$$
The helicopter flies $103$ km (nearest km).
criteria: Finds $\angle UVW$ and applies trigonometry to find $UW$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Diagram 1544_q14_s1 already referenced in source; needs to show the bearings, north lines at U, V, W, angles 55 and 30 degrees, and sides 70 and 82 km. Source solution sketch_id is 1544_q14_s2 but figure key 1544_q14_s1 kept as written.

solutions.latex:
Applying the sine rule in triangle $UVW$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle VWU}{70}=\dfrac{\sin 85^\circ}{103.07}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\angle VWU&=\dfrac{70\times\sin 85^\circ}{103.07} \\ &\approx 0.67656 \end{aligned}$$
$$\angle VWU\approx 42.575^\circ$$
Since $WZ$ and $VY$ are parallel north lines, $\angle ZWV=30^\circ$ (alternate angles). So
$$\angle UWZ\approx 30^\circ+43^\circ=73^\circ$$
The bearing of $U$ from $W$ is
$$360^\circ-73^\circ=287^\circ$$
Alternatively, find $\angle VUW\approx 52.4^\circ$ by the sine rule, then $\angle XUW\approx 55^\circ+52^\circ=107^\circ$ and $\angle UWZ=180^\circ-107^\circ=73^\circ$.

Or use the cosine rule:
$$\cos\angle VWU=\dfrac{82^2+103.07^2-70^2}{2\times82\times103.07}\approx 0.73638$$
This gives $\angle VWU\approx 42.576^\circ$ and the same bearing, $287^\circ$.
criteria: Finds a correct acute angle by any method but does not find the bearing, or finds an acute angle incorrectly and applies it correctly to find the bearing

meta.format_note: Source's cosine-rule value was quoted to more decimals; shortened to 5 places. Could reference the part (a) diagram.

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle at time $(t)$ seconds is given by:

$$x=3e^{-2t}+4e^{-t}+2t.$$

Find the exact time at which the particle comes to rest.

dif.r: Velocity zero gives hidden quadratic in e^{-t}, reject negative root

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when the velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-6e^{-2t}-4e^{-t}+2$$
Setting this to zero:
$$-6e^{-2t}-4e^{-t}+2=0$$
Let $u=e^{-t}$, so $e^{-2t}=u^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6u^2+4u-2&=0 \\ 3u^2+2u-1&=0 \\ (u+1)(3u-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-t}>0$, $e^{-t}=-1$ has no solution. So $e^{-t}=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} -t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\ t&=-(\ln 1-\ln 3) \\ &=\ln 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\ln 3 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Correct differentiation and progress towards solving $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$

meta.format_note: Source substituted x=e^{-t}, clashing with displacement x; renamed to u.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show $\dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}=3\sec 3x\,\operatorname{cosec}3x$

dif.r: Short identity proof via sin and cos

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise find $\displaystyle\int 3\sec 3x\,\operatorname{cosec}3x\,dx$

dif.r: Hence recognise f'/f form, giving ln|tan 3x|

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec$ and $\tan$ in terms of $\sin$ and $\cos$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{\cos^2 3x}}{\frac{\sin 3x}{\cos 3x}} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{\cos^2 3x}\times\dfrac{\cos 3x}{\sin 3x} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{\cos 3x\sin 3x} \\ &=3\sec 3x\operatorname{cosec}3x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes correct equivalent fractions in terms of sine and cosine

solutions.latex:
By part (a), the integrand equals $\dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}$, which has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ with $f(x)=\tan 3x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int 3\sec 3x\operatorname{cosec}3x\,dx&=\int\dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{\tan 3x}\,dx \\ &=\ln|\tan 3x|+C \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave ln(tan 3x)+C; modulus signs added since the integral of f'/f is ln|f|.

dif.r: Read amplitude, period and phase from graph

figures.cap: cosine curve, amplitude 2, from -3pi to 3pi, y(0)=-2

solutions.latex:
The curve has the form $y=k\cos(ax+b)$.

The amplitude is $2$ and $k>0$, so $k=2$.

The graph completes $3$ cycles for $0\le x\le 2\pi$, so $a=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=-2$:
$$\begin{aligned} -2&=2\cos b \\ \cos b&=-1 \\ b&=\pi \end{aligned}$$
This is the value with $0\le b\le\pi$.
$$\therefore\ y=2\cos(3x+\pi)$$
Equivalently, from the graph, there is a phase shift of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the left, giving $y=2\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$.

As a transformation of $y=\cos x$: dilate in the $y$ direction by a factor of $2$ (replace $y$ by $\dfrac{y}{2}$), dilate in the $x$ direction by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ (replace $x$ by $3x$), and translate $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the left (replace $x$ by $x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{y}{2}&=\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ y&=2\cos 3\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Any two of $k$, $a$, $b$ correct, or equivalent merit
Any one of $k$, $a$, $b$ correct, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The gradient of a curve is given by $y'=1-6\sin 3x$.

The curve passes through the point $(0,7)$.

What is the equation of the curve?

dif.r: Integrate trig gradient and find constant from point

solutions.latex:
Integrate the gradient:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\int(1-6\sin 3x)\,dx \\ &=x+2\cos 3x+C \end{aligned}$$
The curve passes through $(0,7)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7&=0+2\cos 0+C \\ 7&=2+C \\ C&=5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=x+2\cos 3x+5$$
criteria: Correct integration but does not find $C$, or small error in solution, or equivalent merit
Some attempt to integrate, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: For an arithmetic series the third term ($T_3$) is 32 and the sixth term ($T_6$) is 17.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the common difference.

dif.r: Two term equations, subtract to find d

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the sum of the terms from $T_{10}$ to $T_{20}$ inclusive.

dif.r: Find a, then S20 minus S9 with negative d; careful arithmetic

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic series, $T_n=a+(n-1)d$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} T_3&=a+2d=32 &&(1)\\ T_6&=a+5d=17 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtract $(1)$ from $(2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3d&=-15 \\ d&=-5 \end{aligned}$$
The common difference is $d=-5$.
criteria: Sets up the two equations, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $d=-5$ into equation (1): $a-10=32$, so $a=42$.

The sum of the terms from $T_{10}$ to $T_{20}$ is $S_{20}-S_9$, using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{20}&=\dfrac{20}{2}[2\times42+(20-1)(-5)]=-110 \\ S_9&=\dfrac{9}{2}[2\times42+(9-1)(-5)]=198 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum}&=S_{20}-S_9 \\ &=-110-198 \\ &=-308 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Sum}=-308$$

questions.stem: At 7 pm on a Wednesday evening after a storm, Jack's water tank was full. The capacity of the tank was 3 000 litres. The tap on the tank, however, was leaking such that the change in volume at any time ($t$) hours was proportional to the volume ($V$) of the tank and can be modelled by the equation $V=V_0e^{-kt}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $V_0$, the initial volume of the tank.

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into exponential model; one step

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that the volume of the tank after 3 hours is 1 900 litres, find the value of $k$ correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for k using logarithms

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By the time Jack discovered that the tank was leaking, there were only 250 litres of water remaining. At what time and on which day did Jack discover the leak (correct to the nearest minute)?

dif.r: Solve for t with logs, convert hours to clock time and day

solutions.latex:
The model is $V=V_0e^{-kt}$.

When $t=0$, $V=3\,000$:

$$3\,000=V_0e^0$$

$$\therefore\ V_0=3\,000 \text{ litres}$$

The model is $V=3\,000e^{-kt}$. When $t=3$, $V=1\,900$:

$$\begin{aligned} 1\,900&=3\,000e^{-3k} \\ \dfrac{19}{30}&=e^{-3k} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{19}{30}\right)&=-3k \\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left(\dfrac{19}{30}\right) \\ &\approx 0.1522528008 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k\approx 0.1523 \text{ (4 decimal places)}$$
criteria: Correct progress towards finding $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When $V=250$:

$$\begin{aligned} 250&=3\,000e^{-kt} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{25}{300}\right)&=-kt \\ t&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{25}{300}\right)}{-0.1522528008} \end{aligned}$$

So $t=16$ hours $19$ minutes.

Adding this to 7 pm Wednesday gives 11:19 am Thursday.

$$\therefore\ \text{The leak was discovered at 11:19 am on Thursday.}$$

parts.latex:
Consider the geometric series below:

$$\left(\dfrac{4}{x+1}\right)+\left(\dfrac{4}{x+1}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{4}{x+1}\right)^3+\cdots$$

Show that the series will have a sum to infinity when $x=4$, but not when $x=-4$.

dif.r: Identify ratio, test |r|<1 for two values

solutions.latex:
The ratio is $r=\dfrac{4}{x+1}$. A sum to infinity exists if $|r|<1$.

When $x=4$:

$$r=\dfrac{4}{4+1}=\dfrac{4}{5},\qquad \left|\dfrac{4}{5}\right|<1$$

So there is a limiting sum.

When $x=-4$:

$$r=\dfrac{4}{-4+1}=-\dfrac{4}{3},\qquad \left|-\dfrac{4}{3}\right|=\dfrac{4}{3}>1$$

So there is no limiting sum.
criteria: Sets up and evaluates $r$ for either value, or equivalent merit
