parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y = x\cos x$ at the point where $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

dif.r: Product rule then standard normal equation at exact point

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$

$$y' = \cos x - x\sin x$$

When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $y = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0$.

The gradient of the tangent is

$$m_1 = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_1 m_2 = -1$:

$$m_2 = \dfrac{2}{\pi}$$

The normal passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$:

$$\begin{aligned} y - y_1 &= m_2(x - x_1) \\ y - 0 &= \dfrac{2}{\pi}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ y &= \dfrac{2x}{\pi} - 1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ y = \dfrac{2x}{\pi} - 1$$
criteria: Correctly obtains the normal gradient, or equivalent merit
Correctly differentiates $y = x\cos x$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The weights of metal drums are normally distributed with a mean of 8.1kg and a standard deviation of 2kg.

\exfigure{1321_q26_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What weight would have a $z$-score of $-2$?

dif.r: Direct z-score formula used in reverse, one step

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Use the $z$-score table provided at the back of the paper to answer this question.

Find $P(8.4 \le X \le 11)$, where $X$ is a random variable, representing the weight of the drums?

dif.r: Two z-scores and table subtraction, standard technique

figures.cap: normal curve with mean 8.1 marked

solutions.latex:
The $z$-score formula is $z = \dfrac{x - \bar{x}}{\sigma}$, with $\bar{x} = 8.1$ and $\sigma = 2$.

$$\begin{aligned} -2 &= \dfrac{x - 8.1}{2} \\ x - 8.1 &= -4 \\ x &= 4.1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the weight is } 4.1 \text{ kg}$$

Convert each weight to a $z$-score using $z = \dfrac{x - \bar{x}}{\sigma}$.

$$z = \dfrac{8.4 - 8.1}{2} = 0.15 \qquad z = \dfrac{11 - 8.1}{2} = 1.45$$

Using the $z$-score table:

$$\begin{aligned} P(0.15 \le z \le 1.45) &= P(z \le 1.45) - P(z \le 0.15) \\ &= 0.9265 - 0.5596 \\ &= 0.3669 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P(8.4 \le X \le 11) = 0.3669$$
criteria: Finds the probabilities for both $z$-scores but does not subtract correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds the $z$-score for both weights, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3$ in the domain $-1 \le x < 3$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary point(s) and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of cubic with second derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the point(s) of inflection.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and check concavity change; two routine steps

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Sketch the graph of $y = f(x)$ showing all features. Do not find the $x$-intercepts.

\exfigure{1321_q27_1}

dif.r: Standard cubic sketch from found features, restricted domain endpoints

figures.cap: blank axes for sketch
solution sketch: sketch of y=f(x)

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= x^3 - 3x^2 + 3 \\ f'(x) &= 3x^2 - 6x \\ f''(x) &= 6x - 6 \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2 - 6x &= 0 \\ 3x(x-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x = 0$ or $x = 2$, both in the domain $-1 \le x < 3$.

When $x = 0$, $y = 3$. When $x = 2$, $y = 8 - 12 + 3 = -1$.

The second derivative decides the nature:

$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -6 < 0 &&\text{maximum turning point}\\ f''(2) &= 6 > 0 &&\text{minimum turning point}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ (0, 3) \text{ is a maximum and } (2, -1) \text{ is a minimum turning point}$$

meta.format_note: Added $y=-1$ calculation line. Sketch for the whole question is in part (c).

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection need $f''(x) = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 6x - 6 &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

When $x = 1$, $y = 1 - 3 + 3 = 1$.

Test for a change in concavity:

\extable{Ts3959_1}

The concavity changes at $x = 1$.

$$\therefore\ (1, 1) \text{ is a point of inflection}$$

dif.r: Rewrite with base 2, quadratic substitution, reject negative root

solutions.latex:
Write each term with base $2$: $4^x = 2^{2x} = (2^x)^2$ and $2^{x+2} = 2^2\cdot 2^x$.

$$(2^x)^2 - 4(2^x) = 32$$

Let $u = 2^x$.

$$\begin{aligned} u^2 - 4u - 32 &= 0 \\ (u - 8)(u + 4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $u = 8$ or $u = -4$.

$2^x > 0$ for all $x$, so $2^x = -4$ has no solution.

$$2^x = 8 = 2^3$$

$$\therefore\ x = 3$$
criteria: Correctly obtains $u = 8$ or $u=-4$, or equivalent merit
Correctly reduces the exponential to a quadratic equation and factorises, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Double-angle identity for intersection, curves swap, two trig integrals

figures.cap: curves f(x)=sin x and g(x)=1-cos 2x with shaded region between x=0 and pi/2

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $\sin x = 1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x$, so $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ in the shaded region.

On $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]$ the curve $f$ is above $g$. On $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ the curve $g$ is above $f$.

$$A = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \big(\sin x - 1 + \cos 2x\big)\,dx + \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \big(1 - \cos 2x - \sin x\big)\,dx$$

$$A = \left[-\cos x - x + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} + \left[x - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x + \cos x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}$$

First integral:

$$\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - \left(-\cos 0 - 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 0\right)$$

Second integral:

$$\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\pi + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

Adding the two integrals:

$$A \approx 0.66 \text{ units}^2 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Obtains correct primitive, or equivalent merit
Obtains correct definite integral, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 3^x & \text{for } 0 \le x \le k \\ 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$ correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Integrate exponential pdf to 1 and solve with logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Evaluate the $8^{\text{th}}$ decile correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Build CDF then solve F(x)=0.8 with logarithms

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is $1$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k 3^x\,dx &= 1 \\ \left[\dfrac{3^x}{\ln 3}\right]_0^k &= 1 \\ \dfrac{3^k}{\ln 3} - \dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} &= 1 \\ 3^k &= \ln 3 + 1 \\ k &= \log_3(\ln 3 + 1) \\ &\approx 0.67 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.67$$
criteria: Writes an equation involving a definite integral set equal to $1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The $8^{\text{th}}$ decile is the value $x$ with $F(x) = 0.8$, where $F$ is the cumulative distribution function.

$$F(x) = \int 3^x\,dx = \dfrac{3^x}{\ln 3} + C$$

Since $F(0) = 0$:

$$0 = \dfrac{3^0}{\ln 3} + C, \quad \text{so } C = -\dfrac{1}{\ln 3}$$

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \le 0 \\[6pt] \dfrac{3^x - 1}{\ln 3}, & 0 \le x \le 0.67 \\[6pt] 1, & x > 0.67 \end{cases}$$

Solve $F(x) = 0.8$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3^x - 1}{\ln 3} &= 0.8 \\ 3^x &= 0.8\ln 3 + 1 \\ x &= \log_3(0.8\ln 3 + 1) \\ &\approx 0.57 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the } 8^{\text{th}} \text{ decile is } 0.57$$

parts.latex: Given $f''(t) = t + \sqrt{t}$, find the equation of the curve $f(t)$, given $f(1) = 1$ and $f'(1) = 2$.

dif.r: Integrate twice with fractional powers, two constants from conditions

solutions.latex:
Integrate $f''(t) = t + t^{\frac{1}{2}}$:

$$f'(t) = \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \dfrac{2}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}} + C$$

Using $f'(1) = 2$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{2}{3} + C \\ C &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$f'(t) = \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \dfrac{2}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}} + \dfrac{5}{6}$$

Integrate again:

$$f(t) = \dfrac{t^3}{6} + \dfrac{4}{15}t^{\frac{5}{2}} + \dfrac{5}{6}t + D$$

Using $f(1) = 1$:

$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{4}{15} + \dfrac{5}{6} + D \\ D &= -\dfrac{4}{15} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f(t) = \dfrac{t^3}{6} + \dfrac{4}{15}t^{\frac{5}{2}} + \dfrac{5}{6}t - \dfrac{4}{15}$$
criteria: Obtains correct primitive of $f'(t)$, or equivalent merit
Obtains correct primitive of $f''(t)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line so that its distance $x$ metres from the origin is given by $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Where is the particle initially?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 and evaluate exact cosine

parts.label: b
parts.latex: When does the particle first come to rest?

dif.r: Differentiate trig displacement, solve v=0 for first time

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: When does the particle first pass through the origin?

dif.r: Solve simple cosine equation for first positive solution

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find when the rate of change of velocity is zero.

dif.r: Second derivative of trig function, solve a=0

parts.label: e
parts.latex:
Hence or otherwise, draw a neat sketch of $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$, showing its main features.

\exfigure{1321_q32_1}

dif.r: Sketch phase-shifted cosine on restricted domain using found features

parts.label: f
parts.latex: Calculate the total distance travelled between $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $t = \dfrac{6\pi}{7}$.

dif.r: Must split at turning point and handle crossing origin

figures.cap: blank axes (t horizontal, x vertical) for sketch
solution sketch: sketch of x=4cos(t-pi/3)

solutions.latex:
Initially $t = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is initially } 2 \text{ m from the origin}$$

The particle is at rest when $v = 0$.

$$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -4\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first comes to rest when } t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly to find $v$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at the origin when $x = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first passes through the origin when } t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

The rate of change of velocity is the acceleration $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$.

$$a = -4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

Set $a = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ a = 0 \text{ when } t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly to find $a$ and substitutes $a = 0$, or equivalent merit

Incorrect graph showing all features, or equivalent merit

Sketch still to draw if not yet drawn: $x=4\cos\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ on $0\le t\le\pi$, start $(0,2)$, maximum $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},4\right)$, inflection and $t$-intercept $\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6},0\right)$, end point $(\pi,-2)$. Check: $4\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=-2$. Marking: 3 | Correct answer.

solutions.latex:
From the graph, the particle moves towards the maximum at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ ($x = 4$), then reverses and moves back towards the origin. Split the motion at the turning point.

At $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:

$$x = 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

At $t = \dfrac{6\pi}{7}$, $t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{11\pi}{21}$:

$$x = 4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)$$

From $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ the particle travels $4 - 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

From $x = 4$ to the final position (which is negative, as $\dfrac{6\pi}{7} > \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$) it travels $4 + \left|4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)\right|$.

$$\text{Total distance} = \left(4 - 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right) + 4 + \left|4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)\right|$$

$$\therefore\ \text{total distance} \approx 4.835 \text{ m (3 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Finds either $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ or $f\left(\dfrac{6\pi}{7}\right)$ with $+4$, or equivalent merit
Separates the distances, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A radioactive substance is decaying such that its mass, $m$ grams, at a time $t$ years after initial observation is given by

$$m = 60e^{kt}, \text{ where } k \text{ is a constant.}$$

After 100 years, the mass of radioactive substance is 42 grams.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: Substitute values, take logs for exact k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $t$ when $m = 30$.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for time using logarithms

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 100$ and $m = 42$ into $m = 60e^{kt}$.

$$\begin{aligned} 42 &= 60e^{100k} \\ 0.7 &= e^{100k} \\ 100k &= \ln 0.7 \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k = \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7$$

Using $k = \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7$ and $m = 30$:

$$\begin{aligned} 30 &= 60e^{\frac{t}{100}\ln 0.7} \\ 0.5 &= e^{\frac{t}{100}\ln 0.7} \\ \ln 0.5 &= \dfrac{t}{100}\ln 0.7 \\ t &= 100\times\dfrac{\ln 0.5}{\ln 0.7} \\ &\approx 194.34 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ t \approx 194.34 \text{ years}$$

questions.stem: \$2000 is invested into a credit union account at the beginning of each year and interest is paid at the end of each year, at a rate of $6.5\%$ per annum, on the balance in the account at that time.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of the investment at the end of the 3 years is \$6814.35.

dif.r: Write three compounded deposits and sum to given value

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At the end of how many years, before the next \$2000 is invested, would the accumulated amount in the account first exceed \$100,000?

dif.r: Build GP for annuity, solve inequality with logs, interpret

solutions.latex:
Each \$2000 earns interest at the end of each year it is in the account: the first deposit for $3$ years, the second for $2$ years and the third for $1$ year.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Value} &= 2000(1.065)^3 + 2000(1.065)^2 + 2000(1.065) \\ &= \$6814.35 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly obtains the series, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ year, the deposits have grown for $n, n-1, \ldots, 1$ years.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Amount} &= 2000(1.065)^n + 2000(1.065)^{n-1} + \cdots + 2000(1.065) \\ &= 2000\left(1.065 + 1.065^2 + \cdots + 1.065^n\right) \end{aligned}$$

This is a GP with $a = 1.065$, $r = 1.065$ and $n$ terms, so $S_n = \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$.

$$\text{Amount} = 2000\times\dfrac{1.065(1.065^n - 1)}{1.065 - 1} = \dfrac{2130}{0.065}\left(1.065^n - 1\right)$$

We need the amount to exceed \$100000.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2130}{0.065}\left(1.065^n - 1\right) &> 100000 \\ 1.065^n &> 4.0516 \\ n &> \dfrac{\log 4.0516}{\log 1.065} \\ n &> 22.2 \end{aligned}$$

$n$ is a whole number of years, so $n = 23$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the amount first exceeds \$100000 at the end of 23 years}$$
criteria: Identifies the sum of a GP correctly, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds the series for the amount accumulated at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ year, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
From a circular disc of metal whose area is $100\text{m}^2$, a sector is cut out and used to make a right cone. The radius of the disc is $R$ metres. The perpendicular height of the cone with radius $r$ metres, is $h$ metres.

\exfigure{1321_q35_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the height of the cone is given by $h = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{\pi} - r^2}$.

dif.r: Recognise slant height equals disc radius, apply Pythagoras

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the volume of the cone is given by $V = \dfrac{r^2\sqrt{100\pi - \pi^2 r^2}}{3}$.

dif.r: Substitute h into cone volume, manipulate surd to form

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the volume is maximised when $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}}$.

dif.r: Chain rule on messy root, solve, justify maximum

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Given that the area of the sector used to make the cone is $A = \pi Rr$, show that the angle in this sector $\theta$, which gives a maximum volume for the cone, is $\dfrac{2\pi\sqrt{6}}{3}$ radians.

dif.r: Equate sector area forms, combine earlier results, simplify surds

figures.cap: circular disc with sector removed (radius R, angle theta) and right cone with height h and radius r

solutions.latex:
The disc has area $\pi R^2 = 100$, so

$$R^2 = \dfrac{100}{\pi}$$

When the sector is formed into a cone, the slant height is $R$. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with sides $h$, $r$ and hypotenuse $R$:

$$\begin{aligned} R^2 &= h^2 + r^2 \\ h &= \sqrt{R^2 - r^2} \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{\pi} - r^2} \end{aligned}$$

The volume of a cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$. Substitute $h$ from part (a).

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2\sqrt{\dfrac{100}{\pi} - r^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2\sqrt{\dfrac{100 - \pi r^2}{\pi}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}r^2\sqrt{\pi^2\times\dfrac{100 - \pi r^2}{\pi}} \\ &= \dfrac{r^2\sqrt{100\pi - \pi^2 r^2}}{3} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had an extra duplicated line; removed duplicate chain step only (value unchanged).

solutions.latex:
Write $V$ as a single power so it can be differentiated by the chain rule.

$$V = \sqrt{\dfrac{r^4(100\pi - \pi^2 r^2)}{9}} = \left(\dfrac{100\pi r^4}{9} - \dfrac{\pi^2 r^6}{9}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

$$\begin{aligned} V' &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{100\pi r^4}{9} - \dfrac{\pi^2 r^6}{9}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times\left(\dfrac{400\pi r^3}{9} - \dfrac{6\pi^2 r^5}{9}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{400\pi r^3}{9} - \frac{6\pi^2 r^5}{9}}{2\sqrt{\frac{100\pi r^4}{9} - \frac{\pi^2 r^6}{9}}} \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $V' = 0$, that is when the numerator is zero.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{400\pi r^3}{9} - \dfrac{6\pi^2 r^5}{9} &= 0 \\ \pi r^3\left(400 - 6\pi r^2\right) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $r = 0$ (rejected, no cone) or $400 - 6\pi r^2 = 0$, giving

$$r = \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}}$$

Test the sign of $V'$ either side of this value; the sign is decided by the numerator, $\pi r^3(400 - 6\pi r^2)$.

\extable{Ts3978_1}

The sign of $V'$ changes from positive to negative, so the volume is a maximum.

$$\therefore\ V \text{ is maximised when } r = \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}}$$
criteria: Correctly obtains $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}}$ but does not check it is a maximum, or equivalent merit
Some significant progress towards obtaining $r$, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds $V'$ in any form, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The area of a sector of radius $R$ and angle $\theta$ is $\dfrac{\theta}{2}R^2$. Equate it to the given $A = \pi Rr$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\theta}{2}R^2 &= \pi Rr \\ \dfrac{\theta}{2}R &= \pi r \\ \theta &= \dfrac{2\pi r}{R} \end{aligned}$$

Substitute $R = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{\pi}}$ and $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}}$ (maximum volume, part (c)).

$$\begin{aligned} \theta &= \dfrac{2\pi\sqrt{\frac{200}{3\pi}}}{\sqrt{\frac{100}{\pi}}} \\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{200}{3\pi}\times\dfrac{\pi}{100}} \\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}} \\ &= 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{6}{9}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\pi\sqrt{6}}{3} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \theta = \dfrac{2\pi\sqrt{6}}{3} \text{ radians}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $y=e^{5x}\cos 3x$

dif.r: Product rule with exponential and trig chain factors.
Quotient rule with algebraic simplification.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{5x} & v&=\cos3x\\ u'&=5e^{5x} & v'&=-3\sin3x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= e^{5x}\times(-3\sin3x)+5e^{5x}\times\cos3x \\ &= -3e^{5x}\sin3x+5e^{5x}\cos3x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct differentiation of $e^{5x}$ or $\cos3x$ and attempts product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=10x-3 & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=10 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{(x^2+1)\times10-(10x-3)\times2x}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{10x^2+10-20x^2+6x}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-10x^2+6x+10}{(x^2+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: The curve $y=f(x)$ has gradient function $f'(x)=3x^2-k$, where $k$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$ if the curve has a stationary point at $(-1,3)$.

dif.r: Set derivative zero at given x, one step.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the equation of the curve $y=f(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate gradient function and find constant from point.

solutions.latex:
A stationary point has $f'(x)=0$. At $x=-1$:

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3\times(-1)^2-k \\ k &= 3 \end{aligned}$$

Integrate $f'(x)=3x^2-3$.

$$f(x)=x^3-3x+C$$

The curve passes through $(-1,3)$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= (-1)^3-3\times(-1)+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore f(x)=x^3-3x+1$$

questions.stem:
The discrete random variable $X$ has this probability distribution.

\extable{1322_q18_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is 0.3.

dif.r: Probabilities sum to one, solve linear equation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the expected value and variance of $X$.

dif.r: Standard expected value and variance calculation.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find $P(X\leq 1)$

dif.r: Add two table probabilities.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find $P(X>1\mid X\leq 3)$

dif.r: Conditional probability formula applied to distribution table.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities must sum to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.2+k+0.1+k+0.1&=1 \\ 2k+0.4&=1 \\ 2k&=0.6 \\ k&=0.3 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Fixed: added the line 2k+0.4=1 that the source skipped.

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=0\times0.2+1\times0.3+2\times0.1+3\times0.3+4\times0.1 \\ &=1.8 \end{aligned}$$
Using $E(X^2)=\sum x^2\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2)&=0^2\times0.2+1^2\times0.3+2^2\times0.1+3^2\times0.3+4^2\times0.1 \\ &=5 \end{aligned}$$
Using $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X)&=5-1.8^2 \\ &=1.76 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\leq1)&=P(X=0)+P(X=1) \\ &=0.2+0.3 \\ &=0.5 \end{aligned}$$

Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>1\mid X\leq3)&=\dfrac{P(X>1\cap X\leq3)}{P(X\leq3)} \\ &=\dfrac{P(X=2)+P(X=3)}{1-P(X=4)} \\ &=\dfrac{0.1+0.3}{1-0.1} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Body mass index (BMI) is a measure that can be used to determine a person's healthy weight range. The following graph indicates z-scores of 'BMI-for age' for boys aged 5-19 years.

\exfigure{1322_q20_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How old is Jackson if he has a BMI of 20 and a z-score of 1?

dif.r: Read value directly from z-score curve graph.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Benjamin is 9 years old. If $97.5\%$ of boys his age have a higher BMI than him, what is his BMI?

dif.r: Convert percentage to z=-2 via empirical rule, then read graph.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: c
parts.latex: George is 16 years old and has a BMI of 23.5. There are 40 people in his Year 10 cohort who have a BMI larger than his. Assuming all students are 16 years old, how many people are in George's cohort?

dif.r: Read z, empirical rule tail, reverse proportion to find total.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

figures.cap: WHO BMI-for-age z-score chart for boys 5 to 19 years

solutions.latex:
Reading the graph at a BMI of 20 on the $z=1$ curve:
$$\text{Jackson is } 12 \text{ years old.}$$

If $97.5\%$ of boys have a higher BMI, then $1-97.5\%=2.5\%$ have a lower BMI.

This corresponds to $z=-2$.

Reading the graph at age 9 on the $z=-2$ curve:
$$\text{BMI}=13.5$$

At age 16 with BMI 23.5, the graph gives $z=1$.

Using the $68\%$ rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(Z>1)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(1-P(-1\leq Z\leq1)\big) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-68\%) \\ &=16\% \end{aligned}$$
So $16\%$ of the cohort is $40$ people.

$$\dfrac{40}{0.16}=250$$

Therefore George's cohort has 250 people.

Manavdeep leaves island $A$ in a boat and sails 164 km on a bearing of $070^\circ$ to island $B$. He then sails on a bearing of $194^\circ$ for 241 km to island $C$, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1322_q22_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the size of $\angle ABC=56^\circ$.

dif.r: Angle from bearings using alternate angles; given result to verify.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the distance from island $C$ to island $A$ is approximately $202\ \text{km}$.

dif.r: Direct cosine rule with given angle and sides.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Manavdeep wants to sail from island $C$ directly to island $A$. On what bearing should he sail? Give your answer to the nearest degree.

solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

meta.format_note: Solution diagram requested by style: figure 1322_q22_s1 should be the question's diagram showing north lines at A and B, bearings 070° and 194°, AB = 164 km, BC = 241 km and angle ABC = 56°.

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule in triangle $ABC$:
$$AC^2=164^2+241^2-2\times164\times241\times\cos56^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} AC&=\sqrt{164^2+241^2-2\times164\times241\times\cos56^\circ} \\ &=201.9255\dots \\ &\approx202\ \text{km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

Using the sine rule in triangle $ABC$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle ACB}{164}=\dfrac{\sin56^\circ}{202}$$
$$\sin\angle ACB=\dfrac{\sin56^\circ}{202}\times164$$
$$\angle ACB=42.305\dots\approx42^\circ\text{ (nearest degree)}$$
The bearing from $C$ to $A$ is
$$\begin{aligned} 360^\circ-\big[42^\circ-(194^\circ-180^\circ)\big]&=332^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $\angle ACB$, or equivalent merit

Since $|r|<1$, the sum to infinity exists:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{0.5}{1-\frac{2}{3}} \\ &=1.5\text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Leonard and Howard start jobs at the beginning of the same year. Leonard's annual salary in the first year is \$53000 and increases by $3\%$ at the beginning of each subsequent year. Howard's annual salary in the first year is \$59000 and increases by \$1500 at the beginning of each subsequent year.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that in the $15^{\text{th}}$ year, Leonard's annual salary is higher than Howard's annual salary.

dif.r: Two nth-term formulas (GP and AP) evaluated and compared.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: In the first 15 years, how much in total, does Leonard earn?

dif.r: Direct substitution into geometric series sum formula.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: In which year will Leonard start to earn a salary more than \$90000 a year?

dif.r: Exponential inequality solved with logarithms, then interpreting integer year.

solutions.latex:
Leonard's salaries form a geometric sequence with $a=53000$, $r=1.03$:
$$\begin{aligned} L_{15}&=53000\times1.03^{14} \\ &=\$80167.25542\dots \\ &\approx\$80167.26 \end{aligned}$$
Howard's salaries form an arithmetic sequence with $a=59000$, $d=1500$:
$$\begin{aligned} H_{15}&=59000+1500\times14 \\ &=\$80000 \end{aligned}$$
Since $80167.26>80000$, $L_{15}>H_{15}$.
criteria: Correct value for Leonard or Howard, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the geometric series sum $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ with $a=53000$, $r=1.03$, $n=15$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15}&=\dfrac{53000\times(1.03^{15}-1)}{1.03-1} \\ &=\$985742.435994\dots \\ &\approx\$985742.44 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into the sum formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's second criterion row says 'sum formula' for a part that uses a term formula; kept as is.

solutions.latex:
Leonard's salary in year $n$ is $53000\times1.03^{n-1}$, so we need
$$\begin{aligned} 53000\times1.03^{n-1}&>90000 \\ 1.03^{n-1}&>\dfrac{90}{53} \\ (n-1)\ln1.03&>\ln\left(\dfrac{90}{53}\right) \\ n&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{90}{53}\right)}{\ln1.03}+1 \\ n&>18.91406\dots \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ is a whole number, $n=19$.
criteria: Correct substitution into the term formula, or equivalent merit

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find $P(X>3)$.

dif.r: Definite integral of pdf with complement; routine arithmetic.

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^5kx(5-x)\,dx&=1 \\ k\int_0^5(5x-x^2)\,dx&=1 \\ k\left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^5&=1 \\ k\times\dfrac{125}{6}&=1 \\ k&=\dfrac{6}{125} \end{aligned}$$

The mode is where $f(x)$ is greatest. Here $f(x)$ is a concave down parabola with $x$-intercepts $x=0$ and $x=5$.

The vertex lies midway between the intercepts:
$$x=\dfrac{0+5}{2}=2.5$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the mode of } f(x) \text{ is } x=2.5$$

The probability that $X>3$ is the complement of $P(X\le 3)$, using $k=\dfrac{6}{125}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>3) &= 1-P(X\le 3) \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\displaystyle\int_0^3 (5x-x^2)\,dx \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\left[\dfrac{5\times 3^2}{2}-\dfrac{3^3}{3}-0\right] \\ &= 1-\dfrac{6}{125}\times\dfrac{27}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{44}{125} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X>3)=\dfrac{44}{125}$$

questions.stem:
On any given day, the depth of water in a river is modelled by the function

$$h(t)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right),\ 0\leq t\leq 24$$

where $h$ is the depth of water, in metres and $t$ is the time, in hours, after 6 am.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the minimum depth of the water in the river.

dif.r: Minimum from sine range; one-step recall.

can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the values of $t$ for which $h(t)=10$.

dif.r: Solve trig equation in restricted domain, two quadrants.

solutions.latex:
The minimum of $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right)$ is $-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} h_{\min} &= 14-8 \\ &= 6 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum depth is } 6 \text{ metres}$$

Set $h(t)=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} 14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= 10 \\ 8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= -4 \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{12}\right) &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with $0\le \dfrac{\pi t}{12}\le 2\pi$.
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{12}=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ t=14 \text{ or } t=22$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{\pi t}{12}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ or one correct value of $t$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the curve given by $y=x^3-x^2-x+6$, for $-3\leq x\leq 3$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of cubic with second derivative test.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that there is a point of inflection at $\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{151}{27}\right)$.

dif.r: Set second derivative zero, check concavity change; given point.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the curve for $-3\leq x\leq 3$, showing all key features.

dif.r: Sketch cubic from found features plus endpoints and intercept.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: For what values of $x$ is the curve decreasing and concaving up?

dif.r: Combine signs of first and second derivatives into one interval.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of the cubic curve with key points

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= x^3-x^2-x+6 \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 3x^2-2x-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-2x-1 &= 0 \\ (3x+1)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $x=1$, giving $y=\dfrac{167}{27}$ and $y=5$ respectively.

The second derivative decides the nature.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-2$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=-\dfrac{1}{3}: \quad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 6\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)-2=-4<0 \\ \text{At } x=1: \quad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 6\times 1-2=4>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(-\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{167}{27}\right) \text{ is a maximum turning point and } (1,5) \text{ is a minimum turning point}$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct $x$ values for the turning points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-2$$
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-2 &= 0 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^3-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2-\dfrac{1}{3}+6 \\ &= \dfrac{151}{27} \end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts4025_1}

There is a change in concavity, therefore the point of inflection is $\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{151}{27}\right)$.

criteria: Correct curve with some key features shown, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve is decreasing for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}<0$, that is $-\dfrac{1}{3}<x<1$, and concave up for $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$, that is $x>\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Both hold together when:
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{3}<x<1$$

questions.stem: A tank contains 50 litres of water. A tap at the base of the tank allows water to flow out at a rate proportional to the quantity of water still in the tank at that time, given by the equation $W=W_0e^{-kt}$, where $W$ is the amount of water in the tank and $t$ is time in minutes. After 2 minutes, 10 litres of water has been released.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5}$.

dif.r: Read W=40 from context, solve exponential with logs.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How much water has been released from the tank after 10 minutes? Give your answer to the nearest litre.

dif.r: Substitute into model then subtract to get amount released.

solutions.latex:
Initially $W_0=50$, so $W=50e^{-kt}$.

After 2 minutes, 10 litres has been released, so $W=40$ when $t=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 40 &= 50e^{-2k} \\ \dfrac{4}{5} &= e^{-2k} \\ \ln\dfrac{4}{5} &= -2k \\ k &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$

When $t=10$, using $k=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5}$:
$$\begin{aligned} W &= 50e^{-10\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{4}{5}\right)} \\ &= 16.384 \end{aligned}$$
So 16.384 litres of water are in the tank.
$$\begin{aligned} 50-16.384 &= 33.616 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 34 \text{ litres of water have been released}$$

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\sqrt{3}\cos x$, $0\leq x\leq 2\pi$. The graphs intersect at points $A$ and $B$.

\exfigure{1322_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that point $A$ has coordinates $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.

dif.r: Verify by substituting exact trig values into both functions.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of point $B$.

dif.r: Convert to tan x = sqrt3, solve in domain, find y.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the shaded area enclosed by the two graphs.

dif.r: Area between trig curves; integration and careful exact-value evaluation.

figures.cap: graphs of y=sin x and y=sqrt3 cos x with shaded region between A and B

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into both functions.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y &= \sqrt{3}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The same $y$ value is obtained, therefore $A\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ is a point of intersection of the two functions.

At an intersection, the two functions are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} \sin x &= \sqrt{3}\cos x \\ \tan x &= \sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
Tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants.
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ B\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$$

meta.format_note: Source line read $x=\pi/3,\ \pi+\pi/3=\pi/3,\ 4\pi/3$ (repeated value); tidied to $\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

solutions.latex:
The sine curve is above $y=\sqrt{3}\cos x$ between $A$ and $B$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\left(\sin x-\sqrt{3}\cos x\right)dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x-\sqrt{3}\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}} \\ &= \left(-\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)-\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}+3\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}-3\right) \\ &= 4 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive function, or equivalent merit
Shows area is $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}(\sin x-\sqrt{3}\cos x)\,dx$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v$ m/s. The displacement is given by $x=2t-3\log_e(t+1)$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find an expression for the velocity $v$.

dif.r: Single differentiation of linear plus log term.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the initial acceleration.

dif.r: Differentiate again with negative power, substitute t=0.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: When does the particle come to rest?

dif.r: Set velocity zero and solve simple rational equation.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first three seconds. Answer correct to four decimal places.

dif.r: Must account for direction change; distance differs from displacement.

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of displacement x against t

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2t-3\log_e(t+1) \\ v &= \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2-\dfrac{3}{t+1} \end{aligned}$$

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$v=2-3(t+1)^{-1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 3(t+1)^{-2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{3}{(0+1)^2} \\ &= 3 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct acceleration equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-\dfrac{3}{t+1} &= 0 \\ \dfrac{3}{t+1} &= 2 \\ t+1 &= \dfrac{3}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest when } t=\dfrac{1}{2} \text{ s}$$

The particle turns at $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ (from part (c)), so find the displacement at the end and at the turning point.
$$\begin{aligned} t=3: \quad x &= 2\times 3-3\log_e 4 \\ &= 6-3\log_e 4 \\ &\approx 1.841116 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t=\dfrac{1}{2}: \quad x &= 2\times\dfrac{1}{2}-3\log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+1\right) \\ &= 1-3\log_e\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &\approx -0.216395 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1322_q30_s1}

The particle goes from $0$ to $-0.216395$, then back past the origin to $1.841116$, so the total distance is
$$\begin{aligned} (6-3\log_e 4)+2\left|1-3\log_e\dfrac{3}{2}\right| &\approx 2.273907 \\ &\approx 2.2739 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Diagram 1322_q30_s1 kept as in source (number line of motion).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right)=-\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x$.

dif.r: Chain rule on reciprocal sine, rewrite as cot cosec.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x\,dx$. Give your answer in exact form.

dif.r: Hence integral using given primitive, exact trig evaluation.

solutions.latex:
Write $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}=(\sin x)^{-1}$ and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^{-1} \\ &= -1\times\cos x\times(\sin x)^{-2} \\ &= -\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x} \\ &= -\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $-\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ is a primitive of $\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\left[\dfrac{1}{\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}\right] \\ &= -\left[1-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive function, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A cylinder is inscribed in a cone of radius 9 cm and perpendicular height 25 cm.

\exfigure{1322_q32_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the perpendicular height $h$ of the cylinder is given by

$$h=\dfrac{25(9-r)}{9},$$

where $r$ is the radius of the cylinder.

dif.r: Set up similar triangles in cone cross-section to relate h, r.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by

$$V=\dfrac{25\pi}{9}(9r^2-r^3)$$

dif.r: Substitute h into cylinder volume formula.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the maximum possible exact volume of this cylinder.

dif.r: Given volume function; routine derivative, nature test, exact maximum.

figures.cap: cylinder inscribed in a cone, radius 9 cm, height 25 cm
solution sketch: similar triangles diagram ABC and EDC

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1322_q32_s1}

In the cross-section, $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle EDC$ are similar (common angle at $C$, both right-angled, equiangular).
$$\dfrac{EC}{AC}=\dfrac{ED}{AB}$$
with $EC=9-r$, $AC=9$, $ED=h$ and $AB=25$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{9-r}{9} &= \dfrac{h}{25} \\ h &= \dfrac{25(9-r)}{9} \end{aligned}$$

The volume of a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$; substitute $h$ from part (a).
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \pi r^2\times\dfrac{25(9-r)}{9} \\ &= \dfrac{25\pi}{9}(9r^2-r^3) \end{aligned}$$

For a maximum, set $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dr}=\dfrac{25\pi}{9}(18r-3r^2)$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{25\pi}{9}(18r-3r^2) &= 0 \\ 3r(6-r) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $r=0$ or $r=6$. If $r=0$ cm, the cylinder doesn't exist, so $r=6$ cm.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2}=\dfrac{25\pi}{9}(18-6r)$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } r=6: \quad \dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2} &= \dfrac{25\pi}{9}(18-6\times 6) \\ &= -50\pi<0 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $r=6$ gives the maximum volume.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{25\pi}{9}(9\times 6^2-6^3) \\ &= 300\pi \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ V_{\max}=300\pi \text{ cm}^3$$
criteria: Shows $r=6$ cm produces maximum volume, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the exact value of $\sec 30^\circ + \tan 30^\circ$?

dif.r: Recall exact values for 30 degrees and add

solutions.latex:
Using $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ with $\cos 30^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\sin 30^\circ=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sec 30^\circ &= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \tan 30^\circ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
Adding:
$$\begin{aligned} \sec 30^\circ+\tan 30^\circ &= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D, $\sqrt{3}$.

parts.latex:
Which type of relationship best describes the curve drawn below?

\exfigure{1323_q2_1}

dif.r: Classify relation from graph using vertical and horizontal line tests

figures.cap: ellipse centred at the origin

solutions.latex:
A relationship is one-to-one, many-to-one, and so on, according to how many $y$ values match each $x$ value and how many $x$ values match each $y$ value.

A vertical line such as $x=0$ cuts the curve twice, so one $x$ value gives two $y$ values.

A horizontal line such as $y=0$ cuts the curve twice, so one $y$ value gives two $x$ values.

So the relationship is many-to-many (it is not a function, and its inverse is not a function).

Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex:
Matthew recorded the number of runs scored by each member of his cricket team this season. The results were:

$$25,\ 85,\ 96,\ 104,\ 110,\ 122,\ 124,\ 129,\ 144,\ 144,\ 160,\ 205$$

According to these results:
parts.note: Outliers in a data set (IQR / quartile test) are removed from 2024 Advanced; this is Standard statistics.

dif.r: Find quartiles, IQR, then apply outlier fences

solutions.latex:
The quartiles are $Q_1=100$ and $Q_3=144$, so
$$IQR=144-100=44$$
Outliers lie below $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$ or above $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1-1.5\times 44&=34\\ Q_3+1.5\times 44&=210\end{aligned}$$
Since $25<34$, the score $25$ is an outlier.

Since $205<210$, the score $205$ is not an outlier.

So only $25$ is an outlier (option B).

parts.latex:
For $t \neq 0$, find the limiting sum of the geometric series

$$t+\dfrac{t}{1+t^2}+\dfrac{t}{\left(1+t^2\right)^2}+\dfrac{t}{\left(1+t^2\right)^3}+\cdots$$

dif.r: Limiting sum formula with algebraic ratio and fraction simplification

solutions.latex:
The first term is $a=t$ and the common ratio is $r=\dfrac{1}{1+t^2}$, with $|r|<1$ since $t\ne 0$. Using $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{t}{1-\frac{1}{1+t^2}}\\ &=\dfrac{t(1+t^2)}{1+t^2-1}\\ &=\dfrac{t(1+t^2)}{t^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1+t^2}{t}\end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

dif.r: Compute mean, median, mode from frequency table and compare

solutions.latex:
From the table, the mean is $7.08$, the mode is $7$ and the median is $7$.

So the mode and median are equal, and the mean is greater than both:
$$\text{Mean}>(\text{Mode}=\text{Median})$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be a quadratic polynomial with $x$ intercepts at $x=-5$ and $x=3$.

Which of the following statements is always true?

dif.r: Vertex midway between intercepts gives zero gradient there

solutions.latex:
A quadratic is symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex, and the vertex lies midway between the $x$ intercepts.
$$x=\dfrac{-5+3}{2}=-1$$
At the vertex the tangent is horizontal, so $f'(-1)=0$.

The other options fail: $f'(0)$, $f'(3)$ and $f'(5)$ are at $x$ values other than the vertex, and the gradient of a quadratic is zero only at its vertex.

Hence the answer is option A.

This is option A.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\,dx$?

dif.r: Combine fractions, Pythagorean identity, recognise sec squared integral

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator, then use $1-\sin^2 x=\cos^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int \left(\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\right)dx&=\int \dfrac{(1-\sin x)+(1+\sin x)}{1-\sin^2 x}\,dx\\ &=\int \dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x}\,dx\\ &=\int 2\sec^2 x\,dx\\ &=2\tan x+c\end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

dif.r: Order of several transformations including two reflections and dilation

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

options.label: A
options.latex: Vertical dilation factor $8$, reflect in $x$-axis, reflect in $y$-axis, translate up $6$ units

options.label: B
options.latex: Vertical dilation factor $\dfrac{1}{8}$, reflect in $x$-axis, reflect in $y$-axis, translate up $6$ units

options.label: C
options.latex: Translate up $6$ units, reflect in $x$-axis, reflect in $y$-axis, vertical dilation factor $8$

options.label: D
options.latex: Translate up $6$ units, reflect in $x$-axis, reflect in $y$-axis, vertical dilation factor $\dfrac{1}{8}$

figures.cap: graphs of y=e^x and y=6-8e^{-x} with asymptote y=6

solutions.latex:
Apply the transformations to $y=e^x$ one at a time, in the order of the options.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=e^x \\ y&=8e^x &&(\text{vertical dilation, factor } 8) \\ y&=-8e^x &&(\text{reflect in the } x\text{-axis}) \\ y&=-8e^{-x} &&(\text{reflect in the } y\text{-axis}) \\ y&=6-8e^{-x} &&(\text{translate up } 6) \end{aligned}$$
This is $g(x)$, and it also matches the horizontal asymptote $y=6$.

Options C and D translate first, which gives $y=-(e^{x}+6)$ or similar, with asymptote $y=-6$ instead of $y=6$ after reflecting, so they fail. Option B uses a dilation factor $\dfrac{1}{8}$, which gives the wrong coefficient.

Hence the answer is option A.

parts.latex: Solve $|3x-8|=7$

dif.r: Routine absolute value equation, two linear cases

solutions.latex:
For $|3x-8|=7$, either $3x-8=7$ or $3x-8=-7$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x-8&=7\\ 3x&=15\\ x&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3x-8&=-7\\ 3x&=1\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=5 \text{ or } x=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Finds one correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A circle has the equation $x^2-6x+y^2+4y+k=0$ for some constant $k$.

Find the set of possible values for $k$.

dif.r: Complete squares then require positive radius squared

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-6x+y^2+4y+k&=0\\ (x-3)^2-9+(y+2)^2-4+k&=0\\ (x-3)^2+(y+2)^2&=13-k\end{aligned}$$
This is a circle only if the right side (the radius squared) is positive.
$$13-k>0$$
$$\therefore\ k<13$$

parts.latex:
Marios thinks about three distinct numbers $x$, $x+4$ and $9x$.

Find all possible sets of these three numbers if they are successive terms in a geometric series.

dif.r: Equal ratios give quadratic; two sets of terms found

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
In a geometric series consecutive terms have equal ratios.
$$\dfrac{9x}{x+4}=\dfrac{x+4}{x}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 9x^2&=(x+4)^2\\ 9x^2&=x^2+8x+16\\ 8x^2-8x-16&=0\\ x^2-x-2&=0\\ (x-2)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=2$ or $x=-1$.

If $x=2$, the numbers are $2,\ 6,\ 18$.

If $x=-1$, the numbers are $-1,\ 3,\ -9$.
criteria: Equates the common ratios, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b

solutions.latex:
A matching pair is two white socks or two black socks.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{13}{20}\times\dfrac{12}{19}+\dfrac{7}{20}\times\dfrac{6}{19}\\ &=\dfrac{99}{190}\end{aligned}$$

Use the complement of selecting two black socks.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-\dfrac{7}{20}\times\dfrac{6}{19}\\ &=\dfrac{169}{190}\end{aligned}$$

dif.r: Factorise exponential equation and solve with logs

solutions.latex:
Factorise:
$$e^x\left(2e^x-1\right)=0$$
Since $e^x\ne 0$, we need $2e^x-1=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ x&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=-\ln 2\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Three people play a game that involves collecting apples that are placed $4$ m apart. The first apple is placed $6$ m from point $P$. Players collect the closest apple, then return it to the bucket before collecting the next closest apple and so on.

\exfigure{1323_q17_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
When collecting her last apple, Hannah ran $130$ m from point $P$ to the apple.

How many apples did she collect in total?

dif.r: Direct arithmetic nth term formula solved for n

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If Katherine collected $41$ apples, how many metres did she run in total?

dif.r: Model return trips as new AP, then sum formula

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Luke aims to run a marathon whilst playing this game. He achieves this by running a total of $42\,432$ metres. How many apples did he collect in total?

dif.r: Sum formula gives quadratic in n with large constant

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: bucket, point P and apples placed 6 m, then 4 m apart

solutions.latex:
The distances to the apples form an arithmetic sequence with first term $a=6$ and common difference $d=4$.

The $n$th term is $T_n=a+(n-1)d$. Setting $T_n=130$:
$$\begin{aligned} 130&=6+(n-1)\times 4\\ 124&=4n-4\\ n&=32\end{aligned}$$
She collected $32$ apples.

Each apple needs a return trip, so the distances run are $12, 20, 28, \dots$, an arithmetic series with $a=12$, $d=8$ and $n=41$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{41}&=\dfrac{41}{2}\left[24+8(41-1)\right]\\ &=\dfrac{41}{2}\left[24+320\right]\\ &=7052 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into the sum formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the same series ($a=12$, $d=8$) with sum $42\,432$:
$$\begin{aligned} 42\,432&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[24+8(n-1)\right]\\ 84\,864&=24n+8n^2-8n\\ 0&=8n^2+16n-84\,864\\ 0&=n^2+2n-10\,608\\ 0&=(n+104)(n-102)\end{aligned}$$
So $n=-104$ or $n=102$.

Since $n>0$, $n\ne -104$.

$$\therefore\ \text{Luke collected } 102 \text{ apples}$$

parts.latex: Solve $2\sin^2 x-3\sin x-2=0$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$

dif.r: Quadratic in sin x, reject 2, solve standard angles

solutions.latex:
Let $u=\sin x$. The equation becomes a quadratic in $u$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2u^2-3u-2&=0\\ 2u^2-4u+u-2&=0\\ (u-2)(2u+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $u=2$ or $u=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Since $-1\le\sin x\le 1$, $\sin x\ne 2$, so $\sin x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

The solutions are in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
criteria: Factorises the quadratic in $\sin x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta$

dif.r: Common denominator, Pythagorean identity, cancel factor

solutions.latex:
Take the left-hand side and use the common denominator $\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)$.
$$\begin{aligned}LHS&=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}+\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2\theta+1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}\\ &=\dfrac{2+2\cos\theta}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)} &&(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1)\\ &=\dfrac{2(1+\cos\theta)}{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{\sin\theta}\\ &=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta\\ &=RHS\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ to obtain $2+2\cos\theta$, or equivalent merit
Uses a common denominator, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Expand into fractional powers and integrate over interval

figures.cap: graph of y=sqrt(x)(1-x) with shaded region between 0 and 1

solutions.latex:
The area under the curve from $x=0$ to $x=1$ is
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,(1-x)\,dx\\ &=\int_0^1\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}-x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-\dfrac{2x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}\right]_0^1\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{2}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{15} \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct antiderivative, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Maddie owns a company, and has noticed that the profits have been decreasing each year, by $8\%$ of the previous years' profit. In 2013, her company made a profit of \$100\,000.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How much profit will the company make in 2022?

dif.r: Identify ratio 0.92 and correct term number

parts.label: b
parts.latex: In total, how much profit has been made in the ten-year period from 2013 to 2022 inclusive?

dif.r: Direct geometric series sum formula with r=0.92 identified from context

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If this trend continues, what is the total amount of profit the company will make?

dif.r: Recognise total as limiting sum, then substitute into formula

solutions.latex:
The profits form a geometric sequence with $a=100\,000$ and $r=1-0.08=0.92$.

2022 is the 10th year, so
$$\begin{aligned}T_{10}&=100\,000\,(0.92)^9\\ &\approx \$47\,216.14\end{aligned}$$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ with $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{10}&=\dfrac{100\,000\left(1-0.92^{10}\right)}{1-0.92}\\ &\approx \$707\,014.43\end{aligned}$$

Since $|r|=0.92<1$, the limiting sum exists, with $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_\infty&=\dfrac{100\,000}{1-0.92}\\ &=\$1\,250\,000\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x\sin x$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

dif.r: Product rule derivative, then routine normal equation at given point

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the product rule:
$$y'=\sin x+x\cos x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, the tangent gradient is
$$\begin{aligned} m_T &= \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-1$.

The $y$ value at this point is
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{\pi}{2} &= -1\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ y &= -x+\pi \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=-x+\pi$$
criteria: Finds the normal gradient, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the curve $y=7+4x^3-3x^4$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Quartic stationary points; y''=0 case needs concavity test for inflection

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Draw a neat sketch of the curve in the domain $[-1,2]$ labelling all stationary points

\exfigure{1323_q29_1}

dif.r: Sketch quartic on restricted domain using found stationary points

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find any values of $x$ such that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}>0$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0$.

dif.r: Solve two derivative inequalities and intersect, excluding x=0

figures.cap: blank grid with axes for sketching
solution sketch: sketch of y = 7 + 4x^3 - 3x^4 on [-1,2] with (0,7) and (1,8) labelled

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 12x^2-12x^3 \\ &= 12x^2(1-x)=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$, giving the points $(0,7)$ and $(1,8)$.

The second derivative is
$$y''=24x-36x^2$$
At $x=1$: $y''=-12<0$, so $(1,8)$ is a maximum turning point.

At $x=0$: $y''=0$, so test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{aligned} x=-1:&\ y''=-60 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=0:&\ y''=0 &&\\ x=\dfrac12:&\ y''=3 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at $x=0$, so $(0,7)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
$$\therefore\ (0,7)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion and }(1,8)\text{ is a maximum turning point}$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points and the nature of one, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1323_q29_s1}
criteria: Sketch with one feature correct, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch drawn (1323_q29_s1); it was to show: $y=7+4x^3-3x^4$ on domain $[-1,2]$, axes labelled; horizontal point of inflexion at $(0,7)$; maximum turning point at $(1,8)$; end points $(-1,0)$ and $(2,7)$ ($y(-1)=7-4-3=0$, $y(2)=7+32-48=-9$, so end point is $(2,-9)$); curve rising through the inflexion to the maximum, then falling.

solutions.latex:
For $y''<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 24x-36x^2 &< 0 \\ 12x(2-3x) &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x<0$ or $x>\dfrac{2}{3}$.

For $y'>0$: $12x^2(1-x)>0$, so $x<1$ and $x\ne0$.

Combining both conditions:
$$\therefore\ x<0 \text{ or } \dfrac{2}{3}<x<1$$
criteria: Solves one condition correctly, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Substitute t=3 into depth equation

solutions.latex:
Depth is the integral of the rate:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \int 4\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\,dt \\ &= -\dfrac{24\pi}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+C \\ &= -24\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the exact area enclosed between the curve $y=\log_e x$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=1$ and $y=3$.

questions.stem:
Chloe records the lifespan of termites, and determines the that the number of weeks a termite lives can be modelled by the function:

$$f(x)=\dfrac{4}{5}-\dfrac{x^2}{45}\qquad \text{for } 3\le x\le 6$$

parts.latex: Find the mean lifespan of a termite

dif.r: Integral of x f(x) over domain, routine evaluation

solutions.latex:
A PDF must integrate to $1$ over its domain (and $f(x)\ge0$ there).
$$\begin{aligned} \int_3^6\left(\dfrac{4}{5}-\dfrac{x^2}{45}\right)dx &= \left[\dfrac{4x}{5}-\dfrac{x^3}{135}\right]_3^6 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{24}{5}-\dfrac{216}{135}\right)-\left(\dfrac{12}{5}-\dfrac{27}{135}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{16}{5}-\dfrac{11}{5} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore $f(x)$ is a PDF.
criteria: Finds the correct antiderivative, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source check: Source line $\frac{16}{5}-\frac{11}{5}$ equals 1 only if the first bracket is $\frac{16}{5}$ and the second $\frac{11}{5}$; check: $\frac{24}{5}-\frac{8}{5}=\frac{16}{5}$ and $\frac{12}{5}-\frac{1}{5}=\frac{11}{5}$, consistent.

solutions.latex:
The CDF is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_3^x f(t)\,dt$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \left[\dfrac{4t}{5}-\dfrac{t^3}{135}\right]_3^x \\ &= \dfrac{4x}{5}-\dfrac{x^3}{135}-\dfrac{11}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{108x-x^3-297}{135} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral setup, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The mean is $\mu=\displaystyle\int_3^6 xf(x)\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= \left[\dfrac{4x^2}{10}-\dfrac{x^4}{180}\right]_3^6 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{144}{10}-\dfrac{1296}{180}\right)-\left(\dfrac{36}{10}-\dfrac{81}{180}\right) \\ &= 4.05 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Pete worked in a National Park in 1942 and he introduced $18$ koalas to the park. By 2002, the number of koalas had grown to $5000$. The number of koalas has grown exponentially according to the rule $N=N_0e^{kt}$, where $t$ is the number of years since 1942. $N_0$ represents the initial amount of koalas and $k$ is a constant. By first finding these values, predict the number of koalas expected to be in the National Park in 2022.

dif.r: Find k via logarithms then substitute to predict

solutions.latex:
The initial number is $N_0=18$.

In 2002, $t=60$ and $N=5000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5000 &= 18e^{60k} \\ \dfrac{5000}{18} &= e^{60k} \\ 60k &= \log_e\left(\dfrac{5000}{18}\right) \\ k &= 0.0937\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $N=18e^{0.0937\ldots t}$.

In 2022, $t=80$:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 18e^{0.0937\ldots\times80} \\ &\approx 32\,624 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 32\,624 \text{ koalas}$$

solutions.latex:
In triangle $ABD$, $AB=AD$, so the base angles are equal. $\angle ABD=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ (from the figure, as $\angle DBC=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$) and $\angle ADB=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Hence $\angle DAB=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $ABD$:
$$\begin{aligned} DB^2 &= 3^2+3^2-2\times3^2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \\ &= 27 \\ DB &= 3\sqrt{3} \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle DAB=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and sets up the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Area of triangle $ABD$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times3^2\times\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{9}{2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Area of sector $BCD$ (radius $3\sqrt{3}$, angle $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times\left(3\sqrt{3}\right)^2\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6} &= \dfrac{135\pi}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{45\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Adding:
$$\therefore\ \text{Total}=\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}+45\pi}{4} \text{ m}^2$$
criteria: Finds the area of the triangle and sector, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has a displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ m/s. Initially the particle is at $O$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use integration to show that $x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.

dif.r: Integrate velocity with reverse chain rule, apply initial condition

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find when the particle is at rest.

dif.r: Set velocity zero and solve simple surd equation

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled in the first $24$ seconds of its motion.

dif.r: Must account for direction change when totalling distance

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\right)dt \\ &= \dfrac{3(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C \\ &= 2(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$ and $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2-0+C \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$$

At rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1} &= 9 \\ \sqrt{t+1} &= 3 \\ t+1 &= 9 \\ t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest at } t=8 \text{ seconds}$$

The particle changes direction at $t=8$, so find the positions at $t=8$ and $t=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(8) &= 2(9)(3)-72-2 \\ &= -20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x(24) &= 2(25)(5)-216-2 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
From $0$ to $-20$ is $20$ m, then from $-20$ to $32$ is $52$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total distance} &= 20+20+32 \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the position at rest $-20$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $A$, the area of triangle $ABC$, is given by $A=(10+x)\sqrt{100-x^2}$

dif.r: Geometric set-up with Pythagoras to show given area formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$, leaving your answer as a single simplified fraction

dif.r: Product and chain rule with careful surd-fraction simplification

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Prove that the triangle with a maximum area is equilateral

dif.r: Optimise, justify maximum, then prove sides equal geometrically

figures.cap: isosceles triangle ABC inscribed in circle centre O, OP = x perpendicular to AB

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $OPB$, Pythagoras' theorem gives
$$\begin{aligned} PB^2 &= 10^2-x^2 \\ PB &= \sqrt{100-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Since $OP$ bisects $AB$, $AB=2\sqrt{100-x^2}$.

The height of the triangle is $x+10$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times2\sqrt{100-x^2}\times(x+10) \\ &= (10+x)\sqrt{100-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

criteria: Combines over a common denominator, or equivalent merit
Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For a maximum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$-2(x+10)(x-5)=0$$
So $x=-10$ or $x=5$. Since $x>0$ is a distance, $x\ne-10$, so $x=5$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side:
$$\begin{aligned} x=4:&\ \dfrac{dA}{dx}\approx3.1 &&\text{increasing}\\ x=5:&\ \dfrac{dA}{dx}=0 &&\\ x=6:&\ \dfrac{dA}{dx}\approx-4 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=5$ gives a maximum.

When $x=5$: $AB=2\sqrt{75}=10\sqrt{3}$, $AP=5\sqrt{3}$ and the height is $15$.

In right-angled triangle $APC$:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= \left(5\sqrt{3}\right)^2+15^2 \\ &= 300 \\ AC &= 10\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
So $AC=CB=AB$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the triangle of maximum area is equilateral}$$
criteria: Shows $x=5$ is a maximum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The second term of a geometric series is $-2$, and the fifth term is $16$. What is the common ratio?

dif.r: Divide two GP terms to get r^3, then cube root

solutions.latex:
For a geometric sequence, $T_2 = ar = -2$ and $T_5 = ar^4 = 16$.

Dividing the second equation by the first:
$$\begin{aligned} r^3 &= \dfrac{16}{-2} \\ &= -8 \end{aligned}$$
so $r = -2$, which is option A.

parts.latex: For what values of $x$ does the geometric series $1 - 4x + 16x^2 + \dots$ have a limiting sum?

dif.r: Identify ratio -4x and apply |r|<1 condition

solutions.latex:
The first term is $1$ and the common ratio is $r = -4x$.

A limiting sum exists when $|r| < 1$, so $|4x| < 1$.
$$-\dfrac{1}{4} < x < \dfrac{1}{4}$$
The inequality is strict (at $|r|=1$ there is no limiting sum), so this is option D.

parts.latex: Which of the following is $e^{2\log_e x}$ equal to ?

dif.r: Direct log law and inverse property recall

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $n\log_e x = \log_e x^n$:
$$\begin{aligned} e^{2\log_e x} &= e^{\log_e x^2} \\ &= x^2 \end{aligned}$$
so the answer is option C.

parts.latex: The function $y = \ln x$ is reflected in the $x$-axis and then translated 5 units vertically up. Which one of the following is the equation of the transformed function?

dif.r: Two standard transformations applied in order

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

solutions.latex:
Reflecting in the $x$-axis replaces $y$ by $-y$, giving $y = -\ln x$.

Translating $5$ units up adds $5$, giving $y = 5 - \ln x$.

This is option C.

parts.latex: If, $y = \dfrac{e^x}{e^x + 1}$, which of the following is correct?

dif.r: Rearrange to isolate e^x, then take logarithm

solutions.latex:
Make $x$ the subject.
$$\begin{aligned} y(e^x + 1) &= e^x \\ ye^x + y &= e^x \\ y &= e^x - ye^x \\ y &= e^x(1 - y) \end{aligned}$$
Then $e^x = \dfrac{y}{1-y}$, so
$$x = \ln\left(\dfrac{y}{1-y}\right)$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: The first three terms of an arithmetic sequence are $7$, $11$ and $15$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Is $113$ a term in this sequence? Justify your answer by performing appropriate calculations.

dif.r: Formula used in reverse; non-integer n shows not a term

solutions.latex:
The sequence has $a = 7$ and common difference $d = 11 - 7 = 4$.

Using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= 7 + (10-1)\times 4 \\ &= 43 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (single mark).

solutions.latex:
Suppose $T_n = 113$, using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 7 + (n-1)\times 4 &= 113 \\ (n-1)\times 4 &= 106 \\ n - 1 &= 26.5 \\ n &= 27.5 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ must be a whole number, $113$ is not a term of the sequence.

parts.latex: The fifth term of an arithmetic series is $21$. The sum of the first five terms is $45$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of the first term and show that the common difference is $6$.

dif.r: Set up and solve two simultaneous equations from term and sum

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, determine the minimum number of terms required to obtain a sum greater than $600$.

dif.r: Sum formula to quadratic inequality, solve, interpret integer n

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$ for the fifth term:
$$a + 4d = 21 \qquad (1)$$
Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$ for the first five terms:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5}{2}(2a + 4d) &= 45 \\ 2a + 4d &= 18 \\ a + 2d &= 9 \qquad (2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (2) from (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 2d &= 12 \\ d &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $d = 6$ into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a + 4(6) &= 21 \\ a &= -3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = -3 \text{ and } d = 6$$
criteria: Forms the two equations in $a$ and $d$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source's middle step $2a+4d=18$ written out.

solutions.latex:
With $a = -3$ and $d = 6$, the sum of $n$ terms is
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(-3) + (n-1)6\right] \\ &= n(3n - 6) \\ &= 3n^2 - 6n \end{aligned}$$
We need $S_n > 600$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3n^2 - 6n &> 600 \\ n^2 - 2n - 200 &> 0 \end{aligned}$$
Solve $n^2 - 2n - 200 = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 800}}{2} \\ &= 15.18\ldots \text{ or } -13.18\ldots \end{aligned}$$
The parabola is positive for $n > 15.18\ldots$ or $n < -13.18\ldots$, and the second is impossible as $n > 0$.

Since $n$ is a whole number, the minimum number of terms is $16$.
criteria: Solves the quadratic to find $n = 15.18\ldots$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the geometric series $1 + \left(1 - \sqrt{e}\right) + \left(1 - \sqrt{e}\right)^2 + \cdots$

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

dif.r: Substitute into limiting sum formula and simplify

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{1 - \sqrt{e}}{1} \\ &= 1 - \sqrt{e} \\ &\approx -0.648 \end{aligned}$$
So $|r| \approx 0.648 < 1$.

Since $|r| < 1$, the geometric series has a limiting sum.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using $S = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a = 1$ and $r = 1 - \sqrt{e}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{1}{1 - (1 - \sqrt{e})} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{e}} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The lengths above the ground form a geometric series $0.3 + 0.6 + \cdots$ with $a = 0.3$, $r = 2$ and $n = 10$.

Each of the $10$ posts is imbedded $0.2$ m:
$$0.2 \times 10 = 2 \text{ m}$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $\dfrac{(x+3)^2}{e^{2x}}$ and simplify your answer.

dif.r: Quotient rule with chain rule, then factorise to simplify

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x+3)^2 & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=2(x+3) & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{e^{2x}\cdot 2(x+3) - (x+3)^2\cdot 2e^{2x}}{\left(e^{2x}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2e^{2x}(x+3)\left[1 - (x+3)\right]}{\left(e^{2x}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2(x+3)(-x-2)}{e^{2x}} \\ &= -\dfrac{2(x+3)(x+2)}{e^{2x}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation $e^{2x} - 2e^x - 15 = 0$ for $x$.

dif.r: Substitution gives quadratic in e^x; reject negative root

solutions.latex:
Let $y = e^x$, so the equation becomes a quadratic in $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} y^2 - 2y - 15 &= 0 \\ (y - 5)(y + 3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $y = 5$ or $y = -3$.

That is, $e^x = 5$ or $e^x = -3$.

Since $e^x > 0$ for all $x$, $e^x = -3$ has no solution.
$$\therefore\ x = \ln 5$$
criteria: Solves the quadratic in $e^x$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $y = e^x$ to form a quadratic, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation $2^{2x} = 5^{2x-1}$ for $x$. Leave your answer to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Take logs both sides and collect x terms

solutions.latex:
Take natural logs of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x\ln 2 &= (2x - 1)\ln 5 \\ 2x\ln 2 &= 2x\ln 5 - \ln 5 \\ \ln 5 &= 2x\ln 5 - 2x\ln 2 \\ &= 2x(\ln 5 - \ln 2) \end{aligned}$$
Since $\ln 5 - \ln 2 = \ln 2.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{\ln 5}{2\ln 2.5} \\ &\approx 0.878\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \approx 0.88 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Takes logs and begins to solve for $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a

dif.r: Convert days to hours and substitute

parts.label: c
parts.latex: A pesticide was introduced 10 hours after the initial count. The pesticide has a positive result in controlling the growth of bacteria. Instead of increasing, bacteria count started reducing by 8% per hour. During which hour from the initial count, will the number of bacteria be reduced to 700?

dif.r: Build two-stage growth-decay model, solve with logs, interpret hour

solutions.latex:
The number of bacteria is multiplied by $1.06$ each hour, starting from $2500$:
$$N = 2500(1.06)^t$$
where $N$ is the number of bacteria and $t$ is in hours.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$2$ days is $48$ hours, so $t = 48$:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 2500(1.06)^{48} \\ &= 40\,984.67\ldots \\ &\approx 40\,985 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
After $10$ hours the number is $2500(1.06)^{10}$. After that it falls by $8\%$ each hour, so it is multiplied by $0.92$ each hour:
$$N = 2500(1.06)^{10}(0.92)^n$$
where $n$ is the number of hours since the pesticide was introduced.

Set $N = 700$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2500(1.06)^{10}(0.92)^n &= 700 \\ (0.92)^n &= \dfrac{700}{2500(1.06)^{10}} \\ &= 0.28(1.06)^{-10} \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln\left[0.28(1.06)^{-10}\right]}{\ln 0.92} \\ &\approx 22.25 \end{aligned}$$
The total time from the start is $10 + 22.25 = 32.25$ hours, which is during the $33$rd hour.
$$\therefore\ \text{the } 33\text{rd hour from the start}$$

parts.latex: Given that $\log 4 + \log 16 + \log 64 + \cdots + \log 16384 = a\log b$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers and $b$ is a prime number.

dif.r: Recognise powers of 2, use log laws, then sum an AP

solutions.latex:
Write each number as a power of $2$ and use $\log 2^k = k\log 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} &\log 4 + \log 16 + \log 64 + \cdots + \log 16384 \\ &= \log 2^2 + \log 2^4 + \log 2^6 + \cdots + \log 2^{14} \\ &= 2\log 2 + 4\log 2 + 6\log 2 + \cdots + 14\log 2 \\ &= \log 2\left[2 + 4 + 6 + \cdots + 14\right] \end{aligned}$$
The bracket is an arithmetic series with first term $2$, last term $14$ and common difference $2$, so $n = \dfrac{14}{2} = 7$.

Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_7 &= \dfrac{7}{2}(2 + 14) \\ &= 56 \end{aligned}$$
So the sum is $56\log 2$.
$$\therefore\ a = 56,\ b = 2$$
criteria: Writes the sum as $\log 2\left[2 + 4 + \cdots + 14\right]$ and attempts the arithmetic sum, or equivalent merit
Writes the terms as powers of $2$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A Year 12 cohort were surveyed on their favourite streaming service, the results are displayed in the following Sector Graph, along with the proportion who chose the service as a percentage. 90 students chose Disney Plus as their favourite streaming service.

\exfigure{634_q15_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How many students are there in the Year 12 cohort?

dif.r: One-step percentage reverse calculation

parts.label: b

dif.r: Compare computed counts with column graph and justify

figures.cap: sector graph: Netflix 35%, Disney Plus 30%, Amazon Prime 25%, Stan 10%
column graph: Netflix 105, Disney Plus 90, Amazon Prime 50, Stan 30

solutions.latex:
Disney Plus is $30\%$ of the cohort, so $90$ students is $30\%$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{cohort} &= 90\times\dfrac{100}{30} \\ &= 300 \text{ students} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Each service's expected number is its percentage of $300$ students.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Netflix: } & 0.35\times 300 = 105 \\ \text{Disney Plus: } & 90 \\ \text{Amazon Prime: } & 0.25\times 300 = 75 \\ \text{Stan: } & 0.1\times 300 = 30 \end{aligned}$$
Netflix, Disney Plus and Stan match the column graph.

Amazon Prime is incorrect: the sector graph shows $25\%$, which corresponds to 75 students, but the column graph shows 50.
criteria: Identifies Amazon Prime without justification, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

The graphs below show the points scored by two teams in a local Rugby League competition.

\exfigure{634_q16_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the difference in ranges of scores between the 2 teams?
parts.note: Range and summary statistics comparing two data sets are not in the 2024 Advanced syllabus (Standard content).

dif.r: Read ranges from graphs and subtract

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If the Digitsville Diagonals scored between 24 and 28 points in 6 games, how many games did they play in total?

dif.r: Recognise quartile interval holds 25% of games, then scale

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Sam, a fan of the Quadtown Parabolas, claims that their team is statistically better than the Digitsville Diagonals as they have the higher maximum score.

Provide 2 statistical reasons you could use to argue against Sam.
parts.note: Comparing data sets using summary statistics (median, IQR, spread, skew) is removed from Advanced (Standard content).

dif.r: Interpret boxplots to argue against claim with statistics

figures.cap: two box plots: Digitsville Diagonals and Quadtown Parabolas

solutions.latex:
The range is the highest score minus the lowest score.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Digitsville Diagonals: } & 34-6=28 \\ \text{Quadtown Parabolas: } & 40-0=40 \end{aligned}$$
The difference in ranges is
$$40-28=12$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The interval $24$–$28$ points is $25\%$ of the games, and it contains $6$ games.

So $6$ games is $25\%$ of the total.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 6 \div 0.25 \\ &= 24 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the Diagonals played } 24 \text{ games in total.}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (single row). The $25\%$ is read from the given graph, which was not checked.

solutions.latex:
Any two of the following statistical reasons.

The Diagonals have a better median.

The Diagonals have a higher $Q_3$ and a higher $Q_1$.

The Diagonals have a smaller spread, so they are more consistent.

The Diagonals have a higher lowest score.
criteria: Gives one correct statistical reason, or equivalent merit
