dif.r: Apply 1.5 IQR outlier rule at both ends

figures.cap: blank grid for cumulative frequency histogram and ogive (page 13 of paper)
solution sketch: handwritten cumulative frequency histogram and ogive

solutions.latex:
The cumulative frequency is the running total of the frequencies.

$$4,\ 16,\ 34,\ 75,\ 95,\ 100$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Frequency table not shown in the source working, values not rechecked.

criteria: Draws the histogram or the ogive correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Figure 634_q17_s1 already present in the source.

solutions.latex:
Reading from the ogive at $25\%$ and $75\%$ of the $100$ players:
$$Q_1 = 50,\qquad Q_3 = 80$$
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 80 - 50 \\ &= 30 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
An outlier lies below $Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR$ or above $Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR &= 50 - 1.5\times 30 \\ &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR &= 80 + 1.5\times 30 \\ &= 125 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{outliers are scores less than } 5 \text{ or greater than } 125$$
criteria: Finds one outlier boundary correctly, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.

dif.r: Single chain rule for tan of linear

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $y = e^{\sin x}$

dif.r: Standard chain rule for e to a function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: $y = \ln\left(\dfrac{3x+2}{x-4}\right)$

dif.r: Log laws then differentiate and simplify fractions
Product rule with derivative of exponential base 2

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan u = \sec^2 u \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}$ with $u = 5x-3$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 5\sec^2(5x-3)$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u} = e^{u}\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}$ with $u = \sin x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= e^{\sin x}\cdot\cos x \\ &= \cos x\, e^{\sin x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the chain rule with an error in one factor, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b} = \ln a - \ln b$:
$$y = \ln(3x+2) - \ln(x-4)$$
Differentiating, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u = \dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{3}{3x+2} - \dfrac{1}{x-4} \\ &= \dfrac{3(x-4)-(3x+2)}{(3x+2)(x-4)} \\ &= \dfrac{-14}{(3x+2)(x-4)} \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, use $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ where $f(x) = \dfrac{3x+2}{x-4}$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x+2 & v&=x-4\\ u'&=3 & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{3(x-4)-(3x+2)}{(x-4)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-14}{(x-4)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{\frac{-14}{(x-4)^2}}{\frac{3x+2}{x-4}} \\ &= \dfrac{-14}{(x-4)(3x+2)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly with an algebraic error, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Two methods kept from source.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2^x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=2^x\ln 2 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \ln(2)\,x^2\,2^x + 2x\cdot 2^x$$
criteria: Applies the product rule with one derivative correct, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{e^{3x+4}}$.

Prove that $f'(x) = \dfrac{1-3x}{e^{3x+4}}$.

dif.r: Quotient rule with exponential, factor and simplify to given result

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{3x+4}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3e^{3x+4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{e^{3x+4} - 3x\,e^{3x+4}}{\left(e^{3x+4}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^{3x+4}(1-3x)}{\left(e^{3x+4}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1-3x}{e^{3x+4}} \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Applies the quotient rule correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex:
Let $g(x) = \cos^2\left(6x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

Find the exact value of $g'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)$.

dif.r: Double chain rule then exact trig values

solutions.latex:
Write $g(x) = \left[\cos\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]^2$ and apply the chain rule twice.
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x) &= 2\cos\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\times\left(-\sin\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)\times 6 \\ &= -12\cos\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\sin\left(6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$, where $6x-\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right) &= -12\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= -12\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= -3\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the chain rule with an error, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent of $y = \dfrac{1}{e^{5x-10}}$ at $x = 2$.

dif.r: Standard tangent equation with exponential derivative

solutions.latex:
Rewrite using index laws:
$$y = e^{-(5x-10)} = e^{-5x+10}$$
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -5e^{-5x+10}$$
At $x=2$, the gradient is
$$\begin{aligned} m &= -5e^{-5(2)+10} \\ &= -5e^0 \\ &= -5 \end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$, the $y$ value is
$$\begin{aligned} y &= e^{-5\times 2+10} \\ &= e^0 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
so the point is $(2,1)$.

Using $y - y_1 = m(x-x_1)$:
$$y - 1 = -5(x-2)$$
criteria: Finds the gradient and the point of tangency, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Tangent left in point-gradient form as in the source.

questions.stem:
The brand new u-Phone 15 was released by Orange inc. at the beginning of 2022. While the production of the u-Phone 15 started slowly, it increased at a rapid rate, and is modelled by the function $f(t) = e^{4t} + 10000$, where $t$ is the number of years after 2022 ($t = 0$ is the beginning of 2022).

While demand for the phones started quite small, the marketing campaign was quite successful, and soon more and more people wanted to get their own u-Phone 15. The demand for the u-Phone is modelled by the function $g(t)$ where $g(t) = f'(t)$, the derivative of the production of the phones.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How many phones were initially produced?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the equation of $g(t)$.

dif.r: Differentiate simple exponential

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Sketch both functions on the axis below.

\exfigure{634_q22_1}

dif.r: Sketch two exponential models on same axes

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

parts.label: d
parts.latex: After how many days does the demand for the u-Phone 15 overtake the number of phones that have been produced?

dif.r: Set demand equal to production, solve with logs, convert units

can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: blank axes, t from 0 to 3, vertical 10000 to 30000
solution sketch: handwritten sketch of f(t) and g(t)

solutions.latex:
Initially $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0) &= e^0 + 10000 \\ &= 10\,001 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} g(t) &= f'(t) \\ &= 4e^{4t} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{634_q22_s1}
criteria: Sketches one function correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch drawn (634_q22_s1); it was to show: confirm figure 634_q22_s1 on the question's axes. $f(t)=e^{4t}+10000$ has $y$-intercept $(0,10001)$ and increases exponentially; $g(t)=4e^{4t}$ has $y$-intercept $(0,4)$, is steeper and crosses $f$ at $t\approx 2.03$ (from part (d)). The source text said the crossing is between $t=1$ and $t=2$, which disagrees with part (d); the sentence was dropped.

solutions.latex:
Demand overtakes production when $g(t) = f(t)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4e^{4t} &= e^{4t} + 10000 \\ 3e^{4t} &= 10000 \\ e^{4t} &= \dfrac{10000}{3} \\ 4t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{10000}{3}\right) \\ t &\approx 2.03 \text{ years} \end{aligned}$$
Converting to days:
$$2.0279\ldots\times 365 \approx 740 \text{ days}$$
criteria: Forms and solves $4e^{4t}=e^{4t}+10000$ for $t$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Checked: $\ln(10000/3)/4 \approx 2.028$, $\times 365 \approx 740$.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the conversion used the rounded $2.03$ ($2.03\times365=740.95$); the unrounded $t=2.0279\ldots$ gives $740$ days.

questions.stem: The line $y = mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$ at a point $P$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the coordinates of $P$ is $(3, -e)$.

dif.r: Tangent through origin: equate gradient and point conditions

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the exact value of $m$.

dif.r: Substitute known point into line equation

solutions.latex:
The curve is $y = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$, so
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$$
At $P$ the line and curve meet, and $m$ equals the gradient of the curve:
$$mx = -e^{\frac{1}{3}x},\qquad m = -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$$
Substituting $m$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{\frac{1}{3}x}\times x &= -e^{\frac{1}{3}x} \\ -\dfrac{1}{3}x &= -1 \\ x &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
(dividing by $-e^{\frac{1}{3}x}$, which is never zero).

At $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -e^{\frac{1}{3}\times 3} \\ &= -e \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the coordinates of } P \text{ are } (3,-e)$$
criteria: Finds the derivative and equates the gradient to $m$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The point $(3,-e)$ lies on $y = mx$.
$$\begin{aligned} -e &= 3m \\ m &= -\dfrac{e}{3} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x},\ x\neq 0$ and $g(x)=x+2$. Find the domain of $f(g(x))$.

dif.r: Form composite then find its domain; two short steps

solutions.latex:
The composite is $f(g(x))=\dfrac{1}{x+2}$.

This is undefined when $x+2=0$, that is $x=-2$.

Hence the domain is $x\neq -2$, which is option B.

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows a sketch of the gradient function of the curve $y=f(x)$.

\exfigure{635_q3_1}

Which of the following is a true statement?

The curve $y=f(x)$ has

dif.r: Interpret gradient graph: touching zero means horizontal inflection

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

options.label: B
options.latex: a horizontal point of inflection at $x=2$

options.label: C
options.latex: a horizontal point of inflection at $x=-4$

figures.cap: graph of y=f'(x)

solutions.latex:
The graph shows $f'(x)=0$ at $x=-4$, and $f'(x)\geq 0$ on both sides because the graph touches the axis there.

The gradient does not change sign, so there is a horizontal point of inflection at $x=-4$.

At $x=2$ the gradient changes from positive to negative, so that point is a maximum.

Hence the true statement is option C.

parts.latex: The point $P(8,-3)$ lies on the graph of $f(x)$. Transformations map the graph of $f(x)$ to the graph of $g(x)$, where $g(x)=-2f(x+7)+5$. The same transformation maps the point $P$ to the point $P'$. What are the coordinates of the point $P'$?

dif.r: Apply dilation, reflection and translations to a single point

solutions.latex:
Apply the transformations to $P(8,-3)$ in turn.

Vertical dilation by factor $-2$:
$$(8,-3)\text{ becomes }(8,6)$$
Vertical translation up 5:
$$(8,6)\text{ becomes }(8,11)$$
Horizontal translation left 7:
$$(8,11)\text{ becomes }(1,11)$$
Hence $P'=(1,11)$, which is option A.

dif.r: Deduce a, b from graph and combine signed areas

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: graph of f(x)=a cos bx with shaded area 2 u^2

solutions.latex:
The graph has $b=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

The shaded area gives
$$\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}f(x)\,dx=2$$
so $a=3$.

Then
$$\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\pi}f(x)\,dx=-4$$
Hence
$$\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}f(x)\,dx=2-4=-2$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: What are the values of $x$ for which $|5-3x|\geq 11$ ?

dif.r: Standard absolute value inequality with sign reversal

solutions.latex:
Since $|u|\geq 11$ means $u\leq -11$ or $u\geq 11$:
$$5-3x\leq -11\ \text{ or }\ 5-3x\geq 11$$
$$-3x\leq -16\ \text{ or }\ -3x\geq 6$$
Dividing by $-3$ reverses the inequalities:
$$x\geq\dfrac{16}{3}\ \text{ or }\ x\leq -2$$
This is option D.

parts.latex: Initially, a water tank holds 800 litres of water. Water drains from the bottom of the tank at a rate of $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ litres per minute where $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-100t$ after $t$ minutes. How long does it take the tank to empty?

dif.r: Integrate rate, use initial volume, solve V=0

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate to find the volume:
$$V=-\dfrac{100t^2}{2}+C=-50t^2+C$$
When $t=0$, $V=800$, so $C=800$ and
$$V=-50t^2+800$$
The tank is empty when $V=0$:
$$t^2=16$$
so $t=4$ minutes (as $t>0$), which is option B.

questions.review_note: Options C and D refer to $a$, which is not defined in the question (printed as is)

parts.latex: What is the equation of the axis of symmetry of the quadratic function $y=-k(x+b)^2+c$ ?

dif.r: Read axis of symmetry directly from vertex form

solutions.latex:
The quadratic $y=-k(x+b)^2+c$ is in vertex form, with vertex at $x=-b$.

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex, so $x=-b$, which is option A.

meta.format_note: Option labels C and D in the question use $a$, which does not appear in the function; kept as in source.

parts.latex: How many solutions are there to the equation $2-x=4\cos x$ ? $(0\leq x\leq 2\pi)$

dif.r: Sketch cosine and line accurately and count intersections

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\leq t\leq 14\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for } 0\leq t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$.

dif.r: Set total probability to 1; log integral of linear denominator

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After how many days will a person have a 75% chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?

dif.r: Set CDF equal to 0.75 and solve log equation

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function the total area is 1:
$$\displaystyle\int_1^{14}\dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k}{2}\ln|2t-1|\right]_1^{14}&=1\\ \dfrac{k}{2}\left(\ln 27-\ln 1\right)&=1\\ \dfrac{k}{2}\ln 27&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. The question's pdf is written in $x$ but uses $t$; kept as in source.

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution must reach $0.75$:
$$F(t)=\displaystyle\int_1^{t}f(u)\,du=0.75$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{\ln 27}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ln|2t-1|-\ln 1\right]&=0.75\\ \ln|2t-1|&=0.75\ln 27\\ 2t-1&=e^{0.75\ln 27}\\ t&=\dfrac{e^{0.75\ln 27}+1}{2}\\ &\approx 6.42 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 6.42\text{ days}$$
criteria: Sets up $F(t)=0.75$ with correct integral, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\sec\theta-\sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta}=\sin\theta\tan\theta$

dif.r: Identity proof needing factorisation of 1-cos^4 by difference of squares

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator and use the difference of two squares.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^4\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta}\\ &=\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\\ &=\sec\theta\sin^2\theta &&(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\times\sin\theta\times\sin\theta\\ &=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\sin\theta\\ &=\sin\theta\tan\theta\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Factorises the numerator, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Identify ratio 2a and apply |r|<1

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=x^2+4x-7$ at the point $(1,-2)$

dif.r: Differentiate, negative reciprocal gradient, point-gradient form

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x+4$$
At $x=1$ the tangent gradient is $6$, so the normal gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y+2&=-\dfrac{1}{6}(x-1)\\ y&=-\dfrac{1}{6}x-\dfrac{11}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x+6y+11=0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The curve $y=f(x)$ has a gradient function $f'(x)=3x^2-k$, where $k$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$ if the curve has a stationary point at $(-1,3)$.

dif.r: Substitute x=-1 into f'(x)=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the equation of the curve $y=f(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate polynomial and find constant from a point

solutions.latex:
A stationary point has $f'(x)=0$, so $3x^2-k=0$ at $x=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3(-1)^2-k&=0\\ k&=3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=3$$

Integrate $f'(x)=3x^2-3$:
$$f(x)=\displaystyle\int(3x^2-3)\,dx=x^3-3x+C$$
The curve passes through $(-1,3)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=-1+3+C\\ C&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-3x+1$$

parts.latex:
A curve is defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}x^4-2x^2+1$.

Sketch the graph of the curve for the domain $[-3,3]$ showing all key features including, classifying the nature of stationary points, and finding any points of inflection. Also state where the curve is concave down. You do not need to find the $x$-intercepts

dif.r: Full quartic curve sketch: stationary points, inflections, concavity

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = x^4/4 - 2x^2 + 1 on [-3,3] with key points

solutions.latex:
The $y$-intercept is $f(0)=1$.

Stationary points: $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x)=x^3-4x=x(x^2-4)=0$$
So $x=0,\ \pm2$, giving $(0,1)$, $(2,-3)$ and $(-2,-3)$.

Nature, using the second derivative $f''(x)=3x^2-4$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=-4<0 &&\text{local maximum at }(0,1)\\ f''(\pm2)&=8>0 &&\text{local minima at }(\pm2,-3) \end{aligned}$$
Possible inflection: $f''(x)=0$ gives $x=\pm\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\approx\pm1.15$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&>0 &&\text{for } x<-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\text{ and } x>\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3} &&\text{concave up}\\ f''(x)&<0 &&\text{for } -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}<x<\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3} &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at both, so $\left(\pm\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3},-\dfrac{11}{9}\right)$ are points of inflection.

End points: $f(\pm3)=3.25$, so $(\pm3,3.25)$.

\exfigure{635_q15_s1}

$$\therefore\ \text{the curve is concave down for } -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}<x<\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$$
criteria: Correct sketch with most features, or equivalent merit
Finds and classifies stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds stationary points, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Robert walks 5.59 km from his house to the shop on a bearing of $063^\circ$. He then turns on a bearing of $124^\circ$ to walk to the post office, where he is 13.34 km from home.

\exfigure{635_q16_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\angle HSP=119^\circ$.

dif.r: Bearing angle chase using parallel north lines and co-interior angles

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the bearing of Robert’s house from the post office. Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Sine rule then convert interior angle to a reverse bearing

figures.cap: triangle House (H), Shop (S), Post office (P) with bearings 63 and 124, sides 5.59 km and 13.34 km

solutions.latex:
In the diagram, the north lines at $H$ and $S$ are parallel, so co-interior angles sum to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle HSP&=360^\circ-124^\circ-(180^\circ-63^\circ)\\ &=119^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Let $\theta=\angle SPH$. Apply the sine rule in triangle $HSP$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{5.59}=\dfrac{\sin 119^\circ}{13.34}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5.59\sin 119^\circ}{13.34}\right)\\ &\approx 21^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Bearing of the house from the post office:
$$360^\circ-21^\circ-(180^\circ-124^\circ)=283^\circ$$
$$\therefore\ \text{bearing}\approx 283^\circ\text{T}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find an expression, in terms of $n$, for the number of sticks required to make a similar arrangement of $n$ squares in the $n^{\text{th}}$ row.

dif.r: Write arithmetic nth term from a pattern

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: James continues to make squares following the same pattern. He makes 4 squares in the fourth row and so on until he has completed 10 rows. Find the total number of sticks James uses in making these 10 rows.

dif.r: Direct arithmetic series sum formula

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: James started with 1750 sticks. Given that James continues the pattern to complete $k$ rows but does not have sufficient sticks to complete the $(k+1)^{\text{th}}$ row. Show that $k$ satisfies $(3k-100)(k+35)<0$.

dif.r: Set up sum inequality in context and factorise to given form

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: d
parts.latex: What is the value of $k$?

dif.r: Solve quadratic inequality and take largest integer

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: rows 1 to 3 of squares made from sticks

solutions.latex:
The first row uses 4 sticks and each extra square adds 3 sticks, so this is an arithmetic sequence with $a=4$, $d=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n&=4+(n-1)\times3\\ &=3n+1 \end{aligned}$$

The total is the sum of the first 10 terms of the arithmetic sequence with $a=4$, $d=3$, $n=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10}&=\dfrac{10}{2}\left[2\times4+(10-1)\times3\right]\\ &=5(8+27)\\ &=175\text{ sticks} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the arithmetic series sum formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Completing $k$ rows uses $S_k$ sticks, which must be less than 1750 for the $k$ rows to be possible (and the next row cannot be completed).
$$\begin{aligned} S_k=\dfrac{k}{2}\left[2\times4+(k-1)\times3\right]&<1750\\ k(8+3k-3)&<3500\\ 3k^2+5k-3500&<0\\ 3k^2+105k-100k-3500&<0\\ 3k(k+35)-100(k+35)&<0\\ (3k-100)(k+35)&<0 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source's inequality strictness kept as written.

solutions.latex:
Since $k+35>0$ for $k\geq0$, the inequality $(3k-100)(k+35)<0$ needs $3k-100<0$.
$$0\leq k<\dfrac{100}{3}=33\dfrac{1}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ k=33$$

parts.latex:
Find the value of $k$ such that

$$\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{x^2}{x^3-2}\,dx=\ln k$$

dif.r: f'/f integral with negative bounds and log algebra for k

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator $x^3-2$, so use $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3-2}\,dx&=\ln k\\ \dfrac{1}{3}\left[\ln|x^3-2|\right]_{-2}^{0}&=\ln k\\ \ln 2-\ln 10&=3\ln k\\ \ln\dfrac{2}{10}&=\ln k^3\\ k^3&=\dfrac{1}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{5}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{5}}$$
criteria: Integrates and substitutes the limits, or equivalent merit
Writes the integral in the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$, or equivalent merit

\exfigure{635_q18b_1}

The sign for ‘Pizza $\pi$’ restaurant is in the shape of a circle with a sector cut out of it. The sector has an angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. If the area of the sign is $30\pi$, what is the radius of the circle?

dif.r: Find remaining sector angle, use area formula in reverse

figures.cap: circular sign with a sector cut out

solutions.latex:
The sign is a sector with the $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ sector removed, so its angle is
$$2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$
Using the sector area $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\times\dfrac{5\pi}{3}&=30\pi\\ r^2&=\dfrac{30\pi\times6}{5\pi}\\ &=36 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r=6\text{ units (since } r>0)$$
criteria: Sets up the sector area equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: For what values of $k$ does the quadratic equation $5x^2-2x+(8k-15)=0$ have real roots?

dif.r: Discriminant condition then solve a linear inequality in k

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
Here $a=5$, $b=-2$, $c=8k-15$. The roots are real when the discriminant $\Delta\ge 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} (-2)^2-4\times5\times(8k-15) &\ge 0\\ 304-160k &\ge 0\\ k &\le \dfrac{304}{160}=\dfrac{19}{10}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k\le\dfrac{19}{10}$$

dif.r: Trapezoidal rule with given values, doubled for symmetry

figures.cap: symmetrical lake between two roads with measurements 30, 40, 60, 80, 60, 40, 30 and width 420

solutions.latex:
The lake is symmetrical, so find the area of the top half with the trapezoidal rule and double it. The half-width is $420$ m split into six strips, so $h=\dfrac{420}{6}=70$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area} &\approx 2\times\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\times 70\Big[30+30+2(40+60+80+60+40)\Big]\right]\\ &=43\,400 \text{ m}^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}\approx 43\,400 \text{ square metres}$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule with correct strip width, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Differentiate with respect to $x$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $e^{x\sin 2x}$

dif.r: Chain rule combined with product rule, routine

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\dfrac{x^2}{\ln(x)}$

dif.r: Standard quotient rule with logarithm

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{u}\right)=e^{u}\dfrac{du}{dx}$ with $u=x\sin 2x$. The product rule gives $\dfrac{du}{dx}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 2x}\right)&=e^{x\sin 2x}\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 2x)\\ &=e^{x\sin 2x}\left[\sin 2x+2x\cos 2x\right]\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the chain rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{\ln x}\right)=\dfrac{2x\ln x-x}{(\ln x)^2}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule with correct $u'$ and $v'$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. Initially, it is travelling to the left at 1 cm/min. Its acceleration as a function of time($t$) is given by $a=\pi\cos\pi t+\pi\sin\pi t$ for $0\leq t\leq 2$ where time and displacement are measured in minutes and cm respectively.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find when the particle changes its direction for the first time.

dif.r: Integrate acceleration, apply initial velocity sign, solve trig equation

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the exact total distance travelled in the first half a minute.

dif.r: Displacement then account for direction change to get total distance

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$. Integrate the acceleration, using $v=-1$ when $t=0$ (travelling left at 1 cm/min).
$$\begin{aligned} v-(-1)&=\int_0^t(\pi\cos\pi t+\pi\sin\pi t)\,dt\\ v+1&=\Big[\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t\Big]_0^t\\ v+1&=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t+1\\ v&=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t\end{aligned}$$
Set $v=0$:
$$\tan\pi t=1$$
So $\pi t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{5\pi}{4},\dots$, giving $t=\dfrac14,\dfrac54$ minutes.
$$\therefore\ \text{the first change of direction is at } t=\dfrac14 \text{ min (15 seconds)}$$
criteria: Finds $v=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity $v=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t$ from part (a), with $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$x=\int(\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t)\,dt=-\dfrac{\cos\pi t}{\pi}-\dfrac{\sin\pi t}{\pi}+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $C=\dfrac{1}{\pi}$. Hence
$$x=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\left[\cos\pi t+\sin\pi t-1\right]$$
The particle turns at $t=\dfrac14$, so find $x$ there and at $t=\dfrac12$.
$$x\left(\dfrac14\right)=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1),\qquad x\left(\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(0+1-1)=0$$
The particle moves to $-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1)$ and then returns to $0$, so the distance travelled for $0\le t\le\dfrac12$ is
$$\therefore\ 2\times\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1) \text{ cm}$$
criteria: Finds the positions at $t=\dfrac14$ and $t=\dfrac12$, or equivalent merit
Finds the displacement function $x$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Integrate the following:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int x^4(x^5-3)^2\,dx =$

dif.r: Reverse chain rule, standard form

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int\left(\sqrt{x}-\dfrac{2}{x}+3e^{-x}+1\right)dx =$

dif.r: Term-by-term standard integrals

solutions.latex:
The factor $5x^4$ is the derivative of $x^5-3$, so use the reverse chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned}\int x^4(x^5-3)^2\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{5}\int5x^4(x^5-3)^2\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}\cdot\dfrac{(x^5-3)^3}{3}+C\\ &=\dfrac{1}{15}(x^5-3)^3+C\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, expand:
$$\int x^4(x^{10}-6x^5+9)\,dx=\dfrac{x^{15}}{15}-\dfrac{3}{5}x^{10}+\dfrac{9}{5}x^5+C$$
criteria: Makes progress towards the integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write each term as a power of $x$ and integrate term by term.
$$\begin{aligned}\int\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}-2x^{-1}+3e^{-x}+1\right)dx&=\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-2\ln|x|-3e^{-x}+x+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates two terms correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)$ is $\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$.

dif.r: Log laws then differentiate and combine fractions to given result

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx$.

dif.r: Hence integral by scaling previous derivative

solutions.latex:
Use the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$ before differentiating.
$$y=\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)=\ln(3+x)-\ln(3-x)$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{3+x}+\dfrac{1}{3-x}\\ &=\dfrac{(3-x)+(3+x)}{(3+x)(3-x)}\\ &=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\end{aligned}$$

From part (a),
$$\int\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx=\ln\left|\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right|+C$$
Divide by $6$:
$$\therefore\ \int\dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{6}\ln\left|\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right|+C$$

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx=\dfrac{10}{3},\ 0\leq a<\pi$, calculate the value of $a$.

dif.r: Definite trig integral with unknown limit, solve trig equation in domain

solutions.latex:
Integrate, then apply the limits.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^a5\sin3x\,dx&=\left[-\dfrac{5}{3}\cos3x\right]_0^a\\ &=-\dfrac{5}{3}\left[\cos3a-\cos0\right]\end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\dfrac{10}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{5}{3}\left[\cos3a-1\right]&=\dfrac{10}{3}\\ \cos3a-1&=-2\\ \cos3a&=-1\end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le a<\pi$, we have $0\le3a<3\pi$, so $3a=\pi$.
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

parts.latex: Solve $2\cos\left[2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]=1$ in the domain $[0,2\pi]$.

dif.r: Compound-angle trig equation, adjusted domain, five solutions

solutions.latex:
Divide by $2$:
$$\cos\left[2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]=\dfrac12$$
The reference angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants.

For $0\le x\le2\pi$, the angle $2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ lies in the range
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}&\le 2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\le\dfrac{11\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 4\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
$$x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ x=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ 2\pi$$
criteria: Finds the correct range for the angle and some solutions, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The probability distribution of a discrete random variable $X$ is shown.

\extable{635_q26_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the value of $t$?

dif.r: Probabilities sum to one, solve quadratic, reject negative root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the expected value of the probability distribution.

dif.r: Direct expected value calculation

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned}t^2+t^2+\dfrac{t}{4}+\dfrac{4t+1}{8}&=1\\ 2t^2+\dfrac{6t+1}{8}&=1\\ 16t^2+6t-7&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$t=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{36+448}}{32}=\dfrac{-6\pm22}{32}$$
Since $0\le P(X=x)\le1$, $t$ cannot be negative (as $t^2$ and $\dfrac{t}{4}$ are probabilities, $t\ge0$), so we take the positive root.
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac12$$
criteria: Obtains the quadratic and solves it, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added a short reason for rejecting the negative root ($t=-\dfrac{7}{8}$ makes $\dfrac{t}{4}$ negative); table is in the question and not shown here.

solutions.latex:
With $t=\dfrac12$: $P(X=-1)=P(X=0)=\dfrac14$, $P(X=1)=\dfrac18$, $P(X=2)=\dfrac38$.
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-1\times\dfrac14+0+1\times\dfrac18+2\times\dfrac38\\ &=-\dfrac14+\dfrac18+\dfrac34\\ &=\dfrac58\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the smallest number of people that can be chosen at random so that the probability that at least ONE has green eyes is greater than $0.4$?

dif.r: Set up exponential inequality, logs, reverse inequality, round up

solutions.latex:
"At least one" is the complement of "none". Each person fails to have green eyes with probability $0.96$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one})&=1-P(\text{none})\\ &=1-0.96\times0.96\\ &=0.0784\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the complementary event, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $n$ people, $P(\text{at least one})=1-(0.96)^n$.
$$\begin{aligned}1-(0.96)^n&>0.4\\ (0.96)^n&<0.6\end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms. Since $\ln0.96<0$, the inequality reverses when dividing.
$$\begin{aligned}n\ln0.96&<\ln0.6\\ n&>\dfrac{\ln0.6}{\ln0.96}=12.51\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n=13 \text{ people}$$

questions.stem:
A section of the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ is shown.

\exfigure{635_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: The curves meet at $A$ and $B$. Show by substitution, that the $x$ values of point $A$ and $B$ are $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $-\pi$ respectively.

dif.r: Verify intersections by substituting exact values

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise, find the exact area of the shaded region.

dif.r: Area between two trig curves, exact evaluation with negative limit

figures.cap: graphs of y=cos(x/2) and y=sin x with points A and B and shaded region

solutions.latex:
Substitute each $x$ value into both functions.

At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\ \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}&=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The values are equal, so the curves meet at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, which is $A$.

At $x=-\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin(-\pi)&=0\\ \cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$
The values are equal, so the curves meet at $x=-\pi$, which is $B$.
criteria: Verifies one of the points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From the graph, $y=\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$ lies above $y=\sin x$ between $B$ and $A$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_{-\pi}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(\cos\dfrac{x}{2}-\sin x\right)dx\\ &=\left[2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}+\cos x\right]_{-\pi}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &=\left(2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}+\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\left(2\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+\cos(-\pi)\right)\\ &=1+\dfrac12+2+1\\ &=4\dfrac12 \text{ square units}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the primitive and substitutes the limits, or equivalent merit
Sets up the correct integral, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
In a laboratory, a food product is heated in an oven at $210^\circ$ C in an effort to kill harmful bacteria. The number of bacteria recorded when the food product is first placed in the oven is 1800. After ten minutes the number of bacteria recorded is 550.

It is found that $N$, the number of bacteria remaining $t$ minutes after being in the oven is given by $N=Ae^{-kt}$ where $A$ and $k$ are constants.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $A$.

dif.r: Initial value substitution t=0

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the value of $k$ correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for k using logs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If an acceptable number of bacteria present is 100 or less, For how long should the food product to be in the oven? Express your answer to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Solve exponential inequality with logs, round appropriately

solutions.latex:
When $t=10$, $N=550$:
$$\begin{aligned}550&=1800e^{-10k}\\ e^{-10k}&=\dfrac{55}{180}\\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\left(\dfrac{55}{180}\right)\\ &\approx0.1186\end{aligned}$$

We need $N\le100$.
$$\begin{aligned}1800e^{-0.1186t}&\le100\\ e^{-0.1186t}&\le\dfrac{1}{18}\\ -0.1186t&\le\ln\dfrac{1}{18}\\ t&\ge\dfrac{\ln18}{0.1186}\approx24.37\end{aligned}$$
The inequality reverses when dividing by $-0.1186$. Rounding $24.37$ to the nearest minute gives $24$, but $N(24)\approx105>100$, so round up to the next whole minute:
$$\therefore\ t=25 \text{ minutes}$$

meta.format_note: The source rounds 24.37 up to 25 minutes (nearest minute would be 24, but 25 is needed for $N\le100$); kept as in source.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the working said the answer came from rounding to the nearest minute; $24.37$ rounds to $24$, which is too early ($N(24)\approx105$), so it must be rounded up to $25$.

questions.stem: After a week of heavy rain, the local dam starts to fill until at 10am on Sunday the dam overflows into the river. At time $t$ (hours after the dam begins spilling), the height ($H$) of the river changes at the rate of $\left[1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right]$ metres per hour. Initially the height of the river is 5 metres.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the height of the river is given by the formula $H=-\dfrac{t^2}{40}+t+5$

dif.r: Integrate rate with initial condition to given formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the maximum height of the river during this flood.

dif.r: Maximum of quadratic model via vertex or derivative

parts.label: c
parts.latex: A bridge over this river will be flooded and closed once the height of the river reaches 12.5 metres. At what time(s) and day(s) will the bridge be closed and reopened?

dif.r: Solve quadratic then interpret both roots as clock times

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate of change, with $H=5$ when $t=0$.
$$\dfrac{dH}{dt}=1-\dfrac{t}{20}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_5^H dH&=\int_0^t\left(1-\dfrac{t}{20}\right)dt\\ H-5&=\left[t-\dfrac{t^2}{40}\right]_0^t\\ H-5&=t-\dfrac{t^2}{40}\\ H&=-\dfrac{t^2}{40}+t+5\end{aligned}$$

$H=-\dfrac{t^2}{40}+t+5$ is a concave-down parabola, so the maximum is at the vertex.
$$t=\dfrac{-1}{2\times\left(-\frac{1}{40}\right)}=20$$
$$H(20)=-\dfrac{20^2}{40}+20+5=15$$
Alternatively, $\dfrac{dH}{dt}=0$ gives $t=20$, and $\dfrac{d^2H}{dt^2}=-\dfrac{1}{20}<0$ confirms a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum height}=15 \text{ metres}$$

The bridge closes when $H=12.5$.
$$\begin{aligned}12.5&=-\dfrac{t^2}{40}+t+5\\ t^2-40t+300&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$t=\dfrac{40\pm\sqrt{1600-1200}}{2}=\dfrac{40\pm20}{2}=10 \text{ or } 30$$
The dam starts spilling at 10am Sunday.

At $t=10$: 10 hours later is 8pm Sunday, when the bridge closes.

At $t=30$: 30 hours later is 10am Monday plus 6 hours, which is 4pm Monday, when the bridge reopens.
$$\therefore\ \text{closed at 8pm Sunday and reopened at 4pm Monday}$$

parts.latex: What are the values of $x$ for which $f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-3x}$ is defined?

dif.r: Domain needs a quadratic inequality solved outside the roots

solutions.latex:
The square root is defined only when $x^2-3x\ge 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-3x &\ge 0 \\ x(x-3) &\ge 0 \end{aligned}$$
The parabola $y=x(x-3)$ opens upwards with roots $0$ and $3$, so it is non-negative outside the roots.
$$\therefore\ x\le 0 \text{ or } x\ge 3$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
In which one of the following ways can the shaded area in the diagram be calculated?

\exfigure{1324_q2_1}

dif.r: Signed area: region below axis needs a negated integral

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with shaded regions between x=-3 and x=6

solutions.latex:
The region from $x=-3$ to $x=1$ lies above the axis, so its area equals $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{1}f(x)\,dx$.

The region from $x=1$ to $x=6$ lies below the axis, so its integral is negative and its area is $-\displaystyle\int_{1}^{6}f(x)\,dx$.

Hence the shaded area is
$$\int_{-3}^{1}f(x)\,dx-\int_{1}^{6}f(x)\,dx$$
This is option D.

What is the perimeter $P$, of the sector given below with angle $36^\circ$ and radius 20 centimetres?

figures.cap: sector with angle 36 degrees and radius 20 cm

solutions.latex:
Convert the angle to radians.
$$36^\circ=\dfrac{36}{180}\times\pi=\dfrac{\pi}{5}$$
Using the arc length formula $l=r\theta$:
$$l=20\times\dfrac{\pi}{5}=4\pi$$
The perimeter is the arc plus two radii.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 20+20+4\pi \\ &= 40+4\pi \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

This is option A.

The population $N$, of a colony of ants grows exponentially according to the formula $N(t)=550e^{kt}$, where $k$ is the growth constant and $t$ is time in days.

parts.latex: What is $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{2-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)$ ?

dif.r: Quotient rule with Pythagorean simplification

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2-\sin\theta & v&=\cos\theta\\ u'&=-\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{2-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) &= \dfrac{\cos\theta(-\cos\theta)-(2-\sin\theta)(-\sin\theta)}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{-\cos^2\theta+2\sin\theta-\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{-(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)+2\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sin\theta-1}{\cos^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

This is option C.

parts.latex: There are 10 green marbles and $W$ white marbles in a bag. The probability of selecting a white marble is $\dfrac{4}{9}$. How many more white marbles need to be added to the bag so that the probability of selecting a white marble from the bag is $\dfrac{3}{5}$?

dif.r: Set up and solve two probability equations for unknowns

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
With $W$ white marbles and 10 green marbles, $P(\text{white})=\dfrac{W}{10+W}=\dfrac{4}{9}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9W &= 40+4W \\ 5W &= 40 \\ W &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
So there are 10 green and 8 white marbles. Let $n$ white marbles be added.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{8+n}{18+n} &= \dfrac{3}{5} \\ 40+5n &= 54+3n \\ 2n &= 14 \\ n &= 7 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: Simplify fully: $\dfrac{3}{x+2}\times\dfrac{x^2+2x}{6x-3}$

dif.r: Routine factorising and cancelling of algebraic fractions

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator and denominator, then cancel common factors.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{x+2}\times\dfrac{x^2+2x}{6x-3} &= \dfrac{3}{x+2}\times\dfrac{x(x+2)}{3(2x-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2x-1} \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: Direct substitution into cosine rule

figures.cap: triangle with sides 11 cm, 13 cm, x cm and included angle 80 degrees

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule, $x^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$, with the sides $11$ and $13$ and the included angle $80^\circ$:
$$x^2=11^2+13^2-2\times 11\times 13\times\cos 80^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \sqrt{11^2+13^2-2\times 11\times 13\times\cos 80^\circ} \\ &\approx 15.50 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The first term of an arithmetic series is 4. The fifth term is four times the third term. Find the sum of the first 10 terms.

dif.r: Form equation for d from term condition, then sum formula

solutions.latex:
Here $a=4$, and the condition is $t_5=4t_3$. Using $t_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} a+4d &= 4(a+2d) \\ a+4d &= 4a+8d \\ 3a &= -4d \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $a=4$ gives $12=-4d$, so $d=-3$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}\left[2a+9d\right] \\ &= 5\left[2\times 4+9\times(-3)\right] \\ &= -95 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms an equation from the condition, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $\log_e(2x+1)-\log_e 3=3$

dif.r: Log law then convert to exponential form

solutions.latex:
Combine the logarithms using $\log_e a-\log_e b=\log_e\dfrac{a}{b}$.
$$\log_e\dfrac{2x+1}{3}=3$$
Write in exponential form.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2x+1}{3} &= e^3 \\ 2x+1 &= 3e^3 \\ 2x &= 3e^3-1 \\ x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3e^3-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes in exponential form, or equivalent merit

Use $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ and $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}-1\right)\times\sin^2\theta \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\right)\times\sin^2\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\times\sin^2\theta \\ &= \cos^2\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}\sec^2 x\,dx$ giving the answer in exact form with rational denominator.

solutions.latex:
The antiderivative of $\sec^2 x$ is $\tan x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\sec^2 x\,dx &= \Big[\tan x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \sqrt{3}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int x^2\left(x^3-1\right)^5\,dx$

dif.r: Reverse chain rule with constant adjustment

solutions.latex:
The derivative of the inner function $x^3-1$ is $3x^2$, so adjust by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int x^2(x^3-1)^5\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{3}\displaystyle\int 3x^2(x^3-1)^5\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{(x^3-1)^6}{6}+C \\ &= \dfrac{(x^3-1)^6}{18}+C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the derivative of the inner function, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A function is given by $f(x)=3+4x^3-x^4$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Stationary points including horizontal inflection where second derivative test fails

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that there is a point of inflexion at $(2,19)$ on the curve.

dif.r: Verify inflection with concavity change either side

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, Sketch the graph of the curve and clearly label the stationary points and the points of inflexion on the curve. DO NOT determine the $x$ intercepts of the curve

dif.r: Sketch quartic from found stationary and inflection points

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = 3+4x^3-x^4 with labelled points
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate.
$$f'(x)=12x^2-4x^3,\qquad f''(x)=24x-12x^2$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x^2-4x^3 &= 0 \\ 4x^2(3-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=3$.

At $x=3$, the second derivative decides the nature.
$$f''(3)=24\times 3-12\times 3^2=-36<0$$
So there is a maximum at $x=3$.
$$f(3)=3+4\times 3^3-3^4=30$$
Hence $(3,30)$ is a maximum.

At $x=0$, $f''(0)=0$, so test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline f''(x) & -36 & 0 & 12 \end{array}$$
The sign of $f''$ changes from negative to positive, so the concavity changes and $x=0$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
$$f(0)=3$$
$$\therefore\ (3,30) \text{ is a maximum and } (0,3) \text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion.}$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points and the nature of one of them, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

Points of inflexion occur where $f''(x)=0$.

parts.latex: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the numerator as $1-e^x+2e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x+2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x}{1-e^x}+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= 1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
Alternative solution, starting from the right-hand side:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= 1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1-e^x+2e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x} \\ &= \text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines or splits the numerator correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use part (a), then write the second term as a multiple of $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ with $f(x)=1-e^x$, $f'(x)=-e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{1+e^x}{1-e^x}\,dx &= \displaystyle\int\left(1+\dfrac{2e^x}{1-e^x}\right)dx \\ &= \displaystyle\int\left(1+(-2)\left(\dfrac{-e^x}{1-e^x}\right)\right)dx \\ &= x-2\ln\left|1-e^x\right|+C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rewrites as a multiple of derivative of the denominator over the denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A normal to the graph of $y=2\sqrt{x}$ has the equation $y=-3x+b$. Find the value of $b$.

dif.r: Reverse: normal gradient gives contact point, then find intercept

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the curve to find the gradient of the tangent.
$$y'=2\times\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$$
The gradient of the normal is the negative reciprocal.
$$m=-\sqrt{x}$$
This equals the gradient $-3$ of the given normal.
$$\begin{aligned} -\sqrt{x} &= -3 \\ x &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
When $x=9$, $y=2\sqrt{9}=6$, so the point of contact is $(9,6)$.

The normal passes through this point.
$$\begin{aligned} 6 &= -3\times 9+b \\ b &= 33 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the point of contact, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: If $f(x)=\log_e\left(x+\sqrt{x}\right)$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{2x\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)}$

dif.r: Chain rule on a log, then factorise surds to reach the given form

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, when $x=2$, Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{2x\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)}$ can be written in the form $a+b\sqrt{2}$

dif.r: Substitute, then rationalise a surd denominator into a+b√2 form

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $f(x)=\log_e\left(x+\sqrt{x}\right)$:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{x+\sqrt{x}}\left[1+\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x+\sqrt{x}}\times\dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{\left(x+\sqrt{x}\right)\times 2\sqrt{x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{\sqrt{x}\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)\times 2\sqrt{x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{x}+1}{2x\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the chain rule form, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=2$ and rationalise the denominator.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(2) &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}+1}{2\times 2\left(\sqrt{2}+1\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}+1}{4\left(\sqrt{2}+1\right)}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}-1} \\ &= \dfrac{4-2\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}-1}{4(2-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{3-\sqrt{2}}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{1}{4}\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes and rationalises, or equivalent merit

$$f(-1)=0.27,\quad f(0)=1,\quad f(1)=0$$

solutions.latex:
There are five function values, so four strips of width $h=\dfrac{1-(-3)}{4}=1$, at $x=-3,-2,-1,0,1$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{1-(-3)}{2\times 4}\Big[f(-3)+f(1)+2\big(f(-2)+f(-1)+f(0)\big)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{4}{8}\Big[0.01+0+2(0.05+0.27+1)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.65 \\ &= 1.325 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct trapezoidal rule set-up, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=1-x \\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=-1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= e^{2x}\times(-1)+(1-x)\times 2e^{2x} \\ &= -e^{2x}+2e^{2x}-2xe^{2x} \\ &= e^{2x}(1-2x) \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $f'(x)=0$, so $e^{2x}(1-2x)=0$.

Since $e^{2x}>0$ for all $x$, $1-2x=0$, so $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$$f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=e^{1}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=\dfrac{e}{2}$$

The curve has only one stationary point, $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{e}{2}\right)$, or $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},1.36\right)$.
criteria: Sets the derivative to zero and uses $e^{2x}>0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2^x+1} \\ &= \dfrac{2^x+1-2}{2\left(2^x+1\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{2^x-1}{2\left(2^x+1\right)} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; single row added.

solutions.latex:
Find $f(-x)$ using the form from part (a), multiplying numerator and denominator by $2^x$.

$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= \dfrac{2^{-x}-1}{2\left(2^{-x}+1\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2^x}-1}{2\left(\frac{1}{2^x}+1\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{1-2^x}{2\left(1+2^x\right)} \\ &= -\dfrac{2^x-1}{2\left(2^x+1\right)} \\ &= -f(x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f(x)\text{ is an odd function.}$$

questions.stem: A wire of length 5 metres is to be bent to form the hypotenuse and base of a right angled triangle $ABC$ with right angle at $B$. Let the length of the base $BC$ be $x$ metres.
questions.review_note: Paper labels the last part (d) with no part (c); relabelled c (solutions also call it (c))

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write an expression for the length of the hypotenuse $AC$ in terms of $x$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the area of the triangle $ABC$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}x\sqrt{25-10x}$ square meters.

dif.r: Use Pythagoras to set up the area expression; a short show-that

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the maximum possible area of the triangle $ABC$.

dif.r: Product rule with a surd, simplify, test the nature, exact maximum area

solutions.latex:
The wire has total length $5$ m and $BC=x$.

$$AC=5-x \text{ metres}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; single row added.

solutions.latex:
By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle $ABC$:

$$\begin{aligned} AB^2 &= (5-x)^2-x^2 \\ &= 25-10x+x^2-x^2 \\ &= 25-10x \end{aligned}$$

So $AB=\sqrt{25-10x}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times BC\times AB \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}x\sqrt{25-10x} \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses Pythagoras' theorem to find $AB$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sqrt{25-10x} \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{-10}{2\sqrt{25-10x}} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{25-10x}+x\times\dfrac{-10}{2\sqrt{25-10x}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{25-10x-5x}{\sqrt{25-10x}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{25-15x}{\sqrt{25-10x}} \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 25-15x &= 0 \\ x &= \dfrac{25}{15}=\dfrac{5}{3}\approx 1.67 \end{aligned}$$

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ either side.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 1 & \dfrac{5}{3} & 2 \\ \hline \dfrac{dA}{dx} & 1.29 & 0 & -1.12 \end{array}$$

The derivative changes sign from positive to negative, so $A$ is a maximum when $x=\dfrac{5}{3}$.

$$\begin{aligned} A_{\max} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{5}{3}\times\sqrt{25-\dfrac{10\times 5}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6}\sqrt{\dfrac{25}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{25}{6\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{25\sqrt{3}}{18} \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Justifies the maximum, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Compare f, f', f'' from graph; needs chord-tangent concavity reasoning.

figures.cap: increasing concave down curve through origin with marked point at x=1

solutions.latex:
Read each quantity from the graph at $x=1$.

$f(1)>0$, since the curve is above the $x$-axis.

$f'(1)>0$, since the curve is increasing.

$f''(1)<0$, since the curve is concave down.

To compare $f'(1)$ with $f(1)$: the curve starts at the origin, so the chord from $(0,0)$ to $(1,f(1))$ has gradient $f(1)$. On a concave down curve the tangent at $x=1$ is flatter than this chord, so $f'(1)<f(1)$.

This matches option A.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=x^3-3x^2 with turning points (0,0) and (2,-4), x-intercept 3

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=x^3-3x^2 \\ f'(x)&=3x^2-6x \\ f''(x)&=6x-6 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x(x-2)&=0 \\ x&=0 \text{ or } x=2 \end{aligned}$$
The second derivative decides the nature.

At $x=0$: $f(0)=0$ and $f''(0)=-6<0$, so $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point.

At $x=2$: $f(2)=2^3-3\times 4=-4$ and $f''(2)=6>0$, so $(2,-4)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds both stationary points and tests one, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{1-\sin^2 x\cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x}=\cot^2 x+\sin^2 x$

dif.r: Short trig identity proof using cot and Pythagorean identity.

solutions.latex:
Start from the right-hand side and use $\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=\cot^2x+\sin^2x \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin^2x}+\sin^2x \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2x+\sin^2x\cdot\sin^2x}{\sin^2x} \end{aligned}$$
Using $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$ for one factor:
$$\begin{aligned} &=\dfrac{\cos^2x+\sin^2x(1-\cos^2x)}{\sin^2x} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2x+\sin^2x-\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x} \\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x} \\ &=\text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the right-hand side over the common denominator $\sin^2x$, or equivalent merit

Substitute $t=0$ into $\dot x=8-8e^{-2t}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dot x&=8-8e^{0} \\ &=8-8 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$$

From part (b) the acceleration is always positive, so the velocity is increasing for all $t$.

parts.latex:
A town planning committee notes that the rate of growth of the town's population since 1985 has followed the formula: $\dfrac{dp}{dt}=(1500+200t)$ people per year

where $t$ is the number of years since 1st January 1985. On 1st January 1992 the population was $25\,000$. Find the formula for the city's population from 1985 onwards.

dif.r: Integrate rate and find constant from condition at t=7.

solutions.latex:
Population is the integral of the rate of growth.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \int (1500+200t)\,dt \\ &= 1500t+\dfrac{200t^2}{2}+K \\ &= 1500t+100t^2+K \end{aligned}$$

On 1 January 1992, $t=7$ and $P=25\,000$.

$$\begin{aligned} 25\,000 &= 1500(7)+100(7)^2+K \\ &= 10\,500+4900+K \\ K &= 9600 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P=100t^2+1500t+9600$$

parts.latex: Hence find the maximum volume of the box, and the value of $x$ at which it occurs.

dif.r: Product rule, factorise, test nature, select feasible maximum.

figures.cap: square sheet 16 cm with corner squares x cm cut out

solutions.latex:
After cutting squares of side $x$ from each corner, the base is a square of side $16-2x$ and the height is $x$.

$$\begin{aligned} V &= (16-2x)^2\,x \\ &= x\big(2(8-x)\big)^2 \\ &= 4x(8-x)^2 \\ &= 4x(x-8)^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ V(x)=4x(x-8)^2$$
criteria: Finds the dimensions of the box, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source line ended with $4x(8-x)^2$, which equals $4x(x-8)^2$; added the final step to match the required form. Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=(x-8)^2\\ u'&=4 & v'&=2(x-8)\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} V'(x) &= 4(x-8)^2+8x(x-8) \\ &= 4(x-8)\big[(x-8)+2x\big] \\ &= 4(x-8)(3x-8) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur when $V'(x)=0$, so $x=8$ or $x=\dfrac{8}{3}$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.

$$V''(x)=24x-128$$

$$\begin{aligned} V''(8) &= 24(8)-128>0 &&\text{minimum turning point}\\ V''\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) &= 24\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right)-128<0 &&\text{maximum turning point} \end{aligned}$$

The maximum volume occurs at $x=\dfrac{8}{3}$.

$$\begin{aligned} V\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) &= 4\times\dfrac{8}{3}\left(\dfrac{8}{3}-8\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{8192}{27} = 303\dfrac{11}{27} \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{maximum volume } 303\dfrac{11}{27}\text{ cm}^3 \text{ at } x=\dfrac{8}{3}$$
criteria: Finds the maximum point and tests its nature, or equivalent merit
Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

$$\therefore\ \text{Shaded area}=\left(\pi-\dfrac{5}{6}\right)\text{ units}^2$$

meta.format_note: Table reference kept as given. Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex: \extable{Ts4294_1}
criteria: Completes some of the table correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Table reference kept as given. Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The expected value is $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 0\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{5}{18}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{2}{9}\right)+3\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right)+5\left(\dfrac{1}{18}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{35}{18} \\ &= 1\dfrac{17}{18} \end{aligned}$$

For the standard deviation, $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-\mu^2$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}$.

$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= 0^2\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)+1^2\left(\dfrac{5}{18}\right)+2^2\left(\dfrac{2}{9}\right)+3^2\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)+4^2\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right)+5^2\left(\dfrac{1}{18}\right) \\ &= 5\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Since $\mu=1\dfrac{17}{18}$, $\mu^2=3\dfrac{253}{324}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= 5\dfrac{5}{6}-3\dfrac{253}{324} \\ &\approx 2.0524 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \sigma\approx 1.43 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$

parts.latex: The sum of the series $1+8+15+\dots$ is $396$. How many terms does the series contain?

dif.r: Arithmetic sum formula in reverse, solve quadratic for n.

solutions.latex:
This is an arithmetic series with first term $a=1$ and common difference $d=7$.

Let there be $n$ terms, so $S_n=396$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2+7(n-1)\big) &= 396 \\ n(7n-5) &= 792 \\ 7n^2-5n-792 &= 0 \\ (7n+72)(n-11) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $n=-\dfrac{72}{7}$ or $n=11$.

The number of terms must be a positive integer, so $n=11$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the series has } 11 \text{ terms}$$
criteria: Obtains the quadratic equation in $n$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes into the formula for $S_n$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Find clock angle then apply cosine rule.

figures.cap: clock face with hands OA = 10 cm and OB = 7 cm, diagram not accurately drawn

solutions.latex:
Each hour on the clock face is $\dfrac{360^\circ}{12}=30^\circ$, so at 5 o'clock:

$$\angle AOB=5\times 30^\circ=150^\circ$$

In triangle $AOB$, using the cosine rule with $AB=x$:

$$\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 10^2+7^2-2\times10\times7\times\cos150^\circ \\ &\approx 270.243 \\ x &\approx 16.439 \\ &\approx 16.4 \text{ cm (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ AB\approx 16.4 \text{ cm}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle AOB$ or substitutes into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: By considering the equation of the tangent to $y=x^2-1$ at the point $(a,a^2-1)$, find the equations of the two tangents to $y=x^2-1$ which pass through $(3,-8)$.

dif.r: Identical to HSC tangent-through-external-point question.

solutions.latex:
For $y=x^2-1$, $y'=2x$, so the gradient at $x=a$ is $2a$.

The tangent at $(a,a^2-1)$ is:

$$\begin{aligned} y-(a^2-1) &= 2a(x-a) \\ y-a^2+1 &= 2ax-2a^2 \\ y &= 2ax-a^2-1 \end{aligned}$$

If the tangent passes through $(3,-8)$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2a(3)-a^2-1 &= -8 \\ a^2-6a-7 &= 0 \\ (a-7)(a+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $a=7$ or $a=-1$.

For $a=7$: $y=14x-50$.

For $a=-1$: $y=-2x-2$.

$$\therefore\ y=14x-50 \text{ and } y=-2x-2$$
criteria: Finds both values of $a$, or equivalent merit
Forms the quadratic equation in $a$, or equivalent merit
Finds the equation of the tangent at $x=a$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Under certain climatic conditions the number $N$ of blue-green algae satisfies the equation

$$N(t)=Ae^{0.15t}$$

where $t$ is measured in days and $A$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the number of algae increases at a rate proportional to the number.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential and express derivative as constant times N.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: When $t=3$ the number of algae was estimated to be $1.7\times10^8$. Evaluate $A$.

dif.r: Substitute values and solve for constant.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: The number of algae doubles every $x$ days. Find the value of $x$.

dif.r: Set up doubling equation and solve using logarithms.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $N(t)=Ae^{0.15t}$.

$$\begin{aligned} N'(t) &= 0.15Ae^{0.15t} \\ &= 0.15\,N(t) \end{aligned}$$

Since $0.15$ is a constant, $N'(t)\propto N(t)$, so the number increases at a rate proportional to the number.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=3$ and $N=1.7\times10^8$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1.7\times10^8 &= Ae^{0.15(3)} \\ &= Ae^{0.45} \\ A &= \dfrac{1.7\times10^8}{e^{0.45}} \\ &\approx 1.0839\times10^8 \\ &\approx 1.1\times10^8 \text{ (2 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$, $N(0)=Ae^{0}=A$, so after $x$ days $N(x)=2A$.

$$\begin{aligned} Ae^{0.15x} &= 2A \\ e^{0.15x} &= 2 \\ 0.15x &= \ln 2 \\ x &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.15} \\ &\approx 4.6209 \\ &\approx 4.6 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms the equation $e^{0.15x}=2$, or equivalent merit

A bag contains 4 maroon coloured marbles and 6 white coloured marbles. Three marbles are selected at random without replacement.

What is the probability that at least one of the marbles selected is maroon?

dif.r: Complement for at least one, without replacement

solutions.latex:
Use the complement: at least one maroon marble is the opposite of no maroon marbles.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one maroon})&=1-P(\text{no maroon}) \\ &=1-\left(\dfrac{6}{10}\times\dfrac{5}{9}\times\dfrac{4}{8}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

On $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ the curve $y=2\sec x$ rises from $y=2$ to $y=4$.

This is option A.

figures.cap: graphs of f(x)=x+sin x and g(x)=x with shaded region

solutions.latex:
The graphs meet where $f(x)=g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} x+\sin x&=x \\ \sin x&=0 \\ x&=k\pi,\quad k\in\mathbb{Z} \end{aligned}$$
From the diagram, $A$ is at the first positive solution.

The shaded area lies between $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ from $x=0$ to $x=\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\tan x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\sec^2x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x\tan x)&=x\sec^2x+\tan x\cdot1 \\ &=x\sec^2x+\tan x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows one correct derivative related to the question, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=\cos^2x \\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=-2\sin x\cos x \end{aligned}$$
Here $v'$ comes from the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x\cos^2x)&=\cos x\cdot\cos^2x+\sin x\left(-2\sin x\cos x\right) \\ &=\cos^3x-2\sin^2x\cos x \\ &=\cos x\left(\cos^2x-2\sin^2x\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule but with an error in the chain rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{e^x}\right)&=\dfrac{e^x\cdot1-x\cdot e^x}{(e^x)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{e^x(1-x)}{e^{2x}} \\ &=\dfrac{1-x}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Coal is extracted from a mine at a rate that is proportional to the amount of coal remaining in the mine. Hence the amount $R$ remaining after $t$ years is given by $R=R_0e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a constant and $R_0$ is the initial amount of coal.

After 20 years, $50\%$ of the initial amount of coal remains.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the exact value of $k$.

dif.r: Half-life condition solved with logarithms

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: How many more years will elapse before only $10\%$ of the original amount remains?

dif.r: Solve exponential decay equation with logs, then subtract elapsed time

solutions.latex:
When $t=20$, $R=\dfrac{1}{2}R_0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}R_0&=R_0e^{-20k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2}&=e^{-20k} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=-20k \\ -\ln2&=-20k \\ k&=\dfrac{1}{20}\ln2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes the given values into the equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (i), $k=\dfrac{1}{20}\ln 2$. Set $R=0.1R_0$ and solve for $t$.
$$\begin{aligned}0.1R_0&=R_0e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ 0.1&=e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ \ln(0.1)&=\ln e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ -\dfrac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t&=-\ln 10\\ t&=\dfrac{20\ln 10}{\ln 2}\\ &\approx 66.44\end{aligned}$$
The question asks for how many more years, so subtract the first 20 years.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{More years}&=66.44-20\\ &=46.44\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 46.44 \text{ more years}$$
criteria: Finds the correct value for $t$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A student was asked to differentiate $f(x)=x^2-2x$ from first principles. The student began the solution as shown below. Complete the solution.

$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$

dif.r: Standard first-principles expansion and limit of a quadratic

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{(x+h)^2-2(x+h)-\left[x^2-2x\right]}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{x^2+2hx+h^2-2x-2h-x^2+2x}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{2hx+h^2-2h}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\,(2x-2+h)\\ &=2x-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f'(x)=2x-2$$
criteria: Writes the first line or skips steps, or equivalent merit

Loudness, in decibels, is given by the formula $L=\log_e\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$, where $I$ is the intensity level and $I_0$ is the threshold sound (or sound that can barely be heard). Sounds louder than 85 dB can damage hearing.

The intensity of a vacuum cleaner is estimated to be 10 000 000 times the threshold level $I_0$. Would using a vacuum cleaner damage your hearing based on this estimate? Justify your answer with appropriate working.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $I=10\,000\,000I_0$ into the formula.
$$\begin{aligned}L&=\log_e\left(\dfrac{10\,000\,000\,I_0}{I_0}\right)\\ &=\ln(10\,000\,000)\\ &\approx 16.11 \text{ dB}\end{aligned}$$
Since $16.11<85$, using this vacuum cleaner would not damage your hearing.

questions.stem: Greg lives in Gosford and is starting a new job in Sydney. He needs to catch a train to get to work and will be late if the trains do not run to schedule. The probability that, on any given day, his train will run to schedule is 0.96.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: What is the probability that Greg arrives late on exactly one of the first three days of his new job?

dif.r: Three arrangements of independent events summed

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Greg is late})&=1-0.96\\ &=0.04\end{aligned}$$

Exactly one late day can happen in 3 ways (late on day 1, 2 or 3), each with probability $0.04\times0.96^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{late on exactly one day})&=0.04\times0.96^2+0.96\times0.04\times0.96+0.96^2\times0.04\\ &\approx 0.11\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some correct working, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $\log_e x-\dfrac{3}{\log_e x}=2$ giving your answers in exact form.

dif.r: Recognise hidden quadratic in ln x, factorise, convert back

solutions.latex:
The equation is a quadratic in $\log_e x$. Multiply through by $\log_e x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\log_e x-\dfrac{3}{\log_e x}&=2\\ (\log_e x)^2-3&=2\log_e x\\ (\log_e x)^2-2\log_e x-3&=0\\ (\log_e x-3)(\log_e x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\log_e x=3$ or $\log_e x=-1$.
$$\therefore\ x=e^3 \text{ or } x=\dfrac{1}{e}$$
criteria: One arithmetic error, or equivalent merit
Recognises that the equation can be considered a quadratic, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan^2 x}=\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$

solutions.latex:
Express the left-hand side in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\cos^2 x}}{\frac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x}\\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^2 x\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some correct working, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The function $f(x)=2-2^x$ is dilated vertically by a factor of 2 and shifted 4 units to the right.

Find the equation of the function formed and sketch the result showing key features.

dif.r: Apply dilation and translation, sketch with asymptote and intercepts

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y=4-2^(x-3)

solutions.latex:
Dilating vertically by a factor of $2$ multiplies the function by $2$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=2\left(2-2^x\right)\\ &=4-2\cdot 2^x\\ &=4-2^{x+1}\end{aligned}$$
Shifting right by $4$ units replaces $x$ with $x-4$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=4-2\cdot 2^{x-4}\\ &=4-2^{x-3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=4-2^{x-3}$$
\exfigure{1326_q27_s1}
criteria: Correct answer (accept different forms of the function)
One error (for example a consequential error), or equivalent merit
One correct element, or equivalent merit

The queueing time, $X$ minutes, of a teacher waiting on the phone with the Department of Education has a probability density function

$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^k\dfrac{3}{32}x(k-x)\,dx&=1\\ \dfrac{3}{32}\int_0^k (kx-x^2)\,dx&=1\\ \left[\dfrac{kx^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^k&=\dfrac{32}{3}\\ \left(\dfrac{k^3}{2}-\dfrac{k^3}{3}\right)-0&=\dfrac{32}{3}\\ \dfrac{k^3}{6}&=\dfrac{32}{3}\\ k^3&=64\\ k&=4\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
\exfigure{1326_q30_1}

A car and a jet plane race one another from rest down a runway. The car increases its speed $v_1$ at a constant rate, while the speed of the jet is given by $v_2=2t^2$. After 5 seconds the car and the jet have the same speed of 50 m/s, as shown on the graph.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: By considering the difference quotient, find the average acceleration of the jet during the $5^{\text{th}}$ second.

dif.r: Interpret fifth second, compute difference quotient

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find an equation for the speed $v_1$ of the car in terms of $t$.

dif.r: Linear equation through origin from one point

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: For what times is the acceleration of the car greater than that of the jet?

dif.r: Differentiate both speeds, solve simple inequality

parts.label: iv
parts.latex: Who is winning the race after 5 seconds and by how many metres?

dif.r: Interpret distance as integral of speed, compare two areas

figures.cap: velocity-time graphs of a car (line) and a jet (curve)

solutions.latex:
The average acceleration is the change in speed over the change in time, from $t=4$ to $t=5$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Average acceleration}&=\dfrac{v_2(5)-v_2(4)}{5-4}\\ &=\dfrac{50-2(4)^2}{1}\\ &=18 \text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some correct working, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The car's speed increases at a constant rate from rest, so $v_1=mt$. At $t=5$, $v_1=50$, so $m=10$.
$$\therefore\ v_1=10t$$

Acceleration is the derivative of speed: $a_{\text{car}}=10$ and $a_{\text{jet}}=4t$.

The car's acceleration is greater when
$$\begin{aligned}10&>4t\\ t&<\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{for } 0\le t<\dfrac{5}{2} \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative of velocity, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Distance is the area under the speed-time graph.

Distance of the car:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^5 10t\,dt&=\left[5t^2\right]_0^5\\ &=5\times5^2-0\\ &=125 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
Distance of the jet:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^5 2t^2\,dt&=\left[\dfrac{2t^3}{3}\right]_0^5\\ &=\dfrac{2\times5^3}{3}-0\\ &\approx 83.3 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Difference}&=125-83.3\\ &\approx 41\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the car is winning by about } 41\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ m}$$
criteria: One correct element, or equivalent merit
