questions.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}a+bx & 0\le x\le 5\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that $10a+25b=2$

dif.r: Integrate linear pdf to 1 and rearrange

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: If $E(X)=\dfrac{35}{12}$, find the values for $a$ and $b$.

dif.r: Expected value integral plus simultaneous equations solving

solutions.latex:
The total area under the density function is $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^5 (a+bx)\,dx&=1\\ \left[ax+\dfrac{bx^2}{2}\right]_0^5&=1\\ \left(5a+\dfrac{25b}{2}\right)-0&=1\\ 10a+25b&=2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises that the integral of the function equals $1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The mean is $E(X)=\displaystyle\int x f(x)\,dx$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{35}{12}&=\int_0^5 x(a+bx)\,dx\\ &=\int_0^5 (ax+bx^2)\,dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{ax^2}{2}+\dfrac{bx^3}{3}\right]_0^5\\ &=\dfrac{25a}{2}+\dfrac{125b}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying by $12$:
$$150a+500b=35\qquad(1)$$
From part (i):
$$10a+25b=2\qquad(2)$$
Multiply (2) by $15$:
$$150a+375b=30\qquad(3)$$
Subtract (3) from (1):
$$\begin{aligned}125b&=5\\ b&=\dfrac{1}{25}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (2):
$$\begin{aligned}10a+25\left(\dfrac{1}{25}\right)&=2\\ a&=\dfrac{1}{10}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{10},\ b=\dfrac{1}{25}$$
criteria: Correct answer (include by inspection if they confirm the result)
Substantial progress with an error, or equivalent merit
Recognises $E(X)=\displaystyle\int x f(x)\,dx$ or recognises the solution is found by simultaneous equations, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Model with Pythagoras, optimise with constant k, justify maximum

figures.cap: rectangular beam cut from a cylindrical log, cross-section diagonal 15

solutions.latex:
In the cross-section, the diagonal is a diameter, so by Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle with sides $w$, $d$ and hypotenuse $15$:
$$d^2=225-w^2$$
Substitute into $S=kwd^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}S&=kw\left(225-w^2\right)\\ &=225kw-kw^3\end{aligned}$$
Differentiate and set equal to zero for a stationary point.
$$\dfrac{dS}{dw}=225k-3kw^2$$
$$\begin{aligned}225k-3kw^2&=0\\ w^2&=75\\ w&=5\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
Here $w>0$ since it is a length.

Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2S}{dw^2}=-6kw$$
At $w=5\sqrt{3}$, with $k>0$ (since $S$, $w$ and $d$ are positive):
$$\dfrac{d^2S}{dw^2}=-6k\left(5\sqrt{3}\right)<0$$
So this is a maximum.
$$\begin{aligned}S_{\max}&=k\left(5\sqrt{3}\right)(225-75)\\ &=750\sqrt{3}\,k\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_{\max}=750\sqrt{3}\,k$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric row read "finding $w=5\sqrt{5}$ (as printed)"; the working gives $w=5\sqrt{3}$, so the criterion was corrected to $5\sqrt{3}$.

questions.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{9}\left(x^2-2x+2\right) & 0\le x\le 3\\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{3} & 3<x\le 4\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: In the space provided, sketch the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$

dif.r: Piecewise CDF with carried constant, concavity analysis, sketch

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the $75^{\text{th}}$ percentile of $X$.

dif.r: Choose correct CDF piece, solve linear equation

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of the CDF

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.

For $0\le x\le3$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{9}\int_0^x\left(t^2-2t+2\right)dt\\ &=\dfrac{1}{9}\left[\dfrac{t^3}{3}-t^2+2t\right]_0^x\\ &=\dfrac{1}{9}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2+2x\right)\end{aligned}$$
At the end of this section:
$$F(3)=\dfrac{1}{9}\left(9-9+6\right)=\dfrac{2}{3}$$
For $3<x\le4$:
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\dfrac{2}{3}+\int_3^x\dfrac{1}{3}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{x-3}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}x-\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
This is a straight line joining $\left(3,\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ to $(4,1)$.

Features of $F(x)$ for $0\le x\le3$:
$$F'(x)=\dfrac{1}{9}\left(x^2-2x+2\right)$$
The discriminant $\Delta=4-8<0$, so $F'(x)>0$ and there are no turning points.
$$F''(x)=\dfrac{1}{9}(2x-2)$$
So $F''(x)=0$ when $x=1$. Test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts4356_1}

The concavity changes at $x=1$, so there is a point of inflection at $\left(1,\dfrac{4}{27}\right)$.

\exfigure{1326_q34_s1}
criteria: Finds the end of the first segment at $\left(3,\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ with correct CDF, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw if 1326_q34_s1 is missing: CDF rising from $(0,0)$ with inflection at $\left(1,\dfrac{4}{27}\right)$, passing $\left(3,\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$, then straight line to $(4,1)$; $F=0$ for $x<0$ and $F=1$ for $x>4$. Source's intermediate line $\dfrac{2}{3}+\left[\dfrac{1}{3}x-1\right]$ was tidied to the same final $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}x-\dfrac{1}{3}$. The table Ts4356_1 is kept as given.

solutions.latex:
The $75^{\text{th}}$ percentile satisfies $F(x)=0.75$. Since $F(3)=\dfrac{2}{3}<0.75$, use the straight-line segment from part (i).
$$\begin{aligned}0.75&=\dfrac{1}{3}x-\dfrac{1}{3}\\ 2.25&=x-1\\ x&=3.25\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the } 75^{\text{th}} \text{ percentile is } 3.25$$

solutions.latex:
For the square root to be defined, $16-x^2\ge 0$, so $-4\le x\le 4$. Then $0\le 16-x^2\le 16$, and the next lines apply one operation each.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le\sqrt{16-x^2}\le 4\\ -8&\le -2\sqrt{16-x^2}\le 0 &&(\text{multiply by } -2,\ \text{reverse inequalities})\end{aligned}$$
Hence the range is $[-8,0]$, which is option C.

solutions.latex:
Enlarging by a factor of 2 with centre the origin replaces $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{2}$ and $y$ by $\dfrac{y}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{x}{2}-2\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{y}{2}+4\right)^2&=9\\ \left(\dfrac{x-4}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{y+8}{2}\right)^2&=9\\ (x-4)^2+(y+8)^2&=36\end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: The period of the function $f(x) = 2\tan\left(4x - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$, where $x \in \mathbb{R}$, is

dif.r: Direct recall of tan period pi over n

solutions.latex:
For $y=a\tan(nx+b)$ the period is $\dfrac{\pi}{n}$. Here $n=4$, so
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Which of the following is equal to $e^{-3\log_e x}$ ?

dif.r: Log power law then exponential-log inverse, two steps

solutions.latex:
Using the log power rule, $-3\log_e x=\log_e x^{-3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{-3\log_e x}&=e^{\log_e x^{-3}}\\ &=x^{-3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{x^3}\end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex:
A particle, initially at the origin, moves in a straight line with velocity $v = 8 - 4t$ m/s.

What is the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 4 seconds?

dif.r: Must notice direction change; two triangle areas for distance

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
The velocity $v=8-4t$ is zero at $t=2$, so the particle changes direction there. The distance is the sum of the two areas between the velocity line and the $t$-axis, for $0\le t\le 2$ and $2\le t\le 4$.

At $t=0$, $v=8$, and at $t=4$, $v=-8$. Each area is a triangle:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 8=8$$
So the total distance is
$$8+8=16 \text{ m}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: If $\displaystyle\int_2^5 f(x)\,dx = 4$, which of the following is $\displaystyle\int_0^3 \left(3f(x+2)\right)dx$ equal to?

dif.r: Recognise horizontal shift of limits and constant multiple in integral

solutions.latex:
Substituting $u=x+2$ shifts the limits from $0,3$ to $2,5$.
$$\begin{aligned}\displaystyle\int_0^3 3f(x+2)\,dx&=3\displaystyle\int_2^5 f(x)\,dx\\ &=3\times 4\\ &=12\end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: In a group of 60 students, 24 have subscribed to SFLIX and 38 have subscribed to NETAN. If 12 students have subscribed to both SFLIX and NETAN, what is the probability that a student chosen at random has subscribed to neither SFLIX nor NETAN?

dif.r: Routine two-set Venn diagram count

solutions.latex:
Students in SFLIX only: $24-12=12$.

Students in NETAN only: $38-12=26$.

Students in at least one: $12+12+26=50$, so $60-50=10$ are in neither.
$$P(\text{neither})=\dfrac{10}{60}=\dfrac{1}{6}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Find the degree of $f(x) \times g(x)$.

dif.r: Expand product and read highest power

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Is $f(x) \times g(x)$ odd or even? Justify your answer.

dif.r: Standard f(-x) test for odd function on a polynomial

solutions.latex:
Expand $f(x)$:
$$f(x)=(x+1)(x-1)=x^2-1$$
Then the product is
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)\times g(x)&=(x^2-1)(x^3)\\ &=x^5-x^3\end{aligned}$$
The highest power is $x^5$, so the degree is $5$.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Let $F(x)=x^5-x^3$. To test for odd or even, find $F(-x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(-x)&=(-x)^5-(-x)^3\\ &=-x^5+x^3\\ &=-(x^5-x^3)\\ &=-F(x)\end{aligned}$$
Since $F(-x)=-F(x)$, the function is odd.

questions.stem: Differentiate the following:

dif.r: Rewrite as negative power then chain rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $y = \dfrac{e^{2x}}{x}$

dif.r: Quotient rule with exponential numerator, routine

solutions.latex:
Rewrite as a power and use the chain rule.
$$y=2(x^2-2x+1)^{-1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=-2(x^2-2x+1)^{-2}(2x-2)\\ &=\dfrac{-2(2x-2)}{(x^2-2x+1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{4-4x}{(x^2-2x+1)^2}\end{aligned}$$
Equivalently, since $x^2-2x+1=(x-1)^2$:
$$y'=\dfrac{4(1-x)}{(x-1)^4}=-\dfrac{4}{(x-1)^3}$$
criteria: Correct use of the chain rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=x\\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{x(2e^{2x})-e^{2x}(1)}{x^2}\\ &=\dfrac{e^{2x}(2x-1)}{x^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Find the following:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{(3x+2)^4}\,dx$

dif.r: Reverse chain rule on linear power, negative index

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x^2}{x^3 - 1}\,dx$

dif.r: f'/f log integral with constant adjustment

solutions.latex:
Write as a power and integrate using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C$.
$$\begin{aligned}\displaystyle\int (3x+2)^{-4}\,dx&=\dfrac{(3x+2)^{-3}}{-3(3)}+C\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{9(3x+2)^3}+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates with correct power, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3-1)=3x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x^2}{x^3-1}\,dx&=\dfrac{2}{3}\displaystyle\int \dfrac{3x^2}{x^3-1}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln|x^3-1|+C\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the logarithmic form, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d\left(x^2 \ln x\right)}{dx}$.

dif.r: Single product rule application

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the primitive of $2x + 4x\ln x$.

dif.r: Hence integration requiring rescaling the derivative from part (a)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=2x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2\ln x)&=(\ln x)(2x)+x^2\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\\ &=2x\ln x+x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $x^2\ln x$ has derivative $2x\ln x+x$, so $2x^2\ln x$ has derivative $4x\ln x+2x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\displaystyle\int (2x+4x\ln x)\,dx&=2\displaystyle\int (x+2x\ln x)\,dx\\ &=2x^2\ln x+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find, in general form, the equation of the normal to the curve $y = 2\sqrt{x}$ at the point on the curve where $x = 4$.

dif.r: Standard normal equation: derivative, perpendicular gradient, general form

solutions.latex:
When $x=4$, $y=2\sqrt{4}=4$, so the point is $(4,4)$.

Differentiate:
$$y=2x^{\frac{1}{2}},\qquad y'=x^{-\frac{1}{2}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$$
At $x=4$, the tangent gradient is $m_T=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so the normal gradient is $m_N=-2$.

The normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-4&=-2(x-4)\\ y&=-2x+12\\ 2x+y-12&=0\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The population of an endangered species of whale can be modelled by:

$$P = 350 - 10e^{0.05t}$$

where $t$ is time in years from $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2022 and $P$ is the whale population.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the number of whales after 40 years from $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2022.

dif.r: Direct substitution into given model

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
At what rate is the number of whales decreasing after 40 years from $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2022?

Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential model and substitute

parts.label: c
parts.latex: In what year does the model predict that the species of whale will become extinct?

dif.r: Solve exponential equation with logs, interpret as calendar year

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=40$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=350-10e^{0.05(40)}\\ &=276.1094\ldots\end{aligned}$$
So there are about $276$ whales.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $P$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-10e^{0.05t}\times 0.05=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{0.05t}$$
At $t=40$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{0.05(40)}\\ &=-3.69\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The population is decreasing at a rate of about $4$ whales per year.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The species is extinct when $P=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=350-10e^{0.05t}\\ e^{0.05t}&=35\\ 0.05t&=\ln 35\\ t&=\dfrac{\ln 35}{0.05}\\ &=71.10696\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The whale population becomes extinct during the year $2093$ ($2094$ also accepted).

questions.stem: The acceleration of a particle moving on a straight line is given by $a = \sqrt{4t + 16}$ m/s$^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the acceleration of the particle after 12 seconds?

dif.r: Direct substitution into acceleration

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If the particle starts from rest, find its velocity after 12 seconds.

dif.r: Integrate root of linear, initial condition for constant

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Is the particle speeding up or slowing down after 12 seconds? Justify your answer.

dif.r: Justify speeding up by comparing signs of velocity and acceleration

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=12$.
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\sqrt{4(12)+16}\\ &=8 \text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the integral of acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\displaystyle\int (4t+16)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{(4t+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}\times 4}+c\\ &=\dfrac{(4t+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}+c\end{aligned}$$
The particle starts from rest, so $v=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=\dfrac{16^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}+c\\ c&=-\dfrac{32}{3}\end{aligned}$$
So $v=\dfrac{(4t+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}-\dfrac{32}{3}$. At $t=12$:
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\dfrac{64^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}-\dfrac{32}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{224}{3} \text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the constant of integration, or equivalent merit
Integrates the acceleration correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The particle is speeding up when the velocity and acceleration have the same sign.

At $t=12$, $a=8>0$ and $v=\dfrac{224}{3}>0$.

Therefore the particle is speeding up, because both the acceleration and the velocity are positive.
criteria: Considers the signs of velocity and acceleration, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: For the arithmetic series defined by $S_n = 2n^2 + 3n$, find the first, second and tenth terms.

dif.r: Use S1, S2 to get a, d, then T10

solutions.latex:
The first term equals the first sum.
$$\begin{aligned} T_1 &= S_1 \\ &= 2(1)^2 + 3(1) \\ &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
Using $S_2 = T_1 + T_2$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_2 &= 2(2)^2 + 3(2) = 14 \\ 14 &= 5 + T_2 \\ T_2 &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
So $a=5$ and $d=9-5=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= a + 9d \\ &= 5 + 9\times 4 \\ &= 41 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T_1 = 5,\ T_2 = 9,\ T_{10} = 41$$
criteria: Finds two of the three terms, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: For the geometric series $4 + 8 + 16 + \ldots$, write an equation for the sum of a geometric series given that $S_n = 508$ and solve the equation to find the value of $n$.

$$S_n = \dfrac{4(2^n - 1)}{2-1}$$
Setting $S_n = 508$:
$$\begin{aligned} 508 &= 4(2^n - 1) \\ 127 &= 2^n - 1 \\ 128 &= 2^n \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n = 7$$
criteria: Writes the correct equation for $S_n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
For the function $y = x^3 + \dfrac{3}{2}x^2 - 6x - 1$, find the stationary points and determine their nature and find any points of inflexion. Sketch the curve for $-4 \le x \le 2$.

Also state the global minimum in the specified domain. Do NOT determine the $x$-intercepts of the curve.

dif.r: Full cubic curve sketch plus endpoint check for global minimum

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of the curve on -4<=x<=2
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the stationary points.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3x^2 + 3x - 6 \\ &= 3(x+2)(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$, so $x=-2$ or $x=1$.

When $x=-2$, $y=9$. When $x=1$, $y=-4.5$.

Nature: $y''=6x+3$ decides the sign.
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-2) &= -9 < 0 &&\text{so } (-2, 9) \text{ is a maximum turning point}\\ y''(1) &= 9 > 0 &&\text{so } (1, -4.5) \text{ is a minimum turning point} \end{aligned}$$
Inflexion: $y''=0$ when $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$, giving $y=2\dfrac{1}{4}$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} y''(-1) &= -3 < 0 &&\text{concave down}\\ y''(0) &= 3 > 0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, 2\dfrac{1}{4}\right)$ is a point of inflexion (not horizontal).

Endpoints of the domain: $(-4,-17)$ and $(2,1)$.

\exfigure{1327_q22_s2}

The global minimum in the domain is $-17$.
criteria: Finds the stationary points, their nature, the point of inflexion and the global minimum, with a sketch that has one error, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
In the diagram, $\triangle ABC$ is right angled at C, $\angle BAC = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and AB $= 5$ cm.

KP is a circular arc with centre A and KQ is a circular arc with centre B.

\exfigure{1327_q23_1}

If AK has length $x$ cm, find the value of $x$, correct to one decimal place, for which the areas of the sectors AKP and BKQ are equal.

dif.r: Set up equal sector areas, solve quadratic, reject invalid root

figures.cap: right triangle ABC with arcs KP and KQ

solutions.latex:
Area of a sector is $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$. Sector AKP has radius $x$ and angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area AKP} &= \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\times\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi x^2}{12} \end{aligned}$$
Since $AB=5$, $BK = 5-x$. In the right-angled triangle, $\angle ABC = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area BKQ} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(5-x)^2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}(5-x)^2 \end{aligned}$$
For equal areas:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x^2}{12} &= \dfrac{(5-x)^2}{6} \\ x^2 &= 2(5-x)^2 \\ &= 2(25 - 10x + x^2) \\ x^2 - 20x + 50 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
By the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{20 \pm \sqrt{400-200}}{2} \\ &= 10 \pm 5\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
So $x \approx 2.9289$ or $x \approx 17.07$.

K lies on AB, so $0<x<5$; reject the larger root.
$$\therefore\ x \approx 2.9$$
criteria: Rejects the root outside $0<x<5$ with one minor error, or equivalent merit
Finds both values of $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the value(s) of $x$ when $\cot^2 x + \operatorname{cosec}^2 x = 3$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$

dif.r: Pythagorean identity then tan x = ±1 in four quadrants

solutions.latex:
Replace $\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$ using the identity $\operatorname{cosec}^2 x = \cot^2 x + 1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \cot^2 x + \cot^2 x + 1 &= 3 \\ 2\cot^2 x &= 2 \\ \cot^2 x &= 1 \\ \tan^2 x &= 1 \\ \tan x &= \pm 1 \end{aligned}$$
The acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, and $\tan x=\pm1$ has a solution in each quadrant.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} - \tan\theta = \sec\theta$

dif.r: Short identity proof using common denominator and Pythagorean identity

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta} - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta - \sin\theta(1-\sin\theta)}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta - \sin\theta + \sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sec\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines into a single fraction, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A game consists of a player throwing three fair coins. You lose \$4 if three heads appear and lose \$2 if two heads appear. You win \$2 if one head appears and win \$3 if no heads appear.

Let $X$ be the amount you win or lose per game.

parts.latex:

dif.r: List coin outcomes to fill distribution table

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: b

dif.r: Routine expected value then multiply by 500

parts.label: c

dif.r: Standard conditional probability from distribution table

solutions.latex:
The outcomes of three coin throws are HHH; HHT, HTH, THH; HTT, THT, TTH; TTT, so there are 8 equally likely outcomes.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X=-4) &= \dfrac{1}{8} \\ P(X=-2) &= \dfrac{3}{8} \\ P(X=2) &= \dfrac{3}{8} \\ P(X=3) &= \dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds two correct probabilities, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A hiker walks 5 km from camp to point A in a direction of $N37^\circ W$. They then walk 3 km due west to point B, as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1327_q27_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
What is the shortest distance between the hiker when at point B and the camp?

(Answer to the nearest metre)

dif.r: Find included angle from bearings, then cosine rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
What is the bearing of the hiker at point B from the camp?

(Answer to the nearest degree)

dif.r: Sine rule angle then convert carefully to true bearing

figures.cap: hiker path camp to A to B

solutions.latex:
In triangle camp-A-B, the angle at A is $\angle CAB = 127^\circ$. Use the cosine rule.
$$\begin{aligned} a^2 &= 3^2 + 5^2 - 2(3)(5)\cos 127^\circ \\ &= 52.05445\ldots \\ a &\approx 7.2149 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance is } 7215 \text{ m to the nearest metre}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Diagram would help (bearings and triangle): sketch not added here, no sketch id for it. Rubric written by us. The source gives $\angle CAB=127^\circ$ without derivation (180° − 37° − ... not shown).

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta$ be the angle at the camp in the triangle. Use the sine rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{3} &= \dfrac{\sin 127^\circ}{7.215} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{3\sin 127^\circ}{7.215} \\ \theta &\approx 19.4^\circ \approx 19^\circ \end{aligned}$$
B is further west than A, so the bearing is
$$\begin{aligned} 360^\circ - (37^\circ + 19^\circ) &= 304^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{bearing } 304^\circ \text{ (or N}56^\circ\text{W)}$$

parts.latex:
Give a possible sequence of transformations that transforms $y = f(x)$ to $y = 3 \times f(2x - 4) + 1$.

Ensure that you use appropriate terminology in your response.

dif.r: Horizontal dilation with translation; order and terminology matter

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the equation to show the structure.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 3\times f(2x-4) + 1 \\ y - 1 &= 3\times f(2(x-2)) \\ \dfrac{y-1}{3} &= f\left(\dfrac{x-2}{\frac{1}{2}}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Vertical changes: dilate vertically by a factor of $3$, then translate vertically up by $1$ unit.

Horizontal changes: dilate horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, then translate right by $2$ units.

Alternatively: translate up by $\dfrac{1}{3}$ unit and then dilate vertically by a factor of $3$; or translate right by $4$ units and then dilate horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

The order of the vertical and horizontal transformations does not matter, but within the vertical (or horizontal) transformations the order does matter.
criteria: Gives three of the four transformations correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Suppose $f(x) = 2x^2 - x - 1$ and $g(x) = \cos x$.

Find vertical asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{f(g(x))}$ $\;(0 \le x \le \pi)$.

dif.r: Composite function, quadratic in cos x, asymptotes on restricted domain

solutions.latex:
Substitute $g(x)=\cos x$ into $f$.
$$\dfrac{1}{f(g(x))} = \dfrac{1}{2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1}$$
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero, so $2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1 = 0$.

Let $u=\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2u^2 - u - 1 &= 0 \\ (2u+1)(u-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $u=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $u=1$, that is $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos x=1$.

For $0\le x\le\pi$:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \text{ or } x=0$$
criteria: Finds $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\cos x=1$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Matt and Ingrid are playing a game. The dice they play with is four-sided and is marked with the numbers 1,2,3,4. They take turns throwing two dice. The game is won by the first player to throw a double four. Matt starts the game.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the probability that Ingrid wins the game on her first throw is $\dfrac{15}{256}$.

dif.r: Product of independent probabilities for a given result

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability that Matt wins the game on the first or on the second throw?

dif.r: Add two mutually exclusive multistage probabilities

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the probability that Matt eventually wins the game.

dif.r: Build infinite geometric series from game turns, limiting sum

solutions.latex:
Ingrid wins on her first throw if Matt fails and then Ingrid throws a double four. The probability of a double four is $\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{16}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Ingrid wins first throw}) &= \dfrac{15}{16}\times\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= \dfrac{15}{256} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Matt wins on his first throw, or both fail and Matt wins on his second throw.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{1}{16} + \dfrac{15}{16}\times\dfrac{15}{16}\times\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{16} + \dfrac{15^2}{16^3} \\ &= \dfrac{481}{4096} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct expression for the probability, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Matt wins on throw 1, 3, 5, ... of the game, so
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{1}{16} + \dfrac{15^2}{16^3} + \dfrac{15^4}{16^5} + \cdots \\ &= \dfrac{1}{16}\left[1 + \dfrac{15^2}{16^2} + \dfrac{15^4}{16^4} + \cdots\right] \end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$ and $r=\dfrac{15^2}{16^2}$, which has $|r|<1$, so it has a limiting sum.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{16}}{1 - \frac{15^2}{16^2}} \\ &= \dfrac{16}{31} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the geometric series with its ratio, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Intersections, chord equation, then area between curve and line

figures.cap: two parabolas meeting at A and B with chord AB, region shaded

solutions.latex:
Find the intersections of the curves.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x^2 - 5x &= 5x - 4x^2 \\ 10x^2 - 10x &= 0 \\ 10x(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$. When $x=1$, $y=1$, so chord AB passes through $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$, and has equation $y=x$.

The shaded region lies between the curve $y=5x-4x^2$ above and the chord below.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \displaystyle\int_0^1 \left[(5x - 4x^2) - x\right]dx \\ &= \displaystyle\int_0^1 (4x - 4x^2)\,dx \\ &= \left[2x^2 - \dfrac{4x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= 2 - \dfrac{4}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up and integrates the correct integral, or equivalent merit
Finds the intersections and the equation of the chord, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that volume of the container is exactly $360\pi\ \text{cm}^3$, show clearly that the total surface area, $S\ \text{cm}^2$, of the exposed surfaces including the container's base is given by $S = \dfrac{5}{3}\pi r^2 + \dfrac{720\pi}{r}$.

dif.r: Model composite solid volume and surface, eliminate h

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, show that $r = h$ when $S$ is minimised.

dif.r: Standard minimisation from given formula, then compute h

figures.cap: cylinder of radius r and height h topped by a hemisphere

solutions.latex:
The volume of the cylinder plus the hemisphere is $360\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} \pi r^2 h + \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 &= 360\pi \\ 360 &= r^2 h + \dfrac{2}{3}r^3 \\ h &= \dfrac{360}{r^2} - \dfrac{2}{3}r \end{aligned}$$
The exposed surfaces are the circular base, the curved surface of the cylinder and the curved surface of the hemisphere.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \pi r^2 + 2\pi r h + \dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\pi r^2 \\ &= 3\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{360}{r^2} - \dfrac{2}{3}r\right) \\ &= 3\pi r^2 + \dfrac{720\pi}{r} - \dfrac{4\pi}{3}r^2 \\ &= \dfrac{5}{3}\pi r^2 + \dfrac{720\pi}{r} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct surface area with $h$ substituted, or equivalent merit
Finds $h$ in terms of $r$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source criteria were one mark per step.

solutions.latex:
Write $S=\dfrac{5}{3}\pi r^2 + 720\pi r^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$S' = \dfrac{10}{3}\pi r - \dfrac{720\pi}{r^2}$$
For stationary points $S'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{10\pi r}{3} &= \dfrac{720\pi}{r^2} \\ r^3 &= 216 \\ r &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$S'' = \dfrac{10}{3}\pi + \dfrac{1440\pi}{r^3}$$
At $r=6$, $S''>0$, so the surface area is a minimum when $r=6$.

Find $h$ using part (a).
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{360}{36} - \dfrac{2}{3}\times 6 \\ &= 10 - 4 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r = h = 6$$
criteria: Finds $r=6$ and shows it is a minimum, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Signed areas of sector, rectangle, triangle; triangle below axis

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x): rectangle, quarter-circle sector and triangle

solutions.latex:
The integral is the signed area between the graph and the $x$-axis, found piece by piece.

For $-3\le x\le 0$ the rectangle has width $3$ and height $2$, above the axis.
$$A_1 = 3\times 2 = 6$$
For $0\le x\le 2$ the sector is a quarter of a circle of radius $2$, above the axis.
$$A_2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi (2)^2 = \pi$$
For $2\le x\le 5$ the triangle has base $3$ and height $1$, below the axis, so its area counts as negative.
$$A_3 = -\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 1 = -\dfrac{3}{2}$$
Adding the three areas,
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-3}^{5} f(x)\,dx &= 6+\pi-\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &= \pi+\dfrac{9}{2} \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x) = x^3 - (k^2 - 4)x + 1$.

For which of the values of $k$ below is $f(x)$ many-to-one?

dif.r: Link many-to-one to sign change of derivative with parameter

solutions.latex:
$f$ is many-to-one when it is not monotonic, that is when $f'(x)$ changes sign.
$$f'(x)=3x^2-(k^2-4)$$
If $k^2-4\le 0$, then $f'(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$ (zero at most at a single point), so $f$ is increasing and one-to-one.

If $k^2-4>0$, then $f'(x)=0$ has two roots and changes sign, so $f$ has a turning point and is many-to-one.
$$\begin{aligned} k=\pm 2 &: k^2-4=0 \\ k=1 &: k^2-4=-3 \\ k=-4 &: k^2-4=12>0 \end{aligned}$$
Only $k=-4$ gives $k^2-4>0$, which is option D.

parts.latex:
For $f(x)$, a differentiable function, $f'(x) < 0$ and $f''(x) > 0$.

If $a$ and $b$ are in the domain of $f(x)$ and $a < b$, which statement is NOT always true?

dif.r: Interpret signs of derivatives for gradient and chord comparisons abstractly

solutions.latex:
$f'(x)<0$ means $f$ is decreasing, and $f''(x)>0$ means $f'$ is increasing, so the graph is decreasing and concave up.

Option A: decreasing, so $a<b$ gives $f(a)>f(b)$. Always true.

Option B says $f'(b)<f'(a)$. Since $f'$ is increasing, $a<b$ gives $f'(a)<f'(b)$, so this is false.

Option C: the gradient at $a$ is less than the gradient of the chord from $a$ to $b$ for a concave up curve. Always true.

Option D: the gradient at $b$ is greater than the gradient of the chord. Always true.

The statement that is not always true is option B.

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{x^2}{1 + x^3}\,dx$ and express your answer in exact form.

dif.r: Recognise f'/f form with constant adjustment, evaluate limits

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a constant multiple of the derivative of $1 + x^3$, so use the form $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)|$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \dfrac{x^2}{1+x^3}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{3}\int_0^1 \dfrac{3x^2}{1+x^3}\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}\ln|1+x^3|\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 2 - \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^1 \dfrac{x^2}{1+x^3}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 2$$
criteria: Correct mathematical working, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to $y = \sin 2x$ at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$.

dif.r: Differentiate trig with chain rule then point-gradient tangent

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the gradient of the tangent.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin 2x \\ y' &= 2\cos 2x \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$y' = 2\cos \pi = -2$$
The tangent has gradient $-2$ and passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y - 0 &= -2\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ y &= -2x + \pi \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y = -2x + \pi$$
criteria: Correct derivative obtained, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $\sec\theta - \tan\theta\sin\theta = \cos\theta$.

dif.r: Short identity proof using tan quotient and Pythagorean identity

solutions.latex:
Start with the left-hand side and use $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, then $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \sec\theta - \tan\theta\sin\theta \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\sin\theta \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \cos\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct common denominator, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: After completing a numeracy test, Hanna had achieved a $z$-score of $-2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How does Hanna’s results compare with those of her peers? Explain your answer in terms of the mean and standard deviation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If the mean test mark was 86 and the standard deviation was 4, calculate Hanna’s actual mark.

dif.r: z-score formula used in reverse to find raw mark

solutions.latex:
A $z$-score of $-2$ means the mark is 2 standard deviations below the mean.

Hanna scored 2 standard deviations ($2\sigma$) below the average.

Use the formula for $z$-score.
$$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$
Substitute $z = -2$, $\mu = 86$, $\sigma = 4$.
$$\begin{aligned} -2 &= \dfrac{x - 86}{4} \\ -8 &= x - 86 \\ x &= 78 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Hanna's mark was } 78$$
criteria: Correct answer only, or correct mathematical working only, or equivalent merit

$$\therefore\ \text{area} \approx 1992.4 \text{ m}^2$$
criteria: Uses the area of a triangle formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle ABC$, use the cosine rule with included angle $\angle ABC = 95^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= 50^2 + 80^2 - 2\cdot 50\cdot 80\cdot\cos 95^\circ \\ &= 9597.2459\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$AC = \sqrt{9597.2459\ldots} \approx 98.0 \text{ m}$$
$$\therefore\ AC \approx 98.0 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct equation using the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a

figures.cap: instrument with strings from 50 cm down to 30 cm

solutions.latex:
The strings form an arithmetic sequence with first term $a = 30$, last term $l = 50$ and sum $1240$. Use the sum formula.
$$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$$
$$\begin{aligned} 1240 &= \dfrac{n}{2}(30 + 50) \\ n &= 1240\cdot\dfrac{2}{80} \\ &= 31 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{there are 31 strings}$$
criteria: Uses the sum formula for an AP, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The 31st term is the longest string. Use the formula for the $n$th term.
$$T_n = a + (n-1)d$$
$$\begin{aligned} 50 &= 30 + (31 - 1)d \\ 30d &= 20 \\ d &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the difference is } \dfrac{2}{3} \text{ cm}$$
criteria: Correct mathematical working, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: $d = -\dfrac{2}{3}$ is also accepted if the terms are reversed.

parts.latex: Calculate the limiting sum of the geometric series $4 - 2 + 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} - \cdots$

dif.r: Identify a and negative r, apply limiting sum formula

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a = 4$ and $r = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. Since $|r| < 1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1 - r} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{1 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{\frac{3}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_\infty = \dfrac{8}{3}$$
criteria: Correct mathematical working, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A discrete random variable $X$ has the probability distribution table shown.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Explain why $p^2 - 2p + 0.64 = 0$. Show mathematical working to support your answer.

dif.r: Probabilities sum to one, simplify to given quadratic

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, show that $p = 0.4$ or $p = 1.6$ and determine which of these solutions is invalid, giving a reason.

dif.r: Solve quadratic and justify rejecting root via probability bounds

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If $p = 0.4$, calculate the expected value of $X$.

dif.r: Direct expected value calculation after substituting p

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.1 + p^2 + 0.54 + (1 - 2p) &= 1 \\ p^2 - 2p + 0.64 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p^2 - 2p + 0.64 = 0$$
criteria: Provides either the sum equal to 1 or the simplification, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Table values read from the source working ($0.1$, $p^2$, $0.54$, $1-2p$).

solutions.latex:
Solve the quadratic using the quadratic formula.
$$\begin{aligned} p &= \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 4(0.64)}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{2 \pm 1.2}{2} \\ &= 1.6 \text{ or } 0.4 \end{aligned}$$
The probability of each score must be between 0 and 1. If $p = 1.6$, then $P(X = 2) = p^2 > 1$ and $P(X = 4) = 1 - 2p < 0$, which is not possible.

$$\therefore\ p = 1.6 \text{ is invalid}$$
criteria: Correct application of the quadratic formula, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: No mark is awarded for reasoning if it is stated that $p$ must be between 0 and 1, because $p$ is not itself a probability.

solutions.latex:
Use $E(X) = \sum x\,P(X = x)$ with $p = 0.4$.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 1\cdot 0.1 + 2\cdot 0.4^2 + 3\cdot 0.54 + 4\cdot(1 - 2\cdot 0.4) \\ &= 2.84 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ E(X) = 2.84$$
criteria: Correct mathematical working, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \sqrt{4x + 1}\,dx$.

dif.r: Standard reverse chain rule for linear inner function

solutions.latex:
Write the root as a power, then adjust for the inner function $4x + 1$ (derivative $4$).
$$\begin{aligned} \int\sqrt{4x+1}\,dx &= \int (4x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\int 4(4x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{(4x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} + C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}(4x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}} + C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int\sqrt{4x+1}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{6}(4x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}} + C$$
criteria: Correct mathematical working (coefficient or substitution), or integral obtained without $\dfrac{1}{4}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The amount of money gained by an entrepreneur doubles every day. On day 1, she earns \$9 and on day 2 she earns \$18.

On which day did she first earn more than a total of \$1 million?

dif.r: GP sum inequality solved with logs, then round to whole day

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The daily earnings $9, 18, 36, 72, \ldots$ form a geometric sequence with $a = 9$ and $r = 2$. The total after $n$ days is the sum of the series.
$$S_n = \dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$$
We need the total to exceed \$1 million.
$$\begin{aligned} 1\,000\,000 &< \dfrac{9(1 - 2^n)}{1 - 2} \\ -\dfrac{1\,000\,000}{9} &> 1 - 2^n \\ -1 - \dfrac{1\,000\,000}{9} &> -2^n \\ 2^n &> 1 + \dfrac{1\,000\,000}{9} \\ n &> \dfrac{\ln 111\,112.11}{\ln 2} \\ n &> 16.76 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ is a whole number, $n = 17$.

$$\therefore\ \text{she first earns a total of more than \$1 million on day 17}$$
criteria: Error made, or correctly calculates $n$ but misinterprets the question (finds the term instead of the total), or equivalent merit
Correct application of the formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The queuing time, $X$ minutes, of a customer at a checkout in a store has the probability density function

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx(4 - x) & \text{for } 0 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{3}{32}$.

dif.r: Standard pdf normalisation: integrate polynomial and set equal to 1

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(1 < X < 2)$.

dif.r: Direct definite integral of pdf over interval

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By finding the expected wait time, determine whether the customer is more likely to wait less than 1 minute, or more than 1 minute.

dif.r: Continuous expected value integral then interpreting result in context

can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function the total area is 1.
$$\int_0^4 kx(4 - x)\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[2kx^2 - \dfrac{kx^3}{3}\right]_0^4 &= 1 \\ 32k - \dfrac{64}{3}k &= 1 \\ \dfrac{32}{3}k &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{3}{32} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates the expression, or recognises that the area from 0 to 4 is 1, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Answer with no or incorrect working earns 0 marks.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the density over $1 < x < 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(1 < X < 2) &= \int_1^2 \dfrac{3}{32}x(4 - x)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{3}{16}x^2 - \dfrac{1}{32}x^3\right]_1^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{3}{16}(2)^2 - \dfrac{1}{32}(2)^3\right) - \left(\dfrac{3}{16} - \dfrac{1}{32}\right) \\ &= 0.34375 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(1 < X < 2) = 0.34375$$
criteria: Correctly integrates the expression, or finds $P(X < 1)$ with correct reasoning, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote $\dfrac{2}{16}(2)^2$ in the third line, an evident slip for $\dfrac{3}{16}(2)^2$; corrected to match the integrated expression. Final value 0.34375 is correct.

solutions.latex:
Use $E(X) = \displaystyle \int x f(x)\,dx$.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \int_0^4 \dfrac{3}{32}x^2(4 - x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{3}{32}\left[\dfrac{4x^3}{3} - \dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^4 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{32}\left(\dfrac{256}{3} - \dfrac{256}{4}\right) \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
The expected wait time is 2 minutes, which is more than 1 minute.

$$\therefore\ \text{the customer is more likely to wait more than 1 minute}$$
criteria: Correct integral for the expected value, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Coal is extracted from a mine at a rate that is proportional to the amount of coal remaining in the mine. Hence, the amount $R$ remaining after $t$ years is given by

$$R = 250e^{-kt}$$

$k$ is a positive constant and $R$ is measured in tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If 80% of the coal remains after 2 years, show that the value of $k$ is approximately 0.1116.

dif.r: Substitute data into exponential model and solve with logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the amount of coal remaining after 8 years, correct to the nearest tonne.

dif.r: Single substitution into given exponential model

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what rate is the amount of coal decreasing after 1 year? Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential model and substitute t=1

parts.label: d
parts.latex:
The coal mine is abandoned when the amount of coal remaining is less than 80 tonnes. After how many years will the coal mine be abandoned?

Express your answer in years, correct to one decimal place.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for time using logarithms

solutions.latex:
After 2 years, 80% of 250 tonnes remains, so $R = 200$ when $t = 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 200 &= 250e^{-2k} \\ 0.8 &= e^{-2k} \\ \ln 0.8 &= -2k \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln 0.8}{-2} \\ &\approx 0.11157 \\ &\approx 0.1116 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.1116$$
criteria: Correctly uses the given information to form an equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 8$ and $k = 0.1116$ into $R = 250e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 250e^{-0.1116\times 8} \\ &= 102 \text{ tonnes (nearest tonne)} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate $R = 250e^{-kt}$.
$$\dfrac{dR}{dt} = -250ke^{-kt}$$
When $t = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= -250\times 0.1116\times e^{-0.1116\times 1} \\ &\approx -25 \text{ tonnes/year} \end{aligned}$$
So the coal is decreasing at about $25$ tonnes per year.
criteria: Correct derivative or solution obtained, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The mine is abandoned when $R < 80$.
$$\begin{aligned} 80 &> 250e^{-0.1116t} \\ \dfrac{80}{250} &> e^{-0.1116t} \\ \ln\dfrac{8}{25} &> -0.1116t \\ t &> 10.2 \end{aligned}$$
The last step divides by $-0.1116$, which reverses the inequality.
$$\therefore \text{After } 10.2 \text{ years the coal mine will have less than 80 tonnes of coal.}$$
criteria: Obtains the inequality or equation, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y=4x^2-2x^3 with maximum at (4/3, 64/27)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate twice.
$$f(x) = 4x^2 - 2x^3,\quad f'(x) = 8x - 6x^2,\quad f''(x) = 8 - 12x$$
For a point of inflection, let $f''(x) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 8 - 12x \\ x &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$, $f\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{32}{27}$.

Test the concavity either side of $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

\extable{Ts4450_1}

The concavity changes at $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a point of inflection at } \left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{32}{27}\right)$$
criteria: Correct first and second derivatives obtained, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1328_q26_s1}

For stationary points, let $f'(x) = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 8x - 6x^2 &= 0 \\ x(4 - 3x) &= 0 \\ x &= 0 \text{ or } \dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The sign of $f''(x) = 8 - 12x$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= 8 > 0 &&\text{concave up} \\ f''\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right) &= -8 < 0 &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum at } (0, 0) \text{ and maximum at } \left(\dfrac{4}{3}, \dfrac{64}{27}\right)$$
The $x$-intercept (other than $x=0$) is at $x = 2$, since $f(x) = 2x^2(2-x)$.
criteria: Correct stationary points and one other feature, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Equate the two expressions.
$$\begin{aligned} 2^{-x} &= \dfrac{1}{2} - 2^{-x} \\ 2\times 2^{-x} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 2^{-x} &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ x &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ A = \dfrac{3}{2\ln 2} - 1 \text{ units}^2$$

questions.stem:
The diagram shows a straight section of a river, one kilometre wide. Tamara is at point $O$ on one bank and she wishes to reach point $B$ on the opposite bank. The point $A$ is directly opposite $O$ and the distance from $A$ to $B$ is 2 kilometres.

Tamara can row at 6 km/h and jog at 10 km/h. Show intends to row in a straight line to a point $P$ on the opposite bank, and then jog directly from $P$ to $B$.

Let $AP = x$

\exfigure{1328_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the total distance Tamara will travel to reach point $B$ is given by

$$d = \sqrt{x^2 + 1} + (2 - x)$$

dif.r: Simple Pythagoras set-up from diagram to show distance

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence, explain why the time $T$, in hours, for Tamara to reach point $B$ is

$$T = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}{6} + \dfrac{2 - x}{10}$$

dif.r: Explain time expression using distance over speed

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the value of $x$ such that Tamara minimises the time taken to complete her journey and show that this value of $x$ is a minimum.

dif.r: Chain rule on root, solve surd equation, test minimum

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Hence, determine the time taken to complete the journey in minimum time.

dif.r: Substitute optimal x into given time formula

figures.cap: river diagram with O, A, P, B; AP = x, AB = 2 km, width 1 km

solutions.latex:
Since $AB = 2$ and $AP = x$, we have $PB = 2 - x$.

In right-angled triangle $OAP$, Pythagoras' theorem gives
$$\begin{aligned} OP^2 &= AP^2 + OA^2 \\ OP &= \sqrt{x^2 + 1} \end{aligned}$$
The total distance is
$$\begin{aligned} d &= OP + PB \\ &= \sqrt{x^2 + 1} + (2 - x) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One expression derived, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Time $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$.

Rowing $OP$ at $6$ km/h and jogging $PB$ at $10$ km/h:
$$T_{OP} = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}{6},\qquad T_{PB} = \dfrac{2 - x}{10}$$
$$\therefore\ T = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}{6} + \dfrac{2 - x}{10}$$

Differentiate $T$ (chain rule for the square root).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{6}\times\dfrac{1}{2}(x^2 + 1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 2x - \dfrac{1}{10} \\ &= \dfrac{x}{6\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} - \dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}$$
For minimum time, let $\dfrac{dT}{dx} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{6\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} &= \dfrac{1}{10} \\ \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} &= \dfrac{6}{10} \\ \dfrac{x^2}{x^2 + 1} &= \dfrac{36}{100} \\ 100x^2 &= 36x^2 + 36 \\ 64x^2 &= 36 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{36}{64} \end{aligned}$$
Since $x > 0$, $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dT}{dx}$ either side of $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$. Take $x = 0$ and $x = 1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dx}(0) &= -\dfrac{1}{10} < 0 &&\text{decreasing} \\ \dfrac{dT}{dx}(1) &= \dfrac{1}{6\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{10} \approx 0.018 > 0 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient changes from negative to positive.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{3}{4} \text{ gives the minimum time}$$
criteria: Differentiates and correctly finds the value of $x$, or equivalent merit
Correctly differentiates one of the two expressions for time, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source only said 'Test left and right of 3/4'; the test values $x=0$ and $x=1$ were worked out here.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$ into $T$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{\sqrt{\frac{9}{16} + 1}}{6} + \dfrac{2 - \frac{3}{4}}{10} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{5}{4}}{6} + \dfrac{\frac{5}{4}}{10} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{24} + \dfrac{1}{8} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} \text{ hour} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Working added to reach the source's value $T=\dfrac{1}{3}$ (20 minutes).

solutions.latex:
Standardise with $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$, where $\mu = 600$ and $\sigma = 5$.

For $595$ mL, $z = -1$. From the table, $P(z < 1) = 0.841$, so by symmetry $P(595 < X < 600) = P(0 < z < 1) = 0.841 - 0.5 = 0.341$.

For $602$ mL:
$$z = \dfrac{602 - 600}{5} = 0.4$$
From the table, $P(z < 0.4) = 0.655$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(0 < z < 0.4) &= 0.655 - 0.5 \\ &= 0.155 \end{aligned}$$
So $P(600 < X < 602) = 0.155$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(595 < X < 602) &= 0.341 + 0.155 \\ &= 0.496 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 49.6\% \text{ of bottles}$$

questions.stem:
A weight is attached to a spring that is connected to the ground. The weight is pushed down towards the ground, and then released so that it bounces up and down.

The spring stretches and contracts such that the distance of the weight from the ground, $x$ (in metres), varies sinusoidally with time, $t$ (in seconds).

It takes 2 seconds for the weight to go from its highest point of 9 centimetres to its lowest point of 5 centimetres.

The motion of the weight can be modelled by the equation

$$x = a\sin(bt + c) + d$$
questions.review_note: Paper states x in metres but heights in centimetres (inconsistent units in paper)

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $d$.

dif.r: Amplitude, centre and period from max, min and half-period

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find a possible value of $c$, given that the weight was initially pushed towards the ground before being released.

dif.r: Interpret initial condition as minimum, solve sin c=-1

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, sketch the graph of the weight’s motion against time, for $0 \le t \le 4$.

dif.r: Sketch phase-shifted sinusoid over one period

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of x=2sin(pi/2 t+3pi/2)+7 for 0<=t<=4

solutions.latex:
The highest point is $9$ cm and the lowest is $5$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{9 - 5}{2} = 2 &&\text{(amplitude)} \\ d &= \dfrac{9 + 5}{2} = 7 &&\text{(middle of the wave)} \end{aligned}$$
Highest to lowest takes $2$ s, which is half a period, so the period is $4$ s.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2\pi}{b} &= 4 \\ b &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = 2,\quad b = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\quad d = 7$$
criteria: Correct values of $a$ and $d$ and working towards $b$, or equivalent merit
Correct amplitude and correct $d$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric was 1 (amplitude), 1 ($d$), 2 ($b$); rewritten top-down. Units kept in cm as the question gives, though it says $x$ is in metres.

solutions.latex:
Initially the weight is pushed down, so at $t = 0$, $x = 5$.
$$\begin{aligned} 5 &= 2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\times 0 + c\right) + 7 \\ -1 &= \sin c \\ c &= \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
This is a possible value, since $\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} = -1$.
criteria: Identifies $x = 5$ when $t = 0$ and substitutes into the formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given $f(x) = x^2 + 4x^3$. For what values of $x$ is the function decreasing?

dif.r: Differentiate cubic, solve quadratic inequality for decreasing interval

solutions.latex:
Differentiating,
$$f'(x) = 2x + 12x^2$$
The function is decreasing when $f'(x) < 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x + 12x^2 &< 0 \\ 2x(1+6x) &< 0 \end{aligned}$$
The roots are $x = -\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $x = 0$, and the parabola $2x(1+6x)$ opens upwards, so it is negative between the roots.
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{1}{6} < x < 0$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx = 3$, what is the value of $\displaystyle\int_4^6 f(2(x-3))\,dx$?

dif.r: Relate area under transformed function: dilation halves, translation preserves

solutions.latex:
$f(2x)$ is a horizontal dilation of $f(x)$ by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, so the area is halved.
$$\displaystyle \int_1^3 f(2x)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx = \dfrac{3}{2}$$
Translating the graph three units to the right does not change the area, so
$$\displaystyle \int_4^6 f(2(x-3))\,dx = \dfrac{3}{2}$$
This is option B.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating each term,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2(3)\cos 3x - 3\sec^2 x$$
At $x = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 6\cos 0 - 3\sec^2 0 \\ &= 6 - 3 \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: Consider the function $f(x) = (x-2)^2(x+1)$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the two stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Standard product rule, stationary points and nature test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of the function, clearly showing the stationary points and the $x$ and $y$ intercepts.

dif.r: Sketch factored cubic using found stationary points and intercepts

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of f(x) = (x-2)^2(x+1) with (-1,0), (0,4), (1,2), (2,0)
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x-2)^2 & v&=x+1\\ u'&=2(x-2) & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2(x-2)(x+1) + (x-2)^2 \\ &= (x-2)(2x+2+x-2) \\ &= 3x(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating again,
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2 - 6x \\ f''(x) &= 6x - 6 \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x) = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = 2$.

Test the second derivative at each point.

At $x = 2$: $f''(2) = 6 > 0$ and $f(2) = 0$, so there is a local minimum at $(2, 0)$.

At $x = 0$: $f''(0) = -6 < 0$ and $f(0) = 4$, so there is a local maximum at $(0, 4)$.

Alternatively, test the sign of $f'(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(-1) &= 9 &&\text{positive}\\ f'(1) &= -3 &&\text{negative}\\ f'(3) &= 9 &&\text{positive} \end{aligned}$$
The sign changes from positive to negative through $x = 0$ (local maximum), and from negative to positive through $x = 2$ (local minimum).
criteria: Finds both stationary points and explains the nature of one, or equivalent merit
Correct first derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $h = \dfrac{27 - r^2}{r}$.

dif.r: Model prism surface area, recognising base side equals 2r

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the volume of the cylinder is given by

$$V = 27\pi r - \pi r^3$$

dif.r: Substitute given h into cylinder volume formula

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $r$ such that the volume of the cylinder is greatest.

dif.r: Routine maximisation of given cubic volume function

figures.cap: cylinder inscribed in a rectangular prism with square base

solutions.latex:
The square base has side equal to the diameter of the circle, which is $2r$.

The container has two square faces and four rectangular faces, so its surface area is
$$2(2r)^2 + 4(2rh) = 216$$
$$8r^2 + 8rh = 216$$
$$r^2 + rh = 27$$
$$rh = 27 - r^2$$
$$\therefore\ h = \dfrac{27 - r^2}{r}$$
criteria: Writes the surface area equation, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source criteria gave a single 1-mark row for a 2-mark part; rubric rewritten by us (2 marks as per the question).

solutions.latex:
The cylinder has volume $V = \pi r^2 h$, where $V$ is in $\text{cm}^3$. Substituting $h$ from part (a),
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \pi r^2 \cdot \dfrac{27 - r^2}{r} \\ &= \pi r(27 - r^2) \\ &= 27\pi r - \pi r^3 \end{aligned}$$

Differentiating $V = 27\pi r - \pi r^3$,
$$\dfrac{dV}{dr} = 27\pi - 3\pi r^2, \qquad \dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2} = -6\pi r$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dV}{dr} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 27\pi - 3\pi r^2 &= 0 \\ r^2 &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
Since $r > 0$, $r = 3$.

At $r = 3$: $\dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2} = -6\pi(3) < 0$, so the volume is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ r = 3$$
criteria: Correct first and second derivatives, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The equation of a curve $C$ is given by $y = x^2 + ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

The tangent to $C$ at $(0, 5)$ passes through $(5, 20)$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$.

dif.r: Link tangent gradient from two points to derivative at zero

solutions.latex:
Differentiating,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x + a$$
The gradient of the tangent through $(0,5)$ and $(5,20)$ is
$$\dfrac{20-5}{5-0} = 3$$
At $x = 0$ the gradient of the curve is $a$, so $a = 3$.

Since $(0,5)$ lies on the curve,
$$5 = 0^2 + a(0) + b$$
$$b = 5$$
$$\therefore\ a = 3,\ b = 5$$
criteria: Correct derivative and gradient, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The tenth term of an arithmetic series is 29 and the fifteenth term is 44

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the common difference?

dif.r: Simple simultaneous equations for arithmetic common difference

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the first term?

dif.r: Back-substitute to find first term

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the sum of the first 85 terms.

dif.r: Substitute into arithmetic sum formula

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic series, $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.

The tenth term is 29 and the fifteenth term is 44.
$$a + 9d = 29 \quad [1]$$
$$a + 14d = 44 \quad [2]$$
Subtracting [1] from [2],
$$5d = 15$$
$$\therefore\ d = 3$$

Substituting $d = 3$ into [1],
$$\begin{aligned} a + 9(3) &= 29 \\ a &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the first term is } 2$$

Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$ with $a = 2$, $d = 3$, $n = 85$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{85} &= \dfrac{85}{2}\left(2(2) + (85-1)\cdot 3\right) \\ &= \dfrac{85}{2}(4 + 252) \\ &= 10880 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
For the given series $(2^1+3)+(2^2+3)+(2^3+3)+(2^4+3)+\ldots\ldots$.

Show that the sum of the first $n$ terms is given by $2^{n+1} - 2 + 3n$

dif.r: Must split series into geometric and constant parts, general show-that

solutions.latex:
Split each term into its power of 2 and the constant 3.
$$(2^1+3)+(2^2+3)+(2^3+3)+\ldots = \left(2^1 + 2^2 + 2^3 + \ldots\right) + \left(3 + 3 + 3 + \ldots\ n \text{ times}\right)$$
The first bracket is a GP with $a = 2$, $r = 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{2(2^n - 1)}{2-1} \\ &= 2(2^n - 1) \\ &= 2^{n+1} - 2 \end{aligned}$$
The second bracket is an arithmetic series with $a = 3$, $d = 0$, so $S_n = 3n$.

Adding the two sums:
$$\text{Total sum} = 2^{n+1} - 2 + 3n$$
criteria: Substantial progress towards solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Jayden works in a Moolworths store and he is making a stack of oranges against a sloping display panel.

The oranges are stacked in layers, as shown, where each layer contains one orange less than the layer below it.

\exfigure{1329_q12c_1}

When he has finished, there are five oranges in the top layer, six in the next and so on.

There are $n$ layers altogether.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show there are $\dfrac{1}{2}n(n+9)$ oranges in the stack.

dif.r: Model layers as arithmetic series with last term n+4

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If Jayden has 300 oranges to create his display, how many full rows can he create, if the top row still contains five oranges?

dif.r: Solve quadratic from sum, round down to complete rows

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: stack of oranges in layers of 5, 6, 7 ... with nth layer

solutions.latex:
The number of oranges per layer forms an arithmetic series $5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + \ldots + (n+4)$, with $a = 5$, $d = 1$, last term $l = n+4$.

Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[5 + (n+4)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}(n+9) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}n(n+9) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Establishes the series and uses the correct formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Set the total number of oranges equal to 300.
$$\begin{aligned} 300 &= \dfrac{1}{2}n(n+9) \\ 600 &= n^2 + 9n \\ n^2 + 9n - 600 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$n = \dfrac{-9 \pm \sqrt{81 - 4\times 1\times(-600)}}{2}$$
So $n \approx 20.4$ or $n \approx -29.4$.

The number of rows must be positive and whole, so $n = 20$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Jayden can make 20 complete rows.}$$
criteria: Sets up the correct quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Consider the geometric series $1 + \left(\sqrt{7}-2\right) + \left(\sqrt{7}-2\right)^2 + \ldots\ldots$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show with calculations why this geometric series has a limiting sum.

dif.r: Compute ratio and check absolute value below one

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the exact value of the limiting sum with a rational denominator.

dif.r: Limiting sum formula plus rationalising surd denominator

solutions.latex:
A geometric series has a limiting sum when $|r| < 1$, where $r = \dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$.
$$r = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}-2}{1} \approx 0.65$$
Since $|r| < 1$, the series has a limiting sum.

meta.format_note: Source gave r ≈ 0.6; written as ≈ 0.65 (√7 ≈ 2.6458).

solutions.latex:
Using $S = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a = 1$ and $r = \sqrt{7}-2$, then rationalising the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{1}{1-(\sqrt{7}-2)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3-\sqrt{7}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3-\sqrt{7}}\times\dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{3+\sqrt{7}} \\ &= \dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{9-7} \\ &= \dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct formula and substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate the definite integral $\displaystyle\int_0^2 2x^2\left(x^3 - 8\right)^3\,dx$. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

dif.r: Reverse chain rule definite integral with constant adjustment

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx = \dfrac{1}{n+1}[f(x)]^{n+1}$ with $f(x) = x^3-8$, $f'(x)=3x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 2x^2(x^3-8)^3\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{3}\int_0^2 3x^2(x^3-8)^3\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\left[\dfrac{(x^3-8)^4}{4}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{(2^3-8)^4}{4}\right) - \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{(0^3-8)^4}{4}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}(0) - \dfrac{2}{3}(1024) \\ &= -\dfrac{2048}{3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $f(x)$ is a probability density function, the total area is 1.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_2^4 k(x-1)^2\,dx &= 1 \\ k\left[\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{3}\right]_2^4 &= 1 \\ k\left(9 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ k\left(\dfrac{26}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{3}{26} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

The cumulative distribution function is $F(x) = \displaystyle\int_2^x f(t)\,dt$.

parts.latex: In Broken Hill, the maximum temperature for each day has been recorded. The mean of these maximum temperatures during spring is $25.8^\circ$C, and their standard deviation is $4.2^\circ$C.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What temperature has a $z$-score of $-1$?.

dif.r: Use z-score formula in reverse, one step

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What percentage of spring days in Broken Hill would have maximum temperatures between $21.6^\circ$C and $38.4^\circ$C?

dif.r: Two z-scores, combine halves of empirical-rule percentages

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Using $z = \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ with $\mu = 25.8$, $\sigma = 4.2$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 &= \dfrac{x - 25.8}{4.2} \\ x &= 21.6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the temperature is } 21.6^\circ\text{C}$$

The temperature $38.4^\circ$C has $z = \dfrac{38.4-25.8}{4.2} = 3$, and $21.6^\circ$C has $z=-1$.

From $z=-1$ to the mean, using the 68% rule:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 68\% = 34\%$$
From the mean to $z=3$, using the 99.7% rule:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 99.7\% = 49.85\%$$
Adding:
$$34\% + 49.85\% = 83.85\%$$

parts.latex:
The lifetime $X$ ( in years) of an electric light bulb has a probability distribution given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{6}{125}x(5-x) & 0 \le x \le 5 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a

dif.r: Integrate polynomial pdf and evaluate; standard technique

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that a standard lamp is fitted with two such new bulbs and that their failures are independent, find the probability that exactly one bulb fails within two years?

dif.r: Exactly one of two independent events; two-branch product sum

solutions.latex:
The probability is $P(X\le 2) = F(2)$, where $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.
$$F(x) = \int_0^x \dfrac{6}{125}\left(5t - t^2\right)dt = \dfrac{6}{125}\left[\dfrac{5x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(X \le 2) &= \dfrac{6}{125}\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\times 2^2 - \dfrac{2^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{44}{125} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress towards the correct solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $B$ be the event that a bulb fails within two years.
$$P(B) = \dfrac{44}{125}, \qquad P(B') = 1 - \dfrac{44}{125} = \dfrac{81}{125}$$
Exactly one fails: either the first fails and the second does not, or the reverse.
$$\begin{aligned} P(BB') + P(B'B) &= \dfrac{44}{125}\times\dfrac{81}{125} + \dfrac{81}{125}\times\dfrac{44}{125} \\ &= \dfrac{7128}{15625} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress towards the correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
It is given that a data value below $Q_1 - 1.5 \times IQR$ or above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR$ is the criteria for recognising the outliers.

A set of data has a lower quartile ($Q_1$) of 10 and an upper quartile ($Q_3$) of 16.

What is the maximum possible range for this set of data if there are no outliers?
parts.note: Outliers using IQR are not in 2024 Advanced; they are now Standard content.

dif.r: Realise maximum range lies between the two outlier fences

solutions.latex:
The interquartile range is
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 16 - 10 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
The lower bound for outliers is
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR &= 10 - 1.5\times 6 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The upper bound for outliers is
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR &= 16 + 1.5\times 6 \\ &= 25 \end{aligned}$$
The maximum range is the upper bound minus the lower bound.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Range} &= 25 - 1 \\ &= 24 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Significant progress towards correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $2\sin x\cos x = \sin x$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.

dif.r: Factorise rather than divide; collect all solutions in domain

solutions.latex:
Move every term to one side and factorise.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin x\cos x - \sin x &= 0 \\ \sin x(2\cos x - 1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Case 1: $\sin x = 0$, so $x = 0, \pi, 2\pi$.

Case 2: $2\cos x - 1 = 0$, so $\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ x = 0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \pi, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}, 2\pi$$
criteria: Correctly solves one case, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\sec\theta - \sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1 + \cos^2\theta} = \sin\theta\tan\theta$

dif.r: Identity proof needing difference-of-squares factorisation of 1−cos⁴θ

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator, using $1-\cos^4\theta = \left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sec\theta - \sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1 - \cos^4\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\left(1 - \cos^2\theta\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\sin^2\theta \\ &= \sin\theta\tan\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Significant progress towards correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$.

dif.r: Direct quotient rule application

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=x\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\right) &= \dfrac{(\cos x)\times x - 1\times\sin x}{x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x\cos x - \sin x}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: By first writing the function $y = 7^x$ in logarithmic form, show that its derivative is $7^x\ln 7$.

dif.r: Unfamiliar route: change of base and dy/dx as reciprocal

solutions.latex:
Write $y = 7^x$ in logarithmic form: $x = \log_7 y$.

Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$x = \dfrac{\ln y}{\ln 7}$$
Differentiate with respect to $y$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dy} &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 7}\cdot\dfrac{1}{y} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{y\ln 7} \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 \div \dfrac{dx}{dy}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= y\ln 7 \\ &= 7^x\ln 7 \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Substantially correct solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A particle is accelerating according to the function $a = -\dfrac{3}{t^2}\ \text{ms}^{-2}$.

If, when $t = 0.5$ s, its velocity, $v = 6\ \text{ms}^{-1}$ and its displacement, $x = 1$ m, find the particle’s displacement function in simplest form.

dif.r: Two integrations with constants, log manipulation of ln 0.5

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity.
$$v = \dfrac{3}{t} + c$$
When $t = 0.5$, $v = 6$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6 &= \dfrac{3}{0.5} + c \\ 6 &= 6 + c \end{aligned}$$
So $c = 0$ and $v = \dfrac{3}{t}$.

Integrate the velocity to find the displacement.
$$x = 3\ln t + c_2$$
When $t = 0.5$, $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 3\ln(0.5) + c_2 \\ &= 3\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + c_2 \\ &= -3\ln 2 + c_2 \end{aligned}$$
So $c_2 = 1 + 3\ln 2$.
$$\therefore\ x = 3\ln t + 3\ln 2 + 1$$
criteria: Significant progress towards solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^2 \left(e^{x-1} - 2\right)dx &= \Big[e^{x-1} - 2x\Big]_1^2 \\ &= \left(e^{2-1} - 2\times 2\right) - \left(e^{1-1} - 2\times 1\right) \\ &= e - 4 - 1 + 2 \\ &= e - 3 \end{aligned}$$

The value of the integral, $e - 3 < 0$, is negative because the curve cuts the $x$-axis at $x = 1 + \ln 2$, which lies between $x = 1$ and $x = 2$. Some of the area is below the $x$-axis and the rest is above.

The integral adds the signed areas.

The actual area would need two integrals, one from $x = 1$ to $x = 1 + \ln 2$ and one from $x = 1 + \ln 2$ to $x = 2$, with their absolute values added.

parts.latex: Find the gradient of the curve $y = xe^x$ at the point where $x = \ln 2$.

dif.r: Product rule, then evaluate with e^{ln 2}

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= xe^x + e^x \\ &= (x+1)e^x \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \ln 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= (1 + \ln 2)e^{\ln 2} \\ &= (1+\ln 2)\times 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient} = 2(1 + \ln 2)$$
criteria: Significant progress towards correct solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $A$ and $B$ are independent, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, so $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{8}&=\dfrac{1}{4}+P(B)\left(1-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\\ \dfrac{3}{4}P(B)&=\dfrac{1}{8}\\ P(B)&=\dfrac{1}{8}\times\dfrac{4}{3}=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option D.

parts.latex: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=\ln(x-1)+\sqrt{2-x}$ ?

dif.r: Two domain conditions intersected; standard log and root restrictions.

solutions.latex:
$\ln(x-1)$ needs $x-1>0$, so $x>1$.

$\sqrt{2-x}$ needs $2-x\ge 0$, so $x\le 2$.

Hence the domain is $1<x\le 2$, that is $(1,2]$, which is option B.

parts.latex: The function $f(x)=e^x$ is transformed into the function $g(x)=e^{x+2}$. Which of the following describes the effect of this transformation?

dif.r: Must recognise translation equals vertical dilation via index law.

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

solutions.latex:
Using an index law:
$$g(x)=e^{x+2}=e^2\cdot e^x=e^2f(x)$$
Hence this is a vertical dilation by a factor $e^2$, which is option B.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_{10}3x$ ?

dif.r: Change of base, differentiate, then rewrite 1/ln10 as log10 e.

solutions.latex:
Using the change of base rule, $\log_{10}3x=\log_{10}3+\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 10}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\log_{10}3x&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log_{10}3+\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 10}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{x\ln 10}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{x\log_e 10}\\ &=\dfrac{\log_{10}e}{x} \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option D.

parts.latex:
The marks on a test are normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

$2.5\%$ of the marks are 34 or less and $16\%$ of the marks are 70 or more. What is the value of $\mu$ ?

dif.r: Translate percentages to empirical-rule z-values, solve simultaneous equations.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
$2.5\%$ of marks are below $\mu-2\sigma$, and $16\%$ are above $\mu+\sigma$ (using the empirical rule).
$$\begin{aligned} \mu-2\sigma&=34\\ \mu+\sigma&=70 \end{aligned}$$
Adding the first to twice the second:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\mu&=34+2\times 70=174\\ \mu&=58 \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option C.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\right)dx$ ?

dif.r: Combine fractions, Pythagorean identity, then integrate sec squared.

solutions.latex:
Combining the fractions over a common denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\right)dx&=\int\dfrac{2}{1-\sin^2x}\,dx\\ &=\int\dfrac{2}{\cos^2x}\,dx\\ &=2\int\sec^2x\,dx\\ &=2\tan x+c \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option C.

parts.latex: A single lump sum investment of $\$P$ earns an amount of interest $\$I$ after 2 years with a rate of interest of $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. Which of the following is an expression for $P$ ?

dif.r: Compound interest formula, interest as amount minus principal, rearranged.

solutions.latex:
The rate per month is $\dfrac{0.06}{12}=0.005$ and there are $24$ months. The interest is the final amount minus $P$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(1.005)^{24}-P&=I\\ P\left\{(1.005)^{24}-1\right\}&=I\\ P&=\dfrac{I}{(1.005)^{24}-1} \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option D.

parts.latex:
If $x>0$ what is the limiting sum of the series

$\log_2 x-\log_4 x+\log_{16}x-\log_{256}x+\dots+(-1)^{n+1}\log_{2^{(2^{n-1})}}x+\dots$ ?

dif.r: Change of base reveals hidden geometric series; abstract general term.

solutions.latex:
Using the change of base rule, the general term is
$$T_n=(-1)^{n+1}\dfrac{\log_2x}{\log_22^{(2^{n-1})}}=(-1)^{n+1}\dfrac{\log_2x}{2^{n-1}}$$
Hence the series is geometric with $a=\log_2x$ and $r=-\dfrac{1}{2}$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\ &=\dfrac{\log_2x}{1+\frac{1}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\log_2x \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option A.

parts.latex: A circle has equation $x^2+y^2-6x+4y+k=0$ for some constant $k$. Find the set of possible values of $k$.

dif.r: Complete the square, then reason radius squared must be positive.

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and $y$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+y^2-6x+4y+k&=0\\ x^2-6x+9+y^2+4y+4&=13-k\\ (x-3)^2+(y+2)^2&=13-k \end{aligned}$$
Hence $r^2=13-k$, and a circle needs $r^2>0$.
$$\therefore\ k<13$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. correct procedure with one error in algebra or quotes $k\le 13$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If $\tan x=3$ and $\sin x<0$ find the exact value of $\cos x$.

dif.r: Quadrant determination plus right-triangle exact ratio.

solutions.latex:
Since $\tan x>0$ and $\sin x<0$, $x$ is a 3rd quadrant angle, so $\cos x<0$.

Let $\alpha$ be the related acute angle, with $\tan\alpha=3$. A right-angled triangle with sides $1$ and $3$ has hypotenuse $\sqrt{10}$ (Pythagoras), so
$$\cos\alpha=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$$
$$\therefore\ \cos x=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds the correct numerical value but with the wrong sign, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Sum of probabilities and expected value give two simple equations.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10p&=1\\ p&=\dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}$$
The mean is $4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4ap+6ap+6ap+4ap&=4\\ 20ap&=4\\ a&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=2,\ p=\dfrac{1}{10}$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. writes one equation for $a$, $p$ using the mean or probability sum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: $A(-1,-5)$ and $B(5,-1)$ are two points. Find in general form the equation of the straight line through the midpoint of $AB$ and perpendicular to $AB$.

dif.r: Midpoint, perpendicular gradient, point-gradient form; standard steps.

solutions.latex:
The midpoint of $AB$ is $(2,-3)$ and the gradient of $AB$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

The perpendicular gradient is $-\dfrac{3}{2}$, so the line is
$$\begin{aligned} y+3&=-\dfrac{3}{2}(x-2)\\ 2y+6&=-3x+6\\ 3x+2y&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 3x+2y=0$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. correct procedure but with one error, or equivalent merit
