parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the point on the curve $y=2\sqrt{x}$ where the tangent to the curve is parallel to the line $2x-y-2=0$.

dif.r: Equate derivative to line gradient and solve; routine.

solutions.latex:
The line $2x-y-2=0$ is $y=2x-2$, so its gradient is $2$.

Differentiate the curve:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$$
Parallel tangent needs equal gradients.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}&=2\\ \sqrt{x}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=2\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}}=1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the point is } \left(\dfrac{1}{4},1\right)$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. correct procedure but with one error, or equivalent merit
Some progress, e.g. differentiates correctly, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
\exfigure{1330_q16_1}

In the diagram, $ABC$ is a triangle in which $AB=10$ cm, $AC=6$ cm and $\angle CAB=120^\circ$. $AD$ is the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$.

parts.label: a

dif.r: Direct cosine rule with obtuse angle.

parts.label: b

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

figures.cap: triangle ABC with AB=10, AC=6, angle A=120 degrees and altitude AD

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2&=10^2+6^2-2\times10\times6\cos120^\circ\\ &=196 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BC=14 \text{ cm}$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. writes a numerical expression for $BC^2$ using the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The area of $\triangle ABC$ can be found two ways, using $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ and using base $BC$ with height $AD$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times10\times6\sin120^\circ=15\sqrt{3}\\ \dfrac{1}{2}\times BC\times AD&=15\sqrt{3}\\ 7AD&=15\sqrt{3}\\ AD&\approx 3.7 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ AD\approx 3.7 \text{ cm (1 decimal place)}$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds $\sin B$, $\sin C$, $\cos B$, $\cos C$ or the area of $\triangle ABC$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A bag contains 1 blue and 4 red balls. A first ball is chosen at random without replacement from the bag. If this first ball is blue, no further balls are chosen. If the first ball is red, a second ball is chosen at random without replacement from the remaining balls. If this second ball is blue, no further balls are chosen. If the second ball is red, a third ball is chosen at random without replacement from the remaining balls.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Complete the probability tree diagram below:

\exfigure{1330_q17_1}

dif.r: Fill tree branches with simple without-replacement probabilities.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the probability that 3 red balls are chosen.

dif.r: Multiply along one tree path.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the probability that at least one ball of each colour is chosen.

dif.r: Identify two relevant paths and add their probabilities.

figures.cap: partially completed probability tree: first ball 1/5 blue, 4/5 red; branches for second and third balls without probabilities
solution sketch: completed probability tree

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1330_q17_s1}

The completed tree has these branches.

First ball: Blue $\dfrac{1}{5}$, Red $\dfrac{4}{5}$.

Second ball (after Red): Blue $\dfrac{1}{4}$, Red $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Third ball (after Red, Red): Blue $\dfrac{1}{3}$, Red $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

meta.format_note: Drawing \exfigure{1330_q17_s1} kept from source; the sketch_id given is 1330_q17_s2, check which is the intended tree figure.

solutions.latex:
Multiply along the branches Red, Red, Red.
$$\begin{aligned} P(R,R,R)&=\dfrac{4}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$$

Both colours are chosen on the paths Red then Blue, or Red, Red then Blue.
$$\begin{aligned} P(R,B)+P(R,R,B)&=\dfrac{4}{5}\times\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{4}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{5}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. identifies one appropriate path through the tree with its probability, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given that $\ln a-\ln b=\ln(a-b)$ where $a>b>1$ show that $a=\dfrac{b^2}{b-1}$.

dif.r: Log quotient law then rearrange to make a subject.

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $\ln a-\ln b=\ln\dfrac{a}{b}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\dfrac{a}{b}&=\ln(a-b)\\ \dfrac{a}{b}&=a-b\\ a&=ab-b^2\\ b^2&=a(b-1)\\ a&=\dfrac{b^2}{b-1} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. writes a relation for $a$ and $b$ using log laws, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find correct to 2 decimal places the gradient of the curve $y=x\sin x$ where $x=1$.

dif.r: Product rule with trig, evaluate in radians.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sin x+x\cos x$$
At $x=1$ (radians):
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sin 1+\cos 1\approx 1.38$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient}\approx 1.38$$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds the first derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the curve $y=x^2-8\ln x$ is concave up for all values of $x>0$.

dif.r: Second derivative and brief positivity argument; routine show-that.

solutions.latex:
Concave up needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2x-\dfrac{8}{x}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=2+\dfrac{8}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
For $x>0$, $\dfrac{8}{x^2}>0$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}>2>0$.

Therefore the curve is concave up for all $x>0$.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds the first derivative, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: At the Oztown school, HSC Trial marks in English Standard had a mean of 72 and a standard deviation of 8, whilst HSC Trial marks in Mathematics Standard 2 had a mean of 68 and a standard deviation of 10.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Otto scored 66 in the English Standard Trial and 63 in the Mathematics Standard 2 Trial. Explain which of these was Otto's better performance.

dif.r: Compute and compare two z-scores.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Anna scored 84 in the English Standard Trial but sat the Mathematics Standard 2 Trial late. Find what mark Anna needed to score in the Mathematics Standard 2 Trial so that she performed equally well in both subjects.

dif.r: Equate z-scores and solve for raw score; reverse use.

solutions.latex:
The better performance is the one with the higher $z$-score, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.
$$\begin{aligned} z_{\text{English}}&=\dfrac{66-72}{8}=-0.75\\ z_{\text{Maths}}&=\dfrac{63-68}{10}=-0.5 \end{aligned}$$
Since $-0.5>-0.75$, Otto's performance in Mathematics was better.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. calculates one $z$-score, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Equal performance means equal $z$-scores. Let $x$ be Anna's Mathematics mark.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x-68}{10}&=\dfrac{84-72}{8}\\ x-68&=15\\ x&=83 \end{aligned}$$
Anna needs to score $83$ in the Mathematics Standard 2 Trial.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. writes an equation for $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the values of any constant $A$ such that $\displaystyle\int_0^3\left(x^2+A\right)dx=2A^2$.

dif.r: Routine definite integral then factorise a simple quadratic in A

solutions.latex:
Integrate term by term, then evaluate between the limits.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^3\left(x^2+A\right)dx &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}x^3+Ax\right]_0^3 \\ &= 9+3A \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $2A^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9+3A &= 2A^2 \\ 2A^2-3A-9 &= 0 \\ (2A+3)(A-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=3 \text{ or } A=-\dfrac{3}{2}$$
criteria: Integrates to find a quadratic equation for $A$, or equivalent merit
Finds the definite integral in terms of $A$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the value of the constant $k>0$ such that $\displaystyle\int_{\ln k}^{\ln k^2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx=\ln 10$.

dif.r: Logarithmic limits need careful log-law simplification before solving

solutions.latex:
Integrate, then substitute the limits.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\ln k}^{\ln k^2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx &= \Big[x+\ln x\Big]_{\ln k}^{\ln k^2} \\ &= (\ln k^2-\ln k)+\big\{\ln(\ln k^2)-\ln(\ln k)\big\} \\ &= 2\ln k-\ln k+\ln(2\ln k)-\ln(\ln k) \\ &= \ln k+\ln 2+\ln(\ln k)-\ln(\ln k) \\ &= \ln 2k \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\ln 10$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln 2k &= \ln 10 \\ 2k &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=5$$
criteria: Evaluates and partially simplifies the definite integral in terms of $k$, or equivalent merit
Evaluates the definite integral in terms of $k$ without simplification, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the coordinates and nature of the stationary points on the curve $y=\dfrac{x^2}{x-2}$.

dif.r: Quotient rule stationary points; nature test across asymptote at x=2

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=x-2\\ u'&=2x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{2x(x-2)-x^2}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2-4x}{(x-2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(x-4)}{(x-2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=4$, $y=8$.

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(4,8)$.

The denominator is positive except at $x=2$, so the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is the sign of $x(x-4)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x<0 &&\text{increasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=0\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 0<x<2 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &\text{ undefined} &&\text{at } x=2\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 2<x<4 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=4\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>4 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
Hence $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point and $(4,8)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the stationary points and the nature of one of them, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit
Applies the quotient rule for differentiation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: An item is purchased for $\$20\,000$. It appreciates in value so that after $t$ years its value $\$V$ is given by the formula $V=20000p^t$ for some constant $p>1$. After 9 years its value is $\$32\,000$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $p$ correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: Substitute and take ninth root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find correct to the nearest $\$10$ per year the rate at which the item is appreciating in value after 9 years.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential with base p and evaluate rate

solutions.latex:
When $t=9$, $V=32000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 20000p^9 &= 32000 \\ p^9 &= \dfrac{8}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p=(1.6)^{\frac{1}{9}}\approx 1.0536$$
criteria: Writes and simplifies a numerical expression for $p^9$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The rate of appreciation is $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$. Differentiating $V=20000p^t$:
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=20\,000\ln p\,(p^t)$$
When $t=9$, $p^9=\dfrac{8}{5}$ and $\ln p=\dfrac{1}{9}\ln 1.6$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 20\,000\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\ln 1.6\right)\times\dfrac{8}{5} \\ &\approx 1670 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the rate of increase is } \$1670 \text{ per year (nearest } \$10\text{)}$$
criteria: Differentiates with respect to $t$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: At the start of year 2000 a colony of 600 animals was established in a sanctuary. Each year the population size grows at a rate of $10\%$ per year and at the end of each year 50 of the animals are released into the wild. The population size $P_n$ at the end of the $n^{\text{th}}$ year can be determined using the recurrence relation $P_n=1.1\times P_{n-1}-50$ where $n=1,2,3,\dots$ and $P_0=600$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write down expressions for $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ in terms of $P_0$ and hence show that $P_n=100\times(1.1)^n+500$.

dif.r: Unroll recurrence, recognise GP sum, derive general closed form

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the year in which the growth in population size from the beginning of that year to the start of the next year first exceeds 100.

dif.r: Model yearly growth as difference, log inequality, interpret calendar year

criteria: Process correct but one error made, or simplification not completed, or equivalent merit
Finds expressions for $P_1,P_2,P_3$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The growth over year $n$ is $P_n-P_{n-1}$. We need the least integer $n$ with $P_n-P_{n-1}>100$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100\left\{(1.1)^n-(1.1)^{n-1}\right\} &> 100 \\ (1.1)^{n-1}(1.1-1) &> 1 \\ (1.1)^{n-1} &> 10 \\ (n-1)\log_{10}(1.1) &> 1 \\ n-1 &> \dfrac{1}{\log_{10}(1.1)}\approx 24.16 \end{aligned}$$
So $n-1=25,26,27,\dots$, and the least value is $n=26$.

$$\text{Year } n \text{ is the calendar year } 1999+n \text{ (year 1 is 2000), so } n=26 \text{ is } 2025.$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the required year is } 2025$$
criteria: Correct procedure but one error in calculation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. Initially the particle is at $O$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use integration to show that $x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.

dif.r: Integrate velocity and find constant from initial condition

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find when and where the particle is at rest.

dif.r: Solve v=0 then substitute into displacement

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 24 seconds of its motion.

dif.r: Distance must account for direction change at t=8

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement, so integrate $v$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9 \\ x &= 2(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+c \end{aligned}$$
Initially $x=0$ when $t=0$, so $0=2-0+c$ and $c=-2$.
$$\therefore\ x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$$
criteria: Integrates with respect to $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9 &= 0 \\ \sqrt{t+1} &= 3 \\ t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
Then $x=2(9)(3)-72-2=-20$.

Also, when $t=0$, $v=-3$, so the particle starts in the negative direction.

The particle is at rest at time 8 seconds, when it is 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of travel.

At $t=24$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2(25)(5)-9(24)-2 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
The particle changes direction at $t=8$, so in the first 24 seconds it travels from $x=0$ to $x=-20$, then to $x=32$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 20+(20+32) \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance travelled is } 72 \text{ m}$$

questions.stem: The cost $\$C$ per hour when employees work $x$ hours per day to complete a project is given by $C=ax^3+d$ for some constants $a$ and $d$. The time $T$ hours to complete the project is given by $T=\dfrac{120}{x}$. In order to complete the project, the cost would be $\$248$ per hour when employees work 4 hours per day on the project and $\$472$ per hour when employees work 8 hours per day on the project.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write down two equations in $a$ and $d$ and solve these equations to find the values of $a$ and $d$.

dif.r: Form and solve two simultaneous linear equations

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the total cost $\$S$ of completing the project when employees work $x$ hours per day on the project is given by $S=60x^2+\dfrac{25\,920}{x}$.

dif.r: Recognise total cost equals time times hourly cost

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Use differentiation to find the minimum total cost of completing the project.

dif.r: Standard optimisation of given function with sign test

solutions.latex:
Substitute each pair of values into $C=ax^3+d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 248 &= 64a+d &&(1)\\ 472 &= 512a+d &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtract (1) from (2).
$$\begin{aligned} 224 &= 448a \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 248-64\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 216 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2},\ d=216$$
criteria: Writes correct simultaneous equations but makes one error in solution, or equivalent merit
Writes one of the equations correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total cost is the time multiplied by the cost per hour, $S=TC$, with $a=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $d=216$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{120}{x}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{2}+216\right) \\ &= 60x^2+\dfrac{25\,920}{x} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate $S=60x^2+25\,920x^{-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dS}{dx} &= 120x-\dfrac{25\,920}{x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{120}{x^2}\left(x^3-216\right) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dS}{dx}=0$, so $x^3=216$ and $x=6$.

Then $S=60(36)+\dfrac{25\,920}{6}=6480$.

Since $\dfrac{120}{x^2}>0$, the sign of $\dfrac{dS}{dx}$ is the sign of $x^3-216$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dS}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } 0<x<6 &&\text{decreasing}\\ \dfrac{dS}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=6\\ \dfrac{dS}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x>6 &&\text{increasing}\end{aligned}$$
So $x=6$ gives a minimum.

$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum cost is } \$6480$$
criteria: Correct procedure but one error or omission, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ or $x>2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

dif.r: Check non-negativity and integral equals one

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ of the random variable $X$.

dif.r: Integrate pdf to piecewise CDF

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that if $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$ are the quartiles of the distribution of $X$ then $\dfrac{1}{Q_1}$, $\dfrac{1}{Q_2}$, $\dfrac{1}{Q_3}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.

dif.r: Solve three quartile equations and justify arithmetic sequence

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf
Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
A probability density function must satisfy $f(x)\ge0$ and $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx=1$.

For $1\le x\le2$, $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}>0$, and $f(x)=0$ elsewhere.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 f(x)\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{x}\right]_1^2 \\ &= -1+2 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Both conditions hold.

Hence $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
criteria: Finds and evaluates the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le 2$, integrate the density from 1 to $x$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_1^x\dfrac{2}{t^2}\,dt \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{2}{t}\right]_1^x \\ &= 2-\dfrac{2}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<1\\[6pt] 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x}\right), & 1\le x\le2\\[6pt] 1, & x>2\end{cases}$$
criteria: Correct procedure but one error or omission, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source integrated with the same variable $x$ as the upper limit; changed the integration variable to $t$, no change to the mathematics.

solutions.latex:
The quartiles satisfy $F(Q_1)=\dfrac{1}{4}$, $F(Q_2)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $F(Q_3)=\dfrac{3}{4}$, using $F(x)=2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$.

For $Q_1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_1}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_1} &= \dfrac{7}{8} \end{aligned}$$
For $Q_2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_2}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_2} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
For $Q_3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{Q_3}\right) &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_3} &= \dfrac{5}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The differences between consecutive terms are
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{Q_2}-\dfrac{1}{Q_1} &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \\ \dfrac{1}{Q_3}-\dfrac{1}{Q_2} &= -\dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}$$
The common difference is $-\dfrac{1}{8}$.

Hence $\dfrac{1}{Q_1},\dfrac{1}{Q_2},\dfrac{1}{Q_3}$ are consecutive terms in an arithmetic sequence.
criteria: Correct procedure but an error in execution or AP not verified, or equivalent merit
Finds one of the quartiles or its reciprocal correctly, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
\exfigure{1330_q33_1}

The diagram shows the graphs of the curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ where $f(x)=e^x$ and $g(x)=6-8e^{-x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: State a sequence of dilations, reflections, translations that would transform the graph of the curve $y=f(x)$ into the graph of the curve $y=g(x)$.

dif.r: Several transformations including two reflections in correct order

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the $x$ coordinates ($x_1$ and $x_2$ where $x_1<x_2$) of the points of intersection of the two curves are the solutions of the equation $e^{2x}-6e^x+8=0$ and solve this equation to find the exact values of $x_1$ and $x_2$.

dif.r: Form hidden quadratic in e^x, factorise, take logs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find in simplest exact form the area of the region enclosed by the two curves.

dif.r: Area between exponential curves with logarithmic limits, exact simplification

figures.cap: graphs of y=e^x and y=6-8e^{-x} with asymptote y=6

solutions.latex:
Start from $y=e^x$ and build $y=6-8e^{-x}$ one step at a time.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=e^x \\ y&=8e^x &&(\text{vertical dilation, factor } 8)\\ y&=-8e^x &&(\text{reflection in the } x\text{-axis})\\ y&=-8e^{-x} &&(\text{reflection in the } y\text{-axis})\\ y&=6-8e^{-x} &&(\text{translation up 6 units})\end{aligned}$$
A vertical dilation by a factor 8, then reflections in the $x$ and $y$ axes, followed by a vertical translation upwards by 6 units.
criteria: Identifies one or two correct transformations, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Intermediate lines in the transformation chain were added by us to show the sequence; the source sequence is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
The curves intersect where $e^x=6-8e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{2x} &= 6e^x-8 &&(\text{multiply by } e^x)\\ e^{2x}-6e^x+8 &= 0 \\ (e^x-2)(e^x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $e^x=2$ or $e^x=4$.
$$\therefore\ x_1=\ln 2,\quad x_2=\ln 4$$
criteria: Finds the equation and the values of $e^x$, or equivalent merit
Obtains the required equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
On $\ln 2\le x\le\ln 4$ the curve $y=6-8e^{-x}$ is above $y=e^x$, so the area is
$$\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\left(6-8e^{-x}-e^x\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \Big[6x+8e^{-x}-e^x\Big]_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4} \\ &= 6(\ln 4-\ln 2)+8\left(e^{-\ln 4}-e^{-\ln 2}\right)-\left(e^{\ln 4}-e^{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= 6\ln 2+8\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-(4-2) \\ &= 6\ln 2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area is } (6\ln 2-4) \text{ square units}$$
criteria: Writes the definite integral and finds the anti-derivative with partial evaluation, or equivalent merit
Writes the definite integral and finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The graph has minimum $0$ and maximum $6$, so the midline is $y=3$ and the amplitude is $3$.

The graph starts at its minimum when $x=0$, so $A=-3$.

The period is $\pi$, so $B=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$.

Hence $A=-3$ and $B=2$, which is option C.

parts.latex:
A data set of thirteen scores has a mean and median of 25. The scores 21, 16, 16, 26, 30, 30 are added to this data set.

What of the following MUST BE TRUE?
parts.note: Effect of added scores on the mean and median of a data set (summary statistics of data): not in the 2024 Advanced course (Standard content).

dif.r: Recompute mean and reason median unchanged after adding balanced scores.

solutions.latex:
Three of the added scores lie below $25$ ($16, 16, 21$) and three lie above it ($26, 30, 30$), so the median stays $25$.

Old total:
$$13\times25=325$$
Total of new scores:
$$21+16+16+26+30+30=139$$
New total:
$$325+139=464$$
New mean:
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= \dfrac{464}{19} \\ &\approx 24.42 \\ &< 25 \end{aligned}$$
So the mean decreases, which is option B.

parts.latex: Which of the following is not equivalent to $\sqrt{(x-1)^2}$?

dif.r: Recall sqrt(a^2)=|a| and recognise x-1 fails for x<1.

options.label: B
options.latex: Distance from $x$ to 1 on the number line?

solutions.latex:
Since $\sqrt{a^2}=|a|$, we have $\sqrt{(x-1)^2}=|x-1|$.

This equals $x-1$ only when $x\ge1$, and is not equal to $x-1$ for $x<1$.

So $x-1$ is not equivalent, which is option D.

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

figures.cap: spinner wheel with numbers 1-20

solutions.latex:
The numbers greater than $15$ are $16,17,18,19,20$, so the probability is $\dfrac{5}{20}=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

parts.latex: What is $\displaystyle\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+h\right)-\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)}{h}$?

dif.r: Must recognise limit as derivative of cos at 3pi/2, then evaluate.

solutions.latex:
The limit is the definition of the derivative of $f(x)=\cos x$ at $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.
$$f'(x)=-\sin x$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) &= -\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: The temperature of a room, in degrees Celsius, is modelled by $T(t)$ where $t$ is the number of minutes after its thermostat is adjusted. What is the best interpretation of $T'(5) = 2$?

dif.r: Interpret derivative value as rate of change in context.

options.label: A
options.latex: The temperature of the room is increasing at a rate of 2 degrees Celsius per minute, 5 minutes after the thermostat is adjusted.

options.label: B
options.latex: The temperature of the room is increasing at a constant rate of $\dfrac{2}{5}$ degree Celsius per minute.

options.label: C
options.latex: The temperature of the room increases by 2 degrees Celsius during the first 5 minutes after the thermostat is adjusted.

options.label: D
options.latex: The temperature of the room is 2 degrees, 5 minutes after the thermostat is adjusted.

solutions.latex:
$T'(5)$ is the rate of change of temperature at $t=5$.

So $T'(5)=2$ means the temperature is increasing at $2$ degrees Celsius per minute, $5$ minutes after the thermostat is adjusted.

This is option A.

parts.latex: The graph of $y = \dfrac{3}{x+1}$ is translated 4 units right and dilated vertically by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$. Which of the following gives the equation of the new function?

dif.r: Apply translation then vertical dilation; match rearranged form.

solutions.latex:
Translating $4$ units right replaces $x$ with $x-4$:
$$y=\dfrac{3}{(x-4)+1}=\dfrac{3}{x-3}$$
Dilating vertically by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ multiplies $y$ by $\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{x-3}\right) \\ 2y &= \dfrac{3}{x-3} \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

dif.r: Signs of f, f', f'' at turning points from graph, then order.

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with local max A at x=-2 and local min B at x=8

solutions.latex:
The local maximum at $A$ lies above the $x$-axis, so $f(-2)>0$.

At a local minimum the tangent is horizontal, so $f'(8)=0$.

The graph is concave down at $A$, so $f''(-2)<0$.

In ascending order: $f''(-2),\ f'(8),\ f(-2)$, which is option B.

parts.latex: Find the largest domain for which $\sqrt{2x-3}$ is defined.

dif.r: Single linear inequality for square root domain.

solutions.latex:
The square root is defined when $2x-3\ge0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-3 &\ge 0 \\ 2x &\ge 3 \\ x &\ge \dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the domain is } \left[\dfrac{3}{2},\infty\right)$$

parts.latex: Factorise $2x^2 + 3x - 2xy - 3y$.

dif.r: Routine factorising by grouping in pairs.

solutions.latex:
Group in pairs and take out common factors.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x^2+3x-2xy-3y &= x(2x+3)-y(2x+3) \\ &= (2x+3)(x-y) \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A circle is given by $x^2 + 2x + y^2 - 4y - 4 = 0$.

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+2x+y^2-4y-4 &= 0 \\ (x^2+2x+1)+(y^2-4y+4) &= 4+1+4 \\ (x+1)^2+(y-2)^2 &= 9 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \sqrt7+\sqrt8=\sqrt{15+4\sqrt{14}}$$
criteria: Squares both sides, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: An arithmetic sequence is given by $4, 13, 22, 31, \dots$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the $25^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence.

dif.r: Substitute into arithmetic term formula.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the sum to the $25^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence.

dif.r: Substitute into arithmetic sum formula using found last term.

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic sequence, $a=4$, $d=9$ and $n=25$.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{25} &= 4+24\times9 \\ &= 220 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies $a$, $d$, $n$ and the formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ with $l=220$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{25} &= \dfrac{25}{2}(4+220) \\ &= 2800 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $4, x, y, \dfrac{32}{27}$ are four consecutive terms of a geometric series. Solve for $x$ and $y$.

dif.r: Find ratio from first and fourth terms of geometric sequence.

can_use: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Method 1. In a geometric sequence consecutive ratios are equal, so
$$\dfrac{x}{4}=\dfrac{32}{27y} \qquad (1)$$
$$\dfrac{x}{4}=\dfrac{y}{x}, \text{ so } y=\dfrac{x^2}{4} \qquad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{4} &= \dfrac{32}{27\left(\frac{x^2}{4}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{128}{27x^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 27x^3 &= 512 \\ x^3 &= \dfrac{512}{27} \\ x &= \dfrac{8}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^2}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{64}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{16}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2. Here $a=4$ and $r=\dfrac{x}{4}$, so
$$T_4=4\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3=\dfrac{32}{27}$$
This gives $x^3=\dfrac{512}{27}$, so $x=\dfrac{8}{3}$. Then
$$y=T_3=4\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{8}{3} \text{ and } y=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
criteria: Forms equations (1) and (2), or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $\dfrac{x}{e^x}$ is $\dfrac{1-x}{e^x}$.

dif.r: Routine quotient rule show-that with given answer.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1-x+e^x}{2e^x}\,dx$.

dif.r: Split fraction and reverse the given derivative to integrate.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{e^x\cdot1-xe^x}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(1-x)}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1-x}{e^x} \end{aligned}$$

Split the fraction and use part (a).
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{1-x+e^x}{2e^x}\,dx &= \int\left(\dfrac{1-x}{2e^x}+\dfrac{e^x}{2e^x}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int\left(\dfrac{1-x}{e^x}+1\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{x}{e^x}+x\right]+c \\ &= \dfrac{x}{2e^x}+\dfrac{x}{2}+c \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the derivative of $x^2 - 1$ using first principles.

dif.r: Standard first principles limit for a simple quadratic.

solutions.latex:
Using first principles, $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{(x+h)^2-1-(x^2-1)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{x^2+2xh+h^2-1-x^2+1}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{2xh+h^2}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to0}(2x+h) \\ &= 2x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expands and simplifies, or equivalent merit
Correct substitution into the first principles formula, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The formula must be correct or 0 marks (critical error, no consequential marks); an answer of $2x$ without first principles also gets 0.

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle travelling in a straight line is given by $v = 2t - 4$, where $t$ is time in seconds and $x$ its displacement from the origin in metres. The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the expression for the particle's displacement as a function of time.

dif.r: Integrate linear velocity, constant zero from initial position.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the total distance travelled for the first 5 seconds.

dif.r: Must detect direction change and add distances, not displacement.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
$$x=\displaystyle\int(2t-4)\,dt=t^2-4t+c$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $c=0$.
$$x=t^2-4t$$

meta.marker_note: $x=t^2-4t$ alone is not sufficient without evaluating $c$.

solutions.latex:
When $t=5$:
$$x=5^2-4(5)=5$$
The particle may change direction when it is stationary, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2t-4 &= 0 \\ t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
When $t=2$:
$$x=2^2-4(2)=-4$$
The particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=-4$, then to $x=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{distance} &= 4+9 \\ &= 13 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the total distance is the area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times4+\dfrac{1}{2}\times3\times6=4+9=13 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the change of direction at $t=2$ and $x=-4$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: 0 marks for an answer of 5.

parts.latex: Solve for $k$ such that $\displaystyle\int_2^k (-3x+1)\,dx = \int_k^6 (-3x+1)\,dx$.

dif.r: Evaluate two definite integrals with variable bound, solve quadratic.

solutions.latex:
Evaluate each side using the antiderivative $-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left[-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x\right]_2^k \\ &= -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k-(-6+2) \\ &= -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k+4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \left[-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x\right]_k^6 \\ &= (-54+6)-\left(-\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k\right) \\ &= -48+\dfrac{3k^2}{2}-k \end{aligned}$$
Equate the two sides.
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k+4 &= -48+\dfrac{3k^2}{2}-k \\ 3k^2-2k-52 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4+624}}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{628}}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{157}}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: At the start of the week Susie has three yellow shirts and two green shirts. She wears one clean shirt each day. On Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of that week, she randomly selects one shirt to wear. In this three day period, what is the probability that Susie does not wear a shirt of the same colour on any two successive days?

dif.r: Must identify alternating cases YGY, GYG without replacement; multi-stage products.

solutions.latex:
The colours must alternate, so the shirts worn are YGY or GYG (no replacement).
$$\begin{aligned} P &= P(YGY)+P(GYG) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{4}\times\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{60}+\dfrac{6}{60} \\ &= \dfrac{18}{60} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{10} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Georgina is training for the Tokyo Olympics. She swims 1.5km on the first day, and on each day after that she swims 200 metres more than the previous day. That is, she swims 1.7km on the second day and 1.9km on the third day and so on.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How many days of training will she require to have swum a combined total of over 100km?

dif.r: Arithmetic sum leads to quadratic in n; interpret and round up.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Georgina wants to have swum over 200 km in total over 20 days. If on the first day she still swims 1.5 km but increases her swim by a distance of $x$ km per day. Find the value of $x$ so that she can reach her goal.

dif.r: Sum formula used in reverse to find common difference.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The distances form an arithmetic series with $a=1.5$ and $d=0.2$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2\times1.5+(n-1)\times0.2\right]=100$$
$$\begin{aligned} n\left(3+\dfrac{n-1}{5}\right) &= 200 \\ 15n+n(n-1) &= 1000 \\ n^2+14n-1000 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$n=\dfrac{-14\pm\sqrt{14^2+4(1)(1000)}}{2}=\dfrac{-14\pm\sqrt{4196}}{2}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=\dfrac{-14+\sqrt{4196}}{2}\approx 25.39$.

So she needs $26$ days of training.
criteria: Substitutes into the $S_n$ formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Here $a=1.5$, $n=20$ and $d=x$.
$$\dfrac{20}{2}\left[2\times1.5+(20-1)x\right]=200$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3+19x &= 20 \\ 19x &= 17 \\ x &= \dfrac{17}{19} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{17}{19}\text{ km}$$

meta.marker_note: The value of $x$ must be given in km.

parts.latex: By writing $0 \cdot \dot{7}\dot{6}$ as a geometric series, use the limiting sum formula to show that $0 \cdot \dot{7}\dot{6} = \dfrac{76}{99}$.

solutions.latex:
Write the decimal as a geometric series.
$$0\cdot\dot{7}\dot{6}=0.76+0.0076+0.000076+\cdots$$
Here $a=0.76$ and $r=0.01$, with $|r|<1$.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{0.76}{1-0.01} \\ &= \dfrac{0.76}{0.99} \\ &= \dfrac{76}{99} \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Must use a geometric series.

parts.latex: Solve for $k$ such that $y = e^{kt}$ satisfies the equation $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} = \dfrac{dy}{dt} + y$.

dif.r: Differentiate twice, substitute into differential equation, solve quadratic in k.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $y=e^{kt}$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dt}=ke^{kt},\qquad \dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}=k^2e^{kt}$$
Substitute into $\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}=\dfrac{dy}{dt}+y$.
$$\begin{aligned} k^2e^{kt} &= ke^{kt}+e^{kt} \\ k^2 &= k+1 \\ k^2-k-1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$k=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{(-1)^2-4(1)(-1)}}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the equation, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} y &= \log_2 x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 2} \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{x\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Consider the curve $y = x(x-2)(x+1)$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any stationary point, to 1 decimal place, and determine their nature.

dif.r: Expand cubic, quadratic formula for stationary points, second derivative test.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any points of inflection.

dif.r: Solve y''=0, check concavity change, evaluate point.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the curve showing all important features.

dif.r: Sketch cubic using intercepts and previously found features.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: For what values of $c$ will $x(x-2)(x+1) = c$ have exactly 1 solution? Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=x(x-2)(x+1) with intercepts, turning points and point of inflection

solutions.latex:
$$y=x^3-x^2-2x,\qquad \dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-2x-2$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$x=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4+24}}{6}$$
So $x\approx 1.2$ or $x\approx -0.5$.

The second derivative is $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-2$.

When $x=1.2$, $y\approx -2.1$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\approx 5.2>0$.

So there is a local minimum at $(1.2,-2.1)$.

When $x=-0.5$, $y\approx 0.6$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\approx -5<0$.

So there is a local maximum at $(-0.5,0.6)$.
criteria: Finds one stationary point and its nature, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$6x-2=0,\quad\text{so } x=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
Test the concavity either side.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3} & 1 \\ \hline y'' & -2 & 0 & 4 \end{array}$$
The concavity changes from concave down to concave up.

When $x=\dfrac{1}{3}$, $y=-\dfrac{20}{27}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{point of inflection at }\left(\dfrac{1}{3},-\dfrac{20}{27}\right)$$
criteria: Finds $x$ and checks the change of concavity, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: On average, Silvester takes 15 mins to walk to the train station, and from there it takes an average of 45mins to get to the city by train once he is at the station. The standard deviations for the walk and the train trip are 2mins and 5 mins, respectively.

parts.label: b

dif.r: Empirical rule in reverse: 97.5% corresponds to mean plus two SD.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$z_{\text{walk}}=\dfrac{18-15}{2}=1.5$$
$$z_{\text{train}}=\dfrac{52-45}{5}=1.4$$

By the empirical rule, $97.5\%$ of values lie below $\mu+2\sigma$, so $z=2$.
$$\dfrac{x-15}{2}=2$$
$$\therefore\ x=19\text{ min (at least 19 min)}$$

questions.stem:
A probability distribution is said to have a \textbf{memoryless property} if the probability of some future event occurring is not affected by the occurrence of past events.

In formal statistic terms, a random variable $X$ is said to follow a probability distribution with a memoryless property if for any $a, x \ge 0$ it is true that:

$$P(X > x + a \mid X > a) = P(X > x)$$

You are given that $X$ is modelled by a continuous random variable with probability density function of the form $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, for some constant $\lambda$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the corresponding cumulative distribution function is given by $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$.

dif.r: Integrate given exponential pdf to obtain CDF; standard technique.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence, prove the memoryless property for the distribution of $X$:

$$P(X > x + a \mid X > a) = P(X > x)$$

dif.r: Abstract proof combining conditional probability with continuous distribution tail.

solutions.latex:
For $x\ge 0$, the cumulative distribution function is the integral of the density.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \displaystyle\int_0^x \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt \\ &= \Big[-e^{-\lambda t}\Big]_0^x \\ &= -e^{-\lambda x}+e^{0} \\ &= 1-e^{-\lambda x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using conditional probability, and noting $X>x+a$ implies $X>a$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>x+a\mid X>a) &= \dfrac{P\big((X>x+a)\cap(X>a)\big)}{P(X>a)} \\ &= \dfrac{P(X>x+a)}{P(X>a)} \end{aligned}$$
Using $P(X>t)=1-F(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{P(X>x+a)}{P(X>a)} &= \dfrac{e^{-\lambda(x+a)}}{e^{-\lambda a}} \\ &= \dfrac{e^{-\lambda x}\cdot e^{-\lambda a}}{e^{-\lambda a}} \\ &= e^{-\lambda x} \end{aligned}$$
Also $P(X>x)=1-\left(1-e^{-\lambda x}\right)=e^{-\lambda x}$.
$$\therefore\ P(X>x+a\mid X>a)=P(X>x)$$
criteria: Uses the cumulative distribution function, or equivalent merit
Writes the conditional probability as a ratio, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $2\log_2 x - 9\log_x 2 = 3$.

dif.r: Reciprocal log change of base, substitution to quadratic, two solutions.

solutions.latex:
Using $\log_x 2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2 x}$:
$$2\log_2 x-\dfrac{9}{\log_2 x}-3=0$$
Let $u=\log_2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2u^2-3u-9 &= 0 \\ (2u+3)(u-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $\log_2 x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$ or $\log_2 x=3$.
$$\therefore\ x=2^{-\frac{3}{2}}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\ (\approx 0.3535)\text{ or } x=8$$
criteria: Solves the quadratic in $\log_2 x$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the series $1 - \tan^2\theta + \tan^4\theta - \tan^6\theta \dots$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: For what values of $\theta$ in the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ does a limiting sum exist for the series?

dif.r: Identify ratio -tan^2θ, apply |r|<1, solve trig inequality.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the expression for this limiting sum in its simplest form.

dif.r: Limiting sum formula then Pythagorean identity to simplify.

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $r=-\tan^2\theta$.

A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan^2\theta &< 1 \\ -1 &< \tan\theta < 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{\pi}{4}<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Uses $|r|<1$ to obtain $-1<\tan\theta<1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=1$ and $r=-\tan^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{1}{1+\tan^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta} \\ &= \cos^2\theta \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Accept $\dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta}$.

questions.stem: A barrel maker charges \$50 per hour for the time spent on each job, as well as the cost to cover the power used on machinery. Depending on the setting chosen, the machine uses power at a rate of $20 + \dfrac{v^2}{10}$ MW per hour, where $v$ barrels/hour is the speed of which the machine makes barrels. (That is, $v = 3$ means the machine can make 3 barrels in an hour). Power costs \$1.25 per MW used. A job is given to make 1200 barrels.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the cost (\$$C$) to pay for this job is given by $C = \dfrac{90000}{v} + 150v$.

dif.r: Build cost model from rates and time; interpret wordy context.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Assuming that $v$ can take any non-negative values, find the speed $v$, that minimizes the cost and determine this cost.

dif.r: Routine minimisation of given function with second derivative check.

solutions.latex:
Cost is the wage plus the power cost, where the time taken is $T=\dfrac{1200}{v}$ hours.
$$C=50T+1.25\left(20+\dfrac{v^2}{10}\right)T$$
Substituting $T$:
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 50\left(\dfrac{1200}{v}\right)+1.25\left(20+\dfrac{v^2}{10}\right)\left(\dfrac{1200}{v}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{60000}{v}+\left(25+\dfrac{v^2}{8}\right)\dfrac{1200}{v} \\ &= \dfrac{60000}{v}+\dfrac{30000}{v}+150v \\ &= \dfrac{90000}{v}+150v \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expression for cost with $T=\dfrac{1200}{v}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate and set $C'=0$.
$$C'=-\dfrac{90000}{v^2}+150=0$$
So $v^2=600$, and $v=\sqrt{600}\approx 24.5$ since $v>0$.

Test the nature:
$$C''=\dfrac{2\times 90000}{v^3}>0 \text{ as } v>0$$
So this is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} C_{\min} &= \dfrac{90000}{\sqrt{600}}+150\sqrt{600} \\ &= \dfrac{18000}{\sqrt{6}} \\ &\approx \$7348.47 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of the function $y = \ln(x^2)$, where $x > 0$.

The points $P(1,0)$, $Q(e,2)$ and $R(t, \ln t^2)$ all lie on the curve.

parts.label: a

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $f(x)=\ln(x^2)$.
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2}=\dfrac{2}{x}$$
The gradient of $PQ$ is:
$$m_{PQ}=\dfrac{2-0}{e-1}=\dfrac{2}{e-1}$$
The tangent at $R$ is parallel to $PQ$, so the gradients are equal.
$$\dfrac{2}{x}=\dfrac{2}{e-1},\quad\text{so } x=e-1$$
Then $y=\ln(e-1)^2$.
$$\therefore\ R=\left(e-1,\ln(e-1)^2\right)$$

Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the angles that $PQ$ and $PR$ make with the positive $x$-axis.
$$m_{PQ}=\dfrac{2}{e-1}=\tan\alpha,\quad \alpha=49^\circ 20'$$
$$m_{RP}=\dfrac{\ln(e-1)^2-0}{(e-1)-1}=\dfrac{\ln(e-1)^2}{e-2}=\tan\beta,\quad \beta=56^\circ 26'$$
So $\angle RPQ=\beta-\alpha=7^\circ 6'$.
$$\therefore\ \angle RPQ\approx 7^\circ$$
Alternatively, by the cosine rule:
$$\cos\theta=\dfrac{PR^2+PQ^2-RQ^2}{2\,PR\cdot PQ}=\dfrac{1.688+6.9527-1.8415}{2\sqrt{1.688\times 6.9527}}$$
criteria: Finds the gradients $m_{PQ}$ and $m_{RP}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}|PQ||PR|\sin\angle RPQ$ with $\angle RPQ=7^\circ$.

Find the side lengths.
$$|PQ|=\sqrt{(e-1)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{e^2-2e+5}=\sqrt{6.9527}\approx 2.6368$$
$$|PR|=\sqrt{(e-2)^2+\left(\ln(e-1)^2\right)^2}=\sqrt{1.688}\approx 1.2992$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\max} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.6368\times 1.2992\times\sin 7^\circ \\ &\approx 0.2088 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A_{\max}\approx 0.21\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Correct area formula using the angle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which expression is a term in the geometric series $2x-20x^2+200x^3-\ldots$ ?

dif.r: Find ratio, general term, then match power and sign

solutions.latex:
This is a geometric series with first term and common ratio
$$a=2x,\quad r=\dfrac{-20x^2}{2x}=-10x$$
The general term is
$$\begin{aligned} T_n&=2x\times(-10x)^{n-1} \\ &=2(-10)^{n-1}x^n \end{aligned}$$
The power of $10$ is one less than the power of $x$, so only options A and B (power $7$ of $x$ with $10^7$) or C and D (power $8$ of $x$ with $10^7$) can fit. Since $10^7$ needs $n-1=7$, we get $n=8$, and the power of $x$ is $8$.

When $n=8$, $(-1)^{n-1}=(-1)^7$ is negative, so the term is $-2\times10^7x^8$.

This is option D.

solutions.latex:
This is an arithmetic series with
$$a=5,\quad d=7$$
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $T_n=292$:
$$\begin{aligned} 292&=5+(n-1)\times7 \\ 287&=7n-7 \\ 294&=7n \\ n&=42 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ there are 42 terms, as required.

Using the sum formula for an arithmetic series, $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{42}&=\dfrac{42}{2}(5+292) \\ &=6237 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_{42}=6237$$

dif.r: Check two consecutive ratios are equal

solutions.latex:
A sequence is geometric if consecutive terms have a common ratio.
$$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\dfrac{\frac13}{\frac12}=\dfrac23$$
$$\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}=\dfrac{\frac29}{\frac13}=\dfrac23$$
Since $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\dfrac{T_3}{T_2}$, the sequence is geometric.

questions.stem:
Andrew borrows \$640 000 which is to be repaid in equal monthly instalments. The interest rate is 4.8% p.a. reducible, calculated monthly. Interest is charged and calculated just before each repayment is made.

Let the amount that Andrew repays each month be $M$ and the amount owing after the $n^{\text{th}}$ repayment be $A_n$.

dif.r: Build A1 then A2 from loan recurrence

parts.label: b

dif.r: General show-that: generalise pattern and sum geometric series

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If Andrew makes monthly repayments of \$4000, how long will it take him to repay the loan?

dif.r: Set A_n=0, solve exponential with logs, round up

solutions.latex:
The monthly rate is $4.8\%\div12=0.4\%=0.004$, so the balance is multiplied by $1.004$ before each repayment.
$$A_1=640000\times1.004-M$$
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1\times1.004-M \\ &=(640000\times1.004-M)\times1.004-M \\ &=640000\times1.004^2-M\times1.004-M \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.format_note: Source criterion 'working shown' converted to Correct answer.

solutions.latex:
Continuing the pattern from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} A_3&=(640000\times1.004^2-M\times1.004-M)\times1.004-M \\ &=640000\times1.004^3-M(1+1.004+1.004^2) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$A_n=640000\times1.004^n-M\left(1+1.004+1.004^2+\ldots+1.004^{n-1}\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=1.004$ and $n$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{1.004^n-1}{1.004-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_n&=640000\times1.004^n-\dfrac{M\left(1.004^n-1\right)}{1.004-1} \\ &=640000\times1.004^n-\dfrac{M\left(1.004^n-1\right)}{0.004} \\ &=640000\times1.004^n-250M\left(1.004^n-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Sets up the series in terms of $M$ and $n$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The loan is repaid when $A_n=0$, with $M=4000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=640000\times1.004^n-250\times4000\left(1.004^n-1\right) \\ 0&=640000\times1.004^n-1000000\times1.004^n+1000000 \\ 360000\times1.004^n&=1000000 \\ 1.004^n&=\dfrac{25}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Taking logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned} n\ln(1.004)&=\ln\left(\dfrac{25}{9}\right) \\ n&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{25}{9}\right)}{\ln(1.004)} \\ &=255.923\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ must be a whole number of months, round up.
$$\therefore\ \text{it will take Andrew 256 months to repay the loan.}$$

questions.stem: Liz and Jo are playing a game. They take turns in tossing 2 fair coins. The first player to toss 2 heads is the winner. Jo has the first turn.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that Jo will win the game on her first or second turn?

dif.r: Two-case sequential probability with complements

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability that Jo will eventually win the game?

dif.r: Model winning chances as infinite geometric series

solutions.latex:
Each toss of 2 coins gives
$$P(HH)=\dfrac14,\quad P(\text{not }HH)=\dfrac34$$
Jo wins on her first turn with probability
$$P(W)=\dfrac14$$
Jo wins on her second turn if both Jo and Liz fail first, then Jo succeeds:
$$P(LLW)=\dfrac34\times\dfrac34\times\dfrac14=\dfrac{9}{64}$$
Adding the two cases:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Jo wins on first or second turn})&=\dfrac14+\dfrac{9}{64} \\ &=\dfrac{25}{64} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Jo wins on turn 1, turn 2, turn 3, and so on, so
$$P(W)+P(LLW)+P(LLLLW)+\ldots=\dfrac14+\left(\dfrac34\right)^2\times\dfrac14+\left(\dfrac34\right)^4\times\dfrac14+\ldots$$
This is a geometric series with
$$a=\dfrac14,\quad r=\left(\dfrac34\right)^2=\dfrac{9}{16}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the sum to infinity exists:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac14}{1-\left(\frac34\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac47 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the probability Jo eventually wins is } \dfrac47$$

questions.stem: Consider the curve $y = 6x^2 - x^3$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of cubic with nature test.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any points of inflexion.

dif.r: Linear second derivative, check concavity change; routine two steps.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the curve, showing the stationary points, the point of inflexion and the $x$ and $y$ intercepts.

dif.r: Sketch cubic using found features plus factorised intercepts.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=6x^2-x^3

solutions.latex:
Differentiate, then stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 12x - 3x^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 12x - 3x^2 \\ &= 3x(4-x) \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 0$ or $x = 4$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{When } x=4,\ y &= 6\times 4^2 - 4^3 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts4660_1}

The slope is decreasing, flat, increasing, flat, decreasing, so there is a maximum turning point at $(4,32)$ and a minimum turning point at $(0,0)$.

Alternatively, use the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12 - 6x$$
At $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12>0$ (concave up), so a minimum.

At $x=4$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -12<0$ (concave down), so a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum at } (4,32),\ \text{minimum at } (0,0)$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or one with its nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct $x$-coordinates of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Original criteria rows: 1 correct x-coordinates; 1 y-coordinates; 1 nature (if only 1 stationary point correctly identified including nature: 2 marks). Sketch id on this part is not needed.

solutions.latex:
Points of inflexion occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12 - 6x$$
$$0 = 12 - 6x$$
So $x = 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{When } x=2,\ y &= 6\times 2^2 - 2^3 \\ &= 16 \end{aligned}$$
This is a possible point of inflexion at $(2,16)$. Test the concavity either side.

\extable{Ts4661_1}

The curve is concave up, then concave down, so the concavity changes.
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a point of inflexion at } (2,16)$$
criteria: Identifies the point $(2,16)$, or equivalent merit

The graphs of the functions $y = x^2 - 2x - 1$ and $y = 3 - x^2$ are shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1595_q2b_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the functions intersect when $x = 2$ and $x = -1$.

dif.r: Equate and factorise a quadratic; one routine step.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the exact area bounded by the two curves.

dif.r: Standard area between two parabolas with given bounds.

figures.cap: graphs of y=x^2-2x-1 and y=3-x^2

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 - 2x - 1 &= 3 - x^2 \\ 2x^2 - 2x - 4 &= 0 \\ 2(x^2 - x - 2) &= 0 \\ 2(x-2)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 2$ or $x = -1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the curves intersect when } x = 2 \text{ and } x = -1$$

meta.format_note: Source also accepts substitution of both values into both equations.

solutions.latex:
The area is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve between the intersections $x=-1$ and $x=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-1}^{2}\left(3 - x^2 - (x^2 - 2x - 1)\right)dx \\ &= \int_{-1}^{2}\left(4 + 2x - 2x^2\right)dx \\ &= \left[4x + x^2 - \dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2} \\ &= \left(4\times 2 + 2^2 - \dfrac{2\times 2^3}{3}\right) - \left(4\times(-1) + (-1)^2 - \dfrac{2\times(-1)^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{20}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right) \\ &= 9 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct set up of the integral, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote '20/3 + 7/3'; the second bracket evaluates to $-\dfrac{7}{3}$ so subtracting it gives the same total 9. Written that way here.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x+1}}\,dx$.

dif.r: Direct reverse chain rule on linear inside power.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite with a negative index, then integrate using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx = \dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x+1}}\,dx &= \int (3x+1)^{-\frac12}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{(3x+1)^{\frac12}}{3\times\frac12} + C \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3x+1}}{3} + C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with five function values to find, correct to 1 decimal place, the approximate value of $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \log_{10}(x+1)\,dx$.

dif.r: Direct trapezoidal rule substitution with four strips.

solutions.latex:
There are five function values, so four strips on $[0,4]$.
$$h = \dfrac{4-0}{4} = 1$$
\extable{Ts4667_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^4 \log_{10}(x+1)\,dx &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\Big(0 + \log_{10}5 + 2(\log_{10}2 + \log_{10}3 + \log_{10}4)\Big) \\ &= 1.729\ldots \\ &\approx 1.7 \text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote h = 1 - 0 = 1 (the spacing between x values); replaced with (4-0)/4 = 1, same value. Original second criterion: answer (no penalty for incorrect rounding).

parts.latex:
The graph of the function $y = f(x)$ is known to have a minimum turning point at the point $P(-4, -6)$.

Therefore, the graph of $y = 2 - f(2x)$ will have a maximum turning point at:

dif.r: Track a point through reflection, dilation and translation.

solutions.latex:
Work from $y=f(x)$ to $y=2-f(2x)$ one transformation at a time, tracking the point $(-4,-6)$.

Reflection in the $x$-axis (from $-f(x)$) gives $(-4, 6)$.

Horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac12$ (from $x\to 2x$) gives $(-2, 6)$.

Vertical translation up 2 gives $(-2, 8)$.

The minimum has become a maximum, as required.

Hence the correct option is A.

meta.format_note: Source said 'reflection about the y-axis' but the point change $(-4,-6)$ to $(-4,6)$ is a reflection in the x-axis; corrected the wording only, the mathematics is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$ and $V = \pi r^2 h$, show that $A = 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{40}{r}$.

dif.r: Substitute h from given volume formula; one step.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $r$ for which the surface area occurs minimum occurs and justify that it is a minimum value.

dif.r: Differentiate given area function, solve cubic, justify minimum.

figures.cap: cylinder with radius r and height h

solutions.latex:
Use $V=20$ in $V=\pi r^2 h$ to eliminate $h$.
$$h = \dfrac{20}{\pi r^2}$$
Substitute into $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\times\dfrac{20}{\pi r^2} \\ &= 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{40}{r} \end{aligned}$$

Write $A = 2\pi r^2 + 40r^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dr} &= 4\pi r - 40r^{-2} \\ &= 4\pi r - \dfrac{40}{r^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{40}{r^2} &= 4\pi r \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{10}{\pi} \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10}{\pi}} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} &= 4\pi + 80r^{-3} \\ &= 4\pi + \dfrac{80}{r^3} \end{aligned}$$
When $r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10}{\pi}}$, $r^3=\dfrac{10}{\pi}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} &= 4\pi + \dfrac{80\pi}{10} \\ &= 12\pi \\ &= 37.6\ldots > 0 \end{aligned}$$
So the surface area is a minimum.

Alternatively, test the slope either side.

\extable{Ts4670_1}

The slope is decreasing, flat, increasing, so there is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{10}{\pi}}$$
criteria: Correct value of $r$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Original third criterion: showing $r=\sqrt[3]{10/\pi}$ is a minimum value. Evaluation of second derivative expanded to $12\pi$ (equal to 37.6...).

parts.latex: Sketch the curve $y = -4 + 3\sin 2x$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.

dif.r: Sketch sine with amplitude, period and vertical shift over two periods.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=-4+3sin2x

solutions.latex:
For $y = -4 + 3\sin 2x$:

the amplitude is $3$,

the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$,

the graph is shifted down 4.

So the range is found in steps.
$$\begin{aligned} -1 &\le \sin 2x \le 1 \\ -3 &\le 3\sin 2x \le 3 &&(\text{multiply by } 3) \\ -7 &\le -4 + 3\sin 2x \le -1 &&(\text{subtract } 4) \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1595_q3c_s1}
criteria: Correct shape with correct amplitude and range, or equivalent merit
Correct shape and amplitude, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Original criteria: 1 shape and amplitude; 1 range; 1 period. Figure 1595_q3c_s1 retained; it should show two periods on $[0,2\pi]$, range $-7$ to $-1$, midline $y=-4$.

dif.r: Compare f, f', f'' from graph; tangent intercept reasoning.

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x), increasing and concave down through marked point at x=1

solutions.latex:
Read each quantity from the graph at $x=1$.

$f''(1) < 0$, as the curve is concave down.

$f'(1) > 0$, as the tangent has positive slope.

$f'(1) < f(1)$, as the tangent's $y$-intercept is positive.

Hence $f''(1) < 0 < f'(1) < f(1)$, so the correct option is D.

parts.latex: Given $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^3 = \dfrac{3\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^2}{2\sqrt{x}}$, find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^2}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$.

dif.r: Hence integral by adjusting constant of given derivative.

solutions.latex:
Divide the given derivative by $\dfrac32$ to match the integrand.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^2}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx &= \dfrac23\int \dfrac{3\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^2}{2\sqrt{x}}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac23\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^3 + C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Without using calculus, sketch the graph of $y = 3 + \dfrac{1}{x+2}$, showing the asymptotes and the $x$ and $y$ intercepts.

dif.r: Standard hyperbola sketch with asymptotes and intercepts.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=3+1/(x+2)

solutions.latex:
Write $y = 3 + \dfrac{1}{x+2}$.

The vertical asymptote is $x=-2$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y=3$.

For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 3 + \dfrac12 \\ &= \dfrac72 \end{aligned}$$
For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3 + \dfrac{1}{x+2} \\ -3 &= \dfrac{1}{x+2} \\ -3x - 6 &= 1 \\ x &= -\dfrac73 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1595_q4c_s1}
criteria: Correct asymptotes and intercepts, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Original criteria: 1 asymptotes; 1 intercepts; 1 shape. Figure 1595_q4c_s1 retained.

questions.stem:
Consider the graph of $y = f(x)$ with intercepts at $(-6,0)$, $(0,0)$ and $(4,0)$ and turning points at $(-4,5)$ and $(2,-2)$ as shown below.

\exfigure{1595_q4d_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: For what values of $k$ will $f(x) = k$ have 3 solutions?

dif.r: Interpret horizontal line intersections using turning point values.

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y = f\left(\dfrac{x}{2} - 1\right)$ showing the $x$-intercepts and the coordinates of the turning points.

dif.r: Combined horizontal dilation and translation; order of transformations matters.

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with intercepts -6, 0, 4 and turning points (-4,5), (2,-2)
solution sketch: sketch of y=f(x/2-1)

solutions.latex:
The line $y=k$ must cut the graph of $y=f(x)$ three times.

This happens between the minimum value $-2$ and the maximum value $5$, not including those values.
$$\therefore\ -2 < k < 5$$

Rewrite the function to read the transformations.
$$y = f\left(\dfrac{x}{2} - 1\right) = f\left(\dfrac12(x-2)\right)$$
This is a horizontal dilation by a factor of 2, then a horizontal translation right 2.

Each $x$-coordinate becomes $2x+2$.

$x$-intercepts: $-6\to -10$, $0\to 2$, $4\to 10$.

Turning points: $(-4,5)\to(-6,5)$ and $(2,-2)\to(6,-2)$.

\exfigure{1595_q4d_s1}
criteria: Correct intercepts at $-10, 2, 10$, or correct turning points at $(-6,5)$ and $(6,-2)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Original criteria: 1 intercepts at -10, 2, 10; 1 turning points (-6,5), (6,-2). Figure 1595_q4d_s1 retained.

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=4xe^{3x}$.

dif.r: Single product rule with exponential; MCQ recognition

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=4x & v&=e^{3x}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=3e^{3x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=4e^{3x}+4x\left(3e^{3x}\right)\\ &=4e^{3x}(3x+1)\end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: Given that $f'(x)=3-2e^{-x}$ and $f(0)=1$, find $f(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate exponential term, then find constant from initial condition

solutions.latex:
Integrate term by term.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int \left(3-2e^{-x}\right)dx\\ &=3x+2e^{-x}+c\end{aligned}$$
Use $f(0)=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=0+2+c\\ c&=-1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=3x+2e^{-x}-1$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to $y=e^{2x}+1$ at $x=1$.

dif.r: Chain rule gradient, perpendicular gradient, line equation with exact surds

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the gradient of the tangent.
$$y'=2e^{2x}$$
When $x=1$, $y=e^{2}+1$ and $m_T=2e^{2}$.

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_N=-\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}$$
Equation of the normal:
$$\begin{aligned} y-(e^{2}+1)&=-\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}(x-1)\\ y&=-\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}x+\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}+e^{2}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2e^{2}}x+\dfrac{1+2e^{4}+2e^{2}}{2e^{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x+2e^{2}y-\left(1+2e^{4}+2e^{2}\right)=0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\dfrac{-2x}{e^{x}}$.

dif.r: Routine quotient rule with simplification; MCQ

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=-2x & v&=e^{x}\\ u'&=-2 & v'&=e^{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{-2e^{x}+2xe^{x}}{e^{2x}}\\ &=\dfrac{2e^{x}(x-1)}{e^{2x}}\\ &=\dfrac{2(x-1)}{e^{x}}\end{aligned}$$
This matches option A.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Differentiate $y=e^{x^{2}}$.

dif.r: One-step chain rule on exponential

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find $\displaystyle\int xe^{x^{2}}\,dx$.

dif.r: Reverse previous derivative, adjust constant factor

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule:
$$y'=2xe^{x^{2}}$$

From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x^{2}}\right)=2xe^{x^{2}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int xe^{x^{2}}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2xe^{x^{2}}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{x^{2}}+c\end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Sketch the curve $y=e^{x}-1$.

dif.r: Vertical translation of familiar exponential graph

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the area between the $x$ axis and the curve $y=e^{x}-1$ between $x=-1$ and $1$.

dif.r: Area split at x-axis crossing; standard exponential integration

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=e^x-1 with asymptote y=-1

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1606_q2c_s1}

meta.marker_note: Full mark awarded for a correct sketch with the asymptote labelled.
meta.format_note: Sketch drawn (1606_q2c_s1); it was to show: $y=e^{x}-1$, increasing curve through the origin $(0,0)$, with horizontal asymptote $y=-1$ labelled (dashed line), curve approaching it as $x\to-\infty$. The figure id in the source is 1606_q2c_s1 while the sketch_id is 1606_q2(c)_s2.

solutions.latex:
The curve is below the $x$ axis for $-1\le x<0$ and above it for $0<x\le 1$, so the area is split at $x=0$.
$$A=\left|\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}(e^{x}-1)\,dx\right|+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}(e^{x}-1)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left|\left[e^{x}-x\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left[e^{x}-x\right]_{0}^{1}\\ &=\left|e^{0}-0-\left(e^{-1}+1\right)\right|+(e-1)-e^{0}\\ &=\left|1-\dfrac{1}{e}-1\right|+e-2\\ &=\dfrac{1}{e}+e-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=e+\dfrac{1}{e}-2 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Sets up the integrals with the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate: $y=\cos^{3}2x$

dif.r: Nested chain rule on power of trig with inner coefficient

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $y=(\cos 2x)^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=3(\cos 2x)^2\cdot(-2\sin 2x)\\ &=-6\sin 2x\cos^{2}2x\end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: The height of water in a tank is initially 50cm. The height is decreasing at a rate of $0.5t$ cm/min. Calculate the time for the tank to empty, to the nearest second.

dif.r: Integrate negative rate, use initial height, solve, convert units

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate, with $h=50$ when $t=0$.
$$\dfrac{dh}{dt}=-0.5t$$
$$\begin{aligned} h&=-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}+c\\ 50&=0+c\\ h&=50-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
The tank is empty when $h=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=50-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}\\ t^{2}&=200\\ t&=\sqrt{200}\end{aligned}$$
We take the positive root since $t>0$.
$$\therefore\ t\approx 14 \text{ min } 9 \text{ s}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line from the origin, and after $t$ seconds its velocity in m/s is given by $v=4-2t$ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find when the particle is stationary.

dif.r: Set velocity zero and solve linear equation

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled during the first 6 seconds.

dif.r: Integrate velocity; distance must account for direction change

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-2t&=0\\ t&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=2 \text{ seconds}$$

Integrate the velocity, with $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int(4-2t)\,dt\\ &=4t-t^{2}+c\end{aligned}$$
Since $c=0$, $x=t(4-t)$.

The particle turns at $t=2$ (from part (a)), so find the positions at $t=2$ and $t=6$.
$$\begin{aligned} t=2:&\ x=4 \text{ m}\\ t=6:&\ x=-12 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The particle moves from $0$ to $4$, then back from $4$ to $-12$.
$$\text{Distance}=4+4+12=20 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the displacement function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\ln\sqrt{4x+1}$.

dif.r: Log law simplification then chain rule

solutions.latex:
Use the log law $\ln a^{n}=n\ln a$ first.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=\ln(4x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(4x+1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{4}{4x+1}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{4x+1}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the log law, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{4x+6}{x^{2}+3x}\,dx$.

dif.r: Recognise f'/f with factor 2, evaluate and simplify logs

solutions.latex:
The numerator is twice the derivative of $x^{2}+3x$, so the integrand has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{4x+6}{x^{2}+3x}\,dx&=2\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{2x+3}{x^{2}+3x}\,dx\\ &=2\Big[\ln\left(x^{2}+3x\right)\Big]_{1}^{2}\\ &=2\left[\ln 10-\ln 4\right]\\ &=2\ln\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the stationary point on the curve $y=e^{x^{2}+4x}$ and determine its nature.

dif.r: Chain rule stationary point, second derivative test via product rule

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$y'=(2x+4)e^{x^{2}+4x}$$
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$. Since $e^{x^{2}+4x}>0$, we need $2x+4=0$, so $x=-2$.

Test the nature using the second derivative, using the product rule.
$$y''=2e^{x^{2}+4x}+(2x+4)^{2}e^{x^{2}+4x}$$
At $x=-2$:
$$y''=2e^{-4}>0$$
So the stationary point is a minimum. When $x=-2$, $y=e^{-4}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum stationary point at } \left(-2,\,e^{-4}\right)$$
criteria: Finds the $x$-value and tests the nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: A table of values of $y'$ at $x=-3,-2,-1$ (negative, zero, positive) is also accepted as the nature test.

questions.stem:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $a=\sin 2t$.

At time $t=0$, $v=0$ m/s and $x=1$ m.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the velocity when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ seconds.

dif.r: Integrate trig acceleration with initial condition, exact evaluation

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find displacement when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ seconds.

dif.r: Second integration with constant, exact trig evaluation

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration, with $v=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\int\sin 2t\,dt\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+c\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-\dfrac{1}{2}+c\\ c&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
So $v=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}$.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$:
$$\begin{aligned} v&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{2-\sqrt{2}}{4} \text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $v$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity from part (a), with $x=1$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}t+c\end{aligned}$$
Since $x=1$ when $t=0$, $c=1$.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{\pi}{16}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{8}+\dfrac{\pi}{16}+1\\ &=\dfrac{\pi-2\sqrt{2}+16}{16} \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The rate of change of $Q$ with respect to time is given by $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$.

If $Q=2$ when $t=1$ and $Q=5$ when $t=2$, find $Q$ when $t=3$.

dif.r: Two unknowns in exponential model solved simultaneously by division

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$, exponential growth gives $Q=Q_0e^{kt}$.

Substitute the two given conditions.
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=Q_0e^{k} &&(1)\\ 5&=Q_0e^{2k} &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Dividing (2) by (1):
$$\begin{aligned} e^{k}&=\dfrac{5}{2}\\ k&=\ln\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=Q_0\cdot\dfrac{5}{2}\\ Q_0&=\dfrac{4}{5}\end{aligned}$$
So $Q=\dfrac{4}{5}e^{\left(\ln\frac{5}{2}\right)t}$.

When $t=3$:
$$Q=\dfrac{4}{5}e^{3\ln\frac{5}{2}}$$
$$\therefore\ Q=\dfrac{4}{5}\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^{3}=\dfrac{25}{2}$$

meta.format_note: Source stopped at $Q=\dfrac45e^{3\ln\frac52}$; simplified to $\dfrac{25}{2}$ (equal value) and checked: $\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac{125}{8}=\dfrac{25}{2}$.

dif.r: Direct recall: classify a graph as many-to-one

figures.cap: arc above the x-axis, endpoints on the axis

solutions.latex:
The curve is a relationship in which many $x$-values map to one $y$-value, so it is many-to-one.

Hence option C is correct.

dif.r: Empirical rule gives the mean and sigma, then square for variance

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

figures.cap: normal curve shaded between 25 and 145

solutions.latex:
The mean is the midpoint of the bounds.

$$\mu = \dfrac{145 + 25}{2} = 85$$

Since the bounded region contains $99.7\%$ of the area, the empirical rule says the bounds are three standard deviations from the mean.

$$\sigma = \dfrac{85 - 25}{3} = 20$$

$$\text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 = 20^2 = 400$$

So $\mu = 85$ and $\text{Var}(X) = 400$, which is option D.

parts.latex:
A circle has the equation $(x + 2)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = d$.

What is the value of $d$ such that the $x$-axis is a tangent to the circle?

dif.r: Read centre and radius; tangency means radius equals distance to axis

figures.cap: solution sketch: circle with centre (-2,-3) tangent to x-axis

solutions.latex:
The equation $(x+2)^2 + (y+3)^2 = d$ is a circle with centre $(-2, -3)$ and radius $\sqrt{d}$.

parts.latex:
Consider the two sets $A = \{5, 7, 9\}$ and $B = \{10, 11, 12\}$. A number is randomly chosen from each set.

What is the probability of selecting a number from each set that have a sum that is equal to or greater than 20?

dif.r: Count favourable pairs from nine equally likely outcomes

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
There are $3 \times 3 = 9$ equally likely pairs.

A sum of at least $20$ occurs only for $9$ and $11$, or $9$ and $12$.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{sum} \ge 20) &= P(9 \text{ and } 11) + P(9 \text{ and } 12) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$$

So option C is correct.

parts.latex: Given that $f(x) = \displaystyle\int_2^x \dfrac{1}{1+t^3}\,dt$, what is the value of $f'(2)$?

dif.r: Direct fundamental theorem of calculus, then substitute

skills: Integral as a function of its upper limit

solutions.latex:
By the fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$f'(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\int_2^x \dfrac{1}{1+t^3}\,dt\right] = \dfrac{1}{1+x^3}$$

Hence:

$$f'(2) = \dfrac{1}{1+2^3} = \dfrac{1}{9}$$

So option C is correct.

parts.latex:
Consider the graphs of $y = px^2$ and $y = qx^2 + r$.

The graphs will have no points of intersection for the real constants $p$, $q$ and $r$ provided that

dif.r: General parameter condition via discriminant, testing options abstractly

can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

options.label: C
options.latex: $p < 0$ and $q > 0$ for all real values of $r$.

options.label: D
options.latex: $p > 0$ and $q < 0$ for all real values of $r$.

solutions.latex:
The curves intersect where they are equal.

$$\begin{aligned} px^2 &= qx^2 + r \\ (p - q)x^2 - r &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

There is no intersection when the discriminant is negative.

$$\Delta = 0^2 - 4(p - q)(-r) = 4r(p - q)$$

So $4r(p - q) < 0$. If $r > 0$, then $p - q < 0$, so $p < q$. This is option A.

Check of the others with values:

B: $p = 3$, $q = 2$, $r = 1$ gives intersections.

C: $p = -1$, $q = 1$, $r = 0$ gives intersections.

D: $p = 1$, $q = -1$, $r = 0$ gives intersections.

So option A is correct.

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\sin A}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} = 2\,\text{cosec}\,A$.

dif.r: Standard identity proof: common denominator, Pythagorean identity, cancel

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sin A}{1 + \cos A} + \dfrac{1 + \cos A}{\sin A} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} + \dfrac{(1 + \cos A)^2}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A + (1 + \cos A)^2}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2 A + 1 + 2\cos A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{2 + 2\cos A}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} &&(\text{since } \sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1) \\ &= \dfrac{2(1 + \cos A)}{\sin A(1 + \cos A)} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sin A} \\ &= 2\operatorname{cosec} A \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines the fractions and applies trigonometric identities to assist with the proof, or equivalent merit
