parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $2x\log_5 x$ is $2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln5}$

dif.r: Product rule with derivative of base-5 logarithm.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln5}\right)dx$.

dif.r: Must use hence result and recognise integral undefined at x=0.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=\log_5 x\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2x\log_5 x\right)&=2\log_5 x+2x\left(\dfrac{1}{x\ln 5}\right)\\ &=2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln 5} \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Need to show the line of substitution, otherwise it is copying from the answer.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), simplify the derivative:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2x}{x\ln 5}&=2\log_5 x+\dfrac{2}{\ln 5}\\ &=2\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right) \end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right)dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}2\left(\log_5 x+\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[2x\log_5 x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=\Big[x\log_5 x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
This is undefined, as $\log_5 0$ is undefined.

why: Checker got a different answer — (b) Stored answer is 'undefined, as log_5 0 is undefined'. This is wrong: x·log_5 x → 0 as x→0⁺, so the improper integral converges to (π/2)log_5(π/2) ≈ 0.441. The question itself is probably flawed (the lower limit is 0), so the owner should review it.

parts.latex:
Ms Alrubai and Mrs Norman are employed as doctors. They both start on the same annual salary. However, Ms Alrubai negotiated an annual salary increase of $\$5\,000$, while Mrs Norman negotiated an annual salary increase of $7\%$.

Find their starting annual salary given that after $16$ years they have both made the same amount of money in total.

dif.r: Model arithmetic and geometric sums, equate, solve for first term.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Alrubai's salaries form an arithmetic series with $d=5000$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{16}&=\dfrac{16}{2}\left[2a+(16-1)5000\right]\\ &=8\left[2a+75\,000\right]\\ &=16a+600\,000 \end{aligned}$$
Norman's salaries form a geometric series with $r=1.07$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{16}&=\dfrac{a\left(1.07^{16}-1\right)}{1.07-1}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a \end{aligned}$$
Equate the totals and solve for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} 16a+600\,000&=\left(\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a\\ \left(16-\dfrac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}\right)a&=-600\,000\\ a&=\dfrac{-600\,000}{16-\frac{1.07^{16}-1}{0.07}}\\ &\approx \$50\,470.84 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the starting salary is } \$50\,470.84$$
criteria: Equates the two sums, or equivalent merit
Finds both sums, or equivalent merit
Finds the AP sum $16a+600\,000$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the probability that Mr Ferrarin exercises on any given Monday.

dif.r: Total probability over two branches.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the probability that Mr Ferrarin woke up on time on a Monday, given that he exercised that day.

dif.r: Reverse conditional probability using previous total probability.

solutions.latex:
The probability of exercising on at least one day is the complement of exercising on neither day. On time: not exercising is $\dfrac{1}{5}$; late: not exercising is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{13}{15} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the complementary probability, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Add the probabilities of exercising after waking on time and after waking late.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exercise})&=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{4}{5}+\dfrac{3}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{3}\\ &=0.45 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct sum of products, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula, with $A$ = wakes on time and $B$ = exercises:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A|B)&=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{4}\times\frac{4}{5}}{0.45}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the conditional probability formula with correct numerator and denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The graphs of $f(x)=-x^2+2$ and $g(x)=x^3-x^2-kx+2$, where $k$ is a constant, are shown below.

The graphs intersect and create two closed regions, A and B.

\exfigure{1338_q33_1}

Show that these two regions have the same area.

dif.r: Parametric intersections, identify upper curve, integrate both regions in terms of k.

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: graphs of f and g enclosing regions A and B

solutions.latex:
The graphs meet where they are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3-x^2-kx+2&=-x^2+2\\ x^3-kx&=0\\ x\left(x^2-k\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt{k}$.

For region A, $g(x)$ is above $f(x)$, and $g(x)-f(x)=x^3-kx$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{k}}^{0}\left(x^3-kx\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{kx^2}{2}\right]_{-\sqrt{k}}^{0}\\ &=0-\left(\dfrac{k^2}{4}-\dfrac{k^2}{2}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
For region B, $f(x)$ is above $g(x)$, and $f(x)-g(x)=-x^3+kx$.
$$\begin{aligned} B&=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\sqrt{k}}\left(-x^3+kx\right)dx\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{x^4}{4}+\dfrac{kx^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{\sqrt{k}}\\ &=-\dfrac{k^2}{4}+\dfrac{k^2}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=B$$
criteria: Finds both areas, or equivalent merit
Finds one area correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds the intersections $x=0,\pm\sqrt{k}$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: If an indefinite integral is used, $-1$ (the constant $C$ needs to cancel). If an incorrect intersection is found, carry the error forward.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the minimum distance, to the nearest kilometre, between the police and Ned Kelly.

dif.r: Minimise D via D squared, justify minimum, evaluate distance.

figures.cap: triangle N H P with 120 degree angle at H

solutions.latex:
After $t$ hours, $HP=20-5t$ and $HN=7t$, with $\angle PHN=120^\circ$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $PHN$, $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$:
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=(20-5t)^2+(7t)^2-2(20-5t)(7t)\cos 120^\circ\\ &=400-200t+25t^2+49t^2-2(20-5t)(7t)\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=400-200t+74t^2+140t-35t^2\\ &=39t^2-60t+400 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$D$ is a minimum when $D^2$ is, so find the minimum stationary point of $D^2$.
$$\dfrac{d\left(D^2\right)}{dt}=78t-60$$
Stationary point when $78t-60=0$:
$$t=\dfrac{60}{78}=\dfrac{10}{13}$$
Test the sign of the derivative:
$$t=0.7,\ \dfrac{10}{13},\ 0.8:\ \dfrac{d\left(D^2\right)}{dt}=-5.4,\ 0,\ 2.4$$
The gradient changes from negative to positive, so this is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=39\left(\dfrac{10}{13}\right)^2-60\left(\dfrac{10}{13}\right)+400\\ &\approx 376.923 \end{aligned}$$
$$D\approx 19.41\text{ km (2 d.p.)}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum distance is about } 19\text{ km}$$
criteria: Finds $t=\dfrac{10}{13}$ and tests for a minimum, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Most students forgot to test to show a minimum, or to use the property of the original function (concave up parabola).
meta.format_note: Question asks for the nearest km; the source gives $D=19.28$ km (2 d.p.), so a final line of 19 km was added from that value.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the working gave $D^2\approx371.60$ and $D\approx19.28$; at $t=\dfrac{10}{13}$, $D^2=400-\dfrac{3600}{156}\approx376.92$ and $D\approx19.41$ (the answer, about $19$ km, is unchanged).

A computer technician notes that 40\% of computers fail because of their hard drive, 25\% because of the monitor, 20\% because of a disk drive, and 15\% because of the microprocessor.

If the problem is not in the monitor, what is the probability that it is in the hard drive?

dif.r: Interpret f' graph for concavity; horizontal-inflection trap

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: graph of y=f'(x)

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection of $y=f(x)$ occur where $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes.

Since $f''$ is the gradient of $f'$, this is where the graph of $y=f'(x)$ has a turning point (its gradient changes sign).

The given graph has two such turning points.

At the horizontal tangent point on the right, the gradient does not change sign, so there is no change in concavity.

Hence there are 2 points of inflection, which is option C.

parts.latex: A series is given as $1-3k+9k^2+\dots$. What is the value of $k$ if the sum to infinity is $\dfrac{3}{4}$?

dif.r: Limiting sum formula used in reverse with ratio -3k

$$r=\dfrac{-3k}{1}=-3k$$

Using $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{3}{4}&=\dfrac{1}{1+3k}\\3(1+3k)&=4\\9k&=1\\k&=\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex:
It is known that $f(x)$ is an odd function and $g(x)$ is an even function.

Given that $f(2)=2$ and $g(2)=-2$, what is the value of $f\big(g(-2)\big)+g\big(f(-2)\big)$?

dif.r: Apply odd/even definitions inside composite evaluation

solutions.latex:
Since $g$ is even, $g(-2)=g(2)=-2$.

Since $f$ is odd, $f(-2)=-f(2)=-2$.
$$\begin{aligned}f\big(g(-2)\big)+g\big(f(-2)\big)&=f(-2)+g(-2)\\&=-2+(-2)\\&=-4\end{aligned}$$
This matches option A.

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\sqrt{x}\right)$.

dif.r: Index form then power rule, one step

solutions.latex:
Write $x\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{3}{2}}$ and use the power rule.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\sqrt{x}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}x^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{x}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, by the product rule, the derivative is $\sqrt{x}+\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{x}}$.

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}\right)\right)$.

dif.r: Log laws then differentiate and simplify fractions

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws, split the logarithm of a quotient into a difference.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln(1-3x)-\ln(1+2x)\Big]\\&=\dfrac{-3}{1-3x}-\dfrac{2}{1+2x}\\&=\dfrac{-3(1+2x)-2(1-3x)}{(1-3x)(1+2x)}\\&=\dfrac{-5}{(1-3x)(1+2x)}\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, by the quotient rule:
$$\dfrac{-5}{(1+2x)^2}\div\dfrac{1-3x}{1+2x}=\dfrac{-5}{(1+2x)(1-3x)}$$
criteria: Splits into a difference of logarithms (or correctly uses the quotient rule), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1340_q13_s1}

Distance sailed by the yacht: $15\times3=45$ km.

The angle at $A$ between $AB$ (due south) and $AY$ (bearing $120^\circ$) is $180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $ABY$:
$$\begin{aligned}YB^2&=30^2+45^2-2(30)(45)\cos60^\circ\\&=1575\\YB&=\sqrt{1575}\\&=39.686\ldots\\&\approx40\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Sketch drawn (1340_q13_s1); it was to show: solution diagram for Q13 (key 1340_q13_s1). Triangle ABY: A at top, B due south of A with AB = 30 km, Y on bearing 120 degrees from A with AY = 45 km; north line at A; angle BAY = 60 degrees marked; YB = 40 km (39.7) marked.

solutions.latex:
Applying the sine rule in triangle $ABY$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle YBA}{45}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{YB}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\angle YBA&=\dfrac{45\sin60^\circ}{YB}\\&=0.98198\ldots\\\angle YBA&=79.1066\ldots^\circ\\&\approx79^\circ\end{aligned}$$
Bearing of $B$ from $Y$:
$$180^\circ+79^\circ=259^\circ\text{T}$$
Using the rounded value $YB=40$ gives $\angle YBA\approx77^\circ$ and bearing $257^\circ\text{T}$. Other methods, such as the cosine rule for the angle at $Y$, also give $259^\circ\text{T}$.
criteria: Correct equation (sine or cosine rule), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=x\tan x$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

dif.r: Product rule then exact trig values; mirrors anchor

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=x & v&=\tan x\\u'&=1 & v'&=\sec^2x\end{aligned}$$
So
$$y'=\tan x+x\sec^2x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $\sec\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\right)^2\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\times\dfrac{4}{3}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\dfrac{2\pi}{9}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}+\dfrac{2\pi}{9}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

Chris and Ann are participating in a charity bicycle ride between Canberra and Liverpool.

Chris leaves Canberra and rides to Liverpool, a distance of 250 km, at an average speed of 20km/h. His distance from Liverpool is modelled by the equation $C=250-20t$, where $C$ is his distance from Liverpool and $t$ is the time in hours he has been riding.

The line has $y$-intercept $250$ and gradient $-20$. It meets the $t$-axis when $250-20t=0$, that is at $t=12.5$.

Ann starts 90 km from Liverpool and rides away from it at 12 km/h, so her distance from Liverpool is
$$A=90+12t$$
Chris: $C=250-20t$. They pass each other when $A=C$:

Graphically, Ann's line from $(0,90)$ with gradient 12 crosses Chris's line at $t=5$.
$$\therefore\ t=5\text{ hours}$$

The distance between them is $A-C$, so set
$$\begin{aligned}90+12t-(250-20t)&=160\\32t-160&=160\\32t&=320\\t&=10\end{aligned}$$
Graphically, at $t=10$ Chris is 50 km and Ann 210 km from Liverpool.
$$\therefore\ t=10\text{ hours}$$

Distance ridden by Chris: $20t$. Distance ridden by Ann: $12t$.
$$\begin{aligned}20t+12t&=264\\32t&=264\\t&=8.25\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=8.25\text{ hours}$$

questions.stem:
A runner is training for a long-distance event.

The first week she runs 1.2 km.

The second week she runs 1.8 km.

The third week she runs 2.7 km, and so on, adding on half of the previous week.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How far does she run in the fourth week?

dif.r: Identify ratio, next term of geometric sequence

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How far does she run in \textbf{total} after the first 6 weeks?

dif.r: Direct substitution into geometric sum formula

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
The event she is training for is 45 km.

In which week will she first exceed this distance?

dif.r: Solve exponential with logarithms, interpret non-integer n

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The common ratio is
$$r=\dfrac{1.8}{1.2}=\dfrac{2.7}{1.8}=1.5$$
Fourth week:
$$T_4=2.7\times1.5=4.05\text{ km}$$
Check: $T_4=1.2\times1.5^3=4.05$ km.

The distances form a geometric series with $a=1.2$, $r=1.5$, $n=6$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_6&=\dfrac{1.2(1.5^6-1)}{1.5-1}\\&=24.9375\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
Check by adding the terms: $1.2+1.8+2.7+4.05+6.075+9.1125=24.9375$.
criteria: Correct substitution into the sum formula (or correct terms), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The $n$th term is $T_n=1.2\times1.5^{n-1}$. Set $T_n=45$:
$$\begin{aligned}45&=1.2\times1.5^{n-1}\\37.5&=1.5^{n-1}\\\ln37.5&=(n-1)\ln1.5\\n&=\dfrac{\ln37.5}{\ln1.5}+1\\&=9.93872\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The terms increase, so the first whole week with $n>9.94$ is week 10.
$$\therefore\ \text{She first exceeds 45 km in the 10th week.}$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric (1 correct equation; 1 for 37.5 = 1.5^(n-1), 1/2 n, 1/2 week) was unclear; rewritten top-down by us.

Ash and Naomi complete a series of games. The series finishes when one player has won two games.

In any game, the probability that Ash wins is $\dfrac{3}{5}$ and the probability that Naomi wins is $\dfrac{2}{5}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Draw a probability tree showing the possible outcomes, in a series of three games.

dif.r: Standard tree, but branches must stop once a player wins two

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability that Naomi wins the series?

dif.r: Find three winning paths in the tree and add their products

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the probability that Naomi wins at least one game?

dif.r: Complement of Ash winning the first two games

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=2-1/(x+4)

solutions.latex:
Let $A$ be "Ash wins" and $N$ be "Naomi wins". Each branch has probability $\dfrac{3}{5}$ for $A$ and $\dfrac{2}{5}$ for $N$. After $AA$ or $NN$ the series stops.

\exfigure{1340_q19_s1}
criteria: Correct first two games, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Figure 1340_q19_s1 already referenced; kept. Rubric rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
Naomi wins the series by $ANN$, $NAN$ or $NN$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Naomi wins}) &= P(ANN)+P(NAN)+P(NN) \\ &= 2\times\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5}\right)+\dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{2}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{44}{125} \end{aligned}$$

Naomi wins at least one game unless Ash wins the first two games.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one}) &= 1-P(AA) \\ &= 1-\dfrac{3}{5}\times\dfrac{3}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{16}{25} \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: b

parts.label: e

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2-x & v&=(x+2)^3\\ u'&=-1 & v'&=3(x+2)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -(x+2)^3+(2-x)\times3(x+2)^2 \\ &= (x+2)^2\left[3(2-x)-(x+2)\right] \\ &= (x+2)^2(6-3x-x-2) \\ &= (x+2)^2(4-4x) \\ &= 4(x+2)^2(1-x) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$, so $x=-2$ or $x=1$.
$$f(-2)=0,\quad f(1)=(2-1)(1+2)^3=27$$
The points are $(-2,0)$ and $(1,27)$.

Nature of $(1,27)$, using $f''(x)=-12x(x+2)$:
$$f''(1)=-12(1)(3)=-36<0$$
so $(1,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

Nature of $(-2,0)$: here $f''(-2)=0$, so test the concavity either side.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-3)&=-36 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(-1)&=12 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(-2,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.
criteria: Finds both stationary points and the nature of one, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

$$-12x(x+2)=0$$

questions.stem:
A particle starts to move from the origin along the $x$-axis.

Its velocity, measured in metres, at some time $t$ seconds, is given by $v=4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}$ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Explain why the particle is never at rest.

dif.r: Solve v=0 and reject the negative time

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the acceleration of the particle at $t=3$ seconds.

dif.r: Chain rule derivative of velocity, then substitute

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the exact distance travelled by the particle between $t=0$ and $t=5$ seconds.

dif.r: Integrate velocity with a log term; no direction change

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the particle’s limiting velocity.

dif.r: Simple limit as t tends to infinity

solutions.latex:
If the particle is at rest, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1} &= 0 \\ 4(3t+1) &= 2 \\ 12t &= -2 \\ t &= -\dfrac16 \end{aligned}$$
But $t\ge0$, so the particle is never at rest.

Write $v=4-2(3t+1)^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} a=\dfrac{dv}{dt} &= -2\times(-1)(3t+1)^{-2}\times3 \\ &= \dfrac{6}{(3t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$a=\dfrac{6}{(3\times3+1)^2}=\dfrac{6}{100}=0.06\ \text{m/s}^2$$
criteria: Correct expression for $a$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By part (a) the particle is never at rest and $v>0$, so it never changes direction. The distance equals the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{distance} &= \int_0^5\left(4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}\right)dt \\ &= \Big[4t-\dfrac23\ln|3t+1|\Big]_0^5 \\ &= 20-\dfrac23\ln16 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, $x=4t-\dfrac23\ln|3t+1|+C$, and $x=0$ when $t=0$ gives $C=0$. At $t=5$, $x=20-\dfrac23\ln16$.

$$\therefore\ \text{distance}=\left(20-\dfrac23\ln16\right)\text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct integral set up, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{2}{3t+1}\to0$, so $v\to4$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the limiting velocity is } 4 \text{ m/s}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln(\sec x+\tan x)\right)=\sec x$.

dif.r: Chain rule, derivative of sec, factorise to cancel

parts.label: b

dif.r: Set equal, rearrange to cos squared, choose first-quadrant solution

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, find the exact area of the shaded region $R$.

dif.r: Area between curves using the earlier derivative for sec integral

figures.cap: graphs of y=cos x and y=(1/2)sec x with region R shaded

solutions.latex:
Apply the chain rule to the logarithm, with $\sec x=(\cos x)^{-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\sec x+\tan x) &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\times\dfrac{d}{dx}\left((\cos x)^{-1}+\tan x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}+\sec^2x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\left(\tan x\sec x+\sec^2x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\sec x(\tan x+\sec x)}{\sec x+\tan x} \\ &= \sec x \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct derivative of $\sec x+\tan x$ used in the chain rule, or equivalent merit
Applies the chain rule to the logarithm, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $\cos x=\dfrac12\sec x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos x &= \dfrac{1}{\cos x} \\ 2\cos^2x &= 1 \\ \cos^2x &= \dfrac12 \\ \cos x &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \end{aligned}$$
The solution in the first quadrant is $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

meta.format_note: Source also listed other solutions $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, etc. and 'or by substitution'; dropped as not needed.

solutions.latex:
The region lies between $y=\cos x$ (above) and $y=\dfrac12\sec x$ from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Part (a) gives $\displaystyle\int\sec x\,dx=\ln(\sec x+\tan x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\cos x-\dfrac12\sec x\right)dx \\ &= \Big[\sin x-\dfrac12\ln(\sec x+\tan x)\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac12\ln\left(\sqrt2+1\right)\right)-\left(0-\dfrac12\ln1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac12\ln\left(\sqrt2+1\right)\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Point $A(2e,1)$ lies on the function $h(x)$. The tangent to $h(x)$ at $A$ has equation $y=\dfrac{x}{2e}$.

Point $B$ is the image of the point $A$ on the function $g(x)=3h(2x+4)$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $B$ has coordinates $(e-2,3)$.

dif.r: Map a point under a combined dilation and translation

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the equation of the tangent to $g(x)$ at point $B$, in general form.

dif.r: Chain rule on abstract h using the given tangent gradient

solutions.latex:
Write $g(x)=3h\left(2(x+2)\right)$. A point $(x,y)$ on $h$ maps to $\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-2,\,3y\right)$ on $g$.
$$B=\left(\dfrac{2e}{2}-2,\,3\times1\right)=(e-2,\,3)$$

Differentiate $g(x)=3h(2x+4)$ using the chain rule.
$$g'(x)=3h'(2x+4)\times2=6h'(2x+4)$$
At $B$, $x=e-2$, so $2x+4=2e$.
$$g'(e-2)=6h'(2e)$$
But $h'(2e)$ is the gradient of the tangent at $A$, which is $\dfrac{1}{2e}$.
$$g'(e-2)=6\times\dfrac{1}{2e}=\dfrac{3}{e}$$
The tangent at $B$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-3 &= \dfrac{3}{e}\left(x-(e-2)\right) \\ ey-3e &= 3x-3e+6 \\ 3x-ey+6 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Gradient at $B$ equals $\dfrac{3}{e}$, or equivalent merit
Some correct progress towards the gradient of the tangent to $g(x)$, or equivalent merit

\exfigure{1340_q29_1}

The diagram above shows a part of the circle $x^2+y^2=25$. The point $P(x,y)$ is on the circle, and point $O$ is the origin. Point $M$ has coordinates $(2,0)$, point $N$ has coordinates $(0,4)$, and $\angle MOP$ is measured in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the area, $A$, of the quadrilateral $OMPN$ is given by

$$A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$$

dif.r: Split into triangles; sine area rule with complementary angle

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $\tan\theta$ which gives the maximum area $A$.

dif.r: Differentiate trig expression, solve for tan, test nature

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence find, in surd form, the coordinates of point $P$ when $A$ is maximum.

dif.r: Link tan to y/x with circle equation for surd coordinates

figures.cap: quarter circle radius 5 with points M(2,0), N(0,4), P(x,y), angle theta; not to scale

solutions.latex:
Triangle $OPM$ has $OP=5$ (radius), $OM=2$ and included angle $\theta$.
$$A_{\triangle OPM}=\dfrac12\times5\times2\times\sin\theta=5\sin\theta$$
Triangle $ONP$ has $ON=4$, $OP=5$ and included angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta$.
$$A_{\triangle ONP}=\dfrac12\times4\times5\times\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=10\cos\theta$$
Therefore
$$A=A_{\triangle OPM}+A_{\triangle ONP}=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$$
as required.
criteria: Area of one triangle, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $A=5\sin\theta+10\cos\theta$.
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=5\cos\theta-10\sin\theta$$
For a stationary point $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10\sin\theta &= 5\cos\theta \\ \tan\theta &= \dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right)\approx0.463$ radians.

Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}=-5\sin\theta-10\cos\theta\approx-11.18<0$$
so this is a maximum turning point.

$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum area occurs when } \tan\theta=\dfrac12$$
criteria: Solves $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$ to get $\tan\theta=\dfrac12$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac12$, we have $y=\dfrac{x}{2}$. Also $P$ lies on $x^2+y^2=25$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+\dfrac{x^2}{4} &= 25 \\ 5x^2 &= 100 \\ x^2 &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
P is in the first quadrant, so $x=2\sqrt5$ and $y=\sqrt5$.

Alternatively, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}$, so $y=5\sin\theta=\sqrt5$ and $x=5\cos\theta=2\sqrt5$.

$$\therefore\ P=\left(2\sqrt5,\ \sqrt5\right)$$
criteria: Some correct progress, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The time taken for an orchard to be harvested varies inversely to the number of people picking fruit.

If the orchard can be harvested by 35 people in 6 days, how many people would be needed to harvest the orchard in 5 days?

dif.r: Direct inverse variation: constant product, one division.

solutions.latex:
For inverse variation, time $\times$ number of people is constant.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{time}\times\text{people} &= 35\times 6 \\ &= 210 \end{aligned}$$
For 5 days:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{people} &= \dfrac{210}{5} \\ &= 42 \end{aligned}$$
So 42 people are needed, which is option A.

parts.latex:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards from ground level and lands 8 seconds later in the same place.

Its motion is described by the equation $x = 3t(8-t)$, with displacement $x$ metres and time $t$ seconds. The displacement-time graph is sketched below.

\exfigure{1341_q2_1}

What is the distance travelled by the ball in the first six seconds of motion?

dif.r: Distance not displacement; must account for turning point at t=4.

figures.cap: displacement-time graph of x = 3t(8-t) with points (2,36), (4,48), (6,36)

solutions.latex:
The ball reaches its maximum at $t=4$, where $x = 3(4)(4) = 48$.

At $t=6$, $x = 3(6)(2) = 36$.

It rises 48 m, then falls $48-36 = 12$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 48 + (48-36) \\ &= 60 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

meta.source_flag: Source working read 'Distance = 48 + (48 - 12)', which would give 84; the correct value of x at t=6 is 36, so I used 48 - 36 = 12 and the result 60 is unchanged.

parts.latex: Which of the following is a primitive of $xe^{x^2}$ ?

dif.r: Standard reverse chain rule primitive of x e^{x^2}.

solutions.latex:
Using the substitution $u = x^2$, so $du = 2x\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int xe^{x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x\,e^{x^2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}e^{x^2} + C \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex: If $f(x) = 2 + 5\cos\left(3x + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, what is the range of $f$ ?

dif.r: Range of shifted, scaled cosine read directly from amplitude and centre.

solutions.latex:
Since $-1\le\cos\left(3x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\le 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} -5 &\le 5\cos\left(3x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \le 5 &&(\text{multiply by } 5)\\ -3 &\le 2+5\cos\left(3x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \le 7 &&(\text{add } 2)\end{aligned}$$
So the range is $-3\le y\le 7$, which is option B.

parts.latex:
The figure shows three towns $X$, $Y$ and $Z$.

There are three roads out of town $X$ and two roads out of town $Y$.

\exfigure{1341_q5_1}

Mr Kent and Mr Wayne leave town $X$ and town $Y$ respectively at the same time.

If they select their ways randomly, what is the probability that they will meet on their way?

dif.r: Interpret road diagram, then multiply two independent probabilities.

can_use: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

figures.cap: roads joining towns X, Y and Z

solutions.latex:
Mr Kent can choose a road that leads to Mr Wayne in 2 of his 3 roads, so the probability is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Mr Wayne must then choose the same road, 1 of his 2 roads, so the probability is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{meet}) &= \dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex:
A certain function $f(x)$ has the following properties: $f(0) = -1$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = -3$.

Which of the following is possible for all values of $x$?

dif.r: Infer signs of f' and f'' from value and asymptotic behaviour.

solutions.latex:
The function starts at $f(0)=-1$ and tends to $-3$, so it must decrease: $f'(x)<0$.

It approaches a horizontal asymptote, so the decrease slows down, meaning the curve is concave up: $f''(x)>0$.

So $f''(x)>0$ and $f'(x)<0$, which is option D.

parts.latex:

parts.latex: Which of the following is $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x}{2x-1}\,dx$ ?

dif.r: Must rewrite improper fraction before integrating to logarithm.

solutions.latex:
Write the numerator in terms of the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned}\int \dfrac{2x}{2x-1}\,dx &= \int \dfrac{(2x-1)+1}{2x-1}\,dx\\ &= \int \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2x-1}\right)dx\\ &= \int \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{2x-1}\right)dx\\ &= x + \dfrac{1}{2}\ln|2x-1| + C\end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: By considering symmetry, which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} x^3 \sin x\,dx$ ?

dif.r: Recognise even integrand and split non-symmetric interval appropriately.

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The function $x^3\sin x$ is even, since $(-x)^3\sin(-x)=x^3\sin x$.

Split the interval at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} = \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} + \int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}}$$
By even symmetry, $\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x^3\sin x\,dx = 2\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x^3\sin x\,dx$.

So the integral equals $2\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x^3\sin x\,dx + \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}} x^3\sin x\,dx$, which is option C.

parts.latex: Calculate the sum of the arithmetic series $32 + 36 + 40 + \dots + 144$.

solutions.latex:
The series is arithmetic with first term $a=32$, common difference $d=4$ and last term $T_n=144$.

Find the number of terms using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} 144 &= 32 + (n-1)\cdot 4 \\ 4n &= 116 \\ n &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
Use $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned}S_{29} &= \dfrac{29}{2}\left[2(32) + 28\times 4\right]\\ &= 14.5\times 176\\ &= 2552\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Differentiate the following functions with respect to $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $x\tan 2x$

dif.r: Product rule with chain rule on tan 2x.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\dfrac{\ln x}{x^2}$

dif.r: Quotient or product rule with log; simplify result.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\tan 2x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2\sec^2 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y' &= 1\cdot\tan 2x + x\cdot 2\sec^2 2x\\ &= \tan 2x + 2x\sec^2 2x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write the function as a product, $\ln x\cdot x^{-2}$, and use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x^{-2}\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=-2x^{-3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y' &= \dfrac{1}{x}\cdot x^{-2} + \ln x\cdot\left(-2x^{-3}\right)\\ &= \dfrac{1}{x^3} - \dfrac{2\ln x}{x^3}\\ &= \dfrac{1 - 2\ln x}{x^3}\end{aligned}$$
The quotient rule gives the same result.
criteria: Correct use of the product or quotient rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ has a vertex at $(3, 1)$ and passes through $(0, 0)$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the other $x$-intercept.

dif.r: Reflect intercept in axis of symmetry.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $a$, $b$ and $c$

dif.r: Use intercept form and vertex to find coefficients.

solutions.latex:
The parabola passes through $(0,0)$ with vertex $(3,1)$, which lies above the origin, so it is concave down.

The axis of symmetry is $x=3$, so the other $x$-intercept is the reflection of $x=0$:
$$\therefore\ x = 6$$

The zeros are $x=0$ and $x=6$, so $y=a(x-0)(x-6)=ax(x-6)$.

The point $(3,1)$ satisfies the equation:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 3a(-3) \\ 1 &= -9a \\ a &= -\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y &= -\dfrac{x}{9}(x-6)\\ &= -\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{2}{3}x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a = -\dfrac{1}{9},\ b = \dfrac{2}{3},\ c = 0$$

questions.stem: Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A) = p$, $P(B) = 2p$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.42$, and $P(A \cap B) = 0.03$.

parts.latex: Show that $p = 0.15$

dif.r: Substitute into addition rule and solve linear equation.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
By use of a Venn diagram, or otherwise, show that $P(A \cup \tilde{B}) = 0.73$,

where $\tilde{B}$ is the complement of $B$.

dif.r: Reason about union with complement via Venn regions.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that $P(A \cap \tilde{B}) = 0.12$ and hence determine, with reasoning, whether the events $A$ and $\tilde{B}$ are independent.

dif.r: Subtract intersection, then test independence with justification.

solutions.latex:
Using $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} p + 2p - 0.03 &= 0.42 \\ 3p &= 0.45 \\ p &= 0.15 \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $P(B)=2p=0.3$, so
$$P(\tilde{B}) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$$
$A\cup\tilde{B}$ is everything except the part of $B$ outside $A$, so it is $\tilde{B}$ together with $A\cap B$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cup\tilde{B}) &= P(\tilde{B}) + P(A\cap B)\\ &= 0.7 + 0.03\\ &= 0.73\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cap\tilde{B}) &= P(A) - P(A\cap B)\\ &= 0.15 - 0.03\\ &= 0.12\end{aligned}$$
For independence we need $P(A\cap\tilde{B}) = P(A)\,P(\tilde{B})$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(A)\times P(\tilde{B}) &= 0.15\times 0.7\\ &= 0.105\end{aligned}$$
Since $0.12\ne 0.105$, $A$ and $\tilde{B}$ are NOT independent.

parts.label: c

dif.r: Standard midpoint, perpendicular gradient, then verify point lies on line

figures.cap: quadrilateral ABCD with diagonals meeting at E

solutions.latex:
The diagonal $BD$ passes through $B(7,12)$ and $D(2,-3)$.

The gradient is
$$\begin{aligned} m_{BD} &= \dfrac{-3 - 12}{2 - 7} \\ &= \dfrac{-15}{-5} \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Using point-gradient form with $B(7,12)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 12 &= 3(x - 7) \\ y - 12 &= 3x - 21 \\ y &= 3x - 9 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of $BD$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric rewritten top-down from source rows (gradient; working out the equation).

solutions.latex:
$E$ lies on both diagonals, so substitute $y = 3x - 9$ into $x + 3y = 23$.
$$\begin{aligned} x + 3(3x - 9) &= 23 \\ x + 9x - 27 &= 23 \\ 10x &= 50 \\ x &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 3\times 5 - 9 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ E = (5, 6)$$
criteria: Finds one coordinate, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric was '1/2 for each coordinate; 1 for working'; rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ passes through the midpoint of $AB$ with gradient perpendicular to $AB$.
$$\begin{aligned} m_{AB} &= \dfrac{12 - 8}{7 - (-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{8} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So the gradient of the perpendicular bisector is $-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Midpoint of } AB &= \left(\dfrac{-1+7}{2}, \dfrac{8+12}{2}\right) \\ &= (3, 10) \end{aligned}$$
The perpendicular bisector is
$$\begin{aligned} y - 10 &= -2(x - 3) \\ y - 10 &= -2x + 6 \\ 2x + y - 16 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Test $E(5,6)$:
$$2(5) + 6 - 16 = 0$$
Hence $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
criteria: Finds the equation of the perpendicular bisector, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$P$ and $Q$ lie on both the line and the circle. Substitute $y = 2x + 5$ into the circle equation.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 + (2x+5)^2 - 6x - 2(2x+5) - 30 &= 0 \\ x^2 + 4x^2 + 20x + 25 - 6x - 4x - 10 - 30 &= 0 \\ 5x^2 + 10x - 15 &= 0 \\ 5(x^2 + 2x - 3) &= 0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = -3$ or $x = 1$. The point $P$ has $x=-3$, so $Q$ has $x = 1$ and
$$y = 2(1) + 5 = 7$$
$$\therefore\ Q = (1, 7)$$

solutions.latex:
Complete the square on the equation from (a).
$$\begin{aligned} (x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 - 2y + 1) &= 30 + 9 + 1 \\ (x-3)^2 + (y-1)^2 &= 40 \end{aligned}$$
So the centre is $C_1 = (3, 1)$ and $r = \sqrt{40}$.

The distances from the centres $C_1$ and $C_2$ to $P$ or $Q$ are all $r$, so $PC_1QC_2$ is a rhombus and its diagonals bisect each other at $M$.

The midpoint of $PQ$ is
$$M = \left(\dfrac{1 - 3}{2}, \dfrac{7 - 1}{2}\right) = (-1, 3)$$
The midpoint of $C_1C_2$, with $C_2 = (x, y)$, is also $M$:
$$(-1, 3) = \left(\dfrac{x+3}{2}, \dfrac{y+1}{2}\right)$$
So
$$x = 2(-1) - 3 = -5, \qquad y = 2(3) - 1 = 5$$
The second circle has the same radius, so
$$\therefore\ (x+5)^2 + (y-5)^2 = 40$$

parts.latex:
A roof of a house has a rectangular base 7 m by 10 m.

Each of the four sloping faces make an angle of $50^\circ$ with the horizontal.

The midpoint of $EF$ lies vertically above intersection of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$.

\exfigure{1341_q30_1}

Calculate the total surface area of the sloping faces, correct to one decimal place.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (sloping roof faces over a rectangular base); now Year 11 Extension 1.

dif.r: 3D hip-roof visualisation; deduce slant height and ridge length

figures.cap: roof with rectangular base ABCD, 10 m by 7 m, ridge EF

solutions.latex:
Each sloping face makes $50^\circ$ with the horizontal. Half the width of the base is $3.5$ m.

In the right-angled triangle formed by the roof height $h_R$ and a horizontal run of $3.5$ m:
$$\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{h_R}{3.5}, \quad\text{so}\quad h_R = 3.5\tan 50^\circ$$
The slant height $h_\triangle$ of the sloping face satisfies
$$\begin{aligned} \sin 50^\circ &= \dfrac{h_R}{h_\triangle} \\ h_\triangle &= \dfrac{3.5\tan 50^\circ}{\sin 50^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
The horizontal run $x$ on the end faces satisfies
$$\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{h_R}{x} = \dfrac{3.5\tan 50^\circ}{x}, \quad\text{so}\quad x = 3.5$$
Then $EF = 10 - 2\times 3.5 = 3$ m.

The two triangular end faces have base $7$ and slant height $\dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ}$. The two trapezium faces have parallel sides $3$ and $10$ and the same slant height.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2 \times 7 + \dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 10)\times 2\right) \\ &\approx 108.9 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total area} \approx 108.9 \text{ m}^2 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Correct expression for the total area, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
In an online game there are various 'power-ups' that players can discover while progressing through the game. The power-ups come in two sizes, major and minor, and they all belong to one of two categories, either combat or survival.

It is known that 85% of the power-ups in the game are minor and the rest are major.

Of the major power-ups it is known that 60 % are combat power-ups, while of the minor power-ups it is known that 30 % are combat power-ups.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Using the given information, complete the tree diagram below.

\exfigure{1341_q31_1}

dif.r: Fill tree branches using complements

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Power-ups that are discovered in the game occur at random.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the probability that when a power-up is discovered it will be a combat power-up.

dif.r: Sum two tree branch products

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Given that a power-up is a combat power-up, find the probability that it is a major power-up

dif.r: Reverse conditional probability from tree

figures.cap: incomplete tree diagram: minor 0.85, major 0.15, minor-combat 0.30, blanks for the other branches

solutions.latex:
The minor power-ups are $85\%$ and the major ones $15\%$. On the minor branch, $30\%$ are combat, so the rest are survival. On the major branch, $60\%$ are combat.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{survival}\mid\text{minor}) &= 0.7 \\ P(\text{combat}\mid\text{major}) &= 0.6 \\ P(\text{survival}\mid\text{major}) &= 0.4 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Tree diagram figure is part of the question; the solution gives the missing branch probabilities. Rubric written by us.

meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the branch values were written as joint probabilities; they are conditional ($P(\text{survival}\mid\text{minor})=0.7$, ...).

solutions.latex:
A combat power-up is either minor and combat, or major and combat.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{combat}) &= 0.85 \times 0.3 + 0.15 \times 0.6 \\ &= 0.345 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Let $A$ be the event that the power-up is major and $B$ the event that it is combat. Using conditional probability:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A \mid B) &= \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.15\times 0.6}{0.345} \\ &= \dfrac{0.09}{0.345} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{23} \\ &\approx 0.2609 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Astronomers classify the brightness of stars according to a scale of magnitudes. The difference in magnitude between two stars is defined by the formula

$$m_1 - m_2 = 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{b_2}{b_1}\right),$$

where $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the magnitudes of the two stars, and $b_1$ and $b_2$ are the corresponding apparent brightnesses measured in watts per metre squared.

The magnitude of a star is a unitless measure, and its value can be positive or negative.

The star Sirius has a magnitude of $-1.4$ and an apparent brightness of $1.04 \times 10^{-7}$ W/m$^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
The star Acrux has an apparent brightness of $1.42 \times 10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$.

Calculate the magnitude of Acrux, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Substitute into log formula and rearrange for magnitude

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The Sun has a magnitude of $-26.7$.

Calculate the apparent brightness of the Sun, correct to three significant figures.

dif.r: Rearrange log formula to exponential form; sign care with magnitudes

solutions.latex:
Take Sirius as star 1 and Acrux as star 2 in the given formula, and make $m_2$ the subject.
$$m_1 - m_2 = 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{b_2}{b_1}\right)$$
In the source working, $m_1 = -1.4$ is the Sirius magnitude and the quantity sought is the Acrux magnitude; the source writes
$$\begin{aligned} m &= -1.4 + 2.5\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1.04\times 10^{-7}}{1.42\times 10^{-8}}\right) \\ &\approx 0.76 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{magnitude of Acrux} \approx 0.76$$

meta.format_note: Source labelling of $m_1$, $m_2$ is loose; the numeric working is kept as given (0.76 checked). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Take the Sun as star 1 and Sirius as star 2, and make $b_1$ the subject. Let $A = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{2.5}$.

The source working gives $A = 10.12$, so
$$\begin{aligned} b_1 &= b_2 \times 10^A \\ &= 1.04 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{10.12} \\ &\approx 1370 \text{ W/m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes $b_1$ the subject or substitutes correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Doctor Hopper is investigating the population of kangaroos in New South Wales.

The doctor found, based on historical data that the population of kangaroos, $P$, could be modelled by

$$P = 7500 + 500(1.09)^t,$$

where $t$ is the number of years since the start of the year 2000, $t \ge 0$.

Find the rate at which the population of kangaroos is growing at the end of 2021.

Leave your answer correct to two significant figures.

dif.r: Differentiate a^t; interpret end of 2021 as t=22

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^t\right) = a^t\ln a$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 500 \times (1.09)^t \ln 1.09$$
The end of 2021 is $t = 22$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 500 \times (1.09)^{22}\ln 1.09 \\ &\approx 290 \text{ per year} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The spiral below is formed by connecting semi-circles of increasing radii.

\exfigure{1341_q35_1}

The lengths of each spiral form a geometric sequence, with the length of the first and second spirals being $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ cm and $\pi$ cm respectively.

Show that the sum of the first $n$ spirals is $\dfrac{\pi\left(2^n - 1\right)}{2}$ cm, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.

dif.r: Identify a and r, apply geometric sum formula

figures.cap: spiral of semicircles on a number line

solutions.latex:
The lengths form a geometric sequence with first term $a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and common ratio
$$r = \dfrac{\pi}{\frac{\pi}{2}} = 2$$
Using the sum of a geometric series:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\times\dfrac{2^n - 1}{2 - 1} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi\left(2^n - 1\right)}{2} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac{3}{2^{2t}}\,dt$

dif.r: Rewrite as 4^{-t}, integrate exponential base, evaluate

solutions.latex:
Write $\dfrac{3}{2^{2t}} = 3\cdot 4^{-t}$ and use $\displaystyle\int a^{kt}\,dt = \dfrac{a^{kt}}{k\ln a}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 \dfrac{3}{2^{2t}}\,dt &= 3\int_0^1 4^{-t}\,dt \\ &= 3\left[\dfrac{4^{-t}}{-\ln 4}\right]_0^1 \\ &= -3\left[\dfrac{1}{4\ln 4} - \dfrac{1}{\ln 4}\right] \\ &= -3\times\left(-\dfrac{3}{4\ln 4}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{4\ln 4} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Intermediate step in source ($-3\int -1\cdot 4^{-t}$) replaced by the equivalent primitive with $-\ln 4$ in the denominator; same result.

questions.stem:
Kay borrows \$60 000 to set up a clothing pop up shop.

She must pay 12% p.a. interest compounded monthly, with repayments at the end of every six months. Let $\$A_n$ be the amount still owed after the $n$th repayment of $\$M$.

dif.r: Recurrence with monthly compounding but six-monthly repayments

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If it takes 15 years to pay off the loan, find the amount of each repayment, $M$.

dif.r: Generalise to A_30, geometric series with ratio 1.01^6

solutions.latex:
$12\%$ p.a. compounded monthly is $1\%$ per month, and repayments are every $6$ months.

After the 1st month Kay owes $60\,000 \times 1.01$. This continues, so at the end of the 5th month she owes $60\,000 \times 1.01^5$.

At the end of the 6th month interest is added and then the repayment is made.
$$A_1 = 60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M$$
At the end of the 7th month Kay owes $\left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)1.01$. This continues, so at the end of the 11th month she owes $\left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)1.01^5$.

At the 12th month, the same process gives
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= A_1 \times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= \left(60\,000 \times 1.01^6 - M\right)\times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= 60\,000 \times 1.01^{12} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6\right) \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$15$ years is $30$ repayments, so we need $A_{30}$.

The same step gives the pattern:
$$\begin{aligned} A_3 &= A_2 \times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= \left[60\,000 \times 1.01^{12} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6\right)\right]\times 1.01^6 - M \\ &= 60\,000 \times 1.01^{18} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6 + 1.01^{12}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$A_{30} = 60\,000 \times 1.01^{180} - M\left(1 + 1.01^6 + 1.01^{12} + \cdots + 1.01^{174}\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a = 1$, $r = 1.01^6$ and $n = 30$ terms:
$$A_{30} = 60\,000 \times 1.01^{180} - M \times \dfrac{\left(1.01^6\right)^{30} - 1}{1.01^6 - 1}$$
The loan is paid off, so $A_{30} = 0$.
$$M = \dfrac{60\,000 \times 1.01^{180}\left(1.01^6 - 1\right)}{1.01^{180} - 1}$$
$$\therefore\ M \approx \$4430.07$$
criteria: Obtains the sum of the geometric series for $A_{30}$, or equivalent merit
Finds $A_3$ or identifies the pattern, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A particle moves along a straight line so that it is $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds. The acceleration of the particle is given by

$$\ddot{x} = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \ \text{ m/s}^2$$

Initially the particle is travelling with a velocity of 3 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the first two times when the particle is stationary.

dif.r: Integrate trig acceleration, find constant, solve cosine equation

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How far does the particle travel in the first four seconds.

dif.r: Distance needs splitting at turning point and absolute values

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x} &= -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \\ \dot{x} &= -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\left(-\dfrac{3}{\pi}\right)\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + C \\ &= 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $v = 3$:
$$3 = 2\cos 0 + C, \quad\text{so}\quad C = 1$$
$$\dot{x} = 1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t$$
The particle is stationary when $v = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + 1 &= 0 \\ \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}t &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 2 \text{ and } t = 4$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
From (a), $v = 1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t$ is positive for $0 \le t < 2$ and negative for $2 < t \le 4$ (it is zero at $t=2$ and $t=4$). So the particle turns at $t = 2$ and the distance is found in two parts.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \int_0^2 \left(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)dt + \left|\int_2^4 \left(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)dt\right| \\ &= \left[t + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right]_0^2 + \left|\left[t + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right]_2^4\right| \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \left|4 - \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \left(2 + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi} + \left|2 - \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right| \\ &= \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\ &\approx 4.96 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integrals with absolute value, or equivalent merit
Identifies the change of direction at $t=2$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Check: $2+\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{\pi}\approx3.654$, $\left|2-\dfrac{6\sqrt3}{\pi}\right|\approx1.308$, sum $\approx4.96$, matching $\dfrac{9\sqrt3}{\pi}$.

dif.r: Build area function, optimise, check endpoints for least value

figures.cap: rectangle PQRS with P on y=8/x, points (1,8) and (4,2) marked

solutions.latex:
Let $P = (x, y)$ with $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$. The rectangle has sides $6 - x$ and $12 - y$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= (6 - x)(12 - y) \\ &= 72 - 6y - 12x + xy \\ &= 72 - \dfrac{48}{x} - 12x + 8 \\ &= 80 - 12x - \dfrac{48}{x} \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx} = -12 + \dfrac{48}{x^2}, \qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{96}{x^3}$$
and $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$ for $x \in [1, 4]$.

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -12 + \dfrac{48}{x^2} &= 0 \\ x^2 &= 4 \\ x &= 2 \quad (x \in [1, 4]) \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$, $x = 2$ gives a maximum, with $A = 32$.

Check the end points:
$$\begin{aligned} x = 1:&\quad A = 20 \\ x = 4:&\quad A = 20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{greatest } A = 32 \text{ at } x = 2;\ \text{least } A = 20 \text{ at } x = 1 \text{ and } x = 4$$
criteria: Finds the maximum and tests the end points, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary point $x=2$, or equivalent merit
Finds $A$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The interval which gives the range of the function $y = 3\sin 2x + 4$ is:

dif.r: Direct range of a sine function from its amplitude and vertical shift.

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is $3$ and the vertical shift is $4$.
$$\begin{aligned} y_{\min} &= 4-3=1 \\ y_{\max} &= 4+3=7 \end{aligned}$$
So the range is $[1,7]$, which is option C.

parts.latex: The best description of $x = y^2 + 1$ is:

dif.r: Recognise a sideways parabola and classify the relation type.

solutions.latex:

Each $x>1$ gives two values of $y$, so the relation is one to many, which is option C.

parts.latex: The first three terms of an arithmetic series are $2, 7$ and $12$. The $15^{\text{th}}$ term of the series is:

dif.r: Substitute into the arithmetic nth term formula.

solutions.latex:
Here $a=2$, $d=5$ and $n=15$.

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_{15} &= 2+(15-1)\times 5 \\ &= 72 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: The anti-derivative of $2^x \ln 4$ is:

dif.r: Exponential antiderivative needing ln4 = 2ln2 simplification.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \int 2^x\ln 4\,dx &= \ln 2^2\int 2^x\,dx \\ &= 2\ln 2\times\dfrac{2^x}{\ln 2}+c \\ &= 2\times 2^x + c \\ &= 2^{x+1}+c \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
On the Richter scale, the magnitude $R$ of an earthquake of intensity $I$ is given by the formula $R = \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$, where $I_0$ is a reference intensity used for comparisons.

The 1989 Newcastle Earthquake measured a magnitude of 5.6 on the Richter scale.

Which of these is closest to $\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$, which is the number of times this earthquake is more intense than the reference intensity?

dif.r: Convert a log equation to index form and estimate.

solutions.latex:
Substituting $R=5.6$:
$$5.6=\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{I}{I_0} &= 10^{5.6} \\ &= 398\,107.17\ldots \\ &\approx 400\,000 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex:
The graph of the parabola $y = x^2 - 2x$ is given. The shaded area is equal to:

\exfigure{1342_q6_1}

dif.r: Area split at an x-intercept to handle the region below the axis.

figures.cap: graph of y=x^2-2x with shaded regions between x=0 and x=4

solutions.latex:
The curve is below the axis for $0<x<2$ and above it for $2<x<4$, so the two areas are found separately.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\int_0^2 (x^2-2x)\,dx\right| + \int_2^4 (x^2-2x)\,dx \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_0^2\right| + \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_2^4 \\ &= \left|\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right| + \left(\dfrac{64}{3}-16\right)-\left(\dfrac{8}{3}-4\right) \\ &= \dfrac{4}{3}+\dfrac{16}{3}+\dfrac{4}{3} \\ &= 8 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
How many terms are there in the following arithmetic sequence:

$$-12, -10\dfrac{1}{2}, -9, \dots, 108$$

dif.r: Formula in reverse to find n, with a fractional common difference.

solutions.latex:
Here $a=-12$ and $d=1.5$. Setting $T_n=108$:
$$\begin{aligned} -12+1.5(n-1) &= 108 \\ 1.5n &= 121.5 \\ n &= 81 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex:
$A$ and $B$ are events of a sample space.

Given that $P(B|A) = \sqrt{p}$, $P(A) = p$ and $P(B) = p^2$, which of these is an expression for $P(A|B)$?

dif.r: Conditional probability formula applied twice with symbolic index algebra.

solutions.latex:
Using $P(B|A)=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)}$:
$$\sqrt{p}=\dfrac{P(B\cap A)}{p}$$
so $P(B\cap A)=p^{\frac{3}{2}}$.

Then
$$\begin{aligned} P(A|B) &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} \\ &= \dfrac{p^{\frac{3}{2}}}{p^2} \\ &= p^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{p}} \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex:
A continuous random variable, $X$, has the following probability density function, where $k > 0$.

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 2x\right) & \text{for } -k \le x \le k \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values} \end{cases}$$

Which of the following is true?

dif.r: Recognise the pdf as even cos2x and deduce symmetry.

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
Since $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2x\right)=\cos 2x$, which is an even function, the distribution is symmetric about $x=0$.

Hence $P(X>0.2)=P(X<-0.2)$, which is option B.

dif.r: Bound tangent gradient and intercept by comparing tangents at x=1 and x=e.

At $x=e$ the gradient is $\dfrac{1}{e}$ and at $x=1$ it is $1$. Since $1<a<e$, we have $\dfrac{1}{e}<m<1$.

The tangent at $x=e$ has $c=0$ and the tangent at $x=1$ has $c=-1$, so for the tangent at $x=a$, $-1<c<0$.

This is option A.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^2}{4x^3-6}\,dx$

dif.r: Standard f'/f logarithmic integral needing a constant adjustment.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a constant multiple of the derivative of $4x^3-6$, which is $12x^2$, so the integral is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x^2}{4x^3-6}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{12}\int\dfrac{12x^2}{4x^3-6}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{12}\ln|4x^3-6|+C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\tan x}{e^{2x}}\right)$. Answer in the simplest exact form.

dif.r: Quotient rule with trig and exponential, then simplifying.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\tan x & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=\sec^2 x & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\tan x}{e^{2x}}\right) &= \dfrac{e^{2x}\sec^2 x-2e^{2x}\tan x}{(e^{2x})^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\sec^2 x-2\tan x}{e^{2x}} \end{aligned}$$
Equivalently $\dfrac{(\tan x-1)^2}{e^{2x}}$, which is not required.

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \left(2\sin x - \sec^2 2x\right)dx$. Leave your answer in the simplest exact form.

dif.r: Definite trig integral with exact values, sec^2 2x needing care.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(2\sin x-\sec^2 2x)\,dx &= \left[-2\cos x-\dfrac{1}{2}\tan 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &= \left(-2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt3\right)-\left(-2-0\right) \\ &= 2-\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{4-3\sqrt3}{2} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 4}\dfrac{x^2-16}{8+2x-x^2}$

dif.r: Factorise and cancel to evaluate a limit.

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator and denominator, then cancel the common factor $x-4$.
$$\begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{x^2-16}{8+2x-x^2} &= \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{(x-4)(x+4)}{(x-4)(-2-x)} \\ &= \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{x+4}{-(2+x)} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{-6} \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Factorises and simplifies, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Chandra is an enthusiastic gardener. She planted a lemon tree on $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2019, when it was 80 centimetres tall. At the end of the first year after planting, it was 130 centimetres tall, that is, it grew 50 centimetres. Each year's growth was then 90% of the growth of the previous year.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How tall was the lemon tree after three years?

dif.r: Sum three geometric growth terms and add the initial height.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Assuming the present growth pattern is maintained, explain why the lemon tree will never reach a height of 10 metres?

dif.r: Use a limiting sum in context, including the initial height.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: In which year will the lemon tree reach a height of 5 metres?

dif.r: Set up a geometric sum equation, solve with logs, interpret the year.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Each year's growth is $90\%$ of the previous year's, so the growths in the first three years are $50$, $50\times0.9$ and $50\times0.9^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} H &= 80+(50+50\times0.9+50\times0.9^2) \\ &= 80+(50+45+40.5) \\ &= 215.5 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Adds the three years' growth to $80$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Removed the source's partial list 'Heights: 80, 130, 175, …' because the third value 175 disagrees with the final working (130 + 45 = 175, consistent; but the line was incomplete and unneeded).

solutions.latex:
The yearly growths form a geometric series with $a=50$ and $r=0.9$. Since $|r|<1$, the sum to infinity exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{50}{1-0.9} \\ &= 500 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Maximum height $=500+80=580$ cm, which is less than $10$ m.

So the tree will never reach $10$ m.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Height after $n$ years is $80$ plus the sum of $n$ terms of the series. Set this equal to $500$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned} 500 &= 80+\dfrac{50(1-0.9^n)}{1-0.9} \\ 420 &= \dfrac{50(1-0.9^n)}{0.1} \\ 0.84 &= 1-0.9^n \\ 0.9^n &= 0.16 \\ n &= \dfrac{\log 0.16}{\log 0.9} \\ &\approx 17.3 \end{aligned}$$
So the height is reached during the 18th year, which is 2036.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

questions.stem: Packets of coffee beans are labelled with a net weight of 300 g. It is found that the weight of a packet can be modelled by a normal distribution, with mean 306 g and standard deviation 3 g.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use the Empirical rule to determine the probability that the weight of one packet of coffee beans is less than the advertised weight of 300 g.

dif.r: Empirical rule: two standard deviations below the mean, then halve the tail.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: In a shipment of 40 boxes, each with 100 packets of coffee beans, how many packets would be expected to be underweight?

dif.r: Expected count is the probability times the total packets.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Manufacturers aim to ensure that the expected number of underweight packets in the shipment will be less than 20. The machine is adjusted to give a mean weight of 308 g, with the standard deviation of 3 g remaining the same. Will they meet their target? Justify your answer.

dif.r: Normal z-score, symmetry, expected count, then justify the target in context.

can_use: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The weight $300$ is two standard deviations below the mean, since $306-2\times3=300$.

By the Empirical rule, $95\%$ of weights lie within two standard deviations, so $5\%$ lie outside, split equally between the two tails.
$$P(\text{weight}<300)=\dfrac{0.05}{2}=0.025=2.5\%$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Part (c) has no solution in the source.

solutions.latex:
The shipment has $40\times100=4000$ packets.
$$0.025\times4000=100 \text{ packets}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The $z$-score for a packet of weight 300 g, with mean 308 g and standard deviation 3 g, is
$$z=\dfrac{300-308}{3}\approx-2.67$$
By symmetry of the normal distribution:
$$\begin{aligned} P(Z<-2.67)&=1-P(Z<2.67) \\ &=1-0.99621 \\ &\approx 0.0038 \ (0.38\%) \end{aligned}$$
The shipment has $40\times100=4000$ packets, so
$$\text{Expected number underweight}=0.0038\times4000\approx15.2<20$$
$$\therefore\ \text{They meet the target.}$$
criteria: Finds the $z$-score or the probability of an underweight packet, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The probability it will rain on any day in June is 0.15. Two days in June are selected at random.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Complete the probability distribution table, where the variable $X$ represents the number of rainy days across the 2 days:

\extable{1342_q21_t1}

dif.r: Two independent days; must count both orders for one rainy day.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate, correct to two decimal places:

parts.label: i
parts.latex: the expected value.

dif.r: Direct expected value from a completed table.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: the variance and standard deviation.

dif.r: Standard variance formula then square root for standard deviation.

solutions.latex:
Each day is rainy with probability $0.15$ and not rainy with probability $0.85$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X=0)&=0.85^2=0.7225 \\ P(X=1)&=2(0.15)(0.85)=0.255 \\ P(X=2)&=0.15^2=0.0225 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Using $\mu=\sum x\,P(X=x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mu&=1\times0.255+2\times0.0225 \\ &=0.30 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Using $\text{Var}(X)=\sum x^2P(X=x)-\mu^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}&=(1^2\times0.255+2^2\times0.0225)-(0.30)^2 \\ &=0.255 \\ &\approx0.26 \end{aligned}$$
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance:
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma&=\sqrt{0.255} \\ &=0.50497\ldots \\ &\approx0.50 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the variance, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\sec\theta + 8\cos\theta = 6$ for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$. Answer correct to 3 decimal places, where necessary.

dif.r: Convert sec to quadratic in cos, factorise, find four solutions in radians.

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and multiply through by $\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}+8\cos\theta&=6 \\ 1+8\cos^2\theta&=6\cos\theta \\ 8\cos^2\theta-6\cos\theta+1&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $x=\cos\theta$.
$$(4x-1)(2x-1)=0$$
so $\cos\theta=\dfrac14$ or $\cos\theta=\dfrac12$.

For $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac12$ gives $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, and $\cos\theta=\dfrac14$ gives $\theta\approx1.318,\ 4.965$.
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 1.318,\ 4.965,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Finds both values of $\cos\theta$ and some solutions in radians, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A plane takes off from an airport (A) and travels in a direction of $258^\circ$ for 3050 kilometres.

The plane lands at (B) and then heads in a direction of $300^\circ$ for 2680 kilometres, landing at (C).

Use the diagram below to mark the given information.

\exfigure{1342_q23_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the distance the plane must travel to return to A. Answer to the nearest kilometre.

dif.r: Must deduce 138° angle from bearings before applying cosine rule.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the bearing that the plane must travel from C to A.

dif.r: Find interior angle by cosine rule, convert to a true bearing.

figures.cap: compass axes with A at the origin and points B and C
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1342_q23_s1}

From the bearings, $\angle ABC=138^\circ$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} b^2&=2680^2+3050^2-2(2680)(3050)\cos138^\circ \\ b&\approx5351 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the cosine rule with $138^\circ$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch drawn (1342_q23_s1); it was to show: solution diagram 1342_q23_s1 on the question's figure: points A, B, C with north lines at A and B, AB = 3050 km on bearing 258° from A, BC = 2680 km on bearing 300° from B, angle ABC = 138°, AC = b ≈ 5351 km. Placed \exfigure at top.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1342_q23_s1}

Applying the cosine rule to find $\angle A$:
$$\cos A=\dfrac{5351^2+3050^2-2680^2}{2\times5351\times3050}$$
so $A\approx19^\circ35'$.

Then
$$\begin{aligned} \alpha&=102^\circ-19^\circ35'\approx82^\circ25' \\ \theta&=180^\circ-82^\circ25'\approx97^\circ35' \end{aligned}$$
so the bearing is approximately $098^\circ\text{T}$.

Alternatively, find $\angle C$:
$$\cos C=\dfrac{2680^2+5351^2-3050^2}{2\times2680\times5351}$$
so $C\approx22^\circ25'$, and
$$\text{bearing}=120^\circ-22^\circ25'\approx97^\circ35'$$
$$\therefore\ \text{bearing}\approx098^\circ\text{T}$$
criteria: Finds the angle at $A$ (or $C$), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Consider the cubic function $y = x^3 + ax^2 + bx + 3$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

At the point $(1, 8)$ on the curve, the equation of the tangent is given by $y = 2x + 6$.

Determine the values of $a$ and $b$.

dif.r: Point and tangent gradient give two simultaneous equations for a, b.

solutions.latex:
The point $(1,8)$ lies on the curve.
$$\begin{aligned} 8&=1+a+b+3 \\ a+b&=4 \end{aligned}\qquad (1)$$
The gradient of the tangent is $2$, and
$$y'=3x^2+2ax+b$$
When $x=1$, $y'=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=3+2a+b \\ 2a+b&=-1 \end{aligned}\qquad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$a=-5$$
Then $-5+b=4$, so $b=9$.
$$\therefore\ a=-5,\ b=9$$
criteria: Finds both equations and $a=-5$, or equivalent merit
Finds both equations, or equivalent merit
Finds one equation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A probability density function is given by $f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}; & 0 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0; & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $a$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $a = 1$.

dif.r: Total probability equals one; integrate a linear-inside power.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate pdf from 0 to x, state piecewise CDF.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the median.

dif.r: Set CDF to one half and solve a simple surd equation.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability must equal 1.
$$\int_0^2\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+4x}}\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{a(1+4x)^{\frac12}}{\frac12\times4}\right]_0^2&=1 \\ \dfrac{a}{2}\sqrt9-\dfrac{a}{2}\sqrt1&=1 \\ \dfrac{3a}{2}-\dfrac{a}{2}&=1 \\ a&=1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets the total probability integral equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $a=1$, and using a second variable $t$ in the integrand:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_0^x(1+4t)^{-\frac12}\,dt \\ &=\left[\dfrac{(1+4t)^{\frac12}}{\frac12\times4}\right]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{1+4x}}{2}-\dfrac12 \\ &=\dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
The complete cumulative distribution function is
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<0\\[6pt] \dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right), & 0\le x\le2\\[6pt] 1, & x>2\end{cases}$$
criteria: Sets up the integral with a second variable and limits, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=\dfrac12$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac12\left(\sqrt{1+4x}-1\right)&=\dfrac12 \\ \sqrt{1+4x}&=2 \\ 1+4x&=4 \\ x&=\dfrac34 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the median is } \dfrac34$$

parts.latex:
The rate of 'flu infection' in a population of a city is proportional to the number of infected individuals. That is the number of infected people $F$ after $t$ weeks is modelled by the equation $F = F_0 e^{kt}$

where $F_0$ and $k$ are constants. It is known that after 3 weeks, there is twice the number of infections to begin with. If there were 1000 cases of flu infection originally, how many are there after 7 weeks? Express your answer correct to three significant figures.

dif.r: Find k from doubling with logs, then substitute t=7.

solutions.latex:
When $t=3$, $F=2F_0$ and $F_0=1000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2000&=1000e^{3k} \\ 2&=e^{3k} \\ k&=\dfrac{\ln2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=7$:
$$\begin{aligned} F&=1000e^{\frac{7\ln2}{3}} \\ &=5039.68\ldots \\ &\approx5040 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about 5040 cases after 7 weeks}$$
criteria: Finds $k$ and substitutes $t=7$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source printed answer was about 5000, but 5039.68 to 3 significant figures is 5040; corrected to 5040 (source note said the same).

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of $y = 6 - 8e^{-x}$.

\exfigure{1342_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: On the diagram, sketch the graph of $y = e^x$, which passes through the point $(1, e)$. Show that the $x$ coordinates of the two points of intersection, ($x_1$ and $x_2$, where $x_1 < x_2$), are the solutions of the equation $e^{2x} - 6e^x + 8 = 0$ and solve this equation to find the exact values of $x_1$ and $x_2$.

dif.r: Sketch, form hidden quadratic in e^x, factorise and solve with logs.

skills: Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find in simplest exact form, the area of the region enclosed by the two curves.

dif.r: Area between exponential curves with log limits needing exact simplification.

figures.cap: graph of y=6-8e^{-x} with asymptote y=6
solution sketch: graph of y=e^x added to the diagram, intersecting the given curve at x1 and x2

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1342_q29_s1}

The curves intersect where $e^x=6-8e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x&=6-\dfrac{8}{e^x} \\ e^{2x}&=6e^x-8 \\ e^{2x}-6e^x+8&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Factorising:
$$(e^x-2)(e^x-4)=0$$
so $e^x=2$ or $e^x=4$.
$$\therefore\ x_1=\ln2,\quad x_2=\ln4$$
criteria: Sketches $y=e^x$, shows the equation and factorises, or equivalent merit
Sketches $y=e^x$ and shows the equation, or equivalent merit
Sketches $y=e^x$ through $(0,1)$ and $(1,e)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch drawn (1342_q29_s1); it was to show: sketch_id 1342_q29_s2 is the sketch asked for; the figure placed is 1342_q29_s1 as in the source. Draw on the given axes the curve y = 6 - 8e^{-x} and y = e^x through (0,1) and (1,e), with intersection points at x = ln 2 (y = 2) and x = ln 4 (y = 4) labelled.

solutions.latex:
The region lies between the curves from $x=\ln2$ to $x=\ln4$, with $y=6-8e^{-x}$ above $y=e^x$.
$$\text{Area}=\int_{\ln2}^{\ln4}\left(6-8e^{-x}-e^x\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} &=\left[6x+8e^{-x}-e^x\right]_{\ln2}^{\ln4} \\ &=6(\ln4-\ln2)+8\left(\dfrac14-\dfrac12\right)-(4-2) \\ &=6\ln2-2-2 \\ &=6\ln2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=6\ln2-4 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Sets up the integral and finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The line is $x=5-y$. Split the region at $y=2$: the line is the right boundary for $2\le y\le5$ and the parabola for $1\le y\le2$.
$$\text{Area}=\int_2^5(5-y)\,dy+\int_1^2(-y^2+6y-5)\,dy$$
$$\begin{aligned} &=\left[5y-\dfrac{y^2}{2}\right]_2^5+\left[-\dfrac{y^3}{3}+3y^2-5y\right]_1^2 \\ &=\dfrac{25}{2}-8+\left(-\dfrac23\right)-\left(-\dfrac73\right) \\ &=4\dfrac12+\dfrac53 \\ &=\dfrac{37}{6} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the triangle $BCD$ with $D(0,2)$ has area $\dfrac12\times3\times3=\dfrac92$, and
$$\int_1^2(-y^2+6y-5)\,dy=\dfrac53$$
so the total is $\dfrac92+\dfrac53=\dfrac{37}{6}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{37}{6} \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Sets up the integral(s) and integrates or substitutes, or equivalent merit
Correct integral set-up, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Karen is retiring next week and her Superannuation Fund contains $\$1\,200\,000$. The Fund is earning $6\%$ p.a. compound interest, compounding monthly. To cover her living expenses in her retirement, Karen wishes to withdraw a regular amount of $\$8\,000$ at the end of each month, after interest has been added.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that after 3 months the amount in her account $A_3$ is given by:

$$A_3 = 1\,200\,000(1.005)^3 - 8\,000\left[(1.005)^2 + (1.005) + 1\right]$$

dif.r: Routine recursive build-up of balance over three months.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By finding a similar expression for the amount remaining after $n$ months, find how many years the money will last.

dif.r: Generalise to A_n with GP sum, set zero, solve with logs.

meta.marker_note: The expanding process must be shown.

solutions.latex:
Continuing the pattern:
$$A_n=1\,200\,000(1.005)^n-8000\left[(1.005)^{n-1}+\cdots+(1.005)+1\right]$$
The bracket is a GP sum with $a=1$, $r=1.005$ and $n$ terms.

The money lasts until $A_n=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=1\,200\,000(1.005)^n-\dfrac{8000\left((1.005)^n-1\right)}{1.005-1} \\ 1200(1.005)^n&=1600\left((1.005)^n-1\right) \\ 400(1.005)^n&=1600 \\ (1.005)^n&=4 \\ n&=\dfrac{\ln4}{\ln1.005} \\ &=277.95 \text{ months} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the money lasts about 23 years}$$
criteria: Uses the GP sum formula correctly, or equivalent merit
Writes the expression for $A_n$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
\exfigure{1342_q32_1}

An open trough of depth $h$ metres and length one metre is constructed out of stainless steel sheeting. The cross-section of the trough is an isosceles trapezium with the acute angles being $45^\circ$ each. The width of the bottom of the trough is $a$ metres. The area of the cross-section measures $60\ \text{m}^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $a = \dfrac{60}{h} - h$.

dif.r: Use 45° geometry and trapezium area to show given relation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the amount of stainless steel, $A$, in $\text{m}^2$, required to construct the trough is given by:

$$A = \dfrac{60}{h} - h + 2h\sqrt{2} + 120.$$

dif.r: Model total surface area of faces, Pythagoras for slant, substitute.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the depth of the trough, to the nearest millimetre (mm), if the amount of stainless steel used is kept to a minimum.

dif.r: Routine derivative of given function, solve, second derivative test.

figures.cap: open trough with trapezium cross-section, depth h, base a, length 1 metre

solutions.latex:
In the cross-section, each slanted side makes $45^\circ$ with the base, so the horizontal extension at each end satisfies $\tan45^\circ=\dfrac{h}{x}$, giving $x=h$.

Hence the top width is $b=a+2h$.

Using the area of a trapezium, $\dfrac12h(a+b)=60$:
$$\begin{aligned} 60&=\dfrac12h(2a+2h) \\ 120&=2ah+2h^2 \\ a&=\dfrac{120}{2h}-\dfrac{2h^2}{2h} \\ &=\dfrac{60}{h}-h \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the area of the trapezium, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The steel is two trapezium ends, two slanted sides and the base (length 1 m).

Each slanted side has length $\sqrt{h^2+h^2}$ by Pythagoras' theorem.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\times\left(\dfrac12h(2a+2h)\right)+2\times\left(\sqrt{h^2+h^2}\times1\right)+(a\times1) \\ &=h(2a+2h)+2\sqrt2h+a \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $a=\dfrac{60}{h}-h$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2h\left(\dfrac{60}{h}-h\right)+2h^2+2\sqrt2h+\left(\dfrac{60}{h}-h\right) \\ &=120+2h\sqrt2+\dfrac{60}{h}-h \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{60}{h}-h+2h\sqrt2+120$$
criteria: Writes the correct expression for $A$, or equivalent merit

meta.source_flag: Possible source slip: part (b) adds the two trapezium ends (area 2 × 60 = 120) to the sides and base, but the trapezium end area is given as 60 m² each, so the working's first line ($2\times\frac12h(2a+2h)$) is consistent with the target. No change made.

solutions.latex:
Write $A=60h^{-1}-h+2h\sqrt2+120$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dA}{dh}=-60h^{-2}-1+2\sqrt2,\qquad \dfrac{d^2A}{dh^2}=\dfrac{120}{h^3}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dA}{dh}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{60}{h^2}&=2\sqrt2-1 \\ h&=\sqrt{\dfrac{60}{2\sqrt2-1}} \\ &\approx5.728 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dh^2}=\dfrac{120}{(5.728)^3}\approx0.638>0$$
so this is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ h\approx5.728 \text{ m}\ (5728 \text{ mm})$$
criteria: Sets the derivative to zero, or equivalent merit
