questions.stem: Annabelle takes 2 cans, without replacement, from a refrigerator that contains 8 cans of Pepsi, 4 cans of Coke and 3 cans of Sprite. Find the probability that Annabelle gets:

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At least one Pepsi

dif.r: Complement for at least one, without replacement.

solutions.latex:
Add the probabilities of two Pepsi, two Coke and two Sprite (15 cans in total, no replacement).
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{8}{15}\times\dfrac{7}{14} + \dfrac{4}{15}\times\dfrac{3}{14} + \dfrac{3}{15}\times\dfrac{2}{14} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{105} \end{aligned}$$

Use the complement: at least one Pepsi is the opposite of no Pepsi (7 of the 15 cans are not Pepsi).
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1 - P(\text{no Pepsi}) \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{7}{15}\times\dfrac{6}{14} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $|7x-12|\ge 16$

solutions.latex:
For $|A| \ge k$, either $A \ge k$ or $A \le -k$.

Case 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 7x - 12 &\ge 16 \\ 7x &\ge 28 \\ x &\ge 4 \end{aligned}$$
Case 2:
$$\begin{aligned} 7x - 12 &\le -16 \\ 7x &\le -4 \\ x &\le -\dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \le -\dfrac{4}{7} \text{ or } x \ge 4$$
criteria: One correct solution, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Jure owns a building supply company. They sell packets of screws which claim to have 75 screws per packet. To avoid customer complaints, the mean amount of screws in a packet is 79 and the variance is 4.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that a packet of screws selected randomly will have less than 75 screws in it?

dif.r: Variance to SD, z-score, empirical rule tail.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The business sets a target of less than 16% of all blocks will have more than 80. The business can change the mean weight of the boxes to meet this target. What is mean amount of screws required to meet the target if the standard deviation is 2?

dif.r: Empirical rule in reverse to set mean; confusing wording.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The standard deviation is $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
$$z = \dfrac{75 - 79}{2} = -2$$
By the 68-95-99.7 rule, 95% lie within 2 standard deviations, so 2.5% lie below $z=-2$.
$$\therefore\ P = 2.5\%$$

About 16% of values lie more than one standard deviation above the mean.

So 80 must be one standard deviation above the mean.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{mean} &= 80 - 2 \\ &= 78 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int \cos x^{\circ}\,dx$

dif.r: Must recognise degrees and convert to radians before integrating.

solutions.latex:
Convert degrees to radians: $x^{\circ} = \dfrac{\pi x}{180}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \cos x^{\circ}\,dx &= \int \cos\dfrac{\pi x}{180}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{180}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{180} + C \\ &= \dfrac{180}{\pi}\sin x^{\circ} + C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Changes to radians, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{x}{2x^2+1}\,dx$

dif.r: f'/f log integral with constant adjustment and log laws.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $2x^2+1$, which is $4x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2 \dfrac{x}{2x^2+1}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{4}\int_1^2 \dfrac{4x}{2x^2+1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\Big[\ln(2x^2+1)\Big]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\ln 9 - \ln 3\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\ln 3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and leave each answer as a single simplified fraction:

$y=(3x-4)\sqrt{5-2x}$

dif.r: Product and chain rule with surd, simplify to single fraction.

solutions.latex:
Write $y = (3x-4)(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 3x - 4 & v &= (5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ u' &= 3 & v' &= -(5-2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}} - \dfrac{3x-4}{(5-2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\ &= \dfrac{3(5-2x) - (3x-4)}{\sqrt{5-2x}} \\ &= \dfrac{19 - 9x}{\sqrt{5-2x}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Working re-set in the u, u', v, v' grid; $v'=\dfrac{1}{2}(5-2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(-2)$ simplified; same result as the source.

parts.latex:
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and leave each answer as a single simplified fraction:

$y=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$

dif.r: Quotient rule with Pythagorean identity simplification.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= \sin x & v &= 1 + \cos x \\ u' &= \cos x & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{(1+\cos x)\cos x - \sin x(-\sin x)}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x + \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x + 1}{(1+\cos x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1+\cos x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Compare two z-scores directly.

solutions.latex:
Compare $z$-scores, $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Science: } z &= \dfrac{86 - 73}{8} = 1.625 \\ \text{English: } z &= \dfrac{83 - 74}{5.5} \approx 1.636 \end{aligned}$$
The English $z$-score is higher.

$\therefore$ Luke performed better in English.

questions.stem: Jasmine's salary in her job increases by the same amount every year. In the $4^{\text{th}}$ year at her job she earned \$81 000. In the $9^{\text{th}}$ year of her job she earned \$98 500.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find how much Jasmine earned in the first year of her job and by how much her pay increases each year.

dif.r: Two arithmetic term equations solved simultaneously.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How much will Jasmine have earned in total after working at her job for 15 years?

dif.r: Substitute into arithmetic series sum formula.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Bree started a job at the same time, and with the same starting salary as Jasmine. Bree's salary, however, increased by 2% per annum. With the use of logarithms, show in which year will her income first be greater than \$100 000?

dif.r: Model geometric growth, solve inequality with logs, interpret year.

solutions.latex:
The salary forms an arithmetic sequence with first term $a$ and common difference $d$, so $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} a + 3d &= 81\,000 \\ a + 8d &= 98\,500 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting:
$$\begin{aligned} 5d &= 17\,500 \\ d &= 3500 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} a + 10\,500 &= 81\,000 \\ a &= 70\,500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{first year pay is } \$70\,500 \text{, with an annual increase of } \$3500$$

meta.format_note: Fixed the id: part (a) working had $T_4$ and $T_9$ equations unchanged.

solutions.latex:
Use the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$, with $n = 15$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15} &= \dfrac{15}{2}\left(2\times 70\,500 + 14\times 3500\right) \\ &= \$1\,425\,000 \end{aligned}$$

Bree's salary is a geometric sequence with $a = 70\,500$ and $r = 1.02$, so $T_n = 70\,500(1.02)^{n-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 70\,500(1.02)^{n-1} &> 100\,000 \\ 1.02^{n-1} &> \dfrac{200}{141} \end{aligned}$$
Take logarithms of both sides (the base $1.02>1$, so the inequality is unchanged):
$$\begin{aligned} n - 1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{200}{141}\right)}{\log 1.02} \\ n - 1 &> 17.65\ldots \\ n &> 18.65\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ she first earns more than $\$100\,000$ in her 19th year at the job.
criteria: Uses logarithms to solve for $n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta}-\tan\theta=\sec\theta$

dif.r: Trig identity proof needing common denominator and cancellation.

solutions.latex:
Express $\tan\theta$ as $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ and use a common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta} - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta - \sin\theta(1-\sin\theta)}{(1-\sin\theta)\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sec\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes over a common denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A school has two History classes that sit an exam. Andy's class has 16 students and has a mean mark of 65%, whilst Juliana's class has 24 students. The combined mean for the 2 classes is 68.6%. Find the mean for the Juliana's class.
parts.note: Mean of a data set (combined means) has no 2024 Advanced dot point.

dif.r: Combined mean equation: form total marks, solve linear equation

solutions.latex:
The combined total of marks equals the sum of the class totals. Let $x$ be the mean of Juliana's class.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{16\times 65 + 24x}{40} &= 68.6 \\ 1040 + 24x &= 2744 \\ 24x &= 1704 \\ x &= 71 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the mean of Juliana's class is } 71\%$$

Peter ties his dog to a post with a 20 m long rope. On one side, the post is 10 m from a fence. Calculate the area correct to 4 significant figures, that the dog can play.

dif.r: Must see circle minus segment, find angle from geometry

figures.cap: circle of radius 20 m, centre 10 m from a fence line

solutions.latex:
The dog covers a full circle of radius 20 m, less the minor segment cut off by the fence 10 m from the post.

The angle $\theta$ at the post subtended by the segment: half the angle satisfies
$$\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$
so $\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Using the segment area $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 400\pi - \dfrac{1}{2}\times 20^2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 400\pi - \dfrac{400\pi}{3} + 200\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &\approx 1011 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct method for the area, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable, $T$, represents the time taken in days to show symptoms after contracting a virus. It has the following probability density function.

$$f(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{2t-1} & \text{for } 1\le t\le 14\\[2mm] 0 & \text{for } 0\le t<1 \text{ or } t>14\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$

dif.r: Integrate pdf to 1, log integral, given answer

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After how many days will a person have a 75% chance of showing symptoms after they have contracted the virus?

dif.r: Set cumulative integral to 0.75, solve log equation, interpret days

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability over the domain is 1.
$$\int_1^{14} \dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k}{2}\int_1^{14} \dfrac{2}{2t-1}\,dt &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{14} &= 1 \\ k\left(\ln 27 - \ln 1\right) &= 2 \\ k\ln 27 &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k = \dfrac{2}{\ln 27}$$
criteria: Sets the total area equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $T$ days be the time at which the cumulative probability is 0.75.
$$\int_1^{T} \dfrac{\frac{2}{\ln 27}}{2t-1}\,dt = \dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\ln 27}\Big[\ln(2t-1)\Big]_1^{T} &= \dfrac{3}{4} \\ \ln(2T-1) &= \dfrac{3\ln 27}{4} \\ 2T - 1 &= e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} \\ T &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{3\ln 27}{4}} + 1}{2} \\ &\approx 6.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after 7 days}$$
criteria: Sets up the integral equal to 0.75, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rounded up to 7 days since 6.4 days is not yet a full day with 75% chance.

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\sqrt{\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}}\right]=\dfrac{2}{4-x^2}$

dif.r: Log laws then differentiate and combine fractions to given result

solutions.latex:
Use the log laws to rewrite the function, then differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right] &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2+x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2-x)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2+x}+\dfrac{1}{2-x}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2-x+2+x}{(2+x)(2-x)}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{4}{4-x^2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{4-x^2} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A drug is used to control a medical condition. It is known that the quantity $Q$ milligrams of drug remaining in the body after $t$ hours satisfies an equation of the form $Q=Q_0e^{kt}$ where $Q_0$ and $k$ are constants. The initial dose is 6 milligrams and after 15 hours the amount remaining in the body is half the initial dose.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $Q_0$ and $k$.

dif.r: Initial value and half-life give k via logarithms

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After how long will one-eighth of the initial dose remain?

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for time using k from (a)

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$, $Q=Q_0$, so $Q_0=6$.

After 15 hours the amount is half the initial dose, so $Q=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 6e^{15k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= e^{15k} \\ 15k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$k = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{15}$$

One-eighth of the initial dose is $\dfrac{6}{8}=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4} &= 6e^{kt} \\ \dfrac{1}{8} &= e^{kt} \\ kt &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $k$ from part (a).
$$t = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\div 15} = 45 \text{ hours}$$
criteria: Sets up equation for one-eighth of the dose, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Kloe has taken up golf, each year she plays 30 rounds of golf. In 2011 she totalled 3300 shots, in 2021 she totalled 2760 shots. The number of shots she took each year decreased by the same amount. To make it as a professional golfer she needs to get under 2115 shots in her 30 rounds. If this trend continues, in what year can she become a professional golfer?

dif.r: Model years as AP, inequality, convert term number to year

solutions.latex:
The yearly totals form an arithmetic progression. From 2011 to 2021 is 10 years, so with $a=3300$:
$$\begin{aligned} a+10d &= 2760 \\ 10d &= -540 \\ d &= -54 \end{aligned}$$
She needs fewer than 2115 shots.
$$\begin{aligned} a+(n-1)d &< 2115 \\ 3300+54-54n &< 2115 \\ -54n &< -1239 \\ n &> 22.944\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $n=23$ years, and Kloe can be a professional golfer in 2033.
criteria: Finds the common difference, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with $u=\tan x$.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\tan^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\tan x}+\dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \cot x+\tan x \end{aligned}$$
which is the required result.
criteria: Finds the derivative $\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x}$, or equivalent merit

The gradient is the derivative from part (a) at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} m &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} \\ &= 1+1 \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \log_e\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= \log_e 1 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} y-0 &= 2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ y &= 2x-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the function $y=4x^3-x^4$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature and find any points of inflection

parts.label: b
parts.latex:

dif.r: Sketch from found features plus factorised intercepts

figures.cap: blank grid for sketching
solution sketch: sketch of y=4x^3-x^4 with (0,0), (2,16), (3,27), (4,0)

solutions.latex:
$$y'=12x^2-4x^3 \qquad y''=24x-12x^2$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x^2-4x^3 &= 0 \\ 4x^2(3-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=3$, giving the points $(0,0)$ and $(3,27)$.

At $x=0$, $y''=0$, so the test is inconclusive and $(0,0)$ is a possible point of inflexion.

At $x=3$, $y''=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

For points of inflexion, $y''=0$.
$$12x(2-x)=0$$
So $x=0$ or $x=2$. Test the concavity either side of each.
$$\begin{aligned} x=1 &: y''=12>0 \\ x=2 &: y''=0 \\ x=2.5 &: y''=-15<0 \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(2,16)$ is a point of inflexion.
$$\begin{aligned} x=-1 &: y''=-36<0 \\ x=0 &: y''=0 \\ x=1 &: y''=12>0 \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes and $y'=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
criteria: Completes all but one of the points of inflexion with test, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Aurelia cuts rectangles of equal height from a strip of paper and arranges them in a row. The first rectangle has a length of 10 cm. The second rectangle has a length of 9.6 cm. The length of each subsequent rectangle is 96% of the length of the previous rectangle.

\exfigure{1303_q36_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the length of the $5^{\text{th}}$ rectangular strip, correct to 3 significant figures

dif.r: Direct geometric term formula substitution

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If Aurelia had a strip of paper 2.4 m in length, explain with working, if this is sufficient to make an unlimited number of rectangles.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: strip of paper cut into rectangles, first of length 10 cm

solutions.latex:
The lengths form a geometric sequence with first term $a=10$ and ratio $r=0.96$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_5 &= 10\times 0.96^4 \\ &\approx 8.49 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Using the sum of a GP, $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ with $n=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10(1-0.96^{10})}{1-0.96} \\ &\approx 83.8 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{10}{1-0.96} \\ &= 250 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Now $2.4 \text{ m}=240 \text{ cm}<250 \text{ cm}$.

So 2.4 m is not sufficient to make an unlimited number of rectangles.

questions.stem:
A cylindrical water tank holds 4000 litres of water, making its volume 4 cubic metres as shown in the diagram (not to scale).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the surface area is given by $S=2\pi r^2+8r^{-1}$

dif.r: Eliminate h using volume to derive given surface area

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the radius that would give the smallest possible surface area.

dif.r: Routine optimisation of given function with second derivative test

figures.cap: cylinder with radius r metres, height h metres, volume 4 m^3

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$, with $V=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= \pi r^2h \\ h &= \dfrac{4}{\pi r^2} \end{aligned}$$
The closed cylinder has surface area $S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= 2\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\dfrac{4}{\pi r^2}\right) \\ &= 2\pi r^2+\dfrac{8}{r} \\ &= 2\pi r^2+8r^{-1} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For a minimum, set $S'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} S' &= 4\pi r-8r^{-2} = 0 \\ 4\pi r-\dfrac{8}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 4\pi r^3-8 &= 0 \\ r^3 &= \dfrac{8}{4\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{2}{\pi}}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$S''=4\pi+\dfrac{16}{r^3}$$
Since $r>0$, $S''>0$, so this is a minimum area.
$$\therefore\ r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{2}{\pi}} \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the radius, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Simultaneously solve the equations $\log_{10}(2-x)-\log_{10}y=1-\log_{10}2$ and $\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y$

dif.r: Several log-law manipulations, eliminate variable, solve simultaneously

solutions.latex:
Rearrange the first equation using log laws.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(2-x)+\log_{10}2-1 &= \log_{10}y \\ \log_{10}(4-2x)-1 &= \log_{10}y \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$
$$\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y \qquad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{4-2x}{2x}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{4-2x}{2x} &= 10 \\ 4-2x &= 20x \\ x &= \dfrac{2}{11} \end{aligned}$$
From (2), $y=2x=\dfrac{4}{11}$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2}{11},\ y=\dfrac{4}{11}$$

questions.stem: Max borrows \$250 000 to purchase a house. He repays his loan in equal monthly instalments of \$$M$ for 25 years. Interest is charged at 3% p.a., compounded monthly.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: By first finding expressions for $A_1,A_2$ and $A_3$ (the amount owing after 1 month, 2 months and 3 months), find an expression for $A_n$ (the amount owing after $n$ months).

dif.r: Standard loan recurrence expansion and pattern recognition

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the amount of each monthly instalment, \$$M$, and hence calculate the amount of interest Max pays on the loan.

dif.r: Set A_n=0, GP sum, solve for M, then interest

criteria: Finds expressions for $A_1$, $A_2$ and $A_3$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The loan is repaid after $25\times 12=300$ months, so $A_{300}=0$.
$$250000(1.0025)^{300}-M\left(1+1.0025+\cdots+1.0025^{299}\right)=0$$
The bracket is a GP sum with $a=1$, $r=1.0025$, $n=300$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= \dfrac{250000(1.0025)^{300}}{\left(\frac{1.0025^{300}-1}{1.0025-1}\right)} \\ &= \$1185.53 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest} &= 300M-250000 \\ &= \$105\,658.49 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the monthly instalment, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The acceleration of a particle is given by $\ddot{x}=4\cos 2t$, where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially the particle is at the origin with a velocity of 1 ms$^{-1}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$

dif.r: Integrate cos 2t, find constant, answer given

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.

dif.r: Solve sin 2t = -1/2, select first positive solution

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the displacement, $x$, of the particle in terms of $t$.

dif.r: Integrate velocity and use initial condition for constant

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\dot{x}=\displaystyle\int 4\cos 2t\,dt=2\sin 2t+C$$
When $t=0$, $\dot{x}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 2\sin 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin 2t+1 &= 0 \\ \sin 2t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first time $2t>0$ with $\sin 2t=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ is in the third quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned} 2t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

Integrate the velocity.
$$x=\displaystyle\int(2\sin 2t+1)\,dt=-\cos 2t+t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -\cos 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-\cos 2t+t+1$$

parts.latex: What is the exact value of $\sin\theta$ such that $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{2}{3}$, where $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \pi$?

dif.r: Pythagorean triangle plus quadrant sign; routine exact-value recall

solutions.latex:
Draw a right-angled triangle with adjacent side 2 and hypotenuse 3. By Pythagoras' theorem, the opposite side is $\sqrt{3^2-2^2}=\sqrt{5}$.

In the second quadrant $\sin\theta>0$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$, which is option A.

parts.latex: Which of the following options is the same as $\sin(\pi - \theta)$?

dif.r: Direct recall of supplementary and complementary angle results

solutions.latex:
Since $\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta$ and $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\sin\theta$ (complementary angles),
$$\sin(\pi-\theta)=\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Two students work independently on a mathematical problem. Each student has a probability of 0.8 of solving it. What is the probability that both students solve the problem?

dif.r: Single multiplication of independent probabilities

solutions.latex:
The students work independently, so the probabilities multiply.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both}) &= 0.8\times 0.8 \\ &= 0.64 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex: If $P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.6, P(A \cup B) = 0.8$, then which of the following option is a true statement?

dif.r: Direct substitution into addition rule

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Using $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B) &= P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cup B) \\ &= 0.5+0.6-0.8 \\ &= 0.3 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: The fourth term of an arithmetic series is 27, and the seventeenth term is -38. What is the common difference?

dif.r: Two term equations solved simultaneously for d

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic series $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.

From $T_4=27$:
$$a+3d=27 \quad (1)$$
From $T_{17}=-38$:
$$a+16d=-38 \quad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 13d &= -65 \\ d &= -5 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: Determine the number of terms in the series $3(2)^{20} + 3(2)^{21} + \ldots + 3(2)^{k-1} + \ldots + 3(2)^{62}$.

dif.r: Count terms from exponent range; one step

solutions.latex:
The powers of 2 run from $20$ to $62$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{number of terms} &= 62-20+1 \\ &= 43 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: It is known that a 4 appears on the die at least once in the two throws. What is the probability that $X$ is greater than 9?

dif.r: Conditional probability; restricted sample space of 11 often miscounted

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
Using a table of the 36 equally likely outcomes, 10 outcomes give $X\le 5$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 5) &= \dfrac{10}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{18} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct sample space or count of favourable outcomes, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Outcomes with at least one 4: $36-25=11$.

Of these, the sums greater than 9 are $(4,6)$ and $(6,4)$, which is 2 outcomes.
$$P(X>9\mid \text{a 4 on a die})=\dfrac{2}{11}$$

parts.latex:
Chemistry, Physics and Biology are three of the subjects students may decide to study. For a group of 50 students, the following is known:

\begin{itemize}
\item 12 students study neither Chemistry nor Physics nor Biology
\item 20 students study Chemistry
\item 25 students study Physics
\item 15 students study Biology
\item 9 students study both Chemistry and Physics
\item 10 students study both Chemistry and Biology
\item 11 students study both Physics and Biology
\end{itemize}

A student is chosen at random. By drawing a Venn diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that the student studies all three subjects.

dif.r: Three-set Venn with unknown centre; set up equation

solutions.latex:
Let $x$ be the number studying all three subjects.

The number studying none is 12, so
$$n(\text{at least one subject})=50-12=38$$
Adding the three subject totals gives $20+25+15=60$, and $60-38=22$.

From the Venn diagram regions:
$$\begin{aligned} (9-x)+(10-x)+(11-x)+2x &= 22 \\ 30-x &= 22 \\ x &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$P(\text{all three})=\dfrac{8}{50}=\dfrac{4}{25}$$
Alternatively, using
$$P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-\big[P(A\cap B)+P(A\cap C)+P(B\cap C)\big]+P(A\cap B\cap C)$$
we get
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B\cap C) &= \dfrac{38}{50}-\dfrac{20+25+15}{50}+\dfrac{9+10+11}{50} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{50} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{25} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct Venn diagram or equation for the overlap, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Sum of probabilities and mean formula; two standard steps

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.1+b+0.3 &= 1 \\ b &= 0.6 \end{aligned}$$
Using $\mu=\sum x\,P(X=x)=25$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10(0.1)+a(0.6)+30(0.3) &= 25 \\ 1+0.6a+9 &= 25 \\ 0.6a &= 15 \\ a &= 25 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One value correct, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta}$

dif.r: Trig identity proof using Pythagorean identity and difference of squares

solutions.latex:
Writing in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{1-\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{(1+\sin\theta)(1-\sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{1-\sin\theta} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the first term of the geometric sequence $3, 3\sqrt{2}, 6, 6\sqrt{2}, \ldots$ which exceeds 800?

dif.r: Geometric term inequality solved with logs, integer interpretation

solutions.latex:
The sequence is geometric with $a=3$ and $r=\sqrt{2}$, so $T_n=3(\sqrt{2})^{n-1}$.

We need $T_n>800$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3(\sqrt{2})^{n-1} &> 800 \\ (\sqrt{2})^{n-1} &> \dfrac{800}{3} \\ (n-1)\log(\sqrt{2}) &> \log\left(\dfrac{800}{3}\right) \\ n-1 &> \dfrac{\log\left(\frac{800}{3}\right)}{\log(\sqrt{2})} \approx 16.11 \\ n &> 17.11 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ is a whole number, the 18th term is the first to exceed 800.
criteria: Correct inequality in $n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: In an arithmetic series, the fourth term is 6 and the sum of the first 16 terms is 120. Find the common difference.

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ and $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(2a+(n-1)d)$.

From $T_4=6$:
$$a+3d=6,\quad\text{so}\quad 2a+6d=12 \quad (1)$$
From $S_{16}=120$:
$$\dfrac{16}{2}(2a+15d)=120,\quad\text{so}\quad 2a+15d=15 \quad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$9d=3$$
$$\therefore\ d=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
criteria: Both equations and progress, or equivalent merit
One correct equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Given that $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, show that the limiting sum of the series

$$\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos^2\theta + \sin\theta\cos^4\theta + \sin\theta\cos^6\theta + \ldots$$

is equal to $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$. Explain why you can find the limiting sum.

dif.r: Identify trig ratio, limiting sum identity, justify |r|<1

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=\sin\theta$ and $r=\cos^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} \\ &= \operatorname{cosec}\theta \end{aligned}$$
A limiting sum exists when $-1<r<1$. For $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0<\cos^2\theta<1$, so the limiting sum can be found.

parts.latex:
For the series $x + \dfrac{x}{5} + \dfrac{x}{25} + \cdots$

What is the value of $x$ for which the series has a limiting sum of $\dfrac{5}{6}$?

dif.r: Limiting sum formula used in reverse to solve for x

solutions.latex:
The first term is $a = x$ and the common ratio is
$$r = \dfrac{x}{5} \div x = \dfrac{1}{5}$$
Using the limiting sum formula:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{x}{1 - \frac{1}{5}} \\ &= \dfrac{5x}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\dfrac{5}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5x}{4} &= \dfrac{5}{6} \\ x &= \dfrac{4}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\cot\theta$, given that $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \pi$ ?

dif.r: Reference triangle plus quadrant sign to get cot

solutions.latex:

In the reference triangle the hypotenuse is $3$ and the adjacent side is $2$. By Pythagoras' theorem, the opposite side is

Then
$$\cot\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{-2}{\sqrt{5}}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

Tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants, with reference angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

Both lie in $-\pi < x < \pi$, so the answer is option B.

questions.stem: A clerk is employed at an initial salary of \$18\,320 per annum and after each year of service he receives an increase of \$780 per year.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: What is his salary for the second year of employment?

dif.r: Single addition of the yearly increase

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: What is his salary for the tenth year of employment?

dif.r: Substitute into arithmetic nth term formula

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: What are his total earnings over ten years of employment?

dif.r: Direct arithmetic series sum with known last term

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The salary rises by $\$780$ after the first year.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Salary} &= \$18\,320 + \$780 \\ &= \$19\,100 \end{aligned}$$

The salaries form an arithmetic sequence with $a = 18\,320$ and $d = 780$, so the tenth term is $a + 9d$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= \$(18\,320 + 9 \times 780) \\ &= \$25\,340 \end{aligned}$$

Using the arithmetic series sum $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$ with $n=10$, $a = 18\,320$ and $l = 25\,340$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}(18\,320 + 25\,340) \\ &= \$218\,300 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the sum formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: $x$, $x^2$ and $7x$ are the first three consecutive terms of an arithmetic series.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that $x(x-4) = 0$

dif.r: Equal common differences condition, simple algebra to given result

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence, find the first 3 terms of this series if all the terms are positive integers.

dif.r: Reject x=0, substitute x=4 into terms

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
In an arithmetic series the common difference is constant, so $T_2 - T_1 = T_3 - T_2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 - x &= 7x - x^2 \\ 2x^2 - 8x &= 0 \\ 2x(x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(x-4) = 0$$
criteria: Correct equation from the common difference, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (i), $x = 0$ or $x = 4$.

The terms are positive, so $x \ne 0$ and $x = 4$.

The terms are $4,\ 16,\ 28$.

parts.latex: Show that the sequence $\log_{10} 3,\ \log_{10} 9,\ \log_{10} 81, \dots$ is a geometric sequence.

dif.r: Justify constant ratio using log power law

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
A sequence is geometric if consecutive ratios are equal. Using $\log_{10} 9 = 2\log_{10} 3$ and $\log_{10} 81 = 4\log_{10} 3$:
$$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{\log_{10} 9}{\log_{10} 3} = 2$$
$$\dfrac{T_3}{T_2} = \dfrac{\log_{10} 81}{\log_{10} 9} = 2$$
Since $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{T_3}{T_2}$, the sequence is geometric.
criteria: Finds one ratio, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: How many terms of the series $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \cdots$ give a sum of $\dfrac{2047}{2048}$?

dif.r: Geometric sum formula in reverse, solve 2^n=2048

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Using $S_n = \dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2047}{2048} &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\right)}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{1}{2^n} \end{aligned}$$
So $2^n = 2048 = 2^{11}$, hence $n = 11$.

There are $11$ terms.
criteria: Correct equation for $S_n$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Calculate the sum of all the numbers between 100 and 400 (non-inclusive), which are not divisible by 7.

dif.r: Plan complement: total sum minus multiples of 7, two series

solutions.latex:
First find the sum of all the integers from 101 to 399, an arithmetic series with $n = 299$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{299}{2}(101 + 399) \\ &= 74\,750 \end{aligned}$$
The multiples of 7 in this range are $105, 112, 119, \cdots, 399$. Find how many there are using $T_n = a + (n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} 399 &= 105 + (n-1)\times 7 \\ n &= 43 \end{aligned}$$
Their sum is
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{43}{2}(105 + 399) \\ &= 10\,836 \end{aligned}$$
Subtract the multiples of 7 from the total.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum} &= 74\,750 - 10\,836 \\ &= 63\,914 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the sum is } 63\,914$$
criteria: Finds the sum of the multiples of 7, or equivalent merit
Finds the number of multiples of 7, or equivalent merit
Finds the sum of all numbers from 101 to 399, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Using the formula for the limiting sum of a geometric series, convert the recurring decimal $4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5}$ into a mixed fraction.

dif.r: Express recurring decimal as geometric series, apply limiting sum

solutions.latex:
Write the decimal as a whole number plus a geometric series.
$$4.353535\ldots = 4 + 0.35 + 0.0035 + 0.000035 + \cdots$$
The terms after $4$ form a geometric series with $a = 0.35$ and $r = 0.01$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum $S = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$ applies.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5} &= 4 + \dfrac{0.35}{1 - 0.01} \\ &= 4 + \dfrac{35}{99} \\ &= 4\dfrac{35}{99} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 4 \cdot \dot{3}\dot{5} = 4\dfrac{35}{99}$$
criteria: Finds correct $a$ and $r$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact values of $\theta$ such that $2\sin^2\theta = 1 - \sin\theta$, where $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.

dif.r: Quadratic in sin, solve two standard trig equations

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to a quadratic in $\sin\theta$.
$$2\sin^2\theta + \sin\theta - 1 = 0$$
Factorising (or using the quadratic formula):
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1^2 - 4(2)(-1)}}{2\times 2} \\ &= -1 \text{ or } \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $\sin\theta = -1$:
$$\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
For $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
criteria: Finds both values of $\sin\theta$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $(1 + \cot^2 x)(\sec^2 x - 1) = \sec^2 x$

dif.r: Short identity proof using Pythagorean identities

solutions.latex:
Use the identities $1 + \cot^2 x = \text{cosec}^2 x$ and $\sec^2 x - 1 = \tan^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= (1 + \cot^2 x)(\sec^2 x - 1) \\ &= \text{cosec}^2 x \times \tan^2 x \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x}\times\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \sec^2 x \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the identities correctly, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The population of salmon in a salmon farm grows and reduces as fish are born and sold.

The population $P$ is given by $P = 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900$ where $t$ is time in days.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Determine the initial population.

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the minimum number of salmon in the farm at any time?

dif.r: Minimum when cosine equals -1

parts.label: c
parts.latex: How many days will it take for salmon population to first reach 1150?

dif.r: Solve trig equation, choose smallest positive solution

solutions.latex:
The initial population is at $t = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 500\cos(0) + 900 \\ &= 1400 \end{aligned}$$

The minimum occurs when $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) = -1$.
$$\begin{aligned} P_{\min} &= -500 + 900 \\ &= 400 \end{aligned}$$

Set $P = 1150$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1150 &= 500\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) + 900 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For the first time, take the smallest positive angle.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{4} &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ t &= \dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ days}$$

parts.latex: If $y = \dfrac{x}{\ln x}$, show that $y^2 - xy + x^2 y' = 0$

dif.r: Quotient rule then careful substitution and algebraic simplification

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$y' = \dfrac{\ln x - 1}{(\ln x)^2}$$
Substitute into the left side.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= y^2 - xy + x^2 y' \\ &= \left(\dfrac{x}{\ln x}\right)^2 - x\times\dfrac{x}{\ln x} + x^2\,\dfrac{\ln x - 1}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2 - x^2\ln x + x^2\ln x - x^2}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= 0 \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative and substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Determine the equation of the normal to the curve $y = \cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ at the point where $x = \pi$.

$$y' = -\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$$
At $x=\pi$:
$$m_{\text{tangent}} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The normal is perpendicular, so $m_{\text{normal}} = 2$.

At $x = \pi$, $y = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y - 0 &= 2(x - \pi) \\ y &= 2x - 2\pi \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct normal gradient, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Combine the logarithms using $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$.
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)&=2 \\ \log_2\big(x(x-3)\big)&=2 \\ x(x-3)&=2^2 \\ x^2-3x-4&=0\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies a log law correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-3x-4&=0 \\ (x-4)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=4$ or $x=-1$.

The logarithms need $x>0$ and $x-3>0$, so $x>3$.

Hence $-1$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x=4$$

meta.format_note: Source factorised as $(x-4)(x-1)$ giving $x=1$; correct factors are $(x-4)(x+1)$ giving $x=-1$. Fixed; conclusion $x=4$ unchanged.

parts.latex: Find the exact arc length $CQ$.

parts.latex: Find the exact area of the sector $OAP$.

dif.r: Direct substitution into sector area formula

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the exact length of interval $AP$, correct to 1 decimal place.

dif.r: Cosine rule in isosceles triangle with radian angle

figures.cap: rectangle OABC with sectors OAP and OCQ

solutions.latex:
Angles at $O$ on a straight line sum to $\pi$; $\angle AOC=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (rectangle) and $\angle AOP=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle COQ&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The radius of arc $CQ$ is $OC=2$ cm, so using $l=r\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}l_{CQ}&=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$

The radius of sector $OAP$ is $OA=7$ cm. Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 7^2\times\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{49\pi}{12}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the formula correctly (recognising the radius), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Apply the cosine rule in triangle $OAP$, where $OP=OA=7$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned}AP^2&=OP^2+OA^2-2\times OP\times OA\cos\angle AOP \\ &=7^2+7^2-2\times 7\times 7\times\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=98-98\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=98-49\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned}AP&=\sqrt{98-49\sqrt{3}} \\ &\approx 3.6234\ldots \\ &\approx 3.6\text{ cm (1 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the cosine rule correctly, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The probability that a student plays badminton is 0.3. The probability that a student plays neither table tennis or badminton is 0.5, and the probability that a student plays both sports is $x$.

parts.latex:

\exfigure{1306_q18_1}

$P(B)=\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$

$P(B\cap T)=\_\_\_\_$

dif.r: Read given probabilities straight into notation

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the probability that a student plays table tennis but not badminton

dif.r: Venn diagram total equals one, algebra with unknown x

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
It is known that if a student plays table tennis, the probability that they also play badminton is 0.5

Find the probability that a student plays both badminton and table tennis.

dif.r: Set up conditional probability equation in x and solve

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, determine the probability that a student plays only badminton.

dif.r: One subtraction using found value of x

figures.cap: Venn diagram with B, T and 0.5 outside

solutions.latex:
The probabilities in the Venn diagram sum to $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}1&=0.5+P(B)+P(T)-P(B\cap T) \\ 0.5&=0.3+P(T)-x \\ P(T)&=0.2+x\end{aligned}$$
Table tennis but not badminton:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(T\cap\overline{B}\right)&=P(T)-P(B\cap T) \\ &=0.2+x-x \\ &=0.2\end{aligned}$$

Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P(B\mid T)&=\dfrac{P(B\cap T)}{P(T)} \\ 0.5&=\dfrac{x}{0.2+x} \\ 0.1+0.5x&=x \\ 0.1&=0.5x \\ x&=0.2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(B\cap T)=0.2$$
criteria: Applies the conditional probability formula and substitutes, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Badminton only is badminton less both sports.
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(B\cap\overline{T}\right)&=0.3-x \\ &=0.3-0.2 \\ &=0.1\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A particle moves such that its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, at a time $t$ seconds is given by $\dot{x}=4-8\cos t$.

The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the two times the particle is first at rest?

dif.r: Set velocity zero, solve basic trig equation for two times

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the equation for displacement $x$ in terms of time $t$.

dif.r: Integrate velocity, then use initial condition to find constant.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the exact distance travelled by the particle between the first two times it is at rest.

dif.r: Solve v=0, check sign, evaluate exact displacements and subtract.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4-8\cos t \\ 8\cos t&=4 \\ \cos t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The first quadrant solution is $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is also positive in the fourth quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The first two times the particle is at rest are $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ seconds and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ seconds.
criteria: Reaches $\cos t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and the first quadrant solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrating the velocity gives the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int(4-8\cos t)\,dt\\&=4t-8\sin t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle is at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4(0)-8\sin 0+C\\C&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=4t-8\sin t$$

The particle is at rest when $4-8\cos t=0$, that is $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$. Since $v>0$ between these times, the distance travelled is the difference in displacement.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=4\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}-8\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-8\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
When $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=4\times\dfrac{5\pi}{3}-8\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+8\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}-\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-4\sqrt{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{16\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}\text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one correct displacement for one of the times, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rest times from part (a) and the sign of $v$ added as brief set-up, not in source.

questions.stem: The population of an island is increasing according to the formula $P=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}$ where $P$ is the population in thousands and $t$ is the time in years after January 1st 2020.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the initial rate of change of the population of the island.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential model, substitute t=0, interpret thousands.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Use the model to predict the population on 1st January 2040, correct to the nearest thousand.

dif.r: Direct substitution into the given model.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Using the model, predict in what year will the population reach 40 000.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation with logs, convert to calendar year.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating the population formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=10\times\dfrac{1}{50}e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}e^{\frac{t}{50}}\end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{5}e^0=\dfrac{1}{5}$$
$P$ is in thousands, so initially the population is increasing at a rate of $200$ people per year.

On 1 January 2040, $t=20$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=20+10e^{\frac{20}{50}}\\&\approx 34.9182\end{aligned}$$
The predicted population on 1 January 2040 is $35\,000$.

The population is $40$ thousand, so $P=40$.
$$\begin{aligned}40&=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\e^{\frac{t}{50}}&=2\\\dfrac{t}{50}&=\ln 2\\t&=50\ln 2\\&\approx 34.657\end{aligned}$$
The population will reach $40\,000$ during 2054.
criteria: Substitutes and starts solving the equation, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The height of water $h$ metres in a harbour can be modelled using the function below:

$h=4-A\sin(bt)$, where $t$ is the time in hours after midnight.

\exfigure{1306_q22_1}

At 2 am the height of water in the harbour is at its minimum.

At 6 am the height of water in the harbour is at its maximum.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $A$ and $b$.

dif.r: Amplitude from min/max; period from half-period gap.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
A boat can only enter the harbour when the height of the water is more than 5 metres.

Express the information given as an equation, and solve the equation to find the first time the boat can enter the harbour.

dif.r: Solve sin(πt/4)=-1/2 in correct quadrants, convert to clock time.

figures.cap: graph of h against t, minimum 2 at t=2, maximum 6 at t=6, period 8

solutions.latex:
The minimum is at 2 am and the maximum at 6 am, so the minimum height is $2$ and the maximum is $6$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{amplitude}&=\dfrac{6-2}{2}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A=2$$
Half a period is $4$ hours (from minimum to maximum), so the period is $8$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{b}&=8\\b&=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A=2,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$
criteria: At least one correct value, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The boat can enter when $h>5$, so first solve $h=5$ with $A=2$, $b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned}5&=4-2\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\\\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\\t&=\dfrac{28}{6},\ \dfrac{44}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The first time is $t=\dfrac{28}{6}=4\text{ h }40\text{ min}$.
$$\therefore\text{ the boat can first enter at } 4{:}40 \text{ am}$$
criteria: Sets up the equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with 4 sub-intervals to estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{x}\,dx$, correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Routine trapezoidal rule with four sub-intervals.

solutions.latex:
There are 4 sub-intervals on $[0,2]$, so $h=\dfrac{2-0}{4}=0.5$ and the $x$ values are $0,\ 0.5,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2\sqrt{x}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{0.5}{2}\left(\sqrt{0}+\sqrt{2}+2\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}}+\sqrt{1}+\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)\right)\\&\approx 1.8194\\&\approx 1.82\text{ (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the table or substitutes correctly into the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the equation $2\cos^2 x=4-5\sin x$ may be written as $2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2=0$.

dif.r: One Pythagorean substitution and rearrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence solve $2\cos^2 x=4-5\sin x$, for $0^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ$.

dif.r: Factorise quadratic in sin x, reject sin x=2, solve.

solutions.latex:
Using $\cos^2 x=1-\sin^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2 x&=4-5\sin x\\2\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)&=4-5\sin x\\2-2\sin^2 x&=4-5\sin x\\2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+4-2&=0\\2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2&=0\end{aligned}$$

From part (a), the equation is $2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2=0$. Factorise.
$$\begin{aligned}2\sin^2 x-4\sin x-\sin x+2&=0\\2\sin x(\sin x-2)-1(\sin x-2)&=0\\(2\sin x-1)(\sin x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\sin x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\sin x=2$.

Since $-1\le\sin x\le 1$, $\sin x=2$ is rejected.
$$\sin x=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ x=30^\circ,\ 150^\circ$$
criteria: Finds the quadratic in terms of $\sin x$ and factorises, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The line $y=24(x-1)$ is tangent to the curve $y=ax^3+bx^2+4$ at $x=2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Using the fact that the tangent meets the curve to show that $2a+b=5$.

dif.r: Find contact point from tangent, substitute into curve.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By finding another relationship between $a$ and $b$, find the values of $a$ and $b$.

dif.r: Equate derivative to tangent gradient, solve simultaneous equations.

solutions.latex:
When $x=2$ the tangent has
$$\begin{aligned}y&=24(2-1)\\&=24\end{aligned}$$
The point of contact is $(2,24)$, which also lies on the curve $y=ax^3+bx^2+4$.
$$\begin{aligned}24&=a\times 2^3+b\times 2^2+4\\24&=8a+4b+4\\20&=8a+4b\\5&=2a+b\quad\ldots(1)\end{aligned}$$

The gradient of the curve at $x=2$ equals the gradient of the tangent, $24$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3ax^2+2bx\\24&=3a\times 2^2+2b\times 2\\24&=12a+4b\\6&=3a+b\quad\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$a=1$$
Substituting into (1): $2+b=5$.
$$\therefore\ a=1,\ b=3$$
criteria: Differentiates and sets the gradient equal to $24$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: d
parts.latex: By considering the symmetry of the table in (a), show that the probability of Jack and Jill obtaining the same score is $\dfrac{73}{648}$.

figures.cap: blank 6 by 6 table for the sum of two dice
partial tree diagram for Die 1 to Die 4 with branches 1,2 and 3,4,5,6
partly completed probability distribution table for X

solutions.latex: \extable{Ts6024_1}

There are $4$ ways of scoring $9$ out of $36$ equally likely outcomes.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Jack gets }9)&=\dfrac{4}{36}\\&=\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$

The two children throw independently, so the probabilities multiply.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Jack and Jill both score }9)&=P(\text{Jack scores }9)\times P(\text{Jill scores }9)\\&=\dfrac{1}{9}\times\dfrac{1}{9}\\&=\dfrac{1}{81}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had an ampersand inside \text; replaced with 'and' to avoid a LaTeX alignment error.

solutions.latex:
By symmetry of the table, $P(k,k)$ for score $k$ equals $P(14-k,14-k)$, so the scores $2$ to $6$ are matched with $12$ to $8$.
$$\begin{aligned}&P(\text{same score})\\&=P(2,2)+P(3,3)+\cdots+P(12,12)\\&=2P(2,2)+2P(3,3)+2P(4,4)+2P(5,5)+2P(6,6)+P(7,7)\\&=P(7,7)+2\big[P(2,2)+P(3,3)+P(4,4)+P(5,5)+P(6,6)\big]\\&=\left(\dfrac{6}{36}\right)^2+2\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{2}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{4}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{5}{36}\right)^2\right]\\&=\dfrac{73}{648}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to work towards the probability, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's middle line used an ellipsis-free full sum; shortened with $\cdots$ in the first expansion only. Symmetry sentence added.

solutions.latex:
The events Jack scores more, less, or the same as Jill are exhaustive. By symmetry, $P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})=P(\text{Jack}<\text{Jill})$, and from part (d) $P(\text{Jack}=\text{Jill})=\dfrac{73}{648}$.
$$\begin{aligned}1&=P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})+P(\text{Jack}<\text{Jill})+P(\text{Jack}=\text{Jill})\\1&=2P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})+\dfrac{73}{648}\\2P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})&=1-\dfrac{73}{648}\\P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})&=\dfrac{575}{1296}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the equation, or uses the previous part to attempt the probability, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$X\le 2$ means every die shows $1$ or $2$. From the diagram, each die shows $1$ or $2$ with probability
$$P(1\text{ or }2\text{ on one die})=\dfrac{2}{6}$$
The four dice are independent.
$$\begin{aligned}P(1\text{ or }2\text{ on every die})&=\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{6}\\&=\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^4\\&=\dfrac{1}{81}\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts6030_1}
criteria: Some correct values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$ with the distribution from part (g):
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=1\times\dfrac{1}{1296}+2\times\dfrac{15}{1296}+3\times\dfrac{65}{1296}+4\times\dfrac{175}{1296}+5\times\dfrac{369}{1296}+6\times\dfrac{671}{1296}\\&\approx 5.24\text{ (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Values checked: $E(X)=\dfrac{6797}{1296}\approx 5.24$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\text{Var}(X)=E\left(X^2\right)-[E(X)]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Var}(X)&=E\left(X^2\right)-\left(\dfrac{6797}{1296}\right)^2\\&=\dfrac{1}{1296}+\dfrac{60}{1296}+\dfrac{585}{1296}+\dfrac{2800}{1296}+\dfrac{9225}{1296}+\dfrac{24156}{1296}-\left(\dfrac{6797}{1296}\right)^2\\&=\dfrac{36827}{1296}-\left(\dfrac{6797}{1296}\right)^2\\&\approx 0.91\text{ (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some correct working towards the variance, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The diagram shows a part of the curve with equation $x=y^2$ and a fixed point $S(1,0)$.

Point $P$ lies on the curve and has $y$-coordinate $k$, where $k\ge 0$.

\exfigure{1306_q27_1}

NOT TO SCALE

The distance of $P$ from the $y$-axis is $d$, and $r$ is the ratio $\dfrac{d}{SP}$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $r=\dfrac{k^2}{\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}$

dif.r: Set up coordinates of P, distance formula, form ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{dr}{dk}=\dfrac{2k-k^3}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$.

dif.r: Quotient and chain rule with careful surd algebra to given form.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By solving $\dfrac{dr}{dk}=0$, find and verify the value of $k$ that gives the maximum of $r$.

dif.r: Solve numerator zero, reject negatives, sign test for maximum.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Hence, find the exact maximum value of $r$.

dif.r: Substitute k=√2 into given expression.

figures.cap: part of curve x=y^2, point S(1,0), point P and distance d to the y-axis

solutions.latex:
$P$ lies on $x=y^2$ with $y=k$, so $P\left(k^2,k\right)$.

The distance from the $y$-axis is the $x$-coordinate, so $d=k^2$.

Using the distance formula with $S(1,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned}PS^2&=\left(k^2-1\right)^2+(k-0)^2\\&=k^4-2k^2+1+k^2\\&=k^4-k^2+1\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{d}{PS}\\&=\dfrac{k^2}{\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the expression for $d$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dk}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=k^2 & v&=\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\u'&=2k & v'&=\dfrac{4k^3-2k}{2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}\end{aligned}$$
where $v'$ comes from the chain rule:
$$v'=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(4k^3-2k\right)$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dr}{dk}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\times 2k-k^2\times\frac{4k^3-2k}{2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}}{\left(\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\right)^2}\\&=\dfrac{4k\left(\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\right)^2-k^2\left(4k^3-2k\right)}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)\times 2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}\\&=\dfrac{4k\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)-k^2\left(4k^3-2k\right)}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{4k^5-4k^3+4k-4k^5+2k^3}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{4k-2k^3}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{2k-k^3}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\end{aligned}$$

$$k=\sqrt{2}$$

parts.latex:
Find the coordinates of any horizontal points of inflexion on the curve with equation

$y=x^4-8x^3+18x^2+4$

dif.r: Combine y''=0, y'=0 conditions and concavity check.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate twice.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^4-8x^3+18x^2+4\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=4x^3-24x^2+36x\\\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=12x^2-48x+36\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflexion occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=12x^2-48x+36\\0&=x^2-4x+3\\0&=(x-3)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=1\text{ or }x=3$$
For a horizontal point of inflexion, the value of $x$ must also be a stationary point, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

When $x=1$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(1)^3-24(1)^2+36(1)=16\ne 0$$
When $x=3$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(3)^3-24(3)^2+36(3)=0$$
So only $x=3$ is stationary. Check for a change of concavity:

\extable{Ts6037_1}

When $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3^4-8(3)^3+18(3)^2+4\\&=31\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (3,31)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion}$$
criteria: Finds which value is also a stationary point and its $y$-value, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let the $x$-value of the point of intersection be $a$. The point lies on both $y=x^2$ and $y=mx$, so $a^2=ma$.
$$m=a$$
The line is above the curve between $x=0$ and $x=a$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{32}{3}&=\int_0^a\left(mx-x^2\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{mx^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^a\\&=\dfrac{ma^2}{2}-\dfrac{a^3}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying by $6$:
$$\begin{aligned}64&=3ma^2-2a^3\\&=3a^3-2a^3\quad(\text{since }m=a)\\a^3&=64\\a&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=a=4$$

questions.stem:
The diagram shows part of the curve with the equation $y=f(x)$, where

$f(x)=x^2-7x+5\log_e x+8$, $x>0$.

\exfigure{1306_q30_1}

The points $A$ and $B$ are stationary points of the curve.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

dif.r: Map point under translation and negative dilation; nature flips.

figures.cap: curve y=f(x) with stationary points A (local max) and B (local min)

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $f(x)=x^2-7x+5\ln x+8$.
$$f'(x)=2x-7+\dfrac{5}{x}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2x-7+\dfrac{5}{x}\\0&=2x^2-7x+5\\0&=2x^2-2x-5x+5\\0&=2x(x-1)-5(x-1)\\0&=(2x-5)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$x=1\text{ or }x=\dfrac{5}{2}$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(1)&=1-7+5\ln 1+8\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{5}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}f\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)&=\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^2-7\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)+5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)+8\\&=5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)-\dfrac{13}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A(1,2),\quad B\left(\dfrac{5}{2},\ 5\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)-\dfrac{13}{4}\right)$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=-2f(x-1)$ is the graph of $f(x)$ shifted $1$ unit right, then dilated vertically by a factor of $-2$.

So $A(1,2)$ maps to
$$A_1=(1+1,\ -2\times 2)=(2,-4)$$
The factor $-2$ reflects the graph in the $x$-axis, so the local maximum at $A$ becomes a local minimum.
$$\therefore\ A_1=(2,-4),\text{ a local minimum}$$
criteria: Finds the coordinates of $A_1$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Build area relation from rectangles and general integral of x^n.

can_use: Area with respect to the y-axis

figures.cap: graph of y=x^n with red region R and blue region B between x=a and x=b

solutions.latex:
Let $B$ be the blue area, $W$ the area of the small rectangle and $R$ the area of the big rectangle.

The blue area is
$$\begin{aligned}B&=\int_a^b x^n\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left[x^{n+1}\right]_a^b\\&=\dfrac{1}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right)\end{aligned}$$
The rectangle areas are
$$\begin{aligned}W&=a\times a^n=a^{n+1}\\R&=b\times b^n=b^{n+1}\end{aligned}$$
The big rectangle is made of the blue area, the red area (three times the blue) and the small rectangle.
$$\begin{aligned}R&=B+3B+W\\&=4B+W\\b^{n+1}&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right)+a^{n+1}\\b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\left(b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}\right)\\1&=\dfrac{4}{n+1}\\n+1&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n=3$$
criteria: Sets up the equation relating the areas, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following expressions is equivalent to $4+\log_2 x^2$ ?

dif.r: Several log-law steps to match an unfamiliar equivalent form.

solutions.latex:
Write $4=4\log_2 2=\log_2 2^4$, then combine using the log laws.
$$\begin{aligned}4+\log_2 x^2&=4\log_2 2+\log_2 x^2\\&=\log_2 2^4+\log_2 x^2\\&=\log_2 16+\log_2 x^2\\&=\log_2 16x^2\\&=\log_2(4x)^2\\&=2\log_2 4x\end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
At a point $P(k-2,y)$ on $f(x)=kx^2-kx-k^2$ the gradient of the tangent is $3k-8$.

What is the value of $k$?

dif.r: Differentiate with parameter, substitute, solve resulting quadratic.

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent is $f'(x)$.
$$f'(x)=2kx-k$$
At $x=k-2$:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(k-2)&=2k(k-2)-k\\&=2k^2-5k\end{aligned}$$
Equate this to the given gradient $3k-8$.
$$\begin{aligned}2k^2-5k&=3k-8\\2k^2-8k+8&=0\\k^2-4k+4&=0\\(k-2)^2&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$k=2$$
This is option A.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=x^3-(m^2-4)x+1$.

For which of the values of $m$ below is $f(x)$ many-to-one?

dif.r: Links many-to-one cubic to turning points via discriminant of derivative.

can_use: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

solutions.latex:
$f(x)$ is many-to-one when the cubic has two stationary points, that is, when $f'(x)=0$ has two real roots, so the discriminant of $f'(x)$ is positive.
$$f'(x)=3x^2-(m^2-4)$$
$$\Delta=b^2-4ac=0+12(m^2-4)$$
Now $\Delta>0$ requires:
$$\begin{aligned}12(m^2-4)&>0\\m^2-4&>0\\(m+2)(m-2)&>0\end{aligned}$$
Hence $m>2$ or $m<-2$.

Only $m=-4$ satisfies this, so the answer is option A.

parts.latex:
Charlie is applying for membership at a new golf club that has a strong reputation. The scores of his current club have a lower quartile of 110 and an upper quartile of 118 and Charlie’s score is not an outlier.

Given that the club he plans to join has scores with a lower quartile of 90 and an upper quartile of 106, can you assure Charlie that his score will not be an outlier in his new club? Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.
parts.note: Quartiles, IQR and outliers are not in 2024 Advanced (Mathematics Standard).

dif.r: Compare outlier fences across clubs and justify conclusion.

solutions.latex:
A score is an outlier if it lies outside $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$ and $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

Current club:
$$IQR=118-110=8$$
$$1.5\times IQR=12$$
$$\text{Upper bound}=118+12=130,\quad\text{Lower bound}=110-12=98$$
$\therefore$ Charlie's score is between $98$ and $130$.

New club:
$$IQR=106-90=16$$
$$1.5\times IQR=24$$
$$\text{Upper bound}=106+24=130,\quad\text{Lower bound}=90-24=66$$
$\therefore$ Charlie is not an outlier in the new club, as his score is not outside the bounds $66$ to $130$.
criteria: Finds the range of Charlie's score between $98$ and $130$, or equivalent merit
Finds the IQR of either club, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Mani is a fruit grower. After his oranges are picked, they are sorted by a machine, according to size. The distribution of the diameter, in centimetres, of oranges is modelled by a continuous random variable, $X$, with probability density function given below.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{3x^3}{4}+15x^2-99x+216 & 6\le x\le 8\\[6pt] 0 & \text{Otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ for the domain $6\le x\le 8$.

dif.r: Integrate polynomial pdf from lower bound to get CDF.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise, find the probability that a randomly selected orange has a diameter greater than 7cm.

dif.r: Complement of CDF value already found; one substitution.

can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the mode of the distribution.

dif.r: Mode via differentiating cubic pdf, factorising quadratic, comparing values.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_6^x f(t)\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_6^x\left(-\dfrac{3t^3}{4}+15t^2-99t+216\right)dt\\&=\left[-\dfrac{3}{16}t^4+5t^3-\dfrac{99}{2}t^2+216t\right]_6^x\\&=-\dfrac{3}{16}x^4+5x^3-\dfrac{99}{2}x^2+216x-351\end{aligned}$$
criteria: States the integral for $F(x)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Corrected from source: the integrand and the antiderivative bracket had the $t^3$ and $t^4$ terms with a missing minus sign (written $+\dfrac{3t^3}{4}$ and $+\dfrac{3}{16}t^4$). The final $F(x)$ was already right and $F(6)=0$ checks.

solutions.latex:
The mode occurs at the global maximum, that is at a stationary point or at an end of the domain.

End points:
$$f(6)=0,\quad f(8)=0$$
To find stationary points, differentiate:
$$f'(x)=-\dfrac{3}{4}\left(3x^2-40x+132\right)$$
Set $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-40x+132 &= 0 \\ (3x-22)(x-6) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $x=6$ or $x=\dfrac{22}{3}$.

Values of $f$ at these points:
$$f(6)=0,\quad f\left(\dfrac{22}{3}\right)=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
The greatest value is $\dfrac{8}{9}$, at $x=\dfrac{22}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the mode of the distribution is } \dfrac{22}{3}$$
criteria: Checks the end points, or finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The time, $X$ minutes, taken by Fred to install a satellite dish may be assumed to be normally distributed, with a mean of 134 and a standard deviation of 16.

The table below provides some values of the probabilities for the standard normal distribution.

i.e. $\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{z}\phi(t)\,dt$

\extable{1309_q20_t1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate $P(X<150)$.

dif.r: Standardise to z=1 and read table directly.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Fred’s company policy states that safe installations require a minimum of $a$ minutes to complete. Fred has been informed that 5.5\% of his installation times do not meet this minimum standard.

Find the value of $a$.

dif.r: Inverse normal lookup using symmetry, then unstandardise.

solutions.latex:
Standardise:
$$z=\dfrac{150-134}{16}=1$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<150) &= P(Z<1) \\ &= 0.841 \text{ (from the table)} \\ &= 84.1\% \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using the empirical rule:
$$68\%+13.5\%+2.35\%+0.15\%=84\%$$

meta.marker_note: Accept $84.1\%$ from the table or $84\%$ from the empirical rule.

solutions.latex:
Fred's times that fail the standard are those below $a$:
$$P(X<a)=0.055$$
So
$$P(X>a)=1-0.055=0.945$$
From the table, $P(Z<1.6)=0.945$, and by symmetry $P(Z>-1.6)=0.945$.

Therefore $a$ corresponds to a $z$-score of $-1.6$.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 134-1.6\times 16 \\ &= 108.4 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given the functions $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-1}$ and $g(x)=e^x$, state the domain of $f\big(g(x)\big)$. Give your answer in \textbf{interval notation}.

dif.r: Form composite, exclude zero denominator, interval notation.

solutions.latex:
Compose the functions:
$$f\big(g(x)\big)=\dfrac{1}{e^x-1}$$
The denominator cannot be zero:
$$\begin{aligned} e^x-1 &\ne 0 \\ e^x &\ne 1 \\ x &\ne 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the domain of } f\big(g(x)\big) \text{ is } (-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $y=2xe^{\frac{x}{2}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Product rule, solve f'=0, sign test; routine.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find coordinates of any points of inflection.

dif.r: Second derivative by product rule, solve, check concavity change.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: For what values of $x$ is the curve concave down?

dif.r: Read sign of given f'' expression; one step.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Draw a sketch of the curve, showing all critical points.

dif.r: Sketch from found features; asymptotic behaviour as x to minus infinity.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=2xe^{x/2} with critical points

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=2 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2e^{\frac{x}{2}}+xe^{\frac{x}{2}} \\ &= (2+x)e^{\frac{x}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$. Since $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$, this needs $2+x=0$, so $x=-2$.
$$f(-2)=-\dfrac{4}{e}\approx -1.47$$
Test the sign of $f'(x)$ either side of $x=-2$:

\extable{Ts6126_1}

The gradient changes from negative to positive.
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a minimum turning point at } \left(-2,-\dfrac{4}{e}\right)$$
criteria: Finds the stationary point, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch for part (d) is a separate solution.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $f'(x)=(2+x)e^{\frac{x}{2}}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2+x & v&=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}+\dfrac{2+x}{2}e^{\frac{x}{2}} \\ &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(1+\dfrac{2+x}{2}\right) \\ &= e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(\dfrac{4+x}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$, $f''(x)=0$ when $4+x=0$, so $x=-4$.

Test the sign of $f''(x)$ either side of $x=-4$:

\extable{Ts6127_1}

The concavity changes at $x=-4$.
$$f(-4)=-\dfrac{8}{e^2}\approx -1.083$$
$$\therefore\ \text{there is a point of inflection at } \left(-4,-\dfrac{8}{e^2}\right)$$

From part (b), $f''(x)=e^{\frac{x}{2}}\left(\dfrac{4+x}{2}\right)$ and $e^{\frac{x}{2}}>0$.

The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$, that is when $4+x<0$.
$$\therefore\ x<-4$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The $y$-intercept is at $x=0$:
$$f(0)=0$$
The $x$-intercept is at $y=0$:
$$2xe^{\frac{x}{2}}=0$$
so $x=0$.

\exfigure{1309_q22_s1}

parts.latex:
The effectiveness of a drug is measured by its ability to reduce the number of bacteria in a culture over time. The culture is reduced according to the model $N=N_0e^{-kt}$ where $N$ is the number of bacteria and $t$ is the time since the drug was administered in minutes.

A drug is tested in a culture initially with 1200 bacteria, which reduces to 200 in 6 minutes. How many bacteria are left in the culture after 3 minutes?

dif.r: Find k from data using logs, then substitute.

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$, $N=1200$:
$$1200=N_0e^0,\quad N_0=1200$$
so $N=1200e^{-kt}$.

When $t=6$, $N=200$:
$$\begin{aligned} 200 &= 1200e^{-6k} \\ e^{-6k} &= \dfrac{200}{1200}=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ -6k &= \ln\dfrac{1}{6} \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{1}{6}}{-6}\approx 0.299 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
So $N=1200e^{-kt}$ with $k=\dfrac{\ln 6}{6}$ (keep $k$ exact: the rounded $0.299$ gives $489.3$).

When $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 1200e^{-\frac{\ln 6}{6}\times 3} = 1200e^{-\frac12\ln 6} = \dfrac{1200}{\sqrt6} \\ &= 489.898\ldots \approx 490 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the line $1200e^{-0.299\times3}=489.898$ is false ($489.349$ with the rounded $k$); with the exact $k=\dfrac{\ln6}{6}$, $N=\dfrac{1200}{\sqrt6}\approx490$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the line $1200e^{-0.299\times3}=489.898$ is false ($489.349$ with the rounded $k$); with the exact $k=\dfrac{\ln6}{6}$, $N=\dfrac{1200}{\sqrt6}\approx490$.

parts.latex: Given that $\sin\theta=\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{19}}$ and $\theta$ is obtuse, find the exact value of $\tan\theta$ in simplest form.

dif.r: Quadrant sign plus recognising 38-12√2 as perfect square surd.

figures.cap: solution sketch: right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 2sqrt19 and side 6+sqrt2

solutions.latex:
Since $\theta$ is obtuse, it lies in quadrant 2, so $\sin\theta>0$ and $\tan\theta<0$. Construct a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $2\sqrt{19}$ and opposite side $6+\sqrt{2}$.

\exfigure{1309_q24_s1}

Let $A$ be the adjacent side. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} A^2 &= \left(2\sqrt{19}\right)^2-\left(6+\sqrt{2}\right)^2 \\ &= 76-\left(36+12\sqrt{2}+2\right) \\ &= 76-\left(38+12\sqrt{2}\right) \\ &= 38-12\sqrt{2} \\ &= 36-12\sqrt{2}+2 \\ &= \left(6-\sqrt{2}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
so $A=6-\sqrt{2}$.

In quadrant 2 the tangent is negative:
$$\therefore\ \tan\theta=-\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{6-\sqrt{2}}$$
or equivalently
$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}-6}$$

meta.marker_note: Accept $-\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{6-\sqrt{2}}$ or $\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}-6}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the total surface area of the can, $A\text{ cm}^2$, is given by:

$$A=2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right)$$

dif.r: Standard show-that: eliminate h using volume constraint.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $r$ for which the tin has a minimum surface area.

dif.r: Routine optimisation of given function with second-derivative test.

figures.cap: cylinder with radius r cm and height h cm

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$. Given $V=192\pi$:
$$h=\dfrac{192\pi}{\pi r^2}=\dfrac{192}{r^2}\qquad(1)$$
The closed can has two circular ends and a curved surface:
$$A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi\left(r^2+rh\right)\qquad(2)$$
Substitute (1) into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\pi\left(r^2+r\left(\dfrac{192}{r^2}\right)\right) \\ &= 2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes $192\pi$ into the volume formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write the area with a negative power:
$$A=2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right)=2\pi\left(r^2+192r^{-1}\right)$$
Differentiate:
$$A'=2\pi\left(2r-192r^{-2}\right),\quad A''=2\pi\left(2+384r^{-3}\right)$$
For stationary points, $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2r-\dfrac{192}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 2r &= \dfrac{192}{r^2} \\ 2r^3 &= 192 \\ r^3 &= 96 \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{96} \end{aligned}$$
Nature: when $r=\sqrt[3]{96}$,
$$A''=2\pi\left(2+\dfrac{384}{r^3}\right)=2\pi\left(2+\dfrac{384}{96}\right)>0$$
so this is a minimum turning point.
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum surface area occurs when } r=\sqrt[3]{96}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit
