parts.latex: Differentiate $\ln\big(\cos(2x)\big)$.

dif.r: Chain rule with log and trig, simplify to tan.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence, or otherwise, evaluate:

$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\tan(2x)\,dx$$

dif.r: Reverse derivative with constant adjustment, exact evaluation using log laws.

solutions.latex:
Let $u=\cos 2x$, so $u'=-2\sin 2x$, and $y=\ln u$.

Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{-2\sin 2x}{\cos 2x} \\ &= -2\tan 2x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates with a single mistake, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\cos 2x)=-2\tan 2x$, so
$$\begin{aligned} I &= \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\tan(2x)\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}-2\tan(2x)\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[\ln(\cos 2x)\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\ln(\cos 0)\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\ln 1\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct answer, in exact form $-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ or $\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2$

meta.marker_note: ECF allowed from part (a).

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows the graphs of $y=2^{-x}$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}$ and the point of intersection.

\exfigure{1309_q28_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: By solving simultaneously, show that the point of intersection occurs when $x=2$.

dif.r: Equate, combine powers of 2, match exponents.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the shaded area of the region bounded by the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis and the two curves, correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: Decompose region into two integrals of base-2 exponentials; find intercept.

figures.cap: graphs of y=2^{-x} and y=1/2-2^{-x} with shaded region

solutions.latex:
At the intersection the two $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x} &= 2^{-x} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= 2\times 2^{-x} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= 2^{1-x} \\ 2^{-1} &= 2^{1-x} \\ -1 &= 1-x \\ x &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Must solve simultaneously.

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-intercept of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x} &= 0 \\ 2^{-1} &= 2^{-x} \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The shaded area is the area under $y=2^{-x}$ from $0$ to $2$, minus the area under $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}$ from $1$ to $2$:
$$A=\int_0^2 2^{-x}\,dx-\int_1^2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= -\left[\dfrac{2^{-x}}{\ln 2}\right]_0^2-\left[\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{2^{-x}}{\ln 2}\right]_1^2 \\ &= -\left(\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}\right)-\left(\left(\dfrac{2}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2\ln 2}\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &\approx 0.9427 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expresses the area using the correct integrals, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: No penalty for a rounding error in the final answer.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that

$$\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$$

dif.r: Direct application of change of base rule.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence, solve the equation

$$6\log_x 2+\log_2 x-5=0$$

dif.r: Use reciprocal identity, hidden quadratic substitution, convert back.

solutions.latex:
To prove: $\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$.

Using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$, with base $c=b$:
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= \log_a b \\ &= \dfrac{\log_b b}{\log_b a} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\log_b a} \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Must use proper setting out for a proof.

solutions.latex:
By part (a), $\log_x 2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2 x}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 6\log_x 2+\log_2 x-5 &= 0 \\ \dfrac{6}{\log_2 x}+\log_2 x-5 &= 0 \\ 6+(\log_2 x)^2-5\log_2 x &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $u=\log_2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u^2-5u+6 &= 0 \\ (u-3)(u-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $u=3$ or $u=2$.

For $\log_2 x=3$: $x=2^3=8$.

For $\log_2 x=2$: $x=2^2=4$.
$$\therefore\ x=4 \text{ or } x=8$$
criteria: Forms the quadratic, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A weight is attached to a spring that is connected to the ceiling. The weight is pulled away from the ceiling and then released so that it bounces up and down.

Let the distance of the weight from the ceiling be $x$ metres. The spring stretches and contracts such that $x$ varies sinusoidally with time, between 1.2 metres and 1.8 metres. It takes 1 second for the weight to go from its highest point to its lowest point.

The motion of the weight can be modelled using a sine wave of the form:

$$x=a\sin(bt+c)+d$$

How far from the ceiling is the weight 2.7 seconds after it is at a high point?

dif.r: Build sinusoidal model from description, locate high point, evaluate later time.

solutions.latex:
Since $x$ is the distance from the ceiling, the high point is at $x=1.2$ and the low point is at $x=1.8$.

Amplitude and centre of motion:
$$a=\dfrac{1.8-1.2}{2}=0.3,\qquad d=\dfrac{1.8+1.2}{2}=1.5$$
The time from high to low is 1 s, which is half a period:
$$\text{period}=2\times 1=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$$
so $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$.

Assuming the weight starts ($t=0$) at the centre of motion, the distance from the ceiling is modelled by
$$x=0.3\sin(\pi t)+1.5$$
The weight is at a high point when $x=1.2$, that is when $\sin(\pi t)=-1$, which first occurs at $t=1.5$.

The required time is 2.7 s after this:
$$1.5+2.7=4.2$$
When $t=4.2$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 0.3\sin(\pi\times 4.2)+1.5 \\ &\approx 1.676 \text{ m (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
As the period is 2, the same answer follows from $t=1.5+0.7$, that is $t=0.2$.
criteria: Substitutes the correct time to find $x$, with one error, or equivalent merit
Finds $t=1.5$ for the highest point (or equivalent), or equivalent merit
Finds $b=\pi$ and recognises that the highest point corresponds to $x=1.2$, or equivalent merit
Finds the amplitude and centre of motion, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Accept $t=4.2$, $2.2$ or $0.2$, or the equivalent for the $t$ used for the highest point.

The graph of the function $y=\cos\big(2a(x-b)\big)+c$ is shown below, where $a,b$ and $c$ are constants. Point $P$ has coordinates $(b,c+1)$.

solutions.latex:
Original function: $y=\cos\big(2a(x-b)\big)+c$.

New function: $y=-c\sin\big(3a(x-b)\big)$.

questions.stem:
A competition is run where 400 raffle tickets are placed in a box.

There are two prizes to be won. The ticket for first prize is drawn from the box without replacement, and then the ticket for second prize is drawn from the box.

Rex has 20 tickets in the raffle. Find the probability that he wins:

parts.label: a
parts.latex: no prizes.

dif.r: Two-stage product without replacement

parts.label: b
parts.latex: at least one prize.

dif.r: Direct complement of previous answer

solutions.latex:
Rex has 20 of the 400 tickets, so 380 tickets are not his. Without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{no prizes}) &= \dfrac{380}{400} \times \dfrac{379}{399} \\ &= \dfrac{379}{420} \\ &\approx 90.2\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

Use the complement of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one prize}) &= 1 - \dfrac{379}{420} \\ &= \dfrac{41}{420} \\ &\approx 9.8\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
There are 25 even numbers among the 50 balls. Without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{25}{50} \times \dfrac{24}{49} \times \dfrac{23}{48} \times \dfrac{22}{47} \times \dfrac{21}{46} \\ &= \dfrac{33}{1316} \\ &\approx 2.5\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(X \mid Y) &= \dfrac{P(X \cap Y)}{P(Y)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.3}{0.4} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4} \text{ or } 75\% \end{aligned}$$

Using the complement and the addition formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\overline{A \cup B}) &= 1 - P(A \cup B) \\ &= 1 - \left[P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\right] \\ &= 1 - \left[\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right] \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{11}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the addition formula, or equivalent merit

Each toss is a tail with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$, and the tosses are independent.

Which one of the following is the expression for the limiting sum of the geometric series below?

$$k + \dfrac{k}{1-k} + \dfrac{k}{(1-k)^2} + \dfrac{k}{(1-k)^3} + \cdots \qquad (k \neq 0, 1)$$

dif.r: Algebraic ratio and simplification of limiting sum in k

solutions.latex:
The first term is $a = k$ and the ratio is:
$$r = \dfrac{\;\frac{k}{1-k}\;}{k} = \dfrac{1}{1-k}$$
The limiting sum is:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{k}{1 - \frac{1}{1-k}} \\ &= \dfrac{k(1-k)}{1-k-1} \\ &= \dfrac{k(1-k)}{-k} \\ &= k-1 \end{aligned}$$
This matches option A.

parts.latex: Jimmy is investing in a superannuation fund to which he contributes $\$100$ at the beginning of each month for 10 years. The fund pays $2.4\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. If the fund matures at the end of the $10^{\text{th}}$ year, find the total value of the Jimmy's investment at maturity.

dif.r: Build annuity-due GP unaided and sum it

solutions.latex:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{2.4\%}{12} = 0.2\%$, so each month multiplies by $r = 1.002$.

Each $\$100$ is invested at the start of a month, so the first earns interest for 120 months, the last for 1 month:
$$\begin{aligned} 1\text{st} &= 100 \times 1.002^{120} \\ 2\text{nd} &= 100 \times 1.002^{119} \\ 3\text{rd} &= 100 \times 1.002^{118} \\ &\ \vdots \\ 120\text{th} &= 100 \times 1.002 \end{aligned}$$
The total is:
$$100\left[1.002 + 1.002^2 + \cdots + 1.002^{120}\right]$$
This is a G.P. with $a = 1.002$, $r = 1.002$, $n = 120$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 100 \times 1.002\left[\dfrac{1.002^{120} - 1}{1.002 - 1}\right] \\ &= \$13\,574.32 \text{ (nearest cent)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the G.P. sum formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Jason borrows $\$400\,000$ at $7.2\%$ p.a. The interest is compounded monthly on the amount owing. The terms of the loan are that no repayments are made for one year and then equal monthly repayments of $\$M$ are made for another 9 years. Hence the terms of the loan are for 10 years in total.

Each repayment is deducted at the end of the month after the interest has been calculated for the month.

Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:

$$A_{15} = 400000 \times 1.006^{15} - M\left(1 + 1.006 + 1.006^2\right)$$

dif.r: Show recurrence with deferred repayment period

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $M$ if the loan is fully repaid at the end of 10 years.

dif.r: Generalise deferred-loan pattern to n=120, sum GP, solve M

solutions.latex:
The monthly rate is $\dfrac{7.2\%}{12} = 0.6\%$, so each month multiplies by $1.006$.

No repayments are made for the first 12 months:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 400000 \times 1.006 \\ A_2 &= 400000 \times 1.006^2 \\ &\ \vdots \\ A_{12} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{12} \end{aligned}$$
The first repayment is at the end of month 13:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{13} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{13} - M \\ A_{14} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{14} - 1.006M - M \\ A_{15} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{15} - 1.006^2M - 1.006M - M \\ &= 400000 \times 1.006^{15} - M\left(1 + 1.006 + 1.006^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Develops the series or the subtraction of repayments, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Following the pattern of part (a), after $n$ months:
$$A_n = 400000 \times 1.006^n - M\left(1 + 1.006 + 1.006^2 + \cdots + 1.006^{n-13}\right)$$
So for $n = 120$:
$$A_{120} = 400000 \times 1.006^{120} - M\left(1 + 1.006 + \cdots + 1.006^{107}\right)$$
The bracket is a G.P. with $a = 1$, $r = 1.006$, $n = 108$.

The loan is repaid, so $A_{120} = 0$:
$$0 = 400000 \times 1.006^{120} - M\left(\dfrac{1.006^{108} - 1}{0.006}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 400000 \times 1.006^{120} \times \dfrac{0.006}{1.006^{108} - 1} \\ &= \$5418.46 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the change in amplitude and period when the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 4x$ is transformed into $g(x)=\sin 2x$?

dif.r: Direct recall of amplitude and period for two sine functions.

options.label: A
options.latex: The amplitude is halved and the period is halved

options.label: B
options.latex: The amplitude is halved and the period is doubled

options.label: C
options.latex: The amplitude is doubled and the period is halved

options.label: D
options.latex: The amplitude is doubled and the period is doubled

solutions.latex:
For $y=a\sin bx$ the amplitude is $|a|$ and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$.

$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 4x: & \text{amplitude}&=\dfrac{1}{2}, & \text{period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\ g(x)&=\sin 2x: & \text{amplitude}&=1, & \text{period}&=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi\end{aligned}$$

The amplitude goes from $\dfrac{1}{2}$ to $1$, so it is doubled.

The period goes from $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ to $\pi$, so it is doubled.

Hence the answer is option D.

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=4x^3-x^4$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points on the curve $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: Standard stationary points; inconclusive second derivative needs sign test.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph, showing clearly the stationary points and any axis intercepts.

dif.r: Sketch quartic using found stationary points and factorised intercepts.

figures.cap: solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $f(x)=4x^3-x^4$:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=12x^2-4x^3\\ &=4x^2(3-x)\end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

$$f(0)=0,\qquad f(3)=4(27)-81=27$$

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(3,27)$.

Nature: the second derivative is

$$f''(x)=24x-12x^2=12x(2-x)$$

At $x=3$: $f''(3)=12(3)(-1)=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a local maximum.

At $x=0$: $f''(0)=0$, so the test is inconclusive and we test the sign of $f'(x)=4x^2(3-x)$ either side.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(-1)&=4(1)(4)=16>0\\ f'(1)&=4(1)(2)=8>0\end{aligned}$$

The gradient is positive on both sides of $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

$$\therefore\ (3,27)\text{ is a local maximum and }(0,0)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflection}$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points and the nature of one of them, or equivalent merit

$$\int_0^2 \sqrt{5^x+2}\;dx$$

dif.r: Routine trapezoidal rule with five function values.

solutions.latex:
Five function values give $4$ strips, so the strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{2-0}{4}=0.5$$
The $x$ values are $0,\ 0.5,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 2$, with $f(x)=\sqrt{5^x+2}$.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 0.5 & 1 & 1.5 & 2 \\ \hline f(x) & 1.7321 & 2.0582 & 2.6458 & 3.6305 & 5.1962 \\ \hline \end{array}$

Using the Trapezoidal Rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(x_0)+2(f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3))+f(x_4)\big]$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 \sqrt{5^x+2}\,dx &\approx \dfrac{0.5}{2}\big[1.7321+5.1962+2(2.0582+2.6458+3.6305)\big] \\ &\approx 5.899 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^2 \sqrt{5^x+2}\,dx\approx 5.899$$
criteria: Correct substitution into the Trapezoidal Rule with $h=0.5$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a \sqrt{4x+1}\;dx=\dfrac{13}{3}$, find $a$.

dif.r: Integrate linear power, then solve equation with fractional index.

solutions.latex:
Integrate using $\displaystyle\int (ax+b)^n\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a \sqrt{4x+1}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{(4x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}\right]_0^a \\ &= \dfrac{(4a+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\dfrac{13}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} (4a+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-1 &= 26 \\ (4a+1)^{\frac{3}{2}} &= 27 \\ 4a+1 &= 9 \\ a &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=2$$

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows an athlete, Paul, who wishes to get from point $A$ (in the ocean) to point $Y$, located on the shore of a straight beach. $P$ is the point on the beach nearest to $A$, such that $AP=2$ km and $PY=2$ km. Paul achieves this by swimming to a point $Q$ located on the beach and running to $Y$.

He is able to swim 1 km in $5\sqrt{5}$ minutes and run 1 km in five minutes.

Let $PQ=x$ km.

\exfigure{1593_q4c_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that an expression for the time, $T$ minutes, taken by the athlete to reach $Y$ is given by:

$$T=5\sqrt{5}\left(\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)+5(2-x)$$

dif.r: Model time using Pythagoras and rates; show given expression.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the minimum time, in minutes, taken for the athlete to reach point $Y$.

dif.r: Chain rule on surd, solve radical equation, justify minimum.

figures.cap: right triangle: A above P (AP = 2 km), Q on beach with PQ = x km, Y with PY = 2 km

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $APQ$, Pythagoras' theorem gives the swimming distance:
$$AQ=\sqrt{x^2+2^2}=\sqrt{x^2+4} \text{ km}$$
Swimming takes $5\sqrt{5}$ minutes per km, so the swimming time is $5\sqrt{5}\left(\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)$ minutes.

The running distance is $QY=PY-PQ=(2-x)$ km, at $5$ minutes per km, so the running time is $5(2-x)$ minutes.
$$\therefore\ T=5\sqrt{5}\left(\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)+5(2-x)$$

meta.self_check: Standard time = distance x time per km.
meta.generated_note: Generated solution.

solutions.latex:
Here $0\le x\le 2$. Differentiate:
$$\dfrac{dT}{dx}=\dfrac{5\sqrt{5}\,x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}-5$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dT}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{5}\,x &= \sqrt{x^2+4} \\ 5x^2 &= x^2+4 \\ x^2 &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $x\ge 0$, $x=1$.

The second derivative decides the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2T}{dx^2}=\dfrac{20\sqrt{5}}{(x^2+4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}>0 \text{ for all } x$$
Hence $x=1$ gives a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} T(1) &= 5\sqrt{5}\cdot\sqrt{5}+5(1) \\ &= 25+5 \\ &= 30 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum time}=30 \text{ minutes}$$
criteria: Finds $x=1$ and shows it is a minimum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\sec x$.

dif.r: Standard derivative of sec x by chain rule, multiple choice

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec x = (\cos x)^{-1}$ and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x)^{-1} &= -(\cos x)^{-2}\cdot(-\sin x) \\ &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \tan x \sec x \end{aligned}$$
Hence the derivative of $\sec x$ is $\tan x \sec x$, which is option D.

From the graph, the curves meet at $x=1$ and $x=2$. Check: $\dfrac{2}{x} = -x+3$ gives $x^2-3x+2=0$, so $x=1$ or $x=2$.

For $1\le x\le 2$ the line is above the curve. For $2\le x\le 4$ the curve is above the line. So the area is
$$A=\int_1^2\left(-x+3-\dfrac{2}{x}\right)dx+\int_2^4\left(\dfrac{2}{x}+x-3\right)dx$$
First integral:
$$\begin{aligned} \left[-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+3x-2\ln x\right]_1^2 &= (-2+6-2\ln 2)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}+3\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3}{2}-2\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Second integral:
$$\begin{aligned} \left[2\ln x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}-3x\right]_2^4 &= (2\ln 4+8-12)-(2\ln 2+2-6) \\ &= 4\ln 2-4-2\ln 2+4 \\ &= 2\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Adding,
$$A=\dfrac{3}{2}-2\ln 2+2\ln 2$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{3}{2}\text{ units}^2$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=x^2e^{-x}$ at $x=1$.

dif.r: Product rule then standard tangent equation

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{-x}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=-e^{-x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 2x e^{-x}-x^2e^{-x} \\ &= e^{-x}(2x-x^2) \end{aligned}$$
At $x=1$:
$$y=e^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{e},\qquad \dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{-1}(2-1)=\dfrac{1}{e}$$
The tangent through $\left(1,\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$ with gradient $\dfrac{1}{e}$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{1}{e} &= \dfrac{1}{e}(x-1) \\ y &= \dfrac{x}{e} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{x}{e}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient and the point of tangency, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the $x$ value of the maximum turning point on the curve $f(x)=\cos x-\sin x$ between $[0,2\pi]$.

dif.r: Solve tan x = -1 in domain, classify with second derivative

solutions.latex:
Turning points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x) = -\sin x - \cos x$$
$$\begin{aligned} -\sin x - \cos x &= 0 \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
For $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, $\tan x = -1$ gives $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ or $x = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$.

The second derivative decides the nature of each point.
$$f''(x) = -\cos x + \sin x$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \sqrt{2} > 0 &&\text{minimum}\\ f''\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = -\sqrt{2} < 0 &&\text{maximum} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$$

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate of change to find $V$.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \int 40\sin(0.5t)\,dt \\ &= -80\cos(0.5t) + C \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 100 &= -80\cos 0 + C \\ C &= 180 \end{aligned}$$
So $V = 180 - 80\cos(0.5t)$. When $t = 2$ (angle in radians):
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 180 - 80\cos 1 \\ &\approx 136.78 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ V \approx 137 \text{ litres}$$

questions.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line.

Its velocity $v$ ms$^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=\dfrac{6}{t+1}-3$
questions.review_note: Part (c) says 'exact distance' but also '(answer to 2 decimal places)' - contradictory as printed

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the acceleration of the particle when the particle is stationary.

Find the exact distance travelled by the particle in the first 5 seconds.

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{6}{t+1} - 3 &= 0 \\ t + 1 &= 2 \\ t &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, with $v = 6(t+1)^{-1} - 3$.
$$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -\dfrac{6}{(t+1)^2}$$
When $t=1$:
$$a = -\dfrac{6}{4} = -\dfrac{3}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the acceleration is } -\dfrac{3}{2} \text{ ms}^{-2}$$
criteria: Finds $t=1$ when stationary, or finds $a=-\dfrac{6}{(t+1)^2}$, or equivalent merit

meta.generated_note: Generated solution.

solutions.latex:
Intercepts and asymptote:
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:\ v &= 6 - 3 = 3 \\ v=0:\ t &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
As $t \to \infty$, $\dfrac{6}{t+1} \to 0$, so $v \to -3$: the horizontal asymptote is $v=-3$.

\exfigure{1604_q5_s1}
criteria: Finds the intercepts or the asymptote, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From the graph, $v \ge 0$ for $0 \le t \le 1$ and $v < 0$ for $1 < t \le 5$. The particle turns round at $t=1$, so the two stages are found separately.

An antiderivative of $v$ is
$$x = 6\ln(t+1) - 3t$$
Distance in the first second:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 v\,dt &= \big[6\ln(t+1) - 3t\big]_0^1 \\ &= (6\ln 2 - 3) - 0 \\ &= 6\ln 2 - 3 \end{aligned}$$
Displacement from $t=1$ to $t=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5 v\,dt &= (6\ln 6 - 15) - (6\ln 2 - 3) \\ &= 6\ln 3 - 12 \end{aligned}$$
This is negative ($\approx -5.41$), so the distance in this stage is $12 - 6\ln 3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total distance} &= (6\ln 2 - 3) + (12 - 6\ln 3) \\ &= 9 + 6\ln 2 - 6\ln 3 \\ &= 9 - 6\ln\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance} = 9 - 6\ln\dfrac{3}{2} \approx 6.57 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Integrates $v$ correctly and evaluates both stages, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $3^4 = 81$ and $3^5 = 243$, and $81 < 100 < 243$, the value of $x$ in $3^x = 100$ lies between 4 and 5.

Alternatively, by the change of base rule:

The graph of $y = \sqrt{1-x^2}$ is the upper half of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, of radius 1.

For $0 \le x \le 1$ it is the quarter of the unit circle in the first quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \int_0^1 \sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac14 \pi r^2 \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an example of a discrete random variable ?

dif.r: Recall definition of discrete variable

options.label: A
options.latex: The time needed to run one kilometre.

options.label: B
options.latex: The heights of trees in a local park.

options.label: C
options.latex: The mass of all parcels delivered by Australia Post on a particular day.

options.label: D
options.latex: The number of visits made by 100 patients to their doctor in a year.

solutions.latex:
A discrete variable takes only separate values, usually whole numbers, and is counted rather than measured.

Time, height and mass are measured, so they are continuous.

The number of visits made by 100 patients to their doctor in a year is counted, so it is discrete.

This is option D.

parts.latex:
It is known that for a particular function, $y = f(x)$, that

\begin{itemize}
\item $f(3) = -6$
\item $f'(3) = 0$
\item $f''(3) = 4$
\end{itemize}

Which statement below is true regarding the graph of $y = f(x)$ ?

dif.r: Direct recall: f'=0, f''>0 means minimum

options.label: B
options.latex: There is a local minimum at $(3, -6)$.

options.label: D
options.latex: There is a point of inflexion at $(3, 4)$.

solutions.latex:
Since $f(3) = -6$, the graph passes through $(3,-6)$, not $(3,0)$.

Since $f'(3) = 0$, there is a stationary point at $(3,-6)$.

Since $f''(3) = 4 > 0$, the graph is concave up there, so the stationary point is a local minimum.

This is option B.

parts.latex: The expression $\tan\theta + \sin\theta < 0$ is true for all values of $\theta$ in the domain,

dif.r: Combine sign of sin and tan by quadrant

solutions.latex:
For the sum to be certainly negative, both $\tan\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ must be negative.

$\sin\theta < 0$ in the third and fourth quadrants, and $\tan\theta < 0$ in the second and fourth quadrants.

Both are negative only in the fourth quadrant, so $\theta$ is in $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, 2\pi\right)$.

This is option D.

why: Checker got a different answer — Two options are correct. tanθ+sinθ = sinθ(1+cosθ)/cosθ is negative on all of (π/2, π) (option B; e.g. θ=2 gives −1.28) as well as on (3π/2, 2π) (option D). The stored working says both terms must be negative, which is wrong because it is not necessary. The key D is valid, but B is also correct, so the question is flawed.

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the equation $x = 2t - \dfrac{1}{2}t^2$, where $x$ is in metres, $t$ is in seconds and $t \ge 0$.

Which of the following statements is FALSE ?

dif.r: Differentiate and check several kinematics statements

options.label: A
options.latex: The particle is initially moving to the left.

options.label: B
options.latex: The particle is at the origin after 4 seconds.

options.label: C
options.latex: The acceleration of the particle is constant.

options.label: D
options.latex: The speed of the particle increases indefinitely.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the displacement.
$$v = 2 - t, \qquad a = -1$$
When $t = 4$:
$$x = 2(4) - \dfrac12(4)^2 = 0$$
So B is true.

The acceleration is constant, so C is true.

For large $t$, $|v| = |2 - t|$ grows without bound, so D is true.

At $t = 0$, $v = 2 > 0$, so the particle is initially moving to the right. Statement A is false.

This is option A.

parts.latex: Factorise fully, $x - xy^2$.

dif.r: Common factor then difference of squares

solutions.latex:
Remove the common factor $x$, then use the difference of two squares.
$$\begin{aligned} x - xy^2 &= x(1 - y^2) \\ &= x(1-y)(1+y) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Removes the common factor $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{x+1}\right)$.

dif.r: Quotient rule applied cleanly with simplification

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=x+1\\ u'&=2x & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{x+1}\right) &= \dfrac{(x+1)\cdot 2x - x^2\cdot 1}{(x+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{2x^2 + 2x - x^2}{(x+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2 + 2x}{(x+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Full marks for correct use of the quotient rule; simplification is not required and any later error is ignored.

parts.latex: Differentiate the function, $y = x^2 e^{2x}$ leaving your answer in simplest factored form.

dif.r: Product rule with exponential, then factorise

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= x^2(2e^{2x}) + e^{2x}(2x) \\ &= 2xe^{2x}(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source criterion was '1 for each line of the solution'; rewritten top-down by us.

questions.stem:
Consider the sector drawn below with radius 4 cm and arc length 10 cm.

\exfigure{1310_q11d_1}

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the exact area of the sector.

dif.r: Substitute into sector area formula

figures.cap: sector with radius 4 cm, arc length 10 cm and angle theta

solutions.latex:
The arc length formula is $l = r\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10 &= 4\theta \\ \theta &= 2.5 \text{ radians} \end{aligned}$$

The sector area formula is $A = \dfrac12 r^2\theta$.

parts.latex: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{3}{2x+1}\, dx$.

dif.r: Standard log integral with constant adjustment

solutions.latex:
Write the integrand so the numerator is the derivative of $2x+1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle \int_0^2 \dfrac{3}{2x+1}\,dx &= \dfrac32\int_0^2 \dfrac{2}{2x+1}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac32\Big[\ln(2x+1)\Big]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac32\ln 5 - \dfrac32\ln 1 \\ &= \dfrac32\ln 5 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: $\dfrac32\Big[\ln(2x+1)\Big]_0^2$, or $\dfrac32\ln 5$ without the previous line, or equivalent merit
Finds a primitive involving $\ln$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The gradient function of a curve is $f'(x) = 4x + 3$. The curve passes through the point $(-2, 5)$. Find $f(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate polynomial and find constant from point

solutions.latex:
Integrate the gradient function.
$$f(x) = 2x^2 + 3x + C$$
The curve passes through $(-2, 5)$, so $f(-2) = 5$.
$$\begin{aligned} 5 &= 2(-2)^2 + 3(-2) + C \\ 5 &= 8 - 6 + C \\ C &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x) = 2x^2 + 3x + 3$$
criteria: Correct primitive (with or without $+C$), or substitutes $(-2,5)$ into an incorrect primitive and correctly completes, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Tom invests \$750 at the end of each quarter into an account which earns $8\%$ per annum with interest compounded quarterly.

He does this for 3 years.

Find the future value of Tom's investment.

parts.latex:
His brother, Jake, finds an account that will earn him $12\%$ per annum. The interest will also be compounded quarterly.

However, Jake is only prepared to contribute for 2 years.

Find the amount that he must contribute quarterly if he is to achieve the same future value as Tom.
parts.note: Annuity future-value interest-factor table look-up (2024 Advanced uses the GP formula only; moved to Standard).

dif.r: Annuity table factor used in reverse

figures.cap: future value of an annuity of $1 table, periods 1-12, rates 1%-12%

solutions.latex:
Interest is compounded quarterly, so the rate per period is $\dfrac{8}{4} = 2\%$ and the number of periods is $3\times 4 = 12$.

From the table, the factor for $2\%$ and $12$ periods is $13.4121$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Future value} &= 750 \times 13.4121 \\ &= \$10059.08 \end{aligned}$$

For Jake, the rate per period is $\dfrac{12}{4} = 3\%$ and the number of periods is $2\times 4 = 8$.

From the table, the factor is $8.8923$. Let his quarterly contribution be $\$M$.
$$\begin{aligned} M \times 8.8923 &= 10059.08 \\ M &= \$1131.21 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Jamjet Industries produce galvanised bolts for the roofing industry. Due to manufacturing constraints, the maximum number of bolts they can produce in a month is 120 000.

The cost of production is \$50 000 plus 95 cents per bolt.

The bolts are sold for \$1.75 each and the graph that represents Jamjet's revenue, $R$, appears on the axes below.

\exfigure{1310_q12a_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the linear equation for the cost, $C$, of producing $n$ bolts.

dif.r: Write linear cost model directly from text

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the practical significance of the gradient of the line in (a) ?

dif.r: Interpret gradient in context

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the number of bolts Jamjet must sell in a month to break even.

dif.r: Equate revenue and cost, solve linear equation

parts.label: d
parts.latex: What is the maximum monthly profit attainable by Jamjet ?

dif.r: Form profit and recognise maximum at production limit

figures.cap: graph of revenue R = 1.75n, cost axis up to 200000, n up to 120000

solutions.latex:
The cost is a fixed \$50 000 plus \$0.95 per bolt.
$$C = 50000 + 0.95n$$
The gradient of the cost line is $0.95$, so it represents the cost of production per bolt (the rate at which cost increases for each extra bolt).
criteria: Correct answer; must reference rate in some way

solutions.latex:
Break-even occurs when revenue equals cost, $1.75n = C$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1.75n &= 50000 + 0.95n \\ 0.8n &= 50000 \\ n &= 62500 \end{aligned}$$
Jamjet must sell 62 500 bolts.

Profit is revenue minus cost.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Profit} &= 1.75n - (50000 + 0.95n) \\ &= 0.8n - 50000 \end{aligned}$$
Profit increases with $n$, so it is greatest at the maximum production $n = 120000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Profit} &= 0.8\times 120000 - 50000 \\ &= \$46000 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct profit expression, or substitutes $n = 120000$ into their expression for profit, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The number plane below shows the interval joining the points $A(-5, -4)$ and $B(-1, -3)$.

The line, $l$, is drawn through $B$ so as to be perpendicular to $AB$ and meets the $x$-axis at $C$ and the $y$-axis at $D$.

Find the area of triangle $COD$.

\exfigure{1310_q12b_1}

dif.r: Routine chain: perpendicular gradient, line, intercepts, area

figures.cap: interval AB and perpendicular line l meeting axes at C and D

solutions.latex:
Gradient of $AB$:
$$m_{AB} = \dfrac{-3-(-4)}{-1-(-5)} = \dfrac14$$
The line $l$ is perpendicular to $AB$, so $m_l = -4$.

It passes through $B(-1,-3)$, so use $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y + 3 &= -4(x+1) \\ y &= -4x - 7 \end{aligned}$$
Point $D$ is the $y$-intercept, so $D$ is $(0,-7)$.

Point $C$ is where $y = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -4x - 7 \\ x &= -\dfrac74 \end{aligned}$$
So $C$ is $\left(-\dfrac74, 0\right)$.

Triangle $COD$ is right-angled at $O$, with $OD = 7$ and $OC = \dfrac74$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac12 \times \dfrac74 \times 7 \\ &= \dfrac{49}{8} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the equation of $l$, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient of $l$, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient of $AB$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b
parts.latex: One of the surveyed people is selected at random. Find the probability that the person selected has holidayed both interstate and within NSW.

dif.r: Read single count from Venn diagram

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
A randomly selected person is known to have travelled.

Find the probability that this person holidayed within NSW.

dif.r: Conditional probability from Venn diagram

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Two people are chosen, in turn, at random. Find the probability that exactly one of those chosen holidayed interstate.

dif.r: Two orders, without replacement

figures.cap: Venn diagram with I and N, x, y, z, and 12 outside
solution sketch: completed Venn diagram 32, 10, 26, 12

solutions.latex:
The total is 80 and 12 people did not holiday, so $80 - 12 = 68$ people holidayed.

Both: $42 + 36 - 68 = 10$.

Interstate only: $42 - 10 = 32$.

NSW only: $36 - 10 = 26$.

\exfigure{1310_q12c_s1}

meta.format_note: Working for the values (32, 10, 26, outside 12) added by us; the existing diagram \exfigure{1310_q12c_s1} kept in place and not checked against these values.

solutions.latex:
Ten people holidayed both interstate and within NSW.
$$P(\text{I}\cap\text{N}) = \dfrac{10}{80} = \dfrac18$$

Of the 80 people, $80 - 12 = 68$ have travelled, and 36 of them holidayed within NSW.
$$P(\text{N}\mid\text{traveller}) = \dfrac{36}{68} = \dfrac{9}{17}$$

$42$ people went interstate, so $80-42 = 38$ did not. Exactly one interstate traveller means the order is (I, not I) or (not I, I), without replacement.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly one I}) &= P(\text{I},\overline{\text{I}}) + P(\overline{\text{I}},\text{I}) \\ &= \dfrac{42}{80}\times\dfrac{38}{79} + \dfrac{38}{80}\times\dfrac{42}{79} \\ &= \dfrac{399}{790} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One of the products, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle, initially at the origin, is moving in a straight line. Its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, after $t$ seconds is given by $v = 2 - 2t$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the initial velocity.

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into velocity

skills: Velocity as a rate of change

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find when the particle is at rest.

dif.r: Set v=0 and solve a linear equation.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find when the particle is next at the origin.

dif.r: Integrate velocity, use the initial condition, solve x=0.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled in the first 4 seconds.

dif.r: Distance, not displacement: must account for the change of direction at t=1.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 0$ into $v = 2 - 2t$.
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 2 - 2(0) \\ &= 2 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2-2t \\ 2t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1 \text{ second}$$

Position is the integral of velocity, so $x=\displaystyle\int v\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int (2-2t)\,dt \\ &= 2t - t^2 + C \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$, giving $C=0$.
$$x = 2t - t^2$$
The particle is at the origin when $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2t - t^2 \\ &= t(2-t) \end{aligned}$$
So $t=0$ or $t=2$. The particle is next at the origin when $t\ne 0$.
$$\therefore\ t = 2 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Correct answer (student must evaluate the constant of integration)
Demonstrates an understanding that $x=\displaystyle\int v\,dt$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when it comes to rest, at $t=1$, so find $x$ at $t=0$, $1$ and $4$ using $x=2t-t^2$.

When $t=0$, $x=0$ (given in the initial conditions).

When $t=1$:
$$x = 2(1)-1^2 = 1$$
When $t=4$:
$$x = 2(4)-4^2 = -8$$
So the particle starts at the origin, moves right to $x=1$ and then travels left to $x=-8$.

Distance travelled:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 1 + (1+8) \\ &= 10 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle travels a total of } 10 \text{ m in the first 4 seconds}$$
criteria: Finds $x$ when $t=1$, or finds $x$ when $t=4$, or states the particle has travelled 8 m, or uses integration to arrive at an answer of 8 m, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added the line $d=1+(1+8)$ to show how 10 m arises (same result as source).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$.

dif.r: Probabilities sum to one; one linear equation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $\mathrm{E}(X)$.

dif.r: Direct expected value calculation from a table.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the standard deviation of the distribution.

dif.r: Standard variance formula, then square root.

figures.cap: spinner with three equal sectors red, yellow, green

solutions.latex:
The probabilities in a distribution sum to 1.
$$\dfrac{32}{243}+k+k+\dfrac{40}{243}+\dfrac{10}{243}+\dfrac{1}{243}=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2k+\dfrac{83}{243} &= 1 \\ 2k &= \dfrac{160}{243} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{80}{243}$$
criteria: Sums the probabilities and equates to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\mathrm{E}(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$ and $k=\dfrac{80}{243}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}(X) &= 0\left(\dfrac{32}{243}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+3\left(\dfrac{40}{243}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{10}{243}\right)+5\left(\dfrac{1}{243}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{405}{243} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{3} \end{aligned}$$

Using $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathrm{E}(X^2)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=\dfrac{5}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(X) &= \left[0\left(\dfrac{32}{243}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+9\left(\dfrac{40}{243}\right)+16\left(\dfrac{10}{243}\right)+25\left(\dfrac{1}{243}\right)\right]-\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{10}{9} \end{aligned}$$
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
$$\therefore\ \sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{9}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{3}$$

parts.latex:
A flagpole, $BD$, lies on flat level ground.

It is supported by two cables, $AD$ and $CD$ as shown below. The cable $AD$ is inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal and is tied 18 metres from the foot of the pole.

The second cable is tied at a point, $C$, 12m from $A$ and on a bearing of $210^\circ$ from $A$.

\exfigure{1310_q13c_1}

Find $\theta$, correct to the nearest degree.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (flagpole with ground cables and a bearing): now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

dif.r: 3D diagram: bearing gives angle, then tan, cosine rule, tan.

figures.cap: flagpole BD with cables AD and CD, bearings and angles

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle $BAD$, $\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{BD}{18}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &= \dfrac{BD}{18} \\ BD &= \dfrac{18}{\sqrt{3}} = 6\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB=18$, $AC=12$ and $\angle BAC=60^\circ$. By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2 &= 18^2+12^2-2(18)(12)\cos 60^\circ \\ &= 468-216 \\ &= 252 \end{aligned}$$
$$BC=\sqrt{252}=6\sqrt{7}$$
In the right-angled triangle $BCD$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{BD}{BC} \\ &= \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{6\sqrt{7}} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{7}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta\approx 33^\circ$$
criteria: Correct value of $BC$ (allowing for errors carried forward), or equivalent merit
Expression for $BC^2$, even if $\angle BAC$ is incorrect, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{6} - \dfrac{x^2}{4} - 3x + 1$ is defined for $x$ in the domain $[-4, 6]$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of a cubic with second derivative test.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the absolute maximum of $f(x)$.

dif.r: Compare endpoint values with the local maximum on a closed interval.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch $f(x)$ showing the stationary points and both endpoints.

dif.r: Sketch cubic from known stationary points and endpoints.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of f(x) with stationary points and endpoints

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the stationary points.
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}-3$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}-3 \\ 0 &= x^2-x-6 \\ &= (x-3)(x+2) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-2$ or $x=3$.

The $y$ values:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-2) &= \dfrac{(-2)^3}{6}-\dfrac{(-2)^2}{4}-3(-2)+1 \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{3}-1+6+1 \\ &= 4\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(3) &= \dfrac{3^3}{6}-\dfrac{3^2}{4}-3(3)+1 \\ &= \dfrac{27}{6}-\dfrac{9}{4}-9+1 \\ &= -5\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Use the second derivative to determine the nature.
$$f''(x)=x-\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-2) &= -2-\dfrac{1}{2}=-2\dfrac{1}{2}<0 \\ f''(3) &= 3-\dfrac{1}{2}=2\dfrac{1}{2}>0 \end{aligned}$$
So there is a local maximum at $\left(-2,\,4\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ and a local minimum at $\left(3,\,-5\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$.
criteria: Correct answer (values of $f''(-2)$ and $f''(3)$ must be given to determine nature; if a table of values is used, numerical values of $f'(x)$ must be given)
Correct derivative and finds both stationary points, including the $y$ values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The absolute maximum on $[-4,6]$ is the greatest of the local maximum and the endpoint values. The local maximum is $4\dfrac{2}{3}$, so evaluate the endpoints.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-4) &= \dfrac{(-4)^3}{6}-\dfrac{(-4)^2}{4}-3(-4)+1 \\ &= -10\dfrac{2}{3}-4+12+1 \\ &= -1\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(6) &= \dfrac{6^3}{6}-\dfrac{6^2}{4}-3(6)+1 \\ &= 36-9-18+1 \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the absolute maximum of } f(x) \text{ is } 10$$
criteria: Calculates either $f(-4)$ or $f(6)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The percentage results of a university entrance examination are normally distributed with a mean mark is 60 and the standard deviation is 8.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If Jimmy's mark corresponds to a negative $z$-score in the range, $-1 < z < 0$ give a possible value for Jimmy's mark.

dif.r: Interpret z-score range as marks between 52 and 60.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Tyler obtains a result of $72\%$. Show that his $z$-score is 1.5.

dif.r: Substitute into the z-score formula.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Zoe's $z$-score was 1. What was her percentage mark?

dif.r: z-score formula used in reverse with z=1.

parts.label: d

dif.r: Empirical rule percentile, subtract percentages, scale to population.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

figures.cap: normal curve with area shaded between Zoe and Tyler

solutions.latex:
Here $\mu=60$ and $\sigma=8$. A $z$-score between $-1$ and $0$ means the mark lies between $\mu-\sigma=52$ and $\mu=60$.

Any mark in the range $52<x<60$ is possible, for example $56$.

meta.source_flag: The source answer is 'any integer in the range $56<x<64$', but $-1<z<0$ with $\mu=60$, $\sigma=8$ gives $52<x<60$; marks from $60$ to $64$ have $z\ge 0$. The range in my working replaces the source range.
meta.format_note: Corrected from source: range $56<x<64$ replaced by $52<x<60$ (derived from $z=\dfrac{x-60}{8}$). Original source text: 'Any integer in the range $56 < x < 64$.'

solutions.latex:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{72-60}{8} \\ &= 1.5 \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Rearranging the $z$-score formula, $x=\mu+z\sigma$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 60+1(8) \\ &= 68 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Zoe's mark was } 68\%$$

By the empirical rule, a $z$-score of 1 means Zoe's result is better than $50\%+34\%=84\%$ of scores.

Tyler's result is better than $93.3\%$ of scores, so the percentage between Zoe and Tyler is
$$93.3\%-84\%=9.3\%$$
Students represented by the shaded region:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 9.3\%\times 85000 \\ &= 7905 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Indicates that Zoe's mark is better than $84\%$ of scores, or equivalent merit

why: Possible error in the source solution: The source answer is 'any integer in the range $56<x<64$', but $-1<z<0$ with $\mu=60$, $\sigma=8$ gives $52<x<60$; marks from $60$ to $64$ have $z\ge 0$. The range in my working replaces the source range.

questions.stem:
$X$ is a continuous random variable that is defined by the probability density function,

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} k(x-1)^2 & 2 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k = \dfrac{3}{26}$.

dif.r: Integrate the pdf over its domain and set it equal to 1.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function.

dif.r: Integrate pdf from lower limit to x.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the upper quartile is approximately 3.74.

dif.r: Set CDF to 0.75 and solve the cubic by cube root.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1.
$$\int_2^4 k(x-1)^2\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k(x-1)^3}{3}\right]_2^4 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k(4-1)^3}{3}-\dfrac{k(2-1)^3}{3} &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{3}\left(3^3-1^3\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{26k}{3} &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{3}{26}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct answer with adequate working given it is a show that question
Sets the integral of the PDF equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is the integral of the PDF from the lower limit, with $k=\dfrac{3}{26}$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_2^x \dfrac{3}{26}(x-1)^2\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{26}\right]_2^x \\ &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3}{26}-\dfrac{1}{26} \\ &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3-1}{26} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integration of the PDF, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric 'one mark for each line with a tick' rewritten by us as a top-down rubric. Source uses $x$ as both the limit and the variable of integration, and gives the CDF only for $2\le x\le 4$; kept as in source.

solutions.latex:
The upper quartile is the value of $x$ where the CDF equals $0.75$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.75 &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3-1}{26} \\ 19.5 &= (x-1)^3-1 \\ 20.5 &= (x-1)^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x-1 &= \sqrt[3]{20.5} \\ x &= \sqrt[3]{20.5}+1 \\ &\approx 3.736851837 \\ &\approx 3.74 \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct answer with adequate working given it is a show that question
Sets the CDF equal to $0.75$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off after a period of time.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation,

$$T = 22 + 162(1.2)^{-0.5t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the temperature of the iron 6 minutes after it has switched off ? Give your answer to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Direct substitution into the exponential model.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what rate is the temperature of the iron's surface changing after 6 minutes ?

dif.r: Differentiate a^u with ln a factor, then evaluate.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=6$ into the model.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 22+162(1.2)^{-0.5(6)} \\ &\approx 116^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric row was 'substitution of 6 for $t$'; changed to 'Correct answer' as the single full-mark row.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{u}\right)=a^{u}\ln a\cdot u'$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= 162(-0.5)(1.2)^{-0.5t}(\ln 1.2) \\ &= -81(1.2)^{-0.5t}(\ln 1.2) \end{aligned}$$
When $t=6$:
$$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-81(1.2)^{-0.5(6)}(\ln 1.2)\approx -8.5^\circ\text{C per minute}$$

meta.marker_note: 1 mark if the student omits $\ln 1.2$ from the derivative but completes the question correctly (they will get $-46.875^\circ$C per minute).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the area of the $10^{\text{th}}$ annulus.

dif.r: Arithmetic sequence nth term formula.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the sum of the first $n$ annuli is found by $S_n = \pi n^2 + 2n\pi$

dif.r: Apply the AP sum formula and simplify to the given form.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the minimum number of annuli needed for a combined area of $300\ \text{u}^2$ ?

dif.r: Quadratic inequality in n, quadratic formula, round up to an integer.

figures.cap: concentric circles with annuli A, B, C

solutions.latex:
The areas of the annuli moving outwards form the arithmetic sequence $3\pi,\ 5\pi,\ 7\pi,\ \ldots$ with $a=3\pi$ and $d=2\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ T_{10} &= 3\pi+(10-1)2\pi \\ &= 21\pi \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area of the } 10^{\text{th}} \text{ annulus is } 21\pi \text{ square units}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; wrote a one-row rubric ('Correct answer', 1 mark) from the question's mark allocation.

solutions.latex:
The sum of $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$, with $a=3\pi$ and $d=2\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(3\pi)+(n-1)2\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[3\pi+(n-1)\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[3\pi+n\pi-\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[n\pi+2\pi\right] \\ &= \pi n^2+2n\pi \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct answer with adequate working given it is a show that question
Substitutes $a=3\pi$ and $d=2\pi$ into the sum formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us from the mark allocation (2 marks).

solutions.latex:
We need the combined area to be at least $300$.
$$\pi n^2+2n\pi\ge 300$$
$$\pi n^2+2n\pi-300\ge 0$$
Solve $\pi n^2+2n\pi-300=0$ using the quadratic formula.
$$n=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}=\dfrac{-2\pi\pm\sqrt{4\pi^2+1200\pi}}{2\pi}$$
Since $n>0$, only the positive root applies.
$$n=\dfrac{-2\pi+\sqrt{4\pi^2+1200\pi}}{2\pi}\approx 8.8$$
The quadratic $f(n)=\pi n^2+2n\pi-300$ is an upward parabola, so $f(n)\ge 0$ for $n\ge 8.8$. Since $n$ is a whole number, the minimum is $n=9$.
$$\therefore\ 9 \text{ annuli are required for a total area of } 300 \text{ u}^2$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us from the mark allocation (3 marks). Checked $S_9=99\pi\approx 311>300$.

questions.stem:
Nick chooses an integer, $x$, between 1 and 20 at random.

He reduces this number by 1, 4 and 9 in turn and then multiplies to find the product, $P$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that, $P = x^3 - 14x^2 + 49x - 36$

dif.r: Form product of factors and expand.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the minimum value of $P$.

dif.r: Stationary points of a cubic; discard non-integer root.

solutions.latex:
Reducing $x$ by 1, 4 and 9 gives the factors, so $P=(x-1)(x-4)(x-9)$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= (x-1)(x^2-13x+36) \\ &= x^3-13x^2+36x-x^2+13x-36 \\ &= x^3-14x^2+49x-36 \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.format_note: Source rubric row was 'establishment of the result through expansion'; changed to 'Correct answer' as the single full-mark row.

solutions.latex:
Minimum values occur where $P'(x)=0$.
$$P'(x)=3x^2-28x+49$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3x^2-28x+49 \\ &= (3x-7)(x-7) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac{7}{3}$ or $x=7$. Since $x$ is an integer, $x=7$ only.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$P''(x)=6x-28$$
When $x=7$, $P''=14>0$, so $x=7$ gives a minimum.

The minimum value:
$$\begin{aligned} P(7) &= (7-1)(7-4)(7-9) \\ &= -36 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum value of } P \text{ is } -36$$
criteria: $x=7$ and establishes that this value minimises $P$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Jelena retires with a balance in her superannuation account of \$700 000.

The fund earns interest at the rate of $3.6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.

At the end of each month, Jelena withdraws \$4000 from the account.

The amount, $A_n$, left in her fund after the $n^{th}$ withdrawal is given by,

$$A_n = 700000(1.003)^n - 4000\left\{1 + 1.003 + (1.003)^2 + \ldots + (1.003)^{n-1}\right\}$$

(Do NOT prove this result)

Find, correct to the nearest month, the time taken for the balance in the fund to reduce to \$400 000.

dif.r: Sum GP, rearrange exponential equation, solve with logarithms.

solutions.latex:
The balance is to reduce to $\$400\,000$. The bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.003$ and $n$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}$.
$$400000=700000(1.003)^n-4000\left(\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}\right)$$
Multiply both sides by $0.003$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1200 &= 2100(1.003)^n-4000\left(1.003^n-1\right) \\ &= 4000-1900(1.003)^n \end{aligned}$$
$$1.003^n=\dfrac{28}{19}$$
Take logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{28}{19}\right)}{\ln 1.003} \\ &\approx 129.448963 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n\approx 129 \text{ months}$$
criteria: $1.003^n=\dfrac{28}{19}$ (accept decimal equivalent on RHS), or equivalent merit
Successful use of the sum to $n$ terms of a GP formula

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows the graph of $y = \ln x$. The region bounded by the graph, the $x$-axis and the line $x = 7$ has been shaded.

\exfigure{1310_q16c_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with 3 function values to approximate the shaded area. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

dif.r: Routine trapezoidal rule with three function values.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x \ln x)$.

dif.r: Single product rule differentiation.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find, $\displaystyle\int_1^7 \ln x\, dx$

dif.r: Reverse the derivative result and rearrange to isolate the integral.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Hence, find an approximation for $\ln 7$.

dif.r: Link trapezoidal estimate to exact integral, solve for ln 7.

figures.cap: graph of y = ln x with area shaded from x=1 to x=7

solutions.latex:
With 3 function values the strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{7-1}{2}=3$$
so the $x$ values are $1$, $4$ and $7$. By the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{3}{2}\left[\ln 1+2(\ln 4)+\ln 7\right] \\ &\approx 7.078 \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x) &= x\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)+\ln x\,(1) \\ &= 1+\ln x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From (b), $x\ln x$ is an antiderivative of $1+\ln x$.
$$\int_1^7(1+\ln x)\,dx=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7$$
$$\int_1^7 1\,dx+\int_1^7\ln x\,dx=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7$$
Rearranging:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^7\ln x\,dx &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\int_1^7 1\,dx \\ &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\Big[x\Big]_1^7 \\ &= (7\ln 7-0)-(7-1) \\ &= 7\ln 7-6 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Rearranges to isolate $\displaystyle\int_1^7\ln x\,dx$, or equivalent merit
Integrates $1+\ln x$ using the result of (b), or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric '1 for each line that has a tick' rewritten by us as a top-down rubric.

solutions.latex:
The trapezoidal estimate from (a) approximates the integral in (c).
$$\begin{aligned} 7\ln 7-6 &\approx 7.078 \\ 7\ln 7 &\approx 13.078 \\ \ln 7 &\approx 1.87 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following graphs does NOT represent a probability density function?

dif.r: Direct recall of pdf conditions; spot graph below axis

figures.cap: option A: graph A: straight line decreasing from the y-axis to the x-axis
option B: graph B: downward parabola arc above the x-axis centred on the y-axis
option C: graph C: downward parabola arc above the x-axis for positive x
option D: graph D: curve starting below the x-axis then rising above it

solutions.latex:
A probability density function on $[a,b]$ needs $f(x)\ge 0$ on $[a,b]$ and $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = 1$.

Graph D has part of its graph below the $x$-axis, so it does not satisfy $f(x)\ge 0$.

Graphs A, B and C satisfy these conditions, so they could be probability density functions.

Hence D is the graph that does not represent a probability density function.

parts.note: Annuity future-value interest-factor table look-up; 2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only.

dif.r: Adjust rate and periods for half-yearly, read table, divide

solutions.latex:
Compounded half-yearly, so the rate per period and number of periods are
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{2\%}{2} = 1\% \text{ per half-year} \\ n &= 4\times 2 = 8 \end{aligned}$$
From the table, the interest factor is $8.2857$.

Using future value $=$ present value $\times$ interest factor:
$$\begin{aligned} 34800 &= \text{present value}\times 8.2857 \\ \text{present value} &= \dfrac{34800}{8.2857} \\ &\approx \$4200 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is B.

parts.latex:
The amount of water that Eleanor uses to wash her car is normally distributed with a mean of 50 litres and a standard deviation of 4 litres.

On what percentage of occasions would Eleanor expect to use between 42 litres and 46 litres of water to wash her car?

dif.r: Standard 68-95 rule between one and two standard deviations

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Here $\mu = 50$ and $\sigma = 4$.

$X=42$ is two standard deviations below the mean and $X=46$ is one standard deviation below the mean.

Using the 68% and 95% rules, the probability between two and one standard deviations below the mean is
$$P(42<\text{amount}<46) = \dfrac{95-68}{2}\% = 13.5\%$$
Hence the answer is A.

parts.latex: What is the domain and range of a circle with the equation $x^2 + 4x + y^2 = 5$?

dif.r: Complete the square, then deduce domain and range of circle

solutions.latex:
Complete the square:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+4x+4+y^2 &= 5+4 \\ (x+2)^2+y^2 &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
This is a circle with centre $(-2,0)$ and radius $3$.

So the domain is $[-2-3,\,-2+3] = [-5,1]$ and the range is $[-3,3]$.

Hence the answer is D.

parts.latex: What is the maximum value of $y = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) + 1$ and the value of $x$ occurring in the domain $[0, 2\pi]$?

dif.r: Maximum from amplitude, then solve simple sine equation

options.label: A
options.latex: The maximum value of $y = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) + 1$ is 2 occurring at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

options.label: B
options.latex: The maximum value of $y = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) + 1$ is 3 occurring at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

options.label: C
options.latex: The maximum value of $y = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) + 1$ is 2 occurring at $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

options.label: D
options.latex: The maximum value of $y = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) + 1$ is 3 occurring at $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is $2$, so the maximum value of $y$ is $2+1=3$.

When $y=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{x}{3} &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ x &= \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
This lies in $[0,2\pi]$.

Hence the answer is D.

dif.r: Match derivative graph to increasing/decreasing and asymptote behaviour

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x), a bell-shaped curve with horizontal asymptote y=1
option A: option A graph, asymptote at y=0
option B: option B graph, asymptote at y=0
option C: option C graph, asymptote at y=0
option D: option D graph

solutions.latex:
From the graph of $y=f(x)$:

$f(x)$ is increasing on $(-\infty,0)$, decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, stationary at $x=0$, and $y\to 1$ as $x\to\pm\infty$.

Hence $y=f'(x)$ must be above the $x$-axis on $(-\infty,0)$, below it on $(0,\infty)$, have an $x$-intercept at $x=0$, and $f'(x)\to 0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$.

A fails as it has no $x$-intercept at $x=0$. C fails as it is below the $x$-axis as $x\to-\infty$. D fails as it does not approach the $x$-axis as $x\to\pm\infty$.

Hence the answer is B.

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx = 3$, what is the value of $\displaystyle\int_4^6 f(2(x-3))\,dx$?

dif.r: Reason how dilation and translation affect a definite integral

solutions.latex:
$f(2x)$ is a horizontal dilation of $f(x)$ by a factor of $\dfrac12$, so the area under the graph is halved:
$$\int_1^3 f(2x)\,dx = \dfrac12\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx = \dfrac32$$
Translating the graph three units to the right gives
$$\int_4^6 f(2(x-3))\,dx = \dfrac32$$
Hence the answer is B.

parts.latex: Given that $f(x)$ is an even function and $g(x)$ is an odd function, which of the following statements is true?

dif.r: Test parity of products, sums and compositions abstractly

solutions.latex:
Let $h(x) = f[g(x)]$. Since $g$ is odd and $f$ is even:
$$\begin{aligned} h(-x) &= f[g(-x)] \\ &= f[-g(x)] \\ &= f[g(x)] \\ &= h(x) \end{aligned}$$
So $f[g(x)]$ is even.

A fails: for $h(x)=f(x)\times g(x)$, $h(-x) = f(x)\times(-g(x)) = -h(x)$, so it is odd.

B fails: for $h(x)=f(x)+g(x)$, $h(-x) = f(x)-g(x)$, which is neither $h(x)$ nor $-h(x)$.

D fails: for $h(x)=g[f(x)]$, $h(-x)=g[f(x)] = h(x)$, so it is even.

Hence the answer is C.

dif.r: Constrained parameter, quadratic in b, optimise expected value on interval

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{10}+a+b+b+2b &= 1 \\ a &= \dfrac{9}{10}-4b \end{aligned}$$
The maximum value of $b$ occurs when $a=0$, giving $b=\dfrac{9}{40}$, so $0\le b\le\dfrac{9}{40}$.

Then
$$E(X) = \sum xp(x) = -\dfrac{1}{10}+b+5ab = -\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{11}{2}b-20b^2 \quad\text{for } 0\le b\le \dfrac{9}{40}$$
Smallest value: $b=0$ gives $E(X)=-\dfrac{1}{10}$.

Largest value: the vertex of the quadratic is at $b = \dfrac{11}{80}$, which is in the interval, giving
$$E(X) = -\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{11}{2}\left(\dfrac{11}{80}\right)-20\left(\dfrac{11}{80}\right)^2 = \dfrac{89}{320}$$
Therefore $-\dfrac{1}{10}\le E(X)\le\dfrac{89}{320}$, and the answer is C.

questions.stem:
Ringo and Greg start at location $P$ and drive in different directions. Ringo drives at a speed of 70 km/h on a bearing of $285^\circ$, while Greg drives at a speed of 60 km/h on a bearing of $030^\circ$, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{1312_q11_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\angle GPR = 105^\circ$.

dif.r: Single angle sum from bearings

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
What will be the distance between Ringo and Greg after travelling for 2 hours?

Give your answer correct to the nearest kilometre.

dif.r: Distances from speeds, then cosine rule

figures.cap: diagram of P, R (bearing 285) and G (bearing 030) with north arrow
solution sketch: annotated diagram showing 75 and 30 degree angles

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1312_q11_s1}

$$\angle GPR = 75^\circ + 30^\circ = 105^\circ$$

After 2 hours, Greg has travelled $120$ km and Ringo $140$ km. Let $d$ be the distance apart.

Using the cosine rule in triangle $GPR$:
$$\begin{aligned} d^2 &= 140^2+120^2-2(140)(120)\cos 105^\circ \\ &\approx 42696.32 \\ d &\approx 206.63 \\ &\approx 207 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
Therefore, they are $207$ km apart.
criteria: Attempts to use the cosine rule to find the distance, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
In a chess tournament, each player has a 'chess rating', which is a value from 1600 to 2000.

Danny wants to know if there is a correlation between the number of years a player has spent playing chess and their chess rating.

Danny randomly surveyed 10 players at the tournament. The results are shown in the table.

\extable{1312_q12_t1}

Beth, a competitor in the tournament, has spent 5 years playing chess.

Use the equation of the least-squares regression line for this data set to determine Beth's chess rating. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
parts.note: Least-squares regression line (bivariate data) is Mathematics Standard, not 2024 Advanced.

dif.r: Calculator regression line then substitute to predict

solutions.latex:
The least-squares regression line has the form $y = Bx + A$.

From the calculator, $A \approx 1554.49$ and $B \approx 34.64$, so
$$y = 34.64x + 1554.49$$
When $x=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 34.64\times5+1554.49 \\ &\approx 1727.69 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore, Beth's chess rating is predicted to be $1728$.

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = \dfrac{1}{4x+1}$ at the point $(0, 1)$.

dif.r: Chain rule derivative then point-gradient tangent equation

solutions.latex:
Write $y = (4x+1)^{-1}$ and differentiate using the chain rule:
$$y' = -4(4x+1)^{-2} = \dfrac{-4}{(4x+1)^2}$$
When $x=0$:
$$y' = \dfrac{-4}{(4\times0+1)^2} = -4$$
The tangent at $(0,1)$ is
$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= -4(x-0) \\ y &= -4x+1 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $\ln\left(x^2\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac12\times\dfrac{2x}{x^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x}{x^2} \\ &= \dfrac1x \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $y = \dfrac{e^x}{\sin x}$ with respect to $x$.

dif.r: Direct quotient rule with standard derivatives.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{x} & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=e^{x} & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\sin x\cdot e^x - e^x\cos x}{\sin^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(\sin x-\cos x)}{\sin^2 x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_{10}(x - 21) = 2 - \log_{10}x$.

dif.r: Combine logs, solve quadratic, reject invalid root

solutions.latex:
The logarithms need $x-21>0$ and $x>0$, so $x>21$.

Collect the logs on one side:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(x-21)+\log_{10}x &= 2 \\ \log_{10}[x(x-21)] &= 2 \\ x(x-21) &= 10^2 \\ x^2-21x-100 &= 0 \\ (x-25)(x+4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-4$ or $x=25$.

Since $x>21$, $x=-4$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x = 25$$
criteria: Correctly applies the log laws to obtain the quadratic equation $x^2-21x-100=0$, or equivalent merit

Shirley uses her car every day. Sometimes, she needs a few attempts to start her car. Let the discrete random variable $X$ represent the number of attempts needed.

The probability function for the random variable $X$ is given by

$$P(X = x) = \begin{cases} a & x = 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{1}{2}P(X = x-1) & x = 2, 3, 4, 5 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a

dif.r: Interpret recursive probabilities, sum to one

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The probability distribution table for the discrete random variable $X$ is shown.

\extable{1312_q20_t1}

Shirley claims that after an entire year, she needs an average of two attempts to successfully start her car.

Calculate the expected value and comment on the accuracy of Shirley's claim.

dif.r: Compute expected value and interpret against claim

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$. Each term is half the previous one:
$$\begin{aligned} a+\dfrac a2+\dfrac a4+\dfrac a8+\dfrac a{16}+0 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{31a}{16} &= 1 \\ a &= \dfrac{16}{31} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the probabilities for at least one of the values of the random variable, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \sum xp(x) \\ &= 1\times\dfrac{16}{31}+2\times\dfrac{8}{31}+3\times\dfrac{4}{31}+4\times\dfrac{2}{31}+5\times\dfrac{1}{31} \\ &\approx 1.84 \end{aligned}$$
Shirley's claim is correct. As the expected value is $1.84$, over a long period of time Shirley would need around two attempts to successfully start her car.
criteria: Correctly calculates the expected value and links this to Shirley's claim

questions.stem:
A teacher surveyed his class of 24 students about the subjects that they have chosen to study in the following year.

The results indicate that:

\begin{itemize}
\item 8 students chose to study neither Physics nor Chemistry
\item 8 students chose to study Chemistry
\item 12 students chose to study Physics.
\end{itemize}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Draw a Venn diagram showing this information.

dif.r: Find intersection by inclusion-exclusion and draw Venn diagram.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
A student choosing to study Chemistry is event 1. A student choosing to study Physics is event 2.

If a student is chosen at random, determine whether these events are independent of each other.

dif.r: Standard independence test from Venn diagram probabilities.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
The entire year group is given the same survey. The results indicate that:

\begin{itemize}
\item the probability that a student chose to study Chemistry is $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item the probability that a student chose to study Physics is $\dfrac{2}{5}$
\item given that a student chose to study Chemistry, the probability that they chose to study Physics is $\dfrac{3}{7}$.
\end{itemize}

Calculate the probability that a student picked at random has chosen to study Chemistry or Physics.

dif.r: Multiplication rule for intersection then addition rule.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

figures.cap: solution sketch: Venn diagram 4, 4, 8, outside 8

solutions.latex:
Using $|\text{CHE}\cup\text{PHY}|=24-8=16$ and
$$|\text{CHE}\cup\text{PHY}|=|\text{CHE}|+|\text{PHY}|-|\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}|$$
we get $16=8+12-|\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}|$, so $|\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}|=4$.

\exfigure{1312_q25_s1}

From the Venn diagram:
$$P(\text{PHY})=\dfrac{12}{24}=\dfrac{1}{2},\quad P(\text{CHE})=\dfrac{8}{24}=\dfrac{1}{3},\quad P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY})=\dfrac{4}{24}=\dfrac{1}{6}$$
Test for independence:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{PHY})\times P(\text{CHE}) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6} \\ &= P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}) \end{aligned}$$
Since $P(\text{CHE})\times P(\text{PHY})=P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY})$, the two events are independent.
criteria: Correctly calculates either $P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY})$ OR $P(\text{CHE})\times P(\text{PHY})$ OR equivalent condition for independence, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the addition rule and $P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY})=P(\text{CHE})\times P(\text{PHY}\mid\text{CHE})$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{CHE}\cup\text{PHY}) &= P(\text{CHE})+P(\text{PHY})-P(\text{CHE}\cap\text{PHY}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{2}{5}-\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{7}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{62}{105} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source wrote $P(\text{CHE}|\text{PHY})$ in the middle line but used $P(\text{PHY}\mid\text{CHE})=\dfrac{3}{7}$ numerically; corrected notation to match the given.

questions.stem:
A particle is moving in a straight line with a velocity given by

$$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 8\cos\left(2t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),$$

where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in metres and $t$ is time measured in seconds.

The particle is initially at rest 4 m to the right of the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the displacement of the particle is given by $x = 4\sin\left(2t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + 8$.

dif.r: Integrate trig velocity, apply initial condition for constant.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the particle comes to rest again when it is 12 m to the right of the origin and $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ s.

dif.r: Solve velocity zero or substitute t to verify rest and position.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: By finding a function for acceleration, describe the motion of the particle after $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ s and before it next comes to rest.

dif.r: Differentiate velocity, interpret acceleration sign to describe motion.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 8\cos\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)dt \\ &= 8\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right]+C \\ &= 4\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=4$:
$$4=4\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+C=-4+C$$
so $C=8$.
$$\therefore\ x=4\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+8$$
criteria: Correctly finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Method 1: the particle is at rest when $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$\cos\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$$
so $2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ldots$, giving $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\pi,\ldots$

Hence the particle next comes to rest at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds.

Method 2: when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=8\cos\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$x=4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+8=12 \text{ m}$$
Therefore, at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ the particle is at rest 12 m to the right of the origin.
criteria: Attempts to solve the trigonometric equation $\cos\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating the velocity:
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-16\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$$
When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-16\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=-16$$
The acceleration is negative, so the particle moves towards the left after being stationary at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
criteria: Correct answer, with description of the motion of the particle
Correctly finds the formula for acceleration, or equivalent merit

solution sketch: sketch of f(t)

solutions.latex:
Since $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)\,dt=1$:
$$\int_1^{14}\dfrac{k}{2t-1}\,dt=1$$
$$\dfrac{k}{2}\Big[\ln|2t-1|\Big]_1^{14}=1$$
$$\dfrac{k}{2}(\ln27-\ln1)=1$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{2}{\ln27}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch drawn (1312_q27_s1); it was to show: on the question's axes, decreasing curve $y=\dfrac{2}{\ln27}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2t-1}$ for $1\le t\le14$, closed endpoints at $\left(1,\dfrac{2}{\ln27}\right)$ and $\left(14,\dfrac{2}{27\ln27}\right)$, open circles at $(1,0)$ and $(14,0)$, and $f(t)=0$ along the $t$-axis elsewhere.

solutions.latex:
Let $T$ be the time by which the probability of showing symptoms is $0.75$.
$$\int_1^T\dfrac{2}{\ln27}\times\dfrac{1}{2t-1}\,dt=\dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\dfrac{1}{\ln27}\Big[\ln|2t-1|\Big]_1^T=\dfrac{3}{4}$$
$$\ln|2T-1|=\dfrac{3\ln27}{4}$$
$$2T-1=e^{\frac{3\ln27}{4}}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{e^{\frac{3\ln27}{4}}+1}{2} \\ &= 6.422\ldots \\ &\approx 7 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the anti-derivative and arrives at the expression $\dfrac{1}{\ln27}\Big[\ln|2t-1|\Big]_1^T=\dfrac{3}{4}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The mass of two substances, $A$ and $B$, are decaying exponentially according to

$$M_A = 200e^{-0.05t}$$
$$M_B = 400 \times 3^{-0.12t},$$

where $M$ is the mass in grams and $t$ is the time in minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the time taken for substance $A$ to decrease to half of its original value. Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation with logs for half-life.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what instance do both particles decay at the same rate? Give your answer correct to the nearest second.

dif.r: Differentiate a^x and e^x, equate rates, combine bases, solve.

solutions.latex:
Half the original mass is $M_A=100$:
$$100=200e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\dfrac{1}{2}=e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=-0.05t$$
$$\ln2=0.05t$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln2}{0.05} \\ &= 13.86\ldots \\ &\approx 14 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly arrives at the expression $100=200e^{-0.05t}$ and attempts to solve for $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating each mass:
$$\dfrac{dM_A}{dt}=-0.05\times200e^{-0.05t}=-10e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\dfrac{dM_B}{dt}=400\times\ln3\times(-0.12)\times3^{-0.12t}=-48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$$
Equate the two rates:
$$-10e^{-0.05t}=-48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$$
Write both sides with base $e$, using $3^{-0.12t}=e^{(-0.12\ln3)t}$:
$$\dfrac{10}{48\ln3}=\dfrac{3^{-0.12t}}{e^{-0.05t}}=\dfrac{e^{(-0.12\ln3)t}}{e^{-0.05t}}=e^{(-0.12\ln3+0.05)t}$$
$$0.1895\ldots=e^{-0.0818\ldots t}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln0.1895\ldots}{-0.0818\ldots} \\ &= 20.317\ldots \text{ minutes} \\ &\approx 20 \text{ minutes } 19 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Therefore both substances decay at the same rate at 20 minutes and 19 seconds.
criteria: Writes an expression using the same base, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds the rates of decay for both substances AND attempts to solve the equation $-10e^{-0.05t}=-48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the rate of change for substance $A$ OR substance $B$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Find intersection, integrate, decompose symmetric logo into pieces.

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: four-petalled logo with points A, B, C and lines y=x, y=-x

solutions.latex:
Point $A$ lies on both $y=4-3x^2$ and $y=-x$:
$$4-3x^2=-x$$
$$3x^2-x-4=0$$
$$(3x-4)(x+1)=0$$
so $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$ or $x=-1$. From the diagram $x=-1$, and then $y=4-3(-1)^2=1$.

So $A(-1,1)$ and, by symmetry, $C(1,1)$.

The area of $ABC$ is the area under the curve less the rectangle of height 1 and width 2:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{ABC} &= \int_{-1}^{1}(4-3x^2)\,dx-A_{\text{rectangle}} \\ &= \left[4x-x^3\right]_{-1}^{1}-2 \\ &= (4-1)-(-4+1)-2 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
The logo is four copies of $ABC$ plus two rectangles:
