questions.stem:
Jonathan's parents decide to set up an investment account to help pay for his university degree. Jonathan's parents deposit \$1000 into the account every year, which earns interest at 4% per annum, compounded yearly. They deposited the first \$1000 at the beginning of the year when Jonathan is born. Jonathan will receive the full amount at the end of the year he turns 18 years old.

Let $A_n$ be the value of the account after $n$ years.

dif.r: Build first three terms of annuity recurrence and factorise.
Generalise pattern to 18 years and sum geometric series.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
The amount in the account continues to earn interest at 4% per annum. Jonathan enrols in a four-year university course, which costs $\$M$ each year, to be paid at the end of the year. As a result:

$$A_{19} = 26000\left(1.04^{18} - 1\right)(1.04) - M.$$

How much can Jonathan withdraw from the account each year if the entire amount is to be withdrawn over the four years?

dif.r: Extended recurrence for withdrawals, geometric sum, solve for M.

criteria: Correctly finds an unsimplified expression for $A_{18}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Each year the balance grows by $1.04$ and then $M$ is withdrawn:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{20} &= \left[26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)-M\right](1.04)-M \\ &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^2-M(1+1.04) \end{aligned}$$
$$A_{21}=26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^3-M\left(1+1.04+1.04^2\right)$$
By the pattern, using the geometric series sum $\dfrac{1.04^4-1}{0.04}=25\left(1.04^4-1\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{22} &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4-M\left(1+1.04+1.04^2+1.04^3\right) \\ &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4-25M\left(1.04^4-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
The account is empty when $A_{22}=0$:
$$M=\dfrac{26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4}{25\left(1.04^4-1\right)}$$
$$\therefore\ M=\$7347.66$$
criteria: Correctly uses $A_{22}=0$ and attempts to solve, or equivalent merit
Correctly uses the pattern to write down an expression for $A_{22}$, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds an expression for $A_{21}$, or equivalent merit
Correctly finds an expression for $A_{20}$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: ii
parts.latex:

$$x_1 = \dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8$$

$$\text{and } x_2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi + \tan^{-1}8\right).$$

dif.r: Tan periodicity with adjusted domain for 4x.

dif.r: Product rule, link derivative to earlier tan equation.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex:
It is known that the $y$-coordinates of the stationary points $Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, \ldots, Y_n$ form a geometric sequence.

Find the exact value of the common ratio for this geometric sequence. Express your answer in simplest form.

dif.r: Evaluate Y1, Y2 exactly with sin(pi+θ), simplify ratio.

can_use: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: damped sine curve with stationary points P1 to P5

solutions.latex:
Rearranging:
$$4\cos4x=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x$$
$$8\cos4x=\sin4x$$
Dividing both sides by $\cos4x$:
$$\tan4x=8$$

The solutions of $\tan4x=8$ with $0\le4x\le4\pi$ are
$$4x=\tan^{-1}8,\ \pi+\tan^{-1}8,\ 2\pi+\tan^{-1}8$$
so
$$x=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8,\ \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right),\ \dfrac{1}{4}\left(2\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
Therefore the first two solutions are
$$x_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8 \quad\text{and}\quad x_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
criteria: Correctly shows ONE solution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote the range as $[0,4\pi]$ for $4x$ (domain $[0,\pi]$ for $x$); kept.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $y=10e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}\sin4x$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{-\frac{1}{2}x} & v&=\sin4x\\ u'&=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{1}{2}x} & v'&=4\cos4x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 10\left[\sin4x\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}+e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}\times4\cos4x\right] \\ &= 10e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x+4\cos4x\right) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $y'=0$. Since $e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}>0$, we need $-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x+4\cos4x=0$, which is $\tan4x=8$ by part (a).

Therefore:
$$X_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8,\qquad X_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
criteria: Finds the derivative of $y$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Consequential on the answer to part (a)(ii).
meta.format_note: Source note about consequential marking moved to marker_note.

solutions.latex:
At $X_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8$:
$$Y_1=10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\tan^{-1}8}\sin\left(\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
At $X_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$, using $\sin(\pi+\theta)=-\sin\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} Y_2 &= 10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)}\sin\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right) \\ &= -10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)}\sin\left(\tan^{-1}8\right) \end{aligned}$$
The common ratio is
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{Y_2}{Y_1} \\ &= -e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)+\frac{1}{8}\tan^{-1}8} \\ &= -e^{-\frac{1}{8}\pi} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds an expression for $Y_1$ and $Y_2$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: In a normal distribution, what is the approximate percentage of scores with a $z$-score less than 1?

dif.r: Recall 68% rule then split tails symmetrically; two steps.

solutions.latex:
In a normal distribution, about $68\%$ of scores lie within one standard deviation of the mean, that is $-1 < z < 1$.

The remaining $32\%$ is split equally between the two tails, so $16\%$ of scores have $z > 1$.

Scores with $z < 1$ are all the rest:
$$\begin{aligned} P(z<1) &= 100\% - 16\% \\ &= 84\% \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

solutions.latex:
The die has 6 faces and the spinner has 4 sections, so there are $6\times 4 = 24$ equally likely outcomes in the table.

Count the outcomes with a score of 7 or more for each spinner number (die number needed is at least $7-s$):
$$\begin{aligned} s=1 &: \text{die } 6 &&\text{1 outcome}\\ s=2 &: \text{die } 5, 6 &&\text{2 outcomes}\\ s=3 &: \text{die } 4, 5, 6 &&\text{3 outcomes}\\ s=4 &: \text{die } 3, 4, 5, 6 &&\text{4 outcomes}\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The ratio $2:3$ has $2+3=5$ parts, so each part is $150\div 5 = 30$ jelly beans.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{red} &= 2\times 30 = 60\\ \text{blue} &= 3\times 30 = 90 \end{aligned}$$
After Sophie eats 10 of each colour:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{red} &= 50\\ \text{blue} &= 80 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A cylindrical pipe with a radius of 12.5 cm is filled with water to a depth, $d$ cm, as shown.

The surface of the water has a width of 20 cm.

\exfigure{300_q12_1}

What is the depth of water in the pipe?

dif.r: Set up right triangle in circle, Pythagoras, then interpret depth from radius.

figures.cap: cross-section of pipe with water of width 20 cm and depth d

solutions.latex:
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so the half-width of the water surface is $10$ cm.

Let $h$ be the distance from the centre to the surface. In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $12.5$ (the radius), Pythagoras' theorem gives
$$\begin{aligned} h^2 + 10^2 &= 12.5^2\\ h^2 &= 156.25 - 100 = 56.25\\ h &= 7.5 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
From the figure the centre is above the water surface, so the depth is the radius minus $h$:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 12.5 - 7.5\\ &= 5.0 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

The diagram shows the location of three places $X$, $Y$ and $C$.

$Y$ is on a bearing of $120^\circ$ and 15 km from $X$.

$P$ lies on the line joining $C$ and $Y$ and is due south of $X$.

\exfigure{300_q27_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the distance from $X$ to $P$.

dif.r: Deduce right-triangle angle from bearing geometry, then cosine ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the bearing of $C$ from $X$, to the nearest degree?

dif.r: Find angle via inverse cosine then convert to true bearing past south.

figures.cap: bearings diagram with X, Y, C, P
solution sketch: bearings diagram with angles marked

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{300_q27_s1}

Due south of $X$ is a straight line, so $\angle PXY$ is supplementary to the bearing $120^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle PXY &= 180^\circ-120^\circ\\ &= 60^\circ\end{aligned}$$
In right-angled triangle $PXY$, $XP$ is adjacent to $\angle PXY$.
$$\begin{aligned}XP &= 15\times\cos 60^\circ\\ &= 7.5 \text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies an angle in triangle $PXY$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{300_q27_s1}

In right-angled triangle $CXP$, let $\theta = \angle CXP$, with $XP = 7.5$ km and $XC = 40$ km.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta &= \dfrac{7.5}{40}\\ \theta &\approx 79^\circ 12'\end{aligned}$$
$C$ is south-west of $X$, so the bearing is measured past south.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Bearing of } C &= 180^\circ+79^\circ 12'\\ &= 259^\circ 12'\\ &\approx 259^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of } C \text{ from } X \text{ is } 259^\circ$$
criteria: Calculates one of the acute angles in triangle $CXP$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Straight-line method, using $S = V_0 - D_n$:
$$\begin{aligned}S &= 60\,000-3500\times 3\\ &= \$49\,500\end{aligned}$$
Declining-balance method, using $S = V_0(1-r)^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}S &= 60\,000(1-0.12)^3\\ &= 60\,000(0.88)^3\\ &= \$40\,888.32\end{aligned}$$
Since $\$40\,888.32 < \$49\,500$:
$$\therefore\ \text{the declining-balance method gives the lower salvage value.}$$
criteria: Correctly calculates the salvage value using the declining-balance method, or equivalent merit

$N$ is the number of standard drinks consumed

$M$ is the person's weight in kilograms

$H$ is the number of hours of drinking

Cameron weighs 75 kg. His BAC was zero when he began drinking alcohol. At 9:00 pm, after consuming 3 standard drinks, his BAC was 0.02.

Using the formula, estimate at what time Cameron began drinking alcohol, to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Solve given formula for H, convert hours, subtract time.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $BAC=0.02$, $N=3$ and $M=75$ into the formula.
$$\begin{aligned}0.02 &= \dfrac{10\times 3-7.5H}{6.8\times 75}\\ 10.2 &= 30-7.5H\\ H &= \dfrac{30-10.2}{7.5}\\ &= 2.64 \text{ hours}\\ &\approx 2 \text{ h } 38 \text{ min}\end{aligned}$$
Subtract from 9:00 pm.
$$9{:}00 \text{ pm} - 2 \text{ h } 38 \text{ min} = 6{:}22 \text{ pm}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Cameron began drinking at 6:22 pm.}$$

Lily wanted to estimate the number of fish in a lake.

She randomly captured 30 fish, then tagged and released them.

One week later she randomly captured 40 fish from the same lake. She found that 12 of these 40 fish were tagged.

What is the best estimate for the total number of fish in the lake?

dif.r: Standard capture-recapture proportion set up and solved

solutions.latex:
Using the capture-recapture method, the proportion of tagged fish in the second sample estimates the proportion in the whole lake.

Let $N$ be the number of fish in the lake.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12}{40}&=\dfrac{30}{N}\\ N&=\dfrac{30\times 40}{12}\\ &=100 \end{aligned}$$
So the best estimate is 100, option D.

parts.latex:
Consider the following dataset.

$$13 \quad 16 \quad 17 \quad 17 \quad 21 \quad 24$$

Which row of the table shows how the median and mean are affected when a score of 5 is added to the dataset?

dif.r: Work out the median and mean before and after adding a score

options.label: B
options.latex: Median: Stays the same; Mean: Stays the same

options.label: C
options.latex: Median: Changes; Mean: Stays the same

options.label: D
options.latex: Median: Stays the same; Mean: Changes

solutions.latex:
Original dataset (6 scores): $13,\ 16,\ 17,\ 17,\ 21,\ 24$.

The median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th scores:
$$\dfrac{17+17}{2}=17$$
The mean is:
$$\dfrac{13+16+17+17+21+24}{6}=\dfrac{108}{6}=18$$
After adding 5 there are 7 scores: $5,\ 13,\ 16,\ 17,\ 17,\ 21,\ 24$.

The median is the 4th score, which is 17, so the median stays the same.

The new mean is:
$$\dfrac{108+5}{7}=\dfrac{113}{7}\approx 16.1$$
so the mean changes.

So the median stays the same and the mean changes, option D.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
For the declining-balance method, the salvage value of the machine after $n$ years is given by the formula

$$S = V_0 \times (0.80)^n,$$

where $S$ is the salvage value and $V_0$ is the initial value of the asset.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:

When will the value of the machine, using this method, be equal to the salvage value found in part (a) (ii)?

dif.r: Find annual depreciation, then solve a linear equation for n

solutions.latex:
The formula is $S = V_0 \times (0.80)^n$, so each year the value is $80\%$ of the previous value.

The annual rate of depreciation is $100\% - 80\% = 20\%$.

Using the given formula with $V_0 = 50\,000$ and $n = 3$:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= 50\,000 \times (0.8)^3 \\ &= \$25\,600 \end{aligned}$$

Straight-line depreciation each year is $12.2\%$ of the purchase price.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Annual depreciation} &= 12.2\% \times 50\,000 \\ &= \$6100 \end{aligned}$$
The value after $n$ years equals the salvage value from part (a)(ii).
$$\begin{aligned} 25\,600 &= 50\,000 - 6100n \\ -24\,400 &= -6100n \\ n &= \dfrac{-24\,400}{-6100} \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n = 4 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds the annual depreciated amount, or equivalent merit

Adding 1.2 L of water gives $2.7 + 1.2 = 3.9$ L of water.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{cordial} : \text{water} &= 0.9 : 3.9 \\ &= 3 : 13 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the ratio of cordial to water is } 3:13$$

parts.latex: Which of the following could represent the graph of $y = -x^2 + 1$?

dif.r: Recognise concave-down parabola and intercepts from familiar equation

figures.cap: option A: straight line graph
option B: exponential growth graph
option C: concave-down parabola
option D: hyperbola through (1, 1)

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=-x^2+1$ is a parabola, since $x$ is squared.

The coefficient of $x^2$ is negative, so it is concave down.

The $y$-intercept is found by letting $x=0$:
$$y=1$$
The $x$-intercepts are found by letting $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -x^2+1 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= 1 \\ x &= \pm 1 \end{aligned}$$
So the graph is a concave down parabola with $y$-intercept $1$ and $x$-intercepts $-1$ and $1$. Only graph C has these features (A is a line, B is exponential, D is a hyperbola).

$$\therefore\ \text{the graph is C}$$

John recently did a class test in each of three subjects. The class scores on each test were normally distributed.

The table shows the subjects and John's scores as well as the mean and standard deviation of the class scores on each test.

\extable{36_q8_t1}

Relative to the rest of the class, which row of the table below shows John's strongest subject and his weakest subject?

dif.r: Compute and compare three z-scores

options.label: A
options.latex: Strongest subject: Commerce; weakest subject: French

options.label: B
options.latex: Strongest subject: French; weakest subject: Music

options.label: C
options.latex: Strongest subject: Music; weakest subject: French

options.label: D
options.latex: Strongest subject: Commerce; weakest subject: Music

solutions.latex:
To compare scores from different normal distributions, use the $z$-score of each score:
$$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$
where $x$ is John's score, $\mu$ the class mean and $\sigma$ the class standard deviation.

The subject with the largest $z$-score is the one where John is furthest above the class mean, so it is his strongest subject. The subject with the smallest $z$-score is his weakest.

Calculating $z$ for each row of the table gives the largest $z$-score for Commerce and the smallest for French.
$$\therefore\ \text{Strongest subject: Commerce; weakest subject: French}$$
This is option A.

An annuity consists of ten payments, each equal to \$1000. Each payment is made on 30 June each year from 2021 through to 2030 inclusive.

The rate of compound interest is $5\%$ per annum.

The present value of the annuity is calculated at 30 June 2020.

The future value of the annuity is calculated at 30 June 2030.

Without performing any calculations, which of the following statements is true?

dif.r: Conceptual reasoning about present and future values without calculation

options.label: A
options.latex: $\text{Present value of the annuity} < \$10\,000 < \text{future value of the annuity}$

options.label: B
options.latex: $\$10\,000 < \text{present value of the annuity} < \text{future value of the annuity}$

options.label: C
options.latex: $\text{Future value of the annuity} < \$10\,000 < \text{present value of the annuity}$

options.label: D
options.latex: $\$10\,000 < \text{future value of the annuity} < \text{present value of the annuity}$

solutions.latex:
The payments total $10 \times \$1000 = \$10\,000$.

The present value is the value at 30 June 2020, before any payment is made. Each payment is discounted back, so each is worth less than \$1000 and the present value is less than \$10\,000.

The future value is the value at 30 June 2030. Every payment except the last has earned interest, so the future value is greater than \$10\,000.
$$\text{Present value} < \$10\,000 < \text{future value}$$
This is option A.

The top of a rectangular table is divided into 8 equal sections as shown.

\extable{36_q15_t1}

A standard die with faces labelled 1 to 6 is rolled onto the table. The die is equally likely to land in any of the 8 sections of the table. If the die does not land entirely in one section of the table, it is rolled again.

A score is calculated by multiplying the value shown on the top face of the die by the number shown in the section of the table where the die lands.

What is the probability of getting a score of 6?

dif.r: Enumerate product outcomes over two-stage experiment with unequal spaces

solutions.latex:
The die is equally likely to land in each of the 8 sections, so each section has probability $\dfrac{1}{8}$. Each face of the die has probability $\dfrac{1}{6}$.

The score is the die value multiplied by the section number. Pairs (section, die) giving a score of 6:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{section } 1 &\text{ and die } 6 \\ \text{section } 2 &\text{ and die } 3 \\ \text{section } 3 &\text{ and die } 2 \\ \text{section } 6 &\text{ and die } 1 \end{aligned}$$
Each section number appears once, so there are 4 such pairs, each with probability $\dfrac{1}{8}\times\dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{48}$.
$$P(\text{score } 6) = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{48} = \dfrac{1}{12}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex:
Consider the following dataset.

$$1 \quad 5 \quad 9 \quad 10 \quad 15$$

Suppose a new value, $x$, is added to this dataset, giving the following.

$$1 \quad 5 \quad 9 \quad 10 \quad 15 \quad x$$

It is known that $x$ is greater than 15. It is also known that the difference between the means of the two datasets is equal to ten times the difference between the medians of the two datasets.

Calculate the value of $x$.

dif.r: Set up equation linking mean and median changes; non-routine

solutions.latex:
For the first dataset:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{mean} &= \dfrac{1+5+9+10+15}{5} = 8 \\ \text{median} &= 9 \end{aligned}$$
For the second dataset, since $x>15$ it is the largest value:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{mean} &= \dfrac{40+x}{6} \\ \text{median} &= \dfrac{9+10}{2} = 9.5 \end{aligned}$$
The difference in means equals ten times the difference in medians:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{40+x}{6}-8 &= 10(9.5-9) \\ \dfrac{40+x}{6}-8 &= 5 \\ \dfrac{40+x}{6} &= 13 \\ 40+x &= 78 \\ x &= 38 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = 38$$
criteria: Calculates the mean and median of the first dataset and the mean of the second dataset, or equivalent merit
Calculates mean and median of first dataset, or equivalent merit
Calculates median of first dataset, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added the sum 40 and median reasoning for clarity.

Mr Ali, Ms Brown and a group of students were camping at the site located at $P$. Mr Ali walked with some of the students on a bearing of $035^\circ$ for 7 km to location $A$. Ms Brown, with the rest of the students, walked on a bearing of $100^\circ$ for 9 km to location $B$.

\exfigure{36_q31_1}

solutions.latex:
North lines at $P$ give the bearings measured clockwise from north.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle APB &= 100^\circ-35^\circ \\ &= 65^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Using the cosine rule in $\triangle APB$:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2 &= 7^2+9^2-2\times 7\times 9\cos 65^\circ \\ &= 76.75\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ AB \approx 8.76 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the cosine rule to find the distance $AB$

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule in $\triangle APB$ to find $\angle PAB$:
$$\dfrac{\sin A}{9} = \dfrac{\sin 65^\circ}{8.76\ldots}$$
$$A = 68.6\ldots^\circ \approx 69^\circ$$
The bearing of $B$ from $A$ is found using the angle at $A$ and the north line at $A$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 180^\circ-(69^\circ-35^\circ) \\ &= 146^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds another angle in $\triangle APB$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The diagram shows a regular decagon (ten-sided shape with all sides equal and all interior angles equal). The decagon has centre $O$.

The perimeter of the shape is 80 cm.

dif.r: Decagon area via central angle, sine rule, triangle area; multi-step

can_use: Area of a triangle (1/2 ab sin C)

figures.cap: regular decagon with centre O

solutions.latex:
The ten sides are equal, so
$$AB = 80\div 10 = 8 \text{ cm}$$
The ten angles at the centre are equal:
$$\angle AOB = 360^\circ\div 10 = 36^\circ$$
Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles ($OA=OB=r$), so
$$\angle OAB = \dfrac{180^\circ-36^\circ}{2} = 72^\circ$$
Using the sine rule in $\triangle OAB$:
$$\dfrac{r}{\sin 72^\circ} = \dfrac{8}{\sin 36^\circ}$$
$$r = 12.944\ldots$$
The area is ten times the area of $\triangle OAB$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 10\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times(12.944\ldots)^2\times\sin 36^\circ \\ &\approx 492.4 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates area of $\triangle AOB$, or equivalent merit

The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) scores for adults in City $A$ are normally distributed with a mean of 108 and a standard deviation of 10.

The IQ scores for adults in City $B$ are normally distributed with a mean of 112 and a standard deviation of 16.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Yin is an adult who lives in City $A$ and has an IQ score of 128.

What percentage of the adults in this city have an IQ score higher than Yin's?

dif.r: z-score then empirical rule tail percentage

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
There are 1 000 000 adults living in City $B$.

Calculate the number of adults in City $B$ that would be expected to have an IQ score lower than Yin's.

dif.r: New distribution z-score, cumulative 84%, scale to population

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Simon, an adult who lives in City $A$, moves to City $B$. The $z$-score corresponding to his IQ score in City $A$ is the same as the $z$-score corresponding to his IQ score in City $B$.

By first forming an equation, calculate Simon's IQ score. Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

dif.r: Form and solve equation equating two z-scores

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{128-108}{10} = 2$$
So $128$ is 2 standard deviations above the mean.

About $95\%$ of scores lie within 2 standard deviations, so $5\%$ lie outside, split equally between the two tails.
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{5\%}{2} = 2.5\% \text{ have an IQ score higher than Yin's}$$
criteria: Demonstrates that $97.5\%$ relates to 2 standard deviations above the mean, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Mean of City $B$ is $112$, so one standard deviation above the mean is
$$112+16 = 128$$
So Yin's score is 1 standard deviation above the mean in City $B$.

The percentage with a lower score is
$$50\%+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 68\% = 84\%$$
The expected number of adults is
$$1\,000\,000\times 0.84 = 840\,000$$
criteria: Demonstrates Yin is 1 standard deviation above the mean in City $B$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $x$ be Simon's IQ score. Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} z_A &= \dfrac{x-108}{10} \\ z_B &= \dfrac{x-112}{16} \end{aligned}$$
The $z$-scores are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x-108}{10} &= \dfrac{x-112}{16} \\ 16(x-108) &= 10(x-112) \\ 16x-1728 &= 10x-1120 \\ 6x &= 608 \\ x &\approx 101.3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Simon's IQ score is } 101.3$$
criteria: Provides correct equation linking City $A$ with City $B$
Provides correct expression for the $z$-score for City $A$ or City $B$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A cricket is an insect. The male cricket produces a chirping sound.

A scientist wants to explore the relationship between the temperature in degrees Celsius and the number of cricket chirps heard in a 15-second time interval.

Once a day for 20 days, the scientist collects data. Based on the 20 data points, the scientist provides the information below.

\begin{itemize}
\item A box-plot of the temperature data is shown.

\exfigure{36_q36_1}
\item The mean temperature in the dataset is $0.525^\circ\text{C}$ below the median temperature in the dataset.
\item A total of 684 chirps was counted when collecting the 20 data points.
\end{itemize}

The scientist fits a least-squares regression line using the data $(x, y)$, where $x$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius and $y$ is the number of chirps heard in a 15-second time interval. The equation of this line is

$$y = -10.6063 + bx,$$

where $b$ is the slope of the regression line.

The least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the temperature data and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the chirp data.

Calculate the number of chirps expected in a 15-second interval when the temperature is $19^\circ$ Celsius. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

dif.r: Combine box-plot, means and regression point to find slope; multi-stage

figures.cap: box plot of temperature data

solutions.latex:
The median temperature is $22$, read from the box-plot, so
$$\bar{x} = 22-0.525 = 21.475$$
$$\bar{y} = \dfrac{684}{20} = 34.2$$
The regression line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$:
$$\begin{aligned} 34.2 &= -10.6063+b(21.475) \\ b &= \dfrac{44.8063}{21.475} \\ &= 2.08644\ldots \end{aligned}$$
When $x=19$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -10.6063+2.08644\ldots\times 19 \\ &= 29.03606\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 29 \text{ chirps are expected}$$
criteria: Finds value of $b$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ into the regression equation, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $\bar{x}$ or $\bar{y}$ or the median of the temperature, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Median 22 taken from the box-plot as in the source.

dif.r: Deferred annuity via difference of table factors; novel construction

solutions.latex:
Present value of the \$1000 annuity for 20 years:
$$16.351\times 1000 = \$16\,351$$
The \$3000 payments are years 21 to 30, so take a 30-year annuity less a 20-year annuity:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{PV}_{30} &= 22.396\times 3000 = \$67\,188 \\ \text{PV}_{20} &= 16.351\times 3000 = \$49\,053 \end{aligned}$$
Total present value:
$$\begin{aligned} PV &= 16\,351+67\,188-49\,053 \\ &= \$34\,486 \end{aligned}$$
Alternate solution: the last 10 payments, discounted back 20 years, have present value
$$\dfrac{3000\times 8.983}{(1+0.02)^{20}}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 16.351\times 1000+\dfrac{3000\times 8.983}{(1+0.02)^{20}} \\ &= \$34\,486.90 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides calculation for the value of the \$1000 annuity for 20 years, or equivalent merit
Identifies an appropriate annuity factor, or equivalent merit

On 14th June, Chris owes $\$950$ on his credit card. He makes no further purchases using the credit card. The period for which the interest is charged includes the date of purchase and the date of payment. Calculate the amount owing on the card on 12th July.

dif.r: Daily compound interest; count days inclusively across two months.

solutions.latex:
The daily rate is the annual rate divided by 365.
$$r = 0.15\div 365 \approx 0.0004109$$
Interest is charged from 14 June to 12 July inclusive of both dates, so
$$n = 29$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Amount} &= 950(1+0.0004109)^{29} \\ &\approx \$961.39 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Explanation of n=29 added: 14 June to 12 July counting both dates gives 17+12=29... source value kept.

parts.latex:
Navneet and her husband want to buy a house. Their combined gross income is $\$9836.67$ per month. They can afford $25\%$ of their gross monthly income for loan repayments. The couple are already paying off a car loan at $\$260$ per month.

The bank offers a loan with monthly repayments of $\$8.36$ per $\$1000$ borrowed.

Calculate the largest loan that this couple can afford, to the nearest thousand.

dif.r: Chain percentage, subtract existing loan, invert per-$1000 repayment rate.

solutions.latex:
Find $25\%$ of the gross monthly income.
$$25\%\times 9836.67 = \$2459.17$$
Subtract the car loan repayment.
$$2459.17 - 260 = \$2199.17$$
The repayment is $\$8.36$ per $\$1000$, so divide to find the number of thousands.
$$2199.17\div 8.36 \approx 263.0586$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Maximum loan} = 263.0586\times 1000 \approx \$263\,000$$
criteria: Finds the available repayment after the car loan ($\$2199.17$), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Michael takes a loan of $\$450\,000$ over a period of 25 years at a reducible interest rate of $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.

Repayments $R$ are made monthly.

Using the table of present value interest factors below and the recurrence relation,

$$A_{n+1} = A_n(1+r) - R$$

Calculate how much interest has been charged on the loan after the second repayment.

\extable{3314_q8_t1}

dif.r: Combine PV table for repayment with two recurrence steps for interest.

solutions.latex:
The monthly rate and number of repayments are
$$r = 6\%\div 12 = 0.5\% ,\qquad n = 25\times 12 = 300$$
From the table, the interest factor is $155.2069$, so
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 450\,000\div 155.2069 \\ &= \$2899.36 \end{aligned}$$
Using $A_{n+1} = A_n(1+r) - R$ with $A_0 = 450\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 450\,000(1.005) - 2899.36 = \$449\,350.64 \\ A_2 &= 449\,350.64(1.005) - 2899.36 = \$448\,698.03 \end{aligned}$$
The loan has reduced by
$$450\,000 - 448\,698.03 = \$1301.97$$
The total repayments are
$$2\times 2899.36 = \$5798.72$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest} &= 5798.72 - 1301.97 \\ &= \$4496.75 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the loan reduction, or equivalent merit

The graphs below show the distribution of the ages of children in Numbertown in 2000 and 2010. In the year 2010, there were 2500 children. The number of children aged 12-18 is the same in 2000 and 2010.

\exfigure{1305_q1a_1}

parts.label: a

dif.r: Reading graph to state median, IQR, range and skew

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many children were aged 0-2 in 2010?

dif.r: Read percentage from graph, multiply by total

parts.label: c
parts.latex: How many children aged 0-18 were there in 2000?

dif.r: Links equal counts across years to proportion; short inference

figures.cap: box plots of ages of children in Numbertown, 2000 and 2010

solutions.latex:
The distribution of children's ages in 2000 is negatively skewed.

The median is 12 (location).

The interquartile range is 8 and the range is 18 (spread).
criteria: Correct mention of skew and median, or equivalent merit
Correct mention of skew, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In 2010, $25\%$ of the children were aged 0-2.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.25\times 2500 &= 625 \text{ children} \end{aligned}$$

In 2010 the children aged 12-18 are those from the upper quartile to the maximum: a quarter of the 2500 children, which is 625.

In 2000 the median is 12, so the 625 children aged 12-18 are half of the data.

Therefore there were 1250 children in 2000.
$$\therefore\ 2\times 625 = 1250 \text{ children}$$

parts.latex: Determine $f(x)$ given that $f'(x)=\sec^2 2x+\sin 2x$ and $f(0)=1$.

dif.r: Standard trig antiderivatives plus initial condition for constant

solutions.latex:
Integrate each term.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{\tan 2x}{2}-\dfrac{\cos 2x}{2}+C$$
Use $f(0)=1$ to find $C$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(0)&=\dfrac{\tan 0}{2}-\dfrac{\cos 0}{2}+C=1 \\ 0-\dfrac{1}{2}+C&=1 \\ C&=\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\tan 2x-\cos 2x+3\right)$$
criteria: Correct integration and attempts to find $C$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ where $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Explain why the particle never changes direction.

dif.r: Justify via range of sine that velocity never negative

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction
Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the displacement $x$ of the particle after 1 second.

dif.r: Integrate trig velocity, find constant, evaluate displacement

parts.label: c
parts.latex: For sufficiently large values of $t$ (as $t\to\infty$), describe the behaviour of the displacement of the particle.

dif.r: Interpret long-term behaviour using bounded cosine term

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the exact acceleration of the particle at $t=4$ seconds.

dif.r: Differentiate velocity once and substitute

solutions.latex:
The range of $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ is $[0,4]$.

So $v\ge 0$ for all $t$.

Therefore the particle is only ever stationary or travelling in the positive direction, so it never changes direction.

Integrate the velocity.
$$x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=0+\dfrac{1}{\pi}+C \\ C&=-\dfrac{1}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)-\dfrac{1}{\pi}$.

When $t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2+\dfrac{1}{\pi}-\dfrac{1}{\pi} \\ &=2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

$$x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)-\dfrac{1}{\pi}$$
The cosine term is bounded, so as $t\to\infty$, $x\to\infty$.

Therefore the displacement approaches infinity.

Students can also use the fact that the particle never changes direction from part (a).

Differentiate the velocity.
$$a=-4\pi\cos(2\pi t)$$
When $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-4\pi\cos(8\pi) \\ &=-4\pi \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct acceleration equation, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right)=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$.

dif.r: Log laws then routine derivative and combine fractions

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{9-x^2}$.

dif.r: Hence integral by scaling previous derivative result

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule inside the logarithm, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right]&=\dfrac{\frac{(3-x)(1)-(3+x)(-1)}{(3-x)^2}}{\frac{3+x}{3-x}} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{(3-x)^2}\cdot\dfrac{3-x}{3+x} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{(3-x)(3+x)} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using log laws:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(3+x)-\ln(3-x)\right]&=\dfrac{1}{3+x}+\dfrac{1}{3-x} \\ &=\dfrac{(3-x)+(3+x)}{(3+x)(3-x)} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the differentiation rule, or equivalent merit
Uses the quotient rule or log laws, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: The source quotient-rule line has been formatted as given; criteria wording mentions integration though the part is differentiation, kept in spirit.

solutions.latex:
From part (a):
$$\int\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx=\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)+C$$
Divide by 6.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{6}\int\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the exact area bounded by the curve $y=x^2-2$, the $x$ axis and the line $y=4$.

dif.r: Identify region, integrate with respect to y using symmetry

skills: Area with respect to the y-axis

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of region bounded by y=x^2-2 and y=4

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1305_q3b_s1}

The curve is $y=x^2-2$, so $x=\pm\sqrt{y+2}$.

By symmetry, integrate with respect to $y$ from $0$ to $4$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\int_0^4\sqrt{y+2}\,dy \\ &=2\left[\dfrac{(y+2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^4 \\ &=\dfrac{4}{3}\left[(y+2)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^4 \\ &=\dfrac{4}{3}\left(6^{\frac{3}{2}}-2^{\frac{3}{2}}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{4}{3}\left(6\sqrt{6}-2\sqrt{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{8}{3}\left(3\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}\right) \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One error in correct method, or finds the area between curves but does not remove the excess area between $-\sqrt{2}\le x\le\sqrt{2}$, or equivalent merit
Two errors with correct procedure, or an error or incomplete solution using area between two curves, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The first term of a geometric series is $e^{x}$ and the fifth term is $81e^{9x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the common ratio can be expressed by $r=3e^{2x}$.

dif.r: Geometric term formula with index laws, fourth root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find an expression for the $8^{\text{th}}$ term of the series.

dif.r: Substitute into T_n formula with index laws

parts.label: c
parts.latex: For what values of $x$ does the series have a limiting sum?

dif.r: Limiting sum condition gives exponential inequality solved by logs

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the exact value of $x$ if the limiting sum is 3.

dif.r: Hidden quadratic in e^x, reject negative root

solutions.latex:
For a geometric series, $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, with $a=e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_5=e^x r^4&=81e^{9x} \\ r^4&=81e^{8x} \\ r&=\sqrt[4]{81e^{8x}} \\ &=3e^{2x} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us from the 2-mark allocation.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} T_8&=ar^7 \\ &=e^x\left(3e^{2x}\right)^7 \\ &=e^x\cdot 2187e^{14x} \\ &=2187e^{15x} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$|3e^{2x}|<1$$
Since $3e^{2x}>0$ for all $x$, this becomes:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&<3e^{2x}<1 \\ 0&<e^{2x}<\dfrac{1}{3} &&(\text{divide by } 3) \\ 2x&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) &&(\text{take } \ln) \\ x&<\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) &&(\text{divide by } 2) \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=\dfrac{e^x}{1-3e^{2x}} \\ 3\left(1-3e^{2x}\right)&=e^x \\ 3-9e^{2x}&=e^x \\ 0&=9e^{2x}+e^x-3 \end{aligned}$$
Let $u=e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=9u^2+u-3 \\ u&=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{1-4(9)(-3)}}{18} \\ &=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{109}}{18} \end{aligned}$$
Since $u=e^x>0$, $u$ cannot be negative.
$$e^x=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{109}}{18}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\ln\left(\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{109}}{18}\right)\approx-0.65$$
criteria: Forms the quadratic in $e^x$ and solves it, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A factory located next to a lake has recently been shut down due to concerns about chemical run off. A bird's eye view of the lake is given in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1305_q5_1}

Local volunteers have begun a clean-up effort to remove these harmful chemicals from the lake. The concentration of chemicals is given by the equation:

$$C=1.5-0.4e^{kt}$$

Let $C$ be the concentration of chemicals in the lake in kg/m$^3$, where $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the number of years after the clean-up effort has started.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: The initial weight of chemical run off in the lake is 38500 kg, and the average depth of the lake is 5 m. Use the trapezoidal rule to show that the initial concentration of chemical run off can be estimated as 1.1 kg/m$^3$.

dif.r: Trapezoidal rule from diagram, then volume and concentration in context

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $k$ to three significant figures if it takes 2.45 years to remove all chemical run off from the lake

dif.r: Set C=0, solve exponential equation with logs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the rate of change in the concentration of chemical run off in the lake at $t=1.8$ years. Round your answer to two decimal places.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential model and substitute value

figures.cap: bird's eye view of lake with five widths 45, 80, 90, 60, 55 m at 25 m spacing

solutions.latex:
Trapezoidal rule with width $h=25$ and the measured widths from the diagram:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{25}{2}\left(45+55+2(80+90+60)\right) \\ &=7000 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Volume $=$ area $\times$ depth:
$$V=7000\times 5=35000 \text{ m}^3$$
Concentration is weight divided by volume:
$$\dfrac{38500 \text{ kg}}{35000 \text{ m}^3}=1.1 \text{ kg/m}^3$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule and finds the volume, or equivalent merit
Applies the trapezoidal rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
All chemical is removed when $C=0$ at $t=2.45$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=1.5-0.4e^{2.45k} \\ \dfrac{1.5}{0.4}&=e^{2.45k} \\ 2.45k&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1.5}{0.4}\right) \\ k&=\dfrac{\ln(1.5\div 0.4)}{2.45} \\ &=0.539 \text{ (3 significant figures)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Working towards correct answer, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $C=1.5-0.4e^{0.539t}$.
$$\dfrac{dC}{dt}=-0.4\times 0.539\,e^{0.539t}$$
When $t=1.8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dC}{dt}&=-0.4\times 0.539\,e^{0.539\times 1.8} \\ &=-0.5699\ldots \\ &\approx -0.57 \text{ kg/m}^3 \text{ per year} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Working towards correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the position of particle $P$ is given by $x=(t-2)^2+4$.

dif.r: Integrate linear velocity, use initial position, complete square

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Explain why particles $P$ and $Q$ will never collide.

dif.r: Justify from graphs or bounds that positions never coincide

skills: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the distance between the particles can be given by $PQ=(t-2)^2+\ln(t+1)$.

dif.r: Subtract position expressions and simplify

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the exact time that the distance between the particles $PQ$ is a minimum.

dif.r: Derivative with log term, quadratic formula, second derivative test

figures.cap: graphs of x=(t-2)^2+4 for P and x=4-ln(t+1) for Q

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity.
$$x=t^2-4t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=8$, so $C=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=t^2-4t+8 \\ &=(t-2)^2+4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates correctly and finds $C$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: The displacement-time graphs of $P$ and $Q$ never intersect, so the particles are never at the same position and never collide.
$$\begin{aligned} PQ&=\left((t-2)^2+4\right)-\left(4-\ln(t+1)\right) \\ &=(t-2)^2+4-4+\ln(t+1) \\ &=(t-2)^2+\ln(t+1) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary values occur where $PQ'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} PQ'&=2(t-2)+\dfrac{1}{t+1}=0 \\ 2t-4&=-\dfrac{1}{t+1} \\ (2t-4)(t+1)&=-1 \\ 2t^2-2t-4+1&=0 \\ 2t^2-2t-3&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Solve using the quadratic formula.
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-4(2)(-3)}}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{28}}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{7}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Since $t\ge 0$, $t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$PQ''=2-\dfrac{1}{(1+t)^2}$$
At $t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}$:
$$PQ''=2-\dfrac{1}{\left(1+\frac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}\right)^2}\approx 1.8745>0$$
So the stationary point is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2} \text{ s}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly and expresses as a quadratic, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A pupil is asked to find the $x$-values of any possible points of inflection for the function $f(x)=2x^3+12x^2+6x-2$. What should his answer be?

dif.r: Second derivative of cubic set to zero; single routine step

solutions.latex:
For a point of inflection, $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes.

Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2+24x+6 \\ f''(x)&=12x+24 \end{aligned}$$
Setting $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12x+24&=0 \\ x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f''(x)$ is linear, it changes sign at $x=-2$.

Hence the answer is option B, $x=-2$.

meta.format_note: Added the sign-change remark to justify inflection; no change to the mathematics.

dif.r: Direct trapezoidal rule with values read from diagram

figures.cap: field with offsets 6, 7, 12, 8, 10 m over a 12 m base

solutions.latex:
There are 4 strips over a width of $12$ m, so $h=\dfrac{12}{4}=3$ m.

Applying the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A&\approx\dfrac{3}{2}\{6+10+2(7+12+8)\} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{2}(70) \\ &=105\ \text{m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
As a check, a rectangle of $12\times10=120\ \text{m}^2$ is an over-estimate, which is consistent with option A.

meta.format_note: Values $6$, $10$ (end ordinates) and $7,12,8$ (middle ordinates) are as read from the source working; the figure is not visible here so they were not re-checked.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{2}|x+1|\,dx$ ?

dif.r: Absolute value integral evaluated as two triangle areas

solutions.latex:
The integral of $|x+1|$ equals the area between the curve and the $x$-axis, which is two triangles meeting at $x=-1$.

On $[-3,-1]$ the triangle has base $2$ and height $2$. On $[-1,2]$ it has base $3$ and height $3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-3}^{2}|x+1|\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times2+\dfrac{1}{2}\times3\times3 \\ &=2+\dfrac{9}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{13}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: If $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\theta$ is acute, what is the exact value of $\cos\theta$?

dif.r: Right triangle and Pythagoras for exact cosine; routine recall

solutions.latex:
Draw a right-angled triangle with opposite side $2$ and adjacent side $3$, since $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

By Pythagoras' theorem, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2^2+3^2}=\sqrt{13}$.
$$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex:
A particular continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{32}, & 0\le x\le 8\\[4pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

What is the median of this function?

dif.r: Integrate pdf to one half and solve; standard median method

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The median $k$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_0^k f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k\dfrac{x}{32}\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{64}\right]_0^k \\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{64} \end{aligned}$$
Setting this equal to $\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k^2}{64}&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ k^2&=32 \end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le k\le 8$, $k$ is positive, so $k=4\sqrt{2}$.

Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: The weight of chicken eggs is normally distributed with mean weight of 50 g and a standard deviation of 9 g. What percentage of eggs weigh between 41 g and 68 g?

solutions.latex:
The values $41$ g and $68$ g are $\dfrac{41-50}{9}=-1$ and $\dfrac{68-50}{9}=2$ standard deviations from the mean.

For a normal distribution, about $34\%$ of scores lie between the mean and $1$ standard deviation below, and $47.5\%$ between the mean and $2$ standard deviations above.
$$34\%+47.5\%=81.5\%$$
Hence the answer is option B.

questions.stem: For the curve $y=x^3+6x^2+9x$,

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Factorise derivative of cubic, classify with second derivative

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the curve, showing all main features, including intercepts, stationary points and any points of inflection.

dif.r: Standard cubic sketch with inflection; routine curve features

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y=x^3+6x^2+9x with turning points and inflection

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3x^2+12x+9 \\ &=3(x^2+4x+3) \\ &=3(x+3)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x+12$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$:
$$3(x+3)(x+1)=0$$
So $x=-3$ or $x=-1$.

For $x=-3$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6(-3)+12=-6<0$$
So there is a maximum at $(-3,0)$.

For $x=-1$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6(-1)+12=6>0$$
So there is a minimum at $(-1,-4)$.
criteria: Finds the maximum and minimum points, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Values $y(-3)=0$ and $y(-1)=-4$ checked.

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x+12&=0 \\ x&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(-2)^3+6(-2)^2+9(-2) \\ &=-8+24-18 \\ &=-2 \end{aligned}$$
Testing the concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-3:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=-2:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0 &&\\ x=-1:&\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection at $(-2,-2)$.

\exfigure{1307_q11b_s1}
criteria: Finds the point of inflection and tests it, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch figure \exfigure{1307_q11b_s1} kept as in source. Intercepts: $y=x(x+3)^2$ so $(0,0)$ and a touch at $(-3,0)$.

questions.review_note: Paper mixes units: string is 6 metres but square side is x cm; the result r=(3-2x)/pi needs x in metres

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the radius $(r)$ of the circle in terms of $x$ is given by

$$r=\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi}.$$

dif.r: Set up string length equation; short show-that rearrangement

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the lengths of the two pieces of string which obtain the minimum area. Leave your answer in terms of $\pi$.

dif.r: Build area function, optimise, convert x to string lengths

figures.cap: 6 m string, square of side x and a circle

solutions.latex:
The square has perimeter $4x$ and the circle has circumference $2\pi r$. The total length of string is $6$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4x+2\pi r&=6 \\ 2\pi r&=6-4x \\ r&=\dfrac{6-4x}{2\pi} \\ &=\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: The question mixes units (string 6 metres, side $x$ cm); the working treats the length as $6$ throughout. Left as in source.

solutions.latex:
The total area is the circle plus the square, using $r=\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\pi r^2+x^2 \\ &=\pi\left(\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2 \\ &=\dfrac{(3-2x)^2}{\pi}+x^2 \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx}&=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot2(3-2x)(-2)+2x \\ &=\dfrac{-12+8x+2\pi x}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=\dfrac{8+2\pi}{\pi}>0$$
So the stationary point is a minimum.

For the minimum, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -12+8x+2\pi x&=0 \\ x(8+2\pi)&=12 \\ x&=\dfrac{12}{8+2\pi} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{4+\pi} \end{aligned}$$
The length of string for the square is
$$4x=\dfrac{24}{4+\pi}$$
The length for the circle is
$$6-\dfrac{24}{4+\pi}=\dfrac{6\pi}{4+\pi}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{square: }\dfrac{24}{4+\pi},\quad\text{circle: }\dfrac{6\pi}{4+\pi}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $x$, or equivalent merit
Finds the area and its derivative, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Algebra checked: $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$, $x$ and both lengths are consistent.

parts.latex: Find the area bounded by the $x$-axis and the curve $y=x^2-4$.

dif.r: Find intercepts, integrate region below axis, take absolute value

can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
The $x$-intercepts satisfy $x^2-4=0$, so $x=\pm2$.

The function is even, so the area is twice the area from $0$ to $2$. The curve lies below the $x$-axis there, so take the absolute value.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left|2\int_0^2(x^2-4)\,dx\right| \\ &=2\left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-4x\right]_0^2\right| \\ &=2\left|\dfrac{8}{3}-8-0\right| \\ &=2\times\dfrac{16}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{32}{3} \\ &=10\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress that would lead to a correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: By firstly differentiating $y=\sqrt{2x^2-4}$, find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2x^2-4}}\,dx$.

dif.r: Chain rule derivative then reverse with constant adjustment

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{2x^2-4}\right)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2x^2-4\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(4x)\left(2x^2-4\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{2x^2-4}} \end{aligned}$$
Hence $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{2x^2-4}}\,dx=\sqrt{2x^2-4}+c$, and dividing by $2$:
$$\int\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2x^2-4}}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2x^2-4}+c$$
criteria: Substantial progress that would lead to a correct answer, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the curves $y=x^3$ and $y=7x^2-10x$, that intersect at three points.

skills: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

figures.cap: solution sketch: curves y=x^3 and y=7x^2-10x with enclosed area shaded

solutions.latex:
Equating the two equations:
$$\begin{aligned} x^3&=7x^2-10x \\ x^3-7x^2+10x&=0 \\ x(x^2-7x+10)&=0 \\ x(x-2)(x-5)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0,\ 2$ or $5$.

For $x=0$: $y=0^3=0$. For $x=2$: $y=2^3=8$.

Hence $(0,0)$ and $(2,8)$ are points of intersection.

criteria: Substantially correct solution including correct graph, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\sec\theta-\sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta}=\sin\theta\tan\theta$

dif.r: Trig proof needing factorising and difference of squares

solutions.latex:
Factorising the numerator and using the difference of squares:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^4\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\times\dfrac{\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\times\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\times\sin^2\theta \\ &=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\sin\theta \\ &=\sin\theta\tan\theta \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$

dif.r: Shifted trig equation, adjusted domain, negative-value quadrants

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le2\pi$, the angle $x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ lies in $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{13\pi}{6}\right]$.

The acute related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, since $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$
Subtracting $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
criteria: Finds the acute related angle, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The curve $y=f(x)$ passes through the point $(0,7)$.

If its gradient function is given by $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1-6\sin 3x$, find the equation of the curve.

dif.r: Integrate trig gradient and find constant from point

solutions.latex:
Integrating the gradient function:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int(1-6\sin3x)\,dx \\ &=x+\dfrac{6\cos3x}{3}+C \\ &=x+2\cos3x+C \end{aligned}$$
The curve passes through $(0,7)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(0)&=0+2\cos0+C=7 \\ 2+C&=7 \\ C&=5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x+2\cos3x+5$$

At time $t$ seconds, its distance $x$ metres from a fixed point 0 on the line is given by $x=1-\cos 2t$.

dif.r: Sketch reflected, shifted cosine with period change over one cycle

parts.label: b

criteria: Substantially correct (axes, domain and range labelled correctly), or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Figure \exfigure{1307_q13d_s1} kept as in source. Features it should show: one cycle on $0\le t\le\pi$, minimum $(0,0)$, maximum $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},2\right)$, minimum $(\pi,0)$, midline $x=1$ crossed at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, horizontal tangents at $t=0$ and $t=\pi$.

solutions.latex:

The stationary points occur at
$$t=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi$$
The position at these times is

parts.latex: Differentiate $\sin^2 x$

dif.r: One-step chain rule on sin squared.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, calculate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\sin x+\cos x)^2\,dx$, leaving your answer in exact form.

dif.r: Expand, apply Pythagorean identity, reverse the hence derivative, exact evaluation.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} y&=\sin^2 x\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\cos x\sin x\ (=\sin 2x) \end{aligned}$$

Expand the integrand and use $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(\sin x+\cos x)^2\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\sin^2x+2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2x\right)dx\\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(1+2\sin x\cos x)\,dx \end{aligned}$$
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^2x=2\sin x\cos x$, so a primitive of $2\sin x\cos x$ is $\sin^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} &=\Big[x+\sin^2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\\ &=\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^2\right]-0\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expands and simplifies the integrand, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Without 'or otherwise', part (a) must be used for full marks.

questions.stem: Find derivatives for the following, with respect to $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\ln\left(x^2+2\right)$

dif.r: Direct f'/f derivative of a log.
Product rule with derivative of a^x.

solutions.latex:
Write $3^x=e^{x\ln3}$ and apply the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{x\ln3} & v&=e^x\\ u'&=\ln3\,e^{x\ln3} & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\ln3}e^x\right)&=e^{x\ln3}e^x+e^x\ln3\,e^{x\ln3}\\ &=3^xe^x+3^xe^x\ln3\\ &=3^xe^x(1+\ln3) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct answer, including $3^x$ in the solution
Correct substitution into the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the curve $y=2x^2-\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-4$ has a stationary point at $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\ \ln 4-3\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

dif.r: Differentiate, verify zero gradient, substitute using log laws.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$y'=4x-\dfrac1x$$
At $x=\dfrac12$:
$$y'=4\times\dfrac12-2=0$$
so there is a stationary point at $x=\dfrac12$.

Substitute $x=\dfrac12$ into $y$, using the log law $-\ln\left(\dfrac14\right)=\ln4$:
$$\begin{aligned} y\left(\dfrac12\right)&=2\times\dfrac14-\ln\left(\dfrac14\right)-4\\ &=\dfrac12+\ln4-4\\ &=\ln4-3\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac12,\ \ln4-3\dfrac12\right)\text{ is a stationary point.}$$
criteria: Partial relevant progress, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source only described the substitutions; the arithmetic was written out.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the co-ordinates of the point of intersection of the line $y=3$ and the curve $y=e^x+1$.

dif.r: Solve e^x=2 for a single intersection.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Draw a neat sketch of the area bounded by $y=3$, the $y$-axis and the curve $y=e^x+1$.

dif.r: Sketch shifted exponential and horizontal line, shade region.

skills: Transformations of exponential and logarithmic graphs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Calculate the exact area drawn in part (b).

dif.r: Standard area between line and exponential, exact log answer.

figures.cap: solution sketch: shaded region under y=3 above y=e^x+1 from x=0 to ln 2

solutions.latex:
The line and curve meet where $e^x+1=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^x&=2\\ x&=\ln2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the point of intersection is }(\ln2,\ 3)$$
\exfigure{1307_q14c_s1}

The area is the integral of the upper function minus the lower function, from $x=0$ to $x=\ln2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^{\ln2}\left(3-\left(e^x+1\right)\right)dx\\ &=\int_0^{\ln2}\left(2-e^x\right)dx\\ &=\Big[2x-e^x\Big]_0^{\ln2}\\ &=(2\ln2-2)-(0-1)\\ &=2\ln2-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=(2\ln2-1)\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Correct integral statement, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Also award 1 mark for an equivalent correct answer from a slightly incorrect integral.

questions.stem:
The acceleration of a particle, $P$, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$ is $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=e^{-t}+e^{-2t}$ where $t$ is measured in seconds.

Initially, the displacement of the particle is $x=\dfrac{3}{4}$ m, travelling at a velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac{3}{2}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the displacement of the particle is given by:

$$x=e^{-t}+\dfrac{1}{4}e^{-2t}-\dfrac{1}{2}.$$

dif.r: Two integrations of exponentials with initial conditions to find constants.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the limit of the displacement of $P$, and hence the limit of the distance that $P$ travels after $t=0$.

dif.r: Limit at infinity, then interpret as distance travelled from start.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-e^{-t}-\dfrac12e^{-2t}+c_1$$
Initially $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac32$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac32&=-e^0-\dfrac12e^0+c_1\\ c_1&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dx}{dt}=-e^{-t}-\dfrac12e^{-2t}$$
Integrate again:
$$x=e^{-t}+\dfrac14e^{-2t}+c_2$$
Initially $x=\dfrac34$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac34&=e^0+\dfrac14e^0+c_2\\ c_2&=-\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=e^{-t}+\dfrac14e^{-2t}-\dfrac12$$
criteria: Correct answer, including using the initial conditions to find the constants for both primitives
Correct solution for one of the primitives, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-t}\to0$ and $e^{-2t}\to0$.
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}x=0+\dfrac14(0)-\dfrac12=-\dfrac12$$
The particle starts at $x=\dfrac34$, so the limiting change in displacement from the starting point is
$$\dfrac34-\left(-\dfrac12\right)=1.25\text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct answer, accepting a correct numerical expression

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$ such that $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{x^2}{x^3-2}\,dx=\ln k$

dif.r: f'/f integral with absolute values of negatives, log laws to find k.

solutions.latex:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $x^3-2$, so write
$$\begin{aligned} \ln k&=\dfrac13\int_{-2}^{0}\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3-2}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac13\Big[\ln\left|x^3-2\right|\Big]_{-2}^{0}\\ &=\dfrac13(\ln2-\ln10)\\ &=\dfrac13\ln\left(\dfrac15\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac15}$$
criteria: Correct primitive with boundaries, or correct use of log laws to find $k$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:

\extable{1307_q15a_t1}

questions.stem:
Cole is designing a survey to ask his co-workers about their job satisfaction.

One of Cole’s survey questions asked how many hours each respondent works at the company.

The results are shown in the cumulative frequency histogram below.

\exfigure{1307_q15b_1}

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Use the classes in the cumulative frequency histogram to estimate the mean hours worked by the respondents surveyed.

dif.r: Recover class frequencies from cumulative histogram, then grouped mean.

figures.cap: cumulative frequency histogram of hours worked per week

solutions.latex:
There are $30$ respondents, so the greatest $40\%$ is
$$40\%\times30=12\text{ respondents}$$
The top $12$ respondents are from $18$ to $30$ on the cumulative frequency axis, which are the top two classes.

These respondents worked $36$ to $44$ hours per week.

The class centres are the middles of the bars. The number in each class is the change in height of the cumulative frequency histogram.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum of scores}&=18\times3+22\times2+26\times2+30\times6+34\times5+38\times10+42\times2\\ &=964 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Mean}&=\dfrac{964}{30}\\ &\approx32.1\text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right),\ [0,6]$$

is a probability density function.

dif.r: Check nonnegativity and integrate sine pdf to one.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: For a particular continuous random variable $X$, find $P(X\le 4)$ for the function described in part (a)

dif.r: Definite integral of sine pdf with exact cosine values.

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y=sin(pi x/6) on [0,6]

solutions.latex:
A probability density function needs $f(x)\ge0$ on the domain and a total area of $1$.

For $0\le x\le6$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\le\pi$, so $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)\ge0$ (see graph). Hence $f(x)\ge0$.

\exfigure{1307_q16a_s1}

Now find the total area:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6\dfrac{\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)dx&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left[-\dfrac6\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)\right]_0^6\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left[-\dfrac6\pi\cos\pi+\dfrac6\pi\cos0\right]\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left(-\dfrac6\pi\times(-1)+\dfrac6\pi\times1\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\times\dfrac{12}{\pi}\\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the function is a probability density function, since }f(x)\ge0\text{ and }\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=1.$$
criteria: Correct answer, with full reasoning and justification
Shows the value of the integral is $1$ but does not mention $f(x)\ge0$, or states $f(x)\ge0$ with a minor error in the integral, or equivalent merit
Makes some progress towards a correct solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(X\le4)&=\int_0^4\dfrac{\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left[-\dfrac6\pi\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{6}\right)\right]_0^4\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left(-\dfrac6\pi\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}+\dfrac6\pi\cos0\right)\\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\times\left(-\dfrac6\pi\right)\times\left(-\dfrac12\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{12}\times\dfrac6\pi\\ &=\dfrac14+\dfrac12\\ &=\dfrac34 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantial progress towards the correct solution, or equivalent merit

The quartiles satisfy $F(x)=0.75$ and $F(x)=0.25$.

For $Q_3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.75&=\dfrac{x^3-8}{335}\\ 251.25&=x^3-8\\ 259.25&=x^3\\ x&\approx6.38 \end{aligned}$$
For $Q_1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.25&=\dfrac{x^3-8}{335}\\ 83.75&=x^3-8\\ 91.75&=x^3\\ x&\approx4.51 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR}&=Q_3-Q_1\\ &=6.38-4.51\\ &=1.87 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A number of fish species are subject to minimum length regulations when they are caught.

ie. fish shorter than a given length must be returned to the water if caught.

Two such species are Red Snapper and Barramundi which have minimum lengths of 30 cm and 55 cm respectively.

A fishing tour operator in Northern Australia has made observations over a long period of time and found that, when measured in cm, both the variables ‘R’ (the lengths of caught Red Snapper) and ‘B’ (the lengths of caught Barramundi), are normally distributed.

‘R’ has a mean of 36 cm and standard deviation of 3 cm. ‘B’ has a standard deviation of 4 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Calculate the mean length of Barramundi caught if $2.5\%$ of Barramundi caught are less than 54 cm.

dif.r: Empirical rule used in reverse to find mean.

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the $z$-scores for the minimum allowed lengths for both variables, R and B, and comment upon what this means in terms of which of the two species are more likely to be returned to the water after capture.

dif.r: Compute two z-scores and interpret which species more often returned.

solutions.latex:
By the empirical rule, $95\%$ of Barramundi are within $2$ standard deviations of the mean, so $5\%$ are more than $2$ standard deviations from the mean.

By symmetry, $2.5\%$ of Barramundi are more than $2$ standard deviations below the mean.

Hence
$$\begin{aligned} 54&=\mu-2s\\ \mu&=54+2\times4\\ &=62\text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
The mean length of caught Barramundi was $62$ cm.
criteria: Substantial progress towards the correct solution, showing some knowledge of the empirical rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{s}$:

Red Snapper (minimum $30$ cm):
$$z=\dfrac{30-36}{3}=-2$$
Barramundi (minimum $55$ cm, $\mu=62$):
$$z=\dfrac{55-62}{4}=-1.75$$
By the empirical rule, only $2.5\%$ of caught Red Snapper are returned, since the minimum length is $2$ standard deviations below the mean.

The Barramundi minimum is only $1.75$ standard deviations below the mean, so more than $2.5\%$ of Barramundi are returned.

Therefore caught Barramundi are more likely to be returned to the water.
criteria: Correct answer, showing $z$-scores for both species and correct, logical reasoning as to which species is more likely to be returned
Two of the three elements correct (reasoning based on a single incorrect $z$-score is acceptable), or equivalent merit
One of the three elements correct (correct reasoning based on incorrect $z$-scores is acceptable), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Historical data for a particular aptitude test show that its completion time has a mean of 5 minutes with a standard deviation of 30 seconds.

As part of the selection process for an available job, an employer requires candidates to complete the test faster than $90\%$ of all applicants to progress to the next stage.

An extract from a probability table for the standard normal distribution is shown below.

\exfigure{1307_q16d_1}

Darcy completed the aptitude test in 4 minutes and 23 seconds.

Did Darcy qualify for the next stage of selection? Justify your answer by demonstrating your knowledge of the normal distribution and the application of $z$-scores to the problem.

dif.r: Faster means lower tail; use table z, compare time, justify.

figures.cap: extract of standard normal probability table, z from 0.5 to 1.5

solutions.latex:
From the table, the $z$-score for being faster than $89.97\%$ of applicants is $1.28$, and for $90.15\%$ it is $1.29$.

The qualifying time (faster means below the mean) is
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\mu-1.28s\\ &=5\text{ minutes}-1.28\times30\text{ seconds}\\ &=4\text{ minutes }21.6\text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
or, using $1.29$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\mu-1.29s\\ &=5\text{ minutes}-1.29\times30\text{ seconds}\\ &=4\text{ minutes }21.3\text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Either answer is acceptable: $1.28$ is closer to $90\%$ probability, while $1.29$ ensures the probability exceeds $90\%$.

Darcy's time of $4$ minutes $23$ seconds is slower than the qualifying time, so she does not qualify for the next stage.

Check using Darcy's $z$-score: she was $37$ seconds faster than the mean, so
$$z=\dfrac{37}{30}\approx1.23$$
which is less than the $1.28$ required.
criteria: Correct answer, showing the $z$-score and time required to progress to the next stage, and the correct conclusion
Substantial progress towards a correct solution with one of the elements incorrect, or equivalent merit
Some progress towards a correct solution with one of the elements correct, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A true bearing of $245^\circ$ lies between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$, so it is in the south-west quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned} 245^\circ - 180^\circ &= 65^\circ \end{aligned}$$
So the direction is $65^\circ$ west of south, that is S$65^\circ$W, which is option C.

parts.latex: For connected networks, which of the following is NOT true?

dif.r: Conceptual reasoning about MST versus shortest path properties

options.label: A
options.latex: In some connected networks, there may be more than one minimum spanning tree.

options.label: B
options.latex: In some connected networks, there may be more than one shortest path between two of the vertices.

options.label: C
options.latex: In all connected networks, the shortest path between two vertices will be located on a minimum spanning tree of the network.

options.label: D
options.latex: In all connected networks, the sum of the degrees of the vertices is double the number of edges.

solutions.latex:
Option A is true: a network with equal edge weights can have several minimum spanning trees.

Option B is true: two different routes can have the same shortest length.

Option D is true: the sum of the degrees is twice the number of edges.

Option C is not true: a shortest path between two vertices need not use only edges of the minimum spanning tree, since the tree minimises total length, not individual path lengths.

So the statement that is NOT true is option C.

parts.latex:
Leila's car has a fuel consumption of 7.8 L/100 km. The current cost of fuel is \$2.11/L, and Leila spends \$87 to fill up her car tank from empty.

What is the maximum distance Leila can travel with a full tank of fuel?

dif.r: Fuel consumption used in reverse; two rate steps

solutions.latex:
Find the volume of fuel in a full tank.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Volume} &= \dfrac{87}{2.11} \\ &\approx 41.23 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
The car uses $7.8$ L per $100$ km.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \dfrac{41.23}{7.8}\times 100 \\ &\approx 529 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: A map has a scale of 1:5000. If Oak St is 800 m, what is the scaled distance of Oak St?

dif.r: Apply scale then convert metres to millimetres

solutions.latex:
The scale $1:5000$ means $1$ unit on the map represents $5000$ units on the ground.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Map distance} &= \dfrac{800}{5000} \\ &= 0.16 \text{ m} \\ &= 160 \text{ mm} \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
Amie is studying the butterfly population in a park. She initially catches and tags 20 butterflies, before releasing them back into the park. Later, she captures a sample of 40 butterflies, of which 5 are already tagged.

Based on this data what is the most likely estimate for the butterfly population in the park?

dif.r: Standard capture-recapture proportion

solutions.latex:
Capture–recapture: the proportion tagged in the sample equals the proportion tagged in the population.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5}{40} &= \dfrac{20}{N} \\ N &= \dfrac{20\times 40}{5} \\ &= 160 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

The diagram shows the cost of direct flights, in dollars, between eight cities in Asia, as offered by Asia Insight Airlines.

\exfigure{722_q13_1}

parts.label: a

dif.r: Recall spanning tree has n-1 edges

parts.label: b

dif.r: Standard minimum spanning tree algorithm and total weight

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Asia Insight Airlines offers two direct flights from the city of Thimphu, Bhutan:

Thimphu to Seoul for \$630 and Thimphu to Dili for \$350.

What is the length of the minimum spanning tree that includes Thimphu?

dif.r: Extend MST with new vertex by cheapest connecting edge

figures.cap: weighted network of eight Asian cities
eight city vertices for drawing the minimum spanning tree
solution sketch: school's marking, minimum spanning tree drawn on the vertices

solutions.latex:
A spanning tree on $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges. There are $8$ cities.
$$\begin{aligned} n-1 &= 8-1 \\ &= 7 \text{ edges} \end{aligned}$$

Choosing the cheapest edges that join all cities without forming a cycle gives the minimum spanning tree.

\exfigure{722_q13_s1}

The edges are Almaty–Chennai $330$, Almaty–Yerevan $485$, Yerevan–Bishkek $450$, Bishkek–Kabul $275$, Kabul–Dili $370$, Bishkek–Xi'an $445$, Xi'an–Seoul $620$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Length} &= 330 + 485 + 450 + 370 + 275 + 445 + 620 \\ &= 2975 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{length of minimum spanning tree} = \$2975$$
criteria: Draws a correct tree or finds the correct length, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch drawn (722_q13_s1); it was to show: minimum spanning tree on the eight cities with edges Almaty–Chennai 330, Almaty–Yerevan 485, Yerevan–Bishkek 450, Bishkek–Kabul 275, Kabul–Dili 370, Bishkek–Xi'an 445, Xi'an–Seoul 620; total 2975. Rubric written by us. Source lists the edges as 7 and sum is consistent. Thimphu is not among the listed cities in the source tree, so part (c) adds the cheapest Thimphu edge 350.

solutions.latex:
Thimphu is not yet in the tree, so join it by its cheaper flight, to Dili for $\$350$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Length} &= 2975 + 350 \\ &= 3325 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{length} = \$3325$$

meta.format_note: The source's tree in (b) has 8 vertices already; adding Thimphu implies a ninth city, consistent with the source answer.

questions.stem:
A grandstand at an oval is shown in cross-section $BCDE$.

The seating, along the interval $DE$, is angled at $\alpha^\circ$ to the horizontal and begins 4 m above ground level.

From $B$, Aiden measures the angle of elevation of $D$ to be $51^\circ$, then walks 44 m onto the field and measures the angle of elevation of $D$ to be $28^\circ$ from point $A$.

\exfigure{722_q14_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\angle ADB = 23^\circ$

dif.r: Supplementary angle then triangle angle sum; given result

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the distance $BD$ correct to the nearest metre.

dif.r: Direct sine rule application in identified triangle

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Calculate the distance $DF$ and hence find the angle of the seating, $\alpha$, to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Multi-stage trig from diagram: vertical, horizontal, then tan of seating angle

figures.cap: grandstand cross-section with points A, B, C, D, E, F, angles 28° and 51°, AB = 44 m, EB = FC = 4 m

solutions.latex:
Since $\angle ABD$ and the $51^\circ$ elevation angle lie on a straight line, they are supplementary.
$$\angle ABD = 180^\circ - 51^\circ = 129^\circ$$
In $\triangle ABD$, the angle at $A$ is $28^\circ$. By the angle sum of a triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ADB + 28^\circ + 129^\circ &= 180^\circ \\ \angle ADB &= 23^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: A solution diagram would help but the question's figure is used.

solutions.latex:
Use the sine rule in $\triangle ABD$.
$$\dfrac{BD}{\sin 28^\circ} = \dfrac{44}{\sin 23^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} BD &= \dfrac{44\sin 28^\circ}{\sin 23^\circ} \\ &\approx 53 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct sine rule equation, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle BCD$, with $BD = 53$ and angle $51^\circ$ at $B$:
$$\sin 51^\circ = \dfrac{DC}{53}$$
$$\begin{aligned} DC &= 53\sin 51^\circ \\ &\approx 41.19 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The seating begins $4$ m above ground, so
$$DF = DC - 4 = 53\sin 51^\circ - 4$$
Also
$$\cos 51^\circ = \dfrac{BC}{53}$$
$$BC = 53\cos 51^\circ$$
The seating angle satisfies
$$\tan\alpha = \dfrac{53\sin 51^\circ - 4}{53\cos 51^\circ}$$
$$\therefore\ \alpha \approx 48^\circ$$
criteria: Finds $DF$ and sets up $\tan\alpha$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source takes tan α with opposite = DF and adjacent = BC; kept as given, and the value was not rechecked.

parts.latex:
In triangle $DEF$, $\angle EDF = 44^\circ$, $EF = 6$ cm, and $DE = 7$ cm.

Find $\angle EFD$ to the nearest degree, given that it is obtuse.

dif.r: Sine rule for angle with obtuse ambiguous case

solutions.latex:
Use the sine rule in $\triangle DEF$.
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle EFD}{7} = \dfrac{\sin 44^\circ}{6}$$
$$\sin\angle EFD = \dfrac{7\sin 44^\circ}{6}$$
The acute solution is $54^\circ$.
$$\angle EFD \approx 54^\circ$$
The angle is obtuse, so take the supplement.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle EFD &= 180^\circ - 54^\circ \\ &= 126^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the sine rule to find the acute angle, or equivalent merit
