parts.latex: Prove the identity $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta}$.

dif.r: Identity proof needing Pythagorean rewrite and difference-of-squares cancellation

solutions.latex:
Rewrite in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, then use $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= (\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{1 - \sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{(1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the left side as $\dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)^2}{\cos^2\theta}$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Tom invented a dice game to play on his own. He throws a pair of six-sided dice repeatedly until the difference between the dice is 2 or 3.

If the difference is 2, Tom wins and the game ends.

If the difference is 3, Tom loses and the game ends.

If the difference is any other number, he continues to throw until the difference is a 2 or 3.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the probability that Tom wins on his first throw of the dice is $\dfrac{2}{9}$.

dif.r: Count favourable dice outcomes out of 36

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the probability that the game continues to a second throw.

dif.r: Count second event and use complement

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events
Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the probability that Tom wins in one of the first three throws? Leave your answer in unsimplified form.

dif.r: Model repeated-trial pattern summing three mutually exclusive cases

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Calculate the probability that Tom wins the game.

dif.r: Recognise infinite geometric series of win probabilities, limiting sum

solutions.latex:
The difference is $2$ for the pairs $(1,3),(2,4),(3,5),(4,6)$ and their reverses, so $8$ of the $36$ equally likely outcomes.
$$P(\text{win on first throw}) = \dfrac{8}{36} = \dfrac{2}{9}$$
criteria: Some appropriate working, or equivalent merit

meta.source_flag: Guideline drawing not cropped: table of the difference between the two dice (die 1 across, die 2 up), showing the difference is 2 in 8 of 36 outcomes.
meta.format_note: Pairs listed to give the count of 8 in words.

solutions.latex:
The difference is $3$ for the pairs $(1,4),(2,5),(3,6)$ and their reverses, which is $6$ outcomes.
$$P(\text{difference } 2 \text{ or } 3) = \dfrac{8 + 6}{36} = \dfrac{14}{36}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{continue}) &= 1 - \dfrac{14}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{11}{18} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Tom wins on throw $1$, or continues once and wins on throw $2$, or continues twice and wins on throw $3$.
$$P = \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{2}{9}$$
This simplifies to $\dfrac{643}{1458}$.
criteria: Writes one or two correct terms, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The probabilities of winning on throw $1, 2, 3, \dots$ form a geometric series with first term $a = \dfrac{2}{9}$ and common ratio $r = \dfrac{11}{18}$.

Since $|r| < 1$, the sum to infinity exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1 - r} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{2}{9}}{1 - \frac{11}{18}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{9} \times \dfrac{18}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the geometric series, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
On the 1st January 2021, Amanda invested \$7000 into a bank account that paid interest at a rate of 6% p.a. compounded annually. Amanda decided to add \$700 to her account on the 1st January each year, beginning in 2022.

Let $A_n$ be the amount in the account on the 1st January after $n$ years, after interest and her deposit has been paid.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $A_2 = A_1 \times 1.06 + 700$.

dif.r: Direct recurrence statement from interest-then-deposit description

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, determine how much was in her account on 1st January 2031, after interest and her deposit has been paid. Give your answer to the nearest dollar.

dif.r: Generalise recurrence, sum geometric series, choose correct n

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Amanda's friend, Bard, invested \$7000 into an account in a different bank on the 1st January 2021 and made no further payments. On 1st January 2031, Bard's balance was \$23\,417.

Calculate the annual rate of compound interest paid on Bard's account. Give your answer to 4 significant figures.

dif.r: Compound interest formula reversed via tenth root

solutions.latex:
$A_1$ is the opening amount after one year's interest and the deposit.
$$A_1 = 7000 \times 1.06 + 700$$
In the second year the balance earns $6\%$ interest and then $\$700$ is added.
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= A_1 + 0.06A_1 + 700 \\ &= A_1 \times 1.06 + 700 \end{aligned}$$
Expanding,
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= (7000 \times 1.06 + 700) \times 1.06 + 700 \\ &= 7000 \times 1.06^2 + 700 \times 1.06 + 700 \end{aligned}$$

Continuing the pattern,
$$A_3 = 7000 \times 1.06^3 + 700 \times 1.06^2 + 700 \times 1.06 + 700$$
$$A_n = 7000 \times 1.06^n + 700 \times 1.06^{n-1} + \cdots + 700 \times 1.06 + 700$$
The terms after the first form a geometric series with $a = 700$, $r = 1.06$ and $n$ terms.
$$A_n = 7000 \times 1.06^n + \dfrac{700(1.06^n - 1)}{0.06}$$
1st January 2031 is $10$ years after 2021, so $n = 10$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{10} &= 7000 \times 1.06^{10} + \dfrac{700(1.06^{10} - 1)}{0.06} \\ &\approx \$21\,762 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the pattern and the geometric series, or equivalent merit
Writes $A_3$ or the general pattern, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Bard's balance after $10$ years at $R\%$ p.a. compounded annually is given by
$$7000\left(1 + \dfrac{R}{100}\right)^{10} = 23\,417$$
Taking the tenth root,
$$\begin{aligned} 1 + \dfrac{R}{100} &= \sqrt[10]{\dfrac{23\,417}{7000}} \\ \dfrac{R}{100} &= \sqrt[10]{\dfrac{23\,417}{7000}} - 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ R \approx 12.83\%$$
criteria: One line of appropriate working, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1318_q33_s1}

The line is $y = \dfrac{2x + 12}{5}$. At the intersections,
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{4x+8} &= \dfrac{2x + 12}{5} \\ 10\sqrt{x+2} &= 2x + 12 \\ 100(x+2) &= (2x+12)^2 \\ 4x^2 - 52x - 56 &= 0 \\ x^2 - 13x - 14 &= 0 \\ (x+1)(x-14) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = -1 \text{ or } x = 14$$
The curve $y = \sqrt{4x+8}$ is above the line $y = \dfrac{2}{5}x + \dfrac{12}{5}$ between the intersection points.
$$A = \int_{-1}^{14}\left(\sqrt{4x+8} - \left(\dfrac{2}{5}x + \dfrac{12}{5}\right)\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \left[\dfrac{(4x+8)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6} - \dfrac{x^2}{5} - \dfrac{12x}{5}\right]_{-1}^{14} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{256}{3} - \dfrac{196}{5} - \dfrac{168}{5}\right) - \left(\dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{12}{5}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{252}{3} - \dfrac{375}{5} \\ &= 84 - 75 \\ &= 9 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the intersection points and sets up the integral with the correct graph above, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Estragon has scored $90\%, 78\%, 81\%,$ and $83\%$ on his first four class tests. After the fifth class test, his mean mark is increased by $1\%$.

What was Estragon's mark in his fifth class test ?
parts.note: Mean of a raw data set (summary statistics) has no 2024 Advanced dot point; Y11 Data only names mode and median.

dif.r: Two steps: find old mean, then work backwards from the new mean.

solutions.latex:
The mean of the first four tests is
$$\dfrac{90+78+81+83}{4} = \dfrac{332}{4} = 83\%$$
The new mean is $84\%$. Let $x$ be the fifth mark.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x+332}{5} &= 84 \\ x &= 5\times 84 - 332 \\ &= 88\% \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

Which of the following is the equation of the translated function $g(x)$ ?

dif.r: Direct recall of horizontal and vertical translation rules.

solutions.latex:
Translating 2 units right replaces $x$ with $x-2$, and 3 units up adds $3$.
$$g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-2} + 3$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: Given that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{2}$ for $0 < \theta < \pi$, what is the exact value of $\sin\theta$ ?

dif.r: Right triangle with Pythagoras plus a quadrant sign check.

solutions.latex:
Since $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{2}$, draw a right-angled triangle with opposite side $3$ and adjacent side $2$. By Pythagoras' theorem, the hypotenuse is
$$\sqrt{3^2+2^2} = \sqrt{13}$$
$\tan\theta$ is positive, so $\theta$ is in quadrant 1 or 3. Since $0<\theta<\pi$, it is in quadrant 1, where $\sin\theta$ is positive.
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: What is the domain and range of $f(x) = \sqrt{x-4}$ ?

dif.r: Standard domain and range of a shifted square root.

solutions.latex:
The square root needs $x-4 \ge 0$, so $x \ge 4$.

A square root is never negative, so $y \ge 0$.

Domain $[4,\infty)$ and range $[0,\infty)$, which is option B.

This is option C.

parts.latex:
For events $A$ and $B$ over a sample space $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$ and $P(A|B) = 0.25$

What is $P(B)$ ?

dif.r: Conditional probability formula used in reverse.

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula, $P(A|B) = \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(B) &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A|B)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.2}{0.25} \\ &= 0.8 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, with a tree diagram, $0.25x = 0.2$, so $x = 0.8$.

This is option D.

figures.cap: velocity-time graph
option A: acceleration graph A

option D: acceleration graph D

solutions.latex:
The velocity curve has 3 turning points, so the acceleration (the gradient of the velocity) is zero three times. The acceleration graph must therefore have exactly 3 $x$-intercepts.

This eliminates B, C and D, so the answer is A.

parts.latex: Which of the following is the gradient of the normal to $y = \log_2 x$ at the point $(8,3)$ ?

dif.r: Differentiate a base-2 log, then take the negative reciprocal for the normal.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $f(x) = \log_2 x$.
$$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{x\ln 2}$$
At $(8,3)$ the tangent gradient is $\dfrac{1}{8\ln 2}$.

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so
$$m_{\text{normal}} = -\dfrac{1}{m_{\text{tangent}}} = -8\ln 2$$
This is option B.

Region $R_1$ lies below the axis between $-1$ and $0$, so $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0} f(x)\,dx=-4$.

solutions.latex:

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$65=\mu-\sigma$. By the empirical rule, $34\%$ of scores lie between $\mu-\sigma$ and $\mu$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 65) &= 50\% - 34\% \\ &= 16\% \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $(\sin x + \cos x)(\sec x - \operatorname{cosec} x) = \tan x - \cot x$

dif.r: Expand and simplify reciprocal trig ratios; short identity proof.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= (\sin x+\cos x)(\sec x - \operatorname{cosec} x) \\ &= \sin x\sec x + \cos x\sec x - \sin x\operatorname{cosec} x - \cos x\operatorname{cosec} x \\ &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} + \dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x} - \dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x} - \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} \\ &= \tan x + 1 - 1 - \cot x \\ &= \tan x - \cot x \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int x(x^2 + 5)^9\,dx$

dif.r: Reverse chain rule with constant adjustment; standard integral.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the integrand in the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=x^2+5$, $f'(x)=2x$, $n=9$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int x(x^2+5)^9\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x(x^2+5)^9\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{n+1}[f(x)]^{n+1} + C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{10}(x^2+5)^{10} + C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int x(x^2+5)^9\,dx = \dfrac{(x^2+5)^{10}}{20} + C$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 - 9x$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ has 2 stationary points at $P\,(1,-5)$ and $Q(-3,27)$ and determine their nature

dif.r: Routine stationary points of cubic and nature test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any points of inflexion

dif.r: Second derivative zero and concavity change check, routine

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Sketch the graph marking and labelling any stationary points or points of inflexion.

Do NOT determine the $x$ intercepts of the curve

dif.r: Sketch cubic from found stationary and inflexion points

figures.cap: solution sketch: Sketch of f(x) with stationary points and point of inflexion

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2+6x-9 \\ &= 3(x+3)(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=-3$ or $x=1$.
$$f(-3) = (-3)^3 + 3(-3)^2 - 9(-3) = 27$$
$$f(1) = 1+3-9 = -5$$
Hence the stationary points are $(-3,27)$ and $(1,-5)$, as required.

Nature (sign of $f'(x)$ either side):

\extable{Ts7262_1}

$\therefore\ (-3,27)$ is a local maximum and $(1,-5)$ is a local minimum.
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds $f'(x)$ and solves $f'(x)=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Kept \extable from source. Part (c) sketch is under sketch id 1319_q31_s2, not part of this solution.

solutions.latex:
Points of inflexion occur where $f''(x)=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$f''(x) = 6x+6 = 0 \text{ so } x=-1$$
$$y = (-1)^3+3(-1)^2-9(-1) = 11$$
Concavity changes at $x=-1$, since $f''(x)=6(x+1)$ changes sign there.

$$\therefore\ (-1,11) \text{ is a point of inflexion}$$

meta.format_note: Source justified by $f''(-1)=0$ and $f'(-1)\ne0$; replaced with the sign change of $f''$, which is the standard test. Rubric written by us.

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} & \text{for } 1 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function

dif.r: Integrate linear pdf from 1 to x, piecewise CDF

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(1.6 \le X \le 2)$

dif.r: Substitute into CDF difference

can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_1^x f(t)\,dt$ for $1\le x\le 2$.

$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_1^x\left(\dfrac{t}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{4}+\dfrac{t}{4}\right]_1^x \\ &= \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{x}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2+x-2}{4} \end{aligned}$$

For $x<1$, $F(x)=0$, and for $x>2$, $F(x)=1$.

$$\therefore\ F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x<1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{x^2+x-2}{4} & 1\le x\le 2 \\[6pt] 1 & x>2 \end{cases}$$
criteria: Integrates $f(x)$ from $1$ to $x$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave $F(x)=0$ otherwise; we wrote the cases $0$ for $x<1$ and $1$ for $x>2$ (standard CDF), which is the meaning of 'otherwise'. Used dummy variable $t$ in the integral (source reused $x$). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using $P(a\le X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)$:

$$\begin{aligned} P(1.6\le X\le 2) &= F(2)-F(1.6) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{2^2}{4}+\dfrac{2}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1.6^2}{4}+\dfrac{1.6}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= 0.46 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P(1.6\le X\le 2)=0.46 \left(=\dfrac{23}{50}\right)$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &= -x^2+x+2 \\ &= -(x^2-x-2) \\ &= -(x-2)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$

The $x$-intercepts are $x=2$ and $x=-1$, and the $y$-intercept is $2$.

The vertex is at $x=\dfrac{-1+2}{2}=0.5$, and $y=-(0.5-2)(0.5+1)=2.25$, so the vertex is $(0.5,\,2.25)$.

questions.stem:
A tank initially holds 8100 litres of Water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. A mathematical model predicts that the volume, $V$ litres, of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V = 8100\left(1 - \dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How long does the tank take to drain fully?

dif.r: Set V=0, solve trivially

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What volume does the model predict will remain after 20 minutes ?

dif.r: Direct substitution into model

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what rate does the model predict that the water will be draining from the tank after 30 minutes ?

dif.r: Chain rule derivative evaluated, interpret sign as draining rate

parts.label: d
parts.latex: At what time does the model predict that the water will drain from the tank at its fastest rate ?

dif.r: Maximise linear rate; must argue endpoint on domain

solutions.latex:
The tank is fully drained when $V=0$.

$$8100\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2=0$$

So $1-\dfrac{t}{90}=0$.

$$\therefore\ t=90 \text{ minutes}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} V &= 8100\left(1-\dfrac{20}{90}\right)^2 \\ &= 8100\times\left(\dfrac{7}{9}\right)^2 \\ &= 4900 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change of volume is $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$. Differentiating using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 8100\times 2\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{90}\right) \\ &= -180\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right) \\ &= 2t-180 \text{ L/min} \end{aligned}$$

At $t=30$:

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2\times 30-180=-120 \text{ L/min}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the water drains at } 120 \text{ L/min}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The rate is $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2t-180$, so $\dfrac{d^2V}{dt^2}=2$.

Since $\dfrac{d^2V}{dt^2}\ne 0$, $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ has no stationary points and no points of inflexion. The greatest draining rate must therefore be at an endpoint of $0\le t\le 90$.

$$\begin{aligned} t=0 &: \dfrac{dV}{dt}=-180 \text{ L/min} \\ t=90 &: \dfrac{dV}{dt}=0 \text{ L/min} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the fastest draining rate is at } t=0$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

dif.r: Split region into two standard integrals and add

figures.cap: graphs of f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=(x-1)^2 with shaded region; top of y-axis label cropped

The shaded area is the area under $f(x)$ from $x=-1$ to $x=0$, plus the area under $g(x)$ from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

questions.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$v = 2 - \dfrac{4}{t+1}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the particle is at rest when $t = 1$

dif.r: Substitute t=1 into velocity

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The particle's initial displacement is 1 m. Find its displacement when at rest (3 decimal points)

dif.r: Integrate with log term, find constant, evaluate

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the expression for the accelaration of the particle at time $t$

dif.r: Single routine differentiation of velocity

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Explain why the displacement of the particle is always positive

dif.r: Argue single stationary minimum is global and positive

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
At $t=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} v &= 2-\dfrac{4}{1+1} \\ &= 2-2 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest when } t=1$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(2-\dfrac{4}{t+1}\right)dt \\ &= 2t-4\ln(t+1)+C \end{aligned}$$

When $t=0$, $x=1$:

$$0-4\ln 1+C=1$$

So $C=1$ and $x=2t-4\ln(t+1)+1$.

At rest, $t=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2(1)-4\ln 2+1 \\ &= 3-4\ln 2 \\ &\approx 0.227 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{displacement} \approx 0.227 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the displacement function including the constant, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source used $d$ for displacement; written $x$ here. Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{dv}{dt} \\ &= \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(2-4(t+1)^{-1}\right) \\ &= 4(t+1)^{-2} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest only when $t=1$, so the displacement has only one stationary point, at $t=1$.

The acceleration there is $\dfrac{4}{(1+1)^2}=1>0$, so the displacement has a local minimum at $t=1$ (concave up).

The displacement at this minimum is $0.227>0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{displacement is always} \ge 0.227, \text{ so always positive}$$

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt} = 20000t - 12000$

dif.r: Differentiate a given quadratic

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence or otherwise find the minimum distance ($r$) between the cars (justify your answer with relevant mathematical arguments)

dif.r: Given derivative: solve, justify minimum, evaluate r

figures.cap: right-angled diagram of cars A and B moving relative to R

solutions.latex:
After $t$ hours, $RA=80t$ and $RB=100-60t$.

The roads meet at a right angle, so by Pythagoras' theorem in triangle $ARB$:

$$\begin{aligned} r^2 &= RB^2+RA^2 \\ &= (100-60t)^2+(80t)^2 \\ &= 10000-12000t+3600t^2+6400t^2 \\ &= 10000t^2-12000t+10000 \\ &= 2000(5t^2-6t+5) \end{aligned}$$

as required.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt} &= \dfrac{d}{dt}\left[2000(5t^2-6t+5)\right] \\ &= 2000(10t-6) \\ &= 20000t-12000 \end{aligned}$$

as required.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$r$ is a minimum when $r^2$ is a minimum.

Stationary point: $\dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 20000t-12000 &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{6}{10}=0.6 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

Nature: $\dfrac{d^2(r^2)}{dt^2}=20000>0$ for all $t$, so $r^2$ is concave up and the stationary point is a minimum.

$$\begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt{2000(5\times 0.6^2-6\times 0.6+5)} \\ &= \sqrt{6400} \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum distance is } 80 \text{ km}$$

meta.format_note: Second derivative written as $20000$ (source wrote $2000(10)$, same value). Rubric written by us.

questions.stem:
Between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18, 2021, the height of the tide in Sydney harbour was given by

$$h(t) = 1 + 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) \text{ for } 0 \le t < 12$$

Where $h$ is the height of the tide in metres, and $t$ is in hours with $t = 0$ at 8 am

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the period of $h(t)$

dif.r: Period formula recall

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What was the height $h(t)$ at low tide, and at what time did this low tide occur

dif.r: Minimum value plus locating minimum time, convert clock time

parts.label: c
parts.latex: A cruise ship is only able to enter the harbour if the tide is at least 1.2 m. Find all the times between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18 2021 that the cruise ship was able to enter the harbour

dif.r: Trig inequality in tidal context, convert interval to times

solutions.latex:
For $h(t)=1+0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$ with $b=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= 2\pi\div\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= 2\pi\times\dfrac{6}{\pi} \\ &= 12 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The minimum value of $\sin$ is $-1$, so the minimum height is $1-0.4=0.6$ m.

The sine curve reaches its minimum at $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of the period:

$$\dfrac{3}{4}\times 12=9 \text{ hours}$$

So the time is $8 \text{ am}+9 \text{ hours}=5$ pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{low tide is } 0.6 \text{ m at } 5 \text{ pm}$$
criteria: Finds the minimum height or the time of low tide, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The ship can enter when $h\ge 1.2$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1+0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge 1.2 \\ 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge 0.2 &&(\text{subtract } 1) \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge \dfrac{1}{2} &&(\text{divide by } 0.4) \end{aligned}$$

For $0\le t<12$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t<2\pi$, and $\sin\theta\ge\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\theta\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t &\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ 1\le t &\le 5 \end{aligned}$$

The times are $8+1=9$ am and $8+5=13$, that is, 1 pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{the ship can enter between 9 am and 1 pm}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
For $y = x^2 - bx - 1$ the coefficient of $x^2$ is positive, so the parabola opens upwards.

When $x = 0$, $y = -1$, so the $y$-intercept is negative.

The axis of symmetry is $x = \dfrac{b}{2}$, and $b > 0$, so the vertex lies to the right of the $y$-axis.

The discriminant is $b^2 + 4 > 0$, so there are two $x$-intercepts.

The graph in option B has all these features.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $2x\sin x$

dif.r: Single routine product rule
Single routine chain rule on a root
Direct chain rule with exponential of tan

parts.label: d
parts.latex: $\dfrac{x}{\log_{10} x}$

dif.r: Change of base to ln then quotient rule

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= 2x & v &= \sin x \\ u' &= 2 & v' &= \cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(2x\sin x) = 2\sin x + 2x\cos x$$
criteria: Applies the product rule with one correct term, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with the outer function $u^{\frac12}$ and inner function $2x^3 - 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(2x^3-4)^{\frac12} &= \dfrac12\cdot 6x^2(2x^3-4)^{-\frac12} \\ &= \dfrac{3x^2}{\sqrt{2x^3-4}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the chain rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x + 1) = \sec^2 x$:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{\tan x+1}\right) = \sec^2 x\, e^{\tan x+1}$$

Applying the change of base rule, $\log_{10} x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 10}$, so
$$\dfrac{x}{\log_{10}x} = \dfrac{\ln 10\cdot x}{\ln x}$$
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= \ln 10\cdot x & v &= \ln x \\ u' &= \ln 10 & v' &= \dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{\log_{10}x}\right) &= \dfrac{\ln 10\cdot\ln x - \ln 10}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln 10(\ln x - 1)}{(\ln x)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Changes base and sets up the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2-1} \\ &= \dfrac{2(x^2-1)+2}{x^2-1} \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{2}{x^2-1} \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator of $\dfrac{2}{x^2-1}$ is zero: $x^2 - 1 = 0$, so $x = \pm 1$.

As $x \to \pm\infty$, $\dfrac{2}{x^2-1} \to 0$, so $y \to 2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{asymptotes at } x = \pm 1 \text{ and } y = 2$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Quintic stationary points including horizontal inflection needing concavity test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the $x$-coordinates of any points of inflection.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and check concavity change

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Sketch the curve $y = f(x)$, showing all important features.

(NB: There is no need to evaluate the $x$-intercepts).

dif.r: Sketch from already found stationary and inflection points

parts.label: d
parts.latex: State the values of $x$ for which the curve is concave up.

dif.r: Solve cubic inequality f''>0 from known zeros

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of y=-x^5+15x^3 with turning points (±3, ±162), origin, inflections at ±3/√2

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -5x^4 + 45x^2 \\ f''(x) &= -20x^3 + 90x \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x) = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -5x^2(x^2 - 9) &= 0 \\ -5x^2(x+3)(x-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 0, \pm 3$.

Test the nature using $f''(x)$.

At $x = 0$, $f''(0) = 0$, so test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-0.1) &= -8.98 < 0 \\ f''(0.1) &= 8.98 > 0 \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a horizontal point of inflection at $x = 0$.

At $x = 3$, $f''(3) = -270 < 0$, so a local maximum.

At $x = -3$, $f''(-3) = 270 > 0$, so a local minimum.

The $y$-values are $f(0) = 0$, $f(3) = 162$ and $f(-3) = -162$.

$$\therefore\ \text{horizontal point of inflection at } (0,0),\ \text{local minimum at } (-3,-162),\ \text{local maximum at } (3,162)$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points and determines their nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the $x$-values of the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For points of inflection, $f''(x) = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -20x^3 + 90x &= 0 \\ -10x(2x^2 - 9) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 0$ or $x = \pm\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$.

\extable{Ts7373_1}

The concavity changes at each of these values.

$$\therefore\ \text{points of inflection at } x = 0 \text{ and } x = \pm\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$$

questions.stem: A particle moves along a straight line so its displacement $x$, in metres, from a fixed point O, is given by $x = 1 - 2\sin 2t$, where the time, $t$, is measured in seconds from $t = 0$.
questions.review_note: Part (c) printed 'when = π/2' with the t missing; transcribed as t = π/2

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Where is the particle initially?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into displacement

dif.r: Differentiate, solve v=0 for first time, find position

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the acceleration of the particle when $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$?

dif.r: Differentiate twice and substitute

solutions.latex:
Initially $t = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 1 - 2\sin 0 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
So the particle is 1 m to the right of the origin.

Differentiating $x = 1 - 2\sin 2t$:
$$\dot x = -4\cos 2t$$
The particle is at rest when $\dot x = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -4\cos 2t &= 0 \\ 2t &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}$$
This is the first time, as it is the smallest positive $t$.

The position then is
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 1 - 2\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
After $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ s the particle is at rest 1 m to the left of the origin.
criteria: Finds the correct time or the correct position, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $\dot x = -4\cos 2t$:
$$\ddot x = 8\sin 2t$$
When $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot x &= 8\sin\pi \\ &= 0 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
On a dark night, two ships, Saga and Hero, sail parallel to a straight coastline on which there are two lights of equal brightness, 16 kilometres apart.

\exfigure{1015_q11_1}

Suppose the coastline is represented by the $x$ axis where the origin $O$ is chosen to be the midpoint of the light sources. It is known that the (total) brightness from the lights on a ship a point $P(x, b)$ is

$$l = \dfrac{1}{b^2 + (x+8)^2} + \dfrac{1}{b^2 + (x-8)^2}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that $\dfrac{dl}{dx} = -\dfrac{2P}{Q}$, where

$P = \left[(x+8)\left(b^2 + (x-8)^2\right)^2 + (x-8)\left(b^2 + (x+8)^2\right)^2\right]$ AND

$Q = \left[\left(b^2 + (x+8)^2\right)^2 \left(b^2 + (x-8)^2\right)^2\right]$

dif.r: Chain rule on two reciprocal terms, combine over common denominator

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
To answer (b) and (c), you may assume the following factorisation:

$$P = 2x\left(x^2 + 64 + b^2 + 16\sqrt{64 + b^2}\right)\left(x^2 + 64 + b^2 - 16\sqrt{64 + b^2}\right)$$

Saga sails parallel to the coast at a distance 15 km from the coast.

By considering $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$, show that, as Saga sails from left to right, the brightness on Saga increases to a maximum when $x = 0$ and then decreases.

dif.r: Substitute, simplify factors, sign argument for derivative in context

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Hero sails parallel to the coast at a distance 6 km from the coast.

Describe how the brightness on Hero changes as Hero sails from left to right. Give clear reasons for your answer.

dif.r: Sign analysis with three stationary points; interpret brightness pattern unprompted

figures.cap: coastline on x-axis with lights at (-8,0) and (8,0), ship path y=b with point P(x,b)

solutions.latex:
Write $l$ using negative powers:
$$l = \left[b^2+(x+8)^2\right]^{-1} + \left[b^2+(x-8)^2\right]^{-1}$$
Differentiating each term with the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dl}{dx} = \dfrac{-2(x+8)}{\left(b^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2} + \dfrac{-2(x-8)}{\left(b^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2}$$
Combining over the common denominator:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dl}{dx} &= \dfrac{-2\left[(x+8)\left(b^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2 + (x-8)\left(b^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2\right]}{\left(b^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2\left(b^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2} \\ &= -\dfrac{2P}{Q} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative of each term, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{dl}{dx} = -\dfrac{2P}{Q}$ with the given factorisation of $P$ and $b = 15$ (so $64 + b^2 = 289$ and $16\sqrt{289} = 272$):
$$\dfrac{dl}{dx} = \dfrac{-4x\left(x^2+64+15^2+16\sqrt{64+15^2}\right)\left(x^2+64+15^2-16\sqrt{64+15^2}\right)}{\left(15^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2\left(15^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2}$$
The numerator simplifies, so for stationary points $\dfrac{dl}{dx} = 0$:
$$-4x(x^2+561)(x^2+17) = 0$$
So $x = 0$ is the only real solution.

The denominator is positive for all real $x$, and $(x^2+561)(x^2+17) > 0$ for all real $x$.

So the sign of $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$ is the sign of $-4x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dl}{dx} &> 0 &&\text{for } x < 0 &&\text{increasing} \\ \dfrac{dl}{dx} &= 0 &&\text{for } x = 0 &&\text{stationary} \\ \dfrac{dl}{dx} &< 0 &&\text{for } x > 0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the brightness increases to a maximum at } x = 0 \text{ and then decreases}$$
criteria: Shows that $x = 0$ is the only stationary point, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $b = 6$ (so $64 + b^2 = 100$ and $16\sqrt{100} = 160$), from the given factorisation:
$$\dfrac{dl}{dx} = \dfrac{-4x\left(x^2+64+6^2+16\sqrt{64+6^2}\right)\left(x^2+64+6^2-16\sqrt{64+6^2}\right)}{\left(6^2+(x+8)^2\right)^2\left(6^2+(x-8)^2\right)^2}$$
For stationary points, $\dfrac{dl}{dx} = 0$:
$$-4x(x^2+260)(x^2-60) = 0$$
So $x = 0$ or $x = \pm\sqrt{60}$.

The denominator and $x^2 + 260$ are always positive, so the sign of $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$ is the sign of $-x(x^2-60)$.

\extable{Ts7381_1}

The signs of $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$ across the intervals are positive, negative, positive, negative (slopes: up, down, up, down).

So the brightness increases to a maximum at $x = -\sqrt{60}$, then decreases to a minimum at $x = 0$, then increases to another maximum at $x = \sqrt{60}$, then decreases.
criteria: Finds the stationary points and the sign of $\dfrac{dl}{dx}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following graphs represents the equation $y+2=\dfrac{4}{x-1}$ ?

dif.r: Rearrange hyperbola, find asymptotes and intercepts to match graph.

figures.cap: option A: hyperbola graph option A
option B: hyperbola graph option B
option C: hyperbola graph option C
option D: hyperbola graph option D

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the equation as

$$y=\dfrac{4}{x-1}-2$$

This is $y=\dfrac{4}{x}$ shifted 1 unit right and 2 units down, so the asymptotes are $x=1$ and $y=-2$.

Find the intercepts.

When $x=0$:

$$y=\dfrac{4}{-1}-2=-6$$

When $y=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4}{x-1}&=2 \\ x-1&=2 \\ x&=3 \end{aligned}$$

So the graph has $y$-intercept $-6$, $x$-intercept $3$, and the branch for $x>1$ lies above the asymptote $y=-2$ and the other branch lies below it.

Only graph B has these intercepts, with the horizontal asymptote $y=-2$ (the other graphs have asymptotes at $y=2$ or $y=-2$ but pass through $(0,0)$ or $(0,4)$).

The answer is B.

meta.self_check: Checked intercepts (3,0) and (0,-6) against graph B in the figure; A and D pass through the origin, C has y-intercept 4.

questions.review_note: Answer key on the answer sheet is A, but translating left 2 then horizontally dilating by 3 gives f(x/3+2)-4 (option C); key kept as extracted

dif.r: Order of translation then horizontal dilation; common trap in composition.

solutions.latex:
Apply the transformations in the order given, each to the previous function.

Translated left 2 units, replace $x$ by $x+2$:

$$f(x+2)$$

Horizontally dilated by a factor of 3, replace $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{3}$ in this new function:

$$f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+2\right)$$

Translated down 4 units, subtract 4:

$$f\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+2\right)-4$$

This is option C.

Option A, $f\left(\dfrac{x+2}{3}\right)-4$, comes from dilating first and then translating left 2, which is the opposite order.

(The school's answer sheet gives A; the transformations in the order given lead to C.)

dif.r: Identify tan period and phase shift from graph features.

figures.cap: graph of a tangent function with asymptotes

solutions.latex:
The graph has $x$-intercepts at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ (and $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$), with vertical asymptotes between them at $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

The distance between consecutive branches gives the period:

$$\text{period}=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$

For $\tan(nx)$ the period is $\dfrac{\pi}{n}$, so

$$\dfrac{\pi}{n}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$

and $n=2$.

The basic $\tan 2x$ has a zero at the origin, so this graph is shifted right by $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (the zero at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ with the curve increasing):

$$f(x)=\tan\left(2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)$$

Check: asymptotes occur when $2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, that is $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, as on the graph.

This is option B.

meta.self_check: Zeros at pi/4 + k pi/2, asymptotes at k pi/2 verified; matches key B.

dif.r: Identify sine phase shift from intercept and maximum on graph.

figures.cap: section of a sine-type graph

solutions.latex:
The graph has amplitude 1 and period $2\pi$ (it crosses zero rising at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and falling at $x=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$, half a period apart).

It has a maximum at $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $y$-intercept $-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

The graph of $y=\sin x$ rises through zero at $x=0$, so this graph is $y=\sin x$ shifted right by $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$:

$$y=\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

Check:

$$\begin{aligned} x&=0:\ y=\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ x&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}:\ y=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1 \end{aligned}$$

This is option B.

Option C, $\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, has $y$-intercept $\dfrac{1}{2}$, and D is the reflection of B.

parts.latex: Find the derivative of $e^{x\sin 3x}$.

dif.r: Chain rule on exponential combined with product rule.

solutions.latex:
This is $e^{u}$ with $u=x\sin 3x$, so by the chain rule

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u}=u'e^{u}$$

To find $u'$ use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(fg)=f'g+fg'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} f&=x & g&=\sin 3x \\ f'&=1 & g'&=3\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$

so

$$u'=\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x$$

Therefore

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{x\sin 3x}=e^{x\sin 3x}\left(\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x\right)$$

This is option B.

meta.self_check: Standard chain and product rule; matches key B.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\left(1+\log_e x\right)^4$ ?

dif.r: Chain rule with log inner function; must include 1/x factor.

solutions.latex:
Use the chain rule with $u=1+\log_e x$, so $y=u^4$ and

$$\dfrac{du}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x}$$

Then

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=4u^3\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx} \\ &=\dfrac{4\left(1+\log_e x\right)^3}{x} \end{aligned}$$

This is option C.

Option A leaves out the factor $\dfrac{1}{x}$.

meta.self_check: Chain rule; matches key C.

dif.r: Integrate polynomial and use initial condition for constant.

solutions.latex:
Integrate $f'(x)$:

$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int (x-3x^2)\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x^3+C \end{aligned}$$

Use $f(0)=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} 1&=0-0+C \\ C&=1 \end{aligned}$$

So

$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{2}-x^3+1$$

This is option D.

meta.self_check: Differentiating D gives x-3x^2 and f(0)=1; matches key D.

questions.stem: A function $f(x)$ is defined by $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: For what values of $x$ is the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ concave up?

dif.r: Two derivatives then solve linear inequality for concavity.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find all the solutions for $f(x)=0$.

dif.r: Factor out x squared and solve; single routine step.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the turning points for the curve $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: Standard stationary points of cubic with second derivative test.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the point of inflexion.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and substitute; routine with fractions.

parts.label: e
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$ showing the essential features.

dif.r: Sketch cubic using features already found in earlier parts.

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of y=2x^3-3x^2 with turning points (0,0), (1,-1), inflexion (1/2,-1/2), x-intercept 3/2, with marking annotations

solutions.latex:
The graph is concave up when $f''(x)>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-6x \\ f''(x)&=12x-6 \end{aligned}$$
So $12x-6>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x&>6 \\ x&>\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{concave up when } x>\dfrac{1}{2}$$
criteria: Finds $f''(x)$ and uses $f''(x)>0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=0 \\ 2x^3-3x^2&=0 \\ x^2(2x-3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=0 \text{ or } x=\dfrac{3}{2}$$

Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x^2-6x&=0 \\ 6x(x-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=1$, $y=2(1)^3-3(1)^2=-1$.

Hence the stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,-1)$.

To find their nature, use $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x-6$.

When $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-6<0$ (concave down), so $(0,0)$ is a maximum turning point.

When $x=1$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6>0$ (concave up), so $(1,-1)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflexion occurs where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x-6&=0 \\ x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3-3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{3}{4} \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{point of inflexion is } \left(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$

NB: The concavity changes either side of $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$. There is no need to check this, since the question states there is a point of inflexion.

meta.format_note: Source NB read 'at the turning point'; reworded to the evident meaning (concavity changes either side of the inflexion).

questions.stem: A particle is moving on the $x$ axis, such that its position in metres, at time $t$ is given by $x=t^3-6t^2+9t$.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the times and positions of the particle when it is at rest.

dif.r: Differentiate, solve quadratic, substitute for positions.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Calculate the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

dif.r: Must account for direction change; distance not displacement.

solutions.latex:
The velocity is the derivative of position.
$$\dot{x}=3t^2-12t+9$$
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} t^2-4t+3&=0 \\ (t-3)(t-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $t=1$ or $t=3$.

When $t=1$, $x=1-6+9=4$.

When $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=3^3-6(3)^2+9(3) \\ &=27-54+27 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore the particle is at rest after 1 second at $x=4$ (4 m to the right of $O$), and after 3 seconds at $x=0$ (the origin, $O$).
criteria: Finds both times and one position, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$, $x=0$. At $t=3$, $x=0$.

The particle moves from the origin to $x=4$ (at rest at $t=1$), then returns to the origin at $t=3$.
$$\text{distance}=4+4=8 \text{ metres}$$
criteria: Finds $x=0$ at $t=0$ and $t=3$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A curve with the equation $y=f(x)$, has $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^3+2x-7$.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$

dif.r: Differentiate a polynomial once.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\ge 2$ for all real values of $x$.

dif.r: Short justification using x squared non-negative.

skills: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: The point $P(2,4)$ lies on the curve. Find $y$ in terms of $x$.

dif.r: Integrate gradient function and find constant from point.

solutions.latex:
We need $3x^2+2\ge 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2&\ge 0 \\ x^2&\ge 0 \end{aligned}$$
This is true for all real $x$.

$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\ge 2 \text{ for all } x\in\mathbb{R}$$

(There are many other ways of showing it.)

Integrating $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$:
$$y=\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2-7x+C$$
Substitute $(2,4)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4&=\dfrac{2^4}{4}+2^2-7(2)+C \\ 4&=4+4-14+C \\ 4&=-6+C \\ C&=10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{1}{4}x^4+x^2-7x+10$$
criteria: Integrates and substitutes $(2,4)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A landscape designer draws up the plan below. It consists of a semi-circular pond in a rectangular shaped lawn. The radius of the pond is $r$ m and the length of the lawn is $l$ m.

\exfigure{1035_q15_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Given that the lawn is $400\ \text{m}^2$, show that $l=\dfrac{200}{r}+\dfrac{\pi}{4}r$.

dif.r: Set up area equation from diagram, rearrange for l.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Given that the perimeter of the lawn is $P$ metres, show that

$$P=\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+2\right)r+\dfrac{400}{r}$$

dif.r: Build perimeter including arc, substitute and simplify.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Given that $r$ and $l$ can vary, find the value of $r$ for which $P$ is a minimum.

dif.r: Optimise given function with negative powers, pi algebra, verify minimum.

figures.cap: semi-circular pond of radius r in rectangular lawn 2r wide and l long

solutions.latex:
The lawn is a rectangle of area $2rl$ with the semicircular pond of area $\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$ removed.
$$2rl-\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}=400$$
So
$$2rl=400+\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$$
Dividing by $2r$:
$$\begin{aligned} l&=\dfrac{400}{2r}+\dfrac{\pi r^2}{4r} \\ &=\dfrac{200}{r}+\dfrac{\pi}{4}r \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ l=\dfrac{200}{r}+\dfrac{\pi}{4}r$$
criteria: Correct area expression, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is two widths $2r$, two lengths $2l$, and the semicircular arc $\pi r$.

Substituting $l$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} P&=2r+2l+\pi r \\ &=2r+2\left(\dfrac{200}{r}+\dfrac{\pi}{4}r\right)+\pi r \\ &=2r+\dfrac{400}{r}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}r+\pi r \\ &=2r+\dfrac{3\pi}{2}r+\dfrac{400}{r} \\ &=\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+2\right)r+\dfrac{400}{r} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes $l$ from part (a), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write $P=\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+2\right)r+400r^{-1}$.

For possible maxima or minima, $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dr}&=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+2-400r^{-2} \\ &=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}+2-\dfrac{400}{r^2}=0 \end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3\pi+4}{2}&=\dfrac{400}{r^2} \\ \dfrac{r^2}{400}&=\dfrac{2}{3\pi+4} \\ r^2&=\dfrac{800}{3\pi+4} \end{aligned}$$
Since $r>0$:
$$\begin{aligned} r&=\sqrt{\dfrac{800}{3\pi+4}} \\ &\approx\sqrt{59.59} \\ &\approx 7.7 \end{aligned}$$
To test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=800r^{-3}=\dfrac{800}{r^3}$$
When $r\approx 7.7$, $\dfrac{d^2P}{dr^2}=\dfrac{800}{(7.7)^3}>0$.

$$\therefore\ P \text{ is a minimum when } r\approx 7.7 \text{ m}$$

NB: Since the area is $400 \text{ m}^2$, the end points of the domain ($r=0$ or $l=0$, which give zero area) need not be considered.
criteria: Finds $r\approx 7.7$ and the second derivative, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Use your knowledge of trigonometric functions to answer the questions below.

The tide in Sydney on Monday May 13 can be modelled by a trigonometric curve in the form

$$h=A\sin[n(t+\varepsilon)]+C$$

where $t$ is in hours after midnight and $h$ is the height of the tide in metres. At 12am (midnight), the graph below starts with the tide measured at 1.29m. High tide of 1.69m occurs at 2.54am. Low tide of 0.46m occurs at 9:43am.

Note: The diagram is not to scale and you may assume that each tide reaches the same heights, for high and low tides.

\exfigure{1035_q16_1}
questions.review_note: Heading prints (6 marks) but parts total 8 and the cover table gives 8; marks_total set to 8

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Explain why $C=1.075$ which is the centre of oscillation.

dif.r: Explain centre as midpoint of high and low tide.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the Amplitude, $A$.

dif.r: Amplitude from maximum minus centre; one step.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine the value of $n$.

dif.r: Half period from tide times, time conversion, then n.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the value of $\varepsilon$.

dif.r: Phase shift from tide timing needs reasoning about sine model.

parts.label: e
parts.latex: Determine the time when the tide is first at a height of 1.25 metres, after 12am. Write your answer to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Solve trig equation in context, choose first valid time, convert.

figures.cap: tide height graph for Mon 13 May

solutions.latex:
The centre of oscillation is midway between the high and low tides.
$$\begin{aligned} C&=\dfrac{1.69+0.46}{2} \\ &=1.075 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
(The average is the median for two values.)

The amplitude is the upper limit minus the centre.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=1.69-1.075 \\ &=0.615 \end{aligned}$$

The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$.

High tide to low tide is 2:54 am to 9:43 am, which is 6 h 49 min. This is half a period, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{period}&=2\times 6\text{ h }49\text{ min} \\ &=13\text{ h }38\text{ min} \\ &=13.63\text{ h}\ \left(=\dfrac{409}{30}\text{ h}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2\pi}{n}&=\dfrac{409}{30} \\ n&=\dfrac{30\times 2\pi}{409} \\ &=\dfrac{60\pi}{409} \\ &\approx 0.46 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the period from the high and low tide times, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
High tide is a maximum of $h=A\sin[n(t+\varepsilon)]+C$, which happens when $n(t+\varepsilon)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

High tide is at 2:54 am, $t=2.9$, and $n=\dfrac{60\pi}{409}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{60\pi}{409}(2.9+\varepsilon)&=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ 2.9+\varepsilon&=\dfrac{409}{120} \\ \varepsilon&=\dfrac{409}{120}-2.9=\dfrac{61}{120}\approx0.508 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds that the curve starts at the centre of oscillation 6 h 49 min before 2:54 am, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the guideline stopped mid-sentence with no value of $\varepsilon$; from the high tide at 2:54 am, $\varepsilon=\dfrac{61}{120}\approx0.508$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the guideline stopped mid-sentence with no value of $\varepsilon$; from the high tide at 2:54 am, $\varepsilon=\dfrac{61}{120}\approx0.508$.

solutions.latex:
With $h=0.615\sin\left[\dfrac{60\pi}{409}(t+0.508)\right]+1.075$, set $h=1.25$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\left[\dfrac{60\pi}{409}(t+0.508)\right]&=\dfrac{1.25-1.075}{0.615}\approx0.28455 \\ \dfrac{60\pi}{409}(t+0.508)&=\sin^{-1}(0.28455)\approx0.28860 \\ t+0.508&\approx0.6262 \\ t&\approx0.118\text{ h}\approx7\text{ min} \end{aligned}$$
This is the first time after midnight, on the rising tide before the 2:54 am high.
$$\therefore\ \text{the tide is first at }1.25\text{ m at about 12:07 am}$$
(The model gives $h(0)\approx1.22$ m, not the $1.29$ m the question states at midnight; the guideline's $\varepsilon=-3.91\dot6$ and answer 4:33 am do not fit the high tide at 2:54 am.)
criteria: Sets up the equation with $h=1.25$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which expression is equal to $\int \tan^2 x\,dx$?

dif.r: Recall tan^2 = sec^2 - 1, then integrate directly

solutions.latex:
Using $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\tan^2 x\,dx&=\int(\sec^2x-1)\,dx \\ &=\tan x-x+C \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is (B).

parts.latex: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e \dfrac{4x^2-9}{2x-3}$ is equal to which of the following?

dif.r: Factorise and cancel inside the log, then differentiate a linear log

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator:
$$\dfrac{4x^2-9}{2x-3}=\dfrac{(2x-3)(2x+3)}{2x-3}=2x+3$$
so
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e(2x+3)=\dfrac{2}{2x+3}$$
Hence the answer is (B).

parts.latex: Which of the following could be a primitive for $f'(x)=\dfrac{x}{e^{x^2-8}}$ ?

dif.r: Rewrite as x e^(8-x^2), reverse chain rule, spot the arbitrary constant

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the integrand and integrate by recognition:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int \dfrac{x}{e^{x^2-8}}\,dx \\ &=\int x\,e^{8-x^2}\,dx \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\int(-2x)e^{8-x^2}\,dx \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{8-x^2}+C \end{aligned}$$
The constant $C$ can be any constant, so $C=-8$ is possible.

Hence the answer is (D).

parts.latex: Results for a test are given as $z$-scores. In this test Angela gained a $z$-score of 3. The test has a mean of 55 and standard deviation of 6. What was Angela's actual mark in this test?

dif.r: Use the z-score formula in reverse, one step

solutions.latex:
A $z$-score of 3 means the mark is 3 standard deviations above the mean.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Mark}&=\mu+3\sigma \\ &=55+3\times 6 \\ &=73 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is (B).

dif.r: Area split above and below the axis with an absolute value, then solve for k

figures.cap: graph of y=k(x-2)^3 with shaded regions between x=1 and x=4

solutions.latex:
The shaded area is the area below the axis from $x=1$ to $2$ plus the area above from $x=2$ to $4$.
$$\begin{aligned} 34&=\left|\displaystyle\int_1^2k(x-2)^3\,dx\right|+\displaystyle\int_2^4k(x-2)^3\,dx \\ &=k\left|\left[\dfrac{(x-2)^4}{4}\right]_1^2\right|+k\left[\dfrac{(x-2)^4}{4}\right]_2^4 \\ &=k\left|0-\dfrac14\right|+k\left[\dfrac{16}{4}-0\right] \\ &=k\left(\dfrac14+4\right) \end{aligned}$$
so $k=8$.

Hence the answer is (B).

parts.latex: The time, $T$, in seconds that divers can hold their breath is normally distributed with $\mu=120$ and $\text{Var}(T)=400$. In what range of time length would you expect to find the middle 95%?

dif.r: Convert variance to standard deviation, then apply the 95% rule

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Since $\text{Var}(T)=\sigma^2=400$, $\sigma=20$.

The middle 95% lies within $2\sigma$ of the mean:
$$\begin{aligned} 120-2\times20&=80 \\ 120+2\times 20&=160 \end{aligned}$$
so $80\le x\le160$.

Hence the answer is (B).

parts.latex: The exact value of $I=\int_1^2 \dfrac{\ln x}{x}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}(\ln 2)^2$. The approximation of $I$ using the Trapezoidal Rule with 2 function values is

dif.r: Single-strip trapezoidal estimate, then a percentage difference from the exact value

solutions.latex:
With 2 function values, $h=1$, so the trapezoidal rule gives
$$\begin{aligned} I&\approx\dfrac h2(\text{first value}+\text{last value}) \\ &=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{\ln1}{1}+\dfrac{\ln2}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac14\ln2 \\ &\approx0.17328 \end{aligned}$$
The exact value is $\dfrac12(\ln2)^2\approx0.2402265$, so the approximation is smaller.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage difference}&=\dfrac{\frac12(\ln2)^2-\frac14\ln2}{\frac12(\ln2)^2}\times100 \\ &\approx27.865\% \\ &\approx 28\% \end{aligned}$$
Hence the approximation is smaller by 28%, so the answer is (A).

parts.latex:
Given a function $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2-5}$

Which of the following statements is true?

dif.r: Test f(-x) for oddness and recognise the function is many-to-one

solutions.latex:
Test for even or odd:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=\dfrac{-x}{(-x)^2-5} \\ &=\dfrac{-x}{x^2-5} \\ &=-f(x) \end{aligned}$$
so $f$ is odd.

The graph has vertical asymptotes at $x=\pm\sqrt5$, and a horizontal line cuts it more than once (horizontal line test), so $f$ is many-to-one.

Hence the answer is (D).

parts.latex:
The amount $M$ of certain medicine present in the blood after $t$ hours is given by $M=9t^2-t^3$ for $0\le t\le 9$.

When is the amount of medicine in the blood increasing most rapidly?

dif.r: Must recognise that the greatest rate means maximising dM/dt

solutions.latex:
The rate of increase of $M$ is
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=18t-3t^2=3t(6-t)$$
This is a concave-down parabola in $t$ with zeros at $t=0$ and $t=6$, so its maximum is at $t=3$.

Hence $M$ increases most rapidly at $t=3$, so the answer is (D).

questions.stem: Differentiate the following

dif.r: Expand the difference of squares and differentiate a polynomial

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: $y=\sin^2 x$

dif.r: Direct chain rule on a squared sine

solutions.latex:
Expand first:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(4x-5)(4x+5) \\ &=16x^2-25 \end{aligned}$$
so
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=32x$$
Alternatively, by the product rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=4(4x+5)+(4x-5)\times4 \\ &=16x+20+16x-20 \\ &=32x \end{aligned}$$

Using the chain rule with $u=\sin x$, $y=u^2$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2\sin x\cos x$$
criteria: Correctly differentiates $\sin^2 x$ to get $2\sin x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: In an arithmetic series, the third term is 5 and the tenth term is 26. Find the sum of the first 14 terms.

dif.r: Simultaneous equations for a and d, then the sum formula

solutions.latex:
The third and tenth terms give two equations:
$$\begin{aligned} a+2d&=5 \\ a+9d&=26 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting gives $7d=21$, so $d=3$ and $a=-1$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac n2\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{14}&=\dfrac{14}{2}\big(2(-1)+13\times3\big) \\ &=259 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds $a$ and $d$, or applies the sum formula correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Evaluate

$$\int_1^4 5(9x-4)^4\,dx$$

dif.r: Reverse chain rule on a linear power, evaluate with heavy arithmetic

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^45(9x-4)^4\,dx&=\left[5\times\dfrac{(9x-4)^5}{5\times9}\right]_1^4 \\ &=\dfrac19\left[(9x-4)^5\right]_1^4 \\ &=\dfrac19\left[(9(4)-4)^5-(9-4)^5\right] \\ &=\dfrac19\left[32^5-5^5\right] \\ &=3727923 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Solve the following equation for $x$.

$$e^{2x}+3e^x-10=0.$$

dif.r: Substitute to get a hidden quadratic, reject the negative root

solutions.latex:
Let $m=e^x$, so the equation becomes
$$\begin{aligned} m^2+3m-10&=0 \\ (m+5)(m-2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
so $m=-5$ or $m=2$.

$e^x=-5$ has no solution, since $e^x>0$.

$e^x=2$ gives $x=\ln2$.
$$\therefore\ x=\ln 2$$
criteria: Correctly reduces to a quadratic equation and solves it, or equivalent merit

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec^2 x)=2\tan x\,\sec^2 x$.

dif.r: Chain rule on (cos x)^-2, then simplify to the given form

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence find $\int \tan x\,\sec^2 x\,dx$.

dif.r: 'Hence' integral using the previous derivative with a factor of 1/2

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec^2x=(\cos x)^{-2}$ and differentiate by the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec^2x)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x)^{-2} \\ &=-2\cos^{-3}x\cdot(-\sin x) \\ &=\dfrac{2\sin x}{\cos^3x} \\ &=\dfrac{2\sin x}{\cos x}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2x} \\ &=2\tan x\sec^2x \end{aligned}$$
as required.

From part (i),
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec^2x)=2\tan x\sec^2x$$
so, ignoring the constant,
$$\sec^2x=\int2\tan x\sec^2x\,dx$$
Hence
$$\int\tan x\sec^2x\,dx=\dfrac12\sec^2x+C$$
(equivalently $\dfrac12(1+\tan^2x)+C$).

questions.stem: Given a function $f(x)=\begin{cases}6x-6x^2 & 0\le x\le 1\\ 0 & \text{Otherwise}\end{cases}$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ represents probability density function.

dif.r: Check non-negative and that the integral equals 1; routine

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the mode of the probability density function $f(x)$.

dif.r: Mode is the vertex of a symmetric parabola

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
$f(x)$ is a probability density function if $f(x)\ge0$ on its domain and $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx=1$.

For $0\le x\le1$, $6x(1-x)\ge0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^1(6x-6x^2)\,dx&=\left[3x^2-2x^3\right]_0^1 \\ &=(3-2)-0 \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
criteria: Finds $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx$ correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The mode is where $f(x)$ is greatest.

Since $f(x)=6x(1-x)$ is a concave-down parabola with zeros at $0$ and $1$, its maximum lies midway between them.
$$\therefore\ \text{mode}=x=\dfrac12$$

parts.latex:
Find the value(s) of $b$ such that $y=2x+b$ is a tangent to the parabola

$$y=2x^2+6x-5.$$

dif.r: Match the gradient to find the contact point, or use discriminant zero

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent is $2$, so set the derivative equal to $2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=4x+6=2 \\ x&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=2(-1)^2+6(-1)-5=-9$, so the point of contact is $(-1,-9)$.

Substituting into $y=2x+b$:
$$\begin{aligned} -9&=2(-1)+b \\ b&=-7 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, equate the two equations:
$$2x+b=2x^2+6x-5$$
so $2x^2+4x-5-b=0$. A tangent means one solution, so $\Delta=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4^2-4(2)(-5-b) \\ &=16+40+8b \end{aligned}$$
so $b=-7$.
$$\therefore\ b=-7$$
criteria: Finds the point of contact using calculus, or forms the quadratic by solving simultaneously and attempts $\Delta=0$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Angela guesses three questions in her multiple choice test, which has four options per question. Find the probability that Angela gets:

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Only one correct answer.

dif.r: Exactly one success: count three orders and multiply probabilities

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: At least one correct answer.

dif.r: Complement of none correct, one step

solutions.latex:
Let $C$ be a correct answer and $IC$ an incorrect answer, with $P(C)=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $P(IC)=\dfrac{3}{4}$. There are three orders for exactly one correct answer.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=P(C\,IC\,IC)+P(IC\,C\,IC)+P(IC\,IC\,C) \\ &=3\times\dfrac{1}{4}\times\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 \\ &=\dfrac{27}{64} \end{aligned}$$

Use the complement: at least one correct is the opposite of none correct.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one correct})&=1-P(\text{no correct}) \\ &=1-\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^3 \\ &=\dfrac{37}{64} \end{aligned}$$

So the $y$-intercept is $\left(0,-\dfrac{5}{4}\right)$.

For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$.

So the $x$-intercept is $(5,0)$.

questions.stem:
Consider the piece-wise defined function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2-1 & x\le 1\\ 4-x^2 & x>1\end{cases}$$

parts.label: i

dif.r: Substitute into the correct branch of the piecewise function

parts.latex: Find $x$ if $f(x)=0$

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} f(1)&=1^2-1 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$$

For $x\le 1$, use $f(x)=x^2-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-1&=0 \\ x&=\pm1 \end{aligned}$$
For $x>1$, use $f(x)=4-x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-x^2&=0 \\ x&=\pm2 \end{aligned}$$
But $x>1$, so $x=2$.

$$\therefore\ x=-1,\ 1,\ 2$$
criteria: Finds all 4 solutions without excluding $x=-2$, or finds $x=\pm1$, or equivalent merit

so there is an open circle at $(1,3)$ on the second branch.

questions.stem:
A surveyor stands at a point $P$, which is due east of the tower $OT$, of height $h$ metres. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower $T$ from $P$ is $30^\circ$. The surveyor then walks 100 metres to point $B$, which is on a bearing of $150^\circ$ from the foot of tower $O$. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from $B$ is now $45^\circ$.

\exfigure{1270_q13b_1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Express the length of $OP$ in terms of $h$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tower seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1, whole question removed

dif.r: Single tangent ratio in a right triangle

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Show that $(100)^2=h^2+\dfrac{h^2}{\tan^2 30^\circ}-\dfrac{h^2}{\tan 30^\circ}$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tower seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1, whole question removed

dif.r: 3D set-up: get the angle from the bearings, then the cosine rule for a given result

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Hence find the height of the tower. Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tower seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1, whole question removed

dif.r: Rearrange given cosine-rule equation for h and evaluate

figures.cap: tower OT with P east of O, B on bearing 150 from O, BP = 100 m, elevations 45 degrees at B and 30 degrees at P

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle OPT$, the angle at $O$ is a right angle, so
$$\begin{aligned} \tan30^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{OP} \\ OP&=\dfrac{h}{\tan30^\circ} \\ &=\sqrt{3}\,h \end{aligned}$$

$P$ is due east of $O$ and $B$ is on a bearing of $150^\circ$ from $O$, so $\angle BOP=150^\circ-90^\circ=60^\circ$.

In $\triangle BOT$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan45^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{BO} \\ BO&=h \end{aligned}$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle OPB$:
$$\begin{aligned} BP^2&=BO^2+OP^2-2\cdot BO\cdot OP\cos\angle BOP \\ 100^2&=h^2+\dfrac{h^2}{\tan^230^\circ}-2h\times\dfrac{h}{\tan30^\circ}\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &=h^2+\dfrac{h^2}{\tan^230^\circ}-\dfrac{h^2}{\tan30^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $OB$ and applies the cosine rule in $\triangle OPB$ correctly, or finds $OB$ and $\angle BOP=60^\circ$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Factorise $h^2$.

questions.stem: Given the function $f(x)=\ln(x^2+1)$.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Find the domain of $f(x)$.

dif.r: Direct domain recall for log of positive expression

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find any stationary point(s) and determine their nature.

dif.r: Differentiate log composite, find and classify one stationary point

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Find any point(s) of inflection.

dif.r: Quotient rule second derivative, test concavity change

parts.label: iv
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $f(x)=\ln(x^2+1)$ showing all features from part (ii) and (iii).

dif.r: Sketch using features already found

figures.cap: solution sketch: marking guideline sketch of y=ln(x^2+1) with minimum and inflexion points

solutions.latex:
The logarithm needs $x^2+1>0$, which is true for all real $x$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the domain is all real } x$$

$$f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$$
For stationary points, set $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1} \\ x&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=\ln(0+1)=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a stationary point.

Nature, by the sign of $f'(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-1&: f'(-1)=-1 &&\text{decreasing}\\ x=0&: f'(0)=0 &&\text{stationary}\\ x=1&: f'(1)=1 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient goes $-,0,+$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.

Alternatively,
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{2-2x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$$
and $f''(0)=2>0$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the stationary point correctly, or determines its nature correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule on $f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$:
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{2(x^2+1)-2x(2x)}{(x^2+1)^2}=\dfrac{2-2x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$$
Set $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-2x^2&=0 \\ x&=\pm1 \end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflexion are $(1,\ln2)$ and $(-1,\ln2)$.

Test the concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-2&: f''=-\dfrac{6}{25} &&\text{concave down}\\ x=-1&: f''=0 \\ x=0&: f''=2 &&\text{concave up}\\ x=1&: f''=0 \\ x=2&: f''=-\dfrac{6}{25} &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at $x=\pm1$.

$$\therefore\ (1,\ln2)\text{ and }(-1,\ln2)\text{ are points of inflexion}$$
\exfigure{1270_q13d_s1}
criteria: Correct shape, or shows the features from parts (ii) and (iii) correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.label: i
parts.latex:
Prove the following identity

$$(1+\tan x)^2=2\tan x+\sec^2 x$$

dif.r: Expand and apply one Pythagorean identity

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Hence find the area bounded by $y=(1+\tan x)^2$ and the $x$-axis between $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

dif.r: Integrate tan x via log form plus sec squared, exact evaluation

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Use $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=(1+\tan x)^2 \\ &=1+2\tan x+\tan^2x \\ &=1+\tan^2x+2\tan x \\ &=\sec^2x+2\tan x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

Since $(1+\tan x)^2\ge0$ for $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the area is the integral, using part (i).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(1+\tan x)^2\,dx \\ &=\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(2\tan x+\sec^2x)\,dx \\ &=\Big[-2\ln|\cos x|+\tan x\Big]_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &=\left(-2\ln\left|\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right|+1\right)-\left(-2\ln\left|\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right|+(-1)\right) \\ &=2 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly uses part (i) and integrates $\tan x$, or equivalent merit
Correctly uses part (i), or correctly integrates $\tan x$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: i
parts.latex: State the amplitude and period.

dif.r: Read amplitude and period from standard form

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the exact values of all intercepts of $y=2\sin\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ with the axes for $0\le x\le\pi$.

dif.r: Solve shifted sine equation within domain, exact values

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Hence sketch the graph of $y=2\sin\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, showing all features from part (i) and (ii) and the global maximum and minimum.

dif.r: Sketch phase-shifted sine with intercepts and extrema

figures.cap: solution sketch: marking guideline sketch of y=2sin(2x-pi/3) on [0,pi]

solutions.latex:
For $y=a\sin(bx-c)$, the amplitude is $|a|$ and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$.
$$\text{Amplitude}=2$$
$$T=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$$
criteria: Correct amplitude or correct period, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= -2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= -\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
So the $y$-intercept is $(0,-\sqrt{3})$.

For the $x$-intercepts, put $y=0$.
$$\sin\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$$
So $2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$, giving
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}$$
The last value is outside the domain $0\le x\le\pi$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the } x\text{-intercepts are } \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},0\right) \text{ and } \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3},0\right)$$
\exfigure{1270_q14b_s1}
criteria: Correct shape and $x$, $y$-intercepts, or equivalent merit
Shows correct maximum and minimum, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A bag contains three red balls and four black balls. Two balls are selected at random without replacement from the bag.

Let $X$ be the number of black balls drawn.

parts.label: i
parts.latex:
Fill in the following table and hence find exact value of $E(X)$.

\extable{1270_q14c_t1}

dif.r: Without-replacement probabilities then expected value

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find $E(X^2)$ and hence find $\text{Var}(X)$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

dif.r: Standard variance and standard deviation calculation

solutions.latex:
Probabilities of the number of black balls drawn, without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(0) &= \dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{2}{6}=\dfrac{1}{7} \\ P(1) &= 2\times\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{6}=\dfrac{4}{7} \\ P(2) &= \dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{2}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline P(X=x) & \dfrac{1}{7} & \dfrac{4}{7} & \dfrac{2}{7} \end{array}$$
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \sum x\,p(x) \\ &= 0\times\dfrac{1}{7}+1\times\dfrac{4}{7}+2\times\dfrac{2}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{7} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds correct $E(X)=\mu$ from an incorrect table of values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= \sum x^2p(x) \\ &= 0\times\dfrac{1}{7}+1^2\times\dfrac{4}{7}+2^2\times\dfrac{2}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= E(X^2)-\mu^2 \\ &= \dfrac{12}{7}-\left(\dfrac{8}{7}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{20}{49} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{49}} \\ &= 0.638876\ldots \\ &\approx 0.639 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct $E(X^2)$, or finds $\text{Var}(X)$, or equivalent merit
