questions.stem: Alice and Raoul take turns throwing darts at a dartboard. The winner is whoever hits the bullseye first. Alice has a $\dfrac{1}{30}$ chance of hitting the bullseye, while Raoul has a $\dfrac{1}{40}$ chance of hitting the bullseye. Alice throws the first dart.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Draw a tree diagram for the first four throws of the games (two throws forAlice and two for Raoul).

dif.r: Draw a simple tree diagram from given probabilities.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability that Alice wins on her first or second throw?

dif.r: Two-path probability: multiply along branches and add.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the probability that Alice will eventually win the game.

dif.r: Recognise infinite geometric series in turn-taking probability, then limiting sum.

figures.cap: solution sketch: Guideline tree diagram for first four throws

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1273_q13_s1}

Here W means win and W$'$ means lose. The game stops once a bullseye is hit.

Alice wins on her first throw, or Alice and Raoul both miss and Alice then hits on her second throw.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Alice wins on 1st or 2nd throw}) &= \dfrac{1}{30}+\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{30}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{259}{4000} \end{aligned}$$

$$P(\text{Alice wins game})=\dfrac{1}{30}+\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{30}\right)+\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{30}\right)+\cdots$$

This is a geometric series with $a=\dfrac{1}{30}$ and $r=\left(\dfrac{29}{30}\right)\left(\dfrac{39}{40}\right)$.

$S_\infty$ exists as $|r|<1$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{1}{30}}{1-\left(\frac{29}{30}\right)\left(\frac{39}{40}\right)} \\ &= \dfrac{40}{69} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies that $S_\infty$ is required and finds the correct ratio

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graphs of $y=4e^{-x}$ and $y=e^x-3$ .

\exfigure{1273_q14_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the curves intersect when $e^{2x}-3e^x-4=0$ .

dif.r: Equate curves and multiply by e^x; one routine step.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, show the $x$ coordinate of the point $P$ is $x=\ln 4$ .

dif.r: Quadratic in e^x, factorise, reject negative root.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the exact shaded area between the two curves .

dif.r: Area between exponential curves; simplifying e^(-ln4) exactly.

figures.cap: graphs of y=4e^{-x} and y=e^x-3 meeting at P with shaded region

solutions.latex:
Equate the two curves:

$$\begin{aligned} 4e^{-x} &= e^x-3 \\ \dfrac{4}{e^x} &= e^x-3 \\ 4 &= e^x(e^x-3) \\ 4 &= e^{2x}-3e^x \end{aligned}$$

Hence $e^{2x}-3e^x-4=0$.

Let $u=e^x$, so $u^2=e^{2x}$. The equation from part (a) becomes

$$\begin{aligned} u^2-3u-4 &= 0 \\ (u-4)(u+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

so $u=4$ or $u=-1$, that is $e^x=4$ or $e^x=-1$.

$e^x\neq-1$ as $e^x>0$.

So $e^x=4$, giving $x=\ln 4$.

Therefore the $x$ coordinate of $P$ is $x=\ln 4$.
criteria: Reduces the equation from (a) to the correct quadratic form and solves for $u$

solutions.latex:
The curve $y=4e^{-x}$ is above $y=e^x-3$ between $x=0$ and $x=\ln 4$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \displaystyle\int_0^{\ln 4}\left(4e^{-x}-e^x+3\right)dx \\ &= \Big[-4e^{-x}-e^x+3x\Big]_0^{\ln 4} \\ &= -4e^{-\ln 4}-e^{\ln 4}+3\ln 4-\left(-4e^0-e^0+3(0)\right) \\ &= -4\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)-4+3\ln 4+4+1 \\ &= 3\ln 4 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line so that after $t$ seconds ($t\geq 0$) its velocity $v$ is given by $v=\left(\dfrac{2}{1+t}-t\right)\ \text{m/s}$ . The displacement of the particle from the origin is given by $x$ metres.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=0$ .

dif.r: Differentiate velocity and substitute t=0.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If the particle is initially at the origin, find the displacement as a function of $t$ .

dif.r: Integrate velocity including log term, use initial condition.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: When is the particle stationary?

dif.r: Set v=0, clear fraction, solve quadratic, reject negative.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: d
parts.latex: How far does the particle travel in the first 2 seconds? Give your answer correct to three significant figures.

dif.r: Distance with direction change needs splitting at t=1.

solutions.latex:
Write $v=2(1+t)^{-1}-t$ and differentiate.

$$\begin{aligned} a &= -2(1+t)^{-2}-1 \\ &= -\dfrac{2}{(1+t)^2}-1 \end{aligned}$$

At $t=0$:

$$a=-2-1=-3 \text{ m/s}^2$$

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \displaystyle\int v\,dt \\ &= 2\ln|1+t|-\dfrac{t^2}{2}+C \end{aligned}$$

At $t=0$, $x=0$:

$$0=2\ln 1-0+C$$

so $C=0$.

Hence

$$x=2\ln|1+t|-\dfrac{t^2}{2}.$$
criteria: Correct answer (finds the constant of integration and gives the correct displacement function)
Correct primitive with constant of integration

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{1+t}-t &= 0 \\ 2-t(1+t) &= 0 \\ 2-t-t^2 &= 0 \\ t^2+t-2 &= 0 \\ (t+2)(t-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $t=1$ (as $t\geq 0$).
criteria: Obtains the correct equation to solve in terms of $t$

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t=1$, so find the displacement at $t=0,1,2$.

$$\begin{aligned} t=0:&\ x=0 \\ t=1:&\ x=2\ln 2-\dfrac{1}{2}\approx 0.88629 \\ t=2:&\ x=2\ln 3-2\approx 0.19722 \end{aligned}$$

The particle moves forward to $0.88629$ at $t=1$, then back to $0.19722$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 0.88629+(0.88629-0.19722) \\ &\approx 1.57536 \\ &\approx 1.58 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Considers and obtains the correct displacements of the particle at $t=0,1,2$ s

questions.stem:
A tank initially holds 3600 litres of water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. The tank takes 60 minutes to empty. A mathematical model predicts that the volume $V$ litres of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V=3600\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)^2,\ \text{where } 0\leq t\leq 60 .$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What volume does the model predict will remain after 10 minutes?

dif.r: Substitute t=10 into given model.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How long will it take for the tank to become half full (to nearest minute)?

dif.r: Solve squared equation, reject root outside domain.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what rate does the model predict that the water will drain from the tank after twenty minutes?

dif.r: Chain rule derivative, substitute, interpret sign as draining rate.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: At what time does the model predict that the water will drain from the tank at its fastest rate?

dif.r: Maximum of |dV/dt| occurs at endpoint, not a stationary point.

solutions.latex:
When $t=10$:

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 3600\left(1-\dfrac{10}{60}\right)^2 \\ &= 2500 \text{ litres} \end{aligned}$$

Half full means $V=1800$.

$$\begin{aligned} 3600\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)^2 &= 1800 \\ \left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 1-\dfrac{t}{60} &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ t &= 60\left(1\mp\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \end{aligned}$$

So $t\approx 17.5736$ or $t\approx 102.4264$.

As $0\leq t\leq 60$, only $t\approx 17.5736$ is valid.

To the nearest minute, $t\approx 18$ minutes.
criteria: Correct answer, explaining why there is only one solution for $t$

meta.format_note: Corrected from source: the guidelines print $t\approx 17$ minutes, but $17.5736$ rounds to $18$ minutes to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 7200\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right)\left(-\dfrac{1}{60}\right) \\ &= -120\left(1-\dfrac{t}{60}\right) \\ &= -120+2t \end{aligned}$$

At $t=20$:

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-80$$

After 20 minutes, water is draining at 80 L/min.

The draining rate is $\left|\dfrac{dV}{dt}\right|$, the steepness of the graph of $V$ against $t$.

This is greatest at $t=0$, where the tangent to the curve is steepest.

So the maximum draining rate occurs when $t=0$ (that is, 120 L/min).
criteria: Correct answer for $t$ with correct reasoning

questions.stem:
\exfigure{1273_q19_1}

The diagram above shows that the distance between a boy's home $H$ and his school $S$ is 6 km. A canal $ABCD$ is 1 km from both his home and school. In winter the canal is frozen, he takes an alternate route $HBCS$, walking $HB$, skating $BC$ and walking $CS$. His walking speed is 4 km/h and his skating speed is 12 km/h. Let $\angle AHB=\angle DSC=\theta$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the time taken for this alternate route is $T=\dfrac{1}{2\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\tan\theta}{6}$ .

dif.r: Build time model from right-triangle trig and speeds.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find, to the nearest minute, the value of $\theta$ which minimizes the time taken for the journey to school.

dif.r: Optimise trig expression: differentiate sec and tan, solve, test nature.

figures.cap: home H, school S, canal ABCD, angle theta

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle HAB$ (right-angled at $A$, with $HA=1$):

$$\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{HB}\quad\text{and}\quad\tan\theta=\dfrac{AB}{1}$$

so $HB=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $AB=\tan\theta$.

Similarly in $\triangle SDC$: $SC=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $DC=\tan\theta$.

Distance walked $=2HB=\dfrac{2}{\cos\theta}$, so the time walked is

$$\dfrac{2}{\cos\theta}\div 4=\dfrac{1}{2\cos\theta}\text{ hours}.$$

Distance skated $=6-2\tan\theta$, so the time skated is $\dfrac{6-2\tan\theta}{12}$ hours.

$$\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{1}{2\cos\theta}+\dfrac{6-2\tan\theta}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2\cos\theta}+\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\tan\theta}{6} \end{aligned}$$

as required.
criteria: Obtains, with working, the correct distances travelled and times taken
Obtains, with working, the correct distances travelled

solutions.latex:
Write $T=\dfrac{(\cos\theta)^{-1}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{\tan\theta}{6}$ and differentiate.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{d\theta} &= -\dfrac{(-\sin\theta)(\cos\theta)^{-2}}{2}-\dfrac{\sec^2\theta}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{1}{6\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{3\sin\theta-1}{6\cos^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$

For a minimum, $\dfrac{dT}{d\theta}=0$. Since $\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}=\sec^2\theta\neq 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin\theta-1 &= 0 \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ \theta &\approx 19^\circ 28' \end{aligned}$$

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dT}{d\theta}$ either side:

$$\begin{aligned} \theta=10^\circ:&\ \dfrac{dT}{d\theta}<0 \\ \theta=19^\circ28':&\ \dfrac{dT}{d\theta}=0 \\ \theta=30^\circ:&\ \dfrac{dT}{d\theta}>0 \end{aligned}$$

The slope changes from negative to positive, so there is a minimum turning point.

$$\therefore\ \theta\approx 19^\circ 28'$$
criteria: Correct answer (must include testing that $\theta$ gives a minimum $T$)
Correct use of the chain rule and correct derivative of $\tan\theta$

parts.latex: Given the function $y=e^{\sqrt{x}}$, which expression is equal to $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$?

figures.cap: sector with radius r, angle theta, arc length 10pi/3

solutions.latex:
The arc length formula is $l=r\theta$, with $0<\theta\le2\pi$.

$$\dfrac{10\pi}{3}=r\theta,\ \text{so } \theta=\dfrac{10\pi}{3r}$$

Now use $0<\theta\le 2\pi$.

$$\begin{aligned} 0<\dfrac{10\pi}{3r} &\le 2\pi \\ 10\pi &\le 6\pi r &&(\text{multiply by } 3r>0) \\ \dfrac{5}{3} &\le r &&(\text{divide by } 6\pi) \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ r\ge\dfrac{5}{3}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The area of a sector is $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, where $\theta=\dfrac{10\pi}{3r}$ and $r=4$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times4^2\times\dfrac{10\pi}{3\times4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times16\times\dfrac{10\pi}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{80\pi}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{20\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

The area of the sector is $\dfrac{20\pi}{3}$ square units.
criteria: Substitutes into the area formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $BY=h\cot 12^o$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: One right-triangle tan ratio rearranged

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $h$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: 3D set-up: Pythagoras in horizontal plane with cot expressions

figures.cap: quadrilateral diagram with hill XY, points A, B, angles 16 and 12 degrees, AB=1600

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle $XYB$ (right angle at $Y$), $\tan 12^\circ=\dfrac{XY}{BY}$.
$$\dfrac{h}{BY}=\tan 12^\circ$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{BY}{h}=\cot 12^\circ$$
$$\therefore\ BY=h\cot 12^\circ$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Question text 'The point is due east' is missing a point label (probably $Y$); left as in source.

solutions.latex:
Similarly, in triangle $XYA$, $AY=h\cot 16^\circ$.

Using Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle $BAY$ (right angle at $A$):
$$\begin{aligned}(h\cot 12^\circ)^2&=(h\cot 16^\circ)^2+1600^2\\ h^2\cot^2 12^\circ-h^2\cot^2 16^\circ&=1600^2\\ h^2\left(\cot^2 12^\circ-\cot^2 16^\circ\right)&=1600^2\\ h^2&=\dfrac{1600^2}{\cot^2 12^\circ-\cot^2 16^\circ}\\ h&=\dfrac{1600}{\sqrt{\cot^2 12^\circ-\cot^2 16^\circ}}\\ &\approx 507\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h\approx 507 \text{ m (nearest whole number)}$$
criteria: Forms and rearranges the Pythagoras equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The maximum occurs where $f'(x)=0$ and changes from positive to negative, at $x=2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2 f'(x)\,dx&=4\\ \Big[f(x)\Big]_0^2&=4\\ f(2)-f(0)&=4\end{aligned}$$
Since $f(0)=0$, $f(2)=4$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^4 f'(x)\,dx&=-4\\ f(4)-f(2)&=-4\end{aligned}$$
Since $f(2)=4$ from part (b), $f(4)=0$.

From $x=4$ to $x=6$ the gradient is $-3$, so
$$\begin{aligned}-3&=\dfrac{f(6)-f(4)}{6-4}\\ f(6)-0&=-3\times 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(6)=-6$$

questions.stem:
The length of a whale species is modelled using the equation

$$L=5.2-4.6e^{-kt}$$

where $L$ is in meters and $t$ is the age in years and $k$ is a positive constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the length of the whale at birth?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into exponential model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If a three year old whale has a length of $4.45$ metres, what is the value of $k$, correct to 2 decimal places?

dif.r: Solve exponential equation for k using logarithms

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the limiting length of the whale species.

dif.r: Exponential term vanishes as t grows; read limit

solutions.latex:
At birth $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}L&=5.2-4.6e^0\\ &=0.6 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=3$, $L=4.45$.
$$\begin{aligned}4.45&=5.2-4.6e^{-3k}\\ 4.6e^{-3k}&=0.75\\ e^{-3k}&=\dfrac{0.75}{4.6}\\ -3k&=\ln\left(\dfrac{0.75}{4.6}\right)\\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left(\dfrac{0.75}{4.6}\right)\\ &\approx 0.60\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k\approx 0.60 \text{ (2 decimal places)}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Write
$$L=5.2-\dfrac{4.6}{e^{kt}}$$
As $t\to\infty$ (with $k>0$), $e^{kt}\to\infty$, so $\dfrac{4.6}{e^{kt}}\to 0$ and $L\to 5.2$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the limiting length is } 5.2 \text{ m}$$

parts.latex:
A wire of length $28\,m$ is to be cut into two pieces. One of the piece is to be made into a square and the other into a circle. Let $r$ be the radius of the circle and $x$ meters be the length of each side of the square. The combined perimeter is given as $2\pi r+4x=28$ and the combined area, $A$, is given by:

$$A=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2$$ (\textbf{DO NOT prove this})

What should be the lengths of each piece so that the combined area of the circle and the square is minimum?

dif.r: Given area function; optimise with pi algebra, convert to lengths

solutions.latex:
Simplify the area expression.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\pi\left(\dfrac{14-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2\\ &=\dfrac{4}{\pi}(7-x)^2+x^2\end{aligned}$$
Differentiate.
$$A'=-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x$$
$$A''=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2$$
Stationary points: $A'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{8}{\pi}(7-x)+2x&=0\\ -\dfrac{56}{\pi}+\dfrac{8x}{\pi}+2x&=0\\ -56+8x+2\pi x&=0\\ -28+4x+\pi x&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{28}{\pi+4}\end{aligned}$$
Since $A''=\dfrac{8}{\pi}+2>0$ for all $x$, this is a minimum.

The lengths of the two pieces are
$$4x=\dfrac{112}{\pi+4}\text{ m}$$
$$28-4x=28-\dfrac{112}{\pi+4}=\dfrac{28\pi}{\pi+4}\text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds $x$ and tests that it is a minimum, or equivalent merit
Finds $A'$ and solves $A'=0$, or equivalent merit
Simplifies $A$ or finds $A'$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Initially a car is at rest. The car then starts from a point $P$ at time $t=0$ seconds and comes to a stop at point $Q$. The distance $x$, in metres covered by the car, in $t$ seconds is given by $x=t^2\left(2-\dfrac{t}{3}\right)$. Find
questions.review_note: Part (b) mark not printed; 1 mark inferred from total of 3

parts.label: a
parts.latex: the time taken by it to reach $Q$.

dif.r: Differentiate displacement and solve velocity equals zero

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction
Velocity as a rate of change

parts.label: b
parts.latex: the distance between $P$ and $Q$.

dif.r: Substitute t=4 into displacement

solutions.latex:
Distance is $x=2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}$, so the velocity is
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=4t-t^2$$
The car is at rest at $Q$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}4t-t^2&=0\\ t(4-t)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=0$ (start) or $t=4$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the car takes 4 seconds to reach } Q$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
At $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=2(4)^2-\dfrac{4^3}{3}\\ &=32-\dfrac{64}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: A simple musical instrument has many strings. The difference between the lengths of adjacent strings is constant, so that the lengths of the strings are the terms of an arithmetics series. The shortest string is $30\,cm$ long and the longest string is $48\,cm$. The sum of the lengths of all the strings is $1209\,cm$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the number of strings.

dif.r: Arithmetic sum formula used in reverse to find n

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the difference in length between adjacent strings.

dif.r: Direct nth term formula to find d

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The series has $a=30$, $l=48$, $S_n=1209$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned}1209&=\dfrac{n}{2}(30+48)\\ 2418&=78n\\ n&=\dfrac{2418}{78}\\ &=31\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{there are 31 strings}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $n=31$:
$$\begin{aligned}48&=30+(31-1)d\\ 30d&=18\\ d&=\dfrac{3}{5}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the difference is } \dfrac{3}{5}\text{ cm}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: There is a large sheet of paper which is $0.1\,mm$ thick that is cut in half. Then one piece is placed on top of the other. This pile is again cut in half and one pile is placed on top of the other. This process is repeated 40 times. How high is the pile of the sheets?

dif.r: Model doubling as GP and identify correct term

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
After the first cut the pile is $0.2$ mm thick, and each cut doubles it. The thicknesses form a GP: $0.2,\ 0.4,\ 0.8,\ \dots$ with $a=0.2$ and $r=2$.

After 40 cuts, the thickness is the 40th term.
$$\begin{aligned}T_{40}&=0.2\times 2^{39}\\ &\approx 1.1\times 10^{11}\text{ mm}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the pile is } 1.1\times 10^{11}\text{ mm, or } 110\,000\text{ km, high}$$
criteria: Identifies the GP with $a=0.2$ and $r=2$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If the $z$ scores on an examination are normally distributed and $P(z<N)=0.6$ for some number $N$, what is the value of $P(-N<z<N)$?

dif.r: Use normal symmetry to combine two tail probabilities

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
Since $P(z<N)=0.6$, the upper tail is $P(z>N)=0.4$.

By symmetry, $P(z<-N)=0.4$.
$$\begin{aligned}P(-N<z<N)&=1-0.4-0.4\\&=0.2\end{aligned}$$
So the answer is option B.

parts.latex: Which one of the following equations is NOT correct?

dif.r: Check four integrals; odd/even property and geometric area

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Test the option that looks false. In D, $x^3$ is odd and $\cos x$ is even, so
$$\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{5}\left(4x^4-x^3+\cos x\right)dx=2\int_0^5\left(4x^4+\cos x\right)dx$$
The integrand $4x^4+\cos x$ is not zero over most of $[0,5]$, so the value is not $0$.

The others hold: A by the reverse chain rule, B is the area of a semicircle of radius $3$, and C by $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}$.

So the answer is option D.

parts.latex: Consider the series $\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{45}+\sqrt{125}+\dots+z=225\sqrt{5}$, the value of $z$ is:

dif.r: Simplify surds to AP, solve sum for n, then term

solutions.latex:
The terms are $\sqrt5,\ 3\sqrt5,\ 5\sqrt5,\dots$, an AP with $a=\sqrt5$ and $d=2\sqrt5$.

The $n$th term is $z=\sqrt5(2n-1)$ and the sum is
$$\begin{aligned}S_n&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(\sqrt5+\sqrt5(2n-1)\right)\\&=n^2\sqrt5\end{aligned}$$
Set $n^2\sqrt5=225\sqrt5$, so $n=15$.
$$z=\sqrt5(2\times15-1)=29\sqrt5$$
So the answer is option B.

questions.stem:
In triangle $ABC$, the length of $AB=5$ cm, $AC=13$ cm and $\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac{1}{8}$.

\exfigure{1275_q13_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the exact value of $\sin\angle BAC$

dif.r: Pythagorean identity and surd simplification for exact value

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the area of triangle $ABC$

dif.r: Substitute into half ab sin C using previous result

skills: Area of a triangle (½ab sin C)

figures.cap: triangle ABC with AB=5cm, AC=13cm

solutions.latex:
Use $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$, or a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $8$ and adjacent side $1$.

The opposite side is $\sqrt{8^2-1^2}=\sqrt{63}=3\sqrt7$.
$$\sin\angle BAC=\dfrac{3\sqrt7}{8}$$
criteria: Finds the opposite side $3\sqrt7$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times5\times13\times\sin\angle BAC\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times5\times13\times\dfrac{3\sqrt7}{8}\\&=\dfrac{195\sqrt7}{16}\\&\approx 32.2\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $2\log x=\log(5x+6)$

dif.r: Log law to quadratic, reject invalid root

solutions.latex:
The logarithms need $x>0$. Using the power law:
$$\begin{aligned}\log x^2&=\log(5x+6)\\x^2&=5x+6\\x^2-5x-6&=0\\(x-6)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=6$ or $x=-1$. Since $x>0$, reject $x=-1$.
$$\therefore\ x=6$$
criteria: Solves the quadratic, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $\left|1-2\cos^2 x\right|=1$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$

dif.r: Absolute value cases, then trig solutions including endpoints

solutions.latex:
Case 1: $1-2\cos^2x=1$
$$\begin{aligned}\cos^2x&=0\\x&=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Case 2: $1-2\cos^2x=-1$
$$\begin{aligned}\cos^2x&=1\\\cos x&=\pm1\\x&=0,\pi,2\pi\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=0,\dfrac{\pi}{2},\pi,\dfrac{3\pi}{2},2\pi$$
criteria: Fully solves one case, or equivalent merit
Sets up both cases, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Differentiate the following expressions.

solutions.latex:
Using the change of base rule, $\log_5(\tan x)=\dfrac{\ln(\tan x)}{\ln5}$.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log_5(\tan x)\right)=\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\ln5\,\tan x}$$

questions.stem: Differentiate the following expressions.

parts.latex: $\dfrac{2^x}{e^x}$

dif.r: Quotient rule with exponential base 2, simplify

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=2^x & v&=e^x\\u'&=\ln2\cdot2^x & v'&=e^x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{2^x}{e^x}\right)&=\dfrac{\ln2\cdot2^x\cdot e^x-2^x\cdot e^x}{(e^x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{e^x2^x(\ln2-1)}{e^{2x}}\\&=\dfrac{2^x(\ln2-1)}{e^x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct application of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned}\displaystyle\int_0^{12}f(x)\,dx&=(6\times6)+(4\times2)+\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\times4^2+\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times2\\&=46+4\pi\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Split the integral; the region from $12$ to $18$ lies below the axis, so it is subtracted.
$$\begin{aligned}\displaystyle\int_0^{18}f(x)\,dx&=\int_0^{12}f(x)\,dx+\int_{12}^{18}f(x)\,dx\\&=46+4\pi-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times2+\left(4\times6-\dfrac{1}{4}\times\pi\times4^2\right)\right)\\&=46+4\pi-(26-4\pi)\\&=20+8\pi\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=x^3+6x^2+9x+4$ in the domain $-4\le x\le 1$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of cubic with second derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the coordinates of its point(s) of inflexion.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and check concavity change

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Draw a sketch of the curve $y=f(x)$ in the domain $-4\le x\le 1$ clearly showing all essential features.

dif.r: Sketch cubic using found features and endpoints

parts.label: d
parts.latex: What is the global maximum value of the curve in the domain $-4\le x\le 1$

dif.r: Compare endpoint value with local maximum on domain

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of cubic with labelled points

solutions.latex:
$$f'(x)=3x^2+12x+9,\qquad f''(x)=6x+12$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3(x^2+4x+3)&=0\\(x+3)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=-3$ or $x=-1$.

For $x=-3$: $y=4$ and $f''(-3)=-6<0$, so there is a maximum turning point at $(-3,4)$.

For $x=-1$: $y=0$ and $f''(-1)=6>0$, so there is a minimum turning point at $(-1,0)$.
criteria: Finds both points, or equivalent merit
Finds $f'(x)$ and sets it to zero, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A possible point of inflexion is where $f''(x)=0$:
$$6x+12=0$$
So $x=-2$ and $y=2$.

Test the concavity:
$$\begin{aligned}f''(-3)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\f''(-2)&=0\\f''(-1)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflexion at $(-2,2)$.

The endpoints are $(-4,0)$ and $(1,20)$, the $y$-intercept is $4$, and the turning points and inflexion are from parts (a) and (b).

\exfigure{1275_q20_s1}
criteria: Partially correct sketch, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The maximum over the domain is at the endpoint $x=1$, where $f(1)=20$, which exceeds the local maximum $4$.
$$\therefore\ \text{global maximum}=20$$

questions.stem:
A pet ownership survey resulted in the following results:

$P(C)=\dfrac{3}{7}$, $P(D\mid\overline{C})=\dfrac{2}{5}$, and $P(\overline{D}\mid C)=\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Where $C$ is the event that "a person has a cat" and $D$ is the event that "a person has a dog"

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Complete the probability tree by marking a probability on each branch.

\exfigure{1275_q22_1}

dif.r: Fill tree using complements and conditional notation; two simple steps.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If one person is chosen at random, find the probability that the person has:

parts.label: i
parts.latex: a cat and a dog

dif.r: Multiply along one pair of tree branches.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: at least one pet (cat or dog)

dif.r: Standard complement for 'at least one' using tree branches.

figures.cap: blank probability tree: C, not C, each followed by D, not D
solution sketch: probability tree completed by hand

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1275_q22_s1}

The branch probabilities are:

$P(C)=\dfrac37$ and $P(\overline C)=\dfrac47$.

From $C$: $P(D\mid C)=\dfrac14$ and $P(\overline D\mid C)=\dfrac34$.

From $\overline C$: $P(D\mid\overline C)=\dfrac25$ and $P(\overline D\mid\overline C)=\dfrac35$.
criteria: Marks some branches correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Multiply along the branches $C$ then $D$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(C\cap D)&=\dfrac37\times\dfrac14 \\ &=\dfrac{3}{28} \end{aligned}$$

Use the complement: the only way to have no pet is $\overline C$ and $\overline D$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least 1 pet})&=1-P(\overline C\cap\overline D) \\ &=1-\dfrac47\times\dfrac35 \\ &=\dfrac{23}{35} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the complement, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The square root needs $x-3\ge0$.

Domain: $x\ge3$, that is $[3,\infty)$.

Since $\sqrt{x-3}\ge0$, we have $f(x)\ge2$.

Range: $y\ge2$, that is $[2,\infty)$.

Gives some correct information, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$g(f(x))=\dfrac{12}{2+\sqrt{x-3}}+2$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} g(f(12))&=\dfrac{12}{2+\sqrt{12-3}}+2 \\ &=\dfrac{12}{5}+2 \\ &=\dfrac{22}{5} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The diagram shows the graphs $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$, $0\le x\le 2\pi$. The graphs intersect at $A$ and $B$.

\exfigure{1275_q24_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $A$ has coordinates $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$.

dif.r: Solve tan x = 1 and substitute; exact value recall.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the area enclosed by the two graphs.

dif.r: Find second intersection, set up trig area integral, exact evaluation.

figures.cap: graphs of y=sin x and y=cos x with region between A and B shaded

solutions.latex:
The graphs meet where $\sin x=\cos x$.

Dividing by $\cos x$:
$$\tan x=1$$
So $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ for $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Substitute into $y=\sin x$:
$$y=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$$
$$\therefore\ A\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)$$

For $B$: $\tan x=1$ with $\pi<x<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, so $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

Between $A$ and $B$, $\sin x\ge\cos x$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{5\pi}{4}}(\sin x-\cos x)\,dx \\ &=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{5\pi}{4}} \\ &=-\Big[\cos x+\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{5\pi}{4}} \\ &=-\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\right) \\ &=2\sqrt2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=2\sqrt2\ \text{units}^2$$
criteria: Correct integral and antiderivative, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: points A(-5,3), B(2,2), C(1,-5) on number plane

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} m_{AC}&=\dfrac{-5-3}{1-(-5)} \\ &=-\dfrac{8}{6} \\ &=-\dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} X&=\left(\dfrac{-5+1}{2},\dfrac{3-5}{2}\right) \\ &=(-2,-1) \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. Its velocity for $t\ge 0$ is given by $v=\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t$, where time is in seconds and displacement in metres.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find when the particle changes direction.

dif.r: Set v=0, clear fraction, solve quadratic, reject negative root.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the exact distance travelled in the first 2 seconds.

dif.r: Split integral at direction change, log integration, absolute values, exact form.

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$.
$$\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t=0$$
Multiply by $t+1$:
$$4-2t^2-2t=0$$
$$t^2+t-2=0$$
$$(t+2)(t-1)=0$$
So $t=-2$ or $t=1$. Since $t\ge0$, reject $t=-2$.
$$\therefore\ t=1\text{ second}$$

The particle changes direction at $t=1$, so split the integral there.
$$d=\left|\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t\right)dt\right|+\left|\displaystyle\int_1^2\left(\dfrac{4}{t+1}-2t\right)dt\right|$$
Integrating:
$$d=\left|\Big[4\ln|t+1|-t^2\Big]_0^1\right|+\left|\Big[4\ln|t+1|-t^2\Big]_1^2\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned} d&=|4\ln2-1|+|4\ln3-3-4\ln2| \\ &=4\ln2-1-(4\ln3-3-4\ln2) \\ &=8\ln2+2-4\ln3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ d=8\ln2+2-4\ln3\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Correct integrals split at $t=1$ with antiderivative, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\left(x^2-2x+2\right) & 1\le x\le 4\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Where $k$ is a constant

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{12}$

dif.r: Standard: integrate pdf over domain, set equal to 1.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Fully define the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate pdf from lower limit and state piecewise CDF.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the median of $X$ lies between $x=3.2$ and $x=3.3$

dif.r: Evaluate CDF at two values and justify median by change across 0.5.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1, so
$$\displaystyle k\int_1^4\left(x^2-2x+2\right)dx=1$$
$$k\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2+2x\right]_1^4=1$$
$$k\left(\left(\dfrac{64}{3}-16+8\right)-\left(\dfrac13-1+2\right)\right)=1$$
$$12k=1$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{12}$$
criteria: Correct antiderivative or set-up, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le4$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{12}\displaystyle\int_1^x\left(t^2-2t+2\right)dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12}\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-x^2+2x-\dfrac43\right] \\ &=\dfrac{x^3}{36}-\dfrac{x^2}{12}+\dfrac{x}{6}-\dfrac19 \end{aligned}$$
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<1\\[6pt] \dfrac{x^3}{36}-\dfrac{x^2}{12}+\dfrac{x}{6}-\dfrac19 & 1\le x\le4\\[6pt] 1 & x>4\end{cases}$$
criteria: Correct middle expression, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} F(3.2)&=\dfrac{3.2^3}{36}-\dfrac{3.2^2}{12}+\dfrac{3.2}{6}-\dfrac19 \\ &\approx0.479 \\ &<0.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} F(3.3)&=\dfrac{3.3^3}{36}-\dfrac{3.3^2}{12}+\dfrac{3.3}{6}-\dfrac19 \\ &\approx0.5296 \\ &>0.5 \end{aligned}$$
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=0.5$, and $F$ is increasing.

$\therefore$ the median lies between $x=3.2$ and $x=3.3$.

questions.stem: Consider the geometric series $1+\dfrac{4}{3}\sin^2 x+\dfrac{16}{9}\sin^4 x+\dfrac{64}{27}\sin^6 x+\dots$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: When the limiting sum exists, find an expression for its value.

dif.r: Identify a and r, substitute into limiting sum formula.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: For what values of $x$ in the interval $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ does the limiting sum of this series exist?

dif.r: Combine |r|<1 condition with solving a trig inequality.

solutions.latex:
The first term is $a=1$ and the common ratio is $r=\dfrac43\sin^2x$.
$$S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac43\sin^2x}$$

The limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$\left|\dfrac43\sin^2x\right|<1$$
For $0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin x>0$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 0&<\dfrac43\sin^2x<1 \\ 0&<\sin^2x<\dfrac34 &&(\text{multiply by } \dfrac34) \\ 0&<\sin x<\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} &&(\text{square root}) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0<x<\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Uses the condition $|r|<1$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \sec^2(2x)\tan^4(2x)\,dx$

dif.r: Reverse chain rule with tan power and inner linear factor.

solutions.latex:
The derivative of $\tan(2x)$ is $2\sec^2(2x)$, so insert a factor of $2$ and compensate with $\dfrac12$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\sec^2(2x)\tan^4(2x)\,dx&=\dfrac12\int2\sec^2(2x)\tan^4(2x)\,dx \\ &=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{\tan^5(2x)}{5}+c \\ &=\dfrac{\tan^5(2x)}{10}+c \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{5x^2}{x^3+1}\,dx$

dif.r: Recognise f'(x)/f(x) form and adjust constant.

solutions.latex:
The derivative of $x^3+1$ is $3x^2$, so the integrand has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{5x^2}{x^3+1}\,dx&=\dfrac53\int\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3+1}\,dx \\ &=\dfrac53\ln|x^3+1|+c \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
An open cone, of radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm is made from a sector of a circle. The area of the sector used is $300\ \text{cm}^2$

\exfigure{1275_q32_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show from Figure 1 that the slant height $l$ is given by $l^2=\dfrac{450}{\pi}$

dif.r: Find sector angle from figure, apply sector area formula.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
In Figure 2 it is given that $h=\sqrt{l^2-r^2}$ (do not prove this).

Show that the volume of the cone is given by $V=\dfrac{1}{3}r^2\sqrt{450\pi-\pi^2r^2}$

dif.r: Substitute into cone volume, manipulate pi inside surd to show result.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
It is known that $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=\dfrac{300\pi r-\pi^2r^3}{\sqrt{450\pi-\pi^2r^2}}$ (do not prove this).

Hence or otherwise, find the value of $r$ for the volume of the cone to be a maximum.

dif.r: Derivative given; solve dV/dr=0 and test sign for maximum.

figures.cap: Figure 1: circle sector with angle 2pi/3 removed, radius l; Figure 2: cone with radius r, height h, slant height l

solutions.latex:
The sector angle is
$$\theta=2\pi-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
Using the sector area $A=\dfrac12l^2\theta$:
$$300=\dfrac12l^2\cdot\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}l^2$$
$$l^2=\dfrac{900}{2\pi}=\dfrac{450}{\pi}$$
criteria: Correct angle or area formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source line '300 = 2/3 pi l^2' kept; intermediate step added.

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac13\pi r^2h$. Substitute $h=\sqrt{l^2-r^2}$ and $l^2=\dfrac{450}{\pi}$.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac13\pi r^2\sqrt{l^2-r^2} \\ &=\dfrac13\pi r^2\sqrt{\dfrac{450}{\pi}-r^2} \\ &=\dfrac13r^2\sqrt{\pi^2\left(\dfrac{450-\pi r^2}{\pi}\right)} \\ &=\dfrac13r^2\sqrt{450\pi-\pi^2r^2} \end{aligned}$$

A stationary point occurs when $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=0$.
$$300\pi r-\pi^2r^3=0$$
$$\pi r\left(300-\pi r^2\right)=0$$
Since $r>0$, $r^2=\dfrac{300}{\pi}$.
$$r=\sqrt{\dfrac{300}{\pi}}=\dfrac{10\sqrt3}{\sqrt\pi}$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dV}{dr}$ on either side:
$$\begin{aligned} r=\sqrt{\dfrac{240}{\pi}}&:\ \dfrac{dV}{dr}\approx64.1>0 &&\text{increasing}\\ r=\sqrt{\dfrac{300}{\pi}}&:\ \dfrac{dV}{dr}=0 &&\text{stationary}\\ r=\sqrt{\dfrac{320}{\pi}}&:\ \dfrac{dV}{dr}=-31.38<0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative, so this is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ r=\sqrt{\dfrac{300}{\pi}}\text{ cm}$$

parts.latex: Simplify $\dfrac{x^2+5x+6}{x^2-9}$

dif.r: Routine factorising and cancelling of a rational expression

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator and the denominator (difference of two squares), then cancel the common factor.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{x^2+5x+6}{x^2-9}&=\dfrac{(x+3)(x+2)}{(x+3)(x-3)}\\ &=\dfrac{x+2}{x-3}\end{aligned}$$
Hence option A.

parts.latex: What values of $x$ is the curve $f(x)=2x^3+x^2$ concave down?

dif.r: Second derivative then solve simple linear inequality

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=6x^2+2x\\ f''(x)&=12x+2\end{aligned}$$
The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$.
$$\begin{aligned}12x+2&<0\\ x&<-\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$
Hence option A.

parts.latex: What is the period and amplitude for the curve $y=\sin \pi x$?

dif.r: Direct recall of period and amplitude formula

solutions.latex:
The amplitude is $1$.

For $y=\sin nx$ the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$, and here $n=\pi$.
$$\text{Period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$$
Hence option A.

solutions.latex:
$y=2-(x+1)^2$ is a downward parabola (negative coefficient of $(x+1)^2$).

Its vertex is $(-1,2)$, to the left of the $y$-axis at height $2$.

When $x=0$, $y=2-1=1$, so the $y$-intercept is $1$.

Hence option D.

parts.latex: What is the value of $f'(x)$ if $f(x)=3x^4(4-x)^3$ ?

dif.r: Product rule with chain rule, then factorise to match option

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=3x^4 & v&=(4-x)^3\\ u'&=12x^3 & v'&=-3(4-x)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=12x^3(4-x)^3-9x^4(4-x)^2\\ &=3x^3(4-x)^2\big(4(4-x)-3x\big)\\ &=3x^3(4-x)^2(16-7x)\end{aligned}$$
Hence option D.

options.label: C

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: What are the solutions to the equation $2\sin x+\sqrt{3}=0$, where $\{x: 0\le x\le 2\pi\}$?

Hence option C.

questions.stem: Sonny repays a loan over a period of $n$ months. His monthly repayments form an arithmetic sequence. He repays \$119 in the first month, \$117 in the second month, \$115 in the third month, and so on. Sonny makes his final repayment in the $n$th month.

solutions.latex:
The repayments form an arithmetic sequence with $a=119$ and $d=-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= 119+(n-1)(-2) \\ &= -2n+121 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} T_{25} &= -2(25)+121 \\ &= 71 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A curve with the equation $y=f(x)$, has $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^3+2x-7$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$

dif.r: Single routine differentiation of a polynomial.

parts.label: b

parts.label: d

dif.r: Gradient, perpendicular gradient, point-gradient form into general form.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^3+2x-7$ term by term.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=3x^2+2$$

meta.format_note: The source scan wrote $3x^2+2x$, a slip; corrected to $3x^2+2$, which part (b) uses. Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Since $x^2\ge0$ for all $x$, we have $3x^2\ge0$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=3x^2+2\ge2$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Integrate $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
$$y=\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2-7x+C$$
Substitute $P(2,4)$ to find $C$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= 4+4-14+C \\ C &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$y=\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2-7x+10$$
criteria: Integrates correctly with constant $C$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent at $P$ is
$$m_1=2^3+2(2)-7=5$$
The normal is perpendicular, so its gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-4 &= -\dfrac{1}{5}(x-2) \\ 5y-20 &= -x+2 \\ x+5y-22 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The functions $y=-x^3+4x$ and $y=x$ are sketched below.

\exfigure{1277_q27_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the functions intersect when $x=0$ and $x=\pm\sqrt{3}$.

dif.r: Equate functions and factorise a simple cubic.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the exact area between the two functions in the first quadrant.

dif.r: Standard area between curves with given limits.

figures.cap: graphs of y = -x^3 + 4x and y = x

solutions.latex:
Set the two functions equal.
$$\begin{aligned} -x^3+4x &= x \\ -x^3+3x &= 0 \\ x(x^2-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x^2=3$.
$$\therefore\ x=0,\ \pm\sqrt{3}$$
criteria: Sets the functions equal and simplifies, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us from the mark allocation [2].

solutions.latex:
The curves meet at $x=0$ and $x=\sqrt{3}$, with $y=-x^3+4x$ above $y=x$ in between.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt{3}}(-x^3+4x-x)\,dx \\ &= \left[-\dfrac{x^4}{4}+\dfrac{3x^2}{2}\right]_0^{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= -\dfrac{9}{4}+\dfrac{9}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{9}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{9}{4} \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Sets up the correct integral, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The average life cycle of an insect is one month. A viable nest of this insect has between 100 000 to 500 000 insects. The population $P$ of a nest of this insect grows exponentially so that:

$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=1200e^{0.3t}$

A nest of these insects had a population of 5000 after one month.

Determine how long it will take the nest to reach the viable stage (i.e. when the population has reached 100 000). Answer correct to the nearest month.

dif.r: Integrate exponential rate, find constant, solve logarithmic equation, round in context.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate of growth.
$$P=\dfrac{1200}{0.3}e^{0.3t}+C=4000e^{0.3t}+C$$
When $t=1$, $P=5000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 5000 &= 4000e^{0.3}+C \\ C &\approx -399.435 \end{aligned}$$
For $P=100\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 4000e^{0.3t} &= 100\,000+399.435 \\ e^{0.3t} &\approx 25.0999 \\ 0.3t &= \ln 25.0999 \\ t &\approx 10.7429 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 11 \text{ months}$$
criteria: Finds $C$ and sets up the equation for $P=100\,000$, or equivalent merit
Integrates to find $P$, or equivalent merit

skills: Maxima and minima from the range

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of x=1+3cos2t on [0, pi]

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 1+3\cos 0 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the initial displacement is } 4 \text{ m}$$

The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$, and $-2\le x\le 4$.

\exfigure{1277_q30_s1}
criteria: Correct period or range, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us from the mark allocation [2].

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the velocity.
$$v=-6\sin 2t$$
At rest, $v=0$.
$$\sin 2t=0,\quad t=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi$$
The first rest after $t=0$ is at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 1+3\cos\pi \\ &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{at } t=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \text{ s, } 2 \text{ m to the left of the origin}$$
criteria: Finds $v=-6\sin 2t$ or the time of rest, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us from the mark allocation [2].

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the velocity to find the acceleration.
$$a=-12\cos 2t$$
The speed is greatest when $a=0$.
$$\cos 2t=0,\quad 2t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ \ldots$$
So $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \ldots$

At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &= -6\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= -6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum speed is } 6 \text{ m/s}$$
criteria: Finds $a=0$ time or the acceleration, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find all solutions of $2\sin^2 x+\cos x-2=0$, where $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: Pythagorean identity to quadratic in cos, factorise, four solutions.

solutions.latex:
Use $\sin^2 x=1-\cos^2 x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2(1-\cos^2 x)+\cos x-2 &= 0 \\ -2\cos^2 x+\cos x &= 0 \\ \cos x(1-2\cos x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
If $\cos x=0$, then $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

If $\cos x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, then $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Factorises to $\cos x(1-2\cos x)=0$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: $A$ and $B$ are events from a sample space such that $P(A) = p$, where $p > 0$, $P(B|A) = m$ and $P(B|A') = n$. $A$ and $B$ are independent events when

solutions.latex:
Events $A$ and $B$ are independent when the probability of $B$ does not depend on whether $A$ occurs:
$$P(B|A) = P(B) = P(B|A')$$
$$\therefore m = n$$
Hence the answer is option A.

Write out the terms:
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^n = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{5^2} + \dfrac{1}{5^3} + \cdots\right)$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a = \dfrac{1}{5}$ and $r = \dfrac{1}{5}$, with $|r| < 1$, so it has a limiting sum $S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} &= 2 \times \dfrac{\frac{1}{5}}{1 - \frac{1}{5}} \\ &= 2 \times \dfrac{1}{5} \times \dfrac{5}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the geometric series with $a = \dfrac{1}{5}$, $r = \dfrac{1}{5}$ and the limiting sum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $f(x) = \ln(x - 1) + 2$ at the point $(2, 2)$.

dif.r: Log derivative, perpendicular gradient, point-gradient line.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-1}$$
Gradient of the tangent at $x = 2$:
$$f'(2) = \dfrac{1}{2-1} = 1$$
The normal is perpendicular, so
$$m_\perp = \dfrac{-1}{1} = -1$$
At $x=2$, $f(2)=\ln 1+2=2$, so the point on the curve is $(2,2)$ (the paper printed $(2,0)$).

Equation of the normal through $(2, 2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 2 &= -1(x - 2) \\ y &= -x + 4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit
Finds the gradient of the tangent, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Describe the transformations applied to $y = x^2$ in order to give the transformed function of $y = (4x + 2)^2$.

dif.r: Factor inside bracket to identify dilation and translation order.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the function:
$$\begin{aligned} y = (4x+2)^2 &= \left(\dfrac{x + \frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{4}}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $y = x^2$ is dilated horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{4}$ and translated to the left by $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Alternatively, $y = \left(\dfrac{x}{\frac{1}{4}} + 2\right)^2$: translate to the left by $2$, then dilate horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{4}$.

Alternatively,
$$y = (2(2x+1))^2 = 4(2x+1)^2$$
so
$$\dfrac{y}{4} = \left(\dfrac{x + \frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^2$$
So $y = x^2$ is dilated horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$, translated to the left by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and dilated vertically by a factor of $4$.

This gives the same curve as the first method, since $4(2x+1)^2=(4x+2)^2$.
criteria: One correct transformation or correct rewriting of the function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $e^{x^2 \cos x}$

dif.r: Chain rule with product rule inside exponent.

solutions.latex:
Let $y = e^{f(x)}$ where $f(x) = x^2\cos x$.

By the product rule,
$$f'(x) = 2x\cos x - x^2\sin x$$
By the chain rule,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= f'(x)e^{f(x)} \\ &= (2x\cos x - x^2\sin x)e^{x^2\cos x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates the index $x^2\cos x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If $\cos\alpha = -\dfrac{4}{5}$ and $\sin\alpha < 0$, find the exact value of $\tan\alpha$.

dif.r: Quadrant from signs, Pythagorean triple, exact tan.

solutions.latex:
Since $\cos\alpha < 0$ and $\sin\alpha < 0$, the angle $\alpha$ is in the third quadrant.

With hypotenuse $5$ and adjacent side $-4$, the opposite side is $-3$ (Pythagoras: $\sqrt{25-16} = 3$).
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \dfrac{-3}{-4} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the quadrant or the third side, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a function $f$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x^3 - x + a, & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ which makes $f(x)$ a valid probability density function

dif.r: Set total integral to one and solve.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the expected value and variance of $X$.

dif.r: Two integrals and variance formula with fraction arithmetic.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1 and $f(x) = 0$ elsewhere, so
$$\int_0^1 (2x^3 - x + a)\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{x^4}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 + ax\right]_0^1 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} + a &= 1 \\ a &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets the integral equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Expected value:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) = \mu &= \int_0^1 x(2x^3 - x + 1)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^1 (2x^4 - x^2 + x)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{5}x^5 - \dfrac{1}{3}x^3 + \dfrac{1}{2}x^2\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{17}{30} \end{aligned}$$
Variance:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 &= \int_0^1 x^2 f(x)\,dx - \mu^2 \\ &= \int_0^1 (2x^5 - x^3 + x^2)\,dx - \left(\dfrac{17}{30}\right)^2 \\ &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}x^6 - \dfrac{1}{4}x^4 + \dfrac{1}{3}x^3\right]_0^1 - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{12} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{375}{900} - \dfrac{289}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{86}{900} \\ &= \dfrac{43}{450} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expected value and variance formula, or equivalent merit
Writes the integral for $E(X)$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: In an arithmetic sequence, the fifth term is 25 and the eighteenth term 181. What is the smallest value of $n$ such that the sum of the first $n$ term in the sequence is at least 27365?

dif.r: Simultaneous equations for a,d then quadratic inequality for n.

solutions.latex:
Use the arithmetic sequence $T_n = a + (n-1)d$:
$$\begin{aligned} a + 4d &= 25 &&(1) \\ a + 17d &= 181 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
Subtract (1) from (2):
$$\begin{aligned} 13d &= 156 \\ d &= 12 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a + 48 &= 25 \\ a &= -23 \end{aligned}$$
Sum of the first $n$ terms:
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a + (n-1)d\big) \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}(12n - 58) \\ &= 6n^2 - 29n \end{aligned}$$
We need $6n^2 - 29n \ge 27365$, that is
$$6n^2 - 29n - 27365 \ge 0$$
The positive root is
$$n = \dfrac{29 + \sqrt{29^2 - 4 \times 6 \times (-27365)}}{2 \times 6} \approx 69.99$$
So $n > 69.99$ and $n$ is a whole number.
$$\therefore n = 70$$
criteria: Forms the quadratic inequality, or equivalent merit
Writes both term equations, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}$ for $x \ge 0$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: State the domain of $f(x)$

dif.r: Domain is the stated restriction; direct reading.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Let $g(x) = x^2 + 4x + 3$, where $x \le c$ and $c \le 0$. Find the largest possible value of $c$ such that the range of $g(x)$ is a subset of the domain of $f(x)$.

dif.r: Relate range of g to domain of f with restricted domain.

solutions.latex:
The square root needs $x + 1 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -1$.

The given restriction is $x \ge 0$, which is stricter.
$$\therefore x \ge 0, \text{ that is } x \in [0, \infty)$$

From part (a), the domain of $f$ is $x \ge 0$, so the range of $g$ must lie in $[0, \infty)$.

Factorise:
$$g(x) = x^2 + 4x + 3 = (x+3)(x+1)$$
We need $g(x) \ge 0$, so
$$x \ge -1 \text{ or } x \le -3$$
But $x \le c$ and $c \le 0$, so the domain of $g$ is $x \le c$ with $c \le 0$.

For $g(x) \ge 0$ on all of $x \le c$, we need $x \le -3$.
$$\therefore\ c = -3$$

questions.stem: Consider the curve $y = \sin x + \cos x$ in the domain $-\pi \le x \le \pi$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $x$-intercepts, express your answer in terms of $\pi$.

dif.r: Rearrange to tan x = -1 and find both solutions in domain

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any stationary points, and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points and second-derivative test for trig function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find any points of inflection.

dif.r: Solve y''=0 and check concavity change; standard procedure

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Explain why the points found in (c) are not points of horizontal inflection.

dif.r: Short justification that y' is nonzero at inflection points

parts.label: e
parts.latex: Hence, sketch the graph of $y = \sin x + \cos x$, for $-\pi \le x \le \pi$, showing all critical features of the graph.

dif.r: Sketch using features already found in earlier parts

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of y = sin x + cos x on [-pi, pi]

solutions.latex:
The $x$-intercepts occur where $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \sin x + \cos x &= 0 \\ \sin x &= -\cos x \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
In $-\pi \le x \le \pi$:
$$\therefore\ x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$
criteria: One correct intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \cos x - \sin x = 0 \\ \tan x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative:
$$y'' = -\sin x - \cos x$$
At $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$y'' = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < 0 \quad \text{(maximum)}$$
At $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$:
$$y'' = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} > 0 \quad \text{(minimum)}$$
The $y$-values are:
$$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}, \qquad y\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -\sqrt{2}$$
$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \sqrt{2}\right) \text{ is a local maximum and } \left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, -\sqrt{2}\right) \text{ is a local minimum.}$$
criteria: Finds the nature of both points, or equivalent merit
Finds the maximum or the minimum, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Points of inflection occur where $y''=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} -\sin x - \cos x &= 0 \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Test concavity:

\extable{Ts8070_1}

Since the concavity changes at each value, the points $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}, 0\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, 0\right)$ are points of inflection.
\exfigure{1279_q24_s1}
criteria: Shows key points (maximum and minimum), or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Key points need to be shown (maximum, minimum); end points: all points required.

solutions.latex:
A horizontal point of inflection needs $y'=0$ as well as a change of concavity.
$$\begin{aligned} y'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)-\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2\ne0 \\ y'\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=-\sqrt2\ne0 \end{aligned}$$
The gradient is not zero at either point, so they are not horizontal points of inflection.
criteria: Shows $y'\ne0$ at both points of inflection

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{1}{1 + \sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1 - \sin\theta} = 2\sec^2\theta$.

dif.r: Two-step identity proof: common denominator then Pythagorean identity

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{1 + \sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1 - \sin\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 - \sin\theta) + (1 + \sin\theta)}{1 - \sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= 2\sec^2\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A class is on a hike as part of their sports course. They are given the following directions from starting point $A$: They are to walk on a bearing of $062^\circ$ for 14 kilometres to point $B$. Then, they continue on a bearing of $136^\circ$ for 8.5 kilometres to point $C$, before returning to starting point $A$.

\exfigure{1279_q28_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\angle ABC = 106^\circ$.

dif.r: Bearings angle using alternate and co-interior angles, two steps

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate $AC$, the distance that the class needs to travel on the final leg of their hike. Give your answer correct to the nearest kilometre.

dif.r: Direct cosine rule calculation for third side

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the bearing that the class needs to take from point $C$ to return to starting point $A$, correct to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Sine rule then converting interior angle to a bearing

figures.cap: triangle ABC with bearings, AB = 14 km, BC = 8.5 km, not to scale

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \angle ABD &= 62^\circ && (\text{alternate angles, parallel north lines}) \\ \angle CBD &= 180^\circ - 136^\circ = 44^\circ && (\text{co-interior angles}) \\ \angle ABC &= 62^\circ + 44^\circ = 106^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source reason for $\angle CBD$ was not given; supplied as co-interior angles. Figure is the question's own.

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle ABC$ use the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} AC^2 &= 14^2 + 8.5^2 - 2 \times 14 \times 8.5\cos 106^\circ \\ AC &\approx 18.27 \\ &\approx 18 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

Use the sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle BCA}{14} = \dfrac{\sin 106^\circ}{18.27}$$
So $\angle BCA = 47.437^\circ$ (the obtuse value $132^\circ$ is not possible, since the angles would exceed $180^\circ$).

The bearing of $B$ from $C$ is $136^\circ+180^\circ=316^\circ$, which is $46^\circ$ north of west.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 270 - (47.437 - 46)^\circ \\ &= 268^\circ 33' \\ &\approx 269^\circ \text{T} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle BCA$ and the $46^\circ$ angle, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Let $f(x) = 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$ for $x \ge 0$. A right-angled triangle $OQP$ has vertex $O$ at the origin, vertex $Q$ on the $x$-axis and vertex $P$ on the graph of $f(x)$, as shown. The coordinates of $P$ are $(x, f(x))$.

\exfigure{1279_q31_1}
questions.review_note: Paper states 8 marks but parts are 1+3+5=9 (guideline also totals 9); Section II then sums to 90; MARKS_MISMATCH

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the area, $A$, of the triangle $OPQ$ in terms of $x$.

dif.r: Simple area expression from diagram coordinates

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the maximum area of triangle $OQP$ and the value of $x$ for which the maximum occurs.

dif.r: Product rule on xe^(-x/5), solve, second-derivative test

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Let $S$ be the point on the graph of $f(x)$ on the $y$-axis and let $T$ be the point on the graph of $f(x)$ with the $y$-coordinate $\dfrac{1}{2}$. Find the area of the region bounded by the graph of $f(x)$ and the line segment $ST$.

\exfigure{1279_q31_2}

dif.r: Find T via logs, trapezium minus exponential integral; several steps

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x) with triangle OQP shaded
graph of y=f(x) with region between curve and chord ST shaded

solutions.latex:
The triangle has base $x$ and height $f(x) = 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times x \times 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ &= xe^{-\frac{x}{5}} \end{aligned}$$

meta.edited_from_original: The question total was recorded as 8 marks while its parts carry 1 + 3 + 5 = 9; the total is now 9 marks (checker flag 24 Nov).

solutions.latex:
A maximum occurs where $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 0$ and $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} < 0$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u &= x & v &= e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= -\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= x\left(-\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\right) + e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \\ &= e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{5}\right) = 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-\frac{x}{5}} > 0$ for all $x$, $x = 5$.

Second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} - \dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} + \dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}} = e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\left(\dfrac{x}{25}-\dfrac{2}{5}\right)$$
At $x = 5$, $\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = e^{-1}\left(\dfrac15-\dfrac25\right) = -\dfrac{1}{5e} < 0$, so this is a maximum.

At $x = 5$:
$$A = 5e^{-1}$$
$$\therefore\ A_{\max} = \dfrac{5}{e} \text{ units}^2 \text{ at } x = 5$$
criteria: Finds $x=5$ and the maximum area, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the second derivative had $-\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$ instead of $+\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$, so "every term is negative" was false; $A^{\prime\prime}(5)=-\dfrac{1}{5e}<0$ still gives a maximum.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the second derivative had $-\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$ instead of $+\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$, so "every term is negative" was false; $A^{\prime\prime}(5)=-\dfrac{1}{5e}<0$ still gives a maximum.

solutions.latex:
Find $S$: $f(0) = 2$, so $S(0, 2)$.

Find $T$: solve $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ e^{-\frac{x}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ x &= -5\ln\dfrac{1}{4} = 5\ln 4 \end{aligned}$$
So $T\left(5\ln 4, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

The region lies between the chord $ST$ (above) and the curve (below) for $0 \le x \le 5\ln 4$. Its area is the trapezium under $ST$ (parallel sides $2$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}$, width $5\ln 4$) minus the area under the curve.

Trapezium:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 5\ln 4\left(2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 \end{aligned}$$
Area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= \displaystyle\int_0^{5\ln 4} 2e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\,dx \\ &= \Big[-10e^{-\frac{x}{5}}\Big]_0^{5\ln 4} \\ &= -10e^{-\ln 4} + 10 \\ &= -10\times\dfrac{1}{4} + 10 \\ &= \dfrac{15}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Required area:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= A_1 - A_2 \\ &= \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 - \dfrac{15}{2} \\ &\approx 1.16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A = \dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4 - \dfrac{15}{2} \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Correct integral and trapezium area, or equivalent merit
Correct area expression, or equivalent merit

meta.overwritten_from_source: The area working ran the trapezium and the integral together in one chain, using undefined $h$, $a$, $b$ and skipping the antiderivative ($-\int = +10[e^{-x/5}]$); it now finds the trapezium area $\dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4$ and the area under the curve $\dfrac{15}{2}$ separately, then subtracts. Answer $\dfrac{25}{4}\ln 4-\dfrac{15}{2}\approx1.16$ units$^2$ unchanged (checker flag 24 Nov).

why: Corrected from source: the second derivative had $-\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$ instead of $+\dfrac{x}{25}e^{-\frac{x}{5}}$, so "every term is negative" was false; $A^{\prime\prime}(5)=-\dfrac{1}{5e}<0$ still gives a maximum.
Part marks add to 9 but the question is worth 8

questions.stem: The population of a white-ant colony can be modelled using the equation $P = Ae^{kt}$, where $A$ and $k$ are positive constants and $t$ is time in weeks. Initially, the population is 1000. Two weeks later, the population has increased to become 1500.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $A$ and $k$. Express your answer in exact form.

dif.r: Initial value then solve exponential with logs for k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the population after four week, correct to the nearest possible number of white-ants.

dif.r: Substitute t=4 into model

parts.label: c
parts.latex: White-ants can cause significant structural timber damages. Assume this particular ant colony was found near a timbre structured home, using the model above to explain why the situation is getting worse. Show all mathematical calculations.

dif.r: Interpret positive, increasing derivative in context

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1000e^{4 \times \frac{\ln 1.5}{2}} \\ &= 1000e^{2\ln 1.5} \\ &= 1000\times1.5^2 \\ &= 2250 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 2250 \text{ white-ants}$$

meta.marker_note: No mark for incorrect rounding.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $1000e^{2\ln1.5}=1000\times1.5^2=2250$; the guideline gave $2449.49$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: $1000e^{2\ln1.5}=1000\times1.5^2=2250$; the guideline gave $2449.49$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the model to find the rate of growth.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= kAe^{kt} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln 1.5}{2} \times 1000 \times e^{\frac{\ln 1.5}{2}t} \end{aligned}$$
Since $\dfrac{dP}{dt} > 0$ for $t > 0$, the population is increasing, and $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ itself increases with $t$, so the population grows faster over time.

$\therefore$ the situation is getting worse.

why: Corrected from source: $1000e^{2\ln1.5}=1000\times1.5^2=2250$; the guideline gave $2449.49$.

parts.latex: What is the value of $f'(x)$ if $f(x)=3x^4(4-x)^3$ ?

dif.r: Product rule with chain rule, then factorising to match option

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3x^4 & v&=(4-x)^3\\ u'&=12x^3 & v'&=-3(4-x)^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=3x^4\times\left(-3(4-x)^2\right)+(4-x)^3\times 12x^3\\ &=3x^3(4-x)^2\left[-3x+4(4-x)\right]\\ &=3x^3(4-x)^2(16-7x)\end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: For what values of $x$ is the curve $f(x)=2x^3+x^2$ concave down?

dif.r: Second derivative then solve simple linear inequality

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=2x^3+x^2\\ f'(x)&=6x^2+2x\\ f''(x)&=12x+2\end{aligned}$$
The curve is concave down when $f''(x)<0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12x+2&<0\\ x&<-\dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}$$
This matches option A.

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=2-(x+1)^2$ is the graph of $y=(x+1)^2$ reflected in the $x$ axis, so it is concave down, and then shifted up 2 units.

The graph of $y=(x+1)^2$ touches the $x$ axis at $x=-1$, so the vertex of $y=2-(x+1)^2$ is at $(-1,2)$.

parts.latex: For what the value of $x$ is $\log x-\log 3=\log\left(\dfrac{x-3}{2}\right)$?

dif.r: Apply log quotient law, equate arguments, solve linear equation

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $\log a-\log b=\log\dfrac{a}{b}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log x-\log 3&=\log\left(\dfrac{x-3}{2}\right)\\ \log\dfrac{x}{3}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x-3}{2}\right)\\ \dfrac{x}{3}&=\dfrac{x-3}{2}\\ 2x&=3x-9\\ x&=9\end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: The continuous random variable $X$ has a normal distribution with a mean of 11 and standard deviation of 2. If the random variable $Z$ has the standard normal distribution, then the probability that $X$ is greater than 16 is equal in value to which expression below?

solutions.latex:

So $P(X>16)=P(Z>2.5)$.

By symmetry of the normal curve, $P(Z>2.5)=P(Z<-2.5)$.

parts.latex: What is the period and amplitude for the curve $y=\sin\pi x$ ?

dif.r: Direct recall of amplitude and period formula

solutions.latex:
For $y=a\sin bx$, the amplitude is $a$ and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$.

Hence $y=\sin\pi x$ has amplitude $1$ and period $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$.

$$\begin{aligned} x&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex: Find the number of terms in the geometric sequence $128, 192, \ldots, 972$.

dif.r: Geometric term formula used in reverse, recognise power of 3/2

solutions.latex:
The first term is $a=128$ and the common ratio is $r=\dfrac{192}{128}=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Suppose there are $k$ terms, so $T_k=972$. Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 972&=128\times\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{k-1}\\ \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{k-1}&=\dfrac{243}{32}=\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^5\\ k-1&=5\\ k&=6\end{aligned}$$
There are 6 terms in the geometric sequence.

solutions.latex:
For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=(x-2)(x^2+1)\\ x&=2\end{aligned}$$
For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(0-2)(0^2+1)\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
The intercepts are $(2,0)$ and $(0,-2)$.
criteria: Finds either the $x$ or $y$ intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x-2 & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=(x-2)\cdot 2x+(x^2+1)\times1\\ &=3x^2-4x+1\\ f''(x)&=6x-4\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-4x+1&=0\\ (3x-1)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
so $x=\dfrac13$ or $x=1$.

When $x=\dfrac13$, $y=-\dfrac{50}{27}$. When $x=1$, $y=-2$.

The stationary points are $\left(\dfrac13,-\dfrac{50}{27}\right)$ and $(1,-2)$.

Nature, using the sign of $f''(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{At } x=\dfrac13:\ f''&=6\times\dfrac13-4=-2<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ \text{At } x=1:\ f''&=6\times1-4=2>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
So $\left(\dfrac13,-\dfrac{50}{27}\right)$ is a maximum and $(1,-2)$ is a minimum.
criteria: Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}\right)&=\dfrac{x^2\cos x-2x\sin x}{(x^2)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{x\cos x-2\sin x}{x^3}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the quotient rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x=2$ and $x=4$, so the area is split at $x=2$. The region from $2$ to $4$ lies below the axis, so its integral is made positive.
$$\text{Area}=\int_0^2(x^3-5x^2+2x+8)\,dx+\left|\int_2^4(x^3-5x^2+2x+8)\,dx\right|$$
An antiderivative is $\dfrac14x^4-\dfrac53x^3+x^2+8x$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\left[\dfrac14x^4-\dfrac53x^3+x^2+8x\right]_0^2+\left|\left[\dfrac14x^4-\dfrac53x^3+x^2+8x\right]_2^4\right|\\ &=\dfrac{32}{3}+\dfrac{16}{3}\\ &=16\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

dif.r: Differentiate a polynomial once

parts.label: b

dif.r: Brief justification using x squared is non-negative

skills: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: c
parts.latex: The point $P(2, 4)$ lies on the curve. Find $y$ in terms of $x$.

dif.r: Integrate gradient function and find constant from a point

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find an equation for the normal to the curve at $P$, in the form $ax+by+c=0$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.

dif.r: Gradient at point, perpendicular gradient, rearrange to general form

solutions.latex:
Since $x^2\ge0$ for all values of $x$, $3x^2\ge0$.

Hence $3x^2+2\ge2$, so $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\ge2$.

meta.marker_note: As a 'show that' question, you cannot start by assuming the result is true.

solutions.latex:
Integrating,
$$y=\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2-7x+C$$
$P(2,4)$ is on the curve, so
$$4=\dfrac{2^4}{4}+2^2-14+C$$
hence $C=10$.
$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2-7x+10$$
criteria: Finds the anti-derivative or correctly finds $C$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent at $P(2,4)$ is
$$m=\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2^3+2\times2-7=5$$
The normal is perpendicular, so $m_1m_2=-1$ and its gradient is $-\dfrac15$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-4&=-\dfrac15(x-2) \\ 5y-20&=-x+2 \\ x+5y-22&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x+5y-22=0$$

meta.marker_note: The question stated the answer was to be in the form $ax+by+c=0$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.

questions.stem: The students in a school were surveyed on the number of hours of sleep per week. The results were normally distributed with a mean of 48 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: The survey indicated that 95% of students had between 42 and $x$ hours of sleep per week. Determine the value of $x$.

dif.r: Recall 95% rule and use symmetry about the mean

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What was the standard deviation?

dif.r: Four standard deviations span known interval; divide

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What percentage of students would have indicated they had between 51 and 57 hours of sleep per week?

dif.r: Two z-scores then combine empirical rule percentages

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
95% of the data lie within two standard deviations of the mean.

So 42 hours has $z$-score $-2$, and $x$ has $z$-score $2$.

The mean 48 is midway between 42 and $x$, so
$$\therefore\ x=54 \text{ hours}$$

There are 4 standard deviations between 42 and 54 hours.
$$\text{Standard deviation}=\dfrac{54-42}{4}=3 \text{ hours}$$

Using $z=\dfrac{x-\bar x}{s}$:
$$z=\dfrac{51-48}{3}=1 \quad\text{and}\quad z=\dfrac{57-48}{3}=3$$
Between $z=1$ and $z=3$, using the 68% and 99.7% rules,
$$\text{Percentage}=\dfrac{99.7\%}{2}-\dfrac{68\%}{2}=15.85\%$$
$$\therefore\ 15.85\% \text{ have between 51 and 57 hours of sleep per week.}$$

parts.latex:
The probability density function for the continuous random variable $X$ is:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}x^3-x+\dfrac{5}{4} & 0\le x\le 1\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Find $E(X)$.

dif.r: Standard integral of x f(x) for expected value

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}xf(x)\,dx \\ &=\displaystyle\int_0^1 x\left(x^3-x+\dfrac{5}{4}\right)dx \\ &=\displaystyle\int_0^1 \left(x^4-x^2+\dfrac{5}{4}x\right)dx \\ &=\left[\dfrac{x^5}{5}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{5x^2}{8}\right]_0^1 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}-\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{5}{8} \\ &=\dfrac{59}{120} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows significant understanding, or equivalent merit

meta.edited_from_original: The paper printed $f(x)=x^3-x+4$ for $0\le x\le 1$, which is not a probability density function ($\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{15}{4}\ne1$; the guideline's $E(X)=\dfrac{28}{15}$ lies outside $[0,1]$). The constant is now $\dfrac{5}{4}$, the value that makes the total probability 1 ($f\ge0$ on $[0,1]$) (checker flag 24 Nov).
meta.overwritten_from_source: Was $E(X)=\int_0^1(x^4-x^2+4x)\,dx=\dfrac{28}{15}$; now $\int_0^1\left(x^4-x^2+\dfrac{5}{4}x\right)dx=\dfrac{59}{120}$ for the corrected $f$ (checker flag 24 Nov).

why: Checker got a different answer — The stored E(X) = 28/15 ≈ 1.87 is the integral of x f(x), but it lies outside the support [0,1], so it cannot be an expected value. The question is defective (it probably meant a different f) and needs the owner's review before it goes to students.

questions.decide: 2020 Hurlstone AT4 Q27: $f(x)=x^3-x+4$ on $[0,1]$ is not a probability density function (its integral is $3.75$, not 1), and the school's $E(X)=\dfrac{28}{15}$ lies outside $[0,1]$. Probably a misprint in $f$. Tell me the intended $f$, or drop the question?

An alarm system is made up of a number of identical components.

The probability that component $X$ fails is 0.05.

parts.label: i
parts.latex:
The alarm system below is wired in series, i.e. the system works only when both components operate properly. Find the probability that the system does not fail. (Give your answer correct to three decimal places.)

\exfigure{1280_q28_1}

dif.r: Multiply two independent complement probabilities

parts.label: ii
parts.latex:
Another alarm system below is wired in parallel i.e. only one component needs to work for the circuit to work. What is the minimum number of components needed so that the probability of the system working is greater than 99.999%? Clearly justify your working.

\exfigure{1280_q28_2}

dif.r: Model at-least-one, solve exponential inequality with logs, reverse sign

figures.cap: two components X wired in series
n components X wired in parallel

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(\text{system does not fail})&=(1-0.05)(1-0.05) \\ &=0.9025 \\ &\approx0.903 \end{aligned}$$

Let the number of components be $n$. The system works if at least one component works, so
$$P(\text{system works})=1-(0.05)^n$$
Require
$$\begin{aligned} 1-(0.05)^n&>0.99999 \\ 0.00001&>(0.05)^n \\ \log 0.00001&>n\log 0.05 \\ 3.843\ldots&<n \end{aligned}$$
The inequality sign reverses because $\log 0.05$ is negative.

Since $n$ is a whole number,
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum number of components is } 4$$
criteria: Correct finding of $n$ with incorrect sign, or equivalent merit
Shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If a coin is tossed $n$ times, where $n>1$, find the probability of obtaining at least one head and at least one tail.

dif.r: General n; complement excluding two disjoint cases

solutions.latex:
Subtract the cases of no heads and no tails (which cannot overlap since $n>1$).
$$\begin{aligned} P&=1-P(\text{no heads})-P(\text{no tails}) \\ &=1-\dfrac{1}{2^n}-\dfrac{1}{2^n} \\ &=1-\dfrac{2}{2^n} \\ &=1-2^{1-n} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The 7th rung is the last, so $T_7=33$.
$$\begin{aligned} 48+(7-1)d&=33 \\ 6d&=-15 \\ d&=-2.5 \end{aligned}$$

meta.source_flag: Source line $T_5=40.5-2.5=38$ is unexplained and looks wrong: $T_5=48+4(-2.5)=38$ is the correct value, but the stated 40.5 is $T_2$ not $T_6$ ($T_6=35.5$); the working as written is inconsistent although the answer 38 is correct.

So the maximum is $n=20$ rungs.

The ladder has 7 rungs, so
$$\therefore\ 20-7=13 \text{ more rungs}$$

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.

From the graph, the turning points occur at
$$t=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi$$
and the positions at these times are
$$x=0,\ 2,\ 0$$
criteria: Finds at least two of the required times or positions, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$x=1-\cos2t,\quad v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2\sin2t$$
At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$v=2\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=2 \text{ m/s}$$

Solve $v=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin2t&=1 \\ \sin2t&=\dfrac12 \\ 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12} \end{aligned}$$
From the graph of $v$, it exceeds 1 between these times.
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{\pi}{12}<t<\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$$

parts.latex: For the curve $y=2x^2-\ln\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)-4$, find the coordinates of the minimum stationary point. Give your answer in exact form.

dif.r: Differentiate log, reject negative root by domain, exact coordinates

solutions.latex:
A minimum occurs where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4x-\dfrac{0.5}{\frac{x}{2}}=4x-\dfrac1x$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4x-\dfrac1x \\ 4x^2&=1 \\ x^2&=\dfrac14 \\ x&=\pm\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
The logarithm needs $x>0$, so $x=\dfrac12$.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2\left(\dfrac12\right)^2-\ln\left(\dfrac{0.5}{2}\right)-4 \\ &=\ln4-3\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4+\dfrac{1}{x^2}$$
At $x=\dfrac12$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4+4=8>0$, so it is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum point is } \left(\dfrac12,\ \ln4-\dfrac72\right)$$
criteria: Finds the minimum value without testing for a minimum, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The least-squares line has the form $y=mx+c$, here:
$$H=1.19t-0.85$$

When $t=5$:
$$H=1.19\times5-0.85\approx5.1 \text{ m}$$

parts.latex: An integer $n$ is chosen at random from the set $\{5,7,9,11\}$. An integer $p$ is also chosen at random from the set $\{2,6,10,14,18\}$. What is the probability that $n+p=23$?
