solutions.latex:
There are $4\times 5=20$ equally likely pairs $(n,p)$.

For $n+p=23$ we need $p=23-n$:
$$\begin{aligned} n=5 &: p=18 &&\text{in the set} \\ n=7 &: p=16 &&\text{not in the set} \\ n=9 &: p=14 &&\text{in the set} \\ n=11 &: p=12 &&\text{not in the set} \end{aligned}$$
So there are $2$ successful pairs.
$$P(n+p=23)=\dfrac{2}{20}=0.1$$
Therefore the answer is option A.

parts.latex: If $\ln 3a=\ln b-2\ln c$ where $a,b,c>0$, which of the following is true?

Using the power law, $2\ln c=\ln c^2$, and the difference law, $\ln b-\ln c^2=\ln\dfrac{b}{c^2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln 3a &= \ln b-\ln c^2 \\ &= \ln\dfrac{b}{c^2} \end{aligned}$$
Since $\ln$ is one-to-one, $3a=\dfrac{b}{c^2}$, so
$$a=\dfrac{b}{3c^2}$$
Therefore the answer is option B.

The integral

evaluates to which of the following?

dif.r: Split absolute value integral into triangle areas

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=|x-2|$ has a corner at $x=2$:
$$|x-2|=\begin{cases} 2-x & x<2 \\ x-2 & x\ge 2 \end{cases}$$
Split the integral at $x=2$:
$$\int_0^6|x-2|\,dx=\int_0^2(2-x)\,dx+\int_2^6(x-2)\,dx$$
The first part is the area of a triangle with base $2$ and height $2$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 2=2$$
The second part is the area of a triangle with base $4$ and height $4$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 4=8$$
So the integral is $2+8=10$.

Therefore the answer is option A.

parts.latex: Find the values of $x$ and $y$ if the first four terms of a geometric sequence are $3,x,y,192$.

dif.r: Find ratio from first and fourth terms, standard GP

solutions.latex:
In a geometric sequence the ratio of consecutive terms is constant:

$$\dfrac{x}{3}=\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{192}{y}$$

So $x^2=3y$ (1) and $y^2=192x$ (2).

Substituting (2) into (1) gives

$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{y^2}{192}\right)^2&=3y \\ \dfrac{y^4}{36864}&=3y \end{aligned}$$

so $y=48$.

Therefore $x=12$ and $y=48$.

Alternatively, using $T_4=ar^{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned} 192&=3r^3 \\ r^3&=64 \\ r&=4 \end{aligned}$$

Then $x=3\times 4=12$ and $y=12\times 4=48$.

$$\therefore\ x=12,\ y=48$$

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $y=3x^4-16x^3+24x^2-9$:

$$\begin{aligned} y'&=12x^3-48x^2+48x \\ &=12x(x^2-4x+4) \\ &=12x(x-2)^2 \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate again:

$$\begin{aligned} y''&=36x^2-96x+48 \\ &=12(3x^2-8x+4) \\ &=12(3x-2)(x-2) \\ &=12(x-2)(3x-2) \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:

$$12x(x-2)^2=0$$

so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$, $y=-9$; when $x=2$, $y=7$. The stationary points are $(0,-9)$ and $(2,7)$.

At $(0,-9)$:

$$y''=12(-2)(-2)=48>0$$

The curve is concave up, so $(0,-9)$ is a minimum.

At $(2,7)$:

$$y''=12(0)(4)=0$$

This is a possible point of inflexion, so test the concavity either side:

\extable{Ts8162_1}

The concavity changes from down to up, so $(2,7)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

Other possible points of inflexion occur when $y''=0$:

$$12(x-2)(3x-2)=0$$

so $x=2$ or $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

\extable{Ts8162_2}

The concavity changes, so $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},-\dfrac{67}{27}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.

$$0.2+0.6p^2+0.1+1-p+0.1=1$$

Simplify:

$$\begin{aligned} 0.6p^2-p+0.4&=0 \\ 3p^2-5p+2&=0 \\ (3p-2)(p-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ p=\dfrac{2}{3}\ \text{ or }\ p=1$$
criteria: Sets the sum of probabilities to 1 and forms the quadratic, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean 4.5. It is given that $P(X>5.5)=0.0465$.

\exfigure{1281_q24_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the standard deviation is 0.595.

dif.r: Reverse z-table lookup then solve for standard deviation.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the probability that a random observation of $X$ lies between 3.8 and 4.8.

dif.r: Standardise two values and combine table probabilities.

figures.cap: normal curve with mean 4.5 and upper tail beyond 5.5 shaded (0.0465)

solutions.latex:
The mean is $\mu=4.5$.

Since $P(X>5.5)=0.0465$, we have $P(Z<z)=1-0.0465=0.9535$.

From the table, $z=1.68$.

Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5.5-4.5}{\sigma}&=1.68 \\ \sigma&=\dfrac{1}{1.68} \\ &=0.5952 \\ &\approx 0.595 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $z=1.68$ from the table, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Differentiate $e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)$.

dif.r: Product rule with exponential and trig, then simplify.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence or otherwise, find

$$\int e^{3x}\sin x\,dx$$

dif.r: Reverse previous derivative to integrate; hence step like anchor.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{3x} & v&=\cos x-3\sin x \\ u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=-\sin x-3\cos x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)\right]&=3e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)+e^{3x}(-\sin x-3\cos x) \\ &=e^{3x}(3\cos x-9\sin x-\sin x-3\cos x) \\ &=-10e^{3x}\sin x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrating the result of part (a):
$$\int \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)\right]dx=-10\int e^{3x}\sin x\,dx$$
The left side is $e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)$, so
$$\int e^{3x}\sin x\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{10}e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)+C$$
criteria: Uses the result of part (a), or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A telecommunications box is to be placed at some point $Q$ along a road $PQR$, as shown in the diagram below. Two cables will connect the box to relay stations at $A$ and $B$. Let $AP=2$ km be the perpendicular distance from $A$ to the road, and similarly, let $BR=1$ km be the perpendicular distance from $B$ to the road. The distance $PR$ is 5 km.

\exfigure{1281_q26_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
By letting $PQ=x$ kilometres, show that the total length $L$ of the cable is given by

$$L=\sqrt{x^2+4}+\sqrt{x^2-10x+26}$$

dif.r: Two Pythagoras applications to set up given expression.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the location of $Q$ such that the total length of the cable is minimised.

dif.r: Surd derivatives, squaring, rejecting extraneous root, nature test.

figures.cap: road PQR with relay stations A and B

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $APQ$, $AP=2$ and $PQ=x$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$AQ=\sqrt{x^2+2^2}$$
In right-angled triangle $BRQ$, $BR=1$ and $QR=5-x$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$QB=\sqrt{(5-x)^2+1^2}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} L&=AQ+QB \\ &=\sqrt{x^2+4}+\sqrt{x^2-10x+26} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dL}{dx}=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}+\dfrac{x-5}{\sqrt{x^2-10x+26}}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=0$:
$$\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}=\dfrac{5-x}{\sqrt{x^2-10x+26}}\qquad(*)$$
Squaring both sides (this can introduce an extra solution):
$$\dfrac{x^2}{x^2+4}=\dfrac{(5-x)^2}{x^2-10x+26}$$
$$x^4-10x^3+26x^2=25x^2-10x^3+x^4+100-40x+4x^2$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=3x^2-40x+100 \\ &=(3x-10)(x-10) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ or $x=10$.

But $x=10$ exceeds $PR=5$ and does not satisfy $(*)$, since the left side is positive and the right side is negative. It is the extra solution introduced by squaring.

Hence $x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ only.

\extable{Ts8183_1}

The table shows $x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ is a local minimum.

$$\therefore\ Q \text{ should be located } \dfrac{10}{3} \text{ km from } P.$$
criteria: Solves to $x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ and rejects $x=10$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The equation of a circle is given by

$$x^2+y^2+4x-2y-20=0$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the centre and radius of the circle.

dif.r: Routine completing the square for circle centre and radius.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence evaluate

$$\int_{-7}^{3} 1+\sqrt{21-4x-x^2}\,dx$$

dif.r: Recognise shifted semicircle; integral as rectangle plus semicircle area.

figures.cap: solution sketch: shaded rectangle plus upper semicircle between x=-7 and x=3

solutions.latex:
Complete the square in $x$ and in $y$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+4x+4+y^2-2y+1&=20+4+1 \\ (x+2)^2+(y-1)^2&=25 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{centre } (-2,1),\ \text{radius } 5 \text{ units}$$
criteria: Completes the square, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the expression under the root:
$$\begin{aligned} 21-4x-x^2&=21-\left((x+2)^2-4\right) \\ &=25-(x+2)^2 \end{aligned}$$
From $(x+2)^2+(y-1)^2=25$, the upper half gives $y-1=\sqrt{25-(x+2)^2}$, so
$$y=1+\sqrt{21-4x-x^2}$$
This is the upper semicircle raised by 1.

\exfigure{1281_q27_s1}

Hence the integral is the area of a rectangle plus the area of a semicircle:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-7}^{3}\left(1+\sqrt{21-4x-x^2}\right)dx&=(3-(-7))\times 1+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(5)^2 \\ &=10+\dfrac{25\pi}{2} \\ &\approx 49.27 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the area as a rectangle plus a semicircle, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A boat travelling in a straight line in a still lake has its engine turned off at time $t=0$ seconds. Its velocity $v$ metres per second at time $t$ seconds thereafter is given by

$$v(t)=\dfrac{100}{(t+2)^2}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Discuss $v(t)$ as $t\to\infty$ and hence the motion of the boat.

dif.r: Limit of velocity and interpretation of motion in context.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the acceleration on the boat is always oppositely directed to its motion.

dif.r: Differentiate velocity, argue signs of velocity and acceleration differ.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: To the nearest metre, how far does the boat travel from $t=5$ to $t=10$ seconds?

dif.r: Integrate velocity over interval using reverse chain rule.

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $(t+2)^2\to\infty$, so
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}v(t)=0^+$$
Also $v(t)>0$ for $t\ge 0$, since $(t+2)^2>0$.

So the boat forever slows, approaching zero velocity but never reaching a complete stop.
criteria: Finds the limit is 0 from above, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $v(t)>0$ for $t\ge 0$, the boat moves in the positive direction.

Differentiating $v(t)=100(t+2)^{-2}$:
$$a(t)=v'(t)=-\dfrac{200}{(t+2)^3}$$
For $t\ge 0$, $(t+2)^3>0$, so $a(t)<0$.

Velocity is always positive and acceleration always negative, so acceleration opposes motion.

The distance is the integral of the (positive) velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int_5^{10}100(t+2)^{-2}\,dt \\ &=-100\Big[(t+2)^{-1}\Big]_5^{10} \\ &=-100\left(\dfrac{1}{12}-\dfrac{1}{7}\right) \\ &=5.95 \\ &\approx 6 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The diagram below shows the area bounded between two curves, $y=\sqrt{x}$ and $y=x$.

\exfigure{1281_q29_1}

Consider the region bounded by the curves, the line $x=0$ and $x=k$, where $k>1$.

For what value of $k$ will the area to the left of point $P$ be equal to the area to the right of $P$?

dif.r: Set up equal-area integral equation, solve with fractional powers.

figures.cap: region between y=sqrt(x) and y=x with line x=k and point P(1,1)

solutions.latex:
The areas left and right of $P$ are equal when
$$\int_0^1\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}-x\right)dx=\int_1^k\left(x-x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)dx$$
$$\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_1^k$$
$$\dfrac{2}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{k^2}{2}-\dfrac{2k^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{2}{3}$$
$$\dfrac{k^2}{2}-\dfrac{2k^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}=0$$
$$k^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\dfrac{k^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2}-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)=0$$
Since $k>1$, $k^{\frac{3}{2}}\ne 0$, so $\sqrt{k}=\dfrac{4}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
criteria: Equates the two areas as integrals, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Consider the probability density function $f$ for a random variable $X$ given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{9+2x}}; & 0\le x\le 8\\[1ex] 0; & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $a$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the value of $a$.

dif.r: Total probability one; reverse chain rule integral.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function, $F(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate pdf to piecewise CDF, standard method.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence find the interquartile range, $Q_3-Q_1$.

dif.r: Invert CDF for two quartiles, careful algebra.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1:
$$1=\int_0^8\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{9+2x}}\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=a\int_0^8(9+2x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx \\ &=a\Big[(9+2x)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big]_0^8 \\ &=a(5-3) \\ &=2a \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le 8$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^x(9+2t)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\Big[\sqrt{9+2t}\Big]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{9+2x}-3\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<0\\[1ex] \dfrac{\sqrt{9+2x}-3}{2} & 0\le x\le 8\\[1ex] 1 & x>8\end{cases}$$

Make $x$ the subject of $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{9+2x}-\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$x=\dfrac{\left[2\left(\frac{3}{2}+F(x)\right)\right]^2-9}{2}$$
$Q_3$ occurs when $F(x)=\dfrac{3}{4}$:
$$Q_3=\dfrac{\left(2\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{4}\right)\right)^2-9}{2}=\dfrac{45}{8}=5.625$$
$Q_1$ occurs when $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$Q_1=\dfrac{\left(2\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\right)\right)^2-9}{2}=\dfrac{13}{8}=1.625$$
$$\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1=4$$
criteria: Finds $x$ in terms of $F(x)$, or equivalent merit

Let $X$ denote a normally distributed random variable with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

The random variable $X$ has probability density function

$$f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}$$

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows a sphere of radius $R$ and centre $O$ circumscribing a square pyramid. The points $A,B,C,D$ and $S$ all lie on the surface of the sphere and form the vertices of the pyramid with $ABCD$ the base. The point $T$ lies directly beneath $O$ and lies in the base of the pyramid such that $AT\perp OT$.

\exfigure{1281_q32_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Let $x=OT$. Show that the volume of the pyramid is

$$V=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)^2(R-x)$$
parts.note: 3D question (square pyramid inscribed in a sphere): all 3D content is Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

dif.r: 3D geometry: Pythagoras, square from diagonal, pyramid volume show-that.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the maximum volume a square pyramid may take when its vertices are circumscribed by a sphere of radius $R$.
parts.note: 3D question (square pyramid inscribed in a sphere): all 3D content is Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

dif.r: Optimise cubic with parameter R, factorise derivative, second derivative test.

figures.cap: sphere with square pyramid SABCD inscribed

solutions.latex:
The base $ABCD$ is a square. Since $AT\perp OT$, in right-angled triangle $OTA$ Pythagoras' theorem gives $AT=\sqrt{R^2-x^2}$.

$AT$ is half a diagonal of the square, so the diagonal is $2\sqrt{R^2-x^2}$.

Area of a square $=\dfrac{1}{2}d^2$, so
$$\text{base area}=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(2\sqrt{R^2-x^2}\right)^2=2(R^2-x^2)$$
Height $=x+R$ (from $T$ up through $O$ to $S$).
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times 2(R^2-x^2)\times(x+R) \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)(R-x)(R+x) \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)^2(R-x) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the base area and the height, or equivalent merit
Finds the base area or the height, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source line for the base area ($2\sqrt{R^2-x^2}\sqrt{R^2-x^2}$) is the same value as written here; a short reason for the diagonal was added.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $V=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)^2(R-x)$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(R+x)^2 & v&=R-x \\ u'&=2(R+x) & v'&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[2(R+x)(R-x)-(R+x)^2\right]$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=(R+x)\left[2(R-x)-(R+x)\right] \\ &=R-3x \end{aligned}$$
The factor $R+x\ne 0$, since $R,x>0$ are lengths, so $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$.

Nature test:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[2(-2x)-2(R+x)\right]=-\dfrac{4}{3}(3x+R)$$
At $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{4}{3}(R+R)<0 \text{ as } R>0$$
So $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$ gives a local maximum.

Maximum volume:
$$\begin{aligned} V\left(\dfrac{R}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{2}{3}\left(R+\dfrac{R}{3}\right)^2\left(R-\dfrac{R}{3}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{16R^2}{9}\times\dfrac{2R}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{64}{81}R^3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows the stationary point is a maximum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The $7^{\text{th}}$ term of an arithmetic sequence is 45 and the $11^{\text{th}}$ term is 77.

Find the first term ($a$) and the common difference ($d$).

dif.r: Two simultaneous term equations solved for a and d

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic sequence, $T_n = a+(n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_7 &= a+6d = 45 \\ T_{11} &= a+10d = 77 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting the first equation from the second:
$$\begin{aligned} 4d &= 32 \\ d &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $a+6d=45$:
$$\begin{aligned} a+48 &= 45 \\ a &= -3 \end{aligned}$$
So $a=-3$ and $d=8$, which is option A.

Differentiate the following with respect to $x$.

$$\dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=\dfrac{(-x)^3}{(-x)^2-1}\\ &=-\dfrac{x^3}{x^2-1}\\ &=-f(x) \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A swimming pool is to be emptied for maintenance. The quantity of water, $Q$ litres, remaining in the pool at a time, $t$ minutes after it starts to drain, is given by:

$$Q(t)=2000(25-t)^2,\quad t\ge 0$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How long will it take to remove half of the water from the pool to the nearest minute?

dif.r: Find initial amount, solve quadratic, reject invalid root

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what time does the rate of flow of water from the pool reach 20 000 L/minute?

dif.r: Chain-rule derivative set equal to given rate, solve linear equation

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$:
$$Q(0)=2000\times25^2=1\,250\,000\ \text{L}$$
Half the quantity is $625\,000$ L.
$$\begin{aligned} 625\,000&=2000(25-t)^2\\ 312.5&=(25-t)^2\\ 25-t&=\pm\sqrt{312.5} \end{aligned}$$
Since $t\le25$, take $25-t=\sqrt{312.5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} t&=25-\sqrt{312.5}\\ &=7.3223\ldots\\ &\approx7\ \text{minutes} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the time but fails to reject the incorrect root, or equivalent merit
Finds the original quantity and then half the quantity, or substitutes the wrong amount for $Q(t)$ and finds a reasonable but incorrect time, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The rate of flow is the rate of change of $Q$.
$$Q'(t)=-4000(25-t)$$
The water flows out at $20\,000$ L/minute, so $Q'(t)=-20\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} -20\,000&=-4000(25-t)\\ 5&=25-t\\ t&=20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the rate reaches $20\,000$ L/minute after 20 minutes.
criteria: Finds the correct derivative of $Q(t)$, or forgets the negative ($Q'(t)=4000(25-t)$) and finds an incorrect time, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source line was garbled and printed $-200000=-4000(25-t)$, which gives $t=-25$ not 20; the consistent equation $-20\,000=-4000(25-t)$ is used, giving the source's answer $t=20$.

questions.stem:
A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=3e^{t}+6e^{-t}$ with $t$ measured in minutes and $v$ in ms$^{-1}$.

The particle begins its motion at the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the initial velocity?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into given velocity

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find an equation for $x$, the displacement of the particle.

dif.r: Integrate exponentials and use initial condition for constant

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that when $x=10$, $3e^{2t}-7e^{t}-6=0$.

dif.r: Substitute and multiply through by e^t to reach given form

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $t$ when $x=10$.

dif.r: Factorise quadratic in e^t, reject negative root, take log

solutions.latex:
Initially $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 3e^0+6e^0 \\ &= 3+6 \\ &= 9 \text{ ms}^{-1} \end{aligned}$$

Integrate the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int (3e^t+6e^{-t})\,dt \\ &= 3e^t-6e^{-t}+c \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3e^0-6e^0+c \\ c &= 6-3 = 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3e^t-6e^{-t}+3$$
criteria: Correct working to find the anti-derivative but not the constant, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10 &= 3e^t-6e^{-t}+3 \\ 3e^t-6e^{-t}-7 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Multiply both sides by $e^t$.
$$3e^{2t}-7e^t-6=0$$
criteria: Substitutes and shows the equation but does not explicitly show the multiplication by $e^t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Factorise the quadratic in $e^t$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3e^{2t}-7e^t-6 &= 0 \\ (3e^t+2)(e^t-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $e^t=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $e^t=3$.

The first has no solution as $e^t>0$ for all $t$.

Hence $e^t=3$.
$$\therefore\ t=\ln 3$$
criteria: Correct solutions for $e^t$ but an error finding $t$ or does not discard the negative solution, or equivalent merit
Attempts the substitution $u=e^t$ or otherwise shows the equation reduces to a quadratic, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The queueing time, $X$ minutes, of a customer at the checkout of a supermarket has the probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{12}{625}x^2(k-x) & 0\le x\le k\\[1ex] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is 5.

dif.r: Set pdf integral to 1, polynomial integration, solve k^4=625

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Is a customer more likely to wait less than 3 minutes, or more than 3 minutes? Justify your answer with calculations.

dif.r: Definite integral of pdf with fraction arithmetic, compare with 0.5

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
Total probability is 1.
$$\int_0^k \dfrac{12}{625}x^2(k-x)\,dx=1$$
$$\dfrac{12}{625}\int_0^k (kx^2-x^3)\,dx=1$$
$$\left[\dfrac{kx^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^k=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
$$\dfrac{k^4}{3}-\dfrac{k^4}{4}=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
$$\dfrac{k^4}{12}=\dfrac{625}{12}$$
So $k^4=625$, and since $k\ge 0$,
$$\therefore\ k=5$$
criteria: Correctly integrates between $0$ and $k$ and sets the result equal to $1$, or equivalent merit
Sets up a correct integral equal to $1$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Find the probability of waiting at least 3 minutes.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 3) &= \int_3^5 \dfrac{12}{625}x^2(5-x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\int_3^5 (5x^2-x^3)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\dfrac{5x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_3^5 \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\left(\dfrac{625}{3}-\dfrac{625}{4}\right)-\left(45-\dfrac{81}{4}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{12}{625}\left[\dfrac{625}{12}-\dfrac{99}{4}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{328}{625} \\ &= 0.5248 \end{aligned}$$
Since $0.5248>0.5$, a customer is more likely to wait more than 3 minutes.
criteria: Correctly integrates between appropriate bounds and finds a probability but does not interpret it, or equivalent merit
Attempts to integrate between $0$ and $3$, or $3$ and $5$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: For the curve $y=x^3+6x^2+9x$,

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points of cubic with second derivative test

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the curve, showing all main features, including intercepts, stationary points and any points of inflection. Use the lines below for any relevant working.

dif.r: Standard cubic sketch: inflection, intercepts, using known stationary points

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=x^3+6x^2+9x with labelled features

solutions.latex:
Differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+12x+9$$
Stationary points: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2+12x+9 &= 0 \\ x^2+4x+3 &= 0 \\ (x+3)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-3$ or $x=-1$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x+12$$
When $x=-3$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-6<0,\qquad y=(-3)^3+6(-3)^2+9(-3)=0$$
Therefore $(-3,0)$ is a maximum turning point.

When $x=-1$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6>0,\qquad y=(-1)^3+6(-1)^2+9(-1)=-4$$
Therefore $(-1,-4)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the coordinates of the turning points, or finds the $x$-coordinates and determines nature correctly, or equivalent merit
Correct differentiation and $x$-coordinates found, or incorrect $x$-coordinates used to determine nature or coordinates, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Possible point of inflection: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$6x+12=0$$
So $x=-2$.

Test the concavity.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= -6 &&\text{at } x=-3 &&\text{concave down}\\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 0 &&\text{at } x=-2 && \\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} &= 6 &&\text{at } x=-1 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection. When $x=-2$:
$$y=(-2)^3+6(-2)^2+9(-2)=-2$$
So $(-2,-2)$ is a point of inflection.

For $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^3+6x^2+9x &= 0 \\ x(x^2+6x+9) &= 0 \\ x(x+3)^2 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=-3$.

\exfigure{1283_q25_s1}
criteria: All the information for 5 marks but with a minor error, or equivalent merit
Correct cubic with the stationary points and either the intercepts or the point of inflection correctly shown with working, or equivalent merit
Cubic with correct turning points and an attempt at the point of inflection or intercepts, or correct working but no graph, or equivalent merit
Cubic with the stationary points sketched, or $x$-coordinate of inflection found, or $x$-intercepts found, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The average life cycle of an insect is one month. A viable nest of this insect has between 100 000 to 500 000 insects. The population $P$ of a nest of this insect grows exponentially so that:

$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=1200e^{0.3t}$$

where $t$ is in months.

A nest of these insects had a population of 5000 after one month.

Determine how long it will take the nest to reach the viable stage (i.e. when the population has reached 100 000). Answer correct to the nearest month.

dif.r: Integrate, find constant at t=1, solve exponential with logs

solutions.latex:
Integrate $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \int 1200e^{0.3t}\,dt \\ &= 1200\times\dfrac{1}{0.3}e^{0.3t}+c \\ &= 4000e^{0.3t}+c \end{aligned}$$
When $t=1$, $P=5000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 5000 &= 4000e^{0.3}+c \\ c &= 5000-4000e^{0.3} = -399.435\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $P=4000e^{0.3t}-399.435\ldots$

When $P=100\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 100\,399.435\ldots &= 4000e^{0.3t} \\ 25.0999\ldots &= e^{0.3t} \\ \ln(25.0999\ldots) &= 0.3t \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln(25.0999\ldots)}{0.3} \\ &= 10.7429\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 11 \text{ months}$$
criteria: Finds the anti-derivative and constant and attempts to substitute $100\,000$ but does not find the correct $t$, or finds the anti-derivative without the constant and substitutes $100\,000$ to find $t$, or equivalent merit
Correct anti-derivative without the constant, or a reasonable but incorrect anti-derivative with $100\,000$ substituted, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $2\cos\left[2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]=1$ in the domain $[0,2\pi]$.

dif.r: Adjusted domain for compound angle; five solutions including endpoints

solutions.latex:
The equation becomes
$$\cos\left[2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]=\dfrac{1}{2},\quad 0\le x\le 2\pi$$
Find the range of the angle, one operation per line.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&\le x\le 2\pi \\ -\dfrac{\pi}{6}&\le x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le \dfrac{11\pi}{6} &&(\text{subtract } \dfrac{\pi}{6}) \\ -\dfrac{\pi}{3}&\le 2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\le \dfrac{11\pi}{3} &&(\text{multiply by } 2) \end{aligned}$$
So
$$2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}$$
$$x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ x=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ 2\pi$$
criteria: Correct working to find three correct solutions, or equivalent merit
One correct solution with relevant working, or uses $u=2\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ to show $u=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: b
parts.latex: By finding the area of $\Delta AOB$, or otherwise, find the width of the river.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

dif.r: Equate two area expressions to find perpendicular width

figures.cap: river with flagpole OF, points A, B and angles of elevation 60 and 30 degrees

solutions.latex:
In $\Delta OFB$, $\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{h}{OB}$.
$$OB=\dfrac{h}{\tan 30^\circ}=\sqrt{3}\,h$$
In $\Delta OFA$, $\tan 60^\circ=\dfrac{h}{OA}$.
$$OA=\dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\Delta OAB$.
$$\begin{aligned} 7^2 &= OA^2+OB^2-2(OA)(OB)\cos 60^\circ \\ 49 &= \dfrac{h^2}{3}+3h^2-2\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}\,h\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{10h^2}{3}-h^2 \\ &= \dfrac{7h^2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
So $h^2=21$, and since $h>0$,
$$\therefore\ h=\sqrt{21} \text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct expressions and cosine rule used to find $h$ but not simplified to show $h=\sqrt{21}$, or equivalent merit
Finds correct expressions for $OA$ and $OB$, or attempts the cosine rule with incorrect expressions, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $h=\sqrt{21}$, $OA=\sqrt{7}$ and $OB=3\sqrt{7}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of } \Delta AOB &= \dfrac{1}{2}(OA)(OB)\sin 60^\circ \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{7}\times 3\sqrt{7}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The width $w$ is the perpendicular height from $O$ to $AB$, so
$$\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times w\times 7$$
Equate the two areas.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{7w}{2} &= \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4} \\ 7w &= \dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ w=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{ m}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the area formulas to find the width but makes an error, or equivalent merit

criteria: Reasonable progress towards the derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the area, $A$, of $\Delta ABC$ is given by $A=(10+x)\sqrt{100-x^2}$

dif.r: Geometric setup with Pythagoras to derive given area formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
By first showing that the derivative is

$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\dfrac{100-10x-2x^2}{\sqrt{100-x^2}}$$

prove that the triangle with maximum area is equilateral.

dif.r: Product rule with surd, optimise, then prove equilateral: extended reasoning

figures.cap: isosceles triangle ABC inscribed in a circle with centre O, OP perpendicular to AC

solutions.latex:
$P$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $OP\perp AC$, so $BP=OB+OP=10+x$.

In right-angled $\Delta OPC$, by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$PC^2=OC^2-OP^2=10^2-x^2$$
so $PC=\sqrt{100-x^2}$ and
$$AC=2PC=2\sqrt{100-x^2}$$
Using area $=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times AC\times BP \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\sqrt{100-x^2}\times(10+x) \\ &= (10+x)\sqrt{100-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts Pythagoras' theorem to find $PC$ and uses the area of a triangle formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=10+x & v&=\sqrt{100-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{100-x^2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= \sqrt{100-x^2}+(10+x)\times\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{100-x^2}} \\ &= \dfrac{100-x^2-x(10+x)}{\sqrt{100-x^2}} \\ &= \dfrac{100-10x-2x^2}{\sqrt{100-x^2}} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100-10x-2x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2+5x-50 &= 0 \\ (x+10)(x-5) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-10$ or $x=5$. Since $x>0$, $x=5$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{dx}$.
$$\begin{aligned} x=4:\ \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= 3.055\ldots>0 &&\text{increasing}\\ x=5:\ \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= 0 && \\ x=6:\ \dfrac{dA}{dx} &= -4<0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
So the area is a maximum when $x=5$ cm.

Then
$$BP=5+10=15,\qquad PC=\sqrt{100-5^2}=5\sqrt{3},\qquad AC=2\times 5\sqrt{3}=10\sqrt{3}$$
In right-angled $\Delta BPC$:
$$BC=\sqrt{15^2+(5\sqrt{3})^2}=\sqrt{300}=10\sqrt{3}$$
Since $AB=BC$, we have $AB=BC=AC=10\sqrt{3}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the triangle of maximum area is equilateral}$$
criteria: Shows the derivative and that $x=5$ gives a maximum area, but the equilateral conclusion is incomplete, or equivalent merit
Correct derivative and finds $x=5$ with an attempt to show it is a maximum, or equivalent merit
Correct derivative using the product or quotient rule, or equivalent merit
Finds $u'$ and $v'$ and attempts the rule, or finds a value of $x$ for which there is a maximum or minimum, or equivalent merit

A bag contains 100 raffle tickets. Five of these tickets are golden.

Augustus is permitted to select two tickets, consecutively, without replacement.

By drawing a tree diagram, or otherwise, find the probability that,

dif.r: Two-stage product without replacement, routine tree branch

parts.label: c
parts.latex: at least one ticket is golden.

dif.r: At least one via complement of previous result

solutions.latex:
There are 5 golden tickets among 100.

$$P(\text{first golden})=\dfrac{5}{100}=\dfrac{1}{20}$$

Neither ticket golden: the first is not golden, then the second (without replacement) is not golden.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither golden}) &= \dfrac{95}{100}\times\dfrac{94}{99} \\ &= \dfrac{893}{990} \end{aligned}$$

"At least one golden" is the complement of "neither golden".

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one golden}) &= 1-\dfrac{893}{990} \\ &= \dfrac{97}{990} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct answer (allow for errors carried forward from part (b))

questions.stem: Consider the finite arithmetic series $30, 28.5, 27, \dots, -6$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the sequence contains 25 terms.

dif.r: nth term formula used in reverse with decimal difference

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the sum of the sequence.

dif.r: Substitute into arithmetic sum formula

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic sequence, the $n$th term is $T_n=a+(n-1)d$, with $a=30$ and $d=-1.5$. The last term is $-6$.

$$\begin{aligned} -6 &= 30+(n-1)(-1.5) \\ -36 &= -1.5n+1.5 \\ -37.5 &= -1.5n \\ n &= 25 \end{aligned}$$

So the sequence contains 25 terms.

Using the sum formula $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ with $n=25$, $a=30$, $l=-6$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_{25} &= \dfrac{25}{2}(30-6) \\ &= 300 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_{25} &= \dfrac{25}{2}\left[60+24(-1.5)\right] \\ &= 300 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Max is given an old coin by his grandfather. The current value of the coin is \$600.

Each year, it is predicted that the coin's value will be 10% greater than in the previous year.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How much, to the nearest dollar, will the coin be worth after 6 years?

dif.r: Substitute into compound growth formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Max decides that he will sell the coin when the value of the coin exceeds \$3000.

For how many complete years must Max keep the coin?

dif.r: Exponential inequality solved with logarithms, round up

solutions.latex:
Using the compound interest formula with $P=600$, $r=0.1$, $n=6$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= P(1+r)^n \\ &= 600(1+0.1)^6 \\ &\approx \$1063 \end{aligned}$$

The value exceeds \$3000 when

$$\begin{aligned} 600(1.1)^n &> 3000 \\ 1.1^n &> 5 \end{aligned}$$

Taking logarithms of both sides (base $1.1>1$, so the inequality is preserved):

$$\begin{aligned} \log_{1.1}1.1^n &> \log_{1.1}5 \\ n &> \dfrac{\ln 5}{\ln 1.1} \\ n &> 16.88\dots \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ 17 \text{ years are required.}$$
criteria: Writes the initial inequality, or equivalent merit

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find $\sigma$ correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Square root of given variance

figures.cap: spinner with sectors 1, 2 and 3

solutions.latex:
The probabilities in a distribution sum to 1.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{4}+3k+\dfrac{5}{18}+k+\dfrac{1}{36} &= 1 \\ 4k &= \dfrac{4}{9} \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Probability table (extable) not shown in the context; values taken from the source working.

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,p(x)$:

$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \left(2\times\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+\left(3\times\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\left(4\times\dfrac{5}{18}\right)+\left(5\times\dfrac{1}{9}\right)+\left(6\times\dfrac{1}{36}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{10}{3} \end{aligned}$$

Using $Var(X)=\sum x^2p(x)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=\dfrac{10}{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned} Var(X) &= \left(4\times\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+\left(9\times\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\left(16\times\dfrac{5}{18}\right)+\left(25\times\dfrac{1}{9}\right)+\left(36\times\dfrac{1}{36}\right)-\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{10}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expression with one error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{9}} \\ &\approx 1.05 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A coin is biased so that the probability of the coin showing tails on any throw is $p$.

The probability that the coin shows tails exactly once in two throws is $0.32$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find, in terms of $p$, the probability that the coin shows heads on any throw.

dif.r: Complement expressed in terms of p

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the possible values of $p$.

dif.r: Build equation 2p(1-p)=0.32 from tree, solve quadratic

figures.cap: solution sketch: handwritten tree diagram for two throws of the biased coin

solutions.latex:
Heads is the complement of tails.

$$P(\text{Heads})=1-p$$

Exactly one tail in two throws means tail then head, or head then tail.

\exfigure{1576_q4e_s1}

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly one tail}) &= p(1-p)+(1-p)p \\ &= 2p(1-p) \end{aligned}$$

This equals $0.32$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2p(1-p) &= 0.32 \\ p(1-p) &= 0.16 \\ p-p^2 &= 0.16 \\ p^2-p+0.16 &= 0 \\ 100p^2-100p+16 &= 0 \\ 25p^2-25p+4 &= 0 \\ (5p-1)(5p-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ p=\dfrac{1}{5} \text{ or } p=\dfrac{4}{5}$$
criteria: Writes the equation $2p(1-p)=0.32$, or equivalent merit

Each square has side $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of the previous one, and $EFGH$ is the second square after the unit square.

questions.stem:
Nick borrows \$380 000 to buy an apartment. The loan is repaid in equal monthly instalments. The interest, which is charged at 0.3% per month, is reducible and calculated monthly. The amount owing after $n$ months, $\$A_n$, is given by,

$$A_n = Pr^n - M(1 + r + r^2 + \dots + r^{n-1}),$$

(Do NOT prove this)

where $\$P$ is the amount borrowed, $r = 1.003$ and $\$M$ is the monthly repayment.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: The loan is to be repaid over 25 years. Show that the monthly repayment is \$1923 to the nearest dollar.

dif.r: Set A_300=0, sum geometric series, solve for M

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Using the monthly repayment found in part (a), find how many months are needed for the balance of the loan to be less than half of the original amount borrowed?

dif.r: Rearrange loan formula, solve exponential equation with logarithms

solutions.latex:
With $P=380000$, $r=1.003$, $n=25\times12=300$ and the loan fully repaid, $A_{300}=0$.

$$0=380000(1.003)^{300}-M\left(1+1.003+1.003^2+\dots+1.003^{299}\right)$$

The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$, ratio $1.003$ and 300 terms.

$$0=380000(1.003)^{300}-M\left[\dfrac{1.003^{300}-1}{0.003}\right]\quad(*)$$

$$\begin{aligned} M &= 380000(1.003)^{300}\times\dfrac{0.003}{1.003^{300}-1} \\ &= 1922.810307\ \text{(by calculator)}\quad(*) \\ &\approx \$1923 \end{aligned}$$

as required.
criteria: Correct answer (working must include the lines marked $(*)$)

solutions.latex:
Half the original amount is $\$190000$, so find $n$ when $A_n=190000$.

$$190000=380000(1.003)^n-1923\left[\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}\right]$$

Since $\dfrac{1923}{0.003}=641000$:

$$\begin{aligned} 190000 &= 380000(1.003)^n-641000(1.003^n-1) \\ 190000 &= 380000(1.003)^n-641000(1.003)^n+641000 \\ 261000(1.003)^n &= 451000 \\ 1.003^n &= 1.7279\dots \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln(1.7279\dots)}{\ln(1.003)} \\ &= 182.58\dots \end{aligned}$$

The balance decreases as $n$ increases, so we need the next whole month.

$$\therefore\ 183 \text{ months are required.}$$
criteria: Writes the expression for $A_n$ and sets it equal to $190000$, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Must rewrite as curve meeting y=-x and argue intersections by regions

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: graph of y = e^x(1+x)

solutions.latex:
The solutions of $e^{x}(1+x)+x=0$ are the points where $y=e^{x}(1+x)$ meets the line $y=-x$.

For $x<-1$ the curve is below the $x$-axis while the line $y=-x$ is above it, so there is no intersection.

For $x>0$ the curve is above the $x$-axis while the line is below it, so there is no intersection.

For $-1\le x\le 0$ the curve rises from $0$ to $1$ and the line falls from $1$ to $0$, so they cross exactly once.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = x^{2} - 1$ and $g(x) = 1 - 2x$, find

dif.r: Direct numerical evaluation of a composite function

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $f \circ g(x)$

dif.r: Substitute and expand a simple composite

solutions.latex:
First find $f(2)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(2)&=2^{2}-1\\ &=3\end{aligned}$$
Then apply $g$.
$$\begin{aligned} g\circ f(2)&=g(3)\\ &=1-2(3)\\ &=-5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ g\circ f(2)=-5$$

Substitute $g(x)$ into $f$.
$$\begin{aligned} f\circ g(x)&=(1-2x)^{2}-1\\ &=1-4x+4x^{2}-1\\ &=4x^{2}-4x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f\circ g(x)=4x^{2}-4x$$

$$\therefore\ \text{centre is } (2,-3),\ \text{radius is } 5$$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0.5}^{2} \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Write the integrand as a power of $x$.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=4$ into each function.
$$\begin{aligned} f(4)&=\dfrac{4}{2}(4-2)=4\\ g(4)&=2\sqrt{4}=4\end{aligned}$$
Since $f(4)=g(4)$, the graphs meet where $x=4$, so the $x$ coordinate of $A$ is $4$.

Between $x=0$ and $x=4$ the curve $g$ is above $f$, so the integrand is $g(x)-f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sqrt{x}-\dfrac{x}{2}(x-2)&=2x^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}+x\end{aligned}$$
The area is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}\left(2x^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}+x\right)dx\\ &=\left[\dfrac{4}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{6}x^{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2}\right]_{0}^{4}\\ &=\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\cdot 8-\dfrac{1}{6}\cdot 64+8\right)-0\\ &=8\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $y = 4x^{3} - x^{4}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = 4x^3 - x^4 with intercepts, stationary point (3,27) and inflexion (2,16)

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=12x^{2}-4x^{3}\\ 0&=4x^{2}(3-x)\end{aligned}$$
so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

When $x=0$, $y=0$. When $x=3$, $y=27$.

Test the nature using $y''=24x-12x^{2}$.

At $x=0$: $y''=0$, so the test fails and $(0,0)$ is a possible horizontal point of inflexion.

At $x=3$: $y''=24(3)-12(9)=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

Alternatively, test the nature using $y'$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline y' & 16 & 0 & 8 \end{array}$$
The gradient is positive on both sides of $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a possible point of inflexion.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline y' & 16 & 0 & -64 \end{array}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative, so $(3,27)$ is a maximum turning point.

Confirm the inflexion at $(0,0)$ by checking the concavity.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline y'' & -36 & 0 & 12 \end{array}$$
The concavity changes, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
$$\therefore\ (3,27)\text{ is a maximum turning point and }(0,0)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion}$$
criteria: Finds $x=0,3$ and the nature at both points (with numbers), or equivalent merit
Finds $x=0,3$ and the nature at one point (with numbers), or equivalent merit

The concavity changes at $x=2$.

$$\int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx .$$

parts.latex: If $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$ then $y'' = \dfrac{2}{x^{3}}$. Briefly explain how this implies that your approximation found in part (a) overestimates the exact value of the definite integral.

solutions.latex:
Five function values give four strips, so
$$h=\dfrac{3-1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
and the $x$ values are $1,\ \dfrac{3}{2},\ 2,\ \dfrac{5}{2},\ 3$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} x & 1 & \dfrac{3}{2} & 2 & \dfrac{5}{2} & 3 \\ \hline f(x) & 1 & \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{3} \end{array}$$
Using the trapezoidal rule, $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f_0+2(f_1+f_2+f_3)+f_4\big]$:
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}\dfrac{1}{x}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{1}{4}\left[1+2\left(\dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{2}{5}\right)+\dfrac{1}{3}\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{67}{15}\\ &=\dfrac{67}{60}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct function values, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Checked: $\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{67}{15}=\frac{67}{60}$ is correct.

solutions.latex:
For $1\le x\le 3$, $y''=\dfrac{2}{x^{3}}>0$, so the curve is concave up.

On a concave up curve the chords (the tops of the trapezoids) lie above the curve.

Therefore the approximation in part (a) is an overestimate.

questions.stem:
\exfigure{1591_q5c_1}

In the diagram above, the curve $y = \dfrac{h}{x^{2} + k}$ where $h$ and $k$ are constants, has a minimum turning point at $(0, -6)$ and passes through the point $(5, -1)$. The rectangle $PQRS$ is inscribed within the curve as shown with its axis of symmetry, $x = 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $h = -30$ and $k = 5$.

dif.r: Substitute two points, solve simultaneous equations

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If $Q$ has co-ordinates $(\alpha, 0)$, find the co-ordinates of $R$ in terms of $\alpha$.

dif.r: Substitute x=alpha into the known curve

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that the area, $A$, of rectangle $PQRS$ is $A = \dfrac{60\alpha}{\alpha^{2} + 5}$.

dif.r: Build area from symmetry and positive height of negative curve

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Hence, find the exact value of $\alpha$ that gives the maximum area of the rectangle $PQRS$.

dif.r: Quotient rule optimisation of given area function with sign test

figures.cap: curve y = h/(x^2+k) with inscribed rectangle PQRS, minimum at (0,-6), point (5,-1)

solutions.latex:
Substitute each given point into $y=\dfrac{h}{x^{2}+k}$.

The point $(0,-6)$ gives
$$-6=\dfrac{h}{k}$$
so $h=-6k$.

The point $(5,-1)$ gives
$$-1=\dfrac{h}{25+k}$$
so $h=-k-25$.

Equate the two expressions for $h$.
$$\begin{aligned} -6k&=-k-25\\ -5k&=-25\\ k&=5\end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} h&=-6k\\ &=-6(5)\\ &=-30\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h=-30,\ k=5,\ \text{so } y=\dfrac{-30}{x^{2}+5}$$
criteria: Establishes the equations in $h$ and $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$R$ lies on the curve directly below $Q$, so its $x$ coordinate is $\alpha$.

When $x=\alpha$,
$$y=\dfrac{-30}{\alpha^{2}+5}$$
$$\therefore\ R\text{ is }\left(\alpha,\ \dfrac{-30}{\alpha^{2}+5}\right)$$

The rectangle is symmetric about $x=0$, so the width is $PQ=2\alpha$.

The height is $QR=\dfrac{30}{\alpha^{2}+5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=PQ\times QR\\ &=2\alpha\cdot\dfrac{30}{\alpha^{2}+5}\\ &=\dfrac{60\alpha}{\alpha^{2}+5}\end{aligned}$$

The area is a maximum where $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=0$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\alpha}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^{2}}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=60\alpha & v&=\alpha^{2}+5\\ u'&=60 & v'&=2\alpha\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=\dfrac{60(\alpha^{2}+5)-60\alpha\cdot 2\alpha}{(\alpha^{2}+5)^{2}}$$
Set the numerator to zero.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=60\alpha^{2}+300-120\alpha^{2}\\ &=300-60\alpha^{2}\\ 0&=5-\alpha^{2}\end{aligned}$$
Since $\alpha>0$, $\alpha=\sqrt{5}$.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}$ either side of $\alpha=\sqrt{5}$, where $\sqrt{5}\approx 2.24$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \alpha & 2 & \sqrt{5} & 3 \\ \hline \dfrac{dA}{d\alpha} & \dfrac{60}{81} & 0 & -\dfrac{60}{49} \end{array}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative, so this is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \alpha=\sqrt{5}\text{ gives the maximum area}$$

The weekly pay for workers at the Prosper Factory is normally distributed, with a mean of \$750 and a standard deviation of \$35.

A weekly pay of $\$680$ has $z$-score
$$z=\dfrac{680-750}{35}=-2$$
so below $\$680$ means $z<-2$.

\exfigure{1299_q4_s1}

Using the 95% rule, $95\%$ lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, so $5\%$ lie outside, split equally between the two tails.

Therefore $2.5\%$ of workers earn below $\$680$.

parts.latex:
The $7^{\text{th}}$ term of an arithmetic sequence is 45 and the $11^{\text{th}}$ term is 77.

Find the first term ($a$) and the common difference ($d$).

dif.r: Two simultaneous term equations for a and d; standard technique.

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic sequence, $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_7=45:\quad a+6d&=45 &&(1) \\ T_{11}=77:\quad a+10d&=77 &&(2) \\ (2)-(1):\quad 4d&=32 \\ d&=8 &&(3) \end{aligned}$$
Substituting (3) into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} 45&=a+6\times 8 \\ a&=-3 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $a=-3$ and $d=8$.

Adding the two late scores gives the new mean for 22 students:
$$\bar{x}_{\text{new}}=\dfrac{1560+95+83}{22}=79$$

parts.latex: What is the equation of the axis of symmetry of the quadratic function $y = -k(x+b)^2 + c$ ?

dif.r: Recall axis of symmetry from vertex form, with parameters.

solutions.latex:
Since $(x+b)$ means the parabola is translated $b$ units to the left, the axis is $x=-b$.

Alternatively, expand and use the axis $x=-\dfrac{B}{2A}$ for $y=Ax^2+Bx+C$:

parts.latex: Find the derivative of $e^{x\sin 3x}$.

dif.r: Chain rule combined with product rule on exponential.

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule,
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 3x}\right)=e^{x\sin 3x}\times\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)$$
For $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)$ use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin 3x \\ u'&=1 & v'&=3\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)=\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 3x}\right)=e^{x\sin 3x}(\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x)$$

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{(x+3)(2x+1)}{\sqrt{x}},\quad x>0$

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that $f(x)$ can be written in the form $Ax^{\frac{3}{2}}+Bx^{\frac{1}{2}}+Cx^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

Find the values of $A$, $B$, and $C$.

dif.r: Expand numerator and divide by root x using index laws.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $f'(x)$

dif.r: Power rule on fractional indices, termwise.

solutions.latex:
Expand the numerator, then divide each term by $\sqrt{x}=x^{\frac{1}{2}}$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\dfrac{(x+3)(2x+1)}{\sqrt{x}} \\ &=\dfrac{2x^2+7x+3}{\sqrt{x}} \\ &=2x^{\frac{3}{2}}+7x^{\frac{1}{2}}+3x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=2,\ B=7,\ C=3$$

Differentiating each term of $f(x)=2x^{\frac{3}{2}}+7x^{\frac{1}{2}}+3x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$:
$$f'(x)=3x^{\frac{1}{2}}+\dfrac{7}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{3}{2}x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$$

parts.latex: Find the common ratio of a geometric series with a first term of 3 and a limiting sum of 18.

dif.r: Limiting sum formula used in reverse to find r.

solutions.latex:
For a limiting sum, $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ with $a=3$ and $S=18$.
$$\begin{aligned} 18&=\dfrac{3}{1-r} \\ 18-18r&=3 \\ 18r&=15 \\ r&=\dfrac{15}{18}=\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the common ratio is } \dfrac{5}{6}$$
criteria: Uses the limiting sum with at least one correct value

meta.format_note: Source had $18r=-15$, $r=-\dfrac{5}{6}$, which is a slip: $18-18r=3$ gives $18r=15$, $r=\dfrac{5}{6}$ (and $|r|<1$ holds). Corrected in the solution.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int 6x^2+2+x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx$, giving each term in its simplest form.

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} \int 6x^2+2+x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,dx&=\dfrac{6x^3}{3}+2x+\dfrac{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}}+C \\ &=2x^3+2x+2x^{\frac{1}{2}}+C \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
Fred sits his Trial exams in Modern History and Ancient History.

The marks for the Modern History class have a mean of 54 and a standard deviation of 5.6.

The marks for the Ancient History class have a mean of 76 and a standard deviation of 2.1.

parts.latex:
Fred scored 65 for Modern History and 80 for Ancient History.

Using $z$-score calculations, explain which subject he performed better in and why.

dif.r: Two z-score calculations and a comparison statement.

solutions.latex:
The Ancient History class has a higher mean and a smaller standard deviation, so its marks are grouped more closely around the mean and are more consistent.

The Modern History class has a lower mean and a larger standard deviation, so its marks are more spread out around the lower mean and are less consistent.
criteria: Comments on only the mean or only the standard deviation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

Modern History: $x=65$, $\mu=54$, $\sigma=5.6$
$$z_{\text{MH}}=\dfrac{65-54}{5.6}\approx 1.96$$
Ancient History: $x=80$, $\mu=76$, $\sigma=2.1$
$$z_{\text{AH}}=\dfrac{80-76}{2.1}\approx 1.90$$
Fred performed better in Modern History, as his higher positive $z$-score means he was further above the mean than in Ancient History, even though his raw mark was lower.
criteria: Correct $z$-scores but incorrect analysis, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Set the two expressions for $y$ equal and square both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x+1}&=11-x \\ x+1&=(11-x)^2 \\ x+1&=121-22x+x^2 \\ x^2-23x+120&=0 \\ (x-8)(x-15)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=8$ or $x=15$.

When $x=8$, $y=3$. When $x=15$, $y=-4$.

The radical sign means the positive square root, so $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ is never negative. Hence $(15,-4)$ is not a solution.

The only point of intersection is $(8,3)$.

solutions.latex:
The curves meet at $(8,3)$. The area is under $y=\sqrt{x+1}$ from $x=-1$ to $x=8$, then under $y=11-x$ from $x=8$ to $x=11$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-1}^{8}(x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx+\int_8^{11}(11-x)\,dx \\ &=\left[\dfrac{2(x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{-1}^{8}+\left[11x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_8^{11} \\ &=\left[\dfrac{2(9)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}-0\right]+\left[\left(121-\dfrac{121}{2}\right)-\left(88-\dfrac{64}{2}\right)\right] \\ &=18+4.5 \\ &=22.5 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=3e^{t}+6e^{-t}$ with $t$ measured in minutes and $v$ in $\text{ms}^{-1}$.

The particle begins its motion at origin.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the initial velocity?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into velocity.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find an equation for $x$, the displacement of the particle.

dif.r: Integrate exponentials and use initial condition for constant.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that when $x=10$, $3e^{2t}-7e^{t}-6=0$.

dif.r: Substitute and multiply through by e^t to reach given quadratic.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $t$ when $x=10$.

dif.r: Quadratic in e^t, factorise, reject negative root, take logs.

solutions.latex:
Initial velocity is at $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=3e^0+6e^0\\ &=9\text{ ms}^{-1}\end{aligned}$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int\left(3e^t+6e^{-t}\right)dt\\ &=3e^t-6e^{-t}+c\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$:
$$0=3-6+c$$
So $c=3$.

$$\therefore\ x=3e^t-6e^{-t}+3$$
criteria: Correct integration but does not find $c$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}10&=3e^t-6e^{-t}+3\\ 7&=3e^t-6e^{-t}\\ 7&=3e^t-\dfrac{6}{e^t}\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying by $e^t$:
$$7e^t=3\left(e^t\right)^2-6$$
Hence
$$3e^{2t}-7e^t-6=0$$
criteria: Correct substitution and some manipulation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $u=e^t$ to give a quadratic in $u$.
$$\begin{aligned}3u^2-7u-6&=0\\ 3u^2-9u+2u-6&=0\\ 3u(u-3)+2(u-3)&=0\\ (3u+2)(u-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $u=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $u=3$.

Since $e^t>0$, $e^t\ne-\dfrac{2}{3}$, so $e^t=3$.

Taking $\ln$ of both sides:
$$t=\ln 3\text{ minutes}$$
criteria: Substitution and attempt at solving the quadratic, or equivalent merit

The mean is

$$\therefore\ \text{Var}(X)=1.2$$

questions.stem: John started work at 18 and at the beginning of each month he invested \$400 into a superannuation fund. Interest was paid at $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly on the investment. John retired at 63 after having contributed to the fund for 45 years.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How much did John contribute to the fund over 45 years?

dif.r: Single multiplication of contributions.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How much did John's investment amount to after 45 years?

dif.r: Annuity due future value set up as geometric series sum.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: John plans to reinvest some of the money into an account which offers $8\%$ p.a. compound interest compounded annually. He plans to have \$300 000 at the end of the 10 year investment period. How much does John need to reinvest to achieve this amount. Answer correct to the nearest dollar.

dif.r: Compound interest formula used in reverse for present value.

solutions.latex:
There are 12 contributions each year for 45 years.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total}&=400\times 12\times 45\\ &=\$216\,000\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ John contributed \$216 000 over the 45 years.

The monthly rate is
$$r=\dfrac{0.06}{12}=0.005\text{ (that is, } 0.5\%)$$
After 1 month:
$$A_1=400\times 1.005^1$$
After 2 months:
$$A_2=400\times 1.005^2+400\times 1.005^1$$
After 45 years (540 months):
$$A_{540}=400\times 1.005^{540}+400\times 1.005^{539}+\cdots+400\times 1.005^1$$
This is a GP with first term $400\times 1.005$, ratio $1.005$ and 540 terms, so using the sum of a GP:
$$A_{540}=400\times\dfrac{1.005\left(1.005^{540}-1\right)}{1.005-1}=\$1\,107\,909.03$$
$\therefore$ John's investment is worth \$1 107 909.03 after 45 years.
criteria: Makes some progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the compound interest formula:
$$\begin{aligned}FV&=PV(1+r)^n\\ 300\,000&=PV(1+0.08)^{10}\\ PV&=138\,958.0464\ldots\\ &\approx\$138\,958\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ John needs to reinvest \$138 958.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^3+2x-7$:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=3x^2+2$$

Since $x^2\ge 0$ for all $x$, we have $3x^2\ge 0$.

Adding 2:
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=3x^2+2\ge 2$$

solutions.latex:
Finding the anti-derivative:
$$y=\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2-7x+C$$
The point $P(2,4)$ lies on the curve, so it satisfies the equation.
$$4=\dfrac{2^4}{4}+2^2-14+C$$
So $C=10$.

$$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2-7x+10$$

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent at $P(2,4)$ is
$$m=\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2^3+2\times 2-7=5$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_1m_2=-1$ and the gradient of the normal is $-\dfrac{1}{5}$.

Equation of the normal, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$y-4=-\dfrac{1}{5}(x-2)$$
$$\therefore\ x+5y-22=0$$

The average life cycle of an insect is one month. A viable nest of this insect has between 100 000 to 500 000 insects. The population $P$ of a nest of this insect grows exponentially so that:

parts.latex: What is the value of $x$ for which $4^{3-5x} = 8^{2x}$?

dif.r: Rewrite both sides base 2, equate indices, solve linear

solutions.latex:
Write both sides as powers of $2$, using $4=2^2$ and $8=2^3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4^{3-5x} &= 8^{2x} \\ 2^{2(3-5x)} &= 2^{3(2x)} \\ 2^{6-10x} &= 2^{6x} \end{aligned}$$
The bases are equal, so the indices are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} 6-10x &= 6x \\ 6 &= 16x \\ x &= \dfrac{3}{8} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Which one of the following is the set of all solutions to $2x^2-5x+2\ge 0$?

dif.r: Factorise quadratic and select region outside roots

solutions.latex:
Factorise to find where the quadratic is zero.
$$2x^2-5x+2=(2x-1)(x-2)$$
The roots are $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x=2$.

The parabola opens upwards (coefficient of $x^2$ is positive), so it is above or on the $x$-axis outside the roots.
$$x\le \dfrac{1}{2} \text{ or } x\ge 2$$
The inequality is $\ge$, so the endpoints are included. The solution set is $\left(-\infty,\dfrac{1}{2}\right]\cup[2,\infty)$, which is option D.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\tan x$ given that $\sin x=\dfrac{1}{3}$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\pi$.

dif.r: Pythagorean identity plus correct quadrant sign for cosine

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<x<\pi$, $x$ is in the second quadrant, so $\cos x<0$.

Using $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos^2 x &= 1-\dfrac{1}{9}=\dfrac{8}{9} \\ \cos x &= -\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} \tan x &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\times\left(-\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: Given the function $f(x)=x^2-4x$ and $g(x)=x^2-9$, write an expression for $g\big(f(x)\big)$ in its simplest form.

$$\begin{aligned}g\big(f(x)\big)&=g(x^2-4x)\\&=(x^2-4x)^2-9\\&=x^4-8x^3+16x^2-9\end{aligned}$$

The graph is a transformation of $f(x)=x^2$, so $g(x)=k(x+b)^2+c$.

Substitute the $y$-intercept $\left(0,-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{7}{3}&=k(0-5)^2+6\\ 25k&=-\dfrac{25}{3}\\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ g(x)=-\dfrac{1}{3}f(x-5)+6$$

questions.stem: A sequence is given by $\sqrt{8},\ \sqrt{32},\ \sqrt{72},\ \cdots$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the terms form an arithmetic sequence.

dif.r: Simplify surds and check common difference

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The sum of the first $n$ terms is $132\sqrt{2}$. Find the value of $n$.

dif.r: Sum formula in reverse with surds, solve quadratic, reject negative

solutions.latex:
Simplify each term:
$$\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2},\quad \sqrt{32}=4\sqrt{2},\quad \sqrt{72}=6\sqrt{2}$$
Check for a common difference:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3-T_2&=6\sqrt{2}-4\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}\\T_2-T_1&=4\sqrt{2}-2\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
So $T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1$.

Hence the terms form an arithmetic sequence.

From part (a), $a=2\sqrt{2}$ and $d=2\sqrt{2}$. Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$:
$$\begin{aligned}132\sqrt{2}&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2\times 2\sqrt{2}+(n-1)\times 2\sqrt{2}\right)\\&=n\left(2\sqrt{2}+n\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}\right)\\&=n^2\sqrt{2}+n\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
Divide by $\sqrt{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}n^2+n-132&=0\\(n-11)(n+12)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $n=11$ or $n=-12$.

But $n\ge 1$, hence $n=11$ only.
$$\therefore\ n=11$$
criteria: Correct manipulation to the quadratic, or equivalent merit
Forms the equation for the arithmetic sum, or equivalent merit

The perimeter is two straight edges of length $r-\dfrac{1}{r}$ plus the inner arc $\dfrac{1}{r}\theta$ and the outer arc $r\theta$ (arc $=$ radius $\times$ angle).
$$P=2\left(r-\dfrac{1}{r}\right)+\dfrac{1}{r}\theta+r\theta$$
Set $P=6$:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)+2\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta\\&=2+2(1+\cot^2\theta)\\&=4+2\cot^2\theta\end{aligned}$$

In $\triangle DBU$, right-angled at $B$, with $UB=880$:
$$\tan 66^\circ=\dfrac{880}{DB}$$
$$DB=\dfrac{880}{\tan 66^\circ}$$
$$\therefore\ DB=880\cot 66^\circ$$
In $\triangle DCT$, right-angled at $C$, with $TC=1044$:
$$\tan 57^\circ=\dfrac{1044}{DC}$$
$$DC=\dfrac{1044}{\tan 57^\circ}$$
$$\therefore\ DC=1044\cot 57^\circ$$
criteria: Correct expression for $DB$ or $DC$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use the area formula in $\triangle BDC$ with $DB=880\cot 66^\circ$ and $DC=1044\cot 57^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}(880\cot 66^\circ)(1044\cot 57^\circ)\sin\angle BDC\\112\,860&=459\,360\cot 66^\circ\cot 57^\circ\sin\angle BDC\end{aligned}$$
$$\sin\angle BDC=\dfrac{57\tan 66^\circ\tan 57^\circ}{232}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle BDC=58^\circ 11'$$
criteria: Forms the equation for the area, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use the cosine rule in $\triangle BDC$ with $\angle BDC=58^\circ 11'$:
$$BC^2=(880\cot 66^\circ)^2+(1044\cot 57^\circ)^2-2(880\cot 66^\circ)(1044\cot 57^\circ)\cos 58^\circ 11'$$
$$BC=577.13$$
So $UV=BC=577.13$, where $V$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $U$ to $TC$, and
$$TV=1044-880=164$$
In right-angled $\triangle UVT$, by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$UT^2=(577.13)^2+164^2$$
$$\therefore\ UT=599.98 \text{ m}$$
Hence the ropeway is $599.98$ m long.
criteria: Forms the expression for $BC$ using the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1, and $E(X)=\Sigma\, x\,p(x)$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}x&1&2&3&4\\\hline P(X=x)&0.35&a&0.2&b\\\hline x\cdot p(x)&0.35&2a&0.6&4b\end{array}$$
$$\begin{aligned}0.35+a+0.2+b&=1\\a+b&=0.45 &&(1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)=0.35+2a+0.6+4b&=2.15\\2a+4b&=1.2\\a+2b&=0.6 &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtract (1) from (2):
$$b=0.15$$
Substitute into (1):
$$a+0.15=0.45$$
$$\therefore\ a=0.3,\ b=0.15$$
criteria: Forms both equations, or equivalent merit

Each day, $\dfrac{3}{5}$ of the cookies produced are chocolate chip and the rest are oatmeal. According to demand, $\dfrac{5}{7}$ of the chocolate chip cookies are regular and the rest of the chocolate chip cookies are sugar free, while $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of the oatmeal cookies are sugar free and the rest of the oatmeal cookies are regular.

parts.latex: A cookie is selected at random. Given that a sugar free cookie is selected, find the probability that the cookie was chocolate-chip.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1286_q20_s1}

Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P(C\mid S)&=\dfrac{P(C\cap S)}{P(S)}\\&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{2}{7}}{\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{2}{7}+\frac{2}{5}\times\frac{2}{3}}\\&=\dfrac{6}{35}\div\dfrac{46}{105}\\&=\dfrac{9}{23}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A company tracked the number of sales made by each sales staff in a day. Using the data from a large number of days, the company estimated the probability of the number of sales made by each sales staff in a day.

Let the random variable $S$ be the number of sales made by Linda per day.

The following table shows the probability data for Linda's daily sales.

\extable{1286_q21_t1}

Linda is expected to make 5.05 sales per day. Find Linda's variance and standard deviation, correct to two decimal places.

(Hint: Add any required rows in the table using the space provided above.)

dif.r: Standard variance formula from table with given mean

solutions.latex:
Variance uses $\mathrm{Var}(S)=\Sigma s^2p(s)-E(S)^2$, so add a row for $s^2p(s)$.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c}s&2&3&4&5&6&7\\\hline P(S=s)&0.05&0.1&0.15&0.35&0.15&0.2\\\hline s^2&4&9&16&25&36&49\\\hline s^2p(s)&0.2&0.9&2.4&8.75&5.4&9.8\end{array}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(S)&=(0.2+0.9+2.4+8.75+5.4+9.8)-5.05^2\\&=27.45-25.5025\\&=1.9475\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \mathrm{Var}(S)\approx 1.95$$
$$\sigma=\sqrt{1.9475}\approx 1.40$$
$$\therefore\ \sigma\approx 1.40$$
criteria: Correct values of $s^2p(s)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
An ice cream company launches a promotion in which customers have a chance of winning a limited edition item. The probability of winning this prize is 0.07 with each individual purchase. Each person can only win the prize once.

Benjamin decides to purchase one ice block each day until he wins the prize.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the probability that he wins the item on the first or second day, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Two-stage probability: win now, or lose then win

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the smallest number of days for which the probability that Benjamin will win the limited edition item, is greater than 80%.

dif.r: Builds geometric sum inequality, solves with logs, rounds up

solutions.latex:
Let $W$ be the event that Benjamin wins on a given day, so $P(W)=0.07$ and $P(\overline{W})=0.93$.

He wins on the first or second day if he wins on day 1, or loses on day 1 and wins on day 2:
$$\begin{aligned}P(A)&=P(W)+P(\overline{W})P(W)\\&=0.07+0.93\times 0.07\\&=0.1351\end{aligned}$$
Hence the probability that Benjamin wins on the first or second day is $0.14$.
criteria: Forms the expression for the probability, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The probabilities that Benjamin first wins on day $1, 2, 3,\cdots$ are
$$0.07,\ 0.93\times 0.07,\ 0.93^2\times 0.07,\ \cdots$$
This is a geometric sequence with $a=0.07$ and $r=0.93$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$, we need
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{0.07(1-0.93^n)}{1-0.93}&>0.8\\1-0.93^n&>0.8 &&(\text{since } 1-0.93=0.07)\\-0.93^n&>-0.2\\0.93^n&<0.2\end{aligned}$$
Take logs (dividing by $\log 0.93<0$ reverses the inequality):
$$\begin{aligned}n&>\log_{0.93}0.2\\&=\dfrac{\log_{10}0.2}{\log_{10}0.93}\\&\approx 22.18\end{aligned}$$
Hence the smallest number of days is $23$.
criteria: Solves for $n$ with minor error, or equivalent merit
Significant progress in solving for $n$, or equivalent merit
Forms the equation for the geometric sum, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A function is given by $f(x)=-(x-2)(x+2)(x-1)$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Sketch the curve in space provided without using calculus. Show all intercepts with the axes.

dif.r: Sketch factorised cubic with negative leading coefficient

skills: Graphs of cubic and polynomial functions

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the exact area bounded by the curve and the $x$-axis.

dif.r: Area split across sign change; cubic integration with fractions

figures.cap: solution sketch: guideline sketch of f(x) = -(x-2)(x+2)(x-1)

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1286_q23_s1}

Expand the factorised form.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=-(x^2-4)(x-1)\\ &=-(x^3-x^2-4x+4) \end{aligned}$$
The curve lies below the $x$-axis for $-2\le x\le 1$ and above it for $1\le x\le 2$, so the area uses the negative of the signed area on $[-2,1]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=-\int_{-2}^{1}\left[-(x^3-x^2-4x+4)\right]dx+\int_{1}^{2}\left[-(x^3-x^2-4x+4)\right]dx\\&=\int_{-2}^{1}\left(x^3-x^2-4x+4\right)dx-\int_{1}^{2}\left(x^3-x^2-4x+4\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+4x\right]_{-2}^{1}-\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+4x\right]_{1}^{2}\\&=[F(1)-F(-2)]-[F(2)-F(1)]\\&=\left(\dfrac{23}{12}-\left(-\dfrac{28}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\dfrac{4}{3}-\dfrac{23}{12}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area}=\dfrac{71}{6}\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Forms the area using signed areas, or equivalent merit
Correct integral of $f(x)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A function is given by $f(x)=-\dfrac{1}{2}x^4+2x^3+\dfrac{3}{2}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points; f''=0 needs concavity table check

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that there is another point of inflexion at $x=2$.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and check concavity change

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence sketch the curve in the space provided, showing all stationary points and points of inflexion. (Do not find the $x$-intercepts)

dif.r: Sketch quartic using found stationary and inflexion points

figures.cap: solution sketch: guideline sketch of f(x) with stationary points and inflexions

solutions.latex:
$$f'(x)=-2x^3+6x^2$$
$$f''(x)=-6x^2+12x$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2x^3+6x^2&=0\\ -2x^2(x-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=3$.

When $x=0$: $f(0)=\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $f''(0)=0$, so there is a potential point of inflexion at $x=0$. Test the concavity either side.

\extable{Ts8410_1}

The concavity changes, hence $\left(0,1\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

When $x=3$: $f(3)=15$ and $f''(3)=-18<0$.

Hence $(3,15)$ is a maximum stationary point.
criteria: Correctly tests the nature of both stationary points, or equivalent merit
Correct coordinates for both stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Points of inflexion occur when $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-6x^2+12x&=0\\ -6x(x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=2$.

From part (a), there is a horizontal point of inflexion at $\left(0,1\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

When $x=2$: $f(2)=\dfrac{19}{2}$. Test the concavity either side of $x=2$.

\extable{Ts8411_1}

The concavity changes at $x=2$.

Hence $\left(2,9\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.
criteria: Finds $x=2$ as a solution of $f''(x)=0$, or equivalent merit
