questions.stem:
A company is designing a closed cylindrical container of radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm for their new product. The container is to have a surface area of $112\pi\ \text{cm}^2$.

\exfigure{1286_q25_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the volume of the container is given by the expression:

$$V=56\pi r-\pi r^3$$

dif.r: Set up volume from surface area constraint, eliminate h

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the radius for which the volume of the container is maximised, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Differentiate cubic, solve, verify maximum with second derivative

figures.cap: closed cylinder with radius r and height h

solutions.latex:
The surface area of a closed cylinder is $SA=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$.
$$\begin{aligned}112\pi&=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\\ 112\pi-2\pi r^2&=2\pi rh\\ h&=\dfrac{56-r^2}{r}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into $V=\pi r^2h$.
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\pi r^2\left(\dfrac{56-r^2}{r}\right)\\ &=56\pi r-\pi r^3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dV}{dr}=56\pi-3\pi r^2$$
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2}=-6\pi r$$
Turning points occur when $\dfrac{dV}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}56\pi-3\pi r^2&=0\\ r^2&=\dfrac{56}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Since $r\ge 0$, $r=\sqrt{\dfrac{56}{3}}$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dr^2}=-6\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{56}{3}}<0$$
Hence the volume is maximised when $r\approx 4.32$ cm.
criteria: Correct value of $r$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=e^{-\sin x}$ at $x=\pi$.

dif.r: Chain rule with exponential-trig, then point-gradient tangent

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\cos x\cdot e^{-\sin x}$$
When $x=\pi$: $y=1$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$.

So the gradient is $m=1$ at $(\pi,1)$.

Using the point-gradient form of a straight line:
$$\begin{aligned}y-1&=1\times(x-\pi)\\ y&=x-\pi+1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the tangent is } y=x-\pi+1$$
criteria: Correct gradient at $x=\pi$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source integral wrote dx for dt in part; corrected in id 8416 (see that note).

parts.latex:
The population $P$ of a colony of ants is given by $P(t)$, where $t$ is the time in years after a scientist first discovered the colony. The ant population changes at a rate modelled by the function:

$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=1800e^{0.6t}$$

The colony had a population of 700 ants when first discovered by the scientist. Calculate the number of years for the population to reach 79\,700 ants, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Integrate rate, find constant, solve exponential equation with logs

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate of change.
$$P=\int 1800e^{0.6t}\,dt=3000e^{0.6t}+c$$
When $t=0$, $P=700$:
$$\begin{aligned}700&=3000e^0+c\\ c&=-2300\end{aligned}$$
So $P=3000e^{0.6t}-2300$.

When $P=79\,700$:
$$\begin{aligned}79\,700&=3000e^{0.6t}-2300\\ \dfrac{82}{3}&=e^{0.6t}\\ \ln\dfrac{82}{3}&=0.6t\\ t&=\dfrac{5}{3}\ln\dfrac{82}{3}\end{aligned}$$
Hence the population reaches $79\,700$ after $t\approx 5.51$ years.
criteria: Significant progress in solving for $t$, or equivalent merit
Correct integral of $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote $dx$ in the integral with respect to $t$; corrected to $dt$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Differentiate $y=2\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^5$

dif.r: Nested chain rule with exponential inside power

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find $\displaystyle\int 5x^2e^{x^3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4\,dx$.

dif.r: Reverse previous derivative, adjusting constant factor

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $y=2u^5$ with $u=7-e^{x^3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=10\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4\times\left(-3x^2e^{x^3}\right)\\ &=-30x^2e^{x^3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the chain rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a):
$$\int-30x^2e^{x^3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4dx=2\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^5+c$$
Divide both sides by $-6$.
$$\therefore\ \int5x^2e^{x^3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^4dx=-\dfrac{1}{3}\left(7-e^{x^3}\right)^5+c$$
criteria: Correct use of part (a), or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The functions $f(x)=2-\dfrac{1}{e^x}$ and $g(x)=4e^x-3$ intersect at points $P$ and $Q$ as shown.

\exfigure{1286_q29_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the curves intersect when $4e^{2x}-5e^x+1=0$.

dif.r: Equate curves and multiply through by e^x

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the points of intersection occur at $x=0$ and $x=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}$.

dif.r: Factorise quadratic in e^x and take logs

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence find the area of the region bounded by $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, correct to three decimal places.

dif.r: Area between exponential curves with log limits, careful evaluation

figures.cap: graphs of f(x) and g(x) intersecting at P and Q with the region between shaded

solutions.latex:
Equate $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned}4e^x-3&=2-\dfrac{1}{e^x}\\ 4e^{2x}-3e^x&=2e^x-1 &&(\text{multiply by } e^x)\\ 4e^{2x}-5e^x+1&=0\end{aligned}$$

Factorise the quadratic in $e^x$.
$$(4e^x-1)(e^x-1)=0$$
So $e^x=\dfrac{1}{4}$ or $e^x=1$.

Hence $x=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}$ or $x=0$.

From the graph, $f(x)$ is above $g(x)$ between the intersections.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\left[\left(2-\dfrac{1}{e^x}\right)-(4e^x-3)\right]dx\\&=\int_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\left(5-e^{-x}-4e^x\right)dx\\&=\left[5x+e^{-x}-4e^x\right]_{\ln\frac{1}{4}}^{0}\\&=\left(0+e^0-4e^0\right)-\left(5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}+e^{-\ln\frac{1}{4}}-4e^{\ln\frac{1}{4}}\right)\\&=(-3)-\left(5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}+4-1\right)\\&=-5\ln\dfrac{1}{4}-6\\&=5\ln 4-6\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A\approx 0.931 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Significant progress in finding the area, or equivalent merit
Forms the integral for the area between $f(x)$ and $g(x)$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x)=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}$.

dif.r: One chain-rule step on (cos x)^-1

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Hence show that the derivative of $y=\dfrac{\sec x}{\sin x+\cos x}$ can be expressed as:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\tan^2 x+2\tan x-1}{1+2\sin x\cos x}$$

dif.r: Quotient rule then trig simplification to a given form

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec x=(\cos x)^{-1}$ and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left((\cos x)^{-1}\right)\\ &=-(\cos x)^{-2}\times(-\sin x)\\ &=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}\end{aligned}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, and part (a), with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=\sec x & v&=\sin x+\cos x\\ u'&=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2x} & v'&=\cos x-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(\sin x+\cos x)\cdot\frac{\sin x}{\cos^2x}-\sec x(\cos x-\sin x)}{(\sin x+\cos x)^2}\\&=\dfrac{\tan^2x+\tan x-1+\tan x}{\sin^2x+\cos^2x+2\sin x\cos x}\\&=\dfrac{\tan^2x+2\tan x-1}{1+2\sin x\cos x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Significant progress in manipulating the derivative, or equivalent merit
Forms the derivative using the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the primitive function $F(x)$ of the function $f(x)=\cot x$, given that $F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=3$.

dif.r: Recognise f'/f form for cot x, find constant

solutions.latex:
Write the function in terms of sine and cosine.
$$f(x)=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$$
$$F(x)=\ln|\sin x|+c$$
Using $F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}3&=\ln 1+c\\ c&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\ln|\sin x|+3$$
criteria: Correct value of $c$, or equivalent merit
Correct integral of $f(x)$ with absolute value signs, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The velocity of a particle is given by:

$$v(t)=-6\cos 2t\qquad\text{for } 0\le t\le 2\pi$$

where $v$ is measured in metres per second and time is measured in seconds.

After $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds, the particle has a displacement of 4 metres.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the displacement of the particle is given by:

$$x(t)=-3\sin 2t+4$$

dif.r: Integrate trig velocity and find constant from condition

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $x(t)$ as a function of $t$ for $0\le t\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: Sketch reflected, shifted sine with period pi over two cycles

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the acceleration of the particle in terms of $t$, and hence state the maximum magnitude of acceleration.

dif.r: Differentiate velocity, read amplitude for maximum

skills: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.label: d
parts.latex: State the values of $t$ for which the displacement of the particle is increasing at an increasing rate.

dif.r: Interpret increasing at increasing rate as x'>0 and x''>0

figures.cap: solution sketch: guideline sketch of x(t)
solution sketch: x(t) with inflexion points and minima marked

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=\int(-6\cos 2t)\,dt\\ &=-6\times\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2t+c\\ &=-3\sin 2t+c\end{aligned}$$
When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=-3\sin\pi+c\\ c&=4\end{aligned}$$
Hence the displacement is $x(t)=-3\sin 2t+4$.
criteria: Correct integral of $v(t)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote $dx$ in the integral with respect to $t$; corrected to $dt$.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1286_q32_s1}
criteria: Correctly sketched shape and period, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}a(t)&=\dfrac{d}{dt}(-6\cos 2t)\\ &=-6(-2\sin 2t)\\ &=12\sin 2t\end{aligned}$$
The amplitude of the acceleration is $12$.

Hence the maximum magnitude of acceleration is $12 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
criteria: Correct equation for acceleration, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The displacement increases at an increasing rate when $x'(t)>0$ and $x''(t)>0$, that is, when the curve is rising and concave up.

From the properties of a sine curve, the displacement graph has:

Points of inflexion at $t=0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ 2\pi$.

Minimum turning points at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

\exfigure{1286_q32_s2}

Hence the displacement is increasing at an increasing rate when
$$\dfrac{\pi}{4}<t<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\dfrac{5\pi}{4}<t<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
criteria: Correctly states one range of $t$-values, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source used the variable $x$ for the time axis in the final ranges; written as $t$ here to match the question.

parts.latex: The period of $f(x)=4\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+1$ is:

dif.r: Direct recall of period formula 2π/b

solutions.latex:
The period of $a\cos(bx)+c$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$, with $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{2\pi}{3}} \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is C.

parts.latex: If $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+1}{4-x^2}$ then the vertical and horizontal asymptotes are respectively:

dif.r: Vertical asymptotes from denominator plus limit for horizontal asymptote

solutions.latex:
The function is undefined when the denominator is zero.
$$4-x^2=0 \text{ gives } x=\pm 2$$
So the vertical asymptotes are $x=-2$ and $x=2$.

As $x\to\infty$, $\dfrac{x^2+1}{4-x^2}\to\dfrac{1}{-1}$, so $y\to-1$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y=-1$.

Hence the answer is B.

parts.latex:
The $7^{\text{th}}$ term of an arithmetic sequence is 45 and the $11^{\text{th}}$ term is 77.

Find the first term ($a$) and the common difference ($d$).

dif.r: Two simultaneous equations from AP terms

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic sequence $T_n=a+(n-1)d$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_7 &= a+6d=45 \\ T_{11} &= a+10d=77 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting, $4d=32$, so $d=8$.

Then $a=45-6\times 8=-3$.

Hence the answer is A.

parts.latex: Find the derivative of $e^{x\sin 3x}$.

dif.r: Chain rule combined with product rule

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u}=u'e^{u}$ with $u=x\sin 3x$.

Using the product rule for $u'$:
$$\begin{aligned} u'&=\sin 3x\cdot 1+x\cdot 3\cos 3x \\ &=\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$
So the derivative is
$$e^{x\sin 3x}\left(\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x\right)$$
Hence the answer is B.

parts.latex:
The graph of a function $f$ is obtained from the graph of the function $g$ with rule $g(x)=\sqrt{2x-5}$ by a reflection in the $x$-axis, followed by a horizontal dilation from the $y$-axis by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Which one of the following is the rule for the function $f$?

dif.r: Two transformations applied in order, dilation factor handling

solutions.latex:
Reflection in the $x$-axis replaces $g(x)$ by $-g(x)$.

A horizontal dilation by factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ replaces $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{\frac{1}{2}}=2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{2x-5} &\text{ becomes } -\sqrt{2x-5} \\ &\text{ becomes } -\sqrt{2(2x)-5} \\ &= -\sqrt{4x-5} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is D.

dif.r: Find a from probabilities summing to 1, then mean

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} a+3a+5a+7a &= 1 \\ 16a &= 1 \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{16} \end{aligned}$$
The mean is $\mu=\sum x\,p(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= 0+3a+10a+21a \\ &= 34a \\ &= \dfrac{34}{16} \\ &= \dfrac{17}{8} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is D.

dif.r: Log laws to quadratic, reject invalid root

solutions.latex:
Using $n\ln a=\ln a^n$:

So $x=3$ or $x=-1$.

But $x=-1$ cannot be substituted into $\ln x$, so it is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x=3$$

The parabola is concave up with roots $-3$ and $6$, so it is above or on the axis outside the roots.
$$\therefore\ x\le -3 \text{ or } x\ge 6$$

questions.stem: For the curve: $y=x^3-3x^2-9x+4$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find any stationary points and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points and second derivative test for cubic

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find any points of inflexion.

dif.r: Solve y''=0 and check concavity change

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Sketch the curve, showing all main features.

dif.r: Sketch cubic using previously found features

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of the cubic with max (-1,9), inflexion (1,-7), min (3,-23), y-intercept 4

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 3x^2-6x-9 \\ &= 3(x^2-2x-3) \\ &= 3(x-3)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
$$y''=6x-6=6(x-1)$$
For stationary points $y'=0$, so $x=3$ or $x=-1$.

When $x=3$, $y=-23$. When $x=-1$, $y=9$.

At $(3,-23)$, $y''=6(3-1)=12>0$, so a local minimum.

At $(-1,9)$, $y''=6(-1-1)=-12<0$, so a local maximum.

$$\therefore\ \text{local minimum at } (3,-23),\ \text{local maximum at } (-1,9)$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For inflexions $y''=0$, so $6(x-1)=0$, giving $x=1$ and $y=-7$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} x=0&: y''=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ x=2&: y''=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is an inflexion.
$$\therefore\ \text{inflexion at } (1,-7)$$
criteria: Finds $x=1$ without the test, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$\cos\theta=0.6=\dfrac{3}{5}$, with $\cos\theta>0$ and $\sin\theta<0$, so $\theta$ is in Quadrant 4 and $\tan\theta<0$.

Using the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5:
$$\tan\theta=-\dfrac{4}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ \cot\theta=-\dfrac{3}{4}$$
Alternatively, since $\sin\theta<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= -\sqrt{1-\cos^2\theta} \\ &= -\sqrt{1-\dfrac{9}{25}} \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \cot\theta &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{3}{5}}{-\frac{4}{5}} \\ &= -\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A geometric progression has $5^{\text{th}}$ term $9$ and $13^{\text{th}}$ term $59\,049$.

dif.r: Divide GP terms, even root gives two ratios

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the $19^{\text{th}}$ term.

dif.r: Substitute into GP term formula

solutions.latex:
Using $T_n=ar^{n-1}$:
$$T_5=ar^4=9,\qquad T_{13}=ar^{12}=59\,049$$
Dividing:
$$\dfrac{ar^{12}}{ar^4}=\dfrac{59\,049}{9}$$
So $r^8=6561$, giving $r=3$ or $r=-3$.

Substituting into $ar^4=9$:
$$a(81)=9$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{9},\ r=\pm 3$$

$$\begin{aligned} T_{19} &= ar^{18} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9}\cdot 3^{18} \\ &= 3^{16} \\ &= 43\,046\,721 \end{aligned}$$
The same result follows from $r=-3$, since $(-3)^{18}=3^{18}$.

questions.stem: The number of bacteria in a culture can be modelled by $B=120\,000\,e^{0.4t}$ where $t$ is the time in hours after the experiment started.

parts.label: a

dif.r: Direct substitution into exponential model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How fast was the culture growing after 6 hours?

dif.r: Differentiate exponential and substitute

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What was the average rate of increase over the first 6 hours?

dif.r: Average rate needs B(6) and a difference quotient, not the derivative

parts.label: d
parts.latex: How long, in hours and minutes, will it take until the number of bacteria doubles?

dif.r: Standard exponential equation solved with logarithms, then converted to hours and minutes

solutions.latex:
The growth rate is the derivative:
$$\dfrac{dB}{dt}=0.4\times 120\,000\,e^{0.4t}=48\,000\,e^{0.4t}$$
At $t=6$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dB}{dt} &= 48\,000\,e^{2.4} \\ &= 529\,112 \text{ per hour} \end{aligned}$$

At $t=0$, $B=120\,000e^0=120\,000$.

Average rate of increase over the first 6 hours:
$$\begin{aligned} &= \dfrac{1\,322\,781-120\,000}{6} \\ &= 200\,463 \text{ per hour} \end{aligned}$$

Doubling means $B=240\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 240\,000 &= 120\,000\,e^{0.4t} \\ e^{0.4t} &= 2 \\ 0.4t &= \ln 2 \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.4} \\ &\approx 1.732867\ldots \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1 \text{ hour } 44 \text{ minutes (nearest minute)}$$

solutions.latex:
At $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$:
$$\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{3}\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3} &= \sqrt{3}\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= \sqrt{3}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So both curves pass through $\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.

Alternatively, $\sin x=\sqrt{3}\cos x$ gives $\tan x=\sqrt{3}$, so $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

The second intersection has $x>\pi$, so $x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ and $y=\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

meta.format_note: Source said 'But $x>4$'; read as $x>\pi$ (second intersection) and corrected here.

solutions.latex:
The shaded region lies below the $x$-axis, so each integral is taken in absolute value:
$$\text{Area}=\left|\int_{\pi}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\sin x\,dx\right|+\left|\int_{\frac{4\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}}\sqrt{3}\cos x\,dx\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= \left|\Big[-\cos x\Big]_{\pi}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\right|+\left|\Big[\sqrt{3}\sin x\Big]_{\frac{4\pi}{3}}^{\frac{3\pi}{2}}\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{1}{2}+(-1)\right|+\left|-\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\left|-\sqrt{3}+\dfrac{3}{2}\right| \end{aligned}$$
As $\sqrt{3}>\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &= \sqrt{3}-1 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: For events $A$ and $B$ from a sample space, $P(A|B)=\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{3}$

dif.r: One multiplication using the conditional probability formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate $P(\bar{A}\cap B)$ where $\bar{A}$ denotes the complement of $A$.

dif.r: Complement within conditional probability, or subtract from P(B)

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If $A$ and $B$ are independent, calculate $P(A\cup B)$

dif.r: Independence gives P(A), then apply the addition rule

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B)&=P(A|B)\cdot P(B) \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

Using the conditional probability formula for $\bar A$ given $B$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\bar A\cap B)&=P(\bar A|B)\cdot P(B) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively,
$$\begin{aligned} P(\bar A\cap B)&=P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$

If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $P(A)=P(A|B)=\dfrac{3}{4}$.

Using the addition rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}+\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Rewrite the gradient so the numerator is the derivative of the denominator:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3x}{x^2+e}=\dfrac{3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2x}{x^2+e}$$
so
$$y=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln(x^2+e)+C$$
The curve passes through $(0,2)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln e+C \\ 2&=\dfrac{3}{2}+C \\ C&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Therefore
$$y=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln(x^2+e)+\dfrac{1}{2}$$

parts.latex: Find the rule for the composite function $f\circ g$

dif.r: Direct substitution to form the composite

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the domain of $f\circ g$

dif.r: Two domain conditions on nested square roots

solutions.latex: $$f\circ g(x)=f(g(x))=\sqrt{2-\sqrt{x}}$$

$\sqrt{x}$ needs $x\ge 0$.

The outer square root needs $2-\sqrt{x}\ge 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{x}&\le 2 \\ x&\le 4 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore the domain is
$$0\le x\le 4 \text{ (i.e. } [0,4])$$
criteria: Finds one correct condition on $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Given the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ below, with turning points as shown, sketch the transformed function $y=3f(x+2)-4$. ($x$-intercepts not required).

\exfigure{1300_q32_1}

dif.r: Apply a translation and a dilation to the given turning points

figures.cap: cubic y=f(x) with turning points (0,6) and (-4,-7)
solution sketch: sketch of y = 3f(x+2) - 4 with turning points (-2,14) and (-6,-25)

solutions.latex:
The transformation $y=3f(x+2)-4$ shifts the graph $2$ units left, stretches it vertically by a factor of $3$, then shifts it $4$ units down.

The point $(0,6)$ becomes
$$x=-2,\quad y=3(6)-4=14,\quad\text{so }(-2,14)$$
The point $(-4,-7)$ becomes
$$x=-6,\quad y=3(-7)-4=-25,\quad\text{so }(-6,-25)$$
\exfigure{1300_q32_s1}
criteria: Finds one correct transformed turning point, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Differentiate $y=\log_e(\cos x)$ with respect to $x$.

dif.r: Routine chain rule on a log of a cosine

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch $y=\tan x$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

dif.r: Familiar tan graph sketched on a restricted domain

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Hence, using parts (a) and (b), find the area bounded by $y=\tan x$, the $x$-axis, and the line $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

(leave answer in simplest exact form)

dif.r: Reverses the earlier derivative with a sign change, exact log simplification

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = tan x on 0 to pi/2 with asymptote and shaded area to pi/3

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $y=\ln(\cos x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=-\sin x\cdot\dfrac{1}{\cos x} \\ &=-\tan x \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1300_q33_s1}

By part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\cos x)=-\tan x$. By part (b), $\tan x\ge 0$ on $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan x\,dx \\ &=-\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}(-\tan x)\,dx \\ &=-\Big[\ln(\cos x)\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &=-\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\ln 1\right] \\ &=-(\ln 1-\ln 2-\ln 1) \\ &=\ln 2\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the primitive and substitutes the limits, or equivalent merit
Finds the primitive, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The diagram shows $y=f'(x)$, the graph of the derivative function of $y=f(x)$.

\exfigure{1300_q34_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Explain why there is a horizontal point of inflection at $x=-2$

dif.r: Justify the inflection from the sign of f' on both sides

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that $f(0)=2$, sketch a possible graph of $y=f(x)$.

dif.r: Reconstructs f from the f' graph, including stationary and inflection features

skills: Graphs of f, f′ and f″

figures.cap: graph of y=f'(x), touching the x-axis at x=-2, crossing at x=1, y-intercept -4
solution sketch: sketch of a possible y = f(x) with horizontal inflexion at x=-2, minimum at x=1, y-intercept 2

solutions.latex:
At $x=-2$, $f'(x)=0$, so it is a stationary point.

Also $f''(x)>0$ to the left of $x=-2$ and $f''(x)<0$ to the right, so the concavity changes.

Therefore there is a horizontal point of inflexion at $x=-2$.

Alternatively, $f'(x)=0$ at $x=-2$ but $f'(x)$ is negative on both sides of $-2$, so the stationary point is a horizontal inflexion.
\exfigure{1300_q34_s1}
criteria: Shows a horizontal inflexion at $x=-2$, a minimum turning point at $x=1$ or the $y$-intercept $2$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to $y=x\sin x$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

dif.r: Product rule, then gradient of the normal and the line equation

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $y=x\sin x$:
$$y'=\sin x\cdot 1+x\cos x$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$y=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$
$$y'=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1$$
So the gradient of the normal is $m_N=-1$.

The normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{\pi}{2}&=-1\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ y&=-x+\pi \end{aligned}$$
Therefore the normal is $y=-x+\pi$ (i.e. $x+y-\pi=0$).
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit
Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Sketch $y=|x|-1$ and $y=2x+2$ neatly on the same number plane.

dif.r: Sketch a familiar absolute value graph and a line

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence solve the equation $|x|-2x=3$

dif.r: Rearranges the equation to match the sketched graphs' intersection

skills: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = |x| - 1 and y = 2x + 2 intersecting at (-1, 0)

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1300_q36_s1}

If $|x|-2x=3$, then $|x|=2x+3$.

Subtracting $1$ from both sides gives
$$|x|-1=2x+2$$
So the solution is where the graphs in part (a) intersect.

Therefore
$$x=-1$$

questions.stem: One half percent ($0.5\,\%$) of a country has a certain viral disease. A test is developed for the disease. The test gives a false positive $3\%$ of the time, and a false negative $2\%$ of the time.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that the probability that Andy, a randomly selected person, tests positive is $0.03475$

[Hint: in this question, let $D$ be the event that Andy has the disease, and $\overline{D}$ be the event Andy does not have it. Let $T$ be the event that Andy's test comes back positive.]

dif.r: Law of total probability with false positive and false negative rates

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Andy just got the bad news that his test came back positive.

Find the probability that Andy actually has the disease.

dif.r: Reverse conditional probability (Bayes) using the earlier result

solutions.latex:
A person tests positive either with the disease or without it, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(T)&=P(T|D)\cdot P(D)+P(T|\bar D)\cdot P(\bar D) \\ &=(0.98)(0.005)+(0.03)(0.995) \\ &=0.03475 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $P(T)$ as the sum of the two correct products, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(D|T)&=\dfrac{P(D\cap T)}{P(T)} \\ &=\dfrac{P(T|D)\cdot P(D)}{P(T)} \\ &=\dfrac{(0.98)(0.005)}{0.03475} \\ &=0.141\ldots \\ &\approx 14\% \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows a sector of a circle of radius $r$ centimetres. The angle at the centre is $\theta$ radians, and the perimeter of the whole sector is $8\ \text{cm}$.

\exfigure{1300_q38_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $r=\dfrac{8}{2+\theta}$.

dif.r: Perimeter of a sector set up from the arc length formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that $A$, the area of the sector in $\text{cm}^2$, is given by

$$A=\dfrac{32\theta}{(\theta+2)^2}$$

dif.r: Substitute r into the sector area formula

parts.label: c
parts.latex: If $0\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, find the maximum area of the sector, and the value of $\theta$ for which this occurs.

dif.r: Quotient rule; stationary points outside domain, so endpoints give maximum

figures.cap: sector of a circle with radius r, arc l and angle theta

solutions.latex:
The arc length is $l=r\theta$, and the perimeter is two radii plus the arc:
$$\begin{aligned} r+r+r\theta&=8 \\ r(2+\theta)&=8 \\ r&=\dfrac{8}{2+\theta} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Using the sector area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ and $r=\dfrac{8}{2+\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{8}{2+\theta}\right)^2\theta \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{64\theta}{(2+\theta)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{32\theta}{(2+\theta)^2} \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=32\theta & v&=(\theta+2)^2 \\ u'&=32 & v'&=2(\theta+2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=\dfrac{(\theta+2)^2\cdot 32-32\theta\cdot 2(\theta+2)}{(\theta+2)^4}$$
For a stationary point $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 32(\theta+2)^2-64\theta(\theta+2)&=0 \\ 32(\theta+2)\left[\theta+2-2\theta\right]&=0 \\ 32(\theta+2)(2-\theta)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
so $\theta=-2$ or $\theta=2$.

But $0\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and both values lie outside this range, so the maximum occurs at an endpoint.

At $\theta=0$:
$$A=0$$
At $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{32\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+2\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{16\pi}{\left(\frac{\pi+4}{2}\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{64\pi}{(\pi+4)^2} \\ &\approx 3.9422\ \text{cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore the maximum area is $\dfrac{64\pi}{(\pi+4)^2}\ \text{cm}^2\approx 3.9422\ \text{cm}^2$, obtained when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ radians.
criteria: Shows that the stationary points lie outside the range and tests the endpoints, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Which of the following represents a many-to-one relation?

\exfigure{1289_q4_1}

dif.r: Classify three relations using many-to-one definition

figures.cap: table of three relations I (lower semicircle graph), II (set of ordered pairs), III (mapping diagram)

solutions.latex:
A many-to-one relation has each $x$-value giving only one $y$-value, but some different $x$-values giving the same $y$-value.

I: it is the lower half of a circle, so each $x$ gives one $y$, and $x$ and $-x$ give the same $y$. This is many-to-one.

II: $(5,-2)$ and $(5,1)$ give two $y$-values for $x=5$, so it is not many-to-one (it is many-to-many).

III: $15$ maps to both $7$ and $9$, so it is not many-to-one (it is many-to-many).
$$\therefore\ \text{I only}$$

parts.latex: If 4 is added to each score in a set, which one of the following statements will be true?
parts.note: Mean and standard deviation of a data set under a shift: summary statistics of data are Standard only, not 2024 Advanced

dif.r: Recall effect of adding constant on mean and standard deviation

options.label: A
options.latex: The mean and standard deviation will remain the same.

options.label: B
options.latex: The mean will increase by 4 and the standard deviation will remain the same.

options.label: C
options.latex: The mean will increase by 4 and the standard deviation will increase by 2.

options.label: D
options.latex: The mean will increase by 4 and the standard deviation will increase by 4.

solutions.latex:
Adding $4$ to every score shifts the whole set up by $4$, so the mean increases by $4$.

The spread of the scores about the mean is unchanged, because each score minus the mean is the same as before. Hence the standard deviation stays the same.
$$\therefore\ \text{the mean increases by } 4 \text{ and the standard deviation is unchanged}$$

parts.latex:
James plays a game involving the tossing of two coins. One turn at this game costs $\$1$. The possible outcomes are listed below along with their payoffs:

\begin{itemize}
\item 2 Heads pays $\$5$
\item 1 Head and 1 Tail pays $\$2$
\item 2 Tails pays nothing
\end{itemize}

What is the financial expectation for this game?

dif.r: Expected payoff then subtract cost of turn

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
For two fair coins, $P(2H)=\dfrac{1}{4}$, $P(1H1T)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $P(2T)=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

The expected payoff is
$$\begin{aligned} E &= \dfrac{1}{4}\times 5+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\times 0 \\ &= 1.25+1 \\ &= \$2.25 \end{aligned}$$
The turn costs $\$1$, so the financial expectation is
$$\$2.25-\$1=\$1.25$$
$$\therefore\ \text{financial expectation}=\$1.25$$

parts.latex: The maximum speed of a train going up a hill is inversely proportional to the square root of its weight. A train weighing 3600 tonnes can go up a hill at 30 km/h. What is the maximum speed at which a train weighing 2500 tonnes could go up the same hill?

dif.r: Inverse variation with square root: find k then substitute

solutions.latex:
Inverse proportion to the square root of the weight $W$ gives
$$v=\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{W}}$$
Using $W=3600$, $v=30$:
$$30=\dfrac{k}{60} \text{ so } k=1800$$
For $W=2500$:
$$v=\dfrac{1800}{\sqrt{2500}}=\dfrac{1800}{50}=36 \text{ km/h}$$
$$\therefore\ v=36 \text{ km/h}$$

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $e^{3\ln x}$?

dif.r: Simplify using log laws before differentiating

solutions.latex:
Since $e^{\ln a}=a$ and $3\ln x=\ln x^3$,
$$e^{3\ln x}=e^{\ln x^3}=x^3$$
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^3\right)=3x^2$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{3\ln x}\right)=3x^2$$

dif.r: Order of transformations matters with horizontal dilation after translation

options.label: A
options.latex:
Step 1: A vertical dilation by a factor of $2$.

Step 2: A horizontal translation to the right by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Step 3: A horizontal dilation by a factor of $2$.

options.label: B
options.latex:
Step 1: A vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Step 2: A horizontal translation to the left by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Step 3: A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

options.label: C

Step 1: A vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Step 2: A horizontal dilation by a factor of $2$.

Step 3: A horizontal translation to the right by $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

options.label: D
options.latex:
Step 1: A vertical dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Step 2: A horizontal dilation by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Step 3: A horizontal translation to the left by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

figures.cap: graph of y=g(x), cosine-shaped with amplitude 0.5

solutions.latex:
From the graph, $g$ has amplitude $0.5$, period $\pi$ (zeros at $\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, maximum at $x=0$), so
$$g(x)=0.5\cos 2x=0.5\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$$
Apply the steps of option B to $\sin x$ in order:
$$\begin{aligned} &\text{Step 1 (vertical dilation by } \dfrac{1}{2}\text{):} && 0.5\sin x \\ &\text{Step 2 (left by } \dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{):} && 0.5\sin\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ &\text{Step 3 (horizontal dilation by } \dfrac{1}{2}\text{, } x \text{ replaced by } 2x\text{):} && 0.5\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
This equals $g(x)$.

Option A has amplitude $2$. Option C has period $4\pi$. Option D gives $0.5\sin(2x+\pi)$, which is $-0.5\sin 2x$, not $g(x)$.
$$\therefore\ \text{option B}$$

parts.latex: Given that $f'(x)=3x^2-7$ and $f(3)=5$, find $f(x)$.

dif.r: Integrate polynomial then find constant from condition

solutions.latex:
Integrate $f'(x)$:
$$f(x)=\dfrac{3x^3}{3}-7x+C=x^3-7x+C$$
Use $f(3)=5$ to find $C$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5&=3^3-7\times3+C\\ &=27-21+C\\ &=6+C\end{aligned}$$
So $C=-1$.
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^3-7x-1$$

parts.latex: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=3^{2x+1}\ln x$ at the point $(1,0)$.

dif.r: Product rule with exponential base 3 and log, substitute

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3^{2x+1} & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=(2\ln3)\,3^{2x+1} & v'&=\dfrac1x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(2\ln3)\left(3^{2x+1}\right)\ln x+3^{2x+1}\times\dfrac1x$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=(2\ln3)(3^3)\ln1+3^3\times\dfrac11\\ &=27\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the gradient is } 27$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence solve the equation $\dfrac{4\cos\theta}{\tan\theta}+15=0$ for $0\leq\theta\leq2\pi$.

dif.r: Factorise quadratic in sin, reject invalid root, two quadrants

solutions.latex:
Use $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4\cos\theta}{\tan\theta}+15&=0\\ 4\cos\theta\times\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}+15&=0\\ 4\cos^2\theta+15\sin\theta&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Use $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4(1-\sin^2\theta)+15\sin\theta&=0\\ 4-4\sin^2\theta+15\sin\theta&=0\\ 4\sin^2\theta-15\sin\theta-4&=0 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Factorise the quadratic in $\sin\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4\sin^2\theta-15\sin\theta-4&=0\\ 4\sin^2\theta-16\sin\theta+\sin\theta-4&=0\\ 4\sin\theta(\sin\theta-4)+(\sin\theta-4)&=0\\ (\sin\theta-4)(4\sin\theta+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\sin\theta=4$ (no solution, since $\sin\theta\le1$) or $\sin\theta=-\dfrac14$.

Since $\sin\theta<0$, $\theta$ is in the third or fourth quadrant.
$$\theta=3.394\ldots,\ 6.031\ldots$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=3.39 \text{ or } 6.03 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Factorises the quadratic, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The continuous random variable $X$ has cumulative distribution function $F$ given by

$$F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & \text{for } x<1,\\ k(x^2-x) & \text{for } 1\leq x\leq 2,\\ 1 & \text{for } x>2,\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{1}{2}$, and hence find the $90^{\text{th}}$ percentile value of $X$, giving your answer correct to three significant figures.

dif.r: Use F(2)=1, then solve quadratic for percentile

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find an expression for $f(x)$ which represents the probability density function of $X$.

dif.r: Differentiate CDF to get PDF

solutions.latex:
Since $F$ is continuous and $F(x)=1$ for $x>2$, $F(2)=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=k(2^2-2)\\ 1&=2k\\ k&=\dfrac12\end{aligned}$$
For the $90^{\text{th}}$ percentile, solve $F(x)=0.9$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.9&=\dfrac12(x^2-x)\\ 1.8&=x^2-x\\ 0&=x^2-x-1.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{-(-1)\pm\sqrt{(-1)^2-4\times1\times(-1.8)}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{8.2}}{2}\\ &=1.932,\ -0.932\end{aligned}$$
Since $1\le x\le2$, we take the positive root.
$$\therefore\ x=1.93 \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$
criteria: Shows $k=\dfrac12$ and sets up the quadratic, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave 1.932 (3 d.p.) though the question asks for 3 significant figures; corrected to 1.93 (3 s.f.). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The density function is the derivative of $F$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=F'(x)\\ &=\dfrac12(2x-1)\\ &=x-\dfrac12\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=\begin{cases}x-\dfrac12 & 1\le x\le2\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

questions.stem:
Helen is creating a mosaic pattern by placing square tiles next to each other in a straight line. Each subsequent tile is half the area of the previous one.

\exfigure{1289_q20_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find, in terms of $w$, the length of the sides of the second largest tile.

dif.r: Side from halved area, one square-root step

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Assume the tiles are in contact with the adjacent tiles, but do not overlap. Show that, no matter how many tiles are in the pattern, the total length of the line of tiles will be less than $3.5w$.

dif.r: Recognise side lengths form GP, bound by limiting sum

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

figures.cap: row of squares, each half the area of the previous, largest side w

solutions.latex:
The areas are $A_1=w^2$ and $A_2=\dfrac12w^2$.

Let the side of the second tile be $x$.
$$x^2=\dfrac12w^2$$
Since $x>0$:
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}w$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Third tile: $A_3=\dfrac14w^2$, so the side length is $\dfrac12w$.

Fourth tile: $A_4=\dfrac18w^2$, so the side length is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}w$.

The side lengths form a geometric sequence with $a=w$ and common ratio
$$r=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.707$$
Since $|r|<1$, a limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\\ &=\dfrac{w}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}\\ &\approx3.414w\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{no matter how many tiles, the total length is less than } 3.5w$$
criteria: Identifies the geometric sequence and ratio, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The heights of female students at NSGHS are normally distributed with a mean of 168 cm and a standard deviation of 4.5 cm.

parts.latex: Find the probability that the height of a randomly selected female student attending NSGHS is between 159 cm and 163.5 cm.

dif.r: Empirical rule between -2 and -1 SD; halve the difference

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
159 cm is 2 standard deviations below the mean ($168-2\times4.5$) and 163.5 cm is 1 standard deviation below ($168-4.5$).

Using the 68%-95% rule, the probability is half the difference of the two percentages.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac12(95\%-68\%)\\ &=13.5\%\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:

Wendy is a student at NSGHS and she is 173.5 cm tall. Caleb is a student at NSBHS and he is 176 cm tall. Who is the taller student relative to their peers in their own school? Justify your answer.

solutions.latex:
Compare $z$-scores, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Wendy: } z&=\dfrac{173.5-168}{4.5}=\dfrac{11}{9}\approx1.22\\ \text{Caleb: } z&=\dfrac{176-170}{6.5}=\dfrac{12}{13}\approx0.92\end{aligned}$$

criteria: Finds one $z$-score correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Caleb would need Wendy's $z$-score of $\dfrac{11}{9}$.
$$\begin{aligned} h&=170+\dfrac{11}{9}\times6.5\\ &=\dfrac{3203}{18}\\ &\approx177.94\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Caleb would need to be about } 178 \text{ cm}$$

solutions.latex:
$OA\perp AT$ since $AT$ is a tangent, so in right-angled triangle $OAT$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{AT}{r}$.

Hence $AT=r\tan\theta$.

The shaded area is the triangle minus the sector.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\text{area }\triangle OAT-\text{sector }OAB\\ &=\dfrac12\times r\times r\tan\theta-\dfrac12r^2\theta\\ &=\dfrac12r^2\tan\theta-\dfrac12r^2\theta\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is $AT$, $BT$ and the arc $AB$.

In right-angled triangle $OAT$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac{r}{OT}$, so $OT=\dfrac{3}{\cos1.2}$, and $BT=OT-OB$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Perimeter}&=AT+BT+\text{arc }AB\\ &=3\tan1.2+(OT-OB)+3\times1.2\\ &=3\tan1.2+\left(\dfrac{3}{\cos1.2}-3\right)+3\times1.2\\ &\approx16.5955\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{perimeter}\approx16.60 \text{ cm}$$
criteria: Finds $AT$, $BT$ and the arc length, or equivalent merit

$$b=0.25$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{[5(x+h)-(x+h)^2]-[5x-x^2]}{h} \\ &=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{5x+5h-x^2-2xh-h^2-5x+x^2}{h} \\ &=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{5h-2xh-h^2}{h} \\ &=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}(5-2x-h) \\ &=5-2x \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Consider the curve $f(x)=2x^3-x^2-4x+6$. Find the stationary points of $f(x)$ and determine their nature. Then sketch the curve, clearly labelling the stationary points.

You do not need to find the $x$-intercepts of $f(x)$.

dif.r: Standard cubic stationary points, nature and sketch

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=2x^3-x^2-4x+6 \\ f'(x)&=6x^2-2x-4=2(3x^2-x-2) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$:
$$0=2(3x+2)(x-1)$$
so $x=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $x=1$.

To find the nature, use the second derivative:
$$f''(x)=12x-2$$
$$f''\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)=12\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)-2=-10<0$$
so there is a maximum turning point at $\left(-\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{206}{27}\right)$.
$$f''(1)=12\times1-2=10>0$$
so there is a minimum turning point at $(1,3)$.

\exfigure{1289_q28_s1}
criteria: Finds both stationary points and their nature, with a sketch with one error, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A teacher in college asks her mathematics students what other subjects they are studying. She finds that, of her 24 students, 12 study physics, 8 study geography and 4 study both.

A student is chosen at random from the class. Determine whether the event ‘the student studies physics’ and the event ‘the student studies geography’ are independent.

dif.r: Standard independence test comparing product to intersection

solutions.latex:
The events are independent if $P(P\cap G)=P(P)\times P(G)$.

Interpretation 1 (12 physics, 8 geography, 4 both, 8 neither):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{4}{24}=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{12}{24}\times\dfrac{8}{24}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
LHS $=$ RHS, $\therefore$ independent.

Interpretation 2 (16 physics, 12 geography, 4 both):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{4}{24}=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{16}{24}\times\dfrac{12}{24}=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
LHS $\neq$ RHS, $\therefore$ not independent.
criteria: Tests $P(P\cap G)=P(P)\times P(G)$ with one correct side, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
It is known that for the whole college:

\begin{itemize}
\item The probability of a student studying mathematics is $\dfrac{1}{5}$
\item The probability of a student studying biology is $\dfrac{1}{6}$
\item The probability of a student studying biology given that they study mathematics is $\dfrac{3}{8}$
\end{itemize}

Calculate the probability that in the whole college a student studies mathematics or biology or both.

dif.r: Conditional probability then addition rule, two steps

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Given $P(M)=\dfrac{1}{5}$, $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{6}$, $P(B|M)=\dfrac{3}{8}$. Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B|M)&=\dfrac{P(B\cap M)}{P(M)} \\ \dfrac{3}{8}&=\dfrac{P(B\cap M)}{\frac{1}{5}} \\ P(B\cap M)&=\dfrac{3}{40} \end{aligned}$$
Using the addition rule:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B\cup M)&=P(M)+P(B)-P(B\cap M) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{1}{6}-\dfrac{3}{40} \\ &=\dfrac{7}{24} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A scientist is researching the effects of caffeine. She models the mass of caffeine in the body using $m=m_0e^{-kt}$ where $m_0$ milligrams is the initial mass of caffeine in the body and $m$ milligrams is the mass of caffeine in the body after $t$ hours.

It takes 5.7 hours for the mass of caffeine in the body to halve.

One cup of strong coffee contains 200 mg of caffeine.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: The scientist drinks two strong cups of coffee at 8 am. By first finding the value of $k$, use the model to estimate the mass of caffeine in the scientist’s body at midday to the nearest gram.

dif.r: Find k from half-life then substitute

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The scientist wants the mass of caffeine in her body to stay below 480 mg. Use the model to find the earliest time that she could drink another cup of strong coffee. Give your answer to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Model reasoning: threshold 280 mg, solve exponential, convert time

solutions.latex:
At $t=5.7$, $m=\dfrac{m_0}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}&=e^{-5.7k} \\ \ln\dfrac{1}{2}&=-5.7k \\ -\ln2&=-5.7k \\ k&=\dfrac{\ln2}{5.7} \end{aligned}$$
Two cups at 8 am give $m_0=400$ mg, and midday is $t=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} m&=400e^{-4k} \\ &=245.929\ldots \\ &\approx 246 \text{ mg} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $k$ and substitutes $m_0=400$, $t=4$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source says nearest gram but gives 246 mg; kept.

solutions.latex:
Another cup adds 200 mg, so before it she needs $480-200=280$ mg in her body, with $m_0=400$.
$$\begin{aligned} 280&=400e^{-kt} \\ \dfrac{280}{400}&=e^{-kt} \\ \ln\dfrac{280}{400}&=-kt \\ t&=-\dfrac{1}{k}\ln\dfrac{280}{400} \\ &=2\text{ h }56\text{ min} \end{aligned}$$
The earliest time is 10:56 am.

questions.stem:
Consider the diagram below.

\exfigure{1289_q35_1}

$OAB$ is a sector of a circle with centre at $O$ and radius $r$ such that $\angle AOB=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$RSTU$ is a rectangle drawn inside the sector and $\angle ROA=\theta$ as shown in the diagram where $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $UT=r\cos\theta-\sqrt{3}\,r\sin\theta$.

dif.r: Geometric show-that combining two right triangles and rectangle

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that the area of the rectangle can be expressed as $A=r^2\left(\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sqrt{3}\sin^2\theta\right)$. Hence find the value of $\theta$ which will maximise the area of the rectangle.

dif.r: Trig optimisation; convert to tan quadratic, select root, verify maximum

figures.cap: sector OAB with inscribed rectangle RSTU

solutions.latex:
Since $UT=UO-OT$, find $UO$ and $OT$.

In $\triangle URO$ (right-angled at $U$):
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\theta&=\dfrac{UO}{OR} \\ UO&=r\cos\theta \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta&=\dfrac{UR}{OR} \\ UR&=r\sin\theta \end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle OTS$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\dfrac{\pi}{6}&=\dfrac{ST}{OT} \\ OT&=ST\div\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt3\,ST \end{aligned}$$
But $ST=UR$ (opposite sides of a rectangle), so
$$OT=\sqrt3\,UR=\sqrt3\,r\sin\theta$$
$$\therefore\ UT=r\cos\theta-\sqrt3\,r\sin\theta$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The area is $A=UT\times UR$ with $UR=r\sin\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=(r\cos\theta-\sqrt3\,r\sin\theta)\,r\sin\theta \\ &=r^2\left(\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sqrt3\sin^2\theta\right) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate and set $\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=r^2\left(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta-2\sqrt3\sin\theta\cos\theta\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta-2\sqrt3\sin\theta\cos\theta \\ 0&=1-\tan^2\theta-2\sqrt3\tan\theta &&(\text{divide by } \cos^2\theta) \\ 0&=\tan^2\theta+2\sqrt3\tan\theta-1 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta&=\dfrac{-2\sqrt3\pm\sqrt{(2\sqrt3)^2-4(1)(-1)}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{-2\sqrt3\pm4}{2} \\ &=-\sqrt3\pm2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $\tan\theta>0$, so $\tan\theta=2-\sqrt3$ and $\theta=15^\circ$.

Test the sign of $A'$ either side:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\theta & 14^\circ & 15^\circ & 16^\circ\\ \hline A' & 0.07r^2 & 0 & -0.07r^2\end{array}$$
Since $r^2>0$, $A'$ changes from positive to negative.
$$\therefore\ \text{the area is a maximum when } \theta=15^\circ \left(=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)$$
criteria: Solves for $\theta$ and attempts to test the nature, or equivalent merit
Shows the area expression, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given $\log_3 5 = 1.46$ and $\log_3 2 = 0.63$, evaluate $\log_3 100$

dif.r: Rewrite 100 as product, apply two log laws

solutions.latex:
Use the log laws, writing $100=2\times 5\times 10$ as $10=2\times 5$ squared.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_3 100 &= 2\log_3 10 \\ &= 2\log_3(2\times 5) \\ &= 2(\log_3 5 + \log_3 2) \\ &= 2(1.46 + 0.63) \\ &= 4.18 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: Given $f(x) = \log_e (x - 3)$ and $g(x) = x + 4$, the domain of $f(g(x))$ is

dif.r: Form composite then apply log domain condition

solutions.latex:
For $f(g(x))$, $g(x)$ is substituted into $f$, so the argument of the logarithm must be positive.
$$\begin{aligned} f(g(x)) &= \log_e[(x+4)-3] \\ &= \log_e(x+1) \end{aligned}$$
This needs $x+1>0$, so $x>-1$.

Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex:
The sample space when a fair die is rolled is $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$.

Each outcome is equally likely.

For which pair of events, $A$ and $B$, are $A$ and $B$ independent?

dif.r: Test independence condition across four event pairs

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
Events $A$ and $B$ are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$ (not the same as mutually exclusive). Test each option.

A: $\dfrac{2}{6}\ne\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{4}{6}$

B: $0\ne\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}$

C: $\dfrac{1}{6}\ne\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{2}$

D: $\dfrac{1}{6}=\dfrac{3}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{6}$

Only option D satisfies the condition, so the answer is option D.

parts.latex:
The function $f(x)$ has derivative $f'(x) = 8\sin(4x)$ and $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1$

Which of the following is $f(x)$?

dif.r: Integrate sine with coefficient, find constant from condition

solutions.latex:
Integrate $f'(x)$, using the substitution-style rule $\displaystyle \int -4\sin 4x\,dx=\cos 4x$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \int 8\sin(4x)\,dx \\ &= -2\int -4\sin(4x)\,dx \\ &= -2\cos(4x)+C \end{aligned}$$
Use $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= -2\cos\left(4\times\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)+C \\ &= -2\times(-1)+C \end{aligned}$$
So $C=-1$.
$$f(x)=-2\cos(4x)-1$$
Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be a differentiable function such that

\begin{itemize}
\item $D:(-\infty,\infty)$
\item $f'(-2) = 0$ ; and
\item $f'(x) > 0$ if $x \ne -2$
\end{itemize}

At $x = -2$, the graph of $y = f(x)$ has a

dif.r: Recognise horizontal inflection from derivative sign conditions

solutions.latex:
The only stationary point is at $x=-2$, and $f'(x)>0$ on both sides of it.

So $f$ is increasing on both sides of $x=-2$ and the gradient does not change sign.

Therefore there is a horizontal point of inflection at $x=-2$, which is option A.

parts.latex:
The graph of $y = f(x)$ undergoes a vertical dilation by a factor of $a$, followed by a horizontal translation of $b$ units to the right, and is then reflected in the $x$ axis.

The resulting graph is

dif.r: Apply three ordered transformations with general parameters

solutions.latex:
Apply the transformations in order.

Vertical dilation by $a$: $y=a\,f(x)$.

Translation $b$ units right: $y=af(x-b)$.

Reflection in the $x$ axis: $y=-af(x-b)$.

Hence the answer is option A.

dif.r: Rectangle approximation with exact trig values

figures.cap: graph of y=2cos x with two rectangles under the curve

solutions.latex:
Each rectangle has width $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and height $2\cos x$ at the right-hand end.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}\times 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{6}\times 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{2\pi}{6}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi(1+\sqrt{3})}{6} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex:
Which of the following is the correct value $S_n$ for the series given below?

$S_n = 5 + 15 + 45 + \dots + 98\,415$

dif.r: Find number of terms, then geometric sum formula

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=5$ and $r=3$. Find the number of terms from the last term.
$$\begin{aligned} 98\,415 &= 5\times 3^{n-1} \\ 19\,683 &= 3^{n-1} \end{aligned}$$
Taking logs, $\log 19\,683=(n-1)\log 3$, so $n-1=9$ and $n=10$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{5(3^{10}-1)}{3-1} \\ &= 147\,620 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex: The correct graph for $y = -2\sin\left(2x + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$ is

dif.r: Identify amplitude, reflection, period and phase shift from equation

figures.cap: option A: sine graph option A
option B: sine graph option B
option C: sine graph option C
option D: sine graph option D

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the equation to read off the phase shift.
$$y=-2\sin\left[2\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]$$
So the graph has amplitude $2$, is reflected in the $x$ axis, has period $\pi$, and is shifted $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to the left.

The graph matching these features is option D.

parts.latex:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution.

\extable{1284_q10_t1}

Let $\mu$ be the mean of $X$.

$P(X < \mu)$ is?

dif.r: Compute expected value then sum probabilities below it

solutions.latex:
The mean is found from $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= 0\times\dfrac{1}{4}+1\times\dfrac{9}{20}+2\times\dfrac{1}{10}+3\times\dfrac{1}{20}+6\times\dfrac{3}{20} \\ &= 1.7 \end{aligned}$$
The values of $X$ below $1.7$ are $0$ and $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X<\mu) &= \dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{9}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{14}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{7}{10} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex: Differentiate $e^{x\sin x}$.

dif.r: Chain rule combined with product rule

solutions.latex:
Use the chain rule: for $y=e^{f(x)}$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f'(x)e^{f(x)}$, with $f(x)=x\sin x$.

By the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=\sin x+x\cos x$.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(\sin x+x\cos x)\,e^{x\sin x}$$
criteria: Correct derivative of the index, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: A shop assistant is building a display of soup cans. The top row will contain 3 cans, and each subsequent row below will have 2 more cans than the previous row above.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: How many cans would be in the $10^{\text{th}}$ row?

dif.r: Direct arithmetic nth term formula

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: The shop assistant has 400 cans. How many rows is the tallest display that he can build using this pattern?

dif.r: Sum formula gives quadratic; solve and round down

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The numbers of cans form an arithmetic series with $a=3$ and $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{10} &= a+(n-1)d \\ &= 3+9\times 2 \\ &= 21 \end{aligned}$$

Use the sum of an arithmetic series, $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$, with $S_n=400$.
$$\begin{aligned} 400 &= \dfrac{n}{2}[6+2n-2] \\ 800 &= 4n+2n^2 \\ 0 &= n^2+2n-400 \end{aligned}$$
By the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+4\times 400}}{2} \\ &= -1\pm\sqrt{401} \\ &\approx 19.02 \text{ or } -21.02 \end{aligned}$$
The number of rows is positive, so $n\approx 19.02$. Only whole rows can be built, so round down.
$$\therefore\ 19 \text{ rows}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into formula, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The completion times for the Oztown triathlon race were normally distributed with mean time 60 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes. Using the empirical rule, find Ozzie's completion time if he finished ahead of 84% of competitors.

dif.r: Empirical rule; interpret finishing ahead as lower time

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
By the empirical rule, about $68\%$ of times lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so $16\%$ lie above $65$ minutes and $16\%$ below $55$ minutes.

To finish ahead of $84\%$ of competitors, Ozzie's time must be faster (lower) than $84\%$ of the times, so only $16\%$ are faster than him. That is one standard deviation below the mean:
$$60-5=55\text{ minutes}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Ozzie's completion time is } 55 \text{ minutes}$$
criteria: Identifies that the time is one standard deviation from the mean, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Two events, $A$ and $B$, are such that $P(A) = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $P(B) = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

If $A'$ denotes the complement of $A$, calculate $P(A' \cap B)$ when

parts.label: i
parts.latex: $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{3}{4}$

dif.r: Addition rule to find P(A' and B)

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: $A$ are $B$ are mutually exclusive.

dif.r: Recognise B lies in A' when mutually exclusive

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

solutions.latex:
Use $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ and $P(A'\cap B)=P(B)-P(A\cap B)$, which equals $P(A\cup B)-P(A)$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(A'\cap B) &= \dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{3}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{20} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Working added by us to reach the source answer $\dfrac{3}{20}$.

solutions.latex:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive then $B$ lies entirely within $A'$, so $P(A'\cap B)=P(B)$.
$$P(A'\cap B)=\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{5}{20}$$

questions.stem: Given the series $\tan^2 x - \tan^4 x + \tan^6 x - \tan^8 x + \dots$ for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Determine the values of $x$ such that the series has a limiting sum.

dif.r: Find ratio, apply |r|<1, solve trig inequality

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Write a fully simplified expression in $x$ for the limiting sum of the given series.

dif.r: Identify a and r in trig form, then simplify with Pythagorean identity.

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric. Find the common ratio.
$$r=\dfrac{-\tan^4 x}{\tan^2 x}=-\tan^2 x$$
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$|-\tan^2 x|<1$$
So $\tan^2 x<1$, which gives $-1<\tan x<1$.
$$\therefore\ -\dfrac{\pi}{4}<x<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Correct inequality for a limiting sum, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=\tan^2 x$ and $r=-\tan^2 x$.

Using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{\tan^2 x}{1-(-\tan^2 x)} \\ &= \dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\sec^2 x} \\ &= \sin^2 x \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S_\infty=\sin^2 x$$

parts.latex: Solve $2\cos(3\theta) = -1$ for $0 \le \theta \le \pi$

dif.r: Trig equation with extended domain 0 to 3π; three solutions needed.

solutions.latex:
For $0\le\theta\le\pi$, we have $0\le 3\theta\le 3\pi$.

Divide by 2:
$$\cos 3\theta=-\dfrac{1}{2}$$
The related acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, so
$$3\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{8\pi}{3}$$

parts.latex:
A particle is moving along the $x$ axis. Its displacement, $x$ metres from the origin after $t$ seconds, is given by $x = e^t - 3e^{2t}$ for $t \ge 0$ .

Explain why the particle never comes to rest.

dif.r: Differentiate, solve v=0, justify root outside domain t≥0.

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=e^t-3e^{2t} \\ v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=e^t-6e^{2t} \end{aligned}$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$e^t\left(1-6e^t\right)=0$$
Since $e^t>0$ for all $t$, $e^t=0$ has no solution (it would need $t=\ln 0$).

Otherwise $1=6e^t$, so
$$\begin{aligned} e^t&=\dfrac{1}{6} \\ t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)\approx -1.79 \end{aligned}$$
This is negative, but $t\ge 0$.

Hence $v=0$ has no solution for $t\ge 0$, so the particle never comes to rest.
criteria: Correct answer, with reasons why $v$ cannot equal $0$
Correct derivative, puts it equal to $0$ and attempts to solve, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Just stating that exponentials cannot equal $0$ earns no marks, as the question says EXPLAIN.

At $x=2$: $f(2)=-4$ and $f''(2)=6>0$ (concave up), so there is a minimum at $(2,-4)$.

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows a rectangular piece of metal, which is bent to form a gutter for the flow of water. The cross-section of a gutter is a trapezium.

\exfigure{1284_q32_1}

parts.label: i
parts.latex:
Show that the cross-sectional area $A(\theta)$, as a function of $\theta$, is given by

$$A(\theta) = 100\sin\theta\,(1 + \cos\theta)$$

dif.r: Model trapezium dimensions with trig to show area formula.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Find the angle $\theta$ that maximizes the cross-sectional area.

dif.r: Product rule, identity gives quadratic in cos θ, then nature test.

figures.cap: trapezium cross-section with sides 10 cm, base 10 cm and base angles theta

solutions.latex:
The cross-section is a trapezium, so $A=\dfrac{h}{2}(a+b)$, with parallel sides $a=10$ and $b=10+2\times 10\cos\theta$ and height $h=10\sin\theta$ (from the right-angled triangle on each side, hypotenuse $10$).
$$\begin{aligned} A(\theta)&=\dfrac{10\sin\theta}{2}\left(10+\left(10+20\cos\theta\right)\right) \\ &=5\sin\theta\left(20+20\cos\theta\right) \\ &=100\sin\theta\left(1+\cos\theta\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some progress, e.g. a correct expression for the area of the rectangle, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=1+\cos\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A'(\theta)&=100\left[\cos\theta(1+\cos\theta)+\sin\theta(-\sin\theta)\right] \\ &=100\left(\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\right) \\ &=100\left(2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1\right) \\ &=100(\cos\theta+1)(2\cos\theta-1) \end{aligned}$$
For a stationary point $A'(\theta)=0$, so $\cos\theta=-1$ or $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Since $\theta$ is acute, $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$A''(\theta)=100\left(-4\cos\theta\sin\theta-\sin\theta\right)=-100\sin\theta(4\cos\theta+1)$$
$$A''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-150\sqrt{3}<0$$
Hence the cross-sectional area is a maximum when
$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Differentiates and solves $A'(\theta)=0$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{1}{1 - \sin x} + \dfrac{1}{1 + \sin x} \equiv 2\sec^2 x$ where $\sin x \ne \pm 1$

parts.label: ii

dif.r: Area between curves reduces via prior identity to integrating sec²x.

figures.cap: shaded region between f(x)=1/(1-sin x) and g(x)=-1/(1+sin x) from x=0 to x=pi/3

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over a common denominator, then use $1-\sin^2 x=\cos^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x} \\ &=\dfrac{(1+\sin x)+(1-\sin x)}{1-\sin^2 x} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x} \\ &=2\sec^2 x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

The area between the curves is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve. Using part (i):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}-\dfrac{-1}{1+\sin x}\right)dx \\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}2\sec^2 x\,dx \\ &=2\Big[\tan x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &=2\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-0\right) \\ &=2\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Simplifies the integrand using part (i), or equivalent merit
Correct expression for the area, or some understanding of the area between two curves, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The lizards on Goanna Island are gradually dying out. The predicted population $P$ of lizards, $t$ years after the first observation was made, is $P = P_0\,e^{-0.01t}$ , where $P_0$ is the initial population.

parts.latex: When will the population decline to 10% of the original population? Leave your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
The population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP$ with $k=-0.01$, since $P=P_0e^{-0.01t}$.

At $t=45$, $P=P_0e^{-0.45}$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-0.01P_0e^{-0.45}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave $-0.1P_0e^{-0.45}$, a slip: with $k=-0.01$ the rate is $-0.01P_0e^{-0.45}$. Fixed here.

solutions.latex:
At $t=45$, $P=P_0e^{-0.45}$.

The percentage remaining is
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{P_0e^{-0.45}}{P_0}\times 100&=63.76\ldots \\ &\approx 64\% \end{aligned}$$

The population is $10\%$ of the original when $P=\dfrac{P_0}{10}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{P_0}{10}&=P_0e^{-0.01t} \\ 0.1&=e^{-0.01t} \\ \ln(0.1)&=-0.01t \\ t&=\dfrac{-\ln 10}{-0.01} \\ &=100\ln 10 \text{ years} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
The monthly sales, $X$ (in units of \$100, 000), of a business are modelled by the two probability density functions:

$$g(x) = \begin{cases} 2x & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{Model 1}$$

OR

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx^3(1 - x^2) & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \text{Model 2}$$

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Determine the value of $k$ in the second model.

dif.r: Set total pdf integral to 1 and solve for k.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Show that the two models have the same median value.

dif.r: Find median of one model, verify it in the other: show-that.

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is $1$:
$$k\int_0^1\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx=1$$
Evaluate the integral:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx&=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{x^6}{6}\right]_0^1 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{k}{12}=1$, giving
$$k=12$$

Let $M$ be the median of model $g$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}&=\int_0^M 2x\,dx \\ &=\Big[x^2\Big]_0^M \\ &=M^2 \end{aligned}$$
So $M^2=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

For model $f$, with $k=12$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^M f(x)\,dx&=\int_0^M 12\left(x^3-x^5\right)dx \\ &=\Big[3x^4-2x^6\Big]_0^M \\ &=3M^4-2M^6 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $M^2=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3M^4-2M^6&=3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{1}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Hence $x=M$ is also the median of model $f$, so the two models have the same median.
criteria: Finds $M^2$ and integrates model 2, but does not substitute $M$, or equivalent merit

look: Compare the wording with the source page

parts.latex:
The graph below shows the cubic curve $y = 9x - x^3$, with domain $[0, 4.5]$.

\exfigure{1284_q36_1}

The curve crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.

The diagram shows two bounded regions:

$R$ bounded by $y = f(x),\ y = 0,\ x = 0$ and $x = 3$

$S$ bounded by $y = f(x),\ y = 0,\ x = 3$ and $x = a$

It is given that $a > 3$. Determine the value of $a$ such that regions $R$ and $S$ have the same area.

dif.r: Equal areas means signed integral zero; solve quartic in a.

figures.cap: cubic y=9x-x^3 with regions R (0 to 3) and S (3 to a)

solutions.latex:
Region $R$ lies above the $x$-axis and region $S$ lies below it (the curve is negative for $x>3$). Equal areas mean the signed integrals cancel:
$$\int_0^3\left(9x-x^3\right)dx+\int_3^a\left(9x-x^3\right)dx=0$$
The two integrals combine into one:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a\left(9x-x^3\right)dx&=0 \\ \left[\dfrac{9x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^a&=0 \\ \dfrac{9a^2}{2}-\dfrac{a^4}{4}&=0 \\ 18a^2-a^4&=0 \\ a^2\left(18-a^2\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $a=0$ or $a=\pm 3\sqrt{2}$.

Since $a>3$, we take the positive root:
$$a=3\sqrt{2}$$
criteria: Integrates with different limits and equates, but makes no further progress, or equivalent merit
Integrates with different limits, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave two methods (separate integrals, then one integral from 0 to a); kept the single-integral method, which the first method reduces to.

questions.stem: Sam invests \$$M$ into an account at the beginning of each month. The account earns 3% p.a. interest, compounded monthly.

parts.label: i
parts.latex: Show that the total amount in the account at the end of the second month, $A_2$ is given by $A_2 = M \times (1.0025 + 1.0025^2)$

dif.r: Track two start-of-month deposits with monthly compounding.

parts.label: ii
parts.latex: Show that the amount in the account after $n$ months, $A_n$, is given by $A_n = 401M(1.0025^n - 1)$

dif.r: General annuity derivation using geometric series sum; abstract show-that.

parts.label: iii
parts.latex: Hence, calculate how much is needed to invest at the beginning of each month if the plan is to have \$6000 at the end of 12 months.

dif.r: Substitute n=12 into given formula and solve for M.

parts.label: iv
parts.latex: After the first five months of contributions, Sam increases his monthly payment to \$600. Given Sam's final contribution is less than \$600, what will be the minimum amount of this contribution (to the nearest \$5) to reach his goal of \$6000?

dif.r: Multi-stage annuity with changed payment and partial final contribution; extended reasoning.

solutions.latex:
Interest per month is $\dfrac{3}{12}\%=0.25\%$, so each month the amount grows by a factor of $1.0025$.
$$A_1=M\times\left(1+\dfrac{3}{1200}\right)=M\times 1.0025$$
At the end of month 2, $A_1$ has grown once more and the second payment has grown for one month:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1\times 1.0025+M\times 1.0025 \\ &=M\times 1.0025^2+M\times 1.0025 \\ &=M\left(1.0025+1.0025^2\right) \end{aligned}$$

Each payment earns interest for the months remaining, so
$$A_n=M\left(1.0025+1.0025^2+\dots+1.0025^n\right)$$
Factor out $1.0025$ to leave a geometric series with first term $1$, ratio $1.0025$ and $n$ terms:
$$A_n=M\times 1.0025\left(1+1.0025+\dots+1.0025^{n-1}\right)$$
Using $S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_n&=M\times 1.0025\left(\dfrac{1.0025^n-1}{1.0025-1}\right) \\ &=401M\left(1.0025^n-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct answer, showing the geometric series
Shows the geometric series, or only uses the formula without showing the series, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's factored line wrote $1.0025+1.0025^2+\dots+1.0025^{n-1}$ inside the bracket; written here as $1+1.0025+\dots+1.0025^{n-1}$, which is what factoring out $1.0025$ gives and what the next line uses.

solutions.latex:
Use $A_{12}=6000$ with the formula from part (ii):
$$\begin{aligned} 6000&=401M\left(1.0025^{12}-1\right) \\ M&=\dfrac{6000}{401\left(1.0025^{12}-1\right)} \\ &=\$491.93 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the equation but does not progress, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
First find the amount after 5 months of contributions of $\$491.93$, using the formula from part (ii):
$$A_5=401\times 491.93\left(1.0025^5-1\right)=\$2478.16$$
Amount still to save:
$$6000-2478.16=\$3521.84$$
Number of $\$600$ payments needed, from $3521.84=401\times 600\left(1.0025^n-1\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1.0025^n&=\dfrac{3521.84}{401\times 600}+1=1.01463 \\ n&=\dfrac{\ln(1.01463)}{\ln 1.0025}=5.81 \end{aligned}$$
So $5<n<6$: five full payments of $\$600$ and a smaller sixth payment.

Five payments of $\$600$:
$$401\times 600\left(1.0025^5-1\right)=\$3022.58$$
The first $\$2478.16$ earns interest for a further 5 months:
$$2478.16\times 1.0025^5=\$2509.29$$
Combined total after 10 months:
$$2509.29+3022.58=\$5531.87$$
Final contribution:
$$6000-5531.87=\$468.13\approx\$470 \text{ (to the nearest } \$5)$$
criteria: Finds the compound interest amount of $\$2509.29$, or the amount $\$3022.57$, or finds two (incorrect) subtotals using compound interest and subtracts them from $\$6000$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which graph could be used to solve the equation $\sin x + 1 = x$?

option B: line and sine curve
option C: decreasing line and cosine curve
option D: decreasing line and sine curve

solutions.latex:
Rearranging,
$$\sin x + 1 = x \quad\text{gives}\quad \sin x = x - 1$$
The solution is where the graphs $y=\sin x$ and $y = x-1$ intersect.

Hence the graph showing these two curves is the correct one, option B.

parts.latex: The function $y = \dfrac{x-3}{2-x}$ has asymptotes at:

dif.r: Vertical and horizontal asymptotes of rational function; sign trap in denominator

solutions.latex:
The function is $y = \dfrac{x-3}{2-x}$.

The vertical asymptote is where the denominator is zero: $2-x=0$, so $x=2$.

For the horizontal asymptote, divide numerator and denominator by $x$:
$$y = \dfrac{1-\frac{3}{x}}{\frac{2}{x}-1}$$

parts.latex: Find the exact solutions to the equation $1+2\sin 3x=2$ in the domain $0\le x\le\pi$.

dif.r: Extended domain for 3x gives four exact solutions

solutions.latex:
Rearrange the equation.
$$\begin{aligned} 1+2\sin 3x &= 2 \\ \sin 3x &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le x\le \pi$, we need $0\le 3x\le 3\pi$.

The solutions of $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ in this range are
$$3x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{6}$$
Dividing by $3$:
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{18},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{18},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{18},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{18}$$
criteria: Finds the values of $3x$ in the domain $0\le 3x\le 3\pi$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: symmetrical lake with offsets 30, 40, 60, 80, 60, 40, 30 and width 420

solutions.latex:
There are $6$ strips across $420$ m, so the strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{420}{6}=70 \text{ m}$$
Using the trapezoidal rule on the top half, with the end values $30$ and $30$,
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{half}} &\approx \dfrac{70}{2}\big(30+30+2(40+60+80+60+40)\big) \\ &\approx 21\,700 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The lake is symmetrical, so double.
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx 2\times 21\,700 \\ &\approx 43\,400 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that the derivative of $\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)$ is $\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$ .

dif.r: Log laws then differentiate and combine fractions

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence show that $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{6}\ln\dfrac{5}{2}$ .

dif.r: Hence integral needs constant adjustment and log evaluation

solutions.latex:
Use the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(3+x)-\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(3-x) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3+x}-\dfrac{-1}{3-x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3+x}+\dfrac{1}{3-x} \\ &= \dfrac{3-x+3+x}{(3+x)(3-x)} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Splits the log and differentiates correctly, or equivalent merit
Splits the log, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
By part (a), $\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$ is the derivative of $\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{6}\int_1^2\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right]_1^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\left[\ln\dfrac{5}{1}-\ln\dfrac{4}{2}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}(\ln 5-\ln 2) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6}\ln\dfrac{5}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the result of part (a) correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Simplify $\dfrac{\tan\theta\sec\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}$ .

dif.r: Pythagorean identity and reciprocal ratios simplify expression

solutions.latex:
Use $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ and $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\tan\theta\sec\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta} &= \dfrac{\tan\theta\sec\theta}{\sec^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\cos\theta \\ &= \sin\theta \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses a correct identity, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A swimming pool is to be emptied for maintenance. The quantity of water, $Q$ litres, remaining in the pool at a time, $t$ minutes after it starts to drain, is given by:

$Q(t)=2000(25-t)^2,\ t\ge 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: At what rate (in litres/min) is the water being removed at any time ($t$)?

dif.r: Chain rule derivative, interpret sign as removal rate

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If the pool is completely full before being emptied, how long will it take to remove half of the water from the pool to the nearest minute?

dif.r: Find full volume, solve quadratic, reject root outside domain

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At what time does the rate of flow of water from the pool reach 20 kL/minute?

dif.r: Unit conversion then solve simple linear equation

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} Q'(t) &= 2\times 2000(25-t)\times(-1) \\ &= -4000(25-t) \end{aligned}$$$$\therefore\ \text{water is removed at the rate of } 4000(25-t) \text{ litres per minute.}$$

The model applies for $0\le t\le 25$.

When full, $t=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} Q(0) &= 2000(25)^2 \\ &= 1\,250\,000 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$Half full means $Q(t)=625\,000$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2000(25-t)^2 &= 625\,000 \\ (25-t)^2 &= 312.5 \\ 25-t &= \sqrt{312.5} \\ t &\approx 7.32 \end{aligned}$$The other solution, $t\approx 42.67$, is outside the domain.

$$\therefore\ \text{it takes 7 minutes (to the nearest minute).}$$
criteria: Forms the quadratic equation, or equivalent merit
Finds the volume at half full ($625\,000$ L), or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Deduct 1/2 mark if $t=43$ is also included.

solutions.latex:
The rate is $20$ kL/min $=20\,000$ L/min.

$$\begin{aligned} 4000(25-t) &= 20\,000 \\ 25-t &= 5 \\ t &= 20 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Use $-20\,000$ if working with $Q'(t)$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence find the exact area between the two functions in the first quadrant.
