solutions.latex:
Solve simultaneously.

$$\begin{aligned} 4x-x^3 &= x \\ 3x-x^3 &= 0 \\ x(3-x^2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$Hence $x=0$ or $x^2=3$, so $x=0$ or $x=\pm\sqrt3$.

Therefore the functions intersect when $x=0$ and $x=\pm\sqrt3$.
criteria: Working towards the answer with correct method, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In the first quadrant the curves meet at $x=0$ and $x=\sqrt3$, and $4x-x^3\ge x$ between them.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^{\sqrt3}(4x-x^3)\,dx-\int_0^{\sqrt3}x\,dx \\ &= \int_0^{\sqrt3}(3x-x^3)\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{\sqrt3} \\ &= \dfrac92-\dfrac94 \\ &= \dfrac94 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral and integration, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 4\times 0\times e^{0}+3 \\ &= 3 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=4t & v&=e^{-t}\\ u'&=4 & v'&=-e^{-t}\end{aligned}$$$$\begin{aligned} v&=\dfrac{dx}{dt} \\ &= 4e^{-t}+4t(-e^{-t}) \\ &= 4e^{-t}(1-t) \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: 1/2 mark for a small error in the product rule.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $v=0$.

$$4e^{-t}(1-t)=0$$Since $e^{-t}\neq 0$, $1-t=0$, so $t=1$ second.

Test the nature using the acceleration:

$$\dfrac{dv}{dt}=4e^{-t}(t-2)$$$$\text{At } t=1:\ \dfrac{dv}{dt}=-\dfrac{4}{e}<0$$Hence the particle is at maximum distance from the origin at $t=1$.

$$\begin{aligned} x(1) &= 4(1)e^{-1}+3 \\ &= \dfrac{4}{e}+3 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $t=1$ and proves a maximum, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: 1/2 mark for explaining that $e^{-t}=0$ has no solution; 1/2 mark for the displacement $\dfrac{4}{e}+3$ cm.

solutions.latex:
Write $x=\dfrac{4t}{e^t}+3$.

As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{t}{e^t}\to 0$, so $\dfrac{4t}{e^t}\to 0$.

Therefore the particle eventually approaches $x=3$.

meta.marker_note: The particle approaches 3 but does not equal 3.

Since $PQ=PR$, $\triangle PQR$ is isosceles, so $\angle QRP=\theta$.

By the angle sum of a triangle, $\angle QPR=180^\circ-2\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac12\times 40\times 40\times\sin(180^\circ-2\theta) \\ &= 800\sin(180^\circ-2\theta) \\ &= 800\sin 2\theta \end{aligned}$$since $\sin(180^\circ-2\theta)=\sin 2\theta$.

$$\dfrac{dA}{d\theta}=1600\cos 2\theta$$For stationary points:

David buys 5 tickets.

dif.r: Complement for at least one, without replacement

solutions.latex:
The complement of "at least one voucher" is "no voucher". Only 2 of the 20 tickets win, so 18 do not win. David holds 5 tickets, and the probability that none of them wins is found by treating the two winning tickets in turn. The source takes the two winning tickets one at a time against David's 5 tickets as follows.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least 1 voucher})&=1-P(\text{no vouchers})\\ &=1-\dfrac{15}{20}\times\dfrac{14}{19}\\ &=1-\dfrac{21}{38}\\ &=\dfrac{17}{38}\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Given that $f''(x)=6x-2$ and that there is a stationary point on $f(x)$ at $(1,2)$, find

dif.r: Integrate twice using stationary point conditions for constants

parts.label: b
parts.latex: The co-ordinates of any point(s) of inflection.

dif.r: Solve f''=0, check concavity change, evaluate

solutions.latex:
Integrate $f''(x)$.
$$f'(x)=\int(6x-2)\,dx=3x^{2}-2x+c$$
The stationary point at $(1,2)$ gives $f'(1)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=3-2+c\\ c&=-1\end{aligned}$$
so $f'(x)=3x^{2}-2x-1$.

Integrate again.
$$f(x)=\int\left(3x^{2}-2x-1\right)dx=x^{3}-x^{2}-x+c$$
The point $(1,2)$ lies on the curve, so $f(1)=2$.
$$\begin{aligned}2&=1-1-1+c\\ c&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=x^{3}-x^{2}-x+3$$
criteria: Finds $f'(x)$ and integrates again, or equivalent merit
Integrates $f''(x)$ to get $f'(x)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric rewritten top-down by us (source: 3 marks total, integrate and find each constant).

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $f''(x)=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$\begin{aligned}6x-2&=0\\ x&=\dfrac{1}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}f\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)&=\dfrac{1}{27}-\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{1}{3}+3\\ &=\dfrac{70}{27}\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $f''(x)$ either side.
$$\begin{aligned}f''(0)&=-2<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(1)&=4>0 &&\text{concave up}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflection.
$$\therefore\ \text{the point of inflection is }\left(\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{70}{27}\right)$$

dif.r: Single chain rule with exponential

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show $y=e^{\sin x}$ has 2 stationary points for $0\le x\le 2\pi$ and find the coordinates of these stationary points in simplest exact form.

dif.r: Solve cos x=0 noting exponential positive, exact coordinates

parts.latex: Find the nature of these stationary points.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Sketch $y=e^{\sin x}$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

dif.r: Sketch using found stationary points and endpoints

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=e^{sin x} with labelled stationary points and endpoints

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{u}=u'e^{u}$ with $u=\sin x$:
$$y'=\cos x\,e^{\sin x}$$

Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$\cos x\,e^{\sin x}=0$$
Since $e^{\sin x}>0$ for all $x$, there is no solution to $e^{\sin x}=0$, so $\cos x=0$.
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\qquad(0\le x\le2\pi)$$
There are exactly 2 stationary points.

At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $y=e^{\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}=e$.

At $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$: $y=e^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{e}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the stationary points are }\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},e\right)\text{ and }\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$$
criteria: Shows only 2 solutions with $e^{\sin x}\ne0$ stated, or finds the coordinates, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric rewritten top-down by us.

solutions.latex:
Test the sign of $y'=\cos x\,e^{\sin x}$ either side of each stationary point.

Near $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&0&\dfrac{\pi}{2}&\pi\\\hline y'&1&0&-1\end{array}$$
The sign of $y'$ changes from positive to negative, so $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},e\right)$ is a local maximum.

Near $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&\pi&\dfrac{3\pi}{2}&2\pi\\\hline y'&-1&0&1\end{array}$$
The sign of $y'$ changes from negative to positive, so $\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{1}{e}\right)$ is a local minimum.

Alternatively, $y''$ is negative at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and positive at $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.
criteria: One nature correct with numerical justification, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the value(s) of $k$ for which the equation $y=(k+1)x^{2}-(2+k)x+3$ is positive definite.

dif.r: Discriminant with parameter, surd quadratic inequality, check a>0

skills: Discriminant and the nature of roots

solutions.latex:
$y$ is positive definite if $\Delta<0$ and $a>0$.

For $y=(k+1)x^{2}-(2+k)x+3$:

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta &= b^{2}-4ac \\ &= (2+k)^{2}-12(k+1) \\ &= k^{2}+4k+4-12k-12 \\ &= k^{2}-8k-8 \end{aligned}$$

So $\Delta<0$ gives $k^{2}-8k-8<0$.

Solving $k^{2}-8k-8=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{8\pm\sqrt{64+32}}{2} \\ &= 4\pm2\sqrt6 \end{aligned}$$

Hence $4-2\sqrt6<k<4+2\sqrt6$.

Also $a>0$ means $k+1>0$, so $k>-1$. This is already satisfied, since $4-2\sqrt6\approx-0.9>-1$.

$$\therefore\ 4-2\sqrt6<k<4+2\sqrt6$$

meta.format_note: Source line read $k^{2}-8k-12<0$ but the next line solved $k^{2}-8k-8=0$; expanding gives $k^{2}-8k-8$, so the slip was fixed here. Final answer unchanged.

questions.stem: Differentiate the following.

parts.latex: $y=\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+4}{x-3}\right)$

dif.r: Log laws then standard log differentiation

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $y=8\sin x\ln x$

dif.r: Routine product rule with trig and log

solutions.latex:
Split the logarithm using the log laws.

$$\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+4}{x-3}\right)=\log_e(x+4)-\log_e(x-3)$$

Differentiating:

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x+4}-\dfrac{1}{x-3}$$

Equivalently, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{-7}{(x+4)(x-3)}$.
criteria: Splits the logarithm, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=8\sin x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=8\cos x & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= uv'+vu' \\ &= \dfrac{8\sin x}{x}+8\cos x\ln x \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: $\frac12$ mark each for $u'$ and $v'$.

questions.stem: Determine

parts.label: a
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int 1+\tan^{2}\theta\,d\theta$

dif.r: Recognise Pythagorean identity, then standard sec squared integral

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{8x+10}{2x^{2}+5x}\,dx$

dif.r: Recognise f'(x)/f(x) form with constant multiple

solutions.latex:
Use the identity $1+\tan^{2}\theta=\sec^{2}\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int(1+\tan^{2}\theta)\,d\theta &= \int\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta \\ &= \tan\theta+C \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: $\frac12$ mark for $\sec^{2}\theta$; $\frac12$ mark for $\tan\theta+C$.

solutions.latex:
The derivative of the denominator $2x^{2}+5x$ is $4x+5$, and the numerator is twice this.

$$\dfrac{8x+10}{2x^{2}+5x}=2\cdot\dfrac{4x+5}{2x^{2}+5x}$$

So

$$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{8x+10}{2x^{2}+5x}\,dx=2\ln\left|2x^{2}+5x\right|+C$$

questions.stem: The velocity, $v$ metres per second, of a body $t$ seconds after starting from rest, is given by $v=3t-t^{2}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find how far the body has travelled when it next comes to rest.

dif.r: Find rest time, integrate velocity, evaluate displacement

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that the acceleration of the body at this time is negative.

Interpret your answer.

dif.r: Differentiate velocity, then interpret sign of acceleration in context

solutions.latex:
The body is at rest when $v=0$.

$$0=t(3-t)$$

So $t=3$ (it next comes to rest).

Integrate the velocity to find the displacement.

$$x=\displaystyle\int(3t-t^{2})\,dt=\dfrac{3t^{2}}{2}-\dfrac{t^{3}}{3}+C$$

Since it starts from rest at the origin, $x(0)=0$, so $C=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} x(3) &= \dfrac{27}{2}-9 \\ &= 4.5 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the body has travelled } 4.5 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds $t=3$ and the correct $x(t)$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: $\frac12$ mark for $t=3$; $\frac12$ mark for correct $x(t)$.

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

$$a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=3-2t$$

At $t=3$:

$$a=3-2(3)=-3<0$$

Interpretation: the body has slowed down, coming to rest. It then changes direction and speeds up.

meta.marker_note: The interpretation must mention the change of direction.

questions.stem: For the curve $y=\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)$ lies on the curve.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

dif.r: Tangent equation using given derivative and exact values

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into the right-hand side.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \dfrac{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{1+\frac12} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\frac32} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\times\dfrac{2}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} \\ &= \text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)\text{ lies on the curve}$$

meta.marker_note: $\frac12$ mark for substitution; $\frac12$ mark for exact values evaluated.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^{2}}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=1+\cos x\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{\cos x(1+\cos x)+\sin^{2}x}{(1+\cos x)^{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos x+\cos^{2}x+\sin^{2}x}{(1+\cos x)^{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\cos x}{(1+\cos x)^{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{1+\cos x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The gradient at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ comes from part (b).

$$\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{1}{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\frac32} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

The tangent passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$.

$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} &= \dfrac23\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ y &= \dfrac23x-\dfrac{2\pi}{9}+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: If the sum of the first 10 terms of the series $\log_2\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)+\log_2\left(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)+\log_2\left(\dfrac{1}{x^{3}}\right)+\ldots$ is $-110$, find the value of $x$.

dif.r: Log laws reveal arithmetic series; solve sum for x

skills: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Use the log laws to rewrite each term.

$$-\log_2x-2\log_2x-3\log_2x-\ldots$$

This is an arithmetic series with $a=-\log_2x$, common difference $d=-\log_2x$, $n=10$ and last term $l=-10\log_2x$.

Using $S_{n}=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:

$$\begin{aligned} -110 &= \dfrac{10}{2}\left(-\log_2x-10\log_2x\right) \\ &= -5\cdot11\log_2x \end{aligned}$$

So $\log_2x=2$.

$$\therefore\ x=2^{2}=4$$
criteria: Substitutes into the correct formula, or equivalent merit
Identifies the AP and common difference

questions.stem:
The probability that a certain girl wakes up late in the morning is 0.6.

When she wakes up late, the probability that she is late to work is 0.85.

When she wakes up on time, the probability that she is late to work is 0.4.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that she is late to work on any morning?

dif.r: Two-branch tree, total probability sum

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Upon seeing the girl arriving late, her boss asks her if she overslept.

What is the probability that the truthful answer is `yes'?

dif.r: Reverse conditional probability from tree, Bayes-style

solutions.latex:
She is late to work either by waking late or by waking on time, so add the two branches.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{late}) &= P(\text{wake late and late})+P(\text{wake on time and late}) \\ &= 0.6\times0.85+0.4\times0.4 \\ &= 0.67 \end{aligned}$$

Use conditional probability.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{wakes up late}\mid\text{arrives late}) &= \dfrac{P(\text{wakes up late}\cap\text{arrives late})}{P(\text{late})} \\ &= \dfrac{0.6\times0.85}{0.67} \\ &= \dfrac{51}{67} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The rate at which liquid is flowing into a vessel after $t$ minutes is given by $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{t+1}$.

If the volume of liquid in the vessel is $(\log_e 2)$ cubic metres after 3 minutes, what is the volume after 8 minutes? Answer correct to 3 significant figures.

dif.r: Integrate rate, find constant from condition, evaluate

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate (with $t\ge0$, so $t+1>0$).

$$V=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{t+1}\,dt=\ln(t+1)+c$$

At $t=3$, $V=\ln2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \ln2 &= \ln4+c \\ c &= \ln2-\ln4=\ln\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$

So $V=\ln(t+1)+\ln\dfrac12$. At $t=8$:

$$\begin{aligned} V &= \ln9+\ln\dfrac12 \\ &\approx 1.50 \text{ m}^{3} \text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct value of $c$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the area bounded by the curve $y=(x+2)^{3}$ and the $x$-axis between $x=-3$ and $x=2$.

dif.r: Area must be split where curve crosses axis

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of y=(x+2)^3 with area from x=-3 to 2 shaded

solutions.latex:
The curve $y=(x+2)^{3}$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-2$, so split the area there.

\exfigure{1292_q30_s1}

A primitive is

$$\displaystyle\int(x+2)^{3}\,dx=\dfrac{(x+2)^{4}}{4}+C$$

The part from $-3$ to $-2$ is below the axis, so subtract its (negative) integral.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}(x+2)^{3}\,dx-\int_{-3}^{-2}(x+2)^{3}\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{(x+2)^{4}}{4}\right]_{-2}^{2}-\left[\dfrac{(x+2)^{4}}{4}\right]_{-3}^{-2} \\ &= 64+\dfrac14 \\ &= \dfrac{257}{4} \text{ square units} \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Correct asymptote, general logarithm shape and passing through the origin.

solutions.latex:
The strip width is

$$h=\dfrac{2-1}{4}=\dfrac14$$

So the $x$ values are $1,\ \dfrac54,\ \dfrac32,\ \dfrac74,\ 2$. With $f(x)=\ln(x+1)$, the trapezoidal rule gives

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^2\ln(x+1)\,dx &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left[f(1)+2\left(f\left(\dfrac54\right)+f\left(\dfrac32\right)+f\left(\dfrac74\right)\right)+f(2)\right] \\ &= \dfrac18\left[\ln2+2\left(\ln\dfrac94+\ln\dfrac52+\ln\dfrac{11}{4}\right)+\ln3\right] \\ &\approx 0.909 \end{aligned}$$

Over the interval the curve is concave down, so each trapezoid lies below the curve.

$$\therefore\ \text{the trapezoidal estimate is less than the exact value}$$

questions.stem:
The population of a town can be estimated by using the formula $P=P_0e^{kt}$, where $t$ is the time in years after the year 2020 and $P_0$ and $k$ are constants.

The population at the beginning of the year 2020 was 300, and at the beginning of 2024 it was 450.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the annual growth rate, $k$, of the population correct to 3 significant figures.

dif.r: Solve exponential model for k using logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: In what year will the town's population be double that of the year 2020?

dif.r: Solve exponential for doubling time, convert to year

meta.marker_note: Expression for $k$ and value to 3 s.f.
meta.format_note: Guidelines allocate 1 mark here although the paper prints [2]; rubric kept as the guidelines give it.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the 2-mark part had a single 1-mark criterion (the guideline mislabelled the marks).
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the 2-mark part had a single 1-mark criterion (the guideline mislabelled the marks).

solutions.latex:
Double the 2020 population is $600$.

$$\begin{aligned} 600 &= 300e^{\frac{\ln3-\ln2}{4}t} \\ 2 &= e^{\frac{\ln3-\ln2}{4}t} \\ \ln2 &= \dfrac{\ln3-\ln2}{4}\,t \\ t &= \dfrac{4\ln2}{\ln3-\ln2} \\ &\approx 6.84 \text{ years} \end{aligned}$$

Hence towards the end of the year 2026 the town will have double the 2020 population.

$$\therefore\ \text{the year is } 2026$$

parts.latex:
The water height in an estuary fluctuates according to the tide. Flooding will occur when the water height reaches 1.5 m. One day the high tide of 1.6 m occurred at 3:00 am and the following low tide at 9:30 am. Assume that the following high tide was also 1.6 m and the height of the tide is modelled by the equation

$$h=1+0.6\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{13}(t+0.25)\right),$$

where $h$ is the height in metres and $t$ is the time in hours after midnight.

Find the time when the next flooding would be expected to occur, to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Solve trig model, choose correct next solution using period

solutions.latex:
Flooding occurs when $h=1.5$.

$$1.5=1+0.6\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{13}(t+0.25)\right)$$

$$\dfrac56=\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{13}+\dfrac{\pi}{26}\right)$$

The first solution is $t\approx1.7882$ (1:47 am), which is before the 9:30 am low tide.

The period is $13$ hours, so adding $13$ hours gives the next time the tide is rising through $1.5$ m.

$$t\approx14.7882$$

The next flooding is expected at 14:47, i.e. 2:47 pm.

Alternatively, the general solution is

$$t=\dfrac{13}{2\pi}(-1)^{k}\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac56\right)+\dfrac{13k}{2}-\dfrac14$$

Then $k=0$ gives $t\approx1.7882$ and $k=2$ gives $t\approx14.7882$.

$$\therefore\ \text{flooding is expected at } 2{:}47 \text{ pm}$$

questions.stem:
Michael borrows \$650 000 to buy a unit at $6\%$ per annum with interest compounded monthly.

The loan is to be repaid with equal monthly repayments of \$4200.

Let \$$A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.

dif.r: Derive loan balance formula via recurrence and GP sum

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
After 15 years, the amount owing is \$373 722 to the nearest dollar.

At this time Michael borrows a further \$200 000 to build an extension.

He adds this onto his previous mortgage. If the monthly repayments remain the same, what is the minimum remaining number of months it will take him to pay off the balance of the loan?

dif.r: Adapt loan formula to new principal, solve with logs, round up

solutions.latex:
The interest rate is $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly, which is $0.5\% = 0.005$ per month.

The amount owing grows by $0.5\%$ and then the repayment is taken off, with $A_0=650\,000$.

$$A_n=1.005A_{n-1}-4200$$

Developing the first terms:

$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 650\,000\times1.005-4200 \\ A_2 &= 650\,000\times1.005^{2}-4200(1+1.005) \\ A_3 &= 650\,000\times1.005^{3}-4200(1+1.005+1.005^{2}) \end{aligned}$$

Hence

$$A_n=650\,000\times1.005^{n}-4200\left(1+1.005+\ldots+1.005^{n-1}\right)$$

The bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.005$ and $n$ terms.

$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= 650\,000\times1.005^{n}-4200\times\dfrac{1.005^{n}-1}{1.005-1} \\ &= 650\,000\times1.005^{n}-840\,000\left(1.005^{n}-1\right) \\ &= 840\,000-190\,000\times1.005^{n} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sums the GP, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
After $180$ months the amount owing is $A_{180}=373\,722$.

The new loan is

$$\$(373\,722+200\,000)=\$573\,722$$

Let $B_n$ be the amount owing after a further $n$ months. The same working as in part (a) gives

$$\begin{aligned} B_n &= 573\,722\times1.005^{n}-840\,000\left(1.005^{n}-1\right) \\ &= 840\,000-266\,278\times1.005^{n} \end{aligned}$$

The loan is paid off when $B_n=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1.005^{n} &= \dfrac{840\,000}{266\,278} \\ n &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{840\,000}{266\,278}\right)}{\ln1.005} \\ &\approx 230.35 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ 231 \text{ months are needed to pay off the loan}$$

parts.latex:
Find the shaded area enclosed by the curves $y=x^{2}$ and $y=9+3x-x^{2}$ and the line $y=1$.

\exfigure{1292_q35_1}

dif.r: Interpret composite region, two intersections, subtract areas

figures.cap: two parabolas and the line y=1 with enclosed region shaded
solution sketch: shaded region with intersection points labelled

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1292_q35_s1}

Find where the two curves meet.

$$\begin{aligned} x^{2} &= 9+3x-x^{2} \\ 2x^{2}-3x-9 &= 0 \\ (2x+3)(x-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=-1.5$ or $x=3$.

The line $y=1$ meets $y=x^{2}$ where $x^{2}=1$, so $x=\pm1$.

First find the area between the curves, then subtract the area between the line $y=1$ and $y=x^{2}$.

$$\displaystyle\int_{-1.5}^{3}\left(9+3x-x^{2}-x^{2}\right)dx \quad\text{and}\quad \int_{-1}^{1}\left(1-x^{2}\right)dx$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left[9x+\dfrac32x^{2}-\dfrac23x^{3}\right]_{-1.5}^{3}-\dfrac43 \\ &= 29\dfrac{1}{24} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the integrals, or equivalent merit

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Show that the least perimeter occurs when $r^{2}=\dfrac{8}{\pi+4}$ and calculate $\theta$.

Write the size of this angle to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Optimise given function, verify minimum, back-substitute for angle

figures.cap: semicircle AXC on diameter AC with sector ABC of radius r and angle theta

solutions.latex:
The semi-circle has diameter $r$, so its perimeter is $r+\dfrac{\pi r}{2}$.

The sector has two radii and an arc, with perimeter $r+r\theta$ on the boundary.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{\pi r}{2}+r+r\theta \\ &= r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+1+\theta\right) \end{aligned}$$

The area is a semi-circle of radius $\dfrac{r}{2}$ plus a sector of radius $r$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac12\pi\left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)^{2}+\dfrac12r^{2}\theta \\ &= \dfrac18r^{2}(\pi+4\theta) \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

So $\pi+4\theta=\dfrac{8}{r^{2}}$, giving

$$\theta=\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$

Substitute into $P$.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+1+\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{2}{r}+r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1\right) \end{aligned}$$

Write $P=2r^{-1}+r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1\right)$ and differentiate.

$$\dfrac{dP}{dr}=-\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}+\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1 \qquad \dfrac{d^{2}P}{dr^{2}}=4r^{-3}$$

The perimeter is stationary when $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{r^{2}} &= \dfrac{\pi+4}{4} \\ r^{2} &= \dfrac{8}{\pi+4} \end{aligned}$$

For $r>0$, $\dfrac{d^{2}P}{dr^{2}}=4r^{-3}>0$, so $P$ is a minimum.

From (b), $\theta=\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, and here $\dfrac{2}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}+1$.

$$\theta=1 \text{ radian}\approx57^\circ$$
criteria: Justifies the minimum, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Two-strip trapezoidal rule straight from a given table

solutions.latex:
The table gives three values of $x$, so there are two strips. The strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{1.6-1.2}{2}=0.2$$
so the $x$ values are $1.2,\ 1.4,\ 1.6$.

Using the trapezoidal rule with two strips:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{1.2}^{1.6} f(x)\,dx &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(1.2)+2f(1.4)+f(1.6)\big] \\ &= \dfrac{0.2}{2}\times 15.4 \\ &= 1.54 \end{aligned}$$
where $f(1.2)+2f(1.4)+f(1.6)=15.4$ comes from the table values.

Hence the best estimate is $1.54$, which is option B.

dif.r: Rearrange, factorise quadratic, choose region outside roots

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to compare with zero, then factorise.
$$\begin{aligned} h^2-3h-4 &> 0 \\ (h-4)(h+1) &> 0 \end{aligned}$$
The parabola $y=(h-4)(h+1)$ opens upwards with roots $h=-1$ and $h=4$, so it is positive outside the roots.
$$\therefore\ h>4 \text{ or } h<-1$$
This is option D.

parts.latex: The correct expression for the integral $\displaystyle\int \sin\dfrac{x}{4}\,dx$ is :

dif.r: Standard integral of sin(ax) with fractional coefficient

solutions.latex:
Use $\displaystyle\int \sin ax\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{a}\cos ax+c$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int \sin\dfrac{x}{4}\,dx &= -\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{4}}\cos\dfrac{x}{4}+c \\ &= -4\cos\dfrac{x}{4}+c \end{aligned}$$
Check by differentiating: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-4\cos\dfrac{x}{4}\right)=-4\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\sin\dfrac{x}{4}\right)=\sin\dfrac{x}{4}$.

This is option C.

meta.self_check: Differentiated the answer to recover the integrand.

parts.latex: The chance of a fisherman catching a fish of legal length is 3 in 5. If three fish are caught at random, what is the probability that exactly one is of legal length?

dif.r: Exactly one of three: count orderings, multiply probabilities

solutions.latex:
Let $L$ be a fish of legal length, with $P(L)=\dfrac{3}{5}$ and $P(\overline{L})=\dfrac{2}{5}$.

Exactly one legal fish out of three can occur in $3$ orders ($L\overline{L}\,\overline{L}$, $\overline{L}L\overline{L}$, $\overline{L}\,\overline{L}L$), each with the same probability.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 3\times\dfrac{3}{5}\times\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{36}{125} \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: If $f(x)=b^{x}+b^{-x}$, then $\left(f(-x)\right)^2=$

dif.r: Notice evenness, expand square, recognise result as f(2x)+2

solutions.latex:
Replacing $x$ by $-x$ gives $f(-x)=b^{-x}+b^{x}=f(x)$.

Square it:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(f(-x)\right)^2 &= \left(b^{x}+b^{-x}\right)^2 \\ &= b^{2x}+2b^{x}b^{-x}+b^{-2x} \\ &= b^{2x}+b^{-2x}+2 \\ &= f(2x)+2 \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent events where $P(X)=0.2$ and $P(Y)=0.52$. What is the value of $P(\overline{X}\cap\overline{Y})$?

dif.r: Complements of independent events, product of complements

solutions.latex:
The complements of independent events are also independent, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(\overline{X}\cap\overline{Y}) &= P(\overline{X})\,P(\overline{Y}) \\ &= (1-0.2)(1-0.52) \\ &= 0.8\times 0.48 \\ &= 0.384 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: If $y=-4\sin^3 3x$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$

dif.r: Double chain rule on power of trig function

solutions.latex:
Write $y=-4(\sin 3x)^3$ and use the chain rule (power rule, then the derivative of $\sin 3x$).
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -4\cdot 3(\sin 3x)^2\cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin 3x) \\ &= -12\sin^2 3x\cdot 3\cos 3x \\ &= -36\sin^2 3x\cdot\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

meta.self_check: Chain rule checked step by step.

parts.latex: A set of data has a lower quartile of 10 and an upper quartile of 16. What is the maximum range for this set of data if there are no outliers?
parts.note: Quartiles, IQR and outliers of a data set are Mathematics Standard content, not 2024 Advanced

dif.r: Apply 1.5 IQR outlier fences to reason about maximum range

solutions.latex:
The interquartile range is
$$IQR=16-10=6$$
A value is an outlier if it is more than $1.5\times IQR=9$ beyond a quartile, so the outlier boundaries are
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1-9 &= 10-9=1 \\ Q_3+9 &= 16+9=25 \end{aligned}$$
With no outliers, every value lies between $1$ and $25$. The largest possible range is
$$25-1=24$$
This is option A.

meta.self_check: Standard 1.5 IQR outlier rule applied; max range uses the extreme allowed values.

parts.latex: The graph of $y=(x-2)^2(3+x)$ is dilated vertically by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and horizontally by a factor of 3. It is then reflected across the $y$ axis. The new equation is given by:

dif.r: Three successive transformations; careful substitution of x/3 then -x

solutions.latex:
Apply the transformations in order, starting from $y=(x-2)^2(3+x)$.

Vertical dilation by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ multiplies $y$ by $\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{2}(x-2)^2(3+x)$$
Horizontal dilation by a factor of $3$ replaces $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{3}$:
$$y=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}-2\right)^2\left(3+\dfrac{x}{3}\right)$$
Reflection in the $y$ axis replaces $x$ by $-x$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-\dfrac{x}{3}-2\right)^2\left(3-\dfrac{x}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}+2\right)^2\left(3-\dfrac{x}{3}\right) \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

meta.self_check: Original x-intercepts 2 and -3 become 6 and -9 after dilation, then -6 and 9 after reflection; option D has roots x=-6 and x=9.

questions.stem: The weight $M$, in kg, of an object on the moon is directly proportional to the weight $E$ of the object on Earth. An astronaut who weighs 90 kg on Earth weighs 16.4 kg on the moon.

parts.latex: An astronaut weighs 120 kg on Earth. How much will the astronaut weigh on the moon?

Since $M$ is directly proportional to $E$, $M=kE$.

Substitute $E=90$, $M=16.4$.

$$\begin{aligned} 16.4&=k\times90\\ k&=\dfrac{16.4}{90}=\dfrac{41}{225}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ M=\dfrac{41}{225}E$$

parts.latex: Given $\cos 2\theta=0.5$ and $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\le\theta\le 2\pi$, what is the value of $\sin\theta$ ?

dif.r: Double-angle equation with restricted domain, choose correct sign

solutions.latex:
Solve $\cos2\theta=\dfrac12$ for $0\le 2\theta\le 4\pi$.

$$2\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}$$

$$\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$

The only value in $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\le\theta\le2\pi$ is $\theta=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$, so

$$\sin\dfrac{11\pi}{6}=-\dfrac12$$

Alternatively, use the double angle identity $\cos2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1-2\sin^2\theta&=\dfrac12\\ 2\sin^2\theta&=\dfrac12\\ \sin^2\theta&=\dfrac14\\ \sin\theta&=\pm\dfrac12\end{aligned}$$

In the fourth quadrant, $\sin\theta<0$.

$$\therefore\ \sin\theta=-\dfrac12$$

dif.r: Average rate needs function values, not derivative; unit conversion

figures.cap: graph of P(t) = 500t/(2t^2+9)

solutions.latex:
Convert 10 months to years: $t=\dfrac{10}{12}=\dfrac56$.

$$P\left(\dfrac56\right)=\dfrac{500\times\frac56}{2\left(\frac56\right)^2+9}\approx 40.107 \text{ thousand}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{about } 40.11 \text{ thousand (2 d.p.)}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=500t & v&=2t^2+9\\ u'&=500 & v'&=4t\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P'(t)&=\dfrac{(2t^2+9)\times500-500t\times4t}{(2t^2+9)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1000t^2+4500-2000t^2}{(2t^2+9)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{4500-1000t^2}{(2t^2+9)^2}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the $x$-values for the points on the graph of $f(x)=-x^3+6x^2$ at which the normal has slope $\dfrac{-1}{9}$.

dif.r: Convert normal slope to tangent slope, solve quadratic

solutions.latex:
Differentiate.

$$f'(x)=-3x^2+12x$$

The normal has slope $m_N=-\dfrac19$, so the tangent has slope $m_T=9$.

Set $f'(x)=9$.

$$\begin{aligned} -3x^2+12x&=9\\ 3x^2-12x+9&=0\\ x^2-4x+3&=0\\ (x-3)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x=1 \text{ or } x=3$$
criteria: Recognises the tangent gradient is $9$, or equivalent merit

So divide by $33$ and multiply by $5$.

$$\therefore\ \int5x^2(x^3+1)^{10}\,dx=\dfrac{5}{33}(x^3+1)^{11}+c$$

dif.r: Product rule with exponential chain rule, factorise

parts.label: b
parts.latex: $f(x)=\ln\left(\dfrac{x^3+4}{6-x}\right)$

dif.r: Log laws then differentiate two log terms

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{-2x} & v&=1+x^2\\ u'&=-2e^{-2x} & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=e^{-2x}\times2x+(1+x^2)\times(-2e^{-2x})\\ &=2e^{-2x}\left(x-(1+x^2)\right)\\ &=2e^{-2x}(x-1-x^2)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule with correct $u'$ and $v'$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Use the log law $\ln\dfrac{a}{b}=\ln a-\ln b$ first.

$$f(x)=\ln(x^3+4)-\ln(6-x)$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3+4}-\dfrac{-1}{6-x}\\ &=\dfrac{3x^2}{x^3+4}+\dfrac{1}{6-x}\end{aligned}$$

Differentiating the quotient directly gives the equivalent form

$$f'(x)=\dfrac{2(9x^2-x^3+2)}{(x^3+4)(6-x)}$$
criteria: Differentiates one log term correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $f(x)=-x^3-5x+1$ is always decreasing.

dif.r: Show derivative always negative; brief justification needed

solutions.latex:
Differentiate.

$$f'(x)=-3x^2-5$$

Since $x^2\ge0$, we have $-3x^2\le0$, so $f'(x)\le-5$.

Hence $f'(x)<0$ for all $x$ (the graph of $f'(x)$ is a downward parabola with maximum value $-5$, so it lies below the $x$-axis).

$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is always decreasing.}$$

parts.latex: Find the area between the curve $y=x^2-3x$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $1\le x\le 5$.

dif.r: Area must be split where curve crosses axis; careful evaluation

solutions.latex:
The curve $y=x^2-3x=x(x-3)$ is below the $x$-axis for $1\le x<3$ and above it for $3<x\le5$, so the two regions are found separately.

$$\text{Area}=\left|\displaystyle\int_1^3(x^2-3x)\,dx\right|+\displaystyle\int_3^5(x^2-3x)\,dx$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}\right]_1^3\right|+\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}\right]_3^5\\ &=\left|\left(9-\dfrac{27}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac13-\dfrac32\right)\right|+\left(\dfrac{125}{3}-\dfrac{75}{2}-\left(9-\dfrac{27}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=\left|-\dfrac{10}{3}\right|+\dfrac{26}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{36}{3}\\ &=12 \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Separates the regions and integrates correctly, or equivalent merit
Separates the regions, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The world population was approximately 6.04 billion at the beginning of 2000. It has been estimated that the population is growing exponentially at the rate of 0.016 per year.

The world population $P$ is modelled by the equation $P=P_0e^{kt}$, where $k$ and $P_0$ are constants and $t$ is the amount of time (in years) since the beginning of 2000.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Estimate the world population at the end of 2030.

dif.r: Substitute into given exponential model; only care needed is t=31

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After how many years will the population be double the population in 2000?

dif.r: Standard doubling time: solve exponential equation using logarithms

solutions.latex:
The model is $P=6.04e^{0.016t}$.

The end of 2030 is 31 years after the beginning of 2000, so $t=31$.

$$\begin{aligned} P_{31}&=6.04e^{0.016\times31}\\ &\approx9.9185\\ &\approx9.919 \text{ billion (3 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: If $t=31$ was not used but the formula was used correctly, 1 mark was awarded.

solutions.latex:
The population doubles when $P=2P_0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2P_0&=P_0e^{0.016t}\\ 2&=e^{0.016t}\\ \ln2&=\ln e^{0.016t}\\ 0.016t&=\ln2\\ t&=\dfrac{\ln2}{0.016}\\ &\approx43.32 \text{ years}\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: If you devised your own $k$ in (a) but used it correctly in (b), two marks were awarded (correct from previous response).

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=2x^3-x^4 on [-2,2] with key points labelled

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-4x^3=0\\ 2x^2(3-2x)&=0\end{aligned}$$

So $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac32$, giving $y=0$ or $y=\dfrac{27}{16}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{stationary points are } (0,0) \text{ and } \left(\dfrac32,\dfrac{27}{16}\right)$$
criteria: Finds $f'(x)$ and the $x$ values, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Test the sign of the slope $f'(x)=2x^2(3-2x)$ either side of each stationary point.

\extable{Ts8775_1}

The slope is increasing, stationary, increasing, stationary, decreasing.

At $x=0$ the slope is positive on both sides, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

At $x=\dfrac32$ the slope changes from positive to negative.

$$\therefore\ (0,0) \text{ is a horizontal point of inflection and } \left(\dfrac32,\dfrac{27}{16}\right) \text{ is a maximum turning point.}$$
criteria: Tests the slope around one stationary point correctly, or equivalent merit

Points of inflection occur where $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x) &= 12x-12x^2 = 0 \\ 12x(1-x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

\extable{Ts8776_1}

The concavity changes at $x=1$, and $y=1$ when $x=1$.

$$\therefore\ (1,1) \text{ is a point of inflection (and } (0,0) \text{ is a horizontal point of inflection, from (b))}$$

questions.stem: Consider the functions $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{3-2x}$ and $g(x)=1+3x^2$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $f\circ g(x)$

dif.r: Direct substitution into composite function and simplify

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Evaluate $g(f'(1))$

dif.r: Chain rule with cube root, evaluate, then substitute into g

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} f\circ g(x) &= f(g(x)) \\ &= f(1+3x^2) \\ &= \sqrt[3]{3-2(1+3x^2)} \\ &= \sqrt[3]{1-6x^2} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Write $f(x)=(3-2x)^{\frac13}$ and differentiate using the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac13(3-2x)^{-\frac23}\times(-2) \\ &= -\dfrac23(3-2x)^{-\frac23} \end{aligned}$$
$$f'(1)=-\dfrac23(3-2)^{-\frac23}=-\dfrac23$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} g\left(f'(1)\right) &= g\left(-\dfrac23\right) \\ &= 1+3\left(-\dfrac23\right)^2 \\ &= 1+\dfrac43 \\ &= \dfrac73 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: If $a=\log_{\frac{1}{x}}\dfrac{1}{N}$ such that $x>0$ and $N>0$, show that $a=\log_x N$.

dif.r: Short general log proof via definition or change of base

solutions.latex:
Method 1: use the definition of a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \log_{\frac1x}\dfrac1N \\ \left(\dfrac1x\right)^a &= \dfrac1N &&(\text{definition of log}) \\ \dfrac{1}{x^a} &= \dfrac1N \\ x^a &= N \\ a &= \log_x N &&(\text{definition of log}) \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: use the change of base rule.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \log_{\frac1x}\dfrac1N \\ &= \dfrac{\log_x\frac1N}{\log_x\frac1x} &&(\text{change of base}) \\ &= \dfrac{\log_x(N^{-1})}{\log_x(x^{-1})} \\ &= \dfrac{-\log_x N}{-\log_x x} &&(\log_a(b^c)=c\log_a b) \\ &= \dfrac{\log_x N}{1} &&(\log_x x=1) \\ &= \log_x N \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the definition of a logarithm or the change of base rule, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The probability density function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}(x^2+1)$ is defined over the interval $[0,1]$.

Find the value of :

dif.r: Standard expected value integral of polynomial pdf

parts.label: b
parts.latex: the variance.

dif.r: Variance formula needs second integral and subtracting squared mean

parts.label: c
parts.latex: the standard deviation, correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Square root of previous variance; one step

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^1 x f(x)\,dx$:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \dfrac13\int_0^1 x(x^2+1)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac13\int_0^1 (x^3+x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac14+\dfrac12\right] \\ &= \dfrac14 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up $\displaystyle\int_0^1 x f(x)\,dx$ or finds a correct primitive, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Using $\text{Var}(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^2 f(x)\,dx-(E(X))^2$ with $E(X)=\dfrac14$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= \dfrac13\int_0^1 (x^4+x^2)\,dx-\left(\dfrac14\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac{x^5}{5}+\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1-\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= \dfrac13\left[\dfrac15+\dfrac13\right]-\dfrac{1}{16} \\ &= \dfrac{83}{720} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up $\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^2 f(x)\,dx-(E(X))^2$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Part labels: output ids 8783/8784 correspond to parts (a)/(b) as given.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} \\ &= \sqrt{\dfrac{83}{720}} \\ &\approx 0.34 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

why: Checker got a different answer — The stored answers E(X)=1/4, Var=83/720 and σ≈0.34 apply the formulas to an invalid pdf (total probability 4/9). If f is rescaled to (3/4)(x^2+1), the answers become E(X)=9/16, Var=107/1280 and σ≈0.29. The question needs an owner decision.

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle travelling along the $x$ axis is given by $v=2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds .

parts.label: a
parts.latex: When is the particle stationary?

dif.r: Set velocity to zero and solve linear equation

skills: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What happens to the velocity as $t\to\infty$ ?

dif.r: Simple limiting behaviour of velocity as t grows

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the acceleration when the particle is stationary.

dif.r: Differentiate velocity using negative power, substitute t=3

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the distance travelled in the first 5 seconds, in exact form.

dif.r: Split integral at direction change, log integration, simplify exactly

figures.cap: solution sketch: velocity-time graph with areas shaded for t from 0 to 5

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-\dfrac{10}{t+2} &= 0 \\ \dfrac{10}{t+2} &= 2 \\ 10 &= 2t+4 \\ 2t &= 6 \\ t &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is stationary at } t=3 \text{ seconds}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{10}{t+2}\to 0$.

So $v\to 2-0=2$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the velocity approaches } 2 \text{ ms}^{-1}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, with $v=2-10(t+2)^{-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= -10\times(-1)(t+2)^{-2} \\ &= 10(t+2)^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 10(3+2)^{-2} \\ &= 0.4 \text{ ms}^{-2} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1293_q32_s1}

The particle moves left from $t=0$ until $t=3$, then turns around and moves right from $t=3$ until $t=5$.

Displacement is the integral of velocity, so the distance travelled in the first 5 seconds is
$$\left|\int_0^3\left(2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\right)dt\right|+\int_3^5\left(2-\dfrac{10}{t+2}\right)dt$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= \Big|\big[2t-10\ln(t+2)\big]_0^3\Big|+\big[2t-10\ln(t+2)\big]_3^5 \\ &= \big|6-10\ln 5-(0-10\ln 2)\big|+10-10\ln 7-(6-10\ln 5) \\ &= -6+10\ln 5-10\ln 2+4-10\ln 7+10\ln 5 \\ &= 20\ln 5-10\ln 2-10\ln 7-2 \\ &= 10\ln\left(\dfrac{25}{14}\right)-2 \end{aligned}$$
The last step uses the log laws.

$$\therefore\ \text{distance} = 10\ln\left(\dfrac{25}{14}\right)-2 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integrals for both stages and integrates, or equivalent merit
Recognises the change of direction at $t=3$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^7 f(x)\,dx$, where $f(x)=3-|x-2|$.

dif.r: Sketch absolute value graph, compute signed areas geometrically

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-intercepts by solving $|x-2|=3$.

So $x-2=3$ giving $x=5$, or $x-2=-3$ giving $x=-1$.

The graph of $f(x)=3-|x-2|$ has vertex $(2,3)$, $y$-intercept $1$ and $x$-intercepts $-1$ and $5$.

The integral is the signed area: a trapezoid from $x=0$ to $x=2$, a triangle above the axis from $x=2$ to $x=5$, and a triangle below the axis from $x=5$ to $x=7$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^7\left(3-|x-2|\right)dx &= \dfrac12\times 2(1+3)+\dfrac12\times 3\times 3-\dfrac12\times 2\times 2 \\ &= 4+\dfrac92-2 \\ &= 6\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the intercepts and the areas, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: plank AB over an 8 m fence, 1 m from a wall, angle theta at A

solutions.latex: $$AB=\dfrac{8}{\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$$
criteria: Finds one of the two parts of $AB$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Source gives no reasoning for the expression; left as is.
meta.edited_from_original: The question total was recorded as 6 marks while parts (a) and (b) carry 2 + 3 = 5; the total is now 5 marks (checker flag 24 Nov).

solutions.latex:
Write $AB=8(\sin\theta)^{-1}+(\cos\theta)^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dAB}{d\theta} &= -8(\sin\theta)^{-2}\cos\theta-(\cos\theta)^{-2}\cdot(-\sin\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{-8\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{-8\cos^3\theta+\sin^3\theta}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dAB}{d\theta}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} -8\cos^3\theta+\sin^3\theta &= 0 \\ \sin^3\theta &= 8\cos^3\theta \\ \tan^3\theta &= 8 \\ \tan\theta &= 2 \\ \theta &\approx 63.43^\circ \end{aligned}$$

\extable{Ts8797_1}

The gradient goes from negative to positive, so this is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} AB &= \dfrac{8}{\frac{2}{\sqrt5}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\sqrt5}} = 4\sqrt5+\sqrt5=5\sqrt5 \\ &\approx 11.18 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the shortest plank is about } 11.18 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $\theta$ for the stationary point, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Neville lives in a town where one third of the days are rainy days. If it is a rainy day, the chance of heavy traffic is $\dfrac{1}{2}$. If it is not a rainy day, the chance of heavy traffic is $\dfrac{1}{4}$. If it is a rainy day and there is heavy traffic, there is a 50% chance that Neville will arrive late to work. On the other hand , the probability of being late is reduced to $\dfrac{1}{8}$ if it is not a rainy day and there is no heavy traffic. In other situations, the probability of Neville being late to work is 0.35. On a random day, Neville arrives late to work. What is the probability that it is a rainy day?

dif.r: Build three-stage tree from wordy data, then reverse conditional

figures.cap: solution sketch: probability tree diagram

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1293_q36_s1}

Let $R$ be a rainy day and $L$ be arriving late. Using conditional probability, $P(R\mid L)=\dfrac{P(L\cap R)}{P(L)}$, with the branches from the tree diagram:
$$P(R\mid L)=\dfrac{\frac13\times\frac12\times\frac12+\frac13\times\frac12\times\frac{35}{100}}{\frac13\times\frac12\times\frac12+\frac13\times\frac12\times\frac{35}{100}+\frac23\times\frac14\times\frac{35}{100}+\frac23\times\frac34\times\frac18}$$
$$\therefore\ P(R\mid L)=\dfrac{34}{63}$$
criteria: Writes $P(R\mid L)=\dfrac{P(L\cap R)}{P(L)}$ or draws a correct tree diagram, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Many students didn't use the conditional probability correctly.
meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Values checked: $\dfrac{34}{63}$ is consistent with the expression.

parts.latex: The graph $y=x^2+4x+7$ is reflected in the $y$-axis, followed by a translation $2$ units to the right. What is the equation of the new graph?

dif.r: Two successive transformations applied in correct order.

solutions.latex:
Reflect in the $y$-axis by replacing $x$ with $-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(-x)^2+4(-x)+7\\ &=x^2-4x+7 \end{aligned}$$
Translate $2$ units to the right by replacing $x$ with $x-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(x-2)^2-4(x-2)+7\\ &=(-x+2)^2+4(-x+2)+7 \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: The function $y=f(x)$ has second derivative $y''=2(x-1)^2(x-3)$. A pupil is asked to find the $x$-coordinate(s) of any point(s) of inflection. What should his final answer be?

dif.r: Recognise repeated factor gives no sign change in y''.

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $y''$ to change sign.

At $x=1$ the factor $(x-1)^2$ is repeated, so $y''$ does not change sign.

At $x=3$ the factor $(x-3)$ changes sign, so $y''$ changes sign.

So the only point of inflection is at $x=3$, which is option C.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x+3}{x^2}\,dx$.

dif.r: Split fraction then integrate including logarithm term.

solutions.latex:
Split the fraction into separate terms.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{2x+3}{x^2}\,dx&=\int\left(\dfrac{2}{x}+\dfrac{3}{x^2}\right)dx\\ &=\int\left(2x^{-1}+3x^{-2}\right)dx\\ &=2\ln x+\dfrac{3x^{-1}}{-1}+c\\ &=2\ln x-\dfrac{3}{x}+c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Splits into separate terms, or one correct term, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Standard absolute value inequality split into two cases.

solutions.latex:
For $|u|>a$, either $u>a$ or $u<-a$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-1&>5 & \text{or}\quad 2x-1&<-5\\ x&>3 & x&<-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x>3 \text{ or } x<-2$$
criteria: One correct inequality, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=\ln(2x-5)$ at $x=3$.

dif.r: Chain rule on log then routine tangent equation.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule.
$$y'=\dfrac{2}{2x-5}$$
At $x=3$ the gradient is
$$m=\dfrac{2}{6-5}=2$$
When $x=3$:
$$y=\ln 1=0$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=2(x-3)\\ y&=2x-6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=2x-6$$
criteria: Finds the gradient and the point, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: On his 1st birthday, Timmy was given \$5 by his Aunty Ruth. On each subsequent birthday, Aunty Ruth gave Timmy \$2 more than the previous year.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How much did Aunty Ruth give Timmy on his 20th birthday?

dif.r: Direct nth term of arithmetic sequence.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If Timmy saves the money every year, how old will he be when he has received over \$100 in total?

dif.r: Set up sum inequality, solve by trial with small numbers.

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
The amounts form an arithmetic sequence with $a=5$ and $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_{20}&=a+(n-1)d\\ &=5+(20-1)\times 2\\ &=5+38\\ &=43 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Timmy was given } \$43.$$

The total after $n$ birthdays is the sum of the arithmetic series with $a=5$, $d=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n&=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)>100\\ \dfrac{n}{2}\left(10+2(n-1)\right)&>100\\ n(n+4)&>100 \end{aligned}$$
By trial and error, $n>8$.

So he has received over \$100 after his 9th birthday.
$$\therefore\ \text{Timmy will be } 9.$$
criteria: Correct inequality or sum formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}$.

parts.label: a

dif.r: Substitute -x and simplify to test oddness.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-x^2}{\left(1+x^2\right)^2}$.

dif.r: Routine quotient rule show-that with simple simplification

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and verify their nature.

dif.r: Standard stationary points from given derivative, nature by sign table

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$, showing the information found in parts (a) and (c). You need not show points of inflection, but any asymptotes should be clear.

dif.r: Curve sketch combining stationary points with horizontal asymptote behaviour

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of y=x/(1+x^2) with turning points at (1, 1/2) and (-1, -1/2)

solutions.latex:
Find $f(-x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=\dfrac{-x}{1+(-x)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{-x}{1+x^2}\\ &=-f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x) \text{ is odd.}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=1+x^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\dfrac{1\times(1+x^2)-x(2x)}{(1+x^2)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1+x^2-2x^2}{(1+x^2)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1-x^2}{(1+x^2)^2}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-x^2&=0\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $y=\dfrac12$; when $x=-1$, $y=-\dfrac12$.

\extable{Ts8826_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative at $x=1$, and from negative to positive at $x=-1$.

Therefore $\left(1,\dfrac12\right)$ is a local maximum and $\left(-1,-\dfrac12\right)$ is a local minimum.
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The concert needs an attendance of at least $2000$ in order to make a profit. Find the maximum distance the concert can be from the city centre and still make a profit.

dif.r: Simple inequality from given inverse variation model

parts.label: c
parts.latex: At a point on the graph, the number of people attending is decreasing at the rate of $5$ people per $4$ metres. Find the value of $D$ for this point.

dif.r: Convert stated rate, differentiate k/D, solve for D

figures.cap: hyperbola N against D passing through (300, 6000)

solutions.latex:
Substitute $D=300$, $N=6000$ into $N=\dfrac{k}{D}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6000&=\dfrac{k}{300}\\ k&=1\,800\,000\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ N=\dfrac{1\,800\,000}{D}$$

meta.format_note: Source wrote k=18×10^5, same as 1 800 000.

solutions.latex:
The concert makes a profit when $N\ge2000$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1\,800\,000}{D}&\ge2000\\ D&\le900\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum distance is } 900 \text{ m}$$

Since $N=\dfrac{k}{D}$, differentiating with respect to $D$ gives
$$\dfrac{dN}{dD}=-\dfrac{k}{D^2}$$
The rate is $-\dfrac{5}{4}=-1.25$ people per metre, so
$$\begin{aligned} D^2&=\dfrac{-k}{dN/dD}\\ &=\dfrac{-1\,800\,000}{-1.25}\\ &=1\,440\,000\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ D=1200 \text{ m}\ (=1.2 \text{ km})$$
criteria: Correct equation for $D^2$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A experimenter records the following data:

$4\quad 6\quad 8\quad 8\quad 9\quad 10\quad 12\quad 12\quad 17\quad 24$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Use the standard criterion for outliers on your reference sheet to determine any outliers in the data.
parts.note: Quartiles, IQR and outliers of a data set are not in 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

dif.r: Quartiles, IQR and standard outlier fences applied cleanly

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the mean and variance for the dataset.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Write down a dataset with the same variance but a mean of $15$.
parts.note: Effect of shifting a data set on its variance (data-set summary statistics) is removed (Standard content).

solutions.latex:
From the ordered data, $Q_1=8$ and $Q_3=12$.
$$\begin{aligned} IQR&=12-8\\ &=4\end{aligned}$$
An outlier is a value above $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$ or below $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times4&=18\\ Q_1-1.5\times4&=2\end{aligned}$$
Only $24$ lies outside the interval from $2$ to $18$.

$$\therefore\ 24 \text{ is an outlier}$$
criteria: Finds the correct fences, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using a calculator on the data:
$$\bar x=11,\qquad \sigma_n\approx5.5$$
$$\text{variance}=\sigma_n^2\approx30.4$$
criteria: One of the mean and variance correct, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean but leaves the variance unchanged. The mean is $11$, so add $4$ to every value:
$$8,\ 10,\ 12,\ 12,\ 13,\ 14,\ 16,\ 16,\ 21,\ 28$$

$$\begin{aligned} 2m+(1-8m)+4m+0.1&=1\\ -2m+1.1&=1\\ m&=0.05\end{aligned}$$
Then $p(x)$ is $0.1,\ 0.6,\ 0.2,\ 0.1$ for $x=1,2,3,4$, all non-negative.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X)&=1\times0.1+2\times0.6+3\times0.2+4\times0.1\\ &=0.1+1.2+0.6+0.4\\ &=2.3\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=0.05 \text{ and } E(X)=2.3$$
criteria: Finds $m=0.05$ and sets up $E(X)$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A $20$ kg block of a radioactive isotope is decaying, and the amount $M$ kg remaining after $t$ years is given by the equation

$$M=20e^{-0.05t}$$

parts.label: a

dif.r: Direct substitution into exponential model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How long until half the isotope has decayed? Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.

dif.r: Solve exponential equation using logarithms for half-life

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Show that $M$ satisfies the equation $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.05M$ and hence find the rate of decay when $5$ kg of the isotope remains. Give your answer correct to $2$ significant figures.

dif.r: Differentiate exponential, express in M, substitute value

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} M&=20e^{-0.05\times2}\\ &=20e^{-0.1}\\ &\approx18.1 \text{ kg}\end{aligned}$$

Half the isotope has decayed when $M=10$.
$$\begin{aligned} 10&=20e^{-0.05t}\\ e^{-0.05t}&=\dfrac12\\ -0.05t&=\ln\dfrac12\\ t&=\dfrac{\ln2}{0.05}\\ &\approx13.9\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after } 13.9 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Correct equation in logarithmic form, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $M=20e^{-0.05t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt}&=20\times(-0.05)e^{-0.05t}\\ &=-0.05\left(20e^{-0.05t}\right)\\ &=-0.05M\end{aligned}$$
When $M=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt}&=-0.05\times5\\ &=-0.25\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the rate of decay is } 0.25 \text{ kg/year}$$
criteria: Shows the differential equation, or equivalent merit

$$P(\text{green}\mid\text{left})=\dfrac{17}{46}$$

Events are independent if $P(\text{green}\mid\text{left})=P(\text{green})$.
$$P(\text{green})=\dfrac{61}{200},\qquad P(\text{green}\mid\text{left})=\dfrac{17}{46}$$

questions.stem:
Janice deposits \$5000 into her savings account every year on January 1. During the year, the account receives compound interest of $6\%$ per annum, where interest is added to her account at the end of each year.

Let $J_n$ be the value of Janice's account immediately after her $n$th investment.

dif.r: One-step recurrence computation of second balance

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Show that

$$J_n=\dfrac{250\,000\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{3}$$

dif.r: Generalise annuity pattern to geometric series and sum it

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine the minimum number of years until Janice's account contains \$100\,000.

dif.r: Rearrange formula, logarithms, interpret rounding to whole years

solutions.latex:
Let $M=5000$ be the annual deposit. Each earlier deposit is multiplied by $1.06$ for each further year.
$$\begin{aligned} J_2&=1.06M+M\\ J_3&=(1.06M+M)\times1.06+M\\ &=M+1.06M+1.06^2M\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$J_n=M+1.06M+1.06^2M+\dots+1.06^{n-1}M$$
This is a geometric series with $n$ terms, first term $M$ and $r=1.06$.
$$\begin{aligned} J_n&=\dfrac{M\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{1.06-1}\\ &=\dfrac{5000\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{0.06}\\ &=\dfrac{250\,000\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{3}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the series for $J_n$ (following from the working), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Solve $J_n=100\,000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100\,000&=\dfrac{250\,000\left(1.06^n-1\right)}{3}\\ \dfrac{30}{25}&=1.06^n-1\\ 1.06^n&=2.2\end{aligned}$$
Taking logarithms,
$$\begin{aligned} n&=\log_{1.06}2.2\\ &=\dfrac{\log2.2}{\log1.06}\\ &\approx13.5\end{aligned}$$
$n$ must be a whole number of instalments, so round up.

$$\therefore\ n=14,\ \text{on the payment of the 14th instalment, at the start of the 14th year}$$

questions.stem: Let $y=xe^{x^2-3x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
Show that

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\left(2x^2-3x+1\right)e^{x^2-3x}$$

dif.r: Product rule with chain rule on exponential, factorise

parts.label: b
parts.latex: For what values of $x$ is $y$ decreasing?

dif.r: Sign of quadratic factor gives decreasing interval

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{x^2-3x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=(2x-3)e^{x^2-3x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=1\times e^{x^2-3x}+x(2x-3)e^{x^2-3x}\\ &=\left(1+2x^2-3x\right)e^{x^2-3x}\\ &=\left(2x^2-3x+1\right)e^{x^2-3x}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the product rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$y$ is decreasing where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}<0$. First find where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x^2-3x+1&=0\\ (2x-1)(x-1)&=0\\ x&=\dfrac12,\ 1\end{aligned}$$
$e^{x^2-3x}>0$, so the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is the sign of the quadratic. It is an upright parabola, so it is negative between its roots.

$$\therefore\ y \text{ is decreasing for } \dfrac12<x<1$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex:

$$A=\dfrac{2V}{r}+4r^2$$

dif.r: Model metal area from diagram, eliminate h using volume

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the minimum area of metal $A$ required to make a barrel. Your result will depend on $V$.

dif.r: Optimisation with general constant V, cube-root algebra to finish

figures.cap: square sheet with inscribed circle of radius r, and rectangle of sides 2*pi*r and h

solutions.latex:
The metal is a square of side $2r$ plus a rectangle of dimensions $2\pi r$ by $h$ for the curved side.
$$A=(2r)^2+2\pi rh$$
The volume of the cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$, so $h=\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}$. Substituting,
$$\begin{aligned} A&=4r^2+2\pi r\times\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}\\ &=4r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $A$ in $r$ and $h$, or substitutes $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $A=\dfrac{2V}{r}+4r^2$ and set $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dA}{dr}&=-\dfrac{2V}{r^2}+8r=0\\ \dfrac{2V}{r^2}&=8r\\ r^3&=\dfrac{V}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}&=\dfrac{4V}{r^3}+8\\ &=\dfrac{4V\times4}{V}+8\\ &=24>0\end{aligned}$$
The curve is concave up, so this is a local minimum.

The minimum area is
$$\begin{aligned} A&=4r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}\\ &=\dfrac{4r^3+2V}{r}\\ &=\dfrac{3V}{r}\qquad(\text{since } 4r^3=V)\\ &=\dfrac{3V}{\sqrt[3]{V/4}}\\ &=3\sqrt[3]{4}\,V^{\frac23}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows the stationary point is a minimum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A company's new logo is the region bounded by $y=\sin x$ and $y=x\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. This region is shown shaded in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1295_q32_1}

Calculate the area of the logo, correct to $2$ decimal places.

You may wish to assume the result

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\cos x\right)=\cos x-x\sin x.$$

dif.r: Find intersection, split regions, reverse hint to integrate x sin x

figures.cap: shaded region between y = sin x and y = x sin x on [0, pi]
solution sketch: logo diagram annotated with regions A1 and A2 and intersection at x=1

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1295_q32_s1}

From the hint, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos x)=\cos x-x\sin x$. Integrating both sides,
$$x\cos x=\sin x-\int x\sin x\,dx$$
$$\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x$$
The curves meet where $x\sin x=\sin x$, that is $x=1$ (for $0<x<\pi$). For $0<x<1$, $\sin x>x\sin x$; for $1<x<\pi$, $x\sin x>\sin x$.

First region:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1&=\int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx\\ &=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x+x\cos x\Big]_0^1\\ &=(-\cos1-\sin1+\cos1)-(-1)\\ &=1-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
Second region:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=\int_1^{\pi}(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx\\ &=\Big[\sin x-x\cos x+\cos x\Big]_1^{\pi}\\ &=(\pi-1)-\sin1\end{aligned}$$
Total area:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=A_1+A_2\\ &=1-\sin1+\pi-1-\sin1\\ &=\pi-2\sin1\\ &\approx1.46 \text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct antiderivative and evaluation of both regions, or equivalent merit
Correct integrals for both regions, or equivalent merit
Splits the area at the intersection, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The probability density function for a continuous random variable $X$ is:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\sin x & 0<x<k\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

What is the value of $k$?

dif.r: Set pdf integral to 1 and solve simple trig equation

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function the total area is $1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k \sin x\,dx &= 1 \\ \left[-\cos x\right]_0^k &= 1 \\ -(\cos k-\cos 0) &= 1 \\ -(\cos k-1) &= 1 \\ \cos k-1 &= -1 \\ \cos k &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
The smallest positive solution is $k=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, option A.

questions.stem:
For the following continuous probability distribution

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3x^2}{511} & \text{for } 1\le x\le 8\\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find $P(X=5)$

dif.r: Recall point probability is zero for continuous variable

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $P(X\le 5)$

dif.r: Integrate simple polynomial pdf over interval; routine

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find $P(X>5)$

dif.r: Complement of previous result; one step

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
For a continuous distribution, the probability at a single point is zero.
$$P(X=5)=0$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Integrate the density from $1$ to $5$.

Write $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ and combine over a common denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}+\tan\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta+\sin\theta(1+\sin\theta)}{(1+\sin\theta)\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta+\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta}{(1+\sin\theta)\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{(1+\sin\theta)\cos\theta} &&(\text{as } \cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sec\theta \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: Consider the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+6$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that stationary points occur at $(-1,11)$ and $(3,-21)$ and determine their nature

dif.r: Routine cubic stationary points with a second derivative test

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and check concavity changes; two routine steps

parts.label: c
parts.latex:

Do not attempt to find the $x$-intercepts.

dif.r: One-mark sketch using points already found

figures.cap: solution sketch: student sketch of y=f(x) with stationary points (-1,11), (3,-21), y-intercept 6 and inflexion (1,-5)

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2-6x-9 \\ 3x^2-6x-9 &= 0 \\ 3(x^2-2x-3) &= 0 \\ 3(x-3)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=3$ or $x=-1$.

When $x=3$, $y=-21$. When $x=-1$, $y=11$.

The second derivative decides the nature.
$$f''(x)=6x-6$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(3) &= 12>0 &&\text{minimum turning point at } (3,-21) \\ f''(-1) &= -12<0 &&\text{maximum turning point at } (-1,11) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points and $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit
Finds $f'(x)$ and solves $f'(x)=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Possible points of inflexion occur where $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-6 &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
When $x=1$, $y=-5$, so the possible point is $(1,-5)$.

Test the concavity either side of $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -6<0 &&\text{concave down} \\ f''(1) &= 0 \\ f''(2) &= 6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflexion.
$$\therefore\ (1,-5)\text{ is a point of inflexion}$$

parts.latex: Determine the equation of a curve given by $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=18x+4$ if it is known that $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point on the curve.

dif.r: Two integrations, using the stationary-point condition to find both constants

solutions.latex:
Integrate once.
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=9x^2+4x+c$$
The point $(1,-2)$ is stationary, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ when $x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9+4+c &= 0 \\ c &= -13 \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=9x^2+4x-13$.

Integrate again.
$$y=3x^3+2x^2-13x+C$$
Substitute $x=1$, $y=-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} -2 &= 3+2-13+C \\ C &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=3x^3+2x^2-13x+6$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ with $c=-13$ and integrates again, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dL}{dt} &= -220(20-5) \\ &= -3300 \text{ L/min} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A factory is producing laptops. The annual production, $M$ laptops at time $t$ years, is given by:

$M=M_0e^{kt}$

Initially the production at the factory was 2000 laptops per annum.

Five years later it had increased to 3200 laptops per annum.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the values of $M_0$ and $k$ (Answer correct to three decimal places).

dif.r: Standard exponential model: initial value then solve for k with logs

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many years will it take for the production to double its original output? Answer correct to one decimal place.

dif.r: Standard doubling-time calculation using logarithms

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$, $M=2000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2000 &= M_0e^0 \\ M_0 &= 2000 \end{aligned}$$
So $M=2000e^{kt}$. When $t=5$, $M=3200$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3200 &= 2000e^{5k} \\ 1.6 &= e^{5k} \\ \ln 1.6 &= 5k \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln 1.6}{5} \\ &\approx 0.094 \text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ M_0=2000,\quad k\approx 0.094$$
criteria: Finds $M_0$, or sets up $3200=2000e^{5k}$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The original output is 2000, so double is $M=4000$. Use $k=\dfrac{\ln 1.6}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4000 &= 2000e^{\frac{\ln 1.6}{5}t} \\ 2 &= e^{\frac{\ln 1.6}{5}t} \\ \ln 2 &= \dfrac{\ln 1.6}{5}t \\ t &= 7.37\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 7.4 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Sets up $2=e^{kt}$ with the correct $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity.
$$a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-4\cos 2t$$
Set $a=0$ for $0\le t\le\pi$, so $\cos 2t=0$ with $0\le 2t\le 2\pi$.

$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-2\sin 2t &= 0 \\ \sin 2t &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
For $0\le 2t\le 2\pi$:
$$2t=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$$

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity to find the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int(1-2\sin 2t)\,dt \\ &= t+\cos 2t+c \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$ and $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 0+\cos 0+c \\ c &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=t+\cos 2t-1$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into $x=t+\cos 2t-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}+\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)-1 \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2}-1 \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.latex:

(The formula for the volume of a cone is $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2\sqrt{l^2-r^2}$ where $l$ is the slant height)

dif.r: Show-that: identify slant height as sector radius, substitute formula

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the value of $\theta$, to 2 decimal places, for which the volume of the cone is maximised.

dif.r: Optimisation with chain rule on a square root, plus nature test

figures.cap: circle radius 2 with shaded major sector of angle pi*theta, points A, B, centre C

solutions.latex:
The arc length is radius times angle.
$$l=r\theta=2\times\pi\theta=2\pi\theta \text{ cm}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (single row).

solutions.latex:
The arc of the sector becomes the circumference of the cone's base, so with $C=2\pi r$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\pi r &= 2\pi\theta \\ r &= \theta \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (single row).

solutions.latex:
The slant height of the cone is the radius of the sector, so $l=2$, and $r=\theta$ from part (b).
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2\sqrt{l^2-r^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\theta^2\sqrt{2^2-\theta^2} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}\sqrt{\theta^4(4-\theta^2)} \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}\sqrt{4\theta^4-\theta^6} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (single row).

solutions.latex:
Write $V=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\left(4\theta^4-\theta^6\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The maximum occurs where $V'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} V' &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}\left(4\theta^4-\theta^6\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(16\theta^3-6\theta^5\right) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi\left(16\theta^3-6\theta^5\right)}{6\sqrt{4\theta^4-\theta^6}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $V'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 16\theta^3-6\theta^5 &= 0 \\ 2\theta^3(8-3\theta^2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $\theta\ne 0$, $\theta^2=\dfrac{8}{3}$.
$$\theta=\sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}}\approx 1.63 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$
Nature test, using the sign of $V'$:
$$\begin{aligned} V'(1) &\approx 3.02>0 &&\text{increasing} \\ V'(1.63) &= 0 && \\ V'(1.8) &\approx -3.72<0 &&\text{decreasing} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient changes from positive to negative.
$$\therefore\ \text{the volume is a maximum when } \theta\approx 1.63$$
criteria: Finds $\theta\approx 1.63$ without testing the nature, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following represents the graph $y=-f(-x)$?

dif.r: Same task as anchor: combine two reflections to identify graph of -f(-x).

figures.cap: graph of y=f(x)
option A: option A graph
option B: option B graph
option C: option C graph

solutions.latex:
The graph $y=-f(-x)$ comes from $y=f(x)$ by two reflections: $x\to -x$ is a reflection in the $y$-axis, and the minus sign in front is a reflection in the $x$-axis. Together they rotate the graph $180^\circ$ about the origin.

The point where $y=f(x)$ touches the $x$-axis, at a positive $x$-value, moves to a point where the new graph touches the $x$-axis at a negative $x$-value.

The positive $y$-intercept of $y=f(x)$ becomes a negative $y$-intercept.

As $x\to -\infty$, $y=-f(-x)=-f(\text{large positive})$, which is positive and large, so the left end goes up. As $x\to\infty$, the right end goes down.

Only the graph in option D has all of these features: it touches the $x$-axis at a negative $x$-value, has a negative $y$-intercept, and goes up on the left and down on the right.

A and B keep the touch point at positive $x$, and C has a positive $y$-intercept, so they fail.

parts.label: iv
parts.latex: $y=\dfrac{(1-x)^3}{x^2}$ and show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ may be expressed as $-\dfrac{(x+2)(1-x)^2}{x^3}$

dif.r: Quotient rule plus careful factorising to reach the given form.

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 3 \times 2(2x+1)^2 \\ &= 6(2x+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the chain rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
$$y = 3x^{-1}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -3x^{-2} \\ &= -\dfrac{3}{x^2} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= x^3 & v &= \cos x \\ u' &= 3x^2 & v' &= -\sin x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= u'v + uv' \\ &= 3x^2\cos x - x^3\sin x \\ &= x^2(3\cos x - x\sin x) \end{aligned}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u &= (1-x)^3 & v &= x^2 \\ u' &= -3(1-x)^2 & v' &= 2x \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{-3x^2(1-x)^2 - 2x(1-x)^3}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{x(1-x)^2\left[-3x - 2(1-x)\right]}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{(1-x)^2\left[-3x - 2 + 2x\right]}{x^3} \\ &= -\dfrac{(x+2)(1-x)^2}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \ln(\sin^2 x) - \ln(\cos^2 x) &= \ln\left(\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}\right) \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right)^2 \\ &= 2\ln(\tan x) \end{aligned}$$

Using part (a):

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(\sin^2 x) - \ln(\cos^2 x)\right] &= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[2\ln(\tan x)\right] \\ &= 2\cdot\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\cos^2 x \cdot \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sin x\cos x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Derivative $2\cdot\dfrac{\sec^2 x}{\tan x}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The logarithm needs its argument positive:
$$x-2>0, \text{ so } x>2$$
The square root needs a non-negative expression:
$$9-x\ge 0, \text{ so } x\le 9$$
Both conditions must hold, so the domain is $x>2$ and $x\le 9$. This is option C.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{20} -(-1)^r$ ?

dif.r: Interpret sigma notation with alternating sign; terms cancel in pairs

solutions.latex:
Write out the terms of the sum:
$$\begin{aligned} T_1&=-(-1)^1=-1\\ T_2&=-(-1)^2=1\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ T_{19}&=-(-1)^{19}=1\\ T_{20}&=-(-1)^{20}=-1\end{aligned}$$
The terms alternate $-1, 1$, so each consecutive pair adds to zero.

There are 10 pairs, so
$$S_{20}=0$$
This is option B.

meta.format_note: Source lists $T_{18}=-1$, $T_{19}=1$, $T_{20}=-1$; kept consistent with alternating pattern, pairing (1,2),...,(19,20) gives 0 (source's listed last terms are consistent with $T_{19}=1,T_{20}=-1$).

solutions.latex:
The mean is the midpoint of the interval containing $99.7\%$ of the data:
$$\mu=\dfrac{25+145}{2}=85$$
About $99.7\%$ of the data lies within $3$ standard deviations of the mean, so
$$\begin{aligned} \mu-3\sigma&=25\\ 85-3\sigma&=25\\ \sigma&=20\end{aligned}$$
The variance is $\sigma^2=400$.

So the mean is $85$ and the variance is $400$. This is option D.

dif.r: Recognise integral of odd function over symmetric interval is zero

skills: Integrals of odd and even functions

figures.cap: odd piecewise-linear function with shaded area between x=-2a and x=2a

solutions.latex:
From the graph, the shaded area to the right of the $y$-axis is a triangle (base $a$, height $2a$) and a rectangle ($a$ by $2a$):
$$\int_0^{2a} f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\times a\times 2a+a\times 2a=3a^2$$
The function $f(x)$ is odd, so the shaded area is $2\times 3a^2=6a^2$, but the integral over the symmetric interval is zero:
$$\int_{-2a}^{2a} f(x)\,dx=0$$
This gives a signed area of $0$, not the shaded area. The other options all give $6a^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{B: } 2\displaystyle\int_0^{-2a} f(x)\,dx &= -2\displaystyle\int_{-2a}^{0} f(x)\,dx = -2\left(-3a^2\right) = 6a^2 \\ \text{C: } 2\displaystyle\int_0^{a} f(x)\,dx+4a^2 &= 2a^2+4a^2 = 6a^2 \\ \text{D: } 3(a\times 2a) &= 6a^2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence option A.

parts.latex:
Let $h(x)=f\big(g(x)\big)$, with $f(4)=1$, $f'(x)=6$, $g(2)=4$ and $g'(2)=4$.

What is the equation of the tangent of the graph of $y=h(x)$ at $x=2$?

dif.r: Chain rule with given values, then point-gradient tangent

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $h'(x)=f'\big(g(x)\big)\cdot g'(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} h'(2)&=f'\big(g(2)\big)\cdot g'(2)\\ &=6\times4\\ &=24\end{aligned}$$
So the gradient of the tangent is $24$.
$$h(2)=f\big(g(2)\big)=f(4)=1$$
Hence the tangent passes through $(2,1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y-1&=24(x-2)\\ y&=24x-47\end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex: Find the exact gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=\log_e(\tan x)$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

dif.r: Chain rule on log of tan, exact trig evaluation

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $\ln u$ with $u=\tan x$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}\cdot\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x)=\dfrac{\sec^2x}{\tan x}$$
At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{\sec^2\frac{\pi}{3}}{\tan\frac{\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt3}\\ &=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient}=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{3}$$
criteria: Recognises the derivative of $\tan x$ is $\sec^2 x$, or equivalent merit
