questions.stem: An arithmetic sequence from start to end is $51, 44, 37, \ldots, -47$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Write a simplified expression for the $n$th term for this sequence.

dif.r: Direct arithmetic nth term formula

parts.label: b
parts.latex: How many terms are there in the sequence?

dif.r: Solve linear equation for number of terms

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the sum of this series.

dif.r: Substitute into sum formula with first and last term

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic sequence $T_n=a+(n-1)d$, with $a=51$ and $d=-7$:
$$\begin{aligned} T_n&=51+(n-1)(-7)\\ &=58-7n\end{aligned}$$

The last term is $-47$, so set $T_n=-47$:
$$\begin{aligned} 58-7n&=-47\\ 58+47&=7n\\ 105&=7n\\ n&=15\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{there are } 15 \text{ terms}$$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ with $n=15$, $a=51$, $l=-47$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{15}&=\dfrac{15}{2}\big(51+(-47)\big)\\ &=30\end{aligned}$$

Differentiate the following:

$y=\sqrt[3]{2x-11}$

dif.r: Rewrite root as power, single chain rule step

solutions.latex:
Rewrite as a power:
$$y=\sqrt[3]{2x-11}=(2x-11)^{\frac13}$$
Using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac13(2x-11)^{-\frac23}\times2\\ &=\dfrac23(2x-11)^{-\frac23}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the power is $-\dfrac23$, or significant attempt at the chain rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Differentiate the following:

$y=e^{x}\tan(5x)$

dif.r: Routine product rule with standard derivatives

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{x} & v&=\tan(5x)\\ u'&=e^{x} & v'&=5\sec^2(5x)\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x\tan(5x)+5e^x\sec^2(5x)$$
criteria: Attempts to use the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Differentiate the following:

$y=\log_e\left[\dfrac{x}{(x+1)^4}\right]$

dif.r: Log laws to split, differentiate, combine fractions

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws to separate the terms:
$$y=\ln x-4\ln(x+1)$$
Differentiating:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac1x-\dfrac{4}{x+1}\\ &=\dfrac{(x+1)-4x}{x(x+1)}\\ &=\dfrac{1-3x}{x(x+1)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses log laws to simplify the expression, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
After $5$ minutes the carriage has completed $\dfrac{5}{20}=\dfrac14$ of a revolution, so it is level with the centre of the wheel.
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac12\times\text{diameter} \\ &= 35 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Added one-line reason for the quarter revolution.

solutions.latex:
The period is $20$ minutes, so
$$\dfrac{2\pi}{b}=20$$
$$b=\dfrac{2\pi}{20}=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$$
The height oscillates between $0$ and $70$, so the centre line is $c=35$ and the amplitude is $35$. The carriage starts at its lowest point ($h=0$ at $t=0$), so the cosine is reflected and $a=-35$.
$$h(t)=-35\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right)+35$$
$$\therefore\ a=-35,\quad b=\dfrac{\pi}{10},\quad c=35$$
criteria: Obtains the correct value for one variable, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Reasons for $a$ and $c$ added.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1763_q16_s1}
criteria: Sine or cosine curve that oscillates between $h=0$ and $h=70$

meta.marker_note: Must have a stationary minimum point at $t=0$ and $t=40$.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change of height is the derivative of $h$.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= h'(t) \\ &= -35\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)\left(-\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{7\pi}{2}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating again gives the rate of change of $R$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= \dfrac{7\pi}{2}\times\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \\ &= \dfrac{7\pi^2}{20}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}t\right) \end{aligned}$$
The maximum value of the cosine is $1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum of } \dfrac{dR}{dt} = \dfrac{7\pi^2}{20}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $R$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Set $h=50$.
$$\begin{aligned} 50 &= -35\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+35 \\ 15 &= -35\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \\ -\dfrac37 &= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \end{aligned}$$
The first time this happens is the first solution of the cosine equation.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi t}{10} &= \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac37\right) \\ t &= \dfrac{10}{\pi}\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac37\right) \\ &\approx 6.41\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 6 \text{ minutes } 25 \text{ seconds}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int x\sqrt{5x^2+1}\,dx$

dif.r: Standard reverse chain rule integral with constant adjustment

solutions.latex:
Method 1: the integrand is of the form $k\,f'(x)[f(x)]^n$ with $f(x)=5x^2+1$, $f'(x)=10x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{5x^2+1}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{10}\int 10x\sqrt{5x^2+1}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{10}\times\dfrac23(5x^2+1)^{\frac32}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{15}(5x^2+1)^{\frac32}+C\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: if $y=(5x^2+1)^{\frac32}$ then
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=15x(5x^2+1)^{\frac12}$$
so
$$\int x\sqrt{5x^2+1}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{15}(5x^2+1)^{\frac32}+C$$
criteria: Attempts to integrate, using the form $k\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
When cooking oil cools down, its temperature, $T$, in degrees Celsius, after $t$ minutes is given by the formula

$$T=60+150e^{-0.1t}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the initial temperature of the oil?

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into exponential model

parts.label: b
parts.latex: At what temperature is the oil decreasing at a rate of $10^\circ$C per minute? Leave your answer to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Set derivative to -10, solve, substitute back for temperature

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What temperature does the oil eventually cool to? Leave your answer to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Limiting value as exponential term decays to zero

solutions.latex:
The initial temperature is at $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 60+150e^0 \\ &= 210^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

The temperature is decreasing at $10^\circ$C per minute when $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-10$.
$$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-15e^{-0.1t}$$
$$\begin{aligned} -10 &= -15e^{-0.1t} \\ \dfrac23 &= e^{-0.1t} \\ -0.1t &= \ln\left(\dfrac23\right) \\ t &= -10\ln\left(\dfrac23\right) \\ &\approx 4.0547 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $e^{-0.1t}=\dfrac23$ into $T$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 60+150\left(\dfrac23\right) \\ &= 160^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source wrote 't = 4.0547 sec' (also in the criteria); $t$ is in minutes, so corrected to minutes.

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.1t}\to 0$, so $T\to 60$.
$$\therefore\ T=60^\circ\text{C}$$

questions.stem:
The velocity, $\dot{x}$, in m/s of a particle moving in a horizontal straight line is given by:

$$\dot{x}=3-\dfrac{9}{t-2}\quad\text{for } t>2,$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.latex:

Justify your answer with calculations.

dif.r: Substitute t=3 and interpret sign of velocity.

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the distance travelled by the particle between $t=3$ and $t=7$. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Split integral at direction change; log antiderivative, careful evaluation.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= 3-\dfrac{9}{3-2} \\ &= -6 \end{aligned}$$
The velocity is negative, so
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is moving left.}$$

The particle changes direction when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3-\dfrac{9}{t-2} &= 0 \\ t-2 &= 3 \\ t &= 5 \end{aligned}$$

The velocity is negative for $3\le t<5$ and positive for $5<t\le 7$, so the distance is found in two parts.
$$\text{Distance}=-\int_3^5\left(3-\dfrac{9}{t-2}\right)dt+\int_5^7\left(3-\dfrac{9}{t-2}\right)dt$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= -\Big[3t-9\ln(t-2)\Big]_3^5+\Big[3t-9\ln(t-2)\Big]_5^7 \\ &= -\Big[\big(15-9\ln 3\big)-\big(9-9\ln 1\big)\Big]+\Big[\big(21-9\ln 5\big)-\big(15-9\ln 3\big)\Big] \\ &= (9\ln 3-6)+\left(6+9\ln\dfrac35\right) \\ &\approx 5.29 \text{ m (2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the distance in one of the directions, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source dropped the minus sign in front of the first bracket when evaluating (the values $9\ln 3-6$ and the final $5.29$ were already consistent with it); restored. Reason line for the sign split added.

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac{3k}{4}$, $P(B)=k$ and $P(\bar{A}\cap B)=k^2$ where $0<k<1$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find an expression for $P(A\cap B)$ in terms of $k$.

dif.r: Partition P(B) into two disjoint events, algebraic expression.

skills: Addition rule and mutually exclusive events

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that the two events are independent, find the value of $k$.

dif.r: Apply independence condition to set up and solve quadratic in k.

solutions.latex:
Since $P(B)=P(A\cap B)+P(\bar{A}\cap B)$, we have
$$\begin{aligned} P(A\cap B)&=P(B)-P(\bar{A}\cap B) \\ &=k-k^2 \end{aligned}$$

If the events are independent, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

$$\begin{aligned} k-k^2&=\dfrac{3k}{4}\times k \\ 4k-4k^2&=3k^2 \\ 7k^2-4k&=0 \\ k(7k-4)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $k=0$ or $k=\dfrac{4}{7}$.

Since $0<k<1$:
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{4}{7}$$
criteria: Writes a correct equation in terms of $k$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source line '3k^2=4k-4k^2' kept as equivalent rearrangement was rewritten as 4k-4k^2=3k^2 (same equation).

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx&=\dfrac{3}{4}\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left[x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left(2^2-\dfrac{2^3}{3}\right)-\dfrac{3}{4}\left(0^2-\dfrac{0^3}{3}\right) \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $f(x)\ge0$ for all $x$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$, $f(x)$ is a probability density function.

questions.stem:
Consider the function:

$$f(x)=\log_e(x^2+1)$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the stationary point(s) of $f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: Chain rule derivative, quotient rule second derivative, classify one point.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the point(s) of inflection of $f(x)$.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 already found, check concavity change.

parts.label: c

\exfigure{1763_q26_1}

parts.latex:
Use the Trapezoidal Rule with four subintervals to find an approximation to:

$$\int_1^3\log_e(x^2+1)\,dx.$$

dif.r: Trapezoidal rule with four subintervals, computing log values.

parts.label: e
parts.latex: State whether the approximation found in part (b) is greater or less than the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_1^3\log_e(x^2+1)\,dx$. Use your sketch in part (c) to provide a brief justification for your answer.

dif.r: Justify under/overestimate from concavity on the interval.

figures.cap: blank x-y axes for sketch
solution sketch: sketch of y=ln(x^2+1)

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}\times2x=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$$
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}=0$$
so $2x=0$, giving $x=0$.

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2x & v&=x^2+1\\ u'&=2 & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=\dfrac{2(x^2+1)-2x(2x)}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{2x^2+2-4x^2}{(x^2+1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{2(1-x^2)}{(x^2+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$f''(0)=\dfrac{2(1-0^2)}{(0^2+1)^2}=2>0$$
So the curve is concave up at $x=0$, a minimum point.
$$f(0)=\ln(0^2+1)=0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum point is } (0,0)$$

Inflection points occur where $f''(x)=0$ and the concavity changes.
$$\begin{aligned} 2(1-x^2)&=0 \\ x^2&=1 \\ x&=\pm1 \end{aligned}$$
$$f(\pm1)=\ln\left((\pm1)^2+1\right)=\ln2$$
Test the sign of $f''(x)=\dfrac{2(1-x^2)}{(x^2+1)^2}$ either side:

\extable{Ts8990_1}

The concavity changes at both, so
$$\therefore\ (-1,\ln2)\text{ and }(1,\ln2)\text{ are points of inflection}$$
\exfigure{1763_q26_s1}
criteria: Shows the curve concave up for $-1<x<1$ and concave down for $|x|>1$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the criterion said "concave down between $-1<x<1$"; the curve is concave up there and concave down for $|x|>1$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the criterion said "concave down between $-1<x<1$"; the curve is concave up there and concave down for $|x|>1$.

solutions.latex:
Write both curves with $x$ in terms of $y$:
$$x=\dfrac{y^2-6}{2},\qquad x=y+1$$
Intersection:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{y^2-6}{2}&=y+1 \\ y^2-6&=2y+2 \\ y^2-2y-8&=0 \\ (y-4)(y+2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $y=4$ or $y=-2$, giving points $(-1,-2)$ and $(5,4)$.

Integrating with respect to $y$, the line is to the right of the parabola:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-2}^{4}\left[(y+1)-\dfrac{y^2-6}{2}\right]dy \\ &=\int_{-2}^{4}\left(-\dfrac{y^2}{2}+y+4\right)dy \\ &=\left[-\dfrac{y^3}{6}+\dfrac{y^2}{2}+4y\right]_{-2}^{4} \\ &=\left[-\dfrac{4^3}{6}+\dfrac{4^2}{2}+4(4)\right]-\left[-\dfrac{(-2)^3}{6}+\dfrac{(-2)^2}{2}+4(-2)\right] \\ &=\dfrac{40}{3}-\left(-\dfrac{14}{3}\right) \\ &=18 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

A random variable is normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The table gives the probability that this random variable lies between 0 and $z$ for different values of $z$.

Maya is training for long jump for the national age championships. To be able to compete at the national age championships her longest jump must be beaten by less than 0.26% of the general population.

The distance jumped by the general population is normally distributed with a mean of 3.48 metres and standard deviation of 1.08 metres.

dif.r: Reverse z-table lookup from tail percentage, then unstandardise.

solutions.latex:
The upper tail is $0.26\%$, so $P(Z<z)=1-0.0026=0.9974$, i.e. $P(0<Z<z)=0.4974$.

From the table, $z\approx2.8$.

Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2.8&=\dfrac{x-3.48}{1.08} \\ x-3.48&=3.024 \\ x&=6.504 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x\approx6.50 \text{ m (nearest cm)}$$
criteria: Uses the table to find $z\approx2.8$, or finds $x$ using a wrong $z$, or equivalent merit

$$\int x^n(1+x)^n\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^n dx.$$

dif.r: Needs insight combining x(1+1/x)=1+x before reverse chain rule.

solutions.latex:
Group the factors using $a^n b^n=(ab)^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int x^n(1+x)^n\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^n dx&=\int(1+x)^n\left[x\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\right]^n dx \\ &=\int(1+x)^n(1+x)^n\,dx \\ &=\int(1+x)^{2n}\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{(1+x)^{2n+1}}{2n+1}+C\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
If the distance $OX=a$ km, show that the time $T$ that it takes Helen to complete the three legs is given by

$$T=\dfrac{4\sqrt{a^2+4}-a+(4+2\pi)}{16}\text{ hours.}$$

dif.r: Model three-leg time from distances, Pythagoras and quarter-circle arc.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the value of $a$ that will allow Helen to minimise the time taken to complete the three legs of her practise course.

dif.r: Optimise with chain rule on root, solve, verify minimum.

figures.cap: triathlon course: swim S to X, bike X to Y, jog quarter-circle Y to F

solutions.latex:
Time is $T=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$. Use Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle SOX$ for the swim.
$$SX=\sqrt{a^2+4}\ \text{ so } T_1=\dfrac{\sqrt{a^2+4}}{4}\text{ hours}$$
Bike ride:
$$XY=4-a\ \text{ so } T_2=\dfrac{4-a}{16}\text{ hours}$$
Jog, a quarter of a circle of radius $2$:
$$YF=\dfrac{2\pi(2)}{4}=\pi\ \text{ so } T_3=\dfrac{\pi}{8}\text{ hours}$$
Combining the three times:
$$\begin{aligned} T&=\dfrac{\sqrt{a^2+4}}{4}+\dfrac{4-a}{16}+\dfrac{\pi}{8} \\ &=\dfrac{4\sqrt{a^2+4}-a+(4+2\pi)}{16}\text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the distance $SX$, $XY$ or $YF$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{da}&=\dfrac{1}{16}\left[4\times\dfrac{1}{2}(a^2+4)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(2a)-1\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{16}\left[\dfrac{4a}{\sqrt{a^2+4}}-1\right] \end{aligned}$$
Stationary point when $\dfrac{dT}{da}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4a}{\sqrt{a^2+4}}-1&=0 \\ 4a&=\sqrt{a^2+4} \\ 16a^2&=a^2+4 \\ 15a^2&=4 \\ a^2&=\dfrac{4}{15} \end{aligned}$$
Since $a>0$, $a=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{15}}\approx0.51$ km.

Test the sign of $\dfrac{dT}{da}$ either side:

\extable{Ts9001_1}

The gradient changes from negative to positive, so
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum occurs at } a=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{15}}\approx0.51 \text{ km}$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be any function with domain all real numbers.

Which of the following is an odd function, regardless of the choice of $f(x)$?

dif.r: Abstract odd-function test for arbitrary f across options

solutions.latex:
Let $p(x)=x\left(f(x)+f(-x)\right)$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} p(-x)&=(-x)\left[f(-x)+f(x)\right] \\ &=-p(x) \end{aligned}$$
So $p$ is odd for any $f$.

This is option B.

dif.r: Set half sector area equal, solve for radius

figures.cap: sector PQR with inner arc XY

solutions.latex:
The area of sector $RPQ$ (radius $60$) is
$$\begin{aligned} A_{RPQ}&=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 60^2\times\theta \\ &=1800\theta \end{aligned}$$
The sector $RXY$ has half this area, with radius $r=RX$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 1800\theta \\ \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta&=900\theta \\ r^2&=1800 \\ r&=30\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: If $f(x+2)=x^2+4x+1$, then $f(x)$ is equal to:

dif.r: Substitution to recover f(x) from shifted argument

solutions.latex:
Let $y=x+2$, so $x=y-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(y)&=(y-2)^2+4(y-2)+1 \\ &=y^2-4y+4+4y-8+1 \\ &=y^2-3 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $f(x)=x^2-3$.

This is option A.

parts.latex:
Two functions, $f$and $g$, are differentiable for all real values of $x$. It is known that

$$f(3)=4,\ g(3)=-2,\ f'(3)=5$$

If the tangent to the curve $y=f(x)g(x)$ at $x=3$ has a gradient $-6$, find the value of $g'(3)$.

dif.r: Product rule with given values, solved in reverse

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g'(x)+g(x)f'(x)$$
At $x=3$ the gradient is $-6$.
$$\begin{aligned} -6&=4g'(3)+(-2)(5) \\ -6&=4g'(3)-10 \\ 4&=4g'(3) \\ g'(3)&=1 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

The diagram shows a part of the graph of $y=f(x)$, which has a local maximum at $x=-1$ and a local minimum at $x=1$. Which of the following shows the correct relationship between $f''(-1)$, $f'(1)$ and $f(0)$?

parts.latex:
A probability density function $f(x)$ is given by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{54}(27x-x^3), & 0\le x\le 2.086\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

The $25^{th}$ percentile $p$ of this distribution satisfies which of the following equations?

dif.r: Integrate pdf to 0.25 and rearrange to quartic

skills: Median, mode and percentiles of a pdf

solutions.latex:
The $25$th percentile $p$ satisfies
$$\displaystyle\int_0^p\dfrac{1}{54}(27x-x^3)\,dx=0.25$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{54}\left[\dfrac{27x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^p&=0.25 \\ \dfrac{27p^2}{2}-\dfrac{p^4}{4}&=13.5 \\ 54p^2-p^4&=54 \\ p^4-54p^2+54&=0 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

$$r=\dfrac{\frac{5}{27}}{\frac{5}{6}}=\dfrac{2}{9}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{5}{6}}{1-\frac{2}{9}} \\ &=\dfrac{15}{14} \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:

\extable{1772_q14_t1}

dif.r: Add two probabilities from table

parts.label: c

dif.r: Standard conditional probability from distribution table

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to $1$.
$$p+0.2+q+0.1=1$$
so
$$p+q=0.7 \quad (1)$$
Using $E(X)=4$:
$$p+0.6+5q+0.7=4$$
so
$$p+5q=2.7 \quad (2)$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$4q=2$$
Hence $q=0.5$ and $p=0.2$.
criteria: Writes both equations, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 5)&=0.5+0.1 \\ &=0.6 \end{aligned}$$

Using conditional probability,
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 5\mid X\ge 3)&=\dfrac{P(X\ge 5\cap X\ge 3)}{P(X\ge 3)} \\ &=\dfrac{0.5+0.1}{0.2+0.5+0.1} \\ &=\dfrac{0.6}{0.8} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=5e^{2x} & v&=5-x^2\\ u'&=10e^{2x} & v'&=-2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(5-x^2)\times 10e^{2x}-5e^{2x}(-2x)}{(5-x^2)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{10e^{2x}(5-x^2+x)}{(5-x^2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
At $x=1$: $y=\dfrac{5e^2}{4}$, so the point is $\left(1,\dfrac{5e^2}{4}\right)$.
$$m_T=\dfrac{10e^2(5-1+1)}{16}=\dfrac{25e^2}{8},\qquad m_N=-\dfrac{8}{25e^2}$$
The normal is
$$y-\dfrac{5e^2}{4}=-\dfrac{8}{25e^2}(x-1)$$
(The school's working found the normal at $x=0$, $x+2y-2=0$, not at the $x=1$ the question asks for.)
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Product rule with factorising, then second derivative

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the stationary points of $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.

dif.r: Routine stationary points and second derivative test

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine the point of inflection of $y=f(x)$.

dif.r: Solve f''=0 and check concavity change

dif.r: Cubic sketch using features already found plus intercepts

parts.label: e
parts.latex: Determine the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)$ is concaving down.

dif.r: Solve linear inequality f''<0

figures.cap: solution sketch: teacher's sketch of y=f(x) with intercepts (-1,0),(0,4), minimum (2,0) and inflexion (1,2)

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x+1 & v&=(x-2)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(x-2)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=(x-2)^2+2(x-2)(x+1) \\ &=(x-2)(x-2+2x+2) \\ &=3x(x-2) \end{aligned}$$
Since $f'(x)=3x^2-6x$,
$$f''(x)=6x-6$$
criteria: Shows $f'(x)$ or finds $f''(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$3x(x-2)=0$$
so $x=0$ or $x=2$.

Then $y=f(0)=4$ and $y=f(2)=0$, giving the points $(0,4)$ and $(2,0)$.

The sign of $f''$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down, so } (0,4) \text{ is a maximum}\\ f''(2)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up, so } (2,0) \text{ is a minimum} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflexion needs $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 6x-6&=0 \\ x&=1 \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=(1+1)(1-2)^2=2$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(0)&=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\\ f''(2)&=6>0 &&\text{concave up} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so the point of inflexion is $(1,2)$.
\exfigure{1772_q18_s1}
criteria: Three features and correct shape, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source key features: $y$-intercept and maximum $(0,4)$, $x$-intercept $(-1,0)$, minimum $(2,0)$, inflexion $(1,2)$; these should be labelled on the guideline figure.

solutions.latex:
The graph is concave down where $f''(x)<0$.
$$6x-6<0$$
$$\therefore\ x<1$$

solutions.latex:
The missing values are:

Form: linear.

Direction: negative.

$$\therefore\ \text{the 6th player is expected to make } 6.36 \text{ successful shots on average}$$

A shooting order of 15 is outside the data range ($1$ to $11$), so the prediction is extrapolation and is not appropriate.

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $y=\ln\sin(2x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{2\cos 2x}{\sin 2x} \\ &=2\cot 2x \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric rows were labelled 1 and 2; rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(\ln\sin 2x\big)=2\cot 2x$, so $\displaystyle\int \cot 2x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|\sin 2x|$.

Also $\displaystyle\int \sec^2 x\,dx=\tan x$.
$$\int(\cot 2x+3\sec^2 x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|\sin 2x|+3\tan x+C$$
criteria: Correct integral for $\cot 2x$ or $\sec^2 x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A music festival is preparing a decorative light display along the main entrance. The lights are arranged in rows. The first row contains 12 lights. Each successive row contains exactly 5 more lights than the previous row.

If there are 792 lights used for this display, how many rows are there?

dif.r: Arithmetic sum formula in reverse, solve quadratic for n

skills: Applications of arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
This is an arithmetic series with $a=12$, $d=5$ and $S_n=792$.

Using the sum formula:
$$S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$$
$$792=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2\times 12+(n-1)\times 5\big)$$
$$1584=24n+5n^2-5n$$
$$5n^2+19n-1584=0$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} n&=\dfrac{-19\pm\sqrt{19^2-4\times 5\times(-1584)}}{10} \\ &=\dfrac{-19\pm 179}{10} \end{aligned}$$
Since $n>0$, $n=\dfrac{160}{10}=16$.
$$\therefore\ \text{there are } 16 \text{ rows}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the quadratic formula, or equivalent merit
Substitutes into the sum formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: Information was collected from a group of employees at a company regarding their modes of transport to work. Each employee indicated whether they travel by train, bus or both. The results showed that 60% of the employees travel by train, 50% of the employees travel by bus, and 25% of the employees travel by both bus and train. It was also found that 36 employees travel by exactly one mode of transport mentioned.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that total number of employees in the company is $60$.

dif.r: Set up Venn equation for exactly one mode, show total

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Two different employees are selected at random from the group. Find the probability that neither travel by bus.

dif.r: Two selections without replacement, standard product of probabilities

solutions.latex:
Let the total number of employees be $n$.

Employees travelling by exactly one mode are those by train only plus those by bus only. Each of these is the total for that mode minus the $25\%$ who travel by both.
$$\begin{aligned} (60\%-25\%)n+(50\%-25\%)n&=36 \\ 60\%\times n&=36 \\ n&=60 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the total number of employees is } 60$$

meta.format_note: Source line $60\%n+50\%n-25\%n-25\%n=36$ rewritten as the equivalent grouped form.

solutions.latex:
Employees not travelling by bus: $50\%$ of $60=30$.

Choosing two different employees without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{neither})&=\dfrac{30}{60}\times\dfrac{29}{59} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{29}{59} \\ &=\dfrac{29}{118} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: In a geometric sequence, the $10th$ term is 768 and the $13th$ term is 6144. Find the first term, and the common ratio.

dif.r: Divide two geometric term equations, cube root, back-substitute

solutions.latex:
For a geometric sequence $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, so
$$ar^9=768 \quad (1)$$
$$ar^{12}=6144 \quad (2)$$
Dividing (2) by (1):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{ar^{12}}{ar^9}&=\dfrac{6144}{768} \\ r^3&=8 \\ r&=2 \end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1):
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{768}{2^9} \\ &=\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{3}{2},\ r=2$$
criteria: Finds the common ratio, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
The graphs of $y=kx$ and $y=12x-x^2$ intersect at the origin and point P. The coordinates of point P are $(8,32)$.

\exfigure{1772_q24_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=4$.

dif.r: Substitute given point into line, one step

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the area enclosed between $y=kx$ and $y=12x-x^2$.

dif.r: Standard area between parabola and line with known bounds

figures.cap: line y=kx and parabola y=12x-x^2 intersecting at origin and P

solutions.latex:
P$(8,32)$ lies on $y=kx$, so substitute it.
$$\begin{aligned} 32&=k\times 8 \\ k&=4 \end{aligned}$$

The parabola is above the line between $x=0$ and $x=8$, so the area is the integral of the difference.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_0^8(12x-x^2-4x)\,dx \\ &=\int_0^8(8x-x^2)\,dx \\ &=\left[4x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^8 \\ &=4(8)^2-\dfrac{8^3}{3} \\ &=256-\dfrac{512}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{256}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=\dfrac{256}{3}\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Correct integral set up, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Alex and Ben are playing a game using a two fair six-sided dice. They take turns rolling both dice with Alex going first, followed by Ben, and then continuing in this alternating pattern.

The objective of the game is to be the first player to roll a total of exactly 10 on the two dice. Once a player rolls a total of exactly 10, the game ends and that player is declared the winner.
questions.review_note: Paper states 4 marks but part marks are 1+2+2 = 5 (booklet 2 totals 45 only if Q25 is 5 marks); MARKS_MISMATCH

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the probability that Alex wins the game on his first turn.

dif.r: Count dice outcomes totalling ten, direct probability

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the probability that Alex wins the game on either his first turn or second turn.

dif.r: Combine first-turn win with lose-lose-win sequence

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Find the probability that Alex eventually wins the game.

dif.r: Build infinite geometric series of alternating turns, limiting sum

solutions.latex:
Totals of $10$: $(5,5),(6,4),(4,6)$, which is 3 outcomes out of 36.
$$P=\dfrac{3}{36}=\dfrac{1}{12}$$

On each turn, $P(\text{win})=\dfrac{1}{12}$ and $P(\text{lose})=\dfrac{11}{12}$.

Alex wins on his second turn if Alex loses, Ben loses, then Alex wins.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{1}{12}+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{12}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{265}{1728} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some progress in identifying the second turn, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Alex can win on turn 1, 2, 3, and so on, each time after both players have lost the earlier rounds.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{1}{12}+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^2\dfrac{1}{12}+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^4\dfrac{1}{12}+\cdots \\ &=\dfrac{1}{12}\left(1+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^4+\cdots\right) \end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a geometric series with $a=1$ and $r=\left(\dfrac{11}{12}\right)^2$. Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{1}{12}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1-\left(\frac{11}{12}\right)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{12}{23} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the geometric series and identifies $a$ and $r$, or equivalent merit

Consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ as shown.

\exfigure{1772_q26_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: State, in the correct order, transformations required to obtain the graph of $y=f(0.5(x-2))$ from the graph of $y=f(x)$.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $y=f(0.5(x-2))$, showing clearly the new position of the points marked in the original graph. .

solution sketch: teacher's sketch of y=f(0.5(x-2)) with points (2,2),(4,0),(7,-3),(10,0),(12,2)

solutions.latex:
The transformations, in order, are:

1. Horizontal dilation by a factor of $2$.

2. Translation $2$ units to the right.

Equivalently: first translate $1$ unit to the right, then dilate horizontally by a factor of $2$.

Each point is mapped by the rule
$$(x,y)\to(2x+2,\,y)$$
So the marked points move as follows:
$$\begin{aligned} (0,2)&\to(2,2) \\ (1,0)&\to(4,0) \\ (2.5,-3)&\to(7,-3) \\ (4,0)&\to(10,0) \\ (5,2)&\to(12,2) \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1772_q26_s1}
criteria: Two points correct, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A rescue helicopter is searching for two hikers, Liam (L) and Sophia (S), who are stranded on the different sides of a flat levelled valley. Both hikers can see the top of Eagle Peak (E) and are communicating with the rescue team by radio.

Liam reports that Eagle Peak has a bearing of $072^\circ$ from his position, and the angle of elevation to the top of Eagle Peak is $18^\circ$. Sophie reports that Eagle Peak has a bearing of $118^\circ$ from her position, and the angle of elevation to the top of the peak is $27^\circ$. The top of the Eagle Peak is 1800 metres above the valley floor.

Find the distance between Liam and Sophie and determine the bearing of Liam from Sophie's position.

\exfigure{1772_q27_1}
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (elevations from two ground points, with bearings): now Year 11 Extension 1.

dif.r: 3D elevation to ground distances, cosine and sine rules, bearing

figures.cap: diagram of hikers S and L, peak E, base B, elevation angles 27 and 18, height 1800 m

solutions.latex:
Let $B$ be the point on the valley floor directly below the peak $E$. In each right-angled triangle $LBE$ and $SBE$, use the tangent ratio with $BE=1800$.
$$\tan 18^\circ=\dfrac{1800}{LB},\quad LB=5539.8\text{ m}$$
$$\tan 27^\circ=\dfrac{1800}{SB},\quad SB=3532.7\text{ m}$$
The bearings of $B$ from $L$ and $S$ differ, so
$$\angle LBS=118^\circ-72^\circ=46^\circ$$
Cosine rule in triangle $LBS$:
$$\begin{aligned} LS&=\sqrt{5539.8^2+3532.7^2-2(5539.8)(3532.7)\cos 46^\circ} \\ &=3997.47\ldots\text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Sine rule to find $\angle S$:
$$\dfrac{\sin S}{LB}=\dfrac{\sin 46^\circ}{LS}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin S&=\dfrac{LB\sin 46^\circ}{LS} \\ &=0.9964 \end{aligned}$$
$LB$ is the longest side and $LB^2\approx30.69\times10^6>LS^2+SB^2\approx28.46\times10^6$, so $S$ is obtuse (the ambiguous case): $S\approx180^\circ-85.5^\circ=94.5^\circ$.

The bearing of Liam from Sophie is
$$118^\circ+94.5^\circ\approx213^\circ$$
$$\therefore\ LS\approx 3997\text{ m and the bearing of Liam from Sophie is } 213^\circ$$
criteria: Either $LB$ or $SB$ correct, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: The sine rule gives $S\approx 85^\circ$ as in source (acute assumed); source also used a $\angle LBS$ taken from bearings.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the sine rule gave $S\approx85^\circ$, but $S$ is obtuse (ambiguous case): $S\approx94.5^\circ$, so the bearing is $213^\circ$, not $203^\circ$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the sine rule gave $S\approx85^\circ$, but $S$ is obtuse (ambiguous case): $S\approx94.5^\circ$, so the bearing is $213^\circ$, not $203^\circ$.

questions.stem:
The amount of time $X$ in minutes that customers spend waiting for a ride at a theme park is modelled by the probability density function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}, & 0\le x\le 5\\[6pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $k=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$.

dif.r: Integrate trig pdf equal to one, solve for k

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the probability that a customer waits between 2 and 4 minutes, give your answer correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: Direct definite integral of known pdf

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.label: c
parts.latex: What is the probability that a customer waits more than 4 minutes? Give answer correct to 4 decimal places.

dif.r: Direct definite integral of known pdf

skills: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$, so
$$\int_0^5 k\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx=1$$
$$\left[\dfrac{10k}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_0^5=1$$
$$\dfrac{10k}{\pi}\left(\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{10}-0\right)=1$$
Since $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1$, $\dfrac{10k}{\pi}=1$.
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{\pi}{10}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P(2\le X\le 4)&=\int_2^4\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx \\ &=\left[\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_2^4 \\ &=\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{10}-\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{10} \\ &=0.36327\ldots \\ &\approx 0.3633 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P(X>4)&=\int_4^5\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\,dx \\ &=\left[\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{10}\right]_4^5 \\ &=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{10} \\ &=0.048943\ldots \\ &\approx 0.0489 \end{aligned}$$

questions.stem:
A rectangular water tank of width $b$ cm and height $h$ cm is designed to fit perfectly inside a cylindrical pipe with diameter of 30 cm as shown, where all vertices of the rectangular prism touch the circumference of the base circles.

\exfigure{1772_q29_1}

The length of the tank is twice its height and the volume ($V$) of the tank is given by

$$V=bhl$$

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $V=2b(900-b^2)$.

dif.r: Recognise cross-section diagonal is diameter, Pythagoras to model volume

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find the dimensions of the rectangular prism that maximises the volume of the tank. Justify your answer.

dif.r: Differentiate given volume, justify maximum, find all three dimensions

parts.label: c
parts.latex: A square based tank with a diagonal 30 cm could also be designed to fit inside the pipe. Show that the rectangular water tank is more than 5% greater in volume compared to square based tank.

dif.r: Model square tank volume, compare with percentage difference

figures.cap: rectangular prism inscribed in a cylindrical pipe, width b, height h, diagonal 30

solutions.latex:
The cross-section is a rectangle inscribed in the circle of diameter $30$, so its diagonal is $30$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$b^2+h^2=30^2,\quad h=\sqrt{900-b^2}$$
The length is $l=2h$.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=bhl \\ &=b\times\sqrt{900-b^2}\times 2\sqrt{900-b^2} \\ &=2b(900-b^2) \end{aligned}$$

Expand the volume, then differentiate to find stationary points.
$$V=1800b-2b^3$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{db}=1800-6b^2=0$$
$$b^2=300$$
Since $b>0$, $b=10\sqrt{3}$.

Then
$$h=\sqrt{900-300}=\sqrt{600}=10\sqrt{6},\quad l=2h=20\sqrt{6}$$
Second derivative test:
$$\dfrac{d^2V}{db^2}=-12b$$
When $b=10\sqrt{3}$, $\dfrac{d^2V}{db^2}=-120\sqrt{3}<0$, so this is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{dimensions are } 10\sqrt{3}\times 10\sqrt{6}\times 20\sqrt{6}\text{ cm}$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric (1 each for b, h and l, justification) rewritten top-down.

solutions.latex:
Rectangular tank:
$$V_{\text{rect}}=10\sqrt{3}\times 10\sqrt{6}\times 20\sqrt{6}=12000\sqrt{3}$$
Square-based tank: the diagonal of the base is $30$, so
$$b^2+b^2=30^2,\quad b=\sqrt{450}=15\sqrt{2},\quad l=2b$$
$$\begin{aligned} V_{\text{sq}}&=b^2l \\ &=(15\sqrt{2})^2\times 2(15\sqrt{2}) \\ &=13500\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$
Percentage increase:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12000\sqrt{3}-13500\sqrt{2}}{13500\sqrt{2}}&=0.0887\ldots \\ &=8.87\%>5\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the rectangular tank is more than } 5\% \text{ greater in volume}$$
criteria: Both volumes correct, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had a ratio line '1:0.8866 (written as 1.0887 ratio)' which was unclear; dropped in favour of the percentage calculation that follows. Source squares-base volume uses l=2b, as stated.

parts.latex:
In a flock of 22400 sheep, the ratio of males to females is $9:15$. The weights of the female sheep are normally distributed with a mean of 78.4 kg and a standard deviation of 5.6 kg. In the flock, 13979 of the female sheep each weigh more than $x$ kg.

Find the value of $x$.

dif.r: Ratio to count females, proportion to z-score, reverse standardise

skills: Normal distribution and the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The ratio of males to females is $9:15$, so
$$\text{Number of females}=\dfrac{15}{24}\times 22400=14000$$

questions.stem:
The temperature, $T^\circ$ C, at a farm over the course of a day is modelled by

$$T(t)=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$$

where $t$ if the time in hours after midnight, $0\le t\le 24$.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the temperature at midnight.

dif.r: Substitute t=0 into trig model, exact value

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$, leave your answer in the simplest form.

dif.r: Routine chain rule differentiation of cosine model

parts.label: c
parts.latex: Determine whether the temperature is initially decreasing or increasing.

dif.r: Evaluate derivative at t=0 and interpret its sign

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Find the maximum temperature and determine the first time at which this occurs.

dif.r: Maximum of cosine is one, solve simple equation

can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} T(0)&=22+8\cos\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{12}\right) \\ &=22+8\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=26^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

Using the chain rule on $T=22+8\cos\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-\dfrac{8\pi}{12}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right) \end{aligned}$$

Initially means $t=0$. The sign of $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$ decides whether $T$ is increasing or decreasing.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt}&=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{12}\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ &>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the temperature is initially increasing}$$
criteria: Correct derivative value at $t=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The maximum of cosine is $1$, so
$$T_{\max}=22+8(1)=30^\circ\text{C}$$
This occurs when
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)\right)=1$$
so $\dfrac{\pi}{12}(t-4)=0$, giving $t=4$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum temperature is } 30^\circ\text{C, first at } t=4 \text{ (4 am)}$$
criteria: Finds the maximum temperature, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A business owner takes an reducing balance loan of \$500000 to expand their company. Interest is charged at $0.4\%$ per month, compounded monthly. At the end of each month, interest is added to the loan balance and then a repayment of \$3200 is made.

Let $A_n$ be the balance owing on the loan at the end of $n$ months.

dif.r: Write first two loan balance steps
Generalise recurrence, sum geometric series, simplify to given form

parts.label: c
parts.latex: After how many months will the balance owing first be less than \$250000.

dif.r: Exponential inequality with logs, sign reversal, round up

solutions.latex:
Interest of $0.4\%$ is added, then the repayment is made.
$$A_1=500000(1.004)-3200$$
Repeating the process:
$$\begin{aligned} A_2&=A_1\times 1.004-3200 \\ &=500000(1.004)^2-3200(1.004)-3200 \end{aligned}$$

criteria: Uses the GP sum, or equivalent merit
Finds the pattern for $A_3$ or $A_n$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
We need $A_n<250000$.
$$800000-300000(1.004)^n<250000$$
$$-300000(1.004)^n<-550000$$
Dividing by $-300000$ reverses the inequality:
$$1.004^n>\dfrac{550000}{300000}=\dfrac{11}{6}$$
Taking logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned} n\ln 1.004&>\ln\dfrac{11}{6} \\ n&>\dfrac{\ln\frac{11}{6}}{\ln 1.004} \\ n&>151.84 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the balance first falls below } \$250000 \text{ after 152 months}$$
criteria: Sets up the inequality, or equivalent merit

An owl is 7 metres above ground level, in a tree. The owl sees a mouse on the ground at an angle of depression of $32^\circ$.

How far must the owl fly in a straight line to catch the mouse, assuming the mouse does not move?

The angle of depression from the owl equals the angle of elevation of the owl from the mouse (alternate angles), so in the right-angled triangle the angle at the mouse is $32^\circ$.

The owl's flight path is the hypotenuse $d$, and the height $7$ m is opposite the $32^\circ$ angle.

$$\sin 32^\circ = \dfrac{7}{d}$$

$$\begin{aligned} d &= \dfrac{7}{\sin 32^\circ} \\ &\approx 13.2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

The scores on an examination are normally distributed with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 6. Michael received a score on the examination between the lower quartile and the upper quartile of the scores.

The lower and upper quartiles cut off the bottom $25\%$ and top $25\%$, so Michael's score is in the middle $50\%$.

Only the first graph has its shading inside the $64$ and $76$ lines, so it is option A.

Apply the sine rule in $\triangle EFG$. Side $EF=81$ is opposite $\angle EGF$, and side $GF=50$ is opposite the $35^\circ$ angle at $E$.

So

$$\angle EGF=180^\circ-68.3^\circ=111.7^\circ$$

Bobbie is charged $0.04\%$ compound interest per day on outstanding balances on a credit card. Bobbie has an outstanding balance of \$740 for 30 days.

Which of the following is an expression for the amount of interest Bobbie is charged?

The interest is the final amount less the original balance.
$$\text{Interest}=\$740(1+0.0004)^{30}-\$740$$

The fastest land mammal, the cheetah, can travel at 104 km/h. The slowest land mammal, the three-toed sloth, travels at 2.4 m/min.

Approximately how many times faster is the cheetah than the sloth?

dif.r: Convert units of speed then compare by division.

solutions.latex:
Convert both speeds to metres per minute.
$$\begin{aligned} 104 \text{ km/h} &= \dfrac{104\times 1000}{60} \text{ m/min} \\ &\approx 1733.3 \text{ m/min} \end{aligned}$$
Divide the cheetah's speed by the sloth's speed.
$$\dfrac{1733.3}{2.4}\approx 722$$
Hence the answer is B.

parts.latex:
A scientist is estimating the population of a bee colony.

The scientist captures $p$ bees but only marks $k\%$ of them and releases them all back into the colony. The next day, the scientist captures $q$ bees and finds that $r$ bees were marked.

Assuming all bees have an equal chance of being captured, which expression gives the best estimate of the total bee population?

dif.r: Capture-recapture set up algebraically with percentage marked; abstract.

solutions.latex:
Let $N$ be the total population. The number of marked bees is $k\%$ of $p$.
$$\text{marked}=\dfrac{kp}{100}$$
Assuming equal chance of capture, the proportion of marked bees in the second sample estimates the proportion in the whole colony.
$$\dfrac{r}{q}=\dfrac{kp}{100N}$$
Solve for $N$.
$$N=\dfrac{kpq}{100r}$$
Hence the answer is A.

meta.self_check: Capture-recapture proportion solved for N.

questions.stem:

$$12, 15, 15, 17, 19, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30 \text{ and } m.$$

dif.r: Quartiles for odd-sized dataset, then interquartile range.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the greatest value of $m$ such that this dataset has no outlier?

dif.r: Outlier criterion used in reverse with whole-number interpretation.

solutions.latex:
With 13 scores, the lower half is the first 6 scores and the upper half is the last 6 scores.

The lower quartile is the average of the 3rd and 4th scores:
$$Q_1 = \dfrac{15+17}{2} = 16$$
The upper quartile is the average of the 10th and 11th scores:
$$Q_3 = \dfrac{27+28}{2} = 27.5$$
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 27.5 - 16 \\ &= 11.5 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the lower or upper quartile, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
An outlier lies above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Upper bound} &= 27.5 + 1.5 \times 11.5 \\ &= 44.75 \end{aligned}$$
Since the number of cars is a whole number, the greatest value of $m$ with no outlier is $44$.
$$\therefore\ m = 44$$
criteria: Attempts to find the upper bound, or equivalent merit

A large rechargeable battery has a maximum storage capacity of 40 kWh when new.

After 1 year, the maximum storage capacity is 32 kWh.

$$y = ka^t$$

parts.label: b

dif.r: Interpret decay factor 0.8 as 20% annual decrease in context

solutions.latex:
When $t = 0$, $y = 40$, so $k = 40$.

When $t = 1$, $y = 32$ and $k = 40$:
$$\begin{aligned} 32 &= 40 \times a^1 \\ a &= \dfrac{32}{40} \\ &= 0.8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k = 40,\ a = 0.8$$

The maximum storage capacity is decreasing at a rate of $20\%$ per year.

Or: $80\%$ of the maximum storage capacity from the previous year remains the following year.

\begin{itemize}
\item $X$, $Y$, 34 and $Z$ are in ascending order, and
\item $Z = X + 38$.
\end{itemize}

The median is the mean of the two middle values, $Y$ and 34.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{Y + 34}{2} &= 26 \\ Y &= 18 \end{aligned}$$
The mean is 28, and $Z = X + 38$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{X + 18 + 34 + Z}{4} &= 28 \\ \dfrac{X + 18 + 34 + X + 38}{4} &= 28 \\ 2X + 90 &= 112 \\ 2X &= 22 \\ X &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ X = 11$$
criteria: Equates a correct expression for the mean to 28, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The blood alcohol content ($BAC$) for males can be estimated by

$$BAC_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$$

where

$N$ = number of standard drinks

$H$ = number of hours drinking

$M$ = the person’s weight in kilograms.

The number of hours for a person’s $BAC$ to reach zero is given by

$$\text{Time} = \dfrac{BAC}{0.015}.$$

Henry, a 72 kg male, consumes a total of three drinks at a family dinner.

The drinks are:

\begin{itemize}
\item two 375 mL cans of beer that hold 1.4 standard drinks each
\item one 250 mL can of mixer that holds 1.8 standard drinks.
\end{itemize}

It took 2 hours and 10 minutes for Henry’s $BAC$ to return to zero.

How many hours did Henry take to consume the three drinks, correct to the nearest hour?

dif.r: Chain two BAC formulas in reverse, convert time, solve for H

solutions.latex:
The time for the $BAC$ to reach zero is 2 hours 10 minutes, so
$$\begin{aligned} 2\dfrac{10}{60} &= \dfrac{BAC}{0.015} \\ BAC &= 2\dfrac{10}{60} \times 0.015 \\ &= 0.0325 \end{aligned}$$
Number of drinks:
$$N = 2 \times 1.4 + 1.8 = 4.6$$
Substituting into the $BAC$ formula with $M = 72$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.0325 &= \dfrac{(10 \times 4.6) - 7.5H}{6.8 \times 72} \\ 15.912 &= 46 - 7.5H \\ -30.088 &= -7.5H \\ H &= \dfrac{-30.088}{-7.5} = 4.0117\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ H \approx 4 \text{ hours}$$
criteria: Uses the $BAC$ formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's $2\frac{10}{60}\times0.015 = 0.0325$ is consistent.

Tax withheld (PAYG):
$$383 \times 52 = \$19\,916$$

The water fills the cross-section not occupied by the cylinders, over height $h$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= (20 \times 50) - (10 \times \pi \times 5^2) \\ &= 214.6018\ldots \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Since $3\text{ L} = 3000\text{ cm}^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= A \times h \\ 3000 &= 214.6018\ldots \times h \\ h &= 13.979\ldots \end{aligned}$$

Since $AX = 7$, the radius is $13 - 7 = 6$ cm.
$$\angle AOB = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right) = 22.62^\circ$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage} &= \dfrac{22.894}{30} \times 100\% \\ &= 76.3\% \text{ (to 1 decimal place)} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A ten-sided die has faces numbered 1 to 10.

The die is constructed so that the probability of obtaining the number 1 is greater than the probability of obtaining any of the other numbers. The numbers 2 to 10 are equally likely to occur.

When the die is rolled 153 times, a 1 is obtained 72 times.

By using the relative frequency of rolling a 1, which of the following is the best estimate for the probability of rolling a 10?

dif.r: Relative frequency then share remaining probability among nine outcomes.

solutions.latex:
The relative frequency of rolling a 1 estimates its probability.
$$P(1) \approx \dfrac{72}{153} = \dfrac{8}{17}$$
The other probabilities add to
$$1 - \dfrac{8}{17} = \dfrac{9}{17}$$
The numbers 2 to 10 are equally likely (9 numbers), so
$$P(10) \approx \dfrac{9}{17} \div 9 = \dfrac{1}{17}$$
Hence the correct option is A.

parts.latex:
The minimum daily temperature, in degrees, of a town each year follows a normal distribution with its mean equal to its standard deviation. The minimum daily temperature was recorded over one year.

What percentage of the recorded minimum daily temperatures was above zero degrees?

dif.r: Abstract mean equals SD gives z=-1, then empirical rule.

solutions.latex:
Let the mean be $\mu$ and the standard deviation be $\sigma$, with $\mu = \sigma$.

Zero is below the mean by
$$\dfrac{\mu - 0}{\sigma} = 1 \text{ standard deviation}$$
so its $z$-score is $-1$.

By the empirical rule, $68\%$ of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so $34\%$ lie between $0$ and $\mu$. Also $50\%$ lie above the mean.
$$P(X > 0) = 50\% + 34\% = 84\%$$
Hence the correct option is D.

One night Bobbie collected 18 snails from the garden. He tagged each snail and released it back into the garden.

The next night 20 snails were captured from the garden.

Approximately how many of the snails in the second sample are expected to have a tag?

dif.r: Capture-recapture proportion used in reverse

solutions.latex:
The tagged fraction of the population is $\dfrac{18}{90}$, so expect that fraction of the second sample.
$$\dfrac{18}{90} \times 20 = 4 \text{ snails}$$
criteria: Provides a correct ratio for tagged snails, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
In a research study, participants were asked to record the number of minutes they spent watching television and the number of minutes they spent exercising each day over a period of 3 months. The averages for each participant were recorded and graphed.

\exfigure{5834_q25_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Describe the bivariate dataset in terms of its form and direction.

dif.r: Read form and direction straight off scatterplot

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The equation of the least-squares regression line for this dataset is

$$y = 64.3 - 0.7x.$$

Interpret the values of the slope and $y$-intercept of the regression line in the context of this dataset.

dif.r: Interpret slope and intercept precisely in context, with units

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Jo spends an average of 42 minutes per day watching television.

Use the equation of the regression line to determine how many minutes on average Jo is expected to exercise each day.

dif.r: Substitute one value into given regression line

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Explain why it is NOT appropriate to extrapolate the regression line to predict the average number of minutes of exercise per day for someone who watches an average of 2 hours of television per day.

dif.r: Explain extrapolation limits: negative prediction or outside data range

figures.cap: scatter plot of exercise minutes against television minutes

solutions.latex:
Form: linear

Direction: negative
criteria: Provides the correct direction, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Slope: for every $1$ minute increase in time spent watching television per day, the time spent exercising decreases by $0.7$ minutes per day.

$y$-intercept: if someone does not watch television, they are expected to exercise for $64.3$ minutes per day.
criteria: Correct interpretation of both slope and $y$-intercept
Correct interpretation of $y$-intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x = 42$ into the regression line.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 64.3 - 0.7 \times 42 \\ &= 34.9 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

A television time of 2 hours is $120$ minutes.

The regression line predicts exercise of $-19.7$ minutes, which is impossible, since a person cannot exercise for a negative time.

Alternative answer: 120 minutes is outside the range of the dataset, so extrapolating is not reliable.

Two applications of the trapezoidal rule, with strip width $5.1$ cm and heights $6$, $3.8$ and $0$ cm:

$$\begin{aligned} 1300 &= (2 \times 34.68) + (10.2 \times 40) + (6 \times 40) + \text{curved surface} \\ 1300 &= 717.36 + \text{curved surface} \\ \text{curved surface} &= 1300 - 717.36 \\ &= 582.64 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\text{Absolute error} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.1 = 0.05 \text{ cm}$$

Solid spheres are placed inside a square-based pyramid as shown.

\exfigure{5834_q32_1}

The base of the pyramid has side lengths of 14 cm. The height of the pyramid is $h$ cm. The radius of each sphere is 1.5 cm.

The amount of empty space remaining inside the pyramid after 30 spheres have been placed inside the pyramid is $634\text{ cm}^3$.

What is the height, $h$, of the pyramid? Give your answer correct to the nearest centimetre.

dif.r: Sphere volumes plus empty space, then solve pyramid formula for h

skills: Volume of pyramids, cones and spheres

figures.cap: square-based pyramid containing spheres (NOT TO SCALE)

solutions.latex:
The volume of 30 spheres is
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 1.5^3 \times 30 \\ &= 424.115\ldots \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
The pyramid volume is the volume of the spheres plus the empty space:
$$\begin{aligned} V_{\text{pyramid}} &= 424.115\ldots + 634 \\ &= 1058.115\ldots \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
Using $V = \dfrac{1}{3}Ah$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1058.115 &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times (14 \times 14) \times h \\ h &= \dfrac{1058.115 \times 3}{14 \times 14} \\ &\approx 16.2 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h = 16 \text{ cm (to the nearest whole number)}$$
criteria: Provides evidence of equating volumes to find $h$, or equivalent merit
Finds the volume of a sphere, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A used car has a sale price of \$24\,200. In addition to the sale price, the following costs are charged:

\begin{itemize}
\item transfer of registration \$50
\item stamp duty which is calculated at \$3 for every \$100, or part thereof, of the sale price.
\end{itemize}

Kat borrows the total amount to be paid for the car, including transfer of registration and stamp duty. Simple interest at the rate of $6.8\%$ per annum is charged on the loan. The loan is to be repaid in equal monthly repayments over 3 years.

Calculate Kat's monthly repayment.

dif.r: Multi-step: stamp duty, total borrowed, simple interest, monthly split

solutions.latex:
Stamp duty is charged per $\$100$ or part thereof:
$$\$24\,200 \div 100 = 242 \text{ lots of } \$100$$
$$\text{Stamp duty} = 242 \times 3 = \$726$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Amount borrowed} &= \$726 + \$24\,200 + \$50 \\ &= \$24\,976 \end{aligned}$$
Using $I = Prn$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest} &= \$24\,976 \times 6.8\% \times 3 \\ &= \$5095.10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total to be repaid} &= \$24\,976 + \$5095.10 \\ &= \$30\,071.10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Monthly repayment} &= \$30\,071.10 \div 36 \\ &= \$835.31 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides total amount to be repaid, or equivalent merit
Calculates the interest on the loan, or equivalent merit
Finds the total amount to be borrowed, or equivalent merit
Finds the number of $\$100$ needed to calculate stamp duty, or equivalent merit

criteria: Finds Lin's correct future value, or equivalent merit

The triangle $PTA$ is shown. The length of $PA$ is 75 m and the length of $PT$ is 51 m.

The angle of depression from $T$ to $A$ is $36^\circ$, and the angle $PTA$ is obtuse.

\exfigure{5834_q35_1}

Find the length of $TA$. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Depression angle, obtuse sine-rule case, then second sine rule

figures.cap: triangle PTA (NOT TO SCALE)
solution sketch: annotated triangle PTA

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{5834_q35_s1}

Let $\angle PTA = \theta$. Using the sine rule in triangle $PTA$ (the angle at $A$ is $36^\circ$, alternate to the angle of depression):
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{75} = \dfrac{\sin 36^\circ}{51}$$
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sin 36^\circ}{51} \times 75$$
$$\theta = 59.813\ldots^\circ$$
Since $\angle PTA$ is obtuse:
$$\angle PTA = 180^\circ - 59.813\ldots^\circ = 120.186\ldots^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle TPA &= 180^\circ - 120.186\ldots^\circ - 36^\circ \\ &= 23.813\ldots^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Using the sine rule again:
$$\dfrac{TA}{\sin 23.813\ldots^\circ} = \dfrac{51}{\sin 36^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} TA &= \dfrac{51}{\sin 36^\circ} \times \sin 23.813\ldots^\circ \\ &= 35.032\ldots \\ &\approx 35.03 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly uses the sine rule, or equivalent merit

The graph shows the salvage value of a car over 5 years.

\exfigure{5834_q36_1}

The salvage values are based on the declining-balance method.

By what amount will the car's value depreciate during the 10th year?

dif.r: Find rate from graph; interpret depreciation during 10th year

figures.cap: graph of salvage value against time

solutions.latex:
Declining-balance formula $S = V_0(1-r)^n$. After 1 year the value is $\$44\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 44\,000 &= 55\,000(1-r) \\ \dfrac{44\,000}{55\,000} &= 1 - r \\ 0.8 &= 1 - r \\ r &= 0.2 = 20\% \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, $55\,000 - 44\,000 = 11\,000$ and $r = \dfrac{11\,000}{55\,000} \times 100\% = 20\%$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Value after 9 years} &= 55\,000(1 - 0.2)^9 \\ &= \$7381.98 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Depreciation in year 10} &= 7381.98 \times 0.2 \\ &= \$1476.40 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the value after 10 years is $55\,000(1-0.2)^{10} = \$5905.58$, and the difference is $\$1476.40$.
criteria: Finds value after 9 years, or equivalent merit
Provides correct rate, or equivalent merit
Uses $44\,000$ correctly in an appropriate formula, or equivalent merit

The grassed triangle has two sides 9 and 3 with an included angle of $60^\circ$ (angle of an equilateral triangle). Using the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} c^2 &= 9^2 + 3^2 - 2 \times 9 \times 3\cos 60^\circ \\ c &\approx 7.937 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The grassed triangle is equilateral, so
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 7.937 \times 7.937 \times \sin 60^\circ \\ &= 27.2798\ldots \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Mowing takes $\dfrac{5}{20}$ minutes per $1 \text{ m}^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Time} &= \dfrac{5}{20} \times 27.2798 \\ &= 6.81 \text{ minutes} \\ &\approx 7 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

When $x = 4$:

In a flock of $12\,600$ sheep, the ratio of males to females is $1 : 20$.

The weights of the male sheep are normally distributed with a mean of 76.2 kg and a standard deviation of 6.8 kg.

In the flock, 15 of the male sheep each weigh more than $x$ kg.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The weights of the female sheep are also normally distributed but have a smaller mean and smaller standard deviation than the weights of male sheep.

Explain whether it could be expected that 300 of the females from the flock each weigh more than $x$ kg, where $x$ is the value found in part (a).

dif.r: Abstract reasoning: smaller mean and SD give larger z, fewer exceed

figures.cap: solution sketch: normal curve with upper 2.5% shaded
solution sketch: male and female normal curves

solutions.latex:
The ratio $1:20$ gives 21 parts:
$$\text{Number of male sheep} = \dfrac{12\,600}{21} = 600$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage of males over } x \text{ kg} &= \dfrac{15}{600} \times 100 \\ &= 2.5\% \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{5834_q40_s1}

The top $2.5\%$ lies above $2$ standard deviations, so the $z$-score is $2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 76.2 + 2 \times 6.8 \\ &= 76.2 + 13.6 \\ &= 89.8 \text{ kg} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use a $z$-score in a calculation, or equivalent merit
Calculates the percentage of males that weigh more than $x$ kg
Calculates the number of male sheep, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For females, $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ will be larger than $2$, as the mean and standard deviation for females are smaller.

So the percentage of female sheep weighing more than $x$ kg will be smaller than $2.5\%$.

Hence fewer than 300 females will weigh more than $x$ kg.

\exfigure{5834_q40_s2}

meta.format_note: Source reasoning: 2.5% of 12 000 females is 300, so fewer than 300 is expected.

dif.r: Build adjacency matrix from graph, including multiple edges

figures.cap: network with vertices A, B, C, D
option A: adjacency matrix
option B: adjacency matrix
option C: adjacency matrix
option D: adjacency matrix

solutions.latex:
In the adjacency matrix, the entry in row $X$, column $Y$ is the number of edges joining $X$ and $Y$. The graph has no loops, so every diagonal entry is $0$, and the matrix is symmetric.

Reading the number of edges from the graph:
$$\begin{aligned} A\text{ to }B &: 1 & A\text{ to }C &: 1 \\ A\text{ to }D &: 1 & B\text{ to }C &: 2 \\ C\text{ to }D &: 1 & B\text{ to }D &: 0 \end{aligned}$$

So the matrix has rows $A: 0,1,1,1$; $B: 1,0,2,0$; $C: 1,2,0,1$; $D: 1,0,1,0$.

The proportion of tagged cats in the second catch should equal the proportion of tagged cats in the whole park.

parts.latex: The network diagrams show the 4 roates that a garbage truck travels in one week. Which diagram will allow the truck driver to travel each road exactly once?

dif.r: Count vertex degrees across four networks; apply Euler path condition.

figures.cap: option A: network A
option B: network B
option C: network C
option D: network D

solutions.latex:
A route can be travelled using every road exactly once when the network has at most two vertices of odd degree (an Euler path).

Count the degree of each vertex in each diagram.

Diagram A:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2, \ B=4, \ C=4, \ D=3 \\ E&=4, \ F=5, \ G=2, \ H=2 \end{aligned}$$
Only $D$ and $F$ are odd, so an Euler path exists (from $D$ to $F$).

Diagram B has four odd vertices: $B, D, F, G$.

Diagram C has four odd vertices: $A, C, F, G$.

Diagram D has four odd vertices: $A, E, F, J$.

So only diagram A allows every road to be travelled exactly once.
$$\therefore\ \text{option A}$$

A true bearing of $250^\circ$ is measured clockwise from north.

parts.latex:
The average energy used in kilojoules per kilogram of body mass by a basketball player in a leisure game is 11.98 kJ/kg per 30 minutes of play. Joshua who weighs 70 kg, drinks a soft drink that contains 162 kilocalories. Joshua is to play a basketball game with his friends.

For approximately how long he should play in order to burn off the energy contained in the drink given that 1 kilocalorie $= 4.184$ kJ?
parts.note: Food energy in kilojoules and kilocalories is not in the 2024 course.

dif.r: Multi-step: kcal conversion, per-kg rate, scale per 30 minutes.

solutions.latex:
First convert the energy in the drink to kilojoules, using $1 \text{ kcal} = 4.184 \text{ kJ}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{energy} &= 162 \times 4.184 \\ &= 677.808 \text{ kJ} \end{aligned}$$
Next find the energy Joshua uses in $30$ minutes of play, using $11.98$ kJ/kg per $30$ minutes and a mass of $70$ kg.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{energy used} &= 11.98 \times 70 \\ &= 838.6 \text{ kJ per 30 minutes} \end{aligned}$$
The time needed is the fraction of $30$ minutes required to use $677.808$ kJ.
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{677.808}{838.6}\times 30 \\ &\approx 24.2 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{approximately 24 minutes (option B)}$$

meta.self_check: Computed in Python: 24.25 min.

parts.latex:
Jon has a mass of 84 kg. He was at a friend's party and consumed six bottles of an alcoholic beverage, each equivalent to 0.9 standard drinks.

Blood alcohol content ($BAC$) is calculated using the following formula:

$$BAC_{Male} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$$

where $N$ is the number of standard drinks consumed, $H$ is the number of hours of drinking, and $M$ is the person's weight in kilograms.

Jon stopped drinking at 10:30 pm and left the party at 2:30 am, just when his Blood Alcohol Content ($BAC$) reached zero.

The time needed for $BAC$ to reach zero after the last drink consumed can be calculated using the formula:

$$\text{Number of hours for } BAC \text{ to reach zero} = \dfrac{BAC}{0.015}$$

At what time did Jon start to have his first drink at the party? Give your answer to the nearest minute.

dif.r: Work backwards through two BAC formulas, solve H, convert time

solutions.latex:
The time for $BAC$ to reach zero is the time from the last drink (10:30 pm) to 2:30 am, which is $4$ hours. Use the given formula.
$$4 = \dfrac{BAC}{0.015}$$
$$BAC = 0.06$$
The number of standard drinks is $N = 6 \times 0.9 = 5.4$. Substitute into the $BAC$ formula with $M = 84$.
$$0.06 = \dfrac{10 \times 5.4 - 7.5H}{6.8 \times 84}$$
$$H = 2 \text{ h } 38 \text{ min}$$
Drinking started $2$ h $38$ min before 10:30 pm.
$$\therefore\ \text{Drinking started at } 7{:}52 \text{ pm.}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the $BAC$ formula, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Jennifer is an environmental scientist who needs to measure the depth of a lake. She drops a rope with a weight on one end and lets it sink to the bottom, labelled $A$. Ensuring the rope is tight, she records the length of rope as 16.2 m, as shown in the diagram below. The angle of depression from the boat to the anchor is $49^\circ$.

\exfigure{497_q35_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the depth of the lake, to the nearest tenth of a metre?

dif.r: Angle of depression to right-triangle trig ratio

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
Due to the difficulty of keeping the rope taught and the movement of the boat in the water, Jennifer estimates that the measurement of the angle has an error of $2^\circ$ and the length of the rope has an error of 0.1 m.

What is the upper and lower bound for the depth of the lake?

dif.r: Reason which angle and length extremes give minimum and maximum depth

figures.cap: boat on lake with rope of 16.2 m to anchor A, angle of depression 49 degrees

solutions.latex:
The angle between the rope and the vertical is $90 - 49 = 41^\circ$.

In the right-angled triangle, the depth $x$ is adjacent to this angle:
$$\cos 41^\circ = \dfrac{x}{16.2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 16.2\cos 41^\circ \\ &\approx 12.2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the angle $41^\circ$ or sets up the ratio, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The depth is $x = L\cos\theta$, which is smallest for the largest angle and shortest rope.

Smallest: angle $41 + 2 = 43^\circ$, rope $16.2 - 0.1 = 16.1$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 16.1 \cos 43^\circ \\ &\approx 11.8 \end{aligned}$$
Largest: angle $41 - 2 = 39^\circ$, rope $16.2 + 0.1 = 16.3$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 16.3 \cos 39^\circ \\ &\approx 12.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{lower bound } 11.8 \text{ m, upper bound } 12.7 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds one bound, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A bag contains six balls numbered 1 to 6. One ball is drawn from the bag and replaced back into the bag. A second ball is then drawn from the bag.

Which of the following outcomes is LEAST likely to occur?

dif.r: Count outcomes in 36-sample space for four events and compare.

options.label: A
options.latex: The two balls drawn have a sum of 5.

options.label: B
options.latex: One ball drawn is odd and the other is even.

options.label: C
options.latex: The two balls drawn are the same number.

options.label: D
options.latex: The two balls drawn differ in value by 2.

solutions.latex:
Drawing with replacement gives $6\times 6 = 36$ equally likely outcomes. Count the outcomes for each option.

Option A: sum of 5.
$$(1,4),\ (2,3),\ (3,2),\ (4,1)$$
This is 4 outcomes, so $P = \dfrac{4}{36}$.

Option B: one odd and one even. There are 3 odd and 3 even numbers, and either order is allowed.
$$2\times 3\times 3 = 18 \text{ outcomes}$$
So $P = \dfrac{18}{36}$.

Option C: the same number.
$$(1,1),\ (2,2),\ \dots,\ (6,6)$$
This is 6 outcomes, so $P = \dfrac{6}{36}$.

Option D: differ by 2.
$$(1,3),\ (2,4),\ (3,5),\ (4,6)$$
Each can be reversed, giving 8 outcomes, so $P = \dfrac{8}{36}$.

The smallest probability is $\dfrac{4}{36}$, so the least likely outcome is the sum of 5.

meta.self_check: Counted outcomes out of 36: A 4, B 18, C 6, D 8; minimum is A, matching the key.
meta.generated_note: MCQ working written for answer key A.

dif.r: Match gradient signs to graph and test intersection point in options.

figures.cap: Lines L1 and L2 intersecting at (2,4); diagram not to scale

solutions.latex:
From the graph, $L_1$ has a negative gradient and a positive $y$-intercept, and $L_2$ has a positive gradient and a positive $y$-intercept. Both lines must pass through $(2,4)$.

$L_1$ slopes downwards, so its gradient is negative. $L_2$ slopes upwards, so its gradient is positive. This rules out A, where $L_1$ has a positive gradient, and C, where $L_2$ has a negative gradient.

Test the point $(2,4)$ in option B, $L_2: y=2x-8$.
$$y = 2(2)-8 = -4 \neq 4$$
So B fails.

Test the point $(2,4)$ in option D.
$$\begin{aligned} L_1: y &= -2(2)+8 = 4 \\ L_2: y &= 2+2 = 4 \end{aligned}$$
Both lines pass through $(2,4)$. Their $y$-intercepts, 8 and 2, are positive, matching the graph.

Therefore the pair of equations is $L_1: y=-2x+8$ and $L_2: y=x+2$.

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
There are 12 equally likely outcomes, and one of them is 3.
$$P(3) = \dfrac{1}{12}$$

solution sketch: Completed probability tree with branch probabilities and outcomes OO, OA, AO, AA, as drawn in the guidelines

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{720_q6_s1}

First piece of fruit (21 pieces):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{8}{21}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{13}{21}$$
If Jack ate an orange, 20 pieces remain (7 oranges, 13 apples):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{7}{20}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{13}{20}$$
If Jack ate an apple, 20 pieces remain (8 oranges, 12 apples):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{8}{20}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{12}{20}$$
criteria: Completes first branch, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Both ate an apple, so multiply along the apple-apple branches.
$$\begin{aligned} P(AA) &= \dfrac{13}{21} \times \dfrac{12}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{35} \end{aligned}$$

Different fruits means orange then apple, or apple then orange. Add the two branch products.
$$\begin{aligned} P(OA \text{ or } AO) &= \dfrac{8}{21} \times \dfrac{13}{20} + \dfrac{13}{21} \times \dfrac{8}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{52}{105} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One correct multiplication for either $OA$ or $AO$, or equivalent merit

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
With her new full time job paying \$1964 per fortnight after tax, she needs to budget for these expenses. The rent on the unit is \$492 per week and the most recent quarterly bills for electricity and water were \$572 and \$260 respectively.

solutions.latex:
Sienna pays one quarter of the rent. Rent is weekly, so a fortnight is 2 weeks.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Share of rent} &= \dfrac{492}{4} \times 2 \\ &= \$246 \end{aligned}$$
Bills are quarterly, so there are 4 sets of bills a year and 26 fortnights.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Yearly utility bills} &= 4 \times (572 + 260) \\ &= \$3328 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Her share of bills} &= (3328 \div 26) \div 4 \\ &= \$32 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Current accommodation expenses} &= 246 + 32 \\ &= \$278 \end{aligned}$$
Add 20% for possible increases.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Budget} &= 1.2 \times 278 \\ &= \$333.60 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards current accommodation expenses, or equivalent merit
Finds share of utility bills, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Monthly payments are 12 a year and there are 26 fortnights in a year.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fortnightly loan payment} &= 572 \times \dfrac{12}{26} \\ &= \$264 \end{aligned}$$
Running costs are weekly, so double them.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Running costs} &= 48 \times 2 \\ &= \$96 \end{aligned}$$
Annual expenses are divided by 26.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fortnightly bills} &= 1831.70 \div 26 \\ &\approx \$70.45 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total car budget} &= 264 + 96 + 70.45 \\ &= \$430.45 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: At least 2 correct fortnightly amounts, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Groceries are weekly, so double them. Lunch is daily, so multiply by 14 days.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fortnightly food and groceries} &= 145 \times 2 \\ &= \$290 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fortnightly lunch and incidentals} &= 40 \times 14 \\ &= \$560 \end{aligned}$$
Using the results of parts (a) and (b):
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total budget} &= 333.60 + 430.45 + 290 + 560 \\ &= \$1614.05 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Savings} &= 1964 - 1614.05 \\ &= \$349.95 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Works out total budget, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: The number of orders received in a particular week is represented by $n$. The company's costs $C$, and revenue $R$ in dollars, producing and delivering these orders, are given by the equations $C = 400 + 5n$ and $R = 25n$.

dif.r: Substitute n=20 into both equations and compare.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
The company made a profit ($P$) of \$600 last week.

Using the equation $P = R - C$, determine the number of internet orders the company delivered last week?

dif.r: Form profit expression from given equations, solve linear equation.

solutions.latex:
At the break-even point $R = C$. Substitute $n = 20$ into each equation.
$$\begin{aligned} C &= 400 + 5(20) \\ &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 25 \times 20 \\ &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
Since $R = C$, the company breaks even when $n = 20$.
criteria: Substitutes $n = 20$ into either equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Profit is revenue minus cost.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= R - C \\ &= 25n - (5n + 400) \\ &= 20n - 400 \end{aligned}$$
Put $P = 600$.
$$\begin{aligned} 600 &= 20n - 400 \\ 1000 &= 20n \\ n &= 50 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore 50 orders were produced and delivered.
criteria: Works towards the profit equation $P = 20n - 400$, or equivalent merit (stating $P = 600$ is not enough for a mark)

solutions.latex:
Each of the 3 players in one team plays each of the 3 players in the other team once.

So the network has 6 vertices, and every vertex is joined to exactly the 3 players of the other team.

Number of matches:
$$3\times 3 = 9 \text{ edges}$$
No two players in the same team are joined, and each vertex has degree 3.

Option D has 9 edges: the 6 sides of the hexagon and 3 diagonals through the centre. Each vertex has degree 3. Alternate vertices of the hexagon form the two teams, since the sides join opposite teams and each diagonal joins opposite vertices (one from each team).

The others fail:

A: the vertices have degree 4, so there are more than 9 edges.

B: every pair of vertices is joined (15 edges), which would include players from the same team.

C: only 6 edges.

Hence the answer is option D.

meta.self_check: Model is K(3,3): 9 edges, all degrees 3; option D is a hexagon with 3 long diagonals, which is K(3,3).

solutions.latex:
From $O$, the point $P$ lies $57^\circ$ east of south.

The return direction from $P$ to $O$ is exactly opposite: north becomes south and east becomes west, with the same angle.

So the bearing from $P$ to $O$ is $N57^\circ W$.

The question asks for the compass bearing, so the answer is $N57^\circ W$ (the equivalent true bearing is $303^\circ$, but that is not in compass form).

Each week she makes $5 \times 2 = 10$ one-way trips. Fuel for a 34 km trip is $\dfrac{34}{17} = 2$ litres.

\exfigure{3307_q3_2}

figures.cap: Triangle with sides a, b, c and Farmer Ellis's handwritten working
Triangle with blanks for angles A, B, C and sides a, b, c

solutions.latex:
Farmer Ellis has assumed the paddock has a right angle and has used side $c$ as the height, which is the wrong formula.

He should have used

$$A = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$$

Using the cosine rule for the angle opposite side $c$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos C &= \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} \\ &= \dfrac{1290^2 + 1260^2 - 880^2}{2 \times 1290 \times 1260} \\ &= 0.762\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} C &= \cos^{-1}(0.762\ldots) \\ &= 40^\circ 21' \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the area formula with the included angle $C$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1290 \times 1260 \times \sin(40^\circ 21') \\ &\approx 526\,200 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into the area formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us (2 marks per the question).

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin B}{1260} &= \dfrac{\sin 40^\circ 21'}{880} \\ B &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sin 40^\circ 21'}{880} \times 1260\right) \\ &= 67^\circ 59' \end{aligned}$$

Using the angle sum of a triangle:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 180^\circ - 67^\circ 59' - 40^\circ 21' \\ &= 71^\circ 40' \end{aligned}$$

The completed triangle has

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 71^\circ 40' & a &= 1290 \text{ m} \\ B &= 67^\circ 59' & b &= 1260 \text{ m} \\ C &= 40^\circ 21' & c &= 880 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one angle using the sine rule, or equivalent merit
Uses the sine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's $B$ value appears slightly off if sine rule is used with side b over sin B (sin B = 1260 sin C / 880 gives about 111 or 69 degrees); kept as source.

dif.r: Pick the right-angled triangle, then one sine ratio

figures.cap: Triangle ABC with perpendicular BD to AC
solution sketch: Triangle with 880 and 71°40' annotated in the guidelines

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{3307_q4_s1}

In right-angled triangle $ABD$, the side $BD$ is opposite the angle $71^\circ 40'$ and $AB = 880$ is the hypotenuse.

$$\sin 71^\circ 40' = \dfrac{BD}{880}$$

$$\begin{aligned} BD &= 880 \times \sin 71^\circ 40' \\ &\approx 835 \\ &\approx 840 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

Angle $C$ could be used instead.
criteria: Correct use of a trigonometric ratio, or equivalent merit
