parts.label: b
parts.latex:
To better understand how he can manage his energy intake, Adrian wishes to discover his Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR). Use the Harris-Benedict Formula below to calculate his BMR in kJ/day. He just turned 17, weighs 63kg and is 1.65m tall.

For Males:

$$\text{BMR (kJ/day)} = 278 + (57.5 \times \text{weight in kg}) + (20.9 \times \text{height in cm}) - (28.2 \times \text{age in years})$$

dif.r: Substitute into a given formula; height must be converted to cm

parts.label: c

dif.r: Convert BMR to hourly, pick PAL from table, substitute

parts.label: d
parts.latex: Adrian decided he wants to cycle laps around Nirimba Falls East rather than run to burn off his excess kilojoules. If one loop around Nirimba Falls East is 2km, how many full loops must Adrian cycle at 16km/h if he wishes to burn off 1000kJ?

dif.r: Formula in reverse for time, then distance, loops, rounding up

solutions.latex:
Convert the Calories burned to kJ:

$$\begin{aligned} 1800 \times 4.184 &= 7531.2 \text{ kJ} \end{aligned}$$

Energy still to burn:

$$\begin{aligned} 8700 - 7531.2 &= 1168.8 \text{ kJ} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Converts Calories to kJ, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substituting into the Harris-Benedict formula, with height $165$ cm:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{BMR} &= 278 + 57.5 \times 63 + 20.9 \times 165 - 28.2 \times 17 \\ &= 6869.6 \text{ kJ/day} \end{aligned}$$

Convert the BMR to kJ per hour:

$$\text{BMR} = \dfrac{7000}{24} = 291\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ kJ/hour}$$

Using the energy formula with PAL $8.6$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Energy out} &= 0.5 \times 291\dfrac{2}{3} \times 8.6 \\ &\approx 1254 \text{ kJ} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Converts BMR to kJ/hour, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Also award the mark if BMR is not converted but the formula is used.

solutions.latex:
Time needed, using the formula with the cycling PAL of $4$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{time} &= \dfrac{1000}{7000 \div 24} \div 4 \\ &= 51 \text{ min } 26 \text{ s} \end{aligned}$$

Distance cycled at $16$ km/h:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \dfrac{16}{60} \times 51 \text{ min } 26 \text{ s} \\ &\approx 13.71 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

Each loop is $2$ km, so the number of full loops is $\dfrac{13.71}{2} \approx 6.9$.

$$\therefore\ 7 \text{ laps are needed}$$
criteria: Finds the total distance, or equivalent merit
Makes time the subject of the formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source says 7 laps although 13.71/2 is under 7 full loops of 2 km (6 full loops); kept as source. The PAL of 4 is read from the source working; table not shown.

parts.latex: A recurrence relation:

dif.r: Direct recall of what a recurrence relation is

options.label: A
options.latex: Is a present value of the annuity.

options.label: B
options.latex: Uses the previous result to obtain the next value in the annuity investment.

options.label: C
options.latex: Uses the final result to obtain the next value in the annuity investment.

options.label: D
options.latex: Is the addition of future and present value of the annuity.

solutions.latex:
A recurrence relation gives each term from the term before it, for example $A_{n+1}=A_n(1+r)+M$ for an annuity investment.

So it uses the previous result to obtain the next value.

Option A and option D describe a present value or a sum of values, not a rule linking one term to the next, and option C uses the final result, which is not known when the relation is applied.
$$\therefore\ \text{the statement that uses the previous result to find the next value is correct}$$

meta.self_check: Definition of a recurrence relation compared with each option.
meta.generated_note: Generated worked solution; key B.

parts.latex: The types of walks that can exist in a network are:

dif.r: Recall of network walk terminology

solutions.latex:
A walk is a sequence of edges in a network. It can be a path (no repeated vertices), a circuit (starts and ends at the same vertex, no repeated edges) or a cycle (a circuit with no repeated vertices except the start and end).

Walks may also be on directed or undirected networks.

So each of options A, B and C is a correct statement about walks, and the keyed option is that all of them are true.
$$\therefore\ \text{all of the above}$$

meta.self_check: Checked against the keyed answer D; options A to C each describe types of walks or networks.
meta.generated_note: Generated worked solution following the supplied key D. Option A (directed and undirected) describes network types rather than walk types, so the wording of the source question is loose.

why: Claude-written solution, confidence 0.8

Checker got a different answer — The key D ('All of the above') matches the school's key, but it is mathematically doubtful: directed and undirected describe types of network, not types of walk. The best answer is B (paths, circuits, cycles). The generated solution's claim that option A is 'a correct statement about walks' is a stretch. Owner should decide whether to keep the question.

questions.decide: 2023 William Clarke AT3 Q3 (\"The types of walks that can exist in a network are\"): the school's key is D (all of the above), which counts \"directed and undirected\" as types of walk; they are types of network. The best answer is B (paths, circuits, cycles). Keep D, change the key to B, or drop the question?

parts.latex: $y = 4^{-x}$ is an example of what relationship?

dif.r: Recognise exponential form from equation

solutions.latex:
Write the function as $y=4^{-x}=\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{x}$.

The variable $x$ is in the exponent with a constant base, so this is an exponential relationship.

It is not quadratic or linear, since $x$ is not raised to a power, and it is not reciprocal, which has the form $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{exponential}$$

questions.stem:
The path of an object projected from the top of a building is shown below.

\exfigure{3306_q10_1}

The equation of the object's path can be modelled by the quadratic function

$$h = 20 + 8t - t^2$$

where $h$ is the height of the object (metres) above the ground and $t$ is the time in seconds the object is in the air.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: How tall is the building?

dif.r: Evaluate quadratic at t equals zero

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the vertical distance ($d$) above the building that the object reaches?

dif.r: Find vertex of quadratic then subtract building height

parts.label: c
parts.latex: The object is 35 metres above the ground 3 seconds after being projected. After how many more seconds will the object be the same distance above the ground?

dif.r: Use parabola symmetry to find other equal-height time

figures.cap: parabolic path of object from building top, d marked, DIAGRAM NOT TO SCALE

solutions.latex:
The building height is the starting height, at $t = 0$.
$$h = 20 \text{ m}$$

The maximum is on the axis of symmetry, $t = -\dfrac{8}{2(-1)} = 4$.
$$\begin{aligned} h &= 20 + 8(4) - (4)^2 \\ &= 36 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 36 - 20 \\ &= 16 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the maximum height $36$ m, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added the axis-of-symmetry step $t=4$ as the set-up.

solutions.latex:
Check the heights at $t = 3$ and $t = 5$.
$$\begin{aligned} h(3) &= 20 + 8(3) - (3)^2 = 35 \text{ m} \\ h(5) &= 20 + 8(5) - (5)^2 = 35 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The values $t = 3$ and $t = 5$ are symmetric about $t = 4$, the axis of symmetry.
$$\therefore\ \text{after } 2 \text{ more seconds}$$
criteria: Provides correct working, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is a tree?

figures.cap: option A: network with a triangle and a pendant edge
option B: network with no cycles
option C: network with cycles
option D: complete network on four vertices

solutions.latex:
A tree is a connected network with no cycles (circuits).

Option A contains a triangle, so it has a cycle.

Option B is connected, has 5 vertices and 4 edges, and has no cycle, so it is a tree.

Options C and D each contain a cycle (a closed loop of edges), so they are not trees.

$$\therefore\ \text{the tree is the network in option B.}$$

Which of the following walks is a path in the network diagram below?

\exfigure{493_q2_1}

dif.r: Recall definition of path; check options for repeated vertices.

figures.cap: network with vertices P, Q, R, S

solutions.latex:
The network has edges $PQ$, $QR$, $RS$ and $SP$.

A path does not repeat a vertex (or an edge).

Option A, $P$–$Q$–$P$–$S$, repeats $P$ and the edge $PQ$.

Option B, $P$–$Q$–$R$–$S$–$P$, returns to $P$, so $P$ is repeated.

Option C uses $Q$–$S$, which is not an edge.

Option D, $P$–$Q$–$R$–$S$, uses edges $PQ$, $QR$, $RS$ and repeats no vertex, so it is a path.

$$\therefore\ \text{the path is option D.}$$

parts.latex:
In a club meeting, 5 regular members and the club president are in attendance.

The club rules state that each regular member must shake the hand of \textbf{two} other regular members, and the club president must shake everyone’s hand.

Which network diagram can be used to represent the handshakes between group members?

dif.r: Model handshake conditions as network; check degrees of options.

skills: Drawing networks from tables and maps

figures.cap: option A: network of six vertices, house shape with centre vertex
option B: star network
option C: network with multiple edges
option D: dense network

solutions.latex:
Represent people as vertices and handshakes as edges.

Each of the 5 regular members shakes hands with exactly two other regular members, so the regular members form a single loop of 5 (each has 2 edges among themselves).

The president shakes hands with all 5 members, so the president's vertex is joined to every other vertex (degree 5).

Then each regular member has degree $2+1=3$, and there is one handshake per pair (no repeated edges).

Option A has an outer loop through the 5 regular members, with the centre vertex joined to all 5. Each outer vertex has degree 3 and the centre has degree 5.

Option B has regular members of degree 1, option C has repeated edges (double handshakes), and in option D the regular members have too many handshakes.

$$\therefore\ \text{the diagram is option A.}$$

meta.self_check: Verified degrees in option A: centre 5, top vertex 3, other four outer vertices 3; outer cycle has 5 vertices.
meta.generated_note: Generated working for MCQ; key A.

parts.latex:
Harper can type 4 pages of text in 24 minutes.

At the same rate, how many minutes will it take Harper to type 7 pages?

dif.r: One-step unitary rate calculation.

solutions.latex:
Since $4$ pages take $24$ minutes, $1$ page takes
$$\dfrac{24}{4} = 6 \text{ minutes}$$
So $7$ pages take
$$7\times 6 = 42 \text{ minutes}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{It takes } 42 \text{ minutes.}$$

At a high school the ratio of male teachers to pupils is $4:9$, whilst the ratio of pupils to female teachers is $12:5$.

Find the ratio of male teachers to female teachers.

dif.r: Combine two ratios via common pupil term, then simplify.

solutions.latex:
Write both ratios with the same number of pupils (LCM of $9$ and $12$ is $108$).
$$\begin{aligned} M:P &= 4:9 = 48:108 \\ P:F &= 12:5 = 108:45 \end{aligned}$$
So
$$M:F = 48:45 = 16:15$$
$$\therefore\ M:F = 16:15$$
criteria: Writes both ratios with a common number of pupils, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Audrey is concerned about the duck population in the local community. She collects 144 ducks and tags them. A couple of months later she collects 15 ducks and found 10 of them were tagged. Using the capture-recapture method, what is her estimate of the duck population?

dif.r: Standard capture-recapture proportion applied directly.

solutions.latex:
Capture-recapture: the proportion tagged in the second sample equals the proportion tagged in the whole population.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Population} &= \dfrac{144 \times 15}{10} \\ &= 216 \text{ ducks} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The estimate is } 216 \text{ ducks.}$$
criteria: Sets up the capture-recapture proportion, or equivalent merit

Eliza is attempting to fill her bathtub with jelly.

In order to dissolve the jelly crystals, she must mix 250 mL of boiling water with every 85 g of crystals.

Eliza can boil up to 10 L at a time in her urn and it takes 8 minutes to boil.

Eliza estimates it will take 10.2 kg of crystals to fill the bath. How long will it take to boil enough water to dissolve this these of crystals?

dif.r: Scale rate with unit conversion, then count batches and time.

solutions.latex:
Water needed per $85$ g of crystals is $250$ mL, so for $10.2$ kg $= 10\,200$ g we multiply by $\dfrac{10\,200}{85} = 120$.
$$250 \times 120 = 30\,000 \text{ mL} = 30 \text{ L}$$
The urn boils $10$ L at a time, so
$$\dfrac{30}{10} = 3 \text{ batches}$$
Time:
$$3 \times 8 = 24 \text{ minutes}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{It takes } 24 \text{ minutes.}$$
criteria: Finds the volume of water needed, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Greg plans to drive from Sydney to Newcastle and can choose between two routes:

\begin{itemize}
\item Route A would take 1 hour and 55 minutes at an average speed of 85 km/h.
\item Route B would take 2 hours and 10 minutes at an average speed of 74 km/h.
\end{itemize}

Greg’s car has a fuel consumption rate of 9.3 L/100 km.

What is the minimum amount of fuel Greg could use to complete this trip?

dif.r: Compare route distances from mixed time units, choose, then fuel rate.

solutions.latex:
Distance $=$ speed $\times$ time for each route.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Route A: } D &= 85 \times 1\dfrac{55}{60} \approx 162.92 \text{ km} \\ \text{Route B: } D &= 74 \times 2\dfrac{10}{60} \approx 160.33 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
Route B is shorter, so it uses less fuel.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Fuel} &= \dfrac{160.33 \times 9.3}{100} \\ &\approx 14.91 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The minimum fuel is about } 14.91 \text{ L.}$$
criteria: Finds both distances and chooses Route B, or equivalent merit

Quarterly compounding at $8\%$ p.a. gives a rate of $\dfrac{8}{4} = 2\%$ per quarter, over $3 \times 4 = 12$ quarters.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 1600(1+0.02)^{12} \\ &= \$2029.19 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The probability of a team winning a particular football match is $\dfrac{3}{7}$, and the probability of drawing this match is $\dfrac{1}{5}$. The probability of this team winning or drawing the match would be closest to:

dif.r: Add probabilities of mutually exclusive events; simple fraction sum.

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
Winning and drawing are mutually exclusive, so the probabilities add.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{win or draw}) &= \dfrac{3}{7} + \dfrac{1}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{22}{35} \\ &\approx 0.63 \end{aligned}$$
So the correct option is A.

parts.latex:
Over 7 cricket matches Adam took the following number of wickets: 4, 2, 6, 4, 0, 1 and 4. In the 8th match he took 3 wickets.

Which of these statements is true when the 8th match is included?

dif.r: Compute mean, judge effect of adding mean value on SD.

options.label: A
options.latex: The mean stays the same and the standard deviation increases.

options.label: B
options.latex: The mean stays the same and the standard deviation decreases.

options.label: C
options.latex: The mean increases and the standard deviation stays the same.

options.label: D
options.latex: The mean decreases and the standard deviation stays the same.

solutions.latex:
Find the mean of the first 7 matches.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Mean} &= \dfrac{4+2+6+4+0+1+4}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{21}{7} = 3 \end{aligned}$$
The 8th score is $3$, which equals the mean, so the mean stays at $3$.

The standard deviation depends on the sum of squared deviations from the mean.
$$\begin{aligned} \sum (x-3)^2 &= 1+1+9+1+9+4+1 \\ &= 26 \end{aligned}$$
The new score $3$ has deviation $0$, so the sum stays $26$ but is now divided by $8$ instead of $7$ (population standard deviation).
$$\sqrt{\dfrac{26}{7}} \approx 1.93 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sqrt{\dfrac{26}{8}} \approx 1.80$$
So the standard deviation decreases. (The sample standard deviation gives the same conclusion: $\sqrt{\dfrac{26}{6}} \approx 2.08$ falls to $\sqrt{\dfrac{26}{7}} \approx 1.93$.)

Therefore the mean stays the same and the standard deviation decreases, which is option B.

meta.self_check: Computed mean 3 and sum of squared deviations 26 in python-free hand check; SD falls under both population and sample formulas.
meta.generated_note: MCQ working written for key B.

What is the salvage value of the furniture after 5 years ?

dif.r: Direct substitution into declining-balance formula.

solutions.latex:
Declining-balance salvage value is $S = V_0(1-r)^n$.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= 15000(1-0.08)^5 \\ &= \$9886.22 \end{aligned}$$
So the correct option is A.

dif.r: Reverse bearing read from diagram; one angle adjustment.

figures.cap: towns A, B, C with north line and 48 degree angle

solutions.latex:
The $48^\circ$ at $A$ is measured from due south ($AC$), so the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is
$$180^\circ - 48^\circ = 132^\circ$$
The bearing of $A$ from $B$ is the reverse direction.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing of } A \text{ from } B &= 132^\circ + 180^\circ \\ &= 312^\circ \end{aligned}$$
So the correct option is D.

dif.r: Fit line by eye, estimate gradient and intercept to match option.

skills: Line of best fit by eye

figures.cap: scatter plot of English vs History marks

solutions.latex:
Draw a line of best fit through the middle of the points. It passes close to $(52, 55)$ on the left and close to $(95, 94)$ on the right.

Find its gradient.
$$\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{94-55}{95-52} \\ &= \dfrac{39}{43} \approx 0.9 \end{aligned}$$
This rules out A and B, which have gradient $2.5$ (at $E = 52$ they would give $H$ well above $100$).

Now find the intercept, using $H = 0.9E + c$ and the point $(52, 55)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 55 &= 0.9 \times 52 + c \\ c &= 55 - 46.8 = 8.2 \approx 8.5 \end{aligned}$$
Option D, $H = 0.9E + 53.5$, gives $H \approx 100$ at $E = 52$, which is far above the data.

Check option C, $H = 0.9E + 8.5$, at $E = 70$.
$$H = 0.9 \times 70 + 8.5 = 71.5$$
This is close to the plotted point $(70, 69)$.

Therefore the best line is $H = 0.9E + 8.5$, which is option C.

A new model washing machine has an energy consumption of 175 kWh per year, and uses an average of 9900 L of water per year.

solutions.latex:

In order to estimate the number of wallabies on an island, 50 are collected and tagged.

At a later date 40 are captured and 16 are found to have been tagged.

solutions.latex:
The proportion tagged in the sample equals the proportion tagged in the population. Let $x$ be the population.

Evelyn owns 3815 shares with a market value of \$9.50 per share. The total dividend received for these shares is \$2671.25.

What is the percentage dividend yield ? Answer correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Market value then dividend yield percentage; two routine steps.

solutions.latex:
First find the total market value of the shares.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Value} &= 3815 \times 9.50 \\ &= \$36242.50 \end{aligned}$$
Then use $\text{yield} = \dfrac{\text{dividend}}{\text{market value}} \times 100$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Yield} &= \dfrac{2671.25}{36242.50} \times 100 \\ &\approx 7.37\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{dividend yield} = 7.37\% \text{ (to 2 decimal places)}$$
criteria: Finds the market value of the shares, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Angles in triangle $PTS$ sum to $180^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle PTS &= 180^\circ - 73^\circ - 49^\circ \\ &= 58^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Using the sine rule, with $x = TS$ opposite the $49^\circ$ angle:
$$\dfrac{x}{\sin 49^\circ} = \dfrac{48}{\sin 58^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{48\sin 49^\circ}{\sin 58^\circ} \\ &\approx 42.72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle PTS$ or sets up the sine rule, or equivalent merit

Jacqueline also wants to save for a home renovation, and her goal is to save \$45 000. She wants to put some money into a savings account at an interest rate of $6\%$ per annum, where the interest is compounded monthly.

What one-off lump sum would Jacqueline need to deposit in order to have \$45 000 in the account after 3 years?

dif.r: Present value formula with monthly rate and periods converted

solutions.latex:
Interest is $\dfrac{6\%}{12} = 0.5\%$ per month, over $3 \times 12 = 36$ months.

Using the present value formula $PV = \dfrac{FV}{(1+r)^n}$:
$$\begin{aligned} PV &= \dfrac{45000}{(1+0.005)^{36}} \\ &\approx 37604.02 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Jacqueline needs to deposit } \$37\,604.02$$
criteria: Sets up the present value formula with $r = 0.005$ and $n = 36$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Corrected from source: the source used $4500$ (giving $3760.40$) but the question asks for $45\,000$, so the answer is $37\,604.02$. Rubric written by us.

Express his fuel consumption in L/100km correct to 1 decimal place.

dif.r: Two steps: tank capacity from cost, then L/100km rate

solutions.latex:
The capacity of the tank is the cost divided by the price per litre.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{capacity} &= 51.60 \div 1.29 \\ &= 40 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
Fuel consumption is the litres used per $100$ km.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{fuel consumption} &= \dfrac{40}{460}\times 100 \\ &\approx 8.7 \text{ L}/100\text{km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{fuel consumption} = 8.7 \text{ L}/100\text{km (to 1 dp)}$$
criteria: Finds the capacity of the tank, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
Two hikers decide to leave a campsite ($C$) to visit some landmarks in the area. One hiker walks 26 km on a bearing of $065^\circ$T to see a lake ($L$), the other hiker walks 16 km on a bearing of $285^\circ$T to see a mountain ($M$).

\exfigure{496_q32_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that $\angle MCL = 140^\circ$.

dif.r: Angle between two bearings by simple addition

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Calculate the distance between the Mountain ($M$) and the Lake ($L$), correct to the nearest kilometre.

dif.r: Direct cosine rule for the third side

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
Hence, find the bearing of the lake from the mountain.

Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

dif.r: Sine rule angle combined with back-bearing geometry to get bearing

figures.cap: campsite C with bearings to lake L and mountain M

solutions.latex:
The angle is made up of the bearing $065^\circ$ and the angle from north back to $285^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle MCL &= 65 + (360 - 285) \\ &= 65 + 75 \\ &= 140^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Let $x = ML$. Using the cosine rule in $\triangle MCL$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 16^2 + 26^2 - 2(16)(26)\cos 140^\circ \\ &= 256 + 676 - 832\cos 140^\circ \\ &= 1569.34897\ldots \\ x &= 39.61500\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance} \approx 40 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The bearing of $C$ from $M$ is the reverse of $285^\circ$, but measured from the north at $M$ it is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{bearing of } C \text{ from } M &= 90 + 15 \\ &= 105^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Let $\theta = \angle CML$. Using the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{26} &= \dfrac{\sin 140^\circ}{39.615\ldots} \\ \theta &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{26\sin 140^\circ}{39.615\ldots}\right) \\ &= 24.95\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{bearing from } M \text{ to } L &= 105 - 25 \\ &= 080^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the angle $CML$, or equivalent merit
Finds the bearing of $C$ from $M$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). I added a short lead-in to the bearing of C from M; the source gave only the calculation.

figures.cap: box and whisker plot of ages, scale 30 to 80

solutions.latex:
The box-and-whisker plot divides the data into four groups, each containing 25% of the residents.

The group between the minimum and the lower quartile, and the group between the lower quartile and the median, are the lower parts of the plot. The interval $30 - 50$ is one of these quarters.

solutions.latex:
Using the area formula for a triangle with two sides and the included angle:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 8\times 12\times\sin 32^\circ \\ &\approx 25.4 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the area is $25.4 \text{ cm}^2$, which is option A.

parts.latex:
Chris purchased a laptop for \$2 999.00 exactly 3 years ago.

He claims 15% depreciation per year using the declining balance method.

Calculate the current salvage value of the laptop.

dif.r: Direct declining-balance formula substitution; same type as the HSC anchor.

solutions.latex:
Using the declining balance (salvage value) formula with $V_0 = 2999$, $r = 0.15$, $n = 3$:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= V_0(1-r)^n \\ &= 2999\times(0.85)^3 \\ &\approx \$1841.76 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex: Which of the following expresses $V$ as the subject of the formula $u=\dfrac{\sqrt{mV}}{2}$ ?
parts.note: Rearranging a formula that has a square root is beyond linear and y = ax^2 + c.

dif.r: Change of subject involving a square root; two inverse steps.

solutions.latex:
Make $V$ the subject of $u=\dfrac{\sqrt{mV}}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2u &= \sqrt{mV} && (\text{multiply by } 2) \\ 4u^2 &= mV && (\text{square both sides}) \\ V &= \dfrac{4u^2}{m} && (\text{divide by } m) \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex:
Adam purchased some office furniture five years ago. It depreciated by \$2300 each year based on the straight-line method of depreciation. The salvage value of the furniture is now \$7500.

Find the initial value of the office furniture.

dif.r: Straight-line depreciation formula used in reverse; identical to the HSC anchor.

solutions.latex:
Using straight-line depreciation, $S = V_0 - Dn$, with $S=7500$, $D=2300$, $n=5$:
$$7500 = V_0 - 5\times 2300$$
$$\begin{aligned} V_0 &= 7500 + 5\times 2300 \\ &= \$19\,000 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the initial value was } \$19\,000$$
criteria: Correct substitution into $S=V_0-Dn$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A formula for the dosage in mL ($D$) of medicine required for a child aged between 1 and 12 years compared to an adult's dosage ($A$) is:

$$D=\dfrac{yA}{y+12}$$

where $y$ is the age of the child (years).

A 6-year-old child is to take 5 mL of a prescribed medicine three times per day.

What is the equivalent daily adult dosage of this medicine?

dif.r: Daily dose conversion, then solving the given formula in reverse.

solutions.latex:
The daily child dosage is $D = 5\times 3 = 15$ mL.

Substitute $D=15$ and $y=6$ into the formula.
$$\begin{aligned} 15 &= \dfrac{6A}{6+12} \\ 15\times 18 &= 6A \\ A &= \dfrac{270}{6} \\ &= 45 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the equivalent daily adult dosage is } 45 \text{ mL}$$

parts.latex:
Sydney is 10 hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC + 10) and New York is 5 hours behind Coordinated Universal Time (UTC $-5$).

Tony travels from Sydney to New York. His plane leaves Sydney at 8:20 pm on Wednesday local time and flies non-stop to New York.

The flight takes 20 hours and 24 minutes.

What time and day is it in New York when the plane lands?

dif.r: Time zones combined with flight duration across days; identical to the HSC anchor.

solutions.latex:
The time difference is
$$10-(-5)=15 \text{ hours}$$
Add the flight time to the departure time (Sydney time): $8{:}20 \text{ pm Wednesday} + 20 \text{ h } 24 \text{ min} = 4{:}44 \text{ pm Thursday}$.

New York is 15 hours behind Sydney, so subtract 15 hours: $4{:}44 \text{ pm} - 15 \text{ h} = 1{:}44 \text{ am}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{it is } 1{:}44 \text{ am Thursday in New York}$$
criteria: Finds the time in Sydney when the plane lands in New York, or equivalent merit
Finds the time difference between Sydney and New York, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A capsule of length 18 cm and diameter 6 cm is formed by joining an open hemisphere at each end of an open cylinder, as shown in the diagram.

\exfigure{500_q10_1}

Water is poured into the capsule and fills one third of its volume.

Calculate the volume of water in the capsule, correct to 2 decimal places.

dif.r: Composite volume: deduce cylinder length, combine sphere and cylinder, then take a third.

skills: Volume of pyramids, cones and spheres

figures.cap: capsule: cylinder with hemispherical ends, length 18 cm, diameter 6 cm, partly filled with water

solutions.latex:
The radius is $3$ cm, so the cylinder length is $18-6=12$ cm.

The two hemispheres make one sphere, so the capsule volume is that of a sphere plus a cylinder.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3+\pi r^2 h \\ &= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\times 3^3+\pi\times 3^2\times 12 \\ &= 36\pi + 108\pi = 144\pi \\ &\approx 452.389 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$
The water fills one third of this.
$$\begin{aligned} V_{\text{water}} &= \dfrac{1}{3}\times 452.389 \\ &\approx 150.80 \text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

After the 8th deposit, Simone stops making deposits but leaves the money in the savings account. The money in her savings account then earns interest at 1.25% per annum, compounded annually, for a further two years.

Find the amount of money in Simone’s savings account at the end of ten years.

dif.r: Annuity table value then further compounding at a new rate; two stages.

figures.cap: table of future value interest factors for an annuity of $1

solutions.latex:
For the first 8 years use the annuity table factor for 8 periods at $0.75\%$, which is $8.2132$.
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= 1000\times 8.2132 \\ &= \$8213.20 \end{aligned}$$
Then compound this for 2 years at $1.25\%$ per annum.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 8213.20\times(1.0125)^2 \\ &\approx \$8419.81 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the balance after 10 years is } \$8419.81$$
criteria: Finds the correct future value of the annuity and attempts to apply the compound interest formula, or equivalent merit

Jacky's car averages fuel use of $8.5$ L/100 km. Jacky fills his fuel tank with 60 litres and travels 550 km.

dif.r: Two steps: fuel used from rate, then subtract from tank

solutions.latex:
The distance is $550$ km, which is $5.5$ lots of $100$ km.

solutions.latex:
The point $P$ lies on the line $3x+4y=26$, so test each option.

$$\begin{aligned} (2,5):\ 3(2)+4(5) &= 6+20 \\ &= 26 \end{aligned}$$

The other options give $25$, $24$ and $23$, so they do not lie on the line.

Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex:
A student used a computer application to graph the following equations,

$x+y=10$ and $2x-3y=10$

\exfigure{718_q4_1}

The program labelled one line as $\boxed{f}$ and the other as $\boxed{g}$. Which of the following correctly matches $f$ and $g$ with their respective equations and gives the solution when the equations are solved simultaneously?

dif.r: Match lines by gradient/intercepts and solve simultaneously

figures.cap: graph of two lines labelled f and g

solutions.latex:
Solve $x+y=10$ and $2x-3y=10$ simultaneously. Substituting $y=10-x$:

$$\begin{aligned} 2x-3(10-x) &= 10 \\ 5x-30 &= 10 \\ x &= 8,\ y=2 \end{aligned}$$

Line $x+y=10$ has intercepts $(10,0)$ and $(0,10)$, so it is the line with negative gradient, $g$. Line $2x-3y=10$ has gradient $\dfrac{2}{3}$, so it is $f$.

Hence $f$: $2x-3y=10$, $g$: $x+y=10$, with solution $x=8$, $y=2$, which is option D.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What is the probability of not drawing an ace card?

dif.r: Single complement probability

skills: Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes

solutions.latex:
There are $26$ black cards, plus the $2$ red 4's.

$$\begin{aligned} P(E) &= \dfrac{28}{52} \\ &= \dfrac{7}{13} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{not an ace}) &= 1-P(\text{an ace}) \\ &= 1-\dfrac{4}{52} \\ &= \dfrac{48}{52} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{13} \end{aligned}$$

Her electricity bill is \$1240. It is due in two weeks time. Alyssa realises she has not put aside enough money to pay this bill.

The weekly allocations must total the net income.

$$\begin{aligned} X &= 1180-(350+90+20+30+180+50+60+140+100+80) \\ &= \$80 \end{aligned}$$

Each week she puts aside $\$80$ for electricity plus $\$80$ for savings, for $3$ weeks.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= (\$80+\$80)\times 3 \\ &= \$480 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Amount still required:

$$\begin{aligned} \$1240-\$480 &= \$760 \end{aligned}$$

She can use her electricity and savings money, and cut entertainment and clothes spending for the 2 weeks.

questions.stem: A cow has a type of bacteria living in it called a methanogen. The methanogen's population exponentially increases with the equation $P = k(1.2)^t$, where $k$ is a constant, and $t$ is time in years. It is known that after 2 years, there are 288 methanogens in the cow.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is 200.

dif.r: Substitute point into exponential model and solve for k.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: After 3 years, what is the population of the methanogens living in the cow?

dif.r: Direct substitution into exponential model.

parts.label: c

dif.r: Initial value at t=0, direct recall.

parts.label: d
parts.latex: If the population grows over 500, the cow will need to have medical treatment. How many years will it take before the cow requires medical treatment?

dif.r: Guess and check whole years against threshold of 500.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 2$ and $P = 288$ into $P = k(1.2)^t$.
$$\begin{aligned} 288 &= k(1.2)^2 \\ k &= \dfrac{288}{1.2^2} \\ &= 200 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 200(1.2)^3 \\ &= 345.6 \\ &\approx 346 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 346 methanogens.

The initial population is at $t = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 200(1.2)^0 \\ &= 200 \end{aligned}$$

Use $P = 200(1.2)^n$ and test whole years.
$$\begin{aligned} n = 4:\ P &= 200(1.2)^4 = 414.72 &&(\text{under } 500) \\ n = 5:\ P &= 497.664 &&(\text{under } 500) \\ n = 6:\ P &= 597.1968 &&(\text{over } 500) \end{aligned}$$
Solving $200(1.2)^t=500$ gives $t=\dfrac{\ln 2.5}{\ln 1.2}\approx5.03$.
$$\therefore\ \text{just over } 5 \text{ years (the population passes } 500 \text{ early in the 6th year)}$$

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{716_q18_s1}

$\angle ABC$ is obtuse and lies on a straight line with the $60^\circ$ angle of depression at $B$.
$$\angle ABC = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ \text{ (straight line)}$$
Using the angle sum of triangle $ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle BCA &= 180^\circ - 42^\circ - 120^\circ \\ &= 18^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Let $AC = x$. By the sine rule in triangle $ABC$:
$$\dfrac{x}{\sin 120^\circ} = \dfrac{15}{\sin 18^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{15\sin 120^\circ}{\sin 18^\circ} \\ &= 42.0375\ldots \\ &\approx 42.04 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Writes the sine rule with correct substitution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Let $h$ be the height of the building. In the right-angled triangle, the angle at $A$ between $AC$ and the vertical is $90^\circ - 42^\circ = 48^\circ$.
$$\cos 48^\circ = \dfrac{h}{42.04}$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= 42.04\cos 48^\circ \\ &= 28.13\ldots \\ &\approx 28 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes a correct trigonometric equation for $h$, or equivalent merit

Geoffrey is planning a bushwalk. He plans to start from his house in Kenthurst ($K$) and walk to Glenhaven ($G$) which is 5 km away at a bearing of $160^\circ\text{T}$. Geoffrey is then planning to walk to Rouse Hill ($R$) which is 4 km from Glenhaven at a bearing of $\text{N}50^\circ\text{E}$.

parts.label: a

solution sketch: diagram labelled with 160 degrees, 5 km, 50 degrees, 4 km

solutions.latex: \exfigure{716_q21_s1}

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The angle between $GK$ and north at $G$ is found from co-interior angles, which add to $180^\circ$:
$$180^\circ - 160^\circ = 20^\circ$$
The bearing of $R$ from $G$ is $\text{N}50^\circ\text{E}$, so
$$\angle KGR = 20^\circ + 50^\circ = 70^\circ$$
as required.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Let $KR = x$. By the cosine rule in triangle $KGR$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 4^2+5^2-2\times 4\times 5\times\cos 70^\circ \\ &= 27.319\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \approx 5.23 \text{ km (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta = \angle GRK$, the angle at $R$ between $RG$ and $RK$. By the sine rule in triangle $KGR$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{5} = \dfrac{\sin 70^\circ}{5.23}$$
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{5\sin 70^\circ}{5.23}$$
$$\theta \approx 64.01^\circ$$
The bearing of $G$ from $R$ is $180^\circ + 50^\circ = 230^\circ\text{T}$, and $K$ lies further round, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 230^\circ + 64^\circ \\ &= 294^\circ\text{T} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the sine rule with correct substitution, or equivalent merit

A bearing of $210^\circ\text{T}$ is measured clockwise from north. It lies between $180^\circ$ (south) and $270^\circ$ (west), so the compass bearing is measured from south towards west.

parts.latex:
A company pays a dividend of 14 cents on every share. Simon has 20 000 shares, valued at \$46 000.

What is the approximate dividend yield?

dif.r: Two steps: total dividend then yield percentage

solutions.latex:
The total dividend is the dividend per share times the number of shares.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Dividend} &= 0.14\times 20\,000 \\ &= \$2800 \end{aligned}$$
The dividend yield is the dividend as a percentage of the value of the shares.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Yield} &= \dfrac{2800}{46\,000}\times 100\% \\ &\approx 6.1\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the dividend yield is approximately } 6\%$$

parts.latex:
A principal is directly in charge of 8 staff members on the executive. Each executive member has 6 people working in their team.

What could we use to represent the staff structure?

dif.r: Recall that a hierarchy with no cycles is a tree

solutions.latex:
A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. In the staff structure, the principal is connected to 8 executive members, and each executive member is connected to 6 team members. There is exactly one path between any two people, and there are no cycles.

A path is a single chain, a cycle is a closed loop, and a weighted graph has values on its edges. None of these describes a branching hierarchy.
$$\therefore\ \text{a tree}$$

meta.self_check: Hierarchy with branching and no cycles is a tree.

The degree of a vertex is the number of edges meeting at it. Counting each vertex in the diagram:

A house plan is drawn to the scale $1:100$.

If the bedroom has an area of $52\ \text{m}^2$, with a length of 8 m, what is the measurement of the width of the house on the drawing?

dif.r: Width from area, then apply the scale with unit conversion

The width of the bedroom is the area divided by the length.

figures.cap: parabola A = 0.5h^2 + 3h

solutions.latex: The height and area cannot be negative, so only the part of the graph with $h>0$ can be used.

Set $A=8$ in $A=0.5h^2+3h$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5h^2+3h &= 8 \\ h^2+6h-16 &= 0 \\ (h+8)(h-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $h=2$ (a height is positive). Then $A=\dfrac12bh$ gives $8=\dfrac12 b(2)$, so $b=8$.

Each equal side $x$ is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with sides $2$ and $4$ (half the base):
$$x^2=2^2+4^2$$
so $x=\sqrt{20}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \sqrt{20}+\sqrt{20}+8 \\ &= 16.9 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the slant side, or equivalent merit
Finds the height $h=2$, or equivalent merit

The distance travelled by a person walking at a constant speed varies directly with the time that they have been walking.

Jacob walked at a constant speed for 20 minutes and travelled a distance of 1 800 metres.

Which graph and equation below would represent this variation relationship?

dif.r: Find direct variation constant and match graph through origin

figures.cap: option A: graph D=180T-1800
option B: graph D=75T
option C: graph D=180T-1800 drawn as a decaying curve
option D: graph D=90X

solutions.latex:
Direct variation has the form $D = kT$, so the graph is a straight line through the origin.

Using $T = 20$ and $D = 1800$ to find $k$:
$$\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{1800}{20} \\ &= 90 \end{aligned}$$
So the equation is $D = 90T$.

Option A is a line that does not pass through the origin ($D = 0$ at $T = 10$). Option B has $D = 75T$, which gives $1500$ m, not $1800$ m, at $20$ minutes. Option C is not a straight line.

Option D is a straight line through the origin with $k = 90$ (it passes through about $(20, 1800)$), so it is the correct choice.

The speeds (in km/h) which are recorded on a radar device approaching a section of road work are normally distributed, with a mean of 58 and a standard deviation of 4.

The speed limit for the section is 60 km/h and 2400 vehicles passed the radar in one day.

How many vehicles were travelling at 2 km/h above the speed limit or more?

dif.r: z=1, empirical rule tail, then scale to count

solutions.latex:
A speed of $2$ km/h above the limit is $62$ km/h or more.

The $z$-score of $62$ is:
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{62 - 58}{4} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
In a normal distribution, about $68\%$ of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean. The remaining $32\%$ is split equally between the two tails, so
$$P(Z \ge 1) = 16\%$$
Number of vehicles:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.16 \times 2400 &= 384 \end{aligned}$$

Two teams of athletes were compared on their endurance, as measured by the number of repetitions that they could complete of a short, mixed-activity training circuit. The results are shown in the back-to-back stem-and-leaf-plot below.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Given that Team B has an interquartile range of 16, show that Team A has a larger interquartile range, and explain what this means in terms of statistical comparison.

dif.r: Compute quartiles for odd set and interpret spread

figures.cap: back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot, Team A and Team B

solutions.latex:
Reading the plot, Team A has 13 scores:
$$5, 6, 8, 14, 17, 17, 18, 20, 22, 27, 31, 33, 40$$
The median is the 7th score, $18$.

Team B has 12 scores:
$$2, 6, 13, 17, 19, 22, 24, 25, 28, 34, 36, 37$$
The median is the mean of the 6th and 7th scores:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{22 + 24}{2} &= 23 \end{aligned}$$
Difference in medians:
$$\begin{aligned} 23 - 18 &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
The medians differ by $5$ repetitions (Team B higher).

meta.self_check: Re-read stem-and-leaf: A n=13 median 18; B n=12 median 23.

solutions.latex:
For Team A (13 scores), the median is the 7th score. The lower half is the first six scores $5, 6, 8, 14, 17, 17$, so
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 &= \dfrac{8 + 14}{2} \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}$$
The upper half is the last six scores $20, 22, 27, 31, 33, 40$, so
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 &= \dfrac{27 + 31}{2} \\ &= 29 \end{aligned}$$
Interquartile range of Team A:
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= 29 - 11 \\ &= 18 \end{aligned}$$
Since $18 > 16$, Team A has the larger interquartile range.

This means the middle $50\%$ of Team A's results are more spread out, so Team A is less consistent than Team B.
criteria: Finds $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ for Team A, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: probability tree: leader A, B, C then mascot M, W

solutions.latex:
Multiply along the branches $A$ then $M$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A \text{ and } M) &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

"Andie or Miao but not both" means either (Andie and Woof) or (not Andie and Miao).

Andie and Woof:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} &= \dfrac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Bec or Cat, with Miao:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{6}\right) \times \dfrac{1}{3} &= \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Add the two cases:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{2}{9} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one of the two required probabilities correctly, or equivalent merit

questions.stem:
A helicopter leaves Underwood and flies 70 km on a bearing of $055^\circ$ to Vanna Beach.

It then flies 82 km on a bearing of $150^\circ$ to Weston.

The diagram below illustrates the journey.

\exfigure{308_q21_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex:
It then plans to fly directly back to Underwood.

Calculate the distance that it will fly.

dif.r: Derive included angle from bearings then cosine rule

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Determine the bearing (from Weston) on which it should fly to return to Underwood.

dif.r: Sine rule angle then convert to bearing from back-bearing

figures.cap: bearings diagram U to V to W
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{308_q21_s1}

The return flight is side $UW$ of triangle $UVW$. First find $\angle UVW$.

The bearing of $U$ from $V$ is $055^\circ+180^\circ=235^\circ$ (co-interior angles with the north lines), and the bearing of $W$ from $V$ is $150^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle UVW &= 235^\circ-150^\circ \\ &= 85^\circ \end{aligned}$$
Apply the cosine rule in triangle $UVW$.
$$\begin{aligned} UW^2 &= UV^2+VW^2-2\cdot UV\cdot VW\cos 85^\circ \\ &= 70^2+82^2-2\times 70\times 82\times\cos 85^\circ \\ &\approx 10\,623.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} UW &\approx 103.07 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the helicopter flies about } 103 \text{ km}$$

meta.self_check: Computed in python: UW = 103.07 km; angle 85 degrees from bearings.
meta.generated_note: Generated solution with diagram.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{308_q21_s1}

Find $\angle UWV$ using the sine rule in triangle $UVW$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin \angle UWV}{70} &= \dfrac{\sin 85^\circ}{103.07} \\ \sin \angle UWV &= \dfrac{70\sin 85^\circ}{103.07} \\ \angle UWV &\approx 42.6^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The angle is acute because $UV<VW$, so $\angle UWV$ is opposite the shorter side.

The bearing of $V$ from $W$ is $150^\circ+180^\circ=330^\circ$. Underwood lies anticlockwise from $WV$ (to the left when facing $V$ from $W$), so subtract.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing of } U \text{ from } W &= 330^\circ-42.6^\circ \\ &\approx 287^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the helicopter should fly on a bearing of about } 287^\circ$$

meta.self_check: Verified with coordinates: W(98.3,-30.8), bearing W to U = 287.4 degrees.

An outdoor spa has a pump which is rated at 350 watts and a heater which is rated at 1.2 kW.

How many kWh of energy would the spa use in a year?

solutions.latex:
Energy $(\text{kWh})$ = power $(\text{kW})\times$ time (hours). The pump is $350 \text{ W}=0.35 \text{ kW}$.

Pump hours per day:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Warmer months} &: 3+1.5=4.5 \text{ h} \\ \text{Cooler months} &: 1.5+1.2=2.7 \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
Pump hours per year:
$$\begin{aligned} 4.5\times 182+2.7\times 183 &= 819+494.1 \\ &= 1313.1 \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
Heater hours per day:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Warmer months} &: 5\times 12=60 \text{ min}=1 \text{ h} \\ \text{Cooler months} &: 12\times 12=144 \text{ min}=2.4 \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
Heater hours per year:
$$\begin{aligned} 1\times 182+2.4\times 183 &= 182+439.2 \\ &= 621.2 \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
Total energy:
$$\begin{aligned} E &= 0.35\times 1313.1+1.2\times 621.2 \\ &= 459.585+745.44 \\ &\approx 1205 \text{ kWh} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the spa uses about } 1205 \text{ kWh in a year}$$
criteria: Finds the yearly running hours of both the pump and the heater, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 0 \\ E &= 8 \\ B &= 9 \\ F &= \min(12,\ 8+5)=12 \\ C &= \min(9+6,\ 12+10)=15 \\ I &= 8+8=16 \\ D &= 15+7=22 \\ G &= \min(12+13,\ 16+7)=23 \\ H &= \min(22+12,\ 23+10,\ 16+19)=33 \end{aligned}$$
The smallest value at $H$ comes via $G$, and $G$'s shortest value comes via $I$, which comes via $E$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Length} &= 8+8+7+10 \\ &= 33 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{shortest path } A\to E\to I\to G\to H \text{, length } 33 \text{ km}$$

questions.stem:
Tahnee bought a car for use with her small business for \$24 000.

For taxation purposes she needed to work out a depreciated value of the car each year.

She initially decided to do this using the declining balance method at a rate of 25%.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Show that the depreciation of the car in the first four years is more than three times greater than the depreciation between the fourth and eighth years using this method.

dif.r: Show-that comparing declining-balance depreciation over two intervals; several calculations

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
She decided to change to the straight-line method of depreciation, as calculations were easier, but wants the value after eight years to be same as she calculated using the declining balance method.

By what amount should she depreciate the car each year, and what percentage is this of the cars new value?

dif.r: Set up straight-line rate to match earlier declining-balance value; reverse reasoning

solutions.latex:
Declining balance: $V=24\,000(0.75)^n$, since the value falls 25% each year.
$$\begin{aligned} V_4 &= 24\,000(0.75)^4 = \$7593.75 \\ V_8 &= 24\,000(0.75)^8 \approx \$2402.71 \end{aligned}$$
Depreciation in the first four years:
$$\begin{aligned} 24\,000-7593.75 &= \$16\,406.25 \end{aligned}$$
Depreciation between the fourth and eighth years:
$$\begin{aligned} 7593.75-2402.71 &= \$5191.04 \end{aligned}$$
Three times the later depreciation:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\times 5191.04 &= \$15\,573.12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 16\,406.25>15\,573.12$$
so the depreciation in the first four years is more than three times the depreciation between the fourth and eighth years.
criteria: Finds $V_4$ and $V_8$, or the depreciation for one of the periods, or equivalent merit

meta.generated_note: Generated solution.

solutions.latex:
The value after eight years must be $\$2402.71$, so the total depreciation is
$$\begin{aligned} 24\,000-2402.71 &= \$21\,597.29 \end{aligned}$$
Straight-line depreciation spreads this equally over 8 years.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Yearly depreciation} &= \dfrac{21\,597.29}{8} \\ &\approx \$2699.66 \end{aligned}$$
As a percentage of the new value:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2699.66}{24\,000}\times 100 &\approx 11.25\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{she should depreciate the car by about } \$2699.66 \text{ each year, which is about } 11.25\% \text{ of its new value}$$
criteria: Finds the yearly amount, or the total depreciation of $\$21\,597.29$, or equivalent merit

Sandy is on holiday in San Francisco and wants to stream a Matilda's World Cup match which is played in Sydney on Monday $31^{\text{st}}$ July and starts at 3:00 pm.

San Francisco is located at UTC $-8$ and Sydney at UTC $+10$.

San Francisco is subject to daylight saving in July and August, but Sydney is not.

At what time and date in San Francisco should Sandy start streaming the match?

dif.r: Time zone conversion across date line with daylight saving adjustment

solutions.latex:
Convert the Sydney start time to UTC. Sydney is UTC $+10$, so subtract 10 hours.
$$\begin{aligned} 3{:}00 \text{ pm Monday} &= 15{:}00 \text{ Monday (Sydney)} \\ \text{UTC} &= 15{:}00-10{:}00 = 5{:}00 \text{ am Monday} \end{aligned}$$
San Francisco is UTC $-8$, but daylight saving makes it UTC $-7$ in July.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{San Francisco} &= 5{:}00 \text{ am Monday}-7 \text{ h} \\ &= 10{:}00 \text{ pm Sunday} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Sandy should start streaming at } 10{:}00 \text{ pm on Sunday } 30^{\text{th}} \text{ July}$$
criteria: Finds the UTC time ($5{:}00$ am Monday) and the correct San Francisco offset, or equivalent merit
Finds the UTC time, or applies the correct time difference of $17$ hours with the wrong direction, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Mr Jensen records the number of days that each student in his Year 11 class is absent during Semester 1 and he also works out their average test mark as a percentage.

He draws the scatterplot below to help him in his discussions with his students in relation to their absences.

\exfigure{308_q28_1}

He calculates the correlation coefficient to be $-0.9419$.

He draws a line of best fit on the scatterplot which has an equation of $m = 96.6 - 3.84n$.

Describe and interpret the data and other information provided and explain how it could be used in discussions with students about absences.

dif.r: Extended interpretation of correlation, gradient, intercept and limitations in context

skills: Line of best fit by eye

figures.cap: scatterplot of days absent vs average semester mark with line of best fit

solutions.latex:
Correlation: $r=-0.9419$ is close to $-1$, so there is a strong negative linear relationship. Students with more days absent tend to have lower average marks.

Strength: the coefficient of determination is
$$\begin{aligned} r^2 &= (-0.9419)^2 \\ &\approx 0.887 \end{aligned}$$
so about $88.7\%$ of the variation in average mark is explained by the number of days absent. The points on the scatterplot lie close to the line.

Line of best fit $m=96.6-3.84n$:

The gradient $-3.84$ means that, on average, each extra day absent is associated with a drop of about $3.84$ marks.

The intercept $96.6$ is the predicted mark for a student with no absences.

The line can be used for prediction within the data range (about $1.5$ to $11$ days). For example, for 5 days absent:
$$\begin{aligned} m &= 96.6-3.84\times 5 \\ &= 77.4 \end{aligned}$$
Limitations: the line should not be used far outside the range (for instance, a very large $n$ would predict a negative mark). Correlation does not prove that absence causes the lower marks, since other factors may affect both.

Use in discussions: Mr Jensen can show students that missing more days is strongly linked to lower marks, with each day missed costing nearly 4 marks on average, and encourage good attendance.
criteria: Interprets the correlation coefficient and the line of best fit (gradient or intercept) and links them to a discussion with students, or equivalent merit
Interprets two features of the data (e.g. the correlation and the gradient), or equivalent merit
Makes one correct statement about the data, e.g. strong negative correlation, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: r^2 = 0.8872; prediction for n=5 gives 77.4, consistent with the plotted line.

The Discount Dapper Corporation produces cummerbunds for sale.

In any production run, the cost ($\$C$) of producing $N$ cummerbunds is given by the equation:

$$C = 8N + 2000$$

The cummerbunds are sold to retailers at the cost of \$12 each, so the equation for the revenue returned to the corporation is $R = 12N$.

Draw the lines representing the cost equation ($C$) and the revenue equation ($R$) on the axes below and use the graph to find the break-even point after which the corporation begins to make a profit on the run of cummerbunds.

\exfigure{308_q29_1}

dif.r: Plot two given linear equations and read break-even intersection

figures.cap: blank axes for cost and revenue lines, N from 0 to 1000
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Plot each line from two points, using $N=0$ and $N=1000$.
$$\begin{aligned} C=8N+2000:\quad & N=0,\ C=2000;\quad N=1000,\ C=10\,000 \\ R=12N:\quad & N=0,\ R=0;\quad N=1000,\ R=12\,000 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{308_q29_s1}

The break-even point is where the lines cross, so $C=R$.
$$\begin{aligned} 8N+2000 &= 12N \\ 2000 &= 4N \\ N &= 500 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 12\times 500 \\ &= 6000 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{break-even point is } (500,\ \$6000)\text{; a profit is made after } 500 \text{ cummerbunds}$$
criteria: Draws both lines correctly, or draws one line correctly and finds the break-even point, or equivalent merit
Draws one line correctly, or equivalent merit

Forward scan (earliest start time, left box): take the largest total along any path into each node.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{after } G &: 7 \\ \text{after } H &: 9 \\ \text{after } I,K &: \max(7+5,\ 9+8) = 17 \\ \text{after } M &: 17+6 = 23 \\ \text{end} &: \max(17+10,\ 23+7,\ 9+11,\ 9+13) = 30 \end{aligned}$$
Backward scan (latest start time, right box): start from the end time $30$ and take the smallest value.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{before } N &: 30-7 = 23 \\ \text{node after } I,K &: \min(30-10,\ 23-6) = 17 \\ \text{node after } H &: \min(17-8,\ 30-11,\ 30-13) = 9 \\ \text{node after } G &: 17-5 = 12 \\ \text{start} &: \min(12-7,\ 9-9) = 0 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{308_q33_s1}
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum completion time} = 30 \text{ minutes}$$

The critical path joins the nodes where the earliest and latest start times are equal.

These are the activities with no float: $H$, $K$, $M$, $N$.

The drawing below is completed from a radial survey centred at point $A$.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

skills: Area of a triangle (1/2 ab sin C)

solution diagram (drawn by Claude)
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{308_q34_s1}

North is the reference line at $A$. $P$ is on a bearing of $336^\circ$, which is $360^\circ - 336^\circ = 24^\circ$ to the west of north.

$Q$ is on a bearing of $042^\circ$, which is $42^\circ$ to the east of north.

North lies between $AP$ and $AQ$, so the angles add.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle PAQ &= 24^\circ + 42^\circ \\ &= 66^\circ \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{308_q34_s2}

In $\triangle PAQ$, $AP = 260$, $\angle PAQ = 66^\circ$ and $\angle PQA = 72^\circ$, so $AP$ is opposite $\angle PQA$ and $PQ$ is opposite $\angle PAQ$.

By the sine rule,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{PQ}{\sin 66^\circ} &= \dfrac{260}{\sin 72^\circ} \\ PQ &= \dfrac{260\sin 66^\circ}{\sin 72^\circ} \\ &\approx 249.7 \\ &\approx 250 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is $PQ + QR + RS + SP$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Perimeter} &= 250 + 190 + 185 + 250 \\ &= 875 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ PQ \approx 250 \text{ m and the perimeter is } 875 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds $PQ$ to the nearest metre, or equivalent merit

$$\therefore\ \text{area of } \triangle SAR \approx 9903 \text{ m}^2$$

parts.latex:
The network diagram shows nine towns and the fifteen roads that connect them.

The length of each road is shown, in kilometres.

All the roads need to be resurfaced after heavy rainfall.

The local council decides to initially resurface the minimum length of roads that will allow all towns to be connected by resurfaced roads.

This is equivalent to finding a minimum spanning tree.

\exfigure{308_q39_1}

Determine the minimum spanning tree and find the total length of roads to be resurfaced, then redraw the minimum spanning tree on the vertices below, showing the distances.

\exfigure{308_q39_2}

Length of roads to be resurfaced = _________ km

dif.r: Routine Kruskal minimum spanning tree on nine vertices

figures.cap: weighted network of nine towns R to Z
blank vertices R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y, Z for redrawing the spanning tree
solution diagram (drawn by Claude)

solutions.latex:
Use Kruskal's algorithm: add the shortest road that does not form a cycle, until all $9$ towns are connected ($8$ roads).
$$\begin{aligned} XY &= 7 &&\text{add} \\ SZ &= 8 &&\text{add} \\ RZ &= 9 &&\text{add} \\ UV &= 9 &&\text{add} \\ ZT &= 10 &&\text{add} \\ VW &= 10 &&\text{add} \\ RT &= 12 &&\text{rejected (cycle } R, Z, T) \\ SU &= 12 &&\text{add (joins } \{S,Z,R,T\} \text{ to } \{U,V,W\}) \\ ZV &= 13,\ TW = 14,\ RS = 15 &&\text{rejected (cycles)} \\ VY &= 15 &&\text{add (joins } \{X,Y\}) \end{aligned}$$
This gives $8$ roads, so the tree is complete.

\exfigure{308_q39_s1}
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= 7+8+9+9+10+10+12+15 \\ &= 80 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$

dif.r: Two independent conditions combined via product of probabilities.

The score is a 2-digit number, tens digit from the first wheel and units digit from the second wheel. Each wheel has equal sectors.

Which of the following formulae could NOT be the result of making $a$ the subject of the following formula?

$$2ab-3c=\dfrac{d}{4}$$

solutions.latex:
Make $a$ the subject of $2ab-3c=\dfrac{d}{4}$.

Add $3c$ to both sides:
$$2ab=\dfrac{d}{4}+3c$$
Divide both sides by $2b$:
$$a=\dfrac{\frac{d}{4}+3c}{2b}=\dfrac{1}{2b}\left(\dfrac{d}{4}+3c\right)$$

Option A gives $a=\dfrac{d}{2b}+3c$. But dividing the whole right-hand side by $2b$ gives $\dfrac{d}{8b}+\dfrac{3c}{2b}$, so A is not equivalent.

$$\therefore\ \text{option A could not be the result}$$

solutions.latex:

parts.latex:
A regular hexagon of side length 5 cm is shown below.

\exfigure{717_q30_1}

The hexagon has been divided into two triangles $AEF$ and $BDC$, and a rectangle $ABDE$, as shown above.

Show that the area of the hexagon is approximately $65\text{ cm}^2$.

dif.r: Cosine rule, sine area formula and rectangle combined in show-that.

skills: Area of a triangle (1/2 ab sin C)

figures.cap: regular hexagon ABCDEF divided into two triangles and a rectangle

solutions.latex:
Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is $120^\circ$, so $\angle AFE=120^\circ$.

Using the cosine rule in $\triangle AEF$:
$$\begin{aligned} AE^2 &= 5^2+5^2-2\times 5\times 5\times\cos 120^\circ \\ &= 25+25-50\cos 120^\circ \\ &= 75 \end{aligned}$$
$$AE \approx 8.7 \text{ cm}$$
Area of $\triangle AEF$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 5\times 5\times\sin 120^\circ \\ &\approx 10.8 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Area of rectangle $ABDE$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 8.7\times 5 \\ &= 43.5 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The hexagon is two triangles plus the rectangle.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of hexagon} &= (2\times 10.8)+43.5 \\ &\approx 65 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the areas of the triangle and the rectangle, or equivalent merit
Finds $\angle AFE$ or sets up the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The maximum speed ($v$), in km/h, of a truck is inversely proportional to the weight ($w$ kg) it carries. A truck carrying a weight of 1600 kg can travel at 80 km/h. What is the maximum speed of the truck if the weight is 1250 kg

dif.r: Find inverse variation constant then substitute.

solutions.latex:
The speed is inversely proportional to the weight.
$$v=\dfrac{k}{w}$$
Substitute $v=80$ and $w=1600$.
$$\begin{aligned} 80 &= \dfrac{k}{1600} \\ k &= 80\times 1600 \\ &= 128\,000 \end{aligned}$$
So $v=\dfrac{128\,000}{w}$.

When $w=1250$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &= \dfrac{128\,000}{1250} \\ &= 102.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the speed is } 102.4 \text{ km/h}$$

questions.stem: A business produces bottles of cola whose capacity is normally distributed with a mean capacity of 600 mL and a standard deviation of 2 mL.

parts.label: a
parts.latex: If 99.7% of bottles pass the quality control check, what limits will the volume of cola in each bottle almost certainly lie?

dif.r: Empirical rule: three standard deviations either side of mean.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: What percentage of bottles with cols lie between 598 mL and 604 mL ?

dif.r: Two z-scores, combine halves of 68% and 95%.

solutions.latex:
About $99.7\%$ of scores lie within 3 standard deviations of the mean, so between $z=-3$ and $z=3$.

Lower limit, using $z=\dfrac{x-600}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned} -3 &= \dfrac{x-600}{2} \\ x &= 2\times(-3)+600 \\ &= 594 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
Upper limit:
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= \dfrac{x-600}{2} \\ x &= 3\times 2+600 \\ &= 606 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the limits are } 594 \text{ mL and } 606 \text{ mL}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Convert each volume to a $z$-score.
$$z=\dfrac{598-600}{2}=-1$$
$$z=\dfrac{604-600}{2}=2$$
So the scores lie between $z=-1$ and $z=2$.

By the $68\%$ and $95\%$ rules, each half is taken on its own side of the mean.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage} &= \dfrac{68\%}{2}+\dfrac{95\%}{2} \\ &= 81.5\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds both $z$-scores and sets up the percentage, or equivalent merit

questions.stem: 45% of the residents in a local community have been administered only one vaccination against a spreading virus and 30% of the residents have been administered two vaccinations (so that they are fully vaccinated).

parts.label: a
parts.latex: What is the probability that a randomly chosen resident from the community has NOT been administered at least ONE vaccination?

dif.r: One-step complement of given probabilities.

parts.label: b
parts.latex: If TWO residents are randomly selected from the community, what is the probability that at least ONE of them has been administered at least ONE vaccination?

dif.r: At least one of two via complement of independent events.

solutions.latex:
The probability of no vaccination is one minus the probability of one or two vaccinations.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-(0.45+0.3) \\ &= 0.25 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 25\% \text{ or } 0.25 \text{ or } \dfrac{1}{4}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Use the complement: at least one vaccinated is one minus neither vaccinated.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-(0.25\times 0.25) \\ &= 1-0.0625 \\ &= 0.9375 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 0.9375 \text{ or } 93.75\%$$
criteria: Uses the complement, or equivalent merit

The diagram below shows a triangle $ABC$ where $AB=20$ cm and $\angle ACB=52^\circ$. Point $D$ lies on $BC$ such that $AD$ is perpendicular to $BC$. The length of $BD$ is 18 cm.

\exfigure{850_q17_1}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Find the length of $AD$, correct to two decimal places.

dif.r: Single Pythagoras calculation in right triangle

parts.label: b
parts.latex: Hence, find the length of $CD$, correct to the nearest centimetre.

dif.r: Tangent ratio using previous result to find side

figures.cap: triangle ABC with altitude AD

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $ABD$, by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned}AD&=\sqrt{20^2-18^2}\\&=8.717797\ldots\\&\approx 8.72 \text{ cm (to 2 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies Pythagoras' theorem, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $ACD$, use the tangent ratio.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan 52^\circ&=\dfrac{AD}{CD}\\CD&=\dfrac{AD}{\tan 52^\circ}\\&=\dfrac{8.717797\ldots}{\tan 52^\circ}\\&=6.811\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore CD=7 \text{ cm (to the nearest centimetre)}$$
criteria: Applies a trigonometric ratio, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The masses of tennis balls produced in a factory are normally distributed with a mean of 58 grams and a standard deviation of 1.2 grams.

Tennis balls with a mass below 56.8 grams are rejected and not packaged for sale.

If the factory produces 4000 tennis balls per day, how many of then are rejected?

dif.r: Empirical rule percentage below z=-1, then scale to count

solutions.latex:
The rejection mass $56.8=58-1.2$ is one standard deviation below the mean ($z=-1$).

Using the empirical rule:
$$13.5\%+2.35\%+0.15\%=16\%$$
of the balls are rejected, so the number rejected is
$$16\%\times 4000=640$$
criteria: Finds the percentage of tennis balls which will be rejected, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Selena uses 420 kilocalories of energy per hour while she is playing tennis.

She eats a meal that contains 2184 kilojoules of energy, where 1 kilocalorie $=4.184$ kilojoules.

How many hours of tennis will Selena need to play to use up all the energy from her meal? Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.note: Food energy in kilocalories and kilojoules is not in the 2024 course.

dif.r: Energy unit conversion then division; mirrors HSC part

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}2184 \text{ kJ}&=\dfrac{2184}{4.184} \text{ kcal}\\&=521.9885\ldots \text{ kcal}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Time taken}&=\dfrac{521.9885\ldots}{420}\\&\approx 1.2 \text{ hours}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the number of kilocalories in 1 kilojoule, or equivalent merit

dif.r: Standard minimum spanning tree algorithm

figures.cap: weighted network
solution sketch: two possible minimum spanning trees

solutions.latex:
